stem:
A 72-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent on echo 3 months ago, NYHA II baseline) and new persistent atrial fibrillation (onset >2 months ago, rate 132 average on Holter, mildly symptomatic with exertional dyspnoea) attends a Maitland cardiology clinic. He is already on optimised guideline-directed medical therapy: bisoprolol 10 mg, sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg BD, spironolactone 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily.

Renal function is normal (Cr 88), thyroid normal, LFT normal, no QT prolongation (QTc 420 ms). He is on apixaban 5 mg BD for AF. He has no symptomatic angina, no valvular disease beyond mild MR, no prior cardiac surgery, no history of substance use. Echo today: LV dilatation, LVEF 26 percent, LA dilated (5.2 cm), no LV thrombus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 AF, BP 124/76, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA. JVP not elevated.
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, S3 gallop, no peripheral oedema, chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: ECG AF rate 132, no LVH on voltage. Echo LVEF 26%, dilated LV, LA 5.2 cm. NT-proBNP 1240 pg/mL. Cr 88, K 4.6, TSH 1.8, LFT normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for rate or rhythm control of his AF, recognising the constraints of HFrEF, optimised GDMT, and the available antiarrhythmic profile?

options.text: Add digoxin 125 microgram daily for rate control given persistent tachycardia despite maximal beta-blocker dose
options.rationale: Digoxin is a reasonable adjunct for rate control in HFrEF + AF when beta-blocker alone is insufficient, but the AFFIRM-AF and CASTLE-AF era has shifted preference toward rhythm control in HFrEF + AF given mortality and HF hospitalisation benefits. Source: ESC/CSANZ AF Guidelines.

options.text: Refer for catheter ablation of AF, recognising mortality and HF hospitalisation reduction in HFrEF demonstrated in CASTLE-AF
options.rationale: MULTI-STEP LADDER CONSTRAINT: in HFrEF + AF, catheter ablation has demonstrated reduced all-cause mortality and HF hospitalisation (CASTLE-AF 2018) and is now Class IIa recommendation in CSANZ + ESC guidelines for symptomatic HFrEF + AF. Patient is on optimised GDMT, has no contraindication, LV thrombus excluded, anticoagulation in place. AAD options are constrained in HFrEF: amiodarone is the only oral AAD with adequate safety profile (flecainide and sotalol contraindicated in HFrEF), but amiodarone carries thyroid, hepatic, pulmonary toxicity and is reserved when ablation is not feasible. Ablation offers the strongest evidence base for prognostic and symptomatic benefit. Source: CSANZ HF Position; ESC AF Guidelines; CASTLE-AF.

options.text: Commence flecainide 50 mg BD for rhythm control with target sinus rhythm restoration
options.rationale: Flecainide is CONTRAINDICATED in structural heart disease including HFrEF (CAST trial: increased mortality). Source: AMH; ESC AF Guidelines.

options.text: Commence sotalol 80 mg BD for combined rate and rhythm control
options.rationale: Sotalol has class III antiarrhythmic effects with negative inotropy and is contraindicated in HFrEF + reduced LVEF. Source: AMH.

options.text: Increase bisoprolol to 15 mg daily for tighter rate control
options.rationale: Maximum recommended bisoprolol dose is 10 mg daily; 15 mg is off-label and adds bradycardia risk without proven benefit over alternative rate or rhythm control. Source: AMH.

explanation.summary: AF management in HFrEF stacks several constraints: (1) most class I antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone) are contraindicated due to CAST trial mortality signal in structural heart disease; (2) sotalol has negative inotropy and is contraindicated in reduced LVEF; (3) amiodarone is the only oral AAD with adequate safety profile in HFrEF but carries thyroid/hepatic/pulmonary toxicity; (4) digoxin has rate-control role but no mortality benefit and possible neutral-to-harmful long-term effect; (5) catheter ablation has level I evidence (CASTLE-AF) for reduced mortality and HF hospitalisation in HFrEF + AF and is now CSANZ/ESC Class IIa recommendation. Workflow: optimise GDMT, ensure anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc + apixaban first-line), exclude LV thrombus on echo, refer for catheter ablation if symptomatic and recurrent.
key_points: Class IC AADs (flecainide, propafenone) contraindicated in structural HD
Sotalol contraindicated in HFrEF
Amiodarone usable but with multi-organ toxicity profile
CASTLE-AF: ablation reduces mortality + HF hospitalisation in HFrEF + AF
Confirm no LV thrombus on echo before cardioversion or ablation
explanation.pearls: When considering rhythm control in HFrEF + AF in 2026 practice, always ask if catheter ablation is available - the evidence base now favours ablation over amiodarone for symptomatic patients on optimised GDMT.

subtopic_detail: AF rhythm vs rate strategy in HFrEF with multi-comorbidity constraints

stem:
A 64-year-old woman with chronic depression on stable citalopram 40 mg daily for 6 years is admitted to Calvary Mater Newcastle with new-onset palpitations, two presyncopal episodes, and one witnessed brief loss of consciousness this morning. She had been started on azithromycin 500 mg daily for community-acquired pneumonia 4 days ago, and was started on ondansetron 8 mg TDS for the nausea associated with her infection 2 days ago.

She has no past cardiac history, no electrolyte disorder, normal renal function, no other medication changes. ECG today: sinus rhythm rate 92 with prolonged QT (QTc 580 ms), no T-wave alternans, no current torsades. Her ECG 6 months ago had QTc 440 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 sinus, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Alert oriented, no neurological deficit, normal heart sounds, chest mild crackles RLL.
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 580 ms (was 440 ms 6 months ago). K 4.1, Mg 0.82, Ca 2.32. Cr 78. Troponin negative. CXR RLL consolidation.

lead_in: Which combination of mechanisms best explains the QT prolongation, and what is the immediate management priority?

options.text: Citalopram alone is responsible; stop citalopram and accept psychiatric relapse risk
options.rationale: Citalopram at 40 mg has been stable for 6 years with prior QTc 440 ms - it has not changed. The TIME-OF-ONSET points to the new drugs as additive contributors. Stopping citalopram alone misses the bigger discontinuation. Source: AMH.

options.text: Additive QT prolongation from three QT-prolonging drugs (citalopram + azithromycin + ondansetron); admit to telemetry, stop both azithromycin (switch antibiotic to doxycycline) and ondansetron, replace IV Mg as prophylaxis
options.rationale: Three QT-prolonging drugs in additive combination: citalopram (FDA black-box at >40 mg), azithromycin (class effect of macrolides), ondansetron (5HT3 antagonists). The TIME-OF-ONSET maps the QT escalation precisely to addition of azithromycin then ondansetron in the past 4 days. QTc 580 ms is a high torsades risk. Management: admit to telemetry, replace IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min as torsades prophylaxis (target Mg 0.9+), stop both new QT-prolongers (switch macrolide to doxycycline; replace ondansetron with metoclopramide which has lower QT signal); continue citalopram (long-term, no acute change). Re-check ECG 24 hours after offending drugs ceased. Source: AMH; eTG Cardiovascular; CredibleMeds QTdrugs.org.

options.text: Hypokalaemia is the cause; replace IV K then continue all current medications
options.rationale: K is 4.1 (within normal). Hypokalaemia is not the issue here. Source: eTG.

options.text: Cardiac ischaemia precipitating QT prolongation; cardiac catheterisation lab activation
options.rationale: Troponin is negative; presentation is presyncope without typical ischaemic symptoms. QT prolongation in this context is drug-induced. Source: eTG.

options.text: Discharge on outpatient cardiology follow-up; QTc will normalise with antibiotic course completion
options.rationale: QTc 580 ms is a high torsades risk and must be treated as a medical emergency until the offending drugs are stopped and Mg restored. Discharge is unsafe. Source: eTG.

explanation.summary: QT prolongation from additive drug interaction is a recurring exam scenario. The TIME-OF-ONSET maps each new drug to the QT change: citalopram has been stable for years and is not the trigger; the addition of azithromycin (macrolide class effect on K+ delayed-rectifier currents) followed by ondansetron (5HT3 antagonists block IKr potassium current) produces additive QT prolongation that pushes a previously controlled QTc into a high-torsades risk range. Management priorities: telemetry, electrolyte correction (Mg first, target >0.9; K target 4.5+), discontinue the most recent QT-prolonging drugs (rarely all of them - choose alternatives), monitor for torsades. CredibleMeds QTdrugs.org maintains an up-to-date list. Risk factors that compound: female sex, older age, baseline cardiac disease, renal impairment, electrolyte abnormality.
key_points: Always check QTc when adding ANY drug to a patient on QT-prolonging therapy
Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) prolong QT
Ondansetron prolongs QT (dose-dependent above 16 mg)
IV magnesium is first-line torsades prophylaxis and treatment
Replace K+ to >4.5 and Mg to >0.9 in any QT prolongation scenario
explanation.pearls: When prescribing for any patient already on a QT-prolonging drug, look up CredibleMeds.org or use eTG to verify additive risk. Doxycycline is the safer macrolide-alternative for CAP when QT is a concern.

subtopic_detail: Additive drug-induced QT prolongation - time-of-onset mapping

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to her GP with progressive cosmetic concerns over the past 9 months. She has noticed coarse facial hair growth requiring weekly waxing, gum swelling that bleeds when she brushes, and her partner has noticed she sounds slightly slurred in the evenings. She also reports new acne, intermittent diplopia at night, and unsteadiness walking down stairs. She started a new daily medication 11 months ago for a chronic condition diagnosed in adolescence. She is not on any other regular medication and is not pregnant.

data_table.Examination: Hirsutism over chin and sideburns, gingival hyperplasia covering proximal third of lower incisors with contact bleeding, mild horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, broad-based gait, finger-nose with end-point intention tremor.
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, LFTs ALT 65 U/L (slightly raised), GGT 110 U/L, urinalysis negative, beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: Which medication is the single most likely cause of this constellation?

options.text: Phenytoin
options.rationale: The classic quartet of gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, cerebellar signs (nystagmus, ataxia, intention tremor), and raised GGT is pathognomonic for chronic phenytoin therapy, mediated by altered fibroblast collagen turnover, androgenic effects, dose-dependent cerebellar toxicity, and hepatic enzyme induction. Coarsening of facial features is also recognised.

options.text: Ciclosporin
options.rationale: Causes gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism but not cerebellar signs or nystagmus; would also expect hypertension and renal impairment. Would be wrong (Source: AMH).

options.text: Amlodipine
options.rationale: Calcium-channel blockers cause gingival hyperplasia but do not cause hirsutism or cerebellar ataxia. Would be wrong (Source: AMH).

options.text: Sodium valproate
options.rationale: Causes tremor, weight gain, hair LOSS (alopecia) not hirsutism, and hepatotoxicity; does not cause gingival hyperplasia. Would be wrong (Source: AMH).

options.text: Topiramate
options.rationale: Causes cognitive slowing, paraesthesiae, weight loss and renal stones; no gingival hyperplasia or hirsutism. Would be wrong (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Three drug classes cause gingival hyperplasia in Australian practice: phenytoin, ciclosporin, and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine). Phenytoin is the only one that ALSO causes the cerebellar triad and hirsutism. The discriminator is the combination, not any single feature. Modern practice has shifted to levetiracetam, lamotrigine and valproate for generalised epilepsy, but phenytoin remains in use for status epilepticus and in patients stable on long-standing therapy.
key_points: Gingival hyperplasia: phenytoin > ciclosporin > CCBs
Hirsutism + gingival hyperplasia = phenytoin or ciclosporin
Add cerebellar signs = phenytoin
GGT rise reflects enzyme induction, not hepatotoxicity
Consider switching to levetiracetam if cosmetic burden is significant
explanation.pearls: Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics in the therapeutic range; a small dose increase can tip into toxicity. Free phenytoin level is more useful than total in hypoalbuminaemia or pregnancy.

subtopic_detail: Adverse effect cluster mapping to anticonvulsant drug class

stem:
A 58-year-old retiree from the Central Coast presents to a Gosford respiratory clinic with 6 months of progressive dyspnoea, dry cough and 4 kg weight loss. He is a lifelong non-smoker. He has been retired for 5 years from his job as an aircraft mechanic. He spends most of his time at home; he keeps a small allotment vegetable garden, has two outdoor cats, and tends to the racing pigeon loft his neighbour asked him to mind during a 12-month overseas trip that began 8 months ago.

He has no occupational asbestos exposure beyond brief brake-pad work in the 1980s. There is no fever, no haemoptysis, no joint pain, no rash. Resting SpO2 96 percent room air, falling to 88 percent after a 6-minute walk test. Fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles are heard but no clubbing. Spirometry shows a restrictive pattern with FEV1/FVC 0.84, TLC 71 percent predicted, DLCO 52 percent predicted. CT chest reports patchy ground-glass and centrilobular nodularity with mid-to-upper lobe predominance.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 deg C, HR 92, RR 22, BP 132/82, SpO2 96% room air resting (88% post 6MWT).
data_table.Examination: Fine bibasal crackles, no clubbing, no rash, no synovitis.
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry restrictive (FEV1/FVC 0.84, TLC 71%, DLCO 52%), CT chest patchy ground-glass + centrilobular nodularity, mid-upper lobe predominant. FBC, UEC, LFT, CRP all normal. ANA, ENA, ANCA negative.

lead_in: Which of the following is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)
options.rationale: IPF is basal-predominant with honeycombing and reticulation, age >60 with insidious onset, and would show a UIP pattern on CT - not mid-upper-lobe ground glass with centrilobular nodules. Source: TSANZ/Lung Foundation Australia IPF guidelines.

options.text: Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis from avian antigen exposure
options.rationale: The discriminator is the pigeon loft, which the candidate must pick out from a long social history. Avian antigens (bird droppings, feathers, bloom proteins) drive a type III/IV hypersensitivity reaction producing centrilobular nodularity and ground-glass with mid-upper-lobe predominance - exactly the imaging described. Restrictive PFTs with reduced DLCO, fine crackles without clubbing in a non-smoker fit. Source: TSANZ Interstitial Lung Disease Position Statement; Cormier 2016.

options.text: Asbestos-related pleural disease
options.rationale: Brief brake-pad exposure 40 years ago is below threshold for asbestos disease, and asbestos causes pleural plaques or asbestosis with basal reticulation - not centrilobular nodularity. Source: ATS/ERS Asbestos guidelines.

options.text: Sarcoidosis stage II
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis would typically show bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with upper-lobe interstitial change and is age 20-40 in most Australian cohorts; ACE level and Ca often abnormal. The imaging here lacks lymphadenopathy and ANA/ENA are non-discriminating. Source: TSANZ Sarcoidosis Guidelines.

options.text: Cryptogenic organising pneumonia (COP)
options.rationale: COP usually has patchy peripheral or peribronchovascular consolidation rather than centrilobular nodularity, and responds rapidly to steroids - the discriminator is the imaging pattern + occupational/animal history. Source: eTG Respiratory.

explanation.summary: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) is driven by inhaled organic antigens (avian proteins, mould, isocyanates) producing a non-IgE immune reaction in alveoli and bronchioles. The chronic form looks like restrictive ILD; the discriminator is exposure history. Mid-upper-lobe predominance and centrilobular nodules differ from IPF (basal, reticular, honeycomb) and sarcoid (lymphadenopathy). Antigen avoidance is the central management step - even before steroids - because continued exposure causes irreversible fibrosis.
key_points: Bird-fancier's lung is the prototypical chronic HP exposure
Mid-upper-lobe centrilobular nodules + ground glass = HP pattern
Restrictive PFTs with low DLCO and exercise desaturation
Antigen avoidance is mandatory and primary therapy
Precipitating IgG (against pigeon serum) supports but does not exclude
explanation.pearls: Always ask explicitly about birds, hot tubs, mould exposure, and farming - patients rarely volunteer these on standard history. The Central Coast and Hunter regions have an active pigeon-racing culture, making this a regionally relevant differential.

sources.label: TSANZ Interstitial Lung Disease Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from avian antigen exposure

stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to a Newcastle hepatology clinic with 6 weeks of fatigue, mild jaundice and a 3 kg weight loss. She is not on any medication and denies herbal supplement use. Alcohol intake is 2 standard drinks per week. She has no risk factors for viral hepatitis on screening interview. There is a remote history of vitiligo and a paternal history of type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Bloods today show ALT 612 U/L, AST 540 U/L, ALP 142 U/L, GGT 88 U/L, total bilirubin 58 micromol/L, conjugated 41 micromol/L, INR 1.2, albumin 36 g/L, IgG 26 g/L (high). Viral hepatitis serology (HBsAg, anti-HCV, anti-HAV IgM, anti-HEV IgM) negative; HIV negative. Caeruloplasmin and alpha-1-antitrypsin normal. Iron studies show normal ferritin and transferrin saturation. Autoimmune panel: ANA 1:640 (homogeneous), anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA) 1:160, anti-LKM-1 negative, anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) negative, anti-soluble liver antigen (SLA) negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 78, BP 112/68, no asterixis.
data_table.Examination: Mild scleral icterus, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, soft non-tender abdomen, no hepatosplenomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Hepatocellular pattern (ALT 612, AST 540, ALP 142). Bilirubin 58 (conj 41). IgG 26 (high). ANA 1:640 homogeneous, ASMA 1:160, anti-LKM-1 negative, AMA negative.

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Primary biliary cholangitis
options.rationale: PBC is cholestatic (ALP-dominant, raised GGT, elevated IgM) with positive AMA in 95 percent. Here ALT/AST dominate, GGT is only mildly elevated, IgG (not IgM) is high, and AMA is negative. Source: eTG Gastrointestinal.

options.text: Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis
options.rationale: The pattern fits AIH type 1: young woman, hepatocellular injury (ALT > ALP), markedly elevated IgG, ANA homogeneous + ASMA positive (the type 1 serology), AMA and anti-LKM-1 negative. The associated autoimmunity (vitiligo, family T1DM) supports. International AIH Group simplified criteria score >=7 (definite). Source: eTG Gastrointestinal; AASLD AIH Practice Guidance.

options.text: Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis
options.rationale: AIH type 2 has anti-LKM-1 or anti-LC1 antibodies (negative here) and typically presents in childhood/adolescence. ASMA-positive AIH is type 1. Source: AASLD.

options.text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
options.rationale: PSC is cholestatic with bile-duct strictures on imaging; ALP > ALT; pANCA positive in 65 percent. Pattern here is hepatocellular and ANCA was not even part of the differential. Source: eTG Gastrointestinal.

options.text: Wilson disease
options.rationale: Wilson is excluded by normal caeruloplasmin and presents with mixed neurological/psychiatric features and Kayser-Fleischer rings. AIH-like ANA + ASMA in Wilson is rare. Source: eTG Gastrointestinal.

explanation.summary: AIH is a T-cell-mediated attack on hepatocytes producing a hepatocellular injury pattern (ALT/AST elevation), polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia (IgG specifically), and characteristic autoantibodies. Type 1 (ANA + ASMA positive, anti-LKM-1 negative) accounts for ~75 percent of cases and presents in young adults, often with associated autoimmunity (thyroid, vitiligo, T1DM). The IAIHG simplified score combines autoantibody titre, IgG level, biopsy histology and exclusion of viral hepatitis. Treatment is prednisolone +/- azathioprine; biopsy is recommended before commencing to grade activity and exclude overlap syndromes.
key_points: Type 1 AIH = ANA + ASMA (anti-LKM-1 negative); type 2 = anti-LKM-1 or anti-LC1
Hepatocellular pattern + raised IgG + ANA/ASMA in a young woman = AIH until proven otherwise
Personal or family history of other autoimmune disease supports
Biopsy: interface hepatitis + plasma cell infiltrate confirms
Treatment: prednisolone 30-60 mg, taper, add azathioprine; long-term remission >80%
explanation.pearls: Beware overlap syndromes (AIH-PBC, AIH-PSC) - if ALP is disproportionately high or AMA is positive, image the biliary tree and consider MRCP.

subtopic_detail: Autoimmune hepatitis type 1 serological pattern

stem:
A 67-year-old man presents to a Maitland general practice with 5 days of progressively severe bilateral thigh and shoulder muscle pain, dark cola-coloured urine and weakness when climbing stairs. He cannot recall recent strenuous exercise or trauma. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism and stable HFrEF. His regular medications are atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg, metformin XR 1 g BD, levothyroxine 100 micrograms, and bisoprolol 5 mg, all unchanged for over 2 years.

Two weeks ago his GP started clarithromycin 500 mg BD for a 7-day course to treat a confirmed Helicobacter pylori eradication regimen. The macrolide course finished 5 days ago. Bloods today: CK 38400 U/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 80), K 4.1, urine dipstick blood ++++, microscopy 2 RBC per high power field, TSH 2.4.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 78, BP 132/78, SpO2 98% room air.
data_table.Examination: Bilateral proximal muscle tenderness in shoulders and thighs, power 4/5 against resistance, reflexes preserved, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: CK 38 400 U/L; Cr 142 (baseline 80); K 4.1; urine dipstick blood ++++ but only 2 RBC/HPF on microscopy (myoglobinuria); TSH 2.4.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely precipitant for this presentation?

options.text: Hypothyroid-induced myopathy from drift in levothyroxine effect
options.rationale: TSH is normal at 2.4, excluding overt hypothyroid myopathy. Source: eTG Endocrinology.

options.text: Clarithromycin-induced atorvastatin toxicity via CYP3A4 inhibition
options.rationale: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor and atorvastatin is a CYP3A4 substrate; co-administration causes a several-fold rise in plasma statin and risk of rhabdomyolysis. The TIME-OF-ONSET is the discriminator: symptoms started during/after the macrolide course on an otherwise unchanged statin regimen of >2 years. Eradication therapy is a recognised trigger. Australian Medicines Handbook and eTG both list this interaction. Source: AMH 2024; eTG Cardiovascular.

options.text: Idiopathic immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (anti-HMGCR)
options.rationale: Anti-HMGCR necrotising myopathy is a recognised but uncommon statin-triggered syndrome; it tends to persist after statin cessation and has a longer subacute onset. Time-of-onset linkage to clarithromycin makes the interaction explanation more likely first. Source: ACR myopathy guidance.

options.text: Strenuous unrecognised exertional rhabdomyolysis
options.rationale: Exertional rhabdo would have a clear inciting episode in the days before symptom onset; the patient denies this and bilateral proximal distribution is unusual. Source: eTG Renal.

options.text: Perindopril-induced AKI causing secondary CK release
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors do not cause primary rhabdomyolysis; the CK 38 400 represents true muscle injury, not a creatinine artefact, and the AKI is secondary to myoglobin nephrotoxicity. Source: KDIGO AKI guidance.

explanation.summary: The discriminating cue is the timing of the macrolide course relative to symptom onset. Atorvastatin is metabolised by CYP3A4; clarithromycin is one of the strongest CYP3A4 inhibitors in clinical use. Co-administration produces dose-dependent rises in atorvastatin exposure and significantly increases rhabdomyolysis risk, with symptoms typically appearing within 5-14 days of macrolide initiation. Management: stop atorvastatin, IV crystalloid to maintain urine output >100 mL/h, monitor K and renal function, repeat CK trend. Restart a non-CYP3A4 statin (rosuvastatin, pravastatin) only once CK and renal function normalise.
key_points: Clarithromycin and erythromycin are strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Atorvastatin, simvastatin, lovastatin are CYP3A4 substrates
Rosuvastatin and pravastatin are NOT CYP3A4 dependent
Statin-macrolide interaction is the single most common drug-induced rhabdomyolysis in AU primary care
Always pause CYP3A4-substrate statins for the duration of macrolide therapy
explanation.pearls: Helicobacter eradication regimens almost always include clarithromycin; flag statin-substrate switching at the time of prescribing.

subtopic_detail: Statin-macrolide CYP3A4 interaction rhabdomyolysis

stem:
A 78-year-old man on long-term warfarin for non-valvular AF (target INR 2.0-3.0) is admitted to Calvary Mater Newcastle with community-acquired pneumonia. He is in atrial fibrillation rate 102, BP 108/68, SpO2 92% on 2 L nasal prongs. His admission bloods show creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 90), urea 18 mmol/L, K 5.1, INR 7.4. He had a witnessed mechanical fall yesterday with a 2x2 cm forehead haematoma but no loss of consciousness; CT brain on arrival shows no intracranial haemorrhage.

He has no active bleeding now; urinalysis no blood. Past history: hypertension, mild Alzheimer dementia, prior PE 4 years ago. Medications: warfarin 5/4 mg alternate days, perindopril 5 mg, donepezil 10 mg. He weighs 72 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2, HR 102 AF, BP 108/68, RR 24, SpO2 92% on 2 L NP.
data_table.Examination: Forehead haematoma 2x2 cm, no active bleed, no neurological deficit. Crepitations RLL. AF irregularly irregular.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124, Plt 220, INR 7.4. Cr 198 (baseline 90), urea 18, K 5.1. CT brain no haemorrhage. CXR RLL consolidation.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step for management of his over-anticoagulation, integrating renal function, recent fall, and continued thromboembolic risk?

options.text: Withhold warfarin only and recheck INR in 24 hours; no other intervention
options.rationale: Withholding alone is appropriate for INR 4.5-10 in a stable patient without bleeding; this patient has multiple bleeding risk factors (recent fall with extracranial haematoma, AKI raising drug-handling unpredictability, age, dementia) that push the threshold for active reversal. Source: BSH Anticoagulation Guidelines; eTG Cardiovascular.

options.text: Stop warfarin and give oral phytomenadione (vitamin K1) 1-2 mg PO once
options.rationale: INR 4.5-10 without bleeding but with elevated bleeding risk (recent head trauma + extracranial haematoma + AKI + age) is reversed with low-dose oral vitamin K1 1-2 mg, plus warfarin withhold and INR recheck at 12-24 hours. IV vitamin K reserved for major bleeding (not present here despite negative CT). PCC is for major bleeding. Continued AF anticoagulation is reassessed after the acute illness; not stopped permanently. Source: eTG Cardiovascular; AHA AF Guidelines; ANZSBT/NBA Massive Transfusion / Warfarin reversal flowchart.

options.text: Stop warfarin, give 4-factor PCC 50 IU/kg plus IV vitamin K1 10 mg
options.rationale: Prothrombinex-VF (Australian 3-factor PCC) plus IV vitamin K1 is for major or life-threatening bleeding, not for non-bleeding over-anticoagulation. CT brain is clear; haematoma is extracranial and not active. This is over-reversal and risks rebound thrombosis. Source: ANZSBT.

options.text: Substitute warfarin with therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD bridging
options.rationale: Enoxaparin at 1 mg/kg BD is contraindicated at this creatinine clearance (estimated <30 mL/min): use renally-dose-reduced enoxaparin (1 mg/kg daily) or UFH if bridging needed - and bridging itself is rarely indicated for AF cessation of <1 week. The over-anticoagulation should be reversed first, not switched. Source: AMH; AHA AF Guidelines.

options.text: Continue warfarin at full dose; treat pneumonia and reassess INR after antibiotics complete
options.rationale: Continuing supratherapeutic warfarin in a patient with AKI, recent head trauma and infection is unsafe; INR will likely climb further as antibiotics displace warfarin from protein binding and inhibit gut vitamin K synthesis. Source: eTG Cardiovascular.

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal sits on a ladder: withhold (INR 4.5-10 stable, no risk factors) → oral vitamin K1 1-2 mg (INR 4.5-10 with bleeding risk factors OR INR >10 stable) → IV vitamin K1 5-10 mg + PCC (major or life-threatening bleeding). This patient is at INR 7.4 without active bleeding but has multiple amplifiers of bleeding risk (recent fall with extracranial haematoma, age, dementia, AKI affecting drug clearance and platelet function). That moves him from 'withhold alone' to 'low-dose vitamin K1', without justifying full PCC reversal. AKI also matters for any LMWH bridging decision: enoxaparin needs dose reduction at CrCl <30 mL/min. Long-term, anticoagulation will be reassessed after acute illness resolves; falls themselves are not an absolute contraindication if HAS-BLED-adjusted benefit favours continuation.
key_points: INR 4.5-10, no bleeding, no risk factors: withhold alone
INR 4.5-10, no bleeding, but bleeding risk factors: add oral vitamin K1 1-2 mg
INR >10 or any major bleed: IV vitamin K1 5-10 mg + Prothrombinex-VF
Renal impairment: enoxaparin at CrCl <30 mL/min needs dose reduction or switch to UFH
AKI also impairs warfarin metabolism and platelet function - lower threshold for reversal
explanation.pearls: Antibiotics that potentiate warfarin: ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, macrolides, azoles. Anticipate INR rise and pre-emptively reduce warfarin dose.

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal ladder in multi-organ dysfunction
Hour-1 bundle initial resuscitation
stem: You are the medical registrar called to ED to review a 72-year-old man with 2 days of dysuria, rigors and now reduced level of consciousness. He has a history of BPH and recent urinary catheterisation 1 week ago for retention. His skin is mottled and his hands are cool. He has been triaged to resus.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 86/48, HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 92% on room air, T 38.9, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Mottled extremities, cool peripheries, mild suprapubic tenderness, no flank tenderness; chest clear, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2, WCC 18.6, neutrophils 16.1, CRP 240, Cr 168 (baseline 88), urine dipstick nitrites +, leukocytes ++; ABG pH 7.28, HCO3 18; blood cultures and urine cultures collected
data_table.Medications: Tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily; finasteride 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic and resuscitation in the first hour?

options.text: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg with amoxicillin 2 g and 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over 1 hour; arrange ICU review for vasopressor
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 bundle: blood cultures, broad spectrum antibiotic within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, lactate and ICU escalation; gentamicin plus amoxicillin covers community-onset urosepsis in Australian practice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily with metronidazole 500 mg and 1 L crystalloid over 4 hours; arrange ward bed and senior review
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone 1 g underdoses serious sepsis; metronidazole not required for urosepsis; 1 L over 4 hours is insufficient for septic shock; ward disposition undertreats severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g and 250 mL hypertonic saline bolus over 30 minutes; commence noradrenaline at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not first line in septic shock resuscitation; balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg precedes vasopressor; pip-taz is acceptable but balanced fluid is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV cefalexin 1 g and 500 mL crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes; defer further escalation until inpatient team reviews
options.rationale: Oral or narrow gram-positive cefalexin underdoses urosepsis and oral route is inappropriate in shock; deferring escalation breaches hour-1 standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV ciprofloxacin 400 mg and 2 L crystalloid bolus over 2 hours; reassess and consider noradrenaline if BP remains below 90 systolic
options.rationale: Ciprofloxacin monotherapy is not first-line for severe urosepsis in Australia given fluoroquinolone resistance; bolus over 2 hours is too slow for septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 bundle comprises lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics where possible, broad-spectrum antibiotic, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and vasopressor for persistent hypotension. Australian empirical therapy for serious urosepsis is gentamicin plus amoxicillin in the absence of beta-lactam allergy or ESBL risk. Lactate above 4 mmol/L is a key trigger for aggressive resuscitation. ICU escalation is required for septic shock not responding to initial fluid.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotic, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor
Empirical urosepsis: gentamicin plus amoxicillin in Australia
Balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg over the first hour
Lactate above 4 indicates need for aggressive resuscitation
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose by lean body weight is the Australian standard for severe gram-negative sepsis; redose at 24 hours guided by levels.

subtopic_detail: Vasopressor selection in septic shock
stem: You are the ICU registrar managing a 64-year-old woman with septic shock from a perforated diverticular abscess. After 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, her MAP is 58 mmHg and she remains tachycardic at 118. She has had source control surgery 2 hours ago and is on piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin. She has a central line in situ. Her ScvO2 is 72 percent and her lactate has fallen from 4.6 to 3.2.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/40 (MAP 58), HR 118, RR 22 ventilated, SpO2 96% on 40% FiO2, T 37.4
data_table.Examination: Warm extremities, cap refill 3 s, urine output 0.4 mL/kg/h over last hour, no new bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.2 (down from 4.6), Hb 96, K 4.2, ScvO2 72%, echo bedside shows hyperdynamic LV, IVC variable
data_table.Medications: Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours; gentamicin loaded

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence dopamine at 5 micrograms/kg/min titrated to MAP 65 mmHg with arterial line monitoring in place
options.rationale: Dopamine is no longer recommended due to greater arrhythmia risk and worse outcomes compared with noradrenaline in septic shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Commence noradrenaline at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min titrated to MAP 65 mmHg with arterial line monitoring
options.rationale: Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor for septic shock with MAP below 65 after adequate fluid resuscitation per Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Commence vasopressin 0.03 units/min as monotherapy; reassess MAP after 30 minutes of stable infusion before escalation
options.rationale: Vasopressin is added when noradrenaline cannot maintain MAP, not as first-line monotherapy; pure vasopressin can cause coronary and digit ischaemia at higher doses. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Administer further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and reassess; defer vasopressor pending response to volume resuscitation
options.rationale: After 30 mL/kg with hyperdynamic LV and variable IVC, further large volume risks pulmonary oedema; vasopressor support is appropriate. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Commence adrenaline at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min; reassess MAP and lactate clearance after 2 hours of infusion at steady state
options.rationale: Adrenaline is reserved for shock not responding to noradrenaline plus vasopressin and can worsen lactate due to beta-mediated metabolic effects. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 recommends noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor for septic shock not responding to 30 mL/kg crystalloid. The MAP target is at least 65 mmHg. Vasopressin 0.03 units/min may be added to noradrenaline if MAP cannot be maintained or to reduce noradrenaline dose. Adrenaline is third line. Dopamine is no longer recommended due to arrhythmia risk and worse outcomes.
key_points: Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor in septic shock
Target MAP at least 65 mmHg
Vasopressin is added second line at 0.03 units/min
Avoid dopamine in septic shock
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone 200 mg per day IV is recommended in septic shock requiring ongoing vasopressor support; consider when noradrenaline is above 0.25 micrograms/kg/min.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and management
stem: You are the medical registrar called to ED to review a 42-year-old woman with Addison's disease who presents with 36 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea from suspected viral gastroenteritis. She has not taken her usual hydrocortisone for 24 hours due to vomiting. She is on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg afternoon and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily.

data_table.Examination: Dry mucosa, sunken eyes, cool peripheries, hyperpigmentation of palmar creases, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Na 124, K 5.8, glucose 2.8, Cr 142 (baseline 64), Hb 142, CRP 18, lactate 2.4, cortisol pending
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20 mg morning, 10 mg afternoon; fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 40 mg with ondansetron 4 mg sublingual and 500 mL crystalloid; observe over 4 hours in ED short stay
options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone is unreliable in vomiting and shock; IV route is mandatory; ED short stay underestimates severity. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Dexamethasone 4 mg IV bolus, 1 L Hartmann's bolus, and oral glucose drinks; admit for slow-stress dosing taper
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has minimal mineralocorticoid activity and is less appropriate; oral glucose in shock is unreliable; hydrocortisone is preferred. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus, 1 L 0.9% saline bolus, and 100 mL 10% glucose bolus; admit for ongoing replacement
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis requires immediate hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, isotonic crystalloid resuscitation, and glucose for hypoglycaemia; this is the standard ESA and Endocrine Society approach. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Fludrocortisone 200 micrograms oral, 1 L saline bolus, and oral glucose; await cortisol level before parenteral steroid
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has no acute glucocorticoid effect; awaiting cortisol delays life-saving treatment; hydrocortisone is given empirically. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV bolus, 2 L 5% dextrose bolus, and noradrenaline infusion for hypotension control
options.rationale: Methylprednisolone is acceptable but hydrocortisone is preferred for mineralocorticoid effect; pure dextrose without sodium worsens hyponatraemia; vasopressor before steroid is wrong order. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency presenting with hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia in a patient with known or unrecognised adrenal insufficiency. Immediate management is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours, isotonic crystalloid resuscitation and glucose for hypoglycaemia. Cortisol level can be sent but treatment should not wait. Sick-day rules require patients to double oral hydrocortisone for febrile illness and use IM emergency hydrocortisone for vomiting.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus is first step in adrenal crisis
Isotonic saline resuscitation, not dextrose alone
Treat glucose with IV dextrose if symptomatic
Sick-day rules: double oral dose for fever, IM if vomiting
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity that fludrocortisone is not needed acutely; restart fludrocortisone when oral intake resumes.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma crisis - blockade sequence
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 38-year-old previously healthy man brought in with sudden onset 'thunderclap' headache, palpitations, drenching sweat and pallor. This is his third such paroxysm in 4 weeks. Today his BP swung from 220/130 to 90/52 within 30 minutes. CT brain excluded haemorrhage. His symptoms have settled but BP is currently 184/108. The endocrine team has been called and an adrenal incidentaloma 4.8 cm was noted on his CT 6 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 184/108 (currently), HR 116, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Pale, mildly diaphoretic, tremor, otherwise unremarkable; no goitre, no exophthalmos
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, no ischaemic change; troponin not elevated; Na 138, K 4.0, glucose 7.4; 24-hour plasma metanephrines previously not done; CT brain normal; CT adrenal 4.8 cm right adrenal mass with washout suggesting phaeochromocytoma
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence labetalol 200 mg twice daily oral; admit and arrange laparoscopic adrenalectomy within 48 hours of admission
options.rationale: Labetalol has predominantly beta-blocking activity at typical oral doses and is not adequate alpha blockade; surgery within 48 hours without preparation has high crisis mortality. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Commence metoprolol 50 mg twice daily oral; titrate based on resting heart rate and clinic blood pressure measurements
options.rationale: Beta blockade without prior alpha blockade in phaeochromocytoma causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and life-threatening hypertensive crisis; this is the classic anti-pattern. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Commence amlodipine 5 mg daily and atenolol 50 mg daily; arrange outpatient endocrine review in 2 weeks for biochemistry
options.rationale: Calcium channel blocker plus beta blocker still includes beta blockade before alpha blockade and outpatient delay risks further crisis; admission is required for alpha blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Commence phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily oral, titrate up over 10 to 14 days; defer beta blockade until alpha blockade established
options.rationale: Alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine is mandatory before any beta blockade in suspected phaeochromocytoma to prevent unopposed alpha stimulation and hypertensive emergency; surgery is planned 10 to 14 days after adequate alpha blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Commence captopril 25 mg three times daily oral; arrange 24-hour fractionated metanephrines as outpatient before biopsy
options.rationale: ACE inhibitor does not address catecholamine excess; biopsy of suspected phaeochromocytoma can precipitate fatal crisis and is contraindicated. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma should be confirmed biochemically with plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and imaged with CT or MRI. Once suspected, preoperative alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated over 10 to 14 days is essential before considering beta blockade, which is reserved for persistent tachycardia after adequate alpha blockade. Surgery is planned only after adequate alpha blockade and volume repletion. Biopsy is contraindicated as it can precipitate catecholamine release. Genetic testing is offered to all phaeochromocytoma patients given the high prevalence of inherited syndromes such as MEN2, VHL, NF1 and SDH mutations.
key_points: Alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine before any beta blockade
Surgery 10 to 14 days after adequate alpha blockade and volume repletion
Biopsy contraindicated in suspected phaeochromocytoma
Genetic testing for all phaeochromocytoma patients
explanation.pearls: Adequate alpha blockade is judged by mild orthostatic hypotension and nasal stuffiness; phenoxybenzamine is irreversible and accumulates, so taper carefully postoperatively to avoid hypotension.

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal osteoporosis - first line
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old postmenopausal woman in osteoporosis clinic. She had a fragility fracture of her right wrist after a fall from standing height 6 weeks ago. Her DEXA shows L1-L4 T-score minus 2.8 and femoral neck T-score minus 2.6. She has stable hypertension on perindopril and no GI symptoms. Her eGFR is 64 mL/min/1.73m^2. She is not lactose intolerant and lives independently.

data_table.Examination: Well; no spinal tenderness; right wrist healing; no peripheral oedema; gait stable with stick
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.42, phosphate 1.0, vitamin D 64 nmol/L, Cr 88, eGFR 64, TSH 1.8, PTH 4.4 (normal), DEXA T-scores as above, beta-CTX baseline 0.62
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily; vitamin D 1000 IU daily; calcium 600 mg twice daily; nil PPI

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological therapy?

options.text: Strontium ranelate 2 g orally daily; review cardiovascular risk and DEXA at 12 months; continue calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Strontium ranelate has been withdrawn from many markets and is not first-line due to cardiovascular safety concerns; not recommended in current AU practice. (Source: AMH: Bone disorders)

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months; review at 12 months with DEXA and serial beta-CTX measurements
options.rationale: Denosumab is second line after bisphosphonate failure or intolerance, primarily because of the rebound vertebral fracture risk on discontinuation, requiring careful long-term planning. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guidelines)

options.text: Teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily for 18 months; sequence to oral bisphosphonate after the course completes
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis with very low T-score, multiple vertebral fractures or bisphosphonate failure; not first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guidelines)

options.text: Raloxifene 60 mg orally daily; advise on VTE risk; review at 12 months with DEXA and bone turnover markers
options.rationale: Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not hip fractures and is reserved for women without vasomotor symptoms or VTE risk; not first-line after hip-relevant DEXA decline. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guidelines)

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg orally weekly; review at 12 months with DEXA and beta-CTX; continue calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Oral bisphosphonate is first-line therapy for postmenopausal osteoporosis after fragility fracture with eGFR above 35; alendronate is PBS-funded and effective. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal osteoporosis with fragility fracture qualifies for pharmacotherapy regardless of T-score. Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) is first-line in the absence of significant GI disease or eGFR below 35. Denosumab is second-line and requires careful long-term planning due to rebound vertebral fracture on discontinuation. Adequate vitamin D and calcium intake are prerequisites and ongoing during therapy. Bone turnover markers and DEXA support monitoring of response.
key_points: Oral bisphosphonate is first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis after fragility fracture
Denosumab requires careful discontinuation planning due to vertebral fracture rebound
Teriparatide is reserved for severe disease
Maintain calcium 1000 to 1300 mg/day and vitamin D 25(OH)D above 50 nmol/L
explanation.pearls: Atypical femur fractures and osteonecrosis of jaw are rare bisphosphonate adverse effects; consider drug holiday after 5 years of oral bisphosphonate in low-risk patients.

subtopic_detail: SJS/TEN initial management
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 56-year-old woman with new-onset painful rash for 36 hours after starting allopurinol 100 mg daily 3 weeks ago for gout. She now has flaccid bullae over the trunk that detach with gentle pressure, oral and conjunctival erosions, and a fever. The dermatology consultant on call estimates 18 percent body surface area involvement with epidermal detachment.

data_table.Examination: Flaccid bullae trunk and arms; Nikolsky positive; oral erosions; conjunctival injection with erosions; dusky targetoid lesions
data_table.Investigations: Hb 132, WCC 6.8, Cr 142 (baseline 76), ALT 122, ALP 184, albumin 28, CRP 96; SCORTEN calculated as 3
data_table.Medications: Allopurinol 100 mg daily for 3 weeks; nil other recent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease allopurinol and transfer to a burns or specialised dermatology unit for supportive care and wound management
options.rationale: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are managed by immediate cessation of the culprit drug and transfer to a burns or specialised dermatology unit; supportive care with fluid balance, wound care, infection control and ocular care is the cornerstone. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

options.text: Continue allopurinol; commence oral prednisolone 50 mg daily and topical corticosteroid; review at 48 hours by dermatology
options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug is dangerous; systemic steroids in SJS/TEN have unclear benefit; cessation and supportive care are the priority. (Source: ASCIA: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

options.text: Cease allopurinol; commence ciclosporin 3 mg/kg twice daily orally with bedside isolation in the medical ward
options.rationale: Ciclosporin has emerging evidence in TEN but is not first-line; specialised burns or dermatology unit transfer takes priority over ward-level care. (Source: ASCIA: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

options.text: Cease allopurinol; commence IV intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 4 days in current medical ward setting
options.rationale: IVIG is controversial in SJS/TEN with conflicting evidence; transfer to specialised unit is the priority intervention. (Source: ASCIA: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

options.text: Continue allopurinol; commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics empirically and arrange skin biopsy in 48 hours for confirmation
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics in SJS/TEN without infection signs increase nosocomial resistance; biopsy can be done but should not delay cessation and transfer. (Source: ASCIA: SCAR)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (less than 10 percent BSA detachment), SJS/TEN overlap (10 to 30 percent) and TEN (greater than 30 percent) are dermatological emergencies. Immediate management is cessation of the culprit drug and transfer to a burns or specialised dermatology unit. Supportive care includes fluid balance, wound care, ocular surface protection, nutrition and infection surveillance. The role of systemic therapies (ciclosporin, IVIG, etanercept, steroids) is debated; SCORTEN at 24 to 72 hours predicts mortality.
key_points: SJS/TEN: cease culprit drug immediately and transfer to burns/dermatology unit
Supportive care is the foundation; specific immunomodulatory therapy is debated
Allopurinol, lamotrigine, sulfonamides, anti-epileptics are common triggers
HLA-B*5801 testing reduces allopurinol risk in high-risk populations
explanation.pearls: SCORTEN parameters: age over 40, malignancy, HR over 120, BSA over 10 percent, urea over 10, glucose over 14, bicarbonate under 20; each adds 1 to predicted mortality.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: SCAR

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation duration after unprovoked PE
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in clinic 6 months after a first unprovoked submassive pulmonary embolism. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily and is asymptomatic with normal exercise tolerance. He has no malignancy on age-appropriate screening and no thrombophilia screen abnormalities. He has no high bleeding risk and is keen to continue if benefit outweighs harm.

data_table.Examination: Well; no oedema; chest clear; no calf swelling
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142, platelets 240, INR not applicable; eGFR 84; LFTs normal; thrombophilia screen negative; CT chest 6 weeks ago shows resolution of PE; HAS-BLED 1
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation strategy beyond 6 months?

options.text: Cease apixaban; arrange repeat D-dimer at 4 weeks off therapy and consider reinitiation only if D-dimer is positive
options.rationale: Off-treatment D-dimer informs risk but is not sufficient alone for cessation in unprovoked PE; extended anticoagulation is generally preferred when bleeding risk is low. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE Guidelines)

options.text: Continue apixaban at reduced dose 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely; review annually for bleeding risk and goals of care
options.rationale: After 6 months for unprovoked PE with low bleeding risk, extended therapy with reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily reduces recurrent VTE without significantly increasing major bleeding (AMPLIFY-EXT data); annual review balances ongoing benefit. (Source: THANZ VTE Guidelines)

options.text: Switch to warfarin INR 2 to 3 indefinitely; arrange community INR monitoring weekly initially then monthly when stable
options.rationale: DOACs are preferred over warfarin for VTE in absence of antiphospholipid syndrome or other contraindication; warfarin offers no advantage and adds monitoring burden. (Source: THANZ VTE Guidelines)

options.text: Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily; arrange GP review in 6 months and resume DOAC if recurrent VTE symptoms develop
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces recurrent VTE by only about 30 percent compared with around 80 percent for low-dose DOAC; not preferred when DOAC is tolerated. (Source: THANZ VTE Guidelines)

options.text: Cease apixaban at 6 months; advise that the risk of recurrent VTE is sufficiently low after 6 months of therapy to stop
options.rationale: Recurrent VTE risk after unprovoked event is 10 percent at 1 year and 30 percent at 5 years after stopping anticoagulation; extended therapy is generally indicated when bleeding risk is acceptable. (Source: THANZ VTE Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Following a first unprovoked PE, anticoagulation should generally continue beyond 3 to 6 months if bleeding risk is acceptable. The AMPLIFY-EXT and EINSTEIN-CHOICE trials demonstrated that reduced-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) effectively reduce recurrent VTE without significantly increasing major bleeding compared with full-dose. Bleeding risk should be reviewed annually. Provoked VTE with a transient major risk factor typically requires only 3 months of anticoagulation.
key_points: Unprovoked PE: extended anticoagulation beyond 6 months if bleeding risk acceptable
Reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily preferred for extended phase
Annual review of bleeding risk and goals of care
Aspirin alone is much less effective than reduced-dose DOAC
explanation.pearls: Provoked VTE with transient major risk factor (surgery, trauma, immobility) typically warrants only 3 months of anticoagulation; cancer-associated VTE requires DOAC or LMWH for 6 months minimum.

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis - Duke criteria
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man with 3 weeks of fever, fatigue and weight loss. He had a dental extraction 6 weeks ago. He has a history of bicuspid aortic valve. Examination reveals a new diastolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages and a tender nodule on his left index finger pulp. Echocardiography shows aortic valve vegetation 8 mm and moderate aortic regurgitation. Two of three sets of blood cultures grow viridans group streptococci.

data_table.Examination: New 2/6 diastolic decrescendo murmur LSE; splinter haemorrhages; Osler node left index finger pulp; no Janeway lesion; spleen tip palpable
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.4, Hb 108, CRP 96, ESR 78, urine dipstick haematuria +, TTE aortic vegetation 8 mm, moderate AR; blood cultures 2 of 3 sets viridans streptococci
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: Which best characterises the diagnostic certainty under the modified Duke criteria?

options.text: Possible endocarditis (1 major plus 1 minor criterion); commence empirical IV flucloxacillin pending further cultures
options.rationale: This patient meets definite criteria with 2 major (typical organism with 2 sets of blood cultures positive plus vegetation on echo) and multiple minor criteria; treatment is targeted not empirical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Possible endocarditis (2 minor criteria only); arrange TOE within 24 hours before commencing any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: The criteria fulfilled exceed possible; TOE may further define vegetation but should not delay treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Definite endocarditis (2 major criteria); commence IV benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly for 4 weeks with gentamicin for the first 2 weeks
options.rationale: Two major Duke criteria (typical organism in 2 cultures plus vegetation with regurgitation) confirm definite endocarditis; targeted treatment for viridans strep native valve endocarditis is benzylpenicillin 4 weeks with gentamicin for the first 2 weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Rejected endocarditis (alternate diagnosis); arrange dental review and broad febrile workup including bone scan and PET
options.rationale: Rejected requires firm alternate diagnosis or resolution within 4 days of antibiotic; this patient has classic endocarditis features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Definite endocarditis (3 minor criteria); commence IV vancomycin and ciprofloxacin pending speciation and sensitivities
options.rationale: Vancomycin plus quinolone is incorrect empirical cover for native-valve streptococcal endocarditis; species is already identified as viridans group streptococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria diagnose infective endocarditis as definite, possible or rejected. Major criteria include typical organism in 2 separate blood cultures and evidence of endocardial involvement on echocardiography (vegetation, abscess, new valve regurgitation). Minor criteria include predisposing valve disease, fever above 38, vascular phenomena (Janeway, emboli) and immunological phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis). Two majors, or one major plus 3 minors, or 5 minors satisfy definite endocarditis. Targeted antimicrobial therapy is selected by organism and valve type.
key_points: Two majors satisfy definite endocarditis
Native valve viridans strep: benzylpenicillin 4 weeks plus gentamicin 2 weeks
Surgical indications: heart failure, abscess, large mobile vegetation, persistent bacteraemia
TOE indicated if TTE non-diagnostic or for prosthetic valves
explanation.pearls: Surgery within 7 days is indicated for heart failure from valve dysfunction, perivalvular abscess, or persistent bacteraemia despite 5 to 7 days of appropriate antibiotic.

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax recognition
stem: You are the medical registrar called to a 64-year-old man with severe COPD on the respiratory ward who has acutely deteriorated. He developed sudden right-sided chest pain and severe dyspnoea 5 minutes ago. He is hypotensive, tachycardic and using accessory muscles. There is decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance on the right with tracheal deviation to the left. SpO2 is 84 percent on 15 L non-rebreather.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 78/44, HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 84% on 15 L NRB, T 36.6, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Severe respiratory distress, accessory muscle use; trachea deviated to the left; right chest hyperresonant with absent breath sounds; distended neck veins
data_table.Investigations: Cannot wait for imaging; ECG sinus tachycardia
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium, salbutamol, prednisolone tapering

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Arrange urgent portable chest X-ray to confirm tension pneumothorax; commence non-invasive ventilation while awaiting result
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; awaiting imaging or starting NIV worsens the tension and delays life-saving decompression. (Source: ANZCOR Guidelines)

options.text: Administer IV crystalloid 1 L bolus; commence noradrenaline infusion to support BP while preparing for theatre
options.rationale: Volume and vasopressor without decompression do not address the obstructive shock; decompression is the only effective treatment. (Source: ATLS Australia)

options.text: Intubate immediately with rocuronium and ketamine; apply positive pressure ventilation to recruit collapsed lung tissue
options.rationale: Positive pressure ventilation in tension pneumothorax worsens the tension and can precipitate cardiac arrest; decompression is required before intubation. (Source: ATLS Australia)

options.text: Perform finger thoracostomy at the 5th intercostal space mid-axillary line on the right; insert intercostal catheter immediately after
options.rationale: Immediate finger thoracostomy in the safe triangle (5th ICS mid-axillary) followed by ICC is the current preferred technique for tension pneumothorax due to reliability in adults with chest wall thickness; needle decompression at 2nd ICS mid-clavicular is an alternative with higher failure rate. (Source: ATLS Australia)

options.text: Administer salbutamol 5 mg and ipratropium 500 micrograms nebulised; increase prednisolone to 50 mg orally daily
options.rationale: Nebulisers and steroids treat COPD exacerbation not tension pneumothorax; do not address the obstructive physiology. (Source: ANZCOR Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis based on respiratory distress, hypotension, ipsilateral hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation and distended neck veins. Immediate decompression is required without waiting for imaging. Australian and ATLS guidance increasingly favours finger thoracostomy at the safe triangle (5th intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line) over the traditional 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular needle decompression because of high failure rates with needles in adults. Definitive intercostal catheter follows immediately. Positive pressure ventilation before decompression is dangerous.
key_points: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; treat before imaging
Finger thoracostomy at 5th ICS mid-axillary is preferred over needle at 2nd ICS
Avoid positive pressure ventilation before decompression
ICC follows immediately after decompression
explanation.pearls: If using needle decompression as first step, a longer 14G cannula (at least 8 cm) is recommended because the standard short cannula fails to reach the pleural space in over half of adults.

subtopic_detail: Primary hyperaldosteronism workup
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 46-year-old woman with resistant hypertension on perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Despite triple therapy her BP remains 162/96. She has muscle cramps and her potassium has consistently been at the lower end (3.0 to 3.4). She has no symptoms of phaeochromocytoma. There is no family history of hypertension before age 40.

data_table.Examination: Well; no abdominal bruit; no Cushingoid features; no goitre; no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Na 142, K 3.2, Cr 78, eGFR 78, plasma renin activity low, aldosterone elevated, ARR pending; TSH normal; HbA1c 5.6%; ECG sinus rhythm; urine ACR 2.4
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 10 mg daily; amlodipine 10 mg daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test; continue current antihypertensive regimen without change before testing
options.rationale: DST screens for Cushing's, not aldosteronism; ARR is the appropriate first test for this clinical picture. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.text: 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines; correct potassium and continue all current antihypertensives during collection
options.rationale: Metanephrines test for phaeochromocytoma; clinical picture is aldosteronism with hypokalaemia; ARR is the appropriate screen. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.text: Renal artery duplex ultrasound; commence empirical spironolactone 25 mg daily while awaiting the result of imaging
options.rationale: Renovascular disease is a differential but ARR screen for aldosteronism comes first given hypokalaemia; spironolactone confounds ARR if started before sampling. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.text: Late-night salivary cortisol; reduce hydrochlorothiazide to 12.5 mg daily and continue ACE inhibitor at full dose
options.rationale: Late-night salivary cortisol screens for Cushing's; no Cushingoid features present and hypokalaemia with resistant hypertension is more characteristic of aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.text: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio screening; correct potassium and switch ACE inhibitor to verapamil before sampling for accuracy
options.rationale: ARR is the screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism in resistant hypertension; medications that affect the RAAS (ACEi, ARB, beta blocker, diuretic) should be stopped where possible and replaced with non-interfering agents like verapamil or doxazosin before sampling, and hypokalaemia corrected. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is the commonest secondary cause of hypertension and is often missed because hypokalaemia is present in only about a third of cases. Screening with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio is indicated for resistant hypertension, hypertension with hypokalaemia, hypertension with adrenal incidentaloma, hypertension under 40 and hypertension with first-degree family history of aldosteronism or early stroke. Hypokalaemia should be corrected and interfering medications swapped before testing. Confirmatory testing (saline suppression or fludrocortisone suppression) follows a positive ARR; adrenal vein sampling guides surgical decision-making.
key_points: ARR is the screening test for primary aldosteronism
Correct hypokalaemia and use non-interfering antihypertensives before sampling
Confirmatory testing follows positive ARR
Adrenal vein sampling guides surgical decisions
explanation.pearls: Verapamil and doxazosin do not interfere significantly with ARR and are the preferred bridging antihypertensives during workup.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

subtopic_detail: Adult sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem: You are the medical registrar in ED reviewing a 68-year-old man with 24 hours of fever, dysuria and confusion. He has a background of well-controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin. He is hypotensive on arrival. The team has placed two large bore IV lines and a urinary catheter for output monitoring. Bloods are at the lab.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.8, HR 122, BP 84/52, RR 26, SpO2 96% on 6 L mask, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; warm peripheries; suprapubic tenderness; cloudy malodorous urine; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2, WCC 18.2 (neutrophils 16.2), CRP 240, Cr 168 (baseline 95), urine dip nitrite and leukocyte positive, blood cultures pending
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline infusion via peripheral line at 0.05 mcg/kg/min; defer fluid resuscitation pending central access
options.rationale: Initial fluid resuscitation precedes vasopressors in sepsis; vasopressors are added if hypotension persists after 30 mL/kg crystalloid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Oral co-trimoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily and oral fluids; admit to short-stay for 24 hours observation with repeat lactate
options.rationale: Septic shock with lactate above 4 requires IV antibiotics and resuscitation; oral therapy is not appropriate for an unstable patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Crystalloid 30 mL/kg IV over 3 hours; IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g; blood cultures and lactate before antibiotics
options.rationale: Sepsis hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, take cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotic within 1 hour, crystalloid 30 mL/kg over 3 hours, vasopressors if MAP below 65 after fluid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Activated protein C infusion 24 mcg/kg/hour for 96 hours; broad-spectrum antibiotics after coagulopathy is excluded
options.rationale: Activated protein C was withdrawn from the market after PROWESS-SHOCK showed no benefit; it is not part of current sepsis management. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as first-line therapy; defer antibiotics until cortisol response confirmed
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone 200 mg per day is added in fluid-refractory and vasopressor-dependent septic shock, not as first-line ahead of antibiotics. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle is: measure lactate, take blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, crystalloid 30 mL/kg over 3 hours if hypotensive or lactate above 4, and add vasopressors if MAP remains below 65 despite fluid. Hydrocortisone 200 mg daily is added in fluid-refractory shock. Source control identifies the focus and removes infected hardware or pus. Reassess perfusion using lactate clearance, capillary refill and dynamic markers.
key_points: Cultures before antibiotics; antibiotics within 1 hour
Crystalloid 30 mL/kg over 3 hours for hypotension or lactate above 4
Vasopressors if MAP below 65 after fluids
Hydrocortisone in fluid-refractory shock
explanation.pearls: Empirical antibiotic for urosepsis in Australia is piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 hours, or ceftriaxone 2 g if community-acquired without risk factors for resistant organisms.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition and LRINEC score
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with 18 hours of right thigh swelling and pain disproportionate to the redness. He has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2 percent). The skin is dusky over a 12 by 8 cm area with bullae forming and crepitus on palpation. He is febrile and unwell. Vitals and bloods are back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.0, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 96% on 4 L mask
data_table.Examination: Pain out of proportion; bullae and dusky discolouration on right thigh; crepitus palpable; reduced sensation over the central plaque
data_table.Investigations: Hb 138, WCC 22, Na 128, glucose 18.4, Cr 132, CRP 380, lactate 4.0
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; gliclazide MR 60 mg daily; insulin glargine 18 units nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Outline cellulitis with marker pen; commence IV cefazolin 2 g and observe for response over 4 hours
options.rationale: Pain disproportionate to skin findings, bullae, crepitus and systemic features suggest necrotising fasciitis; cellulitis monotherapy delays critical surgical intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Bedside ultrasound to exclude deep abscess; commence oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for outpatient management
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency, not a candidate for ultrasound and outpatient oral antibiotics; rapid spread without prompt surgery is fatal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy after first dose of antibiotics; defer surgery pending response to medical therapy and hyperbaric
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive at most and never substitutes for source control; urgent surgical debridement is the definitive treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent surgical consult for debridement; IV meropenem 1 g, vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading, clindamycin 600 mg; activate sepsis pathway
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis features (pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, hypotension, LRINEC 8) mandate urgent surgical debridement plus empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for anti-toxin effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the thigh to delineate fascial involvement; defer antibiotics until imaging completed and reviewed
options.rationale: MRI delays definitive surgery in suspected necrotising fasciitis; clinical diagnosis with prompt surgery and antibiotics is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency suggested by pain out of proportion to skin findings, dusky discolouration, bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia over the lesion, rapid spread and systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, Cr, glucose) supports the diagnosis; score 8 or above indicates high risk but should never delay surgical consultation. Management is urgent surgical debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics (carbapenem, vancomycin, clindamycin for anti-toxin effect), source control and intensive care.
key_points: Necrotising fasciitis features: pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus
LRINEC 8 or above is high risk but not required for surgery
Urgent debridement is the principal intervention
Empirical antibiotics: carbapenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin
explanation.pearls: Mortality in necrotising fasciitis approaches 30 to 50 percent and rises with each hour of delay to surgical debridement; never delay surgery for imaging.

subtopic_detail: Latent TB diagnosis and treatment selection
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 34-year-old asymptomatic nurse before commencing infliximab for rheumatoid arthritis. She was born in Australia and has no known TB contact. She did NOT have BCG as a child. She has a routine pre-biologic screen including chest x-ray and QuantiFERON Gold Plus.

data_table.Examination: No respiratory symptoms; normal chest examination; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray normal; QuantiFERON Gold Plus positive (TB1 1.2 IU/mL, TB2 1.4 IU/mL); HIV negative; HBV and HCV negative; FBC, U&E, LFTs normal
data_table.Medications: Methotrexate 15 mg weekly; folic acid 5 mg weekly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and proceed with infliximab; treat only if active TB develops during therapy on routine monitoring
options.rationale: Positive interferon gamma release assay before TNF inhibitor warrants treatment for latent TB; missed treatment carries up to 10 percent reactivation risk on biologic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Repeat QuantiFERON in 3 months to confirm; proceed with infliximab in the interim while monitoring symptoms
options.rationale: Confirmed positive QuantiFERON does not require repeat for confirmation; biologic should not be started without treating latent TB. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence 6-month course of pyrazinamide and ethambutol with monthly LFTs and visual acuity assessment
options.rationale: Pyrazinamide plus ethambutol is part of treatment for active TB, not latent infection; latent TB is treated with isoniazid, rifampicin or short-course combinations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer to public health for directly observed therapy with daily isoniazid for 24 months as an immunosuppressed patient
options.rationale: Standard latent TB regimens are 6 to 9 months of isoniazid or 4 months of rifampicin; 24-month therapy is not a current standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 9 months; defer infliximab until at least 4 weeks of therapy
options.rationale: Positive QuantiFERON before TNF inhibitor mandates latent TB treatment; isoniazid 9 months (or rifampicin 4 months) is first line; pyridoxine prevents neuropathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
