explanation.summary: Latent TB infection screening with an interferon gamma release assay (QuantiFERON Gold Plus or T-SPOT.TB) is standard before TNF inhibitor or organ transplant. Tuberculin skin testing is an alternative where IGRA is unavailable. Confirmed latent TB is treated with isoniazid for 9 months plus pyridoxine, isoniazid plus rifapentine weekly for 3 months (3HP), or rifampicin alone for 4 months. Biologic therapy is deferred until at least 4 weeks of treatment. Active disease must be excluded before treatment of latent infection.
key_points: IGRA preferred before TNF inhibitor or transplant
Treat latent TB with isoniazid 9 months plus pyridoxine, or 3HP, or rifampicin 4 months
Defer biologic by 4 weeks after starting LTBI treatment
Always exclude active TB before treating latent infection
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine 25 mg daily is added with isoniazid in patients at risk of neuropathy (diabetes, alcohol use, pregnancy, HIV, malnutrition) to prevent peripheral neuropathy.

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis FRAX and bisphosphonate threshold
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 68-year-old postmenopausal woman 6 months after a low-trauma wrist fracture. She is otherwise well, not on glucocorticoids, and her father had a hip fracture aged 78. She has had a DXA scan today. Her calcium and vitamin D are replete and her eGFR is 76 mL/min/1.73m^2. She is keen to consider preventive therapy.

data_table.Examination: No spinal tenderness; height 162 cm (lost 2 cm); BMI 24
data_table.Investigations: DXA T-score lumbar spine -2.6, femoral neck -2.4; corrected calcium 2.40, 25-OH vitamin D 78, PTH 4.2, ALP 80, Cr 76, FRAX 10-year major fracture 22%, hip fracture 6%
data_table.Medications: Vitamin D 1000 IU daily; calcium 600 mg daily; nil other

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological choice?

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg oral once weekly; continue calcium and vitamin D; reassess BMD and clinical risk at 5 years
options.rationale: Prior low-trauma fracture and T-score below -2.5 meet PBS criteria for oral bisphosphonate; alendronate weekly is first line; review at 5 years considers drug holiday. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous 6-monthly indefinitely; cease calcium supplementation to avoid hypercalcaemia
options.rationale: Denosumab is second line where bisphosphonate is poorly tolerated or contraindicated; ceasing calcium is unsafe and risks hypocalcaemia with denosumab. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Hormone replacement therapy with oral oestradiol and progesterone; bone density monitoring annually for 5 years
options.rationale: HRT is not first-line for established osteoporosis in a 68-year-old; absolute thromboembolism risk exceeds vasomotor benefit at this age. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneous daily for 24 months as first-line agent; defer bisphosphonate during teriparatide
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis with multiple vertebral fractures or failure of bisphosphonate, not first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Raloxifene 60 mg daily; reassess BMD at 5 years and consider switch if no response on vertebral measurement
options.rationale: Raloxifene is reserved for vertebral fracture prevention in women intolerant of bisphosphonates; it does not reduce hip fracture risk and is not first line here. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Australian PBS criteria for antiresorptive therapy include prior minimal trauma fracture, T-score -2.5 or below, or high fracture risk by FRAX. First-line is oral alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly, alongside calcium and vitamin D. Intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg annually is an alternative when oral therapy is poorly tolerated. Denosumab is second line; teriparatide is reserved for severe disease. Drug holiday is considered at 5 years for bisphosphonates; denosumab cannot be stopped without follow-on therapy due to rebound vertebral fracture risk.
key_points: Prior minimal-trauma fracture or T-score below -2.5 meets PBS criteria
Oral alendronate or risedronate first line; IV zoledronate alternative
Denosumab second line; never stop without follow-on therapy
Bisphosphonate drug holiday considered at 5 years
explanation.pearls: Denosumab cessation without follow-on bisphosphonate causes multiple vertebral fracture rebound within 9 to 18 months due to rapid loss of antiresorptive effect.

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis surgical indication
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man on day 3 of treatment for native aortic valve endocarditis with methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. He has new dyspnoea overnight. Echocardiogram now shows a 1.2 cm aortic vegetation, moderate to severe aortic regurgitation and a small pericardial effusion. He has bilateral fine inspiratory crackles. He has had 3 days of IV flucloxacillin and remains febrile to 38.7.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, BP 102/56, HR 108, RR 26, SpO2 92% on 4 L mask, JVP 5 cm
data_table.Examination: Bibasal fine crackles; soft S3; collapsing pulse; soft diastolic murmur at LSE; warm extremities
data_table.Investigations: Hb 110, WCC 14, Cr 138 (baseline 92), CRP 180, troponin 84, BNP 1200; echo aortic vegetation 12 mm, severe AR, EF 50%, no abscess yet; chest x-ray pulmonary oedema
data_table.Medications: IV flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly for 3 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue IV flucloxacillin for a further 7 days; reassess vegetation size and clinical response with echo on day 10
options.rationale: Heart failure from severe acute aortic regurgitation in infective endocarditis is a class I indication for urgent surgery; delay risks decompensation and death. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)

options.text: Urgent cardiothoracic referral for aortic valve replacement within 24 to 48 hours; continue antibiotics throughout
options.rationale: New heart failure from severe valvular regurgitation in active endocarditis is a class I indication for urgent surgery within 24 to 48 hours; ongoing antibiotics continue around surgery. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)

options.text: Add IV gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for synergy; reassess response after 5 days before considering operative referral
options.rationale: Routine gentamicin in MSSA native valve endocarditis is no longer recommended due to nephrotoxicity without survival benefit; surgery is indicated here irrespective. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)

options.text: Switch to IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose; defer surgery pending repeat MRI brain to exclude embolic stroke
options.rationale: MSSA is best treated with flucloxacillin; vancomycin is inferior in MSSA. Embolic risk does not generally delay urgent surgery for haemodynamic indications. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)

options.text: Intravenous frusemide 40 mg with non-invasive ventilation for pulmonary oedema; cardiology review in 1 week for assessment
options.rationale: Medical therapy temporises but does not address acute severe AR; delay for 1 week risks fatal decompensation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Endocarditis Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Indications for early surgery in active infective endocarditis include heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (persistent bacteraemia despite appropriate antibiotics, perivalvular extension, abscess, fistula), and prevention of embolism (mobile vegetations greater than 10 mm with prior embolism or larger than 15 mm). Heart failure due to severe valvular regurgitation is the most common class I indication and typically requires surgery within 24 to 48 hours. Antibiotics are continued throughout the perioperative period and adjusted based on intra-operative cultures.
key_points: Heart failure from valve dysfunction is class I urgent surgical indication
Uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteraemia) also class I
Vegetations greater than 10 to 15 mm with embolic risk warrant surgery
Antibiotics continue around surgery
explanation.pearls: MSSA native valve endocarditis is treated with flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours for 4 to 6 weeks; vancomycin is reserved for MRSA or severe penicillin allergy.

subtopic_detail: Cushing's syndrome first-line screening test
stem: You are the medical registrar in an outpatient clinic reviewing a 38-year-old woman with 18 months of weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness when climbing stairs, and new-onset hypertension. Her BMI is 34 and she has wide violaceous abdominal striae. She also reports irregular menses. She is not on glucocorticoids by any route. Her sleep is good and her depression screen is negative.

data_table.Examination: Central obesity; thin extremities; proximal weakness on hip flexion; violaceous striae greater than 1 cm; supraclavicular fat pad
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 6.8 fasting, HbA1c 6.2%, K 3.4, ACTH pending; menstrual irregularity 2 to 3 months; no glucocorticoid use
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily; no inhaled corticosteroid

lead_in: Which screening test sequence is most appropriate?

options.text: Random morning serum cortisol and plasma ACTH; CT adrenals only if cortisol greater than 700 nmol/L
options.rationale: Random cortisol does not screen for Cushing's because of pulsatility; loss of diurnal variation is the key abnormality, requiring late-night cortisol or 1 mg DST. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)

options.text: Adrenal CT alone; biochemical testing only if a mass greater than 1 cm is identified on imaging
options.rationale: Imaging is not a screening test for Cushing's syndrome; biochemical confirmation of hypercortisolism precedes localisation imaging. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)

options.text: Two of: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24-hour urinary free cortisol
options.rationale: Endocrine Society guidance recommends two abnormal first-line tests from 1 mg overnight DST, late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol to confirm Cushing's syndrome before localisation. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)

options.text: Insulin tolerance test for cortisol response; pituitary MRI only if cortisol fails to rise above 500 nmol/L during test
options.rationale: Insulin tolerance test assesses adrenal insufficiency, not Cushing's; it is not a Cushing's screen. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)

options.text: Serum cortisol after 2 mg dexamethasone 8 mg over 2 days; pituitary MRI as first-line localisation if cortisol suppresses
options.rationale: High-dose dexamethasone suppression (8 mg) is used to differentiate Cushing's disease from ectopic ACTH after confirmation; it is not first-line screening. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cushing's syndrome screening uses first-line tests that capture loss of diurnal cortisol rhythm or feedback suppression: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol below 50 nmol/L excludes), late-night salivary cortisol (low at night in normal), and 24-hour urinary free cortisol. Two abnormal first-line tests confirm hypercortisolism. Subsequent ACTH measurement classifies as ACTH-dependent (pituitary adenoma or ectopic) vs ACTH-independent (adrenal). Localisation by MRI pituitary or adrenal CT follows.
key_points: Screen with 1 mg DST, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24-hour UFC
Two abnormal first-line tests confirm hypercortisolism
ACTH classifies dependent vs independent
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation
explanation.pearls: False positives on 1 mg DST occur with oestrogen (raised CBG), depression, alcohol use, obesity and pregnancy; consider these before pursuing further testing.

subtopic_detail: Unprovoked VTE anticoagulation duration
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in clinic 6 months after a first proximal lower limb DVT. He had no surgery, no immobility, no malignancy and no oestrogen use at the time. He has had a CT chest, abdomen and pelvis showing no malignancy, and is well. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily. He has no bleeding history and tolerates apixaban well. He wants to know whether to continue, reduce or stop.

data_table.Examination: No leg swelling; no calf tenderness; cardiorespiratory examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142, plt 220, Cr 92, eGFR 84, INR 1.0, repeat lower limb Doppler shows residual non-occlusive thrombus; D-dimer 360 ng/mL (pending decision)
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily; nil other

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Cease apixaban at 6 months; commence aspirin 100 mg daily for ongoing VTE prevention long-term
options.rationale: Aspirin offers some VTE prevention after stopping anticoagulation but is inferior to extended DOAC at standard or reduced dose for unprovoked VTE. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely; review annually for bleeding risk and recurrence risk
options.rationale: Full-dose extended therapy is appropriate but the AMPLIFY-EXT trial supports reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily as the standard extended-phase dose, with similar efficacy and lower bleeding. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)

options.text: Switch to warfarin with INR target 2.5 to 3.5 indefinitely; cease apixaban after 1 week of overlap with target INR
options.rationale: Higher-intensity warfarin is associated with more bleeding without efficacy benefit; DOACs are preferred in non-cancer non-valvular VTE. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely; review annually for bleeding risk and recurrence risk
options.rationale: Unprovoked proximal DVT carries 10 percent annual recurrence risk; extended-phase apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (AMPLIFY-EXT) is non-inferior to full dose with reduced bleeding and is the Australian standard. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)

options.text: Cease apixaban at 6 months; arrange thrombophilia screen and IVC filter placement if any heritable thrombophilia is found
options.rationale: Routine thrombophilia screening rarely changes management; IVC filters are for contraindication to anticoagulation, not first-line VTE prevention. (Source: ASTH VTE Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Unprovoked proximal DVT or PE carries approximately 10 percent annual recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation. Australian guidance recommends extended-phase anticoagulation beyond 3 to 6 months in patients without high bleeding risk. Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (AMPLIFY-EXT) and rivaroxaban 10 mg daily (EINSTEIN-CHOICE) are non-inferior to full dose with lower bleeding. Provoked VTE with a transient risk factor stops at 3 months. Cancer-associated VTE continues while cancer is active. Bleeding risk is reviewed annually.
key_points: Unprovoked proximal VTE: extended anticoagulation beyond 6 months
Apixaban 2.5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily extended phase
Provoked VTE (transient): stop at 3 months
Cancer-associated VTE: continue while cancer active
explanation.pearls: AMPLIFY-EXT showed extended apixaban 2.5 mg BD reduced recurrence by 80 percent compared with placebo with bleeding rates similar to placebo.

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection acute medical therapy
stem: You are the medical registrar in ED with a 62-year-old man with sudden severe tearing interscapular back pain 2 hours ago. CT aortogram confirms an uncomplicated Stanford type B aortic dissection extending from just distal to the left subclavian artery to the iliac bifurcation. There is no organ malperfusion, no rupture, and no rapid expansion. He has a known background of hypertension. He has no asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 188/108 right arm and 184/106 left arm, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Pain 8/10 between scapulae; equal radial pulses; warm peripheries; no neurological deficit; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: Troponin negative; Cr 96; CXR widened mediastinum; CT aortogram type B dissection without malperfusion
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg daily; amlodipine 10 mg daily at home

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial blood pressure and heart rate target and first-line therapy?

options.text: Sodium nitroprusside infusion alone titrated to systolic 100 to 120 mmHg; no heart rate target during titration
options.rationale: Vasodilator-only therapy causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic wall shear stress; a beta-blocker must be started first or alongside to control heart rate. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

options.text: Intravenous metoprolol 5 mg bolus once; no further treatment if pain settles and discharge home from ED with GP follow-up
options.rationale: Acute aortic dissection requires admission to a critical care setting with continuous IV antihypertensive therapy, not single-bolus management and discharge. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

options.text: Urgent thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) within 4 hours; defer medical therapy until anaesthetic review for surgery
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically first; TEVAR is for complicated dissection (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, rapid expansion). (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

options.text: Intravenous frusemide 40 mg with morphine 5 mg for pain; recheck BP at 30 minutes before further therapy
options.rationale: Frusemide does not address aortic wall shear; pain management is adjunctive; primary therapy is beta blockade plus vasodilator to lower systolic BP and dP/dt. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion targeting systolic 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate below 60 within 20 minutes
options.rationale: Acute type B dissection requires immediate IV beta-blockade with systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate below 60 to reduce aortic wall shear stress and dP/dt; labetalol is the standard first agent in Australia. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Statement)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection requires immediate reduction of aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt) to limit propagation. First-line is intravenous beta blockade (labetalol or esmolol) targeting systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate below 60 per minute within 20 minutes. Vasodilators (sodium nitroprusside or GTN) are added after beta blockade if BP target not met. Pain control (IV opioid) reduces sympathetic drive. Uncomplicated type B is managed medically; type A and complicated type B require surgical or endovascular intervention.
key_points: Target SBP 100 to 120 mmHg and HR below 60 within 20 minutes
Beta blockade first; vasodilator second to avoid reflex tachycardia
Type A and complicated type B require surgery
Uncomplicated type B managed medically in ICU
explanation.pearls: Labetalol IV bolus 20 mg every 10 minutes (max 300 mg) or infusion at 0.5 to 2 mg/min is the Australian first-line agent; esmolol is an alternative when shorter half-life is preferred.

subtopic_detail: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction GDMT
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 64-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent) in clinic 3 months after admission for decompensation. He is now NYHA II symptoms on usual activity. He is on perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, frusemide 40 mg and spironolactone 25 mg, all up-titrated since admission. His latest bloods and observations are stable. He has no peripheral oedema. He is not in atrial fibrillation. He has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 6.9 percent) on metformin only. His renal function is stable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 68 (sinus), RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: JVP 3 cm, no peripheral oedema, clear chest, normal heart sounds
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 62, K 4.4, Na 138, NT-proBNP 980; HbA1c 6.9; recent echo LVEF 28%
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, frusemide 40 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, metformin 1 g BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase perindopril to 10 mg daily and review response in 4 weeks before any additional therapy is added
options.rationale: Up-titration of ACEi is reasonable but the bigger gain is adding the fourth pillar SGLT2 inhibitor, which reduces hospitalisation and mortality in HFrEF irrespective of diabetes status. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)

options.text: Stop spironolactone given normal potassium and stable renal function; add empagliflozin 10 mg daily as the new GDMT pillar
options.rationale: MRA discontinuation in stable HFrEF removes a mortality-reducing pillar; SGLT2i is added in addition, not in place of, MRA. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)

options.text: Add ivabradine 5 mg twice daily to slow heart rate further; defer other medication changes until heart rate is below 60
options.rationale: Ivabradine is added when sinus rhythm with HR 70 or above persists despite maximum tolerated beta-blocker; HR 68 with first-line GDMT incomplete does not warrant ivabradine yet. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)

options.text: Add digoxin 125 micrograms daily for symptom control and review at 6 weeks; defer SGLT2 inhibitor and sacubitril/valsartan
options.rationale: Digoxin is reserved for symptom control after the four pillars are optimised or when AF coexists; it has no mortality benefit. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)

options.text: Switch perindopril to sacubitril/valsartan (after 36-hour washout) and add dapagliflozin 10 mg daily for the fourth pillar of GDMT
options.rationale: Australian guidance for symptomatic HFrEF on ACEi recommends switching to sacubitril/valsartan (after washout) and adding SGLT2 inhibitor; the four pillars (ARNI/ACEi, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) provide additive prognostic benefit. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines)

explanation.summary: HFrEF guideline-directed medical therapy comprises four pillars with additive prognostic benefit: ACEi/ARB (switch to sacubitril/valsartan when tolerated), beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol), MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) and SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin). Each is up-titrated to target or maximum tolerated dose. SGLT2 inhibitors benefit HFrEF regardless of diabetes status, with risk reduction of 25 to 30 percent for HF hospitalisation and CV death. Ivabradine is added when sinus rhythm with HR 70 or above persists despite optimal beta-blocker.
key_points: Four pillars: ARNI/ACEi, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i
SGLT2 inhibitor benefit independent of diabetes
ARNI requires 36-hour washout from ACEi
Ivabradine for sinus rate 70+ despite optimal beta-blocker
explanation.pearls: Sacubitril/valsartan reduces NT-proBNP within 4 weeks; transient hypotension is the commonest reason for dose reduction during titration.

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem: You are the medicine registrar in ED at 0200 reviewing a 68-year-old man with urinary symptoms for 3 days, now confused. He has a known history of BPH. His GP started oral trimethoprim yesterday. His son brought him in after he became confused this evening. On arrival his observations met sepsis criteria. Blood cultures and urine have been taken. The first set of bloods is back. Cefriaxone 2 g has just been given. He has now received 30 mL/kg crystalloid over 60 minutes. His repeat lactate is back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.0, HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 96% on 4 L oxygen, BP 78/42 (now MAP 54 after 2.4 L crystalloid), GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries, dry mucous membranes, suprapubic tenderness, no rash, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L initial, repeat after fluid 3.8; WCC 22 (neutrophils 18), CRP 280, creatinine 168, urea 22, eGFR 38; urine dip 3+ leucocytes 3+ nitrites; ECG normal sinus
data_table.Medications: IV ceftriaxone 2 g given 25 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch ceftriaxone to oral ciprofloxacin once cultures return; continue conservative management while awaiting microbiology
options.rationale: De-escalation occurs after clinical improvement and culture results; immediate priority in septic shock is haemodynamic stabilisation, not antibiotic switching. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Continue intravenous crystalloid at 1 L per hour for the next 4 hours; defer vasopressor until 6 L has been delivered
options.rationale: Persistent MAP under 65 after 30 mL/kg crystalloid defines fluid-refractory septic shock; ongoing fluid risks pulmonary oedema without improving perfusion, and vasopressor is the next step. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion via central access (or peripheral pending central line) to target MAP 65 or above; activate critical care review
options.rationale: Septic shock unresponsive to 30 mL/kg fluid resuscitation requires vasopressor (noradrenaline first-line) to target MAP 65 or above and parallel critical care consultation; further fluid alone risks pulmonary oedema without restoring perfusion. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as a first-line therapy before considering vasopressor or critical care input
options.rationale: Stress-dose hydrocortisone is added in septic shock requiring noradrenaline at moderate dose; it is not first-line ahead of vasopressor. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter and observe for clinical response over the next 2 hours before any further intervention
options.rationale: Source control is important but septic shock unresponsive to fluid demands immediate vasopressor; catheter alone does not restore perfusion. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

explanation.summary: Septic shock is defined by sepsis plus persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor to maintain MAP 65 or above AND serum lactate over 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotic within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4, vasopressor (noradrenaline first-line) if MAP under 65 despite fluid. Source control as soon as feasible. Stress-dose hydrocortisone 200 mg per day is added in fluid- and vasopressor-refractory shock. Critical care input is required.
key_points: Septic shock: vasopressor + lactate over 2 despite fluid
Noradrenaline first-line vasopressor
Lactate, cultures, antibiotics within first hour
Hydrocortisone for refractory shock on rising vasopressor
explanation.pearls: Peripheral noradrenaline can be safely commenced through a large bore (16G or larger) antecubital cannula for up to 24 hours while central access is arranged; do not delay vasopressor waiting for central line.

sources.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / SA Health Sepsis Pathway

subtopic_detail: DOAC selection in AF with chronic kidney disease
stem: You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 78-year-old woman in newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. She has a CHA2DS2-VA score of 5 (hypertension, age, heart failure, female sex). She has chronic kidney disease stage 3b (eGFR 32 mL/min). She has no mechanical valve, no significant mitral stenosis and no recent bleeding. Her weight is 56 kg. She is on no anticoagulant. Liver function is normal. She has no history of intracranial bleed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 118 (irregular), RR 18, SpO2 97% RA, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse; clear chest; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ECG AF rate 118; eGFR 32; creatinine 145; INR 1.0; LFT normal; Hb 124, platelets 220; TFT normal
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, frusemide, atorvastatin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation choice?

options.text: Rivaroxaban 15 mg daily as the preferred once-daily DOAC in CKD stage 3b to improve adherence and minimise bleed risk
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is acceptable in CKD stage 3 at reduced dose but apixaban has lower renal dependence and lower major bleed risk in this population. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Warfarin to a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 because all DOACs are contraindicated when eGFR is below 50 mL/min
options.rationale: DOACs are permitted across CKD stages 1 to 4 with dose adjustment; apixaban is preferred in CKD stage 3 to 4 because of lowest renal clearance. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Dabigatran 110 mg twice daily as the preferred DOAC in renal impairment because of available reversal with idarucizumab
options.rationale: Dabigatran is 80 percent renally cleared and is contraindicated when eGFR is under 30 and used cautiously between 30 and 50; apixaban remains preferred in CKD. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily (or 2.5 mg twice daily if 2 of 3 dose-reduction criteria are met) as the preferred DOAC in CKD stage 3b
options.rationale: Apixaban has the lowest renal clearance of the DOACs and is preferred in CKD stage 3b; dose reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily only when 2 of 3 criteria met (age 80+, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or above). (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily as monotherapy because anticoagulation carries unacceptable risk in CKD stage 3b regardless of CHA2DS2-VA score
options.rationale: Aspirin monotherapy is not effective stroke prevention in AF and is not recommended; anticoagulation is indicated based on CHA2DS2-VA. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is guided by the CHA2DS2-VA score in Australia (replacing CHA2DS2-VASc, sex no longer a modifier). Score 1 or higher: anticoagulation indicated. DOACs are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF. Choice in CKD: apixaban is preferred in CKD stages 3 to 4 due to lowest renal clearance (27 percent); dabigatran is contraindicated when eGFR is under 30 and used cautiously 30 to 50; rivaroxaban dose-reduced to 15 mg daily for eGFR 15 to 49. Apixaban dose reduces to 2.5 mg twice daily only if 2 of 3 criteria met: age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 or above. Warfarin remains preferred for mechanical valves and significant mitral stenosis.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA score (sex removed) guides anticoagulation
Apixaban preferred in CKD stage 3 to 4
Dabigatran contraindicated eGFR under 30
Apixaban dose reduction: 2 of 3 of age 80+, weight 60 or less, creatinine 133+
explanation.pearls: Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban; for dabigatran, idarucizumab reverses fully within 5 minutes for emergency procedures or major bleeding.

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia management with ECG changes
stem: You are the medicine registrar called to ED to review a 72-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 who presents with weakness and palpitations. He is on ramipril, spironolactone and recently started trimethoprim for a UTI. He has not been able to take his medications today. He has no chest pain. Bloods returned 5 minutes ago. The ED ECG was taken urgently and is in front of you. He is haemodynamically stable. He is not in cardiac arrest.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/72, HR 58 (regular), RR 18, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Generalised weakness, no focal neurology, no cardiac murmur, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: K 7.2 mmol/L, urea 28, creatinine 320, eGFR 16, Na 134, HCO3 17, glucose 6.8; ECG: peaked T waves, widened QRS 132 ms, no P waves
data_table.Medications: Ramipril 10 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, trimethoprim 300 mg (started 3 days ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management sequence?

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g and observe over the next 4 hours before any other intervention or further blood test review
options.rationale: Resin therapy has slow onset (hours) and is inadequate as the sole acute intervention; calcium plus insulin/dextrose are required for ECG changes. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50% dextrose alone; no calcium gluconate because the patient is haemodynamically stable currently
options.rationale: QRS widening on ECG indicates membrane instability and calcium gluconate is the immediate priority; insulin acts via slower potassium redistribution. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes for membrane stabilisation, then insulin/dextrose and salbutamol nebuliser
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with QRS widening is a cardiac emergency; calcium gluconate stabilises the membrane within minutes, followed by insulin/dextrose and salbutamol for intracellular shift, then potassium removal (resin or dialysis) and discontinuation of contributing drugs. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis as the first intervention without calcium gluconate, insulin or salbutamol while waiting for vascular access placement
options.rationale: Dialysis is definitive treatment for hyperkalaemia but takes hours to arrange; immediate calcium and shifters must be given in the interim to protect the myocardium. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)

options.text: Frusemide 80 mg IV bolus to promote kaliuresis as the first-line intervention before considering calcium gluconate or shifting therapy
options.rationale: Loop diuretic effectiveness depends on functional nephrons; in advanced CKD with anuria or oliguria, response is limited and calcium stabilisation is needed first. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 mmol/L or above, or any level with ECG changes) requires staged emergency management. Step 1: cardiac membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes (effect within 3 minutes, lasts 30 to 60 minutes; repeat if ECG changes persist). Step 2: intracellular shift with IV insulin 10 units plus 50 mL 50 percent dextrose (effect 15 to 30 minutes); add nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg as adjunct shifter. Step 3: potassium removal via resin (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, patiromer) or dialysis. Step 4: stop ACE inhibitor, MRA, trimethoprim and other contributing drugs. Underlying acidosis correction with bicarbonate is reserved for metabolic acidosis with pH below 7.2.
key_points: Calcium gluconate stabilises membrane within 3 minutes
Insulin/dextrose and salbutamol shift potassium intracellularly
Resins and dialysis remove potassium
Stop ACEi, MRA, trimethoprim and other contributors
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim blocks the epithelial sodium channel similarly to amiloride, causing hyperkalaemia especially when combined with ACEi or MRA; check potassium within 7 days of starting if on these medications.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition versus cellulitis
stem: You are the medicine registrar called to ED to review a 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who presents with a 36-hour history of escalating left lower limb pain. He noticed redness yesterday after a minor abrasion. The pain has rapidly worsened overnight, out of proportion to the visible erythema. He is now febrile and confused. Examination shows tense oedema, dusky skin discolouration with one violaceous patch, and crepitus on palpation. The team is debating cellulitis versus necrotising fasciitis.

data_table.Examination: Tense oedema entire calf; dusky discolouration with violaceous patch; crepitus on palpation; pain disproportionate to visible erythema; reduced sensation over dusky area
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 (neutrophils 18), CRP 320, sodium 128, glucose 18, creatinine 156, lactate 5.2; venous gas: pH 7.28, lactate 5.2; LRINEC score 9
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; gliclazide 60 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for emergency debridement; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics including clindamycin; aggressive resuscitation
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency; immediate debridement, broad antibiotics with anti-toxin coverage (clindamycin) and aggressive resuscitation reduce mortality; LRINEC 8 or above and pain out of proportion are red flags. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence oral cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours for cellulitis; mark the erythema and review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Oral cellulitis treatment is inappropriate for systemic toxicity, crepitus, dusky skin and disproportionate pain; necrotising fasciitis demands surgical and IV antibiotic emergency response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Administer IV vancomycin alone; defer surgical consultation pending blood culture results to confirm a microbiological diagnosis
options.rationale: Antibiotic alone without surgical debridement does not control necrotising soft tissue infection; surgical exploration is the diagnostic and therapeutic gold standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Order urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the limb and defer empirical antibiotics until imaging confirms fascial involvement
options.rationale: Imaging delays definitive surgical management; clinical suspicion plus LRINEC 8+ mandates immediate surgical consultation regardless of imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Elevate the limb, commence subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin and observe over 6 hours for spread of erythema
options.rationale: Observation in suspected necrotising fasciitis is fatal; hourly progression of fascial necrosis demands immediate surgical exploration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality of 20 to 40 percent. Clinical clues: pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapid progression, dusky or violaceous skin, crepitus, bullae, anaesthesia over the involved area, systemic toxicity. LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; score 6 to 7 raises suspicion, 8 or above is high risk. Management: immediate surgical exploration and debridement, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics with clindamycin (toxin suppression) plus piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem and vancomycin for MRSA cover, aggressive resuscitation, ICU admission. Imaging should not delay surgery.
key_points: Pain out of proportion is the cardinal early sign
LRINEC score: 6-7 suspicion, 8+ high risk
Clindamycin for toxin suppression in addition to broad cover
Imaging must not delay surgical exploration
explanation.pearls: Type II necrotising fasciitis (group A Streptococcus) classically affects healthy patients after minor trauma; type I is polymicrobial in diabetes and surgical sites and includes Fournier gangrene.

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative blockade
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 48-year-old woman with biochemically confirmed phaeochromocytoma (24-hour fractionated metanephrines 8-fold raised, normetanephrines 6-fold raised). Imaging shows a 5 cm right adrenal mass. Surgery is planned in 3 weeks. She has episodes of paroxysmal hypertension, sweating and palpitations. She is on no medications currently. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm 84. She is asking about preoperative preparation. There is no history of asthma. She has heart failure symptoms only with severe episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/94 between paroxysms (peaks to 220/130 during episodes), HR 84, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor; mild orthostatic drop; no abdominal mass palpable; no thyroid mass
data_table.Investigations: 24h fractionated metanephrines 8x ULN; normetanephrines 6x ULN; chromogranin A raised; CT: 5 cm right adrenal heterogeneous mass; MIBG positive
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preoperative management plan?

options.text: Commence atenolol 50 mg daily first for tachycardia control; add phenoxybenzamine in the final 48 hours before surgery only as a brief titration
options.rationale: Starting beta-blocker before alpha blockade removes vasodilatory beta-2 effect and unmasks unopposed alpha vasoconstriction, precipitating severe hypertension and myocardial ischaemia. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Commence oral phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily and titrate over 10 to 14 days; add beta-blocker only after adequate alpha blockade is established
options.rationale: Non-selective alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine) is started first and titrated over 10 to 14 days for adequate vascular volume expansion and symptom control; beta-blocker is added only after alpha blockade is established to avoid unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Proceed directly to laparoscopic adrenalectomy within 7 days without preoperative medical blockade; manage crises with intraoperative nitroprusside
options.rationale: Unblocked surgery causes catastrophic intraoperative haemodynamic instability and mortality; preoperative alpha blockade for 10 to 14 days plus volume expansion is standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Administer captopril 25 mg three times daily as first-line preoperative antihypertensive; reserve alpha blockade for refractory cases only
options.rationale: Catecholamine-driven hypertension responds poorly to ACE inhibitors; alpha blockade with volume expansion is the proven preoperative standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Commence labetalol monotherapy 100 mg twice daily; it provides combined alpha and beta blockade in a single agent without sequencing issues
options.rationale: Labetalol provides only weak alpha blockade relative to beta blockade (alpha to beta ratio approximately 1 to 7 oral), risking the same unopposed alpha effect as pure beta blockers; non-selective alpha blocker first is the standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative blockade requires sequential alpha then beta blockade over 10 to 14 days. Phenoxybenzamine (non-selective, irreversible alpha blocker) is started at 10 mg twice daily and titrated to symptom control, target BP under 130/80 seated and orthostasis. High sodium diet and volume expansion accompany alpha blockade because chronic catecholamine excess depletes intravascular volume. Beta-blocker (propranolol or atenolol) is added only after alpha blockade is established, to control reflex tachycardia. Starting beta-blocker first removes vasodilatory beta-2 tone and unmasks alpha-mediated vasoconstriction, precipitating hypertensive crisis. Labetalol has insufficient alpha component for monotherapy.
key_points: Alpha blockade first for 10 to 14 days
High sodium diet and volume expansion alongside alpha block
Beta-blocker added only after alpha blockade established
Labetalol alpha to beta ratio insufficient for monotherapy
explanation.pearls: Alternative selective alpha-1 blockers (doxazosin, prazosin) are reversible and shorter acting than phenoxybenzamine; intraoperative haemodynamic stability is slightly worse but postoperative hypotension less prolonged.

subtopic_detail: Acute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis decision
stem: You are the medicine registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man brought to ED by ambulance with right-sided weakness and expressive aphasia. His last known well time was 2 hours 30 minutes ago. He is on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, last dose 14 hours ago. He has no recent surgery, no head trauma, no known intracranial pathology and no recent bleed. His NIHSS is 14. Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage and no large established infarct; CTA shows a left middle cerebral artery M1 occlusion.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 172/96, HR 84 (irregular), RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, T 36.6, BSL 6.2
data_table.Examination: Right hemiplegia, expressive aphasia, right facial droop, NIHSS 14, GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT: no haemorrhage, ASPECTS 9; CTA: left M1 occlusion; INR 1.0; FBC, UEC normal; platelets 248
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD (last dose 14 hours ago); perindopril 5 mg; atorvastatin 40 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Administer IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg over 1 hour and proceed to endovascular thrombectomy without delay for the proximal large vessel occlusion
options.rationale: Apixaban use within 48 hours is a contraindication to IV thrombolysis regardless of last dose timing; thrombectomy alone is preferred when thrombolysis is contraindicated. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous heparin infusion targeting an APTT of 60 to 80 seconds and monitor for clinical improvement over the next 4 hours observation
options.rationale: Heparin has no role in acute ischaemic stroke reperfusion and increases haemorrhagic transformation risk; mechanical thrombectomy is the indicated reperfusion strategy. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

options.text: Reverse apixaban with andexanet alfa and then administer IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus; defer thrombectomy until thrombolysis is complete
options.rationale: Routine pre-thrombolysis DOAC reversal with andexanet is not recommended due to rebound thrombosis risk; mechanical thrombectomy is the preferred reperfusion strategy. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

options.text: Administer aspirin 300 mg orally and admit to stroke unit; defer mechanical thrombectomy because the time window has been exceeded for reperfusion
options.rationale: Mechanical thrombectomy time window extends to 6 hours from onset and up to 24 hours with perfusion imaging selection; this patient at 2.5 hours qualifies; aspirin alone forfeits proven reperfusion benefit. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

options.text: Withhold thrombolysis due to DOAC use within 48 hours; proceed directly to endovascular thrombectomy for the proven large vessel occlusion
options.rationale: DOAC within 48 hours is a contraindication to thrombolysis but does not preclude mechanical thrombectomy, which is the standard of care for proximal MCA occlusion within 6 hours (and up to 24 hours with imaging selection). (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke reperfusion is governed by time window and contraindications. IV thrombolysis (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg) is offered within 4.5 hours of onset. DOAC use within 48 hours contraindicates thrombolysis unless DOAC level is undetectable or reversed. Mechanical thrombectomy is offered for proven large vessel occlusion (ICA, M1, basilar) within 6 hours of onset, extending to 24 hours with favourable perfusion imaging (DAWN, DEFUSE-3 criteria). DOAC use does not contraindicate thrombectomy. BP target before thrombolysis is under 185/110 and during the first 24 hours under 180/105.
key_points: DOAC within 48 hours contraindicates thrombolysis
DOAC does NOT contraindicate mechanical thrombectomy
Thrombectomy window 6 hours, up to 24 hours with imaging
BP target under 185/110 pre-thrombolysis
explanation.pearls: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus is non-inferior to alteplase for stroke thrombolysis with simpler administration; Australian centres are increasingly switching to tenecteplase as first-line.

subtopic_detail: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis empiric therapy
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old man with two weeks of fever, malaise, anorexia and night sweats. He had a mechanical mitral valve replacement eight months ago for rheumatic mitral regurgitation. On examination he is febrile, looks unwell and has a new pansystolic murmur at the apex that was not documented at his recent valve clinic visit four weeks ago. There are no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. He has no penicillin allergy. Blood cultures have been drawn from two separate sites and are pending.

data_table.Examination: New pansystolic murmur loudest at apex; clear lungs; no peripheral oedema; no splinter haemorrhages or Janeway lesions on inspection
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14, CRP 180, creatinine 95, lactate 1.4; transthoracic echocardiogram shows 8 mm vegetation on prosthetic mitral valve with mild paravalvular regurgitation
data_table.Medications: Warfarin INR target 2.5 to 3.5; bisoprolol 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin combination tailored to streptococcal and enterococcal native valve coverage with no anti-staphylococcal cover
options.rationale: Native valve regimens do not cover the staphylococcal pathogens prevalent in early prosthetic valve endocarditis; vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin combined with gentamicin and oral rifampicin to cover the staphylococcal pathogens of early prosthetic valve endocarditis
options.rationale: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (under 12 months from surgery) is most often Staphylococcus epidermidis or aureus; vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin is the empirical regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy for streptococcus viridans cover until blood culture sensitivities return to guide narrower targeted treatment
options.rationale: Streptococcus viridans is uncommon in early prosthetic valve endocarditis; staphylococcal coverage with vancomycin plus aminoglycoside plus rifampicin is the empirical standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin monotherapy without combination synergy or rifampicin while awaiting blood culture sensitivities and surgical team discussion next day
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy is inadequate for prosthetic valve endocarditis; combination therapy with aminoglycoside synergy and rifampicin biofilm penetration is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Defer empirical antibiotics until two further blood cultures and serology have returned to ensure narrowest appropriate spectrum based on confirmed organism identification
options.rationale: Empirical therapy starts immediately after blood cultures drawn; deferring antibiotics in confirmed endocarditis risks valve destruction, embolic phenomena and septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis is defined as occurring within 12 months of valve surgery and is typically caused by staphylococcal organisms (Staph epidermidis, Staph aureus) acquired perioperatively. Empirical therapy is intravenous vancomycin plus gentamicin plus oral rifampicin pending blood culture results. Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites are drawn before antibiotics. Transthoracic echocardiogram is the initial imaging; transoesophageal echocardiogram is more sensitive for prosthetic vegetations and paravalvular abscess. Cardiothoracic surgical review is mandatory for prosthetic valve endocarditis to assess surgical indications including heart failure, persistent bacteraemia, large vegetations and paravalvular complications.
key_points: Early PVE under 12 months: empirical vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin
Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
TOE more sensitive than TTE for prosthetic vegetations
Cardiothoracic surgical review mandatory
explanation.pearls: Surgical indications in PVE include heart failure, paravalvular extension or abscess, persistent bacteraemia after 5 to 7 days appropriate antibiotics, fungal infection and embolic events with persistent vegetation above 10 mm.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective endocarditis

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis non-severe oral therapy
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 24-year-old non-pregnant woman with 24 hours of fever, right loin pain and dysuria. She has been able to tolerate oral fluids without vomiting and remains haemodynamically stable. She has no past medical history, no allergies, no recent antibiotics and no urological abnormality. She is sexually active and her partner has no symptoms. Urinalysis shows leucocyte esterase strongly positive, nitrites positive and microscopic haematuria. Midstream urine has been sent for culture and sensitivity.

data_table.Examination: Right costovertebral angle tenderness; abdomen otherwise soft; well perfused; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis leucocyte++, nitrite+, blood+; serum lactate 1.4; creatinine 70, eGFR above 90; urine pregnancy test negative
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for three days as standard short-course empirical treatment for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection therapy
options.rationale: Three-day trimethoprim is for uncomplicated cystitis; pyelonephritis requires longer course and an agent with better renal tissue penetration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for five days, which is the preferred narrow-spectrum agent for upper urinary tract infection in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate renal tissue concentrations and is contraindicated in pyelonephritis; it is reserved for lower tract infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily for 14 days through ambulatory care intravenous service even in haemodynamically stable patients tolerating oral fluids
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy is reserved for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, urological abnormality or failure of oral therapy; oral cefalexin is appropriate here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days with follow up at 48 hours to confirm clinical and biochemical improvement on therapy
options.rationale: Acute pyelonephritis in a haemodynamically stable patient tolerating oral intake is treated with oral cefalexin for 10 days with 48-hour clinical review; uropathogen susceptibility is usually adequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Wait for the midstream urine culture sensitivity report before commencing any antibiotic to avoid inappropriate empirical therapy and selection of resistance
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are started immediately after MSU collection in confirmed pyelonephritis to limit renal damage and sepsis progression; sensitivity guides any subsequent narrowing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis is fever, loin pain and lower urinary tract symptoms with evidence of urinary infection. The most common pathogen is E. coli, followed by Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus and Staph saprophyticus. Empirical oral therapy in non-pregnant, haemodynamically stable patients tolerating oral intake is cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days, or amoxicillin-clavulanate. Intravenous therapy (gentamicin plus ampicillin or ceftriaxone) is reserved for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, urological abnormality or failure of oral therapy. Review at 48 hours to confirm clinical improvement and switch to culture-directed therapy.
key_points: Oral cefalexin 500 mg QID for 10 days non-severe pyelonephritis
IV ceftriaxone or gentamicin plus ampicillin for severe or vomiting
Nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim short course only for cystitis
MSU before antibiotics; review at 48 hours
explanation.pearls: An ultrasound or CT kidneys is indicated for pyelonephritis failing to improve within 72 hours, recurrent episodes or any features of obstruction such as oliffuse such as oliguria or worsening loin pain with antibiotic therapy.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Urinary tract infection

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome prevention
stem: You are the general medical registrar admitting a 65-year-old man with alcohol use disorder who has not eaten for five days, drinking only fortified wine. He has lost 15 percent of his body weight over the past three months. He looks cachectic with temporal wasting. He is alert and orientated and his observations are stable. The nutrition team has asked you to write the initial refeeding plan and electrolyte replacement orders before any oral or enteral nutrition is commenced on the ward today.

data_table.Examination: Cachectic with temporal wasting; soft abdomen; no peripheral oedema; alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2, magnesium 0.65, phosphate 0.75, sodium 138, glucose 4.2, albumin 28, INR 1.2
data_table.Medications: Nil regular on admission; pabrinex prescribed pending decision on timing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding plan?

options.text: Give intravenous thiamine, correct potassium, magnesium and phosphate, then commence nutrition at 10 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring and slow titration
options.rationale: High refeeding risk requires thiamine before carbohydrates, proactive electrolyte replacement, slow 10 kcal/kg/day caloric initiation and daily monitoring to prevent cardiac and neurological complications. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

options.text: Commence a standard 1500 kilocalorie oral diet immediately and replace electrolytes only if levels fall below the laboratory reference range during ward observation
options.rationale: Standard caloric load triggers refeeding syndrome in high-risk patients; calories must start at 10 kcal/kg/day with proactive electrolyte and thiamine replacement first. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

options.text: Use 10 percent dextrose intravenously as the sole nutritional source for the first 72 hours and defer enteral feeding until biochemistry has fully normalised after admission
options.rationale: High-carbohydrate intravenous dextrose without thiamine precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy and refeeding hypophosphataemia; enteral or oral is preferred with parallel electrolyte support. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and run full-strength polymeric feed at 80 mL per hour from day one to meet his estimated full caloric requirement immediately on the ward
options.rationale: Full-rate feeding in high refeeding risk overwhelms intracellular shifts and precipitates cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure and seizures; rate must start at 10 kcal/kg/day. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

options.text: Defer all nutrition for a further five days while focusing solely on alcohol withdrawal management and hydration before any oral or enteral feeding plan is restarted
options.rationale: Extending starvation worsens nutritional deficits without addressing refeeding risk; the correct approach is cautious early nutrition with electrolyte and thiamine support. (Source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate reintroduction in chronically starved patients triggers intracellular shifts of potassium, magnesium and phosphate, precipitating cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure, seizures and Wernicke encephalopathy. High-risk criteria include BMI under 16, weight loss over 15 percent in three months, little nutrition for over 10 days, low potassium, phosphate or magnesium pre-feeding. Management is parenteral thiamine 200 to 300 mg before any glucose, proactive electrolyte replacement, slow caloric initiation at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day with stepwise increase over 4 to 7 days, and daily biochemistry monitoring.
key_points: Thiamine 200 to 300 mg IV before carbohydrate refeeding
Start nutrition at 10 kcal/kg/day in high-risk patients
Replace potassium, magnesium and phosphate proactively
Daily electrolytes until stable for at least one week
explanation.pearls: Pabrinex (B and C vitamins) intravenous two pairs three times daily for 5 days is the Australian first-line for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy and prophylaxis prior to refeeding in chronic alcohol misuse.

sources.label: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: Nutrition support in adults

subtopic_detail: Cushing's syndrome first-line screening
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with a six-month history of progressive central weight gain, easy bruising on the forearms, proximal muscle weakness on standing from a chair, and new-onset hypertension requiring two antihypertensive medications. She has facial plethora and purple abdominal striae 1.5 cm wide. She has no exogenous corticosteroid use confirmed on pharmacy records. She takes no medications likely to affect cortisol metabolism. She is keen to know what tests will confirm or exclude hypercortisolism today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/96 on two agents, HR 80, weight 92 kg, BMI 33
data_table.Examination: Moon facies; supraclavicular fat pad; purple striae over abdomen and thighs; proximal weakness in hip flexion grade 4/5
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 7.2 percent, fasting glucose 8.1; FBC and UEC unremarkable; ACTH and a.m. cortisol not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily; amlodipine 5 mg daily; nil corticosteroids confirmed by pharmacy record

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line screening test?

options.text: Random midday serum cortisol drawn during the next clinic visit as the initial screening test before considering further dynamic investigations of the axis
options.rationale: Random cortisol reflects pulsatile secretion and does not detect loss of diurnal rhythm or cortisol excess; it is not a recommended screening test for Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

options.text: Serum adrenocorticotrophic hormone level at 09:00 as the single first-line test that distinguishes ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent forms of Cushing syndrome
options.rationale: ACTH measurement differentiates ACTH-dependent from independent causes but only after hypercortisolism is confirmed; it is not a first-line screen for hypercortisolism. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

options.text: Late-night salivary cortisol on two consecutive nights collected at home with point-of-collection swabs and laboratory cortisol measurement on the samples
options.rationale: Late-night salivary cortisol detects loss of diurnal nadir characteristic of Cushing syndrome and is one of three recommended first-line screening tests with high sensitivity and specificity. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland with gadolinium contrast performed prior to any biochemical screening to identify a pituitary corticotroph adenoma
options.rationale: Pituitary MRI is reserved for confirmed ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism; pre-biochemistry imaging detects incidentalomas in 10 percent of normal people and misleads workup. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

options.text: Insulin tolerance test performed in the endocrine day-stay unit as the first-line dynamic screening method to assess hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis function
options.rationale: Insulin tolerance test assesses ACTH reserve for adrenal insufficiency; it is not used to screen for Cushing syndrome and carries hypoglycaemia risk. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome screening uses three recommended first-line tests, any of which can be chosen depending on patient circumstances: late-night salivary cortisol (collected at home, very sensitive for loss of diurnal nadir), 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol under 50 nmol/L at 08:00 the morning after a 23:00 dose excludes), and 24-hour urinary free cortisol (above three times upper limit of normal is diagnostic). Two abnormal screens are usually required before confirming hypercortisolism. ACTH measurement and dynamic testing (high-dose dexamethasone suppression, CRH stimulation, inferior petrosal sinus sampling) come after confirmed hypercortisolism to localise the source.
key_points: Three first-line screens: salivary cortisol, 1 mg DST, 24-hour UFC
Two abnormal screens needed to confirm hypercortisolism
ACTH differentiates pituitary, ectopic and adrenal sources after confirmation
Pituitary imaging only after ACTH-dependent confirmed
explanation.pearls: Cyclical Cushing syndrome causes intermittent biochemistry; repeat screening is often required over weeks and a single normal late-night salivary cortisol does not exclude when clinical suspicion is high.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis of Cushing syndrome

subtopic_detail: Primary aldosteronism confirmatory testing
stem: You are the medical registrar in the hypertension clinic reviewing a 38-year-old man with three-drug resistant hypertension and persistent hypokalaemia despite oral potassium replacement. His aldosterone to renin ratio screening test taken in the morning after his usual antihypertensives were optimised to non-interfering agents has returned strongly positive. He has no headaches, palpitations or sweating. CT of the adrenal glands has not yet been arranged and he is keen to know what comes next before any imaging or surgical opinion is sought.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/100 on three drugs, HR 76, BMI 28, no orthostatic drop
data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination unremarkable; no abdominal bruit; no Cushingoid features; reflexes brisk symmetric
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.1 (on supplements 40 mmol daily), sodium 142, creatinine 80; aldosterone:renin ratio 110 (normal under 30); morning aldosterone 720 pmol/L, plasma renin 6.5 mU/L
data_table.Medications: Doxazosin 4 mg daily; verapamil 240 mg daily; hydralazine 50 mg three times daily; potassium chloride 40 mmol daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Proceed directly to CT scan of the adrenal glands today to identify a unilateral adenoma before any confirmatory dynamic biochemical testing has been completed
options.rationale: CT is performed after biochemical confirmation; incidentalomas occur in 4 to 8 percent of adults and CT cannot distinguish functioning aldosterone-producing adenoma from non-functioning incidentaloma. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Refer immediately for adrenal vein sampling for lateralisation of aldosterone secretion before any dynamic confirmation of autonomous aldosterone production is undertaken
options.rationale: AVS is reserved for confirmed primary aldosteronism in surgical candidates after biochemical confirmation; performing it before confirmation risks unnecessary invasive testing. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Commence empirical spironolactone 100 mg daily as therapeutic confirmation without further biochemical or radiological investigation in this resistant hypertension setting
options.rationale: Empirical mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism without confirmation misses the opportunity for curative unilateral adrenalectomy in lateralised disease and risks side effects. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Repeat the aldosterone:renin ratio test in three months on the same medications without confirmation testing and review the trend before any further escalation occurs
options.rationale: A clearly positive ARR with biochemical features warrants confirmatory testing rather than repeat screening; delays diagnosis and risks ongoing cardiovascular damage. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Perform saline suppression testing under medical supervision in the day-stay unit to confirm autonomous aldosterone secretion before any imaging or surgical consultation
options.rationale: Confirmatory dynamic testing such as saline suppression, oral salt loading, fludrocortisone suppression or captopril challenge is performed after positive ARR before imaging or adrenal vein sampling. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is the most common secondary cause of hypertension, present in 5 to 10 percent of all hypertensive patients and up to 20 percent of resistant hypertension. Screening uses morning aldosterone to renin ratio after switching to non-interfering antihypertensives (verapamil, hydralazine, doxazosin, prazosin). Positive ARR requires confirmation by one of four dynamic tests (saline suppression, oral salt loading, fludrocortisone suppression, captopril challenge) before subtyping. CT adrenals plus adrenal vein sampling for lateralisation are performed after biochemical confirmation in surgical candidates under 35 with unilateral adenoma on CT or in any patient considering adrenalectomy.
key_points: Confirm ARR with saline or salt loading suppression before imaging
Spironolactone or eplerenone for bilateral or non-surgical disease
Adrenal vein sampling for lateralisation before adrenalectomy
Switch to non-interfering antihypertensives before ARR screen
explanation.pearls: Adrenal vein sampling for primary aldosteronism is operator-dependent and requires cortisol-corrected aldosterone ratios above 4 between sides to confirm lateralisation; centres with low procedural volume should refer.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary aldosteronism

subtopic_detail: Apixaban major intracerebral haemorrhage reversal
stem: You are the medical registrar called to ED to assess a 78-year-old woman on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation who has presented with three hours of sudden headache, right hemiparesis and reduced consciousness following a fall at home. CT brain shows a 28 mL left basal ganglia haemorrhage with intraventricular extension. Her last apixaban dose was four hours ago according to her dosette. She has no current anti-fibrinolytic or platelet inhibitor in addition to her DOAC. Her renal function is stable from clinic two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 178/102, HR 78, RR 18, SpO2 96 percent RA, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Right hemiparesis 2/5; right facial droop; dysarthria; left pupil 3 mm reactive; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: CT 28 mL left basal ganglia haemorrhage with intraventricular extension; INR 1.1; APTT 38; creatinine 90 (eGFR 56); Hb 124; platelets 220
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily; metoprolol 25 mg twice daily; rosuvastatin 20 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal agent?

options.text: Intravenous idarucizumab 5 g given as two consecutive 2.5 g boluses as the targeted reversal antibody binding the active anticoagulant directly in the circulation
options.rationale: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor); it has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban or rivaroxaban. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

options.text: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 25 to 50 units/kg intravenously as the reversal option when andexanet alfa is unavailable in the local hospital
options.rationale: Andexanet alfa is the specific factor Xa inhibitor reversal agent but where unavailable, 4-factor PCC 25 to 50 units/kg is the recommended option for apixaban or rivaroxaban major bleeding. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg intravenously combined with fresh frozen plasma four units transfused over four hours through a peripheral large-bore intravenous access
options.rationale: Vitamin K and FFP reverse warfarin not DOACs; vitamin K has no role in factor Xa inhibitor reversal and FFP volume causes harm without correcting coagulopathy. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

options.text: Protamine sulfate 50 mg intravenously over 10 minutes administered as the recommended reversal agent for any factor Xa inhibitor major bleeding presentation
options.rationale: Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin and partially reverses LMWH; it has no role in DOAC reversal and is not indicated in apixaban bleeding. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g orally via nasogastric tube after intubation as the sole intervention to reduce ongoing absorption of the most recent apixaban dose
options.rationale: Charcoal is reserved for DOAC ingestion within two hours of dose and is adjunctive only; with last dose four hours ago and ICH, primary therapy is haemostatic reversal. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

explanation.summary: Apixaban and rivaroxaban are direct factor Xa inhibitors. In major bleeding (intracranial, retroperitoneal, severe gastrointestinal or any with haemodynamic compromise) the specific reversal agent is andexanet alfa (recombinant decoy factor Xa) given as a bolus and infusion. Where andexanet is unavailable, 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate at 25 to 50 units/kg is the recommended alternative based on observational and limited randomised evidence. Activated charcoal 50 g is given if the last dose was within 2 hours. Tranexamic acid may be added for mucosal bleeding. Dabigatran reversal is specifically idarucizumab. Warfarin is reversed with intravenous vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC.
key_points: Apixaban or rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa, then 4F-PCC if unavailable
Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g as two 2.5 g boluses
Warfarin: vitamin K 10 mg IV plus 4F-PCC 25 to 50 units/kg
Charcoal only if DOAC dose within 2 hours
explanation.pearls: Apixaban-specific calibrated anti-Xa activity assay can quantify drug effect when available; standard APTT and INR are insensitive to therapeutic apixaban concentrations.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Reversal of anticoagulants

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 bundle in septic shock
stem: A 68-year-old man is brought to your emergency department from his nursing home with 24 hours of fevers, confusion and reduced oral intake. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and previously had a transurethral prostatectomy. On arrival he is hypotensive, tachycardic, and confused. He is unable to provide a coherent history. The triage nurse has placed two large-bore peripheral cannulas. You are the ED registrar leading the resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, BP 88/52, HR 118, RR 26, SpO2 92 percent RA, GCS 13 (E3V4M6)
data_table.Examination: Confused, mottled lower limbs, mild suprapubic tenderness; chest clear; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Bedside lactate 4.2 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.30, bicarbonate 17; finger-prick glucose 11.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin, tamsulosin

lead_in: Within the first hour, what is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Obtain blood cultures, administer 30 mL/kg crystalloid, and commence empiric intravenous antibiotics only once culture results return
options.rationale: Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics, but antibiotics must not wait for results; in septic shock each hour of delay increases mortality 7-8 percent. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; ANZICS)

options.text: Obtain blood and urine cultures, give empiric intravenous antibiotics within an hour, administer 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, and recheck lactate at 2 hours
options.rationale: The hour-1 bundle for septic shock includes lactate measurement, blood and other cultures before antibiotics (without delaying antibiotics), empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 or higher, and lactate re-check. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence peripheral noradrenaline infusion without initial fluid resuscitation given the hypotension and rising lactate today
