options.rationale: Vasopressors are second-line after fluid resuscitation; peripheral noradrenaline is acceptable when refractory but not as initial intervention. (Source: Surviving Sepsis)

options.text: Administer a 1 L crystalloid fluid challenge and reassess the need for intravenous antibiotics only after blood pressure normalises
options.rationale: A 1 L challenge is inadequate; ANZICS and Surviving Sepsis recommend 30 mL/kg within 3 hours. Antibiotics must not be deferred until BP normalises. (Source: ANZICS)

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter for source control, perform CT abdomen pelvis, and commence antibiotics only after imaging confirms the source
options.rationale: Source control imaging is important but must not delay early antibiotics; bedside catheterisation can occur alongside but does not replace empiric therapy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Sepsis with septic shock requires the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle: measure lactate (remeasure if elevated), obtain blood cultures before antibiotics (do not delay antibiotics), administer broad-spectrum empiric IV antibiotics, give 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 or higher, and start vasopressors if MAP stays below 65 after fluid. Likely urinary source here (nursing home, suprapubic tenderness, prior prostatic surgery) justifies empirically piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin in line with eTG. Antibiotic timing is the single largest modifiable mortality factor.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors if needed
Each hour of antibiotic delay raises septic shock mortality 7-8 percent
30 mL/kg crystalloid not 1 L
Cultures before antibiotics but never delay antibiotics
explanation.pearls: Lactate over 4 mmol/L on presentation has an associated in-hospital mortality around 27 percent for sepsis even when blood pressure normalises after fluid; serial lactate trend at 2 hours is a stronger prognostic indicator than the initial value.

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic regimen in IVDU native valve IE
stem: A 38-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 2 weeks of fevers, night sweats, and weight loss. He uses intravenous heroin and admits to recent injecting through the femoral vein. Examination shows a new pansystolic murmur loudest at the lower left sternal edge, splinter haemorrhages on two fingernails, and bilateral basal crackles. You suspect infective endocarditis and are awaiting an urgent transthoracic echocardiogram. Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites have been drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, BP 110/72, HR 108, RR 22, SpO2 94 percent RA
data_table.Examination: New PSM 3/6 at LLSE, splinter haemorrhages, JVP elevated 5 cm, bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4 (neutrophils 14.2), CRP 220, Hb 102, platelets 145, creatinine 95; ECG sinus tachycardia; CXR pulmonary congestion with small bilateral effusions; troponin 24 (mildly raised); blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin alone pending culture results and consideration of surgical management
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin alone is inadequate for an intravenous drug user where S. aureus is most likely (over 60 percent of right-sided IE); broader gram-positive coverage including flucloxacillin or vancomycin is required. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate while awaiting echocardiogram and definitive blood culture results
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are not appropriate for empiric IE coverage; intravenous is mandatory. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin plus intravenous gentamicin pending culture results and echocardiogram
options.rationale: For native valve IE in an intravenous drug user, eTG recommends empiric IV flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly plus gentamicin (single daily dosing per renal function) to cover S. aureus and streptococcal species pending culture results; vancomycin substitutes if penicillin-allergic or MRSA likely. (Source: eTG Antibiotic; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone alone with no additional empirical gram-positive coverage at this stage
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone alone misses MSSA at usual doses and does not provide adequate cover for the most likely organism. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin alone with no additional empirical gram-negative coverage at this stage
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy is reserved for confirmed MRSA or penicillin allergy; gram-negative cover via gentamicin enhances activity against streptococci and provides synergy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Suspected infective endocarditis warrants empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics after three sets of blood cultures from separate venepunctures. In a native valve IE with intravenous drug use, S. aureus is the dominant pathogen; empiric flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is first-line per Australian guidelines. Vancomycin replaces flucloxacillin if MRSA suspected (recent hospitalisation, known colonisation, severe penicillin allergy). Duke criteria are applied for diagnostic categorisation. Echocardiography (TTE then TOE if non-diagnostic) is essential and surgical referral is needed for valve perforation, heart failure, persistent bacteraemia, or large vegetations.
key_points: IVDU plus new murmur plus fevers = S. aureus dominant pathogen
Empiric: IV flucloxacillin plus gentamicin
Vancomycin if MRSA risk or penicillin allergy
Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
explanation.pearls: Tricuspid valve IE in intravenous drug users frequently presents with septic pulmonary emboli and bilateral cavitating lung infiltrates rather than left-sided heart failure; CT chest should be considered when there is hypoxia even with a normal initial CXR.

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barre syndrome first-line immunotherapy
stem: A 42-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 5 days of progressive bilateral leg weakness that started in his calves and has ascended to his thighs. He now reports tingling in both hands. He had a brief gastroenteritis illness 2 weeks ago. On examination he has symmetric proximal and distal leg weakness 3/5, areflexia in lower limbs and reduced upper-limb reflexes. He can still walk slowly with assistance. Forced vital capacity is 28 mL/kg. Sensation is intact.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78, HR 88, RR 18, SpO2 99 percent RA, T 36.8, FVC 28 mL/kg
data_table.Examination: Symmetric flaccid lower limb weakness 3/5; areflexia LL; reduced UL reflexes; no bulbar signs; no autonomic features yet
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal; UEC normal; CK 220; CSF protein 1.4 g/L, WCC 2 x10^6/L; nerve conduction studies show demyelinating pattern; MRI spine pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line disease-modifying treatment?

options.text: High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days as initial immunomodulation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no proven benefit in Guillain-Barre syndrome; large meta-analyses show no improvement and possible harm. (Source: Cochrane)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily with proton pump inhibitor cover and slow taper over 12 weeks
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroids are not effective in GBS; do not use. (Source: Cochrane)

options.text: Therapeutic plasma exchange as the most cost-effective Australian first-line treatment for this presentation
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is an alternative first-line therapy with similar efficacy to IVIG but is logistically more demanding and less commonly available outside tertiary neurology centres; IVIG is the preferred Australian first-line in most settings. (Source: NBA; BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 consecutive days targeting a total dose of 2 g/kg
options.rationale: IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (total 2 g/kg) is the Australian first-line treatment for GBS within 4 weeks of symptom onset, particularly when patients are non-ambulant or worsening. Plasma exchange is an equivalent alternative when available. (Source: NBA; BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Pyridostigmine 30 mg every 6 hours with regular cardiopulmonary monitoring during titration
options.rationale: Pyridostigmine is for myasthenia gravis; GBS is a neuromuscular junction-independent demyelinating polyneuropathy. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy classically presenting with ascending symmetrical weakness, areflexia, and CSF albuminocytological dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count). Most cases follow a triggering infection (Campylobacter jejuni is the commonest). FVC less than 20 mL/kg, bulbar weakness, or rapid progression triggers ICU admission. First-line therapies are IVIG 2 g/kg total over 5 days or therapeutic plasma exchange; both are equally efficacious. Corticosteroids are not effective. Treatment is most beneficial within 4 weeks of onset and when patients are unable to walk independently.
key_points: Ascending weakness + areflexia + CSF protein high with normal WCC = GBS
IVIG and plasma exchange are equal first-line
Corticosteroids are NOT effective
Monitor FVC, bulbar function and autonomic status for ICU triggers
explanation.pearls: A 20-30 percent fall in forced vital capacity over 24 hours, or absolute FVC below 20 mL/kg, are objective triggers for ICU admission and elective intubation in Guillain-Barre syndrome; do not wait for desaturation.

subtopic_detail: Intravenous iron when oral fails with time-limited surgical window
stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to your GP clinic with 3 months of fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. She has heavy menstrual bleeding for 18 months, takes ibuprofen frequently for dysmenorrhoea, and has tried oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily for the past 8 weeks. She reports nausea and constipation on the oral iron and intermittent adherence. Her gynaecologist has referred her for endometrial ablation but the procedure is 6 weeks away.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae; no koilonychia; cardiovascular and respiratory examinations normal; mild ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 70 fL, ferritin 8 mcg/L, transferrin saturation 7 percent, CRP 4; UEC normal; LFTs normal; coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue oral ferrous sulfate for another 12 weeks and recheck full blood count then
options.rationale: Oral iron intolerance and ongoing menstrual loss limit oral repletion success; continuing oral iron is unlikely to achieve correction before scheduled surgery. (Source: BloodSafe; eTG)

options.text: Switch to oral iron polymaltose complex 100 mg daily and review tolerance after 4 weeks
options.rationale: Polymaltose is sometimes better tolerated but still requires months to correct severe iron deficiency anaemia with ongoing losses; not suitable for the 6-week timeframe. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Arrange packed red cell transfusion of 2 units to correct the anaemia rapidly before surgery
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia (typically Hb below 70 or acute decompensation); not indicated for stable Hb 88 with time for IV iron correction. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Commence erythropoietin-stimulating agent subcutaneously 4-weekly until ferritin normalises
options.rationale: ESAs are not first-line in iron deficiency anaemia; they require adequate iron stores to be effective and are reserved for chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy-related anaemia. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Arrange intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg infusion at the general practice infusion clinic
options.rationale: Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg single infusion is appropriate when oral iron is ineffective, not tolerated, or where rapid repletion is required (within 8 weeks); reticulocyte response begins within 5-7 days and Hb rises 20-30 g/L by 4 weeks. (Source: AMH; NBA; BloodSafe)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia from ongoing menstrual loss with oral iron failure and a time-limited surgical window is a clear indication for parenteral iron in Australia. Ferric carboxymaltose is the preferred IV iron preparation (single infusion up to 1000 mg over 15 minutes, repeat at 1 week if larger replacement needed). Common adverse effects include hypophosphataemia, infusion-site reactions, and transient skin pigmentation. PBS-subsidised for documented iron deficiency where oral iron has failed or is contraindicated. Address ongoing source (menorrhagia management) in parallel.
key_points: IV iron when oral fails, not tolerated, or rapid repletion needed
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg as single infusion is Australian preferred
Treat the source: tranexamic acid, hormonal management, surgical option
Recheck Hb and ferritin 4-8 weeks after infusion
explanation.pearls: Severe symptomatic hypophosphataemia (phosphate below 0.32 mmol/L) occurs in around 1-3 percent of patients receiving ferric carboxymaltose with bone pain, fatigue and proximal weakness, typically peaking at 2 weeks - check phosphate if symptoms appear at follow-up.

subtopic_detail: Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms
stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to your ED with 2 weeks of new bilateral temporal headache and 2 days of intermittent transient monocular vision loss in the right eye lasting a few minutes each episode. She has 3 weeks of jaw claudication. She was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica 6 months ago and is on prednisolone 5 mg daily. She has no diplopia and no focal neurological deficit. Fundoscopy is normal.

data_table.Examination: Tender thickened right temporal artery; reduced pulsation; visual acuity 6/6 both eyes; pupils equal reactive; visual fields intact at this moment; tongue normal
data_table.Investigations: ESR 110 mm/hr, CRP 96 mg/L; Hb 108, platelets 412; LFTs ALP mildly raised at 142; UEC normal; CT brain normal; carotid Doppler arranged
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone 5 mg daily; metformin; atorvastatin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 14 days
options.rationale: Visual symptoms (amaurosis fugax) in suspected giant cell arteritis mandate immediate high-dose IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days to prevent permanent vision loss; temporal artery biopsy within 7-14 days remains positive despite steroids. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

options.text: Defer steroid escalation until the temporal artery biopsy result is available to avoid masking diagnosis
options.rationale: Delaying steroids until biopsy risks permanent vision loss within hours to days; biopsy positivity remains adequate for 7-14 days after starting steroids. (Source: ARA)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

options.text: Increase oral prednisolone to 40 mg daily and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 4 weeks at the next available slot
options.rationale: 40 mg oral prednisolone is appropriate for non-visual GCA, but visual symptoms warrant IV pulses for the first 3 days. (Source: ARA)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

options.text: Commence aspirin 100 mg daily without altering current prednisolone, and refer to ophthalmology outpatients
options.rationale: Aspirin is adjunctive; alone it does not address the inflammatory mechanism and risk of permanent visual loss is unaddressed. (Source: ARA)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

options.text: Arrange ultrasound of the temporal arteries as the sole confirmatory test and treat empirically based on the ultrasound alone
options.rationale: Temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) has high specificity in expert hands but biopsy remains gold standard in Australia; do not delay treatment for either investigation. (Source: ARA)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement

explanation.summary: Giant cell arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis of older adults presenting with new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual symptoms. Permanent visual loss occurs in 15-30 percent of untreated cases. Australian Rheumatology Association guidelines specify pulsed IV methylprednisolone for visual involvement, oral prednisolone 40-60 mg daily for non-visual disease, with temporal artery biopsy within 7-14 days retaining sensitivity. Adjunctive low-dose aspirin reduces cerebrovascular events. Long-term tocilizumab is steroid-sparing for relapsing GCA. PMR co-occurs in 40-50 percent.
key_points: Visual symptoms - IV methylpred pulses; non-visual - oral prednisolone 40-60 mg
Biopsy within 7-14 days of starting steroids remains diagnostic
ESR and CRP not specific; clinical diagnosis takes priority
Aspirin adjunct; tocilizumab steroid-sparing
explanation.pearls: Bilateral temporal artery biopsy increases yield by 5-10 percent over unilateral but a single 1-2 cm specimen is usually sufficient; skip lesions limit shorter biopsies, so insist on at least 1 cm of artery in the sample.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association (ARA) GCA position statement
BMJ Best Practice: Giant Cell Arteritis

subtopic_detail: Acute adrenal crisis management in primary adrenal insufficiency
stem: A 58-year-old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency presents to your ED with 24 hours of fever, vomiting, abdominal pain and lethargy. She has not been able to take her usual hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg evening due to vomiting. She has type 1 diabetes, hypothyroidism, and a daughter with coeliac disease. She is hypotensive, drowsy and warm peripherally.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, BP 78/45, HR 122, RR 24, SpO2 96 percent RA, GCS 13 (E3V4M6), BSL 3.2 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Hyperpigmented skin and buccal mucosa, dry mucous membranes, soft non-peritonitic abdomen with mild epigastric tenderness; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Na 124, K 5.8, glucose 3.2; creatinine 110 (baseline 70); CRP 84; lactate 3.2; FBC WCC 14.0; cortisol pending; urine ketones positive; CXR clear
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20/10, fludrocortisone 100 mcg, levothyroxine, insulin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold steroids until a random cortisol level is back to confirm the diagnosis before commencing therapy
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis; treatment must not await laboratory confirmation; mortality rises sharply with each hour of delay. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus intravenous 0.9 percent saline 1 L bolus and supplemental dextrose
options.rationale: Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat (then 50 mg 6-hourly or 200 mg/24h infusion), 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 1 hour, and dextrose for hypoglycaemia are the cornerstones of adrenal crisis management. Hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and modest mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: ESA; AMH)

options.text: Administer prednisolone 50 mg via nasogastric tube and commence intravenous saline once the prednisolone is absorbed
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone is unreliable when the patient is vomiting and has potentially impaired gut absorption; IV access is mandatory. (Source: ESA)

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg stat because it does not interfere with subsequent cortisol assay sampling
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is acceptable if hydrocortisone unavailable, but lacks mineralocorticoid activity needed for hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia in primary adrenal crisis. (Source: ESA)

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion centrally before any glucocorticoid replacement to support blood pressure
options.rationale: Vasopressors are second-line if hypotension persists after steroid replacement and fluid resuscitation; replacing the missing hormone treats the cause. (Source: ESA)

explanation.summary: Acute adrenal crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock unresponsive to fluid alone. Mortality is around 1 in 200 per patient-year despite known diagnosis and stress-dose education. Management is immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, followed by 200 mg/24h infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours, plus IV saline and dextrose. Investigate precipitant (infection commonest), continue stress doses until oral tolerated, then halve daily until baseline. All patients with adrenal insufficiency should have a Medic Alert bracelet and emergency hydrocortisone for self-injection.
key_points: Adrenal crisis: hypotension + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia
Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, do not wait for cortisol result
Saline 1 L stat, dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Investigate precipitant (infection most common)
explanation.pearls: Patients with adrenal insufficiency on long-term hydrocortisone must double or triple their daily dose during acute illness or fever above 38 degrees, and switch to IM hydrocortisone 100 mg self-injection for any vomiting episode lasting more than 1 hour - failure to do so is the commonest precipitant of crisis.

subtopic_detail: Migraine prophylaxis with pregnancy planning
stem: A 36-year-old woman presents to your GP clinic for migraine prevention. She has had migraine with aura for 12 years, currently 6 attacks per month each lasting 8-12 hours. She had reasonable benefit from propranolol 40 mg twice daily for 3 months (cutting frequency to 3 per month) but stopped 4 weeks ago after fainting once during a 5 km run and developing exertional bradycardia. She has well-controlled asthma on Symbicort. She is planning pregnancy in the next 12 months.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination including fundi; no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Recent thyroid normal; ECG sinus bradycardia 52 bpm without QT prolongation; FBC normal; pregnancy test negative
data_table.Medications: Stopped propranolol 4 weeks ago; using sumatriptan 50 mg PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next preventive treatment?

options.text: Restart propranolol at a reduced dose of 20 mg twice daily and recommend avoidance of strenuous exercise altogether
options.rationale: Propranolol is contraindicated by recurrent symptomatic bradycardia and risk in asthma; restart is not appropriate. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Commence amitriptyline 25 mg nocte with explicit anti-cholinergic side effect counselling before her planned conception
options.rationale: Amitriptyline is reasonable for migraine plus tension-type headache, but topiramate has stronger evidence as monotherapy; both require pregnancy planning discussion. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as an effective and well-tolerated long-term preventive option
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential because of teratogenicity (neural tube defects 1-2 percent and developmental delay) and requires the Pregnancy Prevention Programme; not appropriate when pregnancy is planned. (Source: AMH; TGA)

options.text: Commence topiramate 25 mg nocte with planned titration to 50 mg twice daily and pregnancy counselling
options.rationale: Topiramate is first-line preventive for migraine with aura, evidence-based for 50 percent or more reduction in frequency; teratogenicity (oral cleft, low birth weight) requires effective contraception and discontinuation 4-6 weeks before planned conception. (Source: AMH; eTG Neurology)

options.text: Commence verapamil 80 mg three times daily as an effective option for migraine with aura prevention
options.rationale: Verapamil is for cluster headache prophylaxis, not migraine; not indicated here. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Migraine prophylaxis is considered for 4 or more attacks per month or significant disability. First-line agents in Australia include propranolol (avoid in asthma, bradycardia), candesartan (good pregnancy profile), topiramate (teratogenic - oral cleft risk), amitriptyline, and sodium valproate (avoid in women of childbearing potential). Newer CGRP-monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) are PBS-restricted to refractory cases with failed 3 prior preventives. Treatment is reviewed at 3 months. Acute attacks treated with triptans or NSAIDs.
key_points: Migraine prevention if 4 or more per month or disabling
First-line AU: propranolol, candesartan, topiramate, amitriptyline
Valproate banned in women of childbearing age (PPP TGA)
Topiramate teratogenic; counsel pre-conception
explanation.pearls: Candesartan 16 mg daily has emerging evidence as a first-line migraine preventive with the best pregnancy compatibility (taper before conception), suiting women planning pregnancy who cannot tolerate propranolol; effect onset is 6-8 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes and trimethoprim trigger
stem: A 67-year-old man presents to your ED with palpitations and weakness for 12 hours. He has stage 4 CKD (baseline eGFR 22), heart failure with reduced EF, and type 2 diabetes. He takes ramipril 10 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, frusemide 40 mg, and metformin. He was recently started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI. Triage ECG shows tall peaked T waves and widening QRS.

data_table.Examination: Mild peripheral oedema; chest with bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: K 7.2 mmol/L, Na 138, urea 18, creatinine 320 (baseline 220), bicarbonate 18, glucose 6.4; VBG pH 7.30; ECG: tall peaked T waves V2-V6, QRS 132 ms, no P waves visible

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first step?

options.text: Administer intravenous insulin 10 units in 50 percent dextrose 50 mL to shift potassium intracellularly
options.rationale: Insulin and dextrose are appropriate but second after membrane stabilisation; insulin lowers K by 0.5-1.2 mmol/L over 30 minutes, acts within 15 minutes. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)

options.text: Administer salbutamol 10 mg nebulised over 10 minutes to shift potassium intracellularly via beta-2 receptors
options.rationale: Salbutamol shifts K but acts more slowly and unreliably than insulin; appropriate as additional shift therapy after membrane stabilisation. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes to shift potassium intracellularly
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for severe metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia and is not the first-line membrane stabiliser. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2-5 minutes to stabilise the myocardial membrane
options.rationale: With ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS, loss of P waves) and K above 6.0 mmol/L, immediate IV calcium stabilises the myocardial membrane within 1-3 minutes (lasts 30-60 minutes), buying time for K-shifting and elimination therapies. (Source: KHA-CARI; ANZCOR)

options.text: Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g orally as the most effective first measure for total body potassium
options.rationale: Polystyrene sulfonate has slow onset (hours), questionable efficacy, and risk of bowel necrosis; not for acute severe hyperkalaemia. (Source: AMH; TGA Safety Alert)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (K above 6.0 mmol/L) with ECG changes is a medical emergency. Management has three phases: membrane stabilisation (IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2-5 min, immediate effect, lasts 30-60 min, repeat if ECG changes persist), potassium shift (insulin plus dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate if acidotic), and elimination (loop diuretic, dialysis if oligoanuric or refractory). Identify and reverse the trigger: ACE inhibitors, MR antagonists, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, beta-blockers, renal failure, tumour lysis. In this patient, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the likely added precipitant.
key_points: K above 6.0 with ECG changes = emergency
Membrane stabilisation FIRST: IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL
Then K-shift: insulin plus dextrose, salbutamol
Identify trigger (trimethoprim, ACEi, K-sparing diuretic, AKI)
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim blocks the renal epithelial sodium channel similar to amiloride and can raise serum K by 1-2 mmol/L within days of starting in CKD patients on ACEi or spironolactone - always check K within 7-10 days of any new trimethoprim prescription in CKD.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic choice for moderate COPD exacerbation in ED
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department with a 68-year-old man presenting with 48 hours of worsening dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, and sputum purulence on a background of GOLD stage 3 COPD. He has had 2 exacerbations in the last year. He takes a long acting bronchodilator and inhaled corticosteroid daily. He has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.2, HR 102, RR 24, SpO2 88 percent on air rising to 92 percent on 2 L/min nasal prongs, BP 138/82
data_table.Examination: Bilateral wheeze, accessory muscle use, no focal consolidation
data_table.Investigations: ABG on 2 L pH 7.36, PaCO2 50, PaO2 70, HCO3 28; CXR no consolidation; CRP 38; FBC normal
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium plus formoterol budesonide combined inhaler daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and treat with prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days alone given absence of fever
options.rationale: Three Anthonisen criteria (dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence) support antibiotic use even in the absence of fever. (Source: Lung Foundation COPD-X)

options.text: Oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 5 days alongside oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Azithromycin is reserved for penicillin-allergic patients due to AU macrolide resistance patterns in Streptococcus pneumoniae. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin clavulanate 875 plus 125 mg twice daily for 5 days alongside oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Clavulanate is reserved for failed first-line therapy or risk factors for resistance; routine first-line is amoxicillin alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 5 days alongside oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Moxifloxacin is reserved for failed first-line therapy or specific resistance; routine use is discouraged due to QT and tendinopathy risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days alongside oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days
options.rationale: AU first-line for moderate exacerbation is amoxicillin for 5 days plus prednisolone 5 days; the combination reduces treatment failure and hospital readmission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: AU practice treats COPD exacerbation with three Anthonisen criteria with amoxicillin first-line for 5 days plus prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days. Doxycycline is an alternative when penicillin is not tolerated. Amoxicillin clavulanate or fluoroquinolones are reserved for failed first-line therapy, severe exacerbation requiring hospitalisation, or risk factors for resistance. Oxygen target in established COPD is SpO2 88 to 92 percent to avoid worsening hypercapnia.
key_points: Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS 5 days plus prednisolone 50 mg 5 days
Doxycycline alternative for penicillin allergy
SpO2 target 88 to 92 percent in COPD
Reserve clavulanate or fluoroquinolone for failure
explanation.pearls: Eosinophil count over 0.3 x10^9/L during exacerbation predicts steroid responsiveness and a lower threshold to use systemic corticosteroids.

subtopic_detail: Occupational HIV postexposure prophylaxis timing and regimen
stem: You are the staff health registrar reviewing a 28-year-old nurse 2 hours after a deep needlestick injury from a hollow bore needle used on a patient who is HIV positive on antiretroviral therapy with a viral load over 50000 copies/mL. The nurse has no chronic illness and is currently well. The source patient is also hepatitis B and C negative.

data_table.Examination: Wound puncture to right index finger; no active bleeding now
data_table.Investigations: Baseline HIV antibody pending; baseline UEC, LFTs, FBC, beta-hCG normal; hepatitis B antibody titre 120 IU/L; source HIV viral load over 50000, hepatitis B and C negative
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive; baseline HIV testing in progress

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a 28 day course of tenofovir disoproxil emtricitabine plus dolutegravir as recommended PEP within 72 hours of exposure
options.rationale: AU PEP guidance recommends a 3 drug regimen of TDF/FTC plus dolutegravir for 28 days starting within 72 hours of high-risk exposure. (Source: ASHM PEP Guidelines)

options.text: Defer PEP until source patient viral load is confirmed below 200 copies/mL by repeat testing within 24 hours
options.rationale: PEP is initiated immediately for high-risk exposure and not delayed for further source testing when initial viral load is detectable. (Source: ASHM)

options.text: Start a 28 day course of zidovudine plus lamivudine as the recommended dual NRTI backbone in AU guidance
options.rationale: Zidovudine has been superseded by tenofovir-based regimens in current AU PEP guidance due to tolerability and efficacy. (Source: ASHM)

options.text: Provide written advice on signs of seroconversion without antiretroviral prophylaxis given the use of source antiretroviral therapy
options.rationale: Use of antiretroviral therapy in a source with detectable high viral load does not eliminate transmission risk; PEP remains indicated. (Source: ASHM)

options.text: Test source for HIV drug resistance before commencing any antiretroviral postexposure prophylaxis regimen
options.rationale: Resistance testing should not delay PEP initiation; modification can be made if resistance is later identified. (Source: ASHM)

explanation.summary: Occupational HIV postexposure prophylaxis is recommended for high-risk exposures including deep injury from a hollow bore needle in a source with detectable HIV. The AU first-line regimen is tenofovir disoproxil plus emtricitabine plus dolutegravir for 28 days. PEP should commence within 72 hours and ideally within 2 hours of exposure. Baseline HIV, hepatitis B and C, and pregnancy testing are arranged with repeat HIV testing at 6 weeks and 3 months. Source resistance can guide regimen changes during the 28 day course.
key_points: Start PEP within 72 hours of high-risk exposure
First-line: tenofovir DF plus emtricitabine plus dolutegravir for 28 days
Follow-up HIV testing at 6 weeks and 3 months
Hepatitis B booster if antibody under 10 IU/L
explanation.pearls: Bictegravir based fixed dose regimens are increasingly used in AU PEP due to single tablet dosing and excellent tolerability; dolutegravir plus tenofovir emtricitabine remains widely available first-line.

subtopic_detail: BP reduction target and agent in hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage
stem: You are the medical registrar in ED reviewing a 58-year-old man with severe headache, blurred vision, and acute breathlessness over 6 hours. His BP is 232/132 with no prior diagnosis of hypertension. He has bibasal crackles, a third heart sound, troponin elevation, and pulmonary oedema on chest X-ray.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 232/132, HR 118, RR 30, SpO2 92 percent on 4 L/min
data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, S3, raised JVP, no focal neurology, fundi show flame haemorrhages and papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, LV strain pattern; CXR pulmonary oedema; troponin 0.18 (upper limit 0.04); creatinine 142; urinalysis 2+ protein; CT brain unremarkable
data_table.Medications: Nil regular; today: IV furosemide 80 mg and nitrate sublingual given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial BP reduction strategy?

options.text: Withhold further antihypertensive therapy until troponin trend confirms or excludes acute myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Hypertensive pulmonary oedema with troponin rise mandates immediate BP reduction; waiting for troponin trend delays critical therapy. (Source: NHF)

options.text: Reduce systolic BP to under 140 within the first hour with rapid bolus dosing of intravenous antihypertensive agents
options.rationale: Rapid normalisation in hypertensive emergency risks watershed cerebral infarction and acute kidney injury; controlled stepwise reduction is recommended. (Source: NHF)

options.text: Reduce systolic BP to under 100 over the next 4 hours using sodium nitroprusside at high titration step infusion
options.rationale: Over-reduction to systolic under 100 risks watershed ischaemia; goal is staged reduction not normalisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Start oral amlodipine 10 mg now and reassess at 1 hour expecting a stepwise reduction over the next 6 hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy is too slow and unpredictable in true hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage; IV titratable agents are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Reduce mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25 percent over the first hour using an intravenous agent then aim 160/100 over the next several hours
options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage other than ischaemic stroke is treated with controlled MAP reduction of 20 to 25 percent in the first hour to balance perfusion and tissue protection. (Source: NHF Hypertension; Therapeutic Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is defined by severe BP elevation with acute end-organ damage including encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema, acute coronary syndrome, AKI, or papilloedema. Controlled BP reduction targets a 20 to 25 percent fall in MAP in the first hour, then 160/100 over several hours, with normalisation over 24 to 48 hours. Agents used in pulmonary oedema include IV glyceryl trinitrate; in aortic dissection, esmolol then sodium nitroprusside or labetalol; in eclampsia, hydralazine or labetalol. Ischaemic stroke has its own permissive hypertension targets.
key_points: MAP reduction 20-25 percent in first hour
Normalisation over 24-48 hours not minutes
GTN for pulmonary oedema; esmolol then SNP for dissection
Aim 160/100 over the next several hours
explanation.pearls: In acute ischaemic stroke, do not lower BP unless above 220/120 (or above 185/110 if thrombolysis planned), as cerebral autoregulation is impaired and over-reduction worsens infarction.

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 bundle interventions in septic shock from urinary source
stem: You are the medical registrar called to the ward at 23 minutes after midnight to assess a 74-year-old woman day 1 admission for pyelonephritis. She has rigors, mottling, and altered mental state. Initial empirical antibiotics for pyelonephritis were given 3 hours ago but her condition has deteriorated.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2, HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 94 percent on 4 L/min, BP 78/42
data_table.Examination: Mottled peripheries, cool, confused (GCS 13), right flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: VBG lactate 4.8 pH 7.28 BE -8; WCC 21, neutrophils 18; CRP 280; creatinine 162 (baseline 78); urinalysis 4+ leucocytes, 3+ nitrites; blood cultures taken on admission and now
data_table.Medications: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily started 3 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next set of immediate interventions in the first hour from recognition of septic shock?

options.text: Crystalloid 10 mL/kg bolus and reassess; defer antibiotic broadening until repeat blood culture results are available tomorrow
options.rationale: 10 mL/kg is below the 30 mL/kg hour-1 target and antibiotic escalation should be considered immediately with rapid clinical deterioration. (Source: SSC)

options.text: Crystalloid 30 mL/kg bolus over the first hour, repeat blood cultures and lactate, broaden antibiotics, start vasopressor for MAP under 65
options.rationale: The hour-1 bundle for septic shock includes 30 mL/kg crystalloid, lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and vasopressors for refractory hypotension. (Source: SSC Guidelines; CEC NSW Sepsis)

options.text: Transfer to ICU for invasive line placement before any fluid or antibiotic action is taken now on the ward
options.rationale: Hour-1 interventions begin where the patient is recognised; ICU transfer must not delay fluid, antibiotics, or vasopressors. (Source: CEC NSW Sepsis)

options.text: Administer hydrocortisone 200 mg IV before fluid bolus as first step in shock from any source in older adults
options.rationale: Steroids in septic shock are reserved for refractory shock on adequate vasopressor support not as first-line therapy. (Source: SSC)

options.text: Start noradrenaline infusion immediately as first step before any fluid resuscitation in the setting of MAP under 65
options.rationale: Concurrent fluid resuscitation should occur with vasopressor commencement; vasopressor alone without fluid does not address hypovolaemia. (Source: SSC)

explanation.summary: The hour-1 bundle for sepsis and septic shock comprises measure lactate and remeasure if elevated, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4, and noradrenaline for MAP under 65 mmHg despite fluid resuscitation. Source control is sought as soon as feasible. Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV is added for refractory septic shock requiring escalating vasopressor support.
key_points: 30 mL/kg crystalloid in first hour for hypotension or lactate over 4
Blood cultures before antibiotics where possible
Noradrenaline first-line vasopressor for MAP under 65
Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV daily for refractory septic shock
explanation.pearls: Beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside is appropriate empirical cover in adult Australian community pyelonephritis with septic shock when local E. coli ESBL rates are above 10 percent.

subtopic_detail: Identifying the underlying mechanism of metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia
stem: You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 56-year-old woman with resistant hypertension despite three agents who has been intermittently using furosemide tablets sourced from her sister. She presents with weakness and muscle cramps over 1 week. She is normovolaemic on examination. She denies vomiting, laxative use, or recent diarrhoea.

data_table.Examination: Normal volume status, no oedema, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Na 138, K 2.6, Cl 88, HCO3 36, urea 6.8, creatinine 78; ABG pH 7.52 PaCO2 49 HCO3 36; urine chloride 32 mmol/L; urine sodium 64; renin and aldosterone pending
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, and intermittent furosemide

lead_in: What is the most likely mechanism contributing to her metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia?

options.text: Primary hyperaldosteronism with autonomous adrenal aldosterone production driving the entire biochemical picture
options.rationale: Primary hyperaldosteronism is possible and is being investigated but the urinary chloride rise during current diuretic use is most directly explained by diuretic effect. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Diuretic induced chloride and potassium loss producing a saline responsive chloride low metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: Loop and thiazide diuretics produce urinary chloride and potassium loss with secondary metabolic alkalosis; urine chloride may be elevated during active use. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Surreptitious vomiting with gastric acid loss producing chloride low metabolic alkalosis with low urine chloride
options.rationale: Vomiting produces low urine chloride below 20 mmol/L; this patient has urine chloride of 32 mmol/L during diuretic use. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Bartter syndrome with congenital tubular dysfunction producing chronic chloride and potassium losses
options.rationale: Bartter syndrome usually presents earlier in life and is associated with normal blood pressure; this presentation is acquired and hypertensive. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Acute respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation accounting for the elevated bicarbonate and PaCO2
options.rationale: The pH of 7.52 indicates alkalosis not acidosis; the elevated PaCO2 is respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis. (Source: KHA-CARI)

explanation.summary: Metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia is classified by urine chloride into saline responsive (low urine chloride from vomiting or post-diuretic state) and saline unresponsive (high urine chloride from current diuretic use, hyperaldosteronism, or Bartter and Gitelman syndromes). Surreptitious diuretic use produces a confusing biochemical picture mimicking primary hyperaldosteronism; the clue is variable urine chloride that falls when diuretics are stopped. Definitive workup includes urine diuretic screen, plasma renin, and aldosterone with aldosterone renin ratio.
key_points: Low urine chloride: vomiting or post-diuretic effect
High urine chloride: current diuretic, hyperaldosteronism, Bartter/Gitelman
Hyperaldosteronism workup with ARR after diuretic cessation
Replace potassium and magnesium together
explanation.pearls: Urine diuretic screen for thiazide and loop diuretics is a reliable test for surreptitious diuretic use and should be considered when biochemistry mimics primary hyperaldosteronism.

subtopic_detail: Induction therapy choice for newly diagnosed ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal involvement
stem: You are the general medical registrar admitting a 62-year-old man with 6 weeks of weight loss, sinusitis with crusting, haemoptysis, and progressive renal impairment over 3 weeks. He has no infection and is haemodynamically stable. ANCA testing is strongly positive for PR3. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis. He has a stable haemoglobin and no requirement for dialysis at present.

data_table.Examination: Nasal crusting; bilateral basal crackles; lower limb purpura sparse
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 320 (baseline 90), eGFR 18, urine red cell casts; PR3-ANCA strongly positive; chest CT pulmonary nodules; renal biopsy crescentic GN
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction regimen?

options.text: Azathioprine plus oral prednisolone as the initial induction regimen with cyclophosphamide reserved for relapse only
options.rationale: Azathioprine is a maintenance agent; it is not effective for induction in AAV which requires rituximab or cyclophosphamide. (Source: KDIGO)

options.text: Plasma exchange alone as primary induction therapy when renal involvement and pulmonary haemorrhage are present
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is an adjunct in selected severe disease and does not replace immunosuppressive induction. (Source: KDIGO)

options.text: Pulse methylprednisolone monotherapy at 1 g IV daily for 3 days as adequate induction therapy in renal involvement
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy is inadequate induction; B cell depletion or cyclophosphamide is required to reduce flare and end stage kidney disease. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Rituximab plus high dose glucocorticoid as induction therapy with rapid steroid tapering protocol over the next several months
options.rationale: Rituximab plus high dose glucocorticoid is at least equivalent to cyclophosphamide for induction in ANCA-associated vasculitis including renal disease and is increasingly preferred in AU. (Source: KHA-CARI; KDIGO Glomerular Disease)

options.text: Mycophenolate mofetil plus oral prednisolone as the recommended first-line induction therapy in PR3 positive AAV
options.rationale: Mycophenolate is less effective than rituximab or cyclophosphamide for AAV induction and is not first-line in PR3 disease. (Source: KDIGO)

explanation.summary: ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal involvement is induced with rituximab plus high dose glucocorticoid or cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoid. Rituximab is at least as effective as cyclophosphamide and is preferred for relapsing disease, women of reproductive age, and patients at high infection risk. Plasma exchange is reserved for severe pulmonary haemorrhage or rapidly progressive AKI. Maintenance is typically rituximab or azathioprine with a steroid taper; PJP prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole is recommended during prolonged immunosuppression.
key_points: Rituximab plus glucocorticoid first-line induction
Cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoid alternative induction
Plasma exchange for severe pulmonary haemorrhage
PJP prophylaxis during prolonged immunosuppression
explanation.pearls: PEXIVAS trial supports a reduced dose glucocorticoid regimen with similar efficacy and lower serious infection risk; AU practice is moving away from the historical high-dose taper.

subtopic_detail: Correction rate in chronic hyponatraemia with mild neurological symptoms
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 72-year-old woman with 2 weeks of progressive nausea, gait unsteadiness, and a fall today. She has been on a thiazide for 6 months and recently started taking sertraline 2 weeks ago. She has no seizure, no severe headache, and remains alert. She is clinically euvolaemic and well hydrated.

data_table.Examination: Alert, ataxic gait, no focal neurology, euvolaemic mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Na 116, K 3.6, urea 4.2, creatinine 78, glucose 5.4, TSH normal, cortisol AM 320; urine osmolality 480, urine sodium 64, plasma osmolality 248
data_table.Medications: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; sertraline 50 mg daily (started 2 weeks ago); calcium and vitamin D

lead_in: What is the most appropriate correction strategy over the next 24 hours?

options.text: Aim to raise serum sodium by 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first 6 hours then no more than 10 mmol/L over 24 hours with frequent reassessment
options.rationale: Chronic hyponatraemia with mild neurology is corrected at a controlled rate of 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first 6 hours and under 10 mmol/L per day to prevent osmotic demyelination. (Source: KHA-CARI; Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Restrict fluids to 800 mL daily without changing existing medications and reassess sodium tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Fluid restriction alone is insufficient in a symptomatic patient and the offending medications should be ceased. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Start hypertonic saline infusion targeting a serum sodium rise of 1 to 2 mmol/L per hour throughout the next 12 hours
options.rationale: Continuous 1 to 2 mmol/L per hour rise overshoots the safe 24 hour limit and risks osmotic demyelination. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Aim to normalise serum sodium to over 135 mmol/L within the first 24 hours using 3 percent hypertonic saline boluses
options.rationale: Rapid full correction risks osmotic demyelination; cautious rate-limited correction is the standard. (Source: KHA-CARI)

options.text: Withhold all fluid replacement and observe with hourly neurological assessment for the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Active correction is required in symptomatic hyponatraemia; observation alone does not address the cerebral oedema risk. (Source: KHA-CARI)

explanation.summary: Chronic hyponatraemia is corrected slowly at 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first 6 hours and under 10 mmol/L over 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Severely symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or coma is treated with bolus 3 percent saline 150 mL until symptoms resolve. Cessation of offending agents (thiazide, SSRI) and management of underlying SIADH with fluid restriction follow. Serum sodium is checked every 2 to 4 hours during active correction.
key_points: Chronic: under 10 mmol/L per 24 hours, 4 to 6 in first 6 hours
Severely symptomatic: 150 mL 3 percent saline boluses
Cease thiazide and SSRI; rule out adrenal and thyroid causes
Overcorrection risks osmotic demyelination
explanation.pearls: If sodium has risen over 8 mmol/L in 24 hours during correction, dextrose 5 percent at 6 mL/kg over 2 hours or DDAVP 2 to 4 micrograms IV can re-lower sodium to prevent osmotic demyelination.

subtopic_detail: Preoperative pharmacological preparation for phaeochromocytoma
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar planning preoperative care for a 48-year-old woman with confirmed adrenal phaeochromocytoma on biochemistry (24 hour fractionated metanephrines 5 times upper limit) and a 5 cm right adrenal mass on CT. She has episodic headache, palpitations, and sweating. Her resting BP is 158/92 with paroxysms to 220/120. She has had no cardiac events and her echocardiogram shows normal LV function.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/92 with paroxysms to 220/120; HR 90 baseline, 130 during paroxysm
data_table.Examination: No tremor at rest; no thyroid enlargement; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: 24 hour fractionated metanephrines 5 times upper limit; CT adrenal 5 cm right mass; ECG sinus rhythm; echocardiogram normal
data_table.Medications: Nil regular cardiovascular medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step in preoperative preparation?

options.text: Commence phenoxybenzamine and titrate over 2 to 3 weeks before introducing a beta blocker if tachycardia persists
options.rationale: Alpha blockade is established before any beta blocker introduction in phaeochromocytoma to prevent unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis. (Source: AU Endocrine Society; Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Commence amlodipine 5 mg daily as a calcium channel blocker first-line before considering more specific therapy
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are second-line adjunct after established alpha blockade; not first-line preoperative preparation. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

options.text: Proceed to surgical resection within the next week without further pharmacological preoperative preparation today
options.rationale: Adequate alpha blockade for at least 10 to 14 days reduces intraoperative haemodynamic instability and morbidity. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

options.text: Commence labetalol 100 mg twice daily as a combined alpha and beta blocker for outpatient preoperative preparation
options.rationale: Labetalol provides predominantly beta blockade and is not recommended as first-line for preoperative phaeochromocytoma preparation. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

options.text: Commence atenolol 50 mg daily first to control the resting tachycardia and add alpha blocker if BP control is incomplete
options.rationale: Unopposed alpha stimulation after beta blockade can precipitate hypertensive crisis in phaeochromocytoma. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

explanation.summary: Preoperative preparation for phaeochromocytoma uses alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin for at least 10 to 14 days before surgery. Beta blockade is introduced only after alpha blockade is established if reflex tachycardia or arrhythmia occurs. Liberal sodium intake and adequate hydration in the days before surgery prevent post-resection hypotension. Calcium channel blockers can be used as adjuncts. Genetic counselling is considered for SDHB and other heritable syndromes especially in younger patients or extra-adrenal disease.
key_points: Alpha blockade first then beta if needed
10 to 14 days minimum alpha blockade preop
Liberal salt and hydration to prevent post-op hypotension
Genetic counselling for younger or extra-adrenal disease
explanation.pearls: Persistent post-resection hypotension may require IV crystalloid plus noradrenaline due to abrupt loss of catecholamine drive; preoperative volume expansion reduces this risk.

subtopic_detail: Differentiating ectopic ACTH from pituitary Cushing disease using dynamic and imaging tests
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 51-year-old man with 8 weeks of rapidly progressive proximal weakness, central weight gain, refractory hypokalaemia, glucose intolerance, and now bilateral lower limb oedema. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history. His skin is hyperpigmented but he has no thin skin or purple striae. Initial screening confirms ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. He has commenced ketoconazole while workup proceeds.

data_table.Examination: Central adiposity; hyperpigmentation of palmar creases; bilateral oedema; no abdominal striae
data_table.Investigations: 24 hour urine cortisol 5 times upper limit; midnight salivary cortisol elevated; ACTH 280 (normal under 50); 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression: cortisol 980 (under 50 percent suppression); pituitary MRI no adenoma; CT chest 18 mm left lower lobe nodule; potassium 2.6 on supplementation
data_table.Medications: Ketoconazole 200 mg twice daily; potassium chloride 600 mg twice daily; perindopril 10 mg daily

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours ectopic ACTH syndrome rather than pituitary Cushing disease as the cause?

options.text: Absence of a visible pituitary lesion on MRI of the sella reliably rules out pituitary Cushing disease entirely
options.rationale: Up to 40 percent of pituitary Cushing adenomas are below MRI resolution; absent MRI lesion does not exclude pituitary disease. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

options.text: Hyperpigmentation of palmar creases without other findings is itself diagnostic of ectopic ACTH syndrome in adults
options.rationale: Hyperpigmentation is seen in any ACTH-dependent state including severe pituitary Cushing disease and is not specifically discriminating. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

options.text: A 24 hour urine cortisol level of more than 4 times the upper limit reliably distinguishes ectopic from pituitary disease
options.rationale: Magnitude of urine cortisol elevation overlaps between aetiologies and is not a discriminating test. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

options.text: Failure of cortisol to suppress below 50 percent after high dose dexamethasone in combination with marked hypokalaemia and rapid onset
options.rationale: Failure to suppress on 8 mg dexamethasone, severe hypokalaemia from cortisol-mediated mineralocorticoid effect, and rapid onset are typical of ectopic ACTH rather than pituitary disease. (Source: AU Endocrine Society Cushing; KDIGO)

options.text: ACTH level over 100 picograms/mL is itself characteristic of pituitary Cushing rather than ectopic ACTH syndrome
options.rationale: Higher ACTH levels typically favour ectopic ACTH; pituitary Cushing more often produces moderate ACTH elevation. (Source: AU Endocrine Society)

explanation.summary: Discrimination of ectopic ACTH from pituitary Cushing disease relies on the high dose dexamethasone suppression test, CRH stimulation, ACTH magnitude, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling when imaging is inconclusive. Ectopic ACTH typically does not suppress on high dose dexamethasone, presents with marked hypokalaemia from cortisol mineralocorticoid effect, and progresses rapidly. Pituitary Cushing usually suppresses by over 50 percent on high dose dexamethasone, has a more indolent course, and is amenable to transsphenoidal surgery. Small cell lung cancer and bronchial carcinoid are common ectopic sources. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is the gold standard discriminator when biochemistry and imaging conflict.
key_points: Ectopic ACTH: no suppression on 8 mg dexamethasone, severe hypokalaemia, rapid onset
Pituitary Cushing: over 50 percent suppression on 8 mg dexamethasone
MRI misses up to 40 percent of pituitary microadenomas
IPSS is the gold standard when discrimination is unclear
explanation.pearls: Ketoconazole, metyrapone, and osilodrostat are used to control cortisol while definitive treatment is planned; etomidate infusion is the rapid parenteral option for severe Cushing crisis.

subtopic_detail: First-line imaging for suspected ureteric calculus in adult with single haematuria episode
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 40-year-old man with acute left flank pain radiating to the groin, microscopic haematuria, and no fever. He has no prior stone history. His eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m2 and bedside ultrasound shows mild left hydronephrosis. He is otherwise well, normotensive, and tolerating oral fluids.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 92, RR 18, BP 124/76, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Left flank tenderness, no rebound, no palpable mass, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 2+ blood, no nitrites, no leucocytes; WCC 8.6; eGFR 88; bedside US mild left hydronephrosis
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line definitive imaging?

options.text: Plain KUB film alone, sufficient to confirm a radiopaque calculus and guide initial treatment now
options.rationale: Plain KUB misses about 30 percent of stones and underestimates obstruction; CT KUB has replaced it for first-line workup. (Source: USANZ; RANZCR)

options.text: Magnetic resonance urogram, providing accurate stone detection without any ionising radiation exposure
options.rationale: MR urogram has limited stone visualisation, restricted availability, and high cost; CT KUB is first-line. (Source: USANZ)

options.text: Intravenous urogram with contrast, providing functional and anatomical imaging in a single examination
options.rationale: IVU is largely superseded by CT KUB for stones because of higher contrast dose and lower sensitivity. (Source: USANZ)

options.text: Repeat formal radiology renal ultrasound with full bladder views and Doppler resistive index measurement
options.rationale: Ultrasound is useful in pregnancy and children but has lower sensitivity for ureteric stones in adults. (Source: USANZ)

options.text: Non-contrast low-dose CT KUB, the first-line investigation for adult suspected ureteric calculus disease
options.rationale: Non-contrast low-dose CT KUB is the first-line imaging in adults with suspected ureteric calculus with sensitivity over 95 percent. (Source: USANZ; RANZCR)

explanation.summary: Non-contrast low-dose CT KUB is the first-line investigation for adult suspected ureteric calculus, providing high sensitivity and specificity, stone characterisation, and assessment of complications. Ultrasound is the preferred first investigation in pregnancy and children to reduce radiation. Indications for urgent urology referral include obstructed infected system, single functioning kidney, bilateral obstruction, refractory pain or vomiting, and acute kidney injury. Stones less than 5 mm typically pass spontaneously.
key_points: CT KUB is first-line imaging in adults
Ultrasound preferred in pregnancy and paediatrics
Urology if obstructed-infected, AKI, solitary kidney, or refractory symptoms
Stones under 5 mm usually pass spontaneously
explanation.pearls: Low-dose CT KUB protocols deliver effective dose around 2 mSv compared with 8 to 10 mSv for standard CT, which has driven its adoption as first-line over IVU in the past decade.

subtopic_detail: First-line pharmacotherapy for newly diagnosed trigeminal neuralgia in 58-year-old woman
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 58-year-old woman with two months of brief electric shock pains in the right cheek triggered by chewing and brushing teeth. Episodes last seconds and resolve completely between attacks. She has no facial numbness, no weakness, and a normal neurological examination. She has no liver disease, normal renal function, and no allergy to anticonvulsants. MRI brain reported as no demyelination and a normal trigeminal nerve.

data_table.Examination: Trigger zone right cheek to light touch, no sensory deficit, normal corneal reflex, normal jaw jerk
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: no demyelination, no vascular loop on trigeminal nerve; LFTs ALT 22; eGFR 90; Na 138
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no Asian heritage HLA-B*1502 risk; no allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Gabapentin 300 mg three times daily titrated up over two weeks against pain and sedation tolerance
options.rationale: Gabapentin is a second-line agent in trigeminal neuralgia; carbamazepine has the best evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg at night titrated upwards as needed for trigeminal neuralgia symptomatic relief
options.rationale: Amitriptyline is used for other neuropathic pain but is not first-line for trigeminal neuralgia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Carbamazepine 100 mg twice daily titrated up against symptoms with sodium and LFT monitoring
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is the first-line evidence-based agent for trigeminal neuralgia with sodium and LFT monitoring during titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Oral paracetamol modified release 1330 mg three times daily as the first-line analgesic regimen
options.rationale: Simple analgesics are ineffective in trigeminal neuralgia which is neuropathic; sodium channel blockers are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for microvascular decompression surgery before any pharmacological trial as definitive treatment
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for medication failure or intolerance; pharmacotherapy is first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterised by brief electric shock pains in the trigeminal distribution triggered by light touch or chewing. Carbamazepine is the first-line evidence-based agent with response rates around 70 percent. Oxcarbazepine is an alternative with fewer drug interactions. Baclofen and lamotrigine are add-on options. Surgical options including microvascular decompression are reserved for medication failure or intolerance. Patients of Han Chinese, Thai, and other South Asian descent require HLA-B*1502 testing before carbamazepine due to risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
key_points: Carbamazepine first-line with 70 percent response
Monitor sodium and LFTs during titration
HLA-B*1502 testing in at-risk ancestry
Surgery reserved for medication failure
explanation.pearls: Carbamazepine response in trigeminal neuralgia is so reliable that lack of response within four weeks at adequate dose should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis or MRI for secondary causes such as a vascular loop or demyelination.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic confirmation manoeuvre and treatment for posterior canal BPPV in 62-year-old
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 62-year-old man with three weeks of brief positional vertigo on rolling over in bed and looking up. Episodes last around 30 seconds, resolve completely, and are accompanied by nausea. He has no hearing loss, no tinnitus, no continuous unsteadiness, and no neurological deficit. His cervical spine has no rotational restriction and he has no significant carotid disease.

data_table.Examination: Cranial nerves normal, no nystagmus at rest, no cerebellar signs, normal gait, no lateralising neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods normal; no imaging performed; audiometry not yet done
data_table.Past history: Hypertension on ramipril; no recent head injury

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next combined diagnostic and therapeutic manoeuvre?

options.text: Order MRI internal auditory meatus to exclude vestibular schwannoma and review imaging report
options.rationale: MRI is reserved for atypical features, neurological signs, or hearing loss; this is classic posterior canal BPPV. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)

options.text: Trial regular oral prochlorperazine 5 mg three times daily for two weeks for vestibular sedation
options.rationale: Vestibular suppressants are not curative in BPPV and prolong recovery; particle repositioning is first-line. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)

options.text: Refer to ENT for diagnostic vestibular testing including videonystagmography and rotational chair tests
options.rationale: Specialist vestibular testing is reserved for atypical or refractory cases; bedside Dix-Hallpike with Epley is first-line. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)

options.text: Perform Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre and if positive then apply Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre
options.rationale: Dix-Hallpike confirms posterior canal BPPV and Epley repositioning is the first-line therapeutic manoeuvre with about 80 percent single-treatment success. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)

options.text: Prescribe vestibular rehabilitation home exercise program alone and review four weeks later in clinic
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation alone is slower than particle repositioning; Epley is the proven first-line treatment. (Source: RACGP: Vertigo)

explanation.summary: Posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is diagnosed by the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre eliciting torsional upbeat nystagmus that latency, fatigues, and resolves. The Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre achieves resolution in about 80 percent after one treatment and over 90 percent after two. Vestibular suppressants prolong recovery and are not first-line. MRI is reserved for atypical features such as central nystagmus, focal neurological signs, hearing loss, or persistent symptoms. Recurrence is common and patients should be taught self-treatment.
key_points: Dix-Hallpike confirms posterior canal BPPV
Epley achieves about 80 percent single-treatment resolution
Vestibular suppressants prolong recovery
MRI for atypical features or persistent symptoms
explanation.pearls: Posterior canal BPPV nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike has a 5 to 20 second latency, lasts under 60 seconds, and fatigues with repetition; absence of these features should prompt evaluation for central causes.

subtopic_detail: Saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention with new lower back pain requires urgent imaging
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 48-year-old man with three days of severe lower back pain after lifting at work. He now describes new perineal numbness, difficulty initiating urination, and reduced erection. Bladder scan shows 700 mL post-void residual. Examination confirms saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone, and bilateral leg weakness. Reflexes are reduced at the ankles. He has no fever and no systemic illness.

data_table.Examination: Saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone, bilateral leg weakness power 4/5, absent ankle jerks, normal plantars
data_table.Investigations: Bladder scan 700 mL post-void residual; WCC 9.2; CRP 6; no fever
data_table.Setting: Tertiary hospital with MRI 24/7 available; spinal team on call

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Outpatient lumbar spine X-ray with flexion and extension views to assess instability and review in clinic
options.rationale: Plain films do not show neural compression; MRI is required for suspected cauda equina syndrome. (Source: RACS; Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Lumbar puncture with measurement of opening pressure and cell count and biochemistry analysis
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated when cord or cauda equina compression is suspected before imaging. (Source: RACS)

options.text: Outpatient CT lumbar spine within 48 hours, scheduled through GP referral pathway after discharge
options.rationale: CT has lower soft tissue and neural resolution than MRI and 48 hour delay risks irreversible deficit. (Source: RACS)

options.text: Outpatient nerve conduction studies in two weeks to assess for peripheral neuropathy or radiculopathy
options.rationale: Nerve conduction studies do not show structural compression and a two-week delay risks permanent loss. (Source: RACS)

options.text: Urgent whole lumbosacral spine MRI within hours to confirm cauda equina compression for surgery
options.rationale: Whole lumbosacral spine MRI within hours is the standard investigation for suspected cauda equina syndrome to confirm compression and guide urgent surgery. (Source: RACS)

explanation.summary: Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency caused by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots, most commonly from a central disc protrusion. Red flag features include saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction with post-void residual over 500 mL, sexual dysfunction, and bilateral leg weakness. Whole lumbosacral spine MRI within hours confirms the diagnosis and surgical decompression within 48 hours of symptom onset preserves the best functional outcome. Delayed diagnosis risks permanent bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction.
key_points: Saddle anaesthesia and retention with PVR over 500 mL are red flags
Urgent MRI within hours
Decompression ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset
Plain films and outpatient pathways are inappropriate
explanation.pearls: Bladder PVR over 500 mL with saddle anaesthesia carries a positive predictive value of about 50 percent for cauda equina on MRI, which is why the imaging threshold is low when both features coexist.

subtopic_detail: Single attack of monocular vision loss with pain on eye movement and normal fundoscopy
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with two days of progressive blurred vision in the right eye with pain on eye movement. Visual acuity is 6/24 right and 6/6 left with a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy is normal in both eyes. There is no headache, no fever, and no systemic symptoms. She has no prior neurological episodes and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Right RAPD, reduced colour vision right, normal fundoscopy bilaterally, normal cranial nerves otherwise, no cerebellar or long tract signs
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods unremarkable; OCT not yet performed
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no prior optic or neurological event

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Visual field testing with Humphrey perimetry in outpatient clinic in two weeks alongside OCT
options.rationale: Outpatient fields delay assessment of demyelinating risk; urgent MRI brain and orbits is the priority. (Source: MSWA; Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Urgent CT brain with contrast to exclude intracranial mass lesion as the diagnostic next step
options.rationale: CT brain has low yield for demyelination; MRI brain and orbits is the standard investigation. (Source: MSWA)

options.text: MRI brain and orbits with contrast to assess for demyelinating lesions and confirm optic neuritis
options.rationale: MRI brain and orbits with contrast is the recommended investigation to confirm optic neuritis and assess demyelinating disease risk. (Source: MSWA)

options.text: Routine outpatient ophthalmology review in six weeks with no imaging pending symptom progression
options.rationale: Delayed review risks missing demyelinating disease that benefits from early disease-modifying therapy. (Source: MSWA)

options.text: Empiric oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days as immediate treatment without imaging input
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone monotherapy at conventional doses worsens outcomes in optic neuritis; high-dose IV methylprednisolone is used when treatment is indicated. (Source: MSWA)

explanation.summary: Optic neuritis presents with subacute monocular vision loss, pain on eye movement, dyschromatopsia, and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy is normal in retrobulbar optic neuritis. MRI brain and orbits with contrast confirms inflammation and stratifies multiple sclerosis risk: T2 white matter lesions raise 10-year MS risk to over 70 percent. Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days speeds recovery but does not improve final acuity. Oral prednisolone at conventional doses worsens outcomes and should be avoided as monotherapy.
key_points: Subacute monocular vision loss with eye movement pain
RAPD plus dyschromatopsia with normal fundoscopy
MRI brain and orbits with contrast
Avoid oral prednisolone monotherapy
explanation.pearls: Among patients with optic neuritis and at least one T2 brain lesion on baseline MRI, the 10-year cumulative risk of multiple sclerosis is around 72 percent versus 25 percent with a normal MRI, which underpins the urgency of imaging for prognostic and treatment decisions.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of acute idiopathic facial nerve palsy at 36 hours of onset
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 36-year-old man with 36 hours of right-sided facial weakness affecting forehead, eyelid, and corner of mouth. He cannot fully close the right eye and has subjective hyperacusis. There is no vesicular rash on the ear or palate, no hearing loss, and no other neurological deficit. He is otherwise well, has no diabetes, no immunosuppression, and is not pregnant.

data_table.Examination: House-Brackmann grade IV right LMN facial palsy, intact corneal reflex, no vesicles, normal otoscopy bilaterally, normal taste anteriorly
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.8 mmol/L; HbA1c not yet done; no further imaging
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no recent zoster or VZV exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management?

options.text: Topical aciclovir cream to the affected side three times daily for two weeks as antiviral monotherapy
options.rationale: Topical aciclovir is not effective in Bell palsy; oral prednisolone is the proven intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for one week as antiviral monotherapy and outpatient review
options.rationale: Antiviral monotherapy without corticosteroid does not improve recovery rates in Bell palsy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three days inpatient with cardiac monitoring after admission
options.rationale: IV pulse steroid is not standard for Bell palsy; oral prednisolone within 72 hours is the proven intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days commenced within 72 hours of symptom onset with eye care
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days started within 72 hours improves recovery rates in Bell palsy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Combined oral prednisolone 50 mg daily plus oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 10 days now
options.rationale: Adding antiviral to prednisolone does not improve outcomes in classic Bell palsy without vesicles. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic facial nerve palsy is the most common cause of acute lower motor neuron facial weakness. Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days started within 72 hours of onset improves recovery rates and is the only intervention with reliable benefit. Antivirals add no clear benefit in classic Bell palsy without vesicles but should be added if Ramsay Hunt syndrome is suspected. Eye care with lubricant drops, ointment, and taping during sleep is essential to prevent exposure keratitis. Improvement typically begins by three weeks and most patients recover by six months.
key_points: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days within 72 hours
Antivirals not routinely added in classic Bell palsy
Add antivirals if Ramsay Hunt vesicles present
Eye care critical to prevent exposure keratitis
