explanation.pearls: Adding aciclovir to prednisolone does not improve House-Brackmann grade I or II recovery at 9 months in classic Bell palsy without vesicles, which is why monotherapy with prednisolone is preferred in Australian practice.

subtopic_detail: Choice of biologic for severe eosinophilic asthma uncontrolled on triple inhaled therapy in adult
stem: You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 42-year-old non-smoking woman with severe asthma referred from her GP. She remains symptomatic with two hospitalisations in 12 months despite high-dose ICS-LABA plus tiotropium and good adherence. Blood eosinophils are 540 cells/microL, FeNO 65 ppb, total IgE 110 IU/mL, and she has nasal polyps. No specific aeroallergen sensitisation is documented. She has no parasitic infection risk and is not pregnant.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 80, RR 18, BP 124/78, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Mild end-expiratory wheeze, nasal polyps on rhinoscopy, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Blood eosinophils 540 cells/microL; FeNO 65 ppb; total IgE 110 IU/mL; spirometry FEV1 62 percent predicted; specific IgE panel negative for perennial allergens
data_table.Medications: ICS-LABA 1000 mcg/250 mcg twice daily, tiotropium 5 mcg daily, montelukast 10 mg daily

lead_in: Which biologic is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Omalizumab subcutaneous monthly dosed by weight and total IgE level as anti-IgE biologic first choice
options.rationale: Omalizumab requires documented sensitisation to a perennial aeroallergen, which is absent in this patient. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)

options.text: Mepolizumab subcutaneous 100 mg every four weeks as IL-5 biologic monotherapy ongoing
options.rationale: Mepolizumab is reasonable but does not address her nasal polyps as effectively as dupilumab in this phenotype. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)

options.text: Reslizumab IV monthly weight-based dosing for severe eosinophilic asthma as the next step now
options.rationale: Reslizumab is IV monthly and reserved when subcutaneous options are unsuitable; not first preference here. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)

options.text: Benralizumab subcutaneous every eight weeks after loading as IL-5 receptor antibody monotherapy
options.rationale: Benralizumab is an option for eosinophilic asthma but does not target the type 2 polyp pathway as broadly as dupilumab. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)

options.text: Dupilumab subcutaneous every two weeks for severe type 2 asthma with nasal polyps as combined indication
options.rationale: Dupilumab targets IL-4 and IL-13 and treats type 2 asthma with nasal polyps as a combined indication on Australian PBS criteria. (Source: TSANZ; PBS criteria)

explanation.summary: Severe asthma not controlled on triple inhaled therapy is eligible for biologic therapy. Choice depends on phenotype: omalizumab requires perennial allergen sensitisation, mepolizumab and benralizumab require elevated eosinophil counts, and dupilumab targets type 2 inflammation including asthma with nasal polyps or atopic dermatitis. Tezepelumab is approved for severe asthma irrespective of phenotype. The Australian Severe Asthma Toolkit and PBS criteria define eligibility. Switching between biologics is reasonable if response is inadequate after four to six months.
key_points: Omalizumab requires perennial allergen sensitisation
Mepolizumab, benralizumab for eosinophilic phenotype
Dupilumab for type 2 asthma plus nasal polyps
Tezepelumab is phenotype-independent
explanation.pearls: Dupilumab reduces nasal polyp size and improves asthma exacerbations by around 50 percent in patients with both conditions and is the only biologic with dual PBS indication for adult asthma plus chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing isolated polymyalgia rheumatica from giant cell arteritis overlap on presentation
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 72-year-old woman with three weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain with morning stiffness over an hour. She also describes a new bitemporal headache that has worsened over five days, jaw claudication after eating tough foods, and a single brief episode of right monocular blurred vision two days ago. There is no rash, no fever, and no joint swelling. ESR is 102 and CRP is 88.

data_table.Examination: Limited shoulder and hip range with pain, no synovitis, mild bitemporal scalp tenderness, no visual deficit on examination, palpable temporal arteries with reduced pulsation right
data_table.Investigations: ESR 102 mm/hr; CRP 88 mg/L; Hb 112; platelets 410; LFTs ALP 180 with normal bilirubin; eGFR 78
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no recent infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily for PMR symptoms with rapid taper over six weeks as monotherapy outpatient
options.rationale: The cranial features and jaw claudication indicate GCA overlap requiring high dose prednisolone, not PMR dose. (Source: ARA; Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Oral NSAID such as celecoxib 200 mg twice daily and book temporal artery biopsy in two weeks for diagnosis
options.rationale: NSAIDs do not treat GCA and biopsy must not delay steroid initiation when visual symptoms are present. (Source: ARA)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 14 days of treatment start
options.rationale: Visual symptoms and jaw claudication mandate immediate high dose prednisolone with biopsy within 14 days for confirmation. (Source: ARA; Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange outpatient rheumatology referral within four weeks without initiating any steroid before assessment
options.rationale: Delay risks permanent visual loss; steroids start before specialist review when GCA is suspected. (Source: ARA)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for three days for monocular visual loss already established prior
options.rationale: IV pulse is reserved for confirmed or progressing visual loss; transient amaurosis without current deficit is treated with high dose oral prednisolone. (Source: ARA)

explanation.summary: Up to 50 percent of patients with giant cell arteritis have polymyalgia rheumatica features and 15 to 20 percent of PMR patients develop GCA. Red flags for GCA overlap include new bitemporal headache, jaw claudication, transient or persistent monocular vision loss, scalp tenderness, and constitutional symptoms. Suspected GCA mandates immediate oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily, or IV pulse for established visual loss, with temporal artery biopsy within 14 days. Methotrexate and tocilizumab are steroid-sparing options. Untreated GCA risks irreversible blindness.
key_points: Jaw claudication and amaurosis are red flags for GCA
Start oral prednisolone immediately, do not delay for biopsy
Biopsy within 14 days of steroid initiation
IV pulse for persistent or progressing visual loss
explanation.pearls: Temporal artery biopsy sensitivity falls from about 80 to 60 percent if delayed beyond 14 days of steroid treatment, which is why the biopsy window is tight even though steroids start immediately.

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic choice for suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 64-year-old man with 3 weeks of fevers, weight loss, and night sweats. He had a mechanical aortic valve replacement 14 months ago. Two sets of blood cultures taken 30 minutes apart are pending. His observations are stable and there is no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis. A transthoracic echocardiogram shows a possible 6 mm vegetation on the prosthetic aortic valve and trivial regurgitation. He has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, HR 96, BP 124/68 mmHg, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Bloods: WCC 12.4 x10^9/L, CRP 88 mg/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L
data_table.Examination: Mechanical second heart sound, no peripheral stigmata, no embolic phenomena
data_table.Imaging: TTE: possible 6 mm vegetation on prosthetic aortic valve, trivial AR, normal LV function

lead_in: Which empiric antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg 8-hourly as initial therapy
options.rationale: Penicillin and gentamicin alone do not cover staphylococcal species (including methicillin-resistant strains) that are common in prosthetic valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly plus gentamicin
options.rationale: This regimen covers native valve endocarditis but does not address methicillin-resistant staphylococci or coagulase-negative staphylococci common on prostheses. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin pending blood culture and susceptibility
options.rationale: Late prosthetic valve endocarditis requires empiric vancomycin (MRSA and coagulase-negative staphylococci), gentamicin (synergy), and rifampicin (biofilm penetration) until pathogen is known. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy until blood cultures result and adjust thereafter
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not adequately cover staphylococci including MRSA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral linezolid 600 mg twice daily monotherapy with outpatient transthoracic review in 1 week
options.rationale: Oral monotherapy is inappropriate for prosthetic valve endocarditis; intravenous combination is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis empiric therapy is stratified by valve type and risk. For native valve endocarditis benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is standard; vancomycin replaces benzylpenicillin and flucloxacillin in severe penicillin allergy or suspected MRSA. For prosthetic valve endocarditis later than 12 months post-surgery the staphylococcal risk plus biofilm formation justifies vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin. Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within 12 months) is dominated by nosocomial pathogens and uses the same regimen but with consideration of fungi. Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites and transoesophageal echo confirm the diagnosis. Surgical referral is indicated for prosthetic involvement, large vegetations, embolic events, heart failure, or perivalvular abscess.
key_points: Three blood culture sets over time before antibiotics where possible
Native valve empiric: benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin
Prosthetic valve empiric: vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin
TOE outperforms TTE for prosthetic valves and complications
Surgical referral for prosthesis, HF, abscess, large vegetation, persistent bacteraemia
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin is added for its biofilm penetration on prosthetic material, but never given alone for staphylococci because of rapid resistance emergence.

subtopic_detail: Application of the sepsis hour-1 bundle in suspected community-acquired sepsis
stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with 24 hours of dysuria, loin pain, and rigors. She presents looking unwell, mottled peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds. Her observations on triage 15 minutes ago triggered an emergency response, and no antibiotics or fluids have yet been given. She is fully alert. She has no documented antibiotic allergy and her usual medications are amlodipine and metformin.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 124, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 95 percent room air
data_table.Bloods: WCC 18.6 x10^9/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 90)
data_table.Examination: Tender right flank, no peritonism, peripheries mottled, mentation intact

lead_in: Within the first hour, which action is most important to perform first?

options.text: Administer empiric intravenous gentamicin and ampicillin within 1 hour after taking blood cultures
options.rationale: The sepsis hour-1 bundle prioritises lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L; this regimen targets pyelonephritis-related sepsis per Australian guidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

options.text: Order computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis before any further escalation or therapy
options.rationale: Imaging is important for source control but must not delay the hour-1 antibiotic and fluid bundle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

options.text: Wait for urine culture susceptibility results before commencing any empiric antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Waiting hours for susceptibilities is unsafe and contravenes the hour-1 bundle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

options.text: Commence intravenous noradrenaline immediately at 0.1 microgram/kg/min as first-line resuscitation
options.rationale: Vasopressor is used when MAP remains under 65 mmHg after 30 mL/kg crystalloid; fluid resuscitation is the initial response unless contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

options.text: Provide 1 L of 5 percent dextrose intravenously as bolus over 30 minutes for volume expansion
options.rationale: Dextrose is not a resuscitation fluid; balanced crystalloid (Hartmann or Plasmalyte) is preferred for septic shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle integrates measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, begin rapid administration of 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at or above 4 mmol/L, and start vasopressors during or after fluid resuscitation if MAP remains below 65 mmHg. For community-acquired pyelonephritis with sepsis, Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend ampicillin plus gentamicin (with renal function adjusted dosing). Source control (urological intervention for obstructive uropathy, surgical debridement, drainage) is sought as soon as possible after stabilisation.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors
30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >= 4
Vasopressor if MAP under 65 mmHg after fluid
Source control as early as feasible after resuscitation
Ampicillin plus gentamicin is first-line for pyelonephritis sepsis
explanation.pearls: Single-dose gentamicin 5 to 7 mg/kg followed by re-dosing only after a 24-hour level minimises nephrotoxicity while achieving high peak-MIC ratios in the first 24 hours of sepsis.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

subtopic_detail: Recognition and surgical urgency of necrotising fasciitis using clinical and LRINEC features
stem: You are the surgical registrar called to the emergency department to review a 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who has 18 hours of severe pain in the right leg out of proportion to the limited erythema. He has had two previous episodes of cellulitis treated with oral antibiotics. He is increasingly distressed by the pain and his observations are deteriorating. There is a small skin break over the shin from a gardening injury 2 days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.0, HR 130, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent
data_table.Bloods: WCC 22 x10^9/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, CRP 220 mg/L, creatinine 152 micromol/L, haemoglobin 132 g/L
data_table.Examination: Localised erythema 5 cm proximal to ankle, exquisite tenderness extending 15 cm proximally, no crepitus, no bullae yet
data_table.Imaging: Plain radiograph shows no soft tissue gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours and review the response in the emergency department in 2 hours
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not cover the spectrum of necrotising soft tissue infection and would dangerously delay surgical debridement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Order urgent magnetic resonance imaging before any decision on surgical exploration is made
options.rationale: Imaging should never delay surgical exploration in suspected necrotising fasciitis; clinical features and LRINEC score are sufficient to act. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for orthopaedic review next day to plan elective wound debridement in the operating room
options.rationale: Delaying debridement beyond hours in necrotising fasciitis substantially increases mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Activate emergency operating theatre booking for surgical exploration plus empiric meropenem and clindamycin
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion to skin findings, systemic toxicity, and an LRINEC score of 8 or more (his is 11) demand emergency surgical exploration with empiric broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for observation on the medical ward and intravenous flucloxacillin alone for severe cellulitis
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin alone does not cover gram-negatives or anaerobes and is insufficient for necrotising fasciitis; surgery is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency where rapid spreading subcutaneous and fascial necrosis develops faster than overlying skin changes can keep up. The hallmark is pain out of proportion to examination, systemic toxicity, and rapidly evolving signs (oedema, bullae, crepitus, skin necrosis, anaesthesia over the affected area). The LRINEC score uses CRP, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose to risk stratify: score 6 or more is intermediate to high risk, 8 or more confirms high risk. Definitive treatment is urgent surgical debridement; empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics include a carbapenem (or piperacillin-tazobactam), vancomycin or linezolid, plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. Repeated debridement at 24 to 48 hours is the norm.
key_points: Pain out of proportion to skin findings is the key early clue
LRINEC score 6 or more raises suspicion; 8 or more confirms it
Surgical debridement within hours saves life
Empiric antibiotics: meropenem + vancomycin + clindamycin
Repeated debridement and ICU support are usually needed
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is added specifically to inhibit streptococcal exotoxin and panton-valentine leukocidin production, distinct from its antibacterial effect.

subtopic_detail: Treatment selection after minimal trauma vertebral fracture in postmenopausal woman
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 72-year-old postmenopausal woman 6 weeks after a thoracic vertebral compression fracture sustained when she stepped down from a kerb. She has had no other fractures. She takes alendronate 70 mg weekly correctly for 5 years and a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement. Recent investigations are back. Her renal function is preserved and there is no history of oesophageal disease.

data_table.DXA: Lumbar spine T score -3.2, femoral neck T score -2.9, total hip -2.7
data_table.Bloods: 25-OH vitamin D 78 nmol/L, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L, eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m^2, TSH 1.4 mIU/L
data_table.Other: PTH 4.6 pmol/L, normal SPEP, no malignant features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next change in management?

options.text: Continue current alendronate at the same dose and review again with repeat DXA in 2 years
options.rationale: Minimal trauma vertebral fracture on alendronate represents treatment failure and demands escalation. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Switch alendronate to teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneously daily for 18 months under specialist review
options.rationale: An incident minimal trauma vertebral fracture despite oral bisphosphonate is an indication for anabolic therapy with teriparatide; PBS subsidy applies under specialist authority. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Add daily high-dose calcitriol 0.5 micrograms to current alendronate to improve fracture healing
options.rationale: Calcitriol is reserved for renal osteodystrophy; it does not address established bisphosphonate failure. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Switch alendronate to oral risedronate 35 mg weekly as an alternative oral bisphosphonate option
options.rationale: Switching between oral bisphosphonates does not address treatment failure; a different drug class is required. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Switch alendronate to raloxifene 60 mg daily as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator
options.rationale: Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not hip or non-vertebral fracture and is not appropriate as escalation after vertebral fracture on a bisphosphonate. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis)

explanation.summary: Osteoporosis treatment in Australia is structured by PBS criteria: minimal trauma vertebral or hip fracture, age 70 or above with T score -2.5 or lower, or prolonged corticosteroid therapy. First line is oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) or intravenous zoledronic acid annually; denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously 6-monthly is an alternative, especially in renal impairment. An incident fracture or further bone density loss while on antiresorptive therapy indicates treatment failure and consideration of anabolic therapy. Teriparatide is approved for 18 months and is followed by an antiresorptive agent (denosumab or bisphosphonate) to preserve gains. Compliance, calcium and vitamin D status, and secondary causes must be reviewed.
key_points: Minimal trauma fracture despite bisphosphonate equals treatment failure
Teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneous daily for 18 months follows
An antiresorptive agent must follow teriparatide to preserve gains
Adherence and secondary causes must be reviewed
Denosumab is an alternative escalation in renal impairment
explanation.pearls: Teriparatide is contraindicated when there is a previous skeletal radiotherapy, hypercalcaemia, Paget disease, or open epiphyses; specialist review is required for PBS authority.

sources.label: Healthy Bones Australia: Clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Workup for suspected acute HIV seroconversion in a man with febrile illness and mucosal ulcers
stem: You are the registrar in a sexual health clinic reviewing a 26-year-old man with 10 days of fevers, sore throat, malaise, painful oral ulcers, a generalised maculopapular rash on the trunk, and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. He had condomless receptive anal sex with a new partner 5 weeks ago. He has not previously been on pre-exposure prophylaxis. His last HIV test was negative 6 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 96, BP 118/70 mmHg, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Bloods: WCC 4.2 x10^9/L (lymphopenia), platelets 116 x10^9/L, ALT 88 U/L, CRP 32 mg/L
data_table.Examination: Oropharyngeal ulcers, tender bilateral posterior cervical lymph nodes, truncal maculopapular rash, no genital ulcers
data_table.STI history: Last negative HIV 4th generation test 6 months ago, no PrEP, single recent exposure

lead_in: Which test most reliably establishes acute HIV infection at this stage?

options.text: Standard 3rd generation HIV antibody test from a venous blood sample as the first investigation
options.rationale: 3rd generation tests detect antibodies only and have a 3 to 6 week window; they may be negative in seroconversion. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)

options.text: Rapid point-of-care fingerprick antibody test as a definitive single test for acute infection
options.rationale: Point-of-care antibody-only tests perform worst in the seroconversion window and may miss acute infection. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)

options.text: Anti-HIV western blot performed on a serum sample collected today to confirm acute infection
options.rationale: Western blot is a confirmatory antibody test and is also negative during seroconversion windows. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)

options.text: Quantitative chest computed tomography to assess for opportunistic infection complicating seroconversion
options.rationale: Imaging does not detect HIV infection; this question is about diagnostic confirmation. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)

options.text: HIV RNA viral load polymerase chain reaction alongside a 4th generation antigen antibody combination test
options.rationale: In suspected acute seroconversion (less than 28 days), HIV RNA PCR detects virus before antibody seroconversion; the 4th generation Ag/Ab test adds p24 antigen detection. Both establish the diagnosis confidently. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing policy)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion classically presents with a mononucleosis-like illness 2 to 4 weeks after high-risk exposure: fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, rash, oral or genital ulcers, with lymphopenia, raised transaminases, and atypical lymphocytes. Diagnostically, HIV RNA viral load detects virus 1 to 2 weeks post-exposure; p24 antigen detected by 4th generation tests becomes positive about 2 weeks post-exposure; antibodies seroconvert at 3 to 6 weeks. A combination of HIV RNA PCR and 4th generation Ag/Ab test maximises sensitivity in the window. Confirmed acute infection requires immediate referral to an s100-prescribing HIV physician for early initiation of antiretroviral therapy, contact tracing, and counselling.
key_points: Acute HIV mimics infectious mononucleosis at 2 to 4 weeks post-exposure
HIV RNA PCR turns positive within 1 to 2 weeks
4th generation Ag/Ab adds p24 antigen detection at ~2 weeks
Antibody-only tests are unreliable in the window period
Immediate referral and rapid ART start are recommended
explanation.pearls: Same-day ART initiation in acute HIV reduces transmission and progression, and is the standard of care at Australian sexual health centres; the rapid test result is no longer required before starting therapy in suspected acute disease.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic sequence for suspected Cushing syndrome in a woman with central obesity and hypertension
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 42-year-old woman with 18 months of progressive central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness in climbing stairs, and new hypertension. She does not take exogenous corticosteroids and denies herbal preparations. She has type 2 diabetes diagnosed last year and her BP is 158/96 mmHg on amlodipine. Her menstrual cycles have become irregular and acne has worsened.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/96 mmHg, HR 84
data_table.Examination: Central obesity, supraclavicular fat pads, dorsocervical fat pad, violaceous abdominal striae, proximal hip and shoulder weakness
data_table.Bloods: HbA1c 7.6 percent, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, fasting glucose 8.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 10 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily; no glucocorticoids or herbal supplements

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

options.text: Random serum cortisol level taken between 08:00 and 10:00 as the first screening investigation
options.rationale: Random cortisol levels are too variable and do not establish or exclude Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)

options.text: Immediate adrenal computed tomography to identify a primary adrenal source of hypercortisolism
options.rationale: Imaging without biochemical confirmation risks discovering incidentalomas and missing pituitary or ectopic sources. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)

options.text: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test or late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol
options.rationale: Any one of these three tests is acceptable as a first-line screen; confirmation requires two abnormal screening tests of different types before further localisation. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)

options.text: Serum adrenocorticotrophic hormone level alone as the first investigation to localise hypercortisolism
options.rationale: ACTH localises but does not establish hypercortisolism; it follows confirmed Cushing syndrome rather than precedes it. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)

options.text: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma at this stage
options.rationale: IPSS is reserved for distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH after confirmed ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome workup starts with confirmation of hypercortisolism using one of three first-line tests: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression (failure to suppress below 50 nmol/L), late-night salivary cortisol (elevated), or 24-hour urinary free cortisol (raised above reference range). Two abnormal tests from different categories are required before proceeding. Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, ACTH is measured. Suppressed ACTH indicates adrenal cause (proceed to adrenal CT or MRI). Normal or raised ACTH indicates ACTH-dependent disease, evaluated next with high-dose dexamethasone suppression, MRI pituitary, then inferior petrosal sinus sampling if non-diagnostic. Treatment is directed at the source: transsphenoidal surgery for pituitary adenoma, adrenalectomy for adrenal source, or treatment of ectopic source.
key_points: First-line: 1 mg overnight DST, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24h UFC
Two abnormal screens of different types confirm hypercortisolism
ACTH then distinguishes ACTH-dependent from independent
MRI pituitary and IPSS localise ACTH-dependent disease
Adrenal imaging follows confirmed ACTH-independent disease
explanation.pearls: Late-night salivary cortisol has the highest sensitivity in the most common form (early ACTH-dependent disease) because the earliest defect is loss of the circadian nadir at midnight.

subtopic_detail: Recognition of Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome in a returned traveller
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 36-year-old man with 4 days of progressively worsening unsteady gait, double vision, and difficulty reading. He returned from Vietnam 3 weeks ago, where he had 24 hours of watery diarrhoea that resolved without treatment. He has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications. He is fully alert with normal language and cognition.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 84, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Bilateral abducens palsy, broad-based ataxic gait, absent ankle and knee reflexes, normal limb power, sensation intact
data_table.Investigations: Pending CSF, normal CT brain, normal FBC and electrolytes, ECG normal
data_table.Travel and exposure: Returned 3 weeks ago from Vietnam; self-limiting gastroenteritis 4 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Order high-resolution MRI of the brainstem to investigate suspected acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
options.rationale: MRI may be done but the clinical triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia is diagnostic for Miller Fisher syndrome and demands immediate treatment. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

options.text: Send GQ1b antibody serology and provide reassurance pending the result with outpatient review
options.rationale: Anti-GQ1b is supportive but treatment should not await serology when the clinical picture is diagnostic. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

options.text: Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 5 days as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not effective in Guillain-Barre or Miller Fisher and may worsen outcomes. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

options.text: Admit to a monitored bed with respiratory observation and commence IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Miller Fisher syndrome is a Guillain-Barre variant treated with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days with cardio-respiratory monitoring because of risk of bulbar and respiratory weakness progression. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

options.text: Order Tensilon test to differentiate from myasthenia gravis before any further treatment is started
options.rationale: Areflexia and ataxia are not features of myasthenia gravis; Tensilon test is not relevant here and is no longer routinely used. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

explanation.summary: Miller Fisher syndrome is the classic variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome characterised by the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia, often preceded by Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis or upper respiratory infection. Anti-GQ1b antibodies are positive in over 85 percent of cases. CSF typically shows raised protein with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation). Treatment is IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or plasma exchange; corticosteroids are not effective and may worsen outcome. Respiratory monitoring with serial forced vital capacity is mandatory because of risk of progression to bulbar weakness and respiratory failure requiring intubation.
key_points: Triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia is diagnostic
Anti-GQ1b antibodies are positive in over 85 percent of cases
CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation
IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days or plasma exchange
Steroids are not effective and not recommended
explanation.pearls: A vital capacity below 20 mL/kg or rapidly falling on serial measurement is a stronger indicator of imminent respiratory failure in GBS than oxygen saturation, which falls late.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists; BMJ Best Practice GBS

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis screening
stem: A 38-year-old woman with newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis is planned to commence adalimumab through your rheumatology clinic. She was born in Vietnam, arrived in Australia six years ago, and received BCG vaccination as a child. She has had no known TB contacts and no respiratory symptoms. She has no chronic liver disease and her bloods are normal. The rheumatologist asks you to organise pre-biologic latent tuberculosis screening.

data_table.Examination: BCG scar present; chest clear; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFTs, renal function within reference range; CXR pending
data_table.Medications: Methotrexate 15 mg weekly, folate 5 mg weekly

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate screening test for latent TB before starting a TNF-alpha inhibitor?

options.text: Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) alone using a 5 mm threshold for positivity in this immunosuppressed cohort
options.rationale: TST is influenced by prior BCG vaccination; in a BCG-vaccinated patient, an interferon-gamma release assay is preferred because it is unaffected by BCG. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)

options.text: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus interferon-gamma release assay together with a baseline plain chest radiograph
options.rationale: IGRA (e.g. QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus) is the preferred screen in BCG-vaccinated individuals before TNF-alpha inhibitors and is paired with CXR to evaluate for active disease before treatment of latent infection. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)

options.text: Three serial induced-sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli over consecutive mornings as the principal screen
options.rationale: Sputum AFB is for suspected active TB with respiratory symptoms; it is not the screening test for latent TB in an asymptomatic patient. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)

options.text: High-resolution CT of the chest as the primary screen for asymptomatic latent tuberculosis before biologic therapy
options.rationale: HRCT does not identify latent infection; latent TB is by definition asymptomatic and radiographically silent and requires immunological detection. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)

options.text: Total serum IgE and peripheral blood absolute eosinophil count to risk-stratify for mycobacterial disease activity
options.rationale: IgE and eosinophils have no role in TB screening; they relate to allergic and parasitic disease. (Source: NTAC IGRA Position Statement 2018)

explanation.summary: Pre-biologic TB screening in Australia uses an interferon-gamma release assay (typically QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus) in BCG-vaccinated patients because TST has poor specificity after BCG. CXR is performed concurrently to exclude active disease before commencing latent TB therapy. If positive, isoniazid for nine months (or rifampicin 4 months or 3HP regimen via specialist clinic) is offered with monthly LFT monitoring. Untreated latent TB carries a markedly elevated reactivation risk on TNF-alpha inhibitors.
key_points: IGRA preferred over TST in BCG-vaccinated patients per NTAC
Always pair IGRA with CXR before treating latent TB
TNF-alpha inhibitors increase reactivation risk substantially
Standard latent TB therapy: isoniazid 9 months or rifampicin 4 months
explanation.pearls: Use QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus, not Mantoux, in any patient born in a high-incidence country who received BCG; if positive and CXR clear, give isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months with pyridoxine 25 mg daily and monthly LFTs.

subtopic_detail: Parkinson's disease initial therapy
stem:
A 72-year-old retired teacher is referred to your geriatric clinic with a six-month history of asymmetric rest tremor of the right hand, micrographia, slowed gait with reduced right arm swing, and difficulty turning in bed. He has fallen once. He has well-controlled hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Examination confirms cogwheel rigidity right greater than left, bradykinesia and a positive pull test for postural instability.

There is no early autonomic failure and no cognitive complaint. He scores 28/30 on MoCA. MRI brain is unremarkable. He asks about treatment options to maintain independence.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 68, BP 128/76 supine to 124/74 standing; no postural drop
data_table.Examination: Asymmetric rest tremor right hand, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability; UPDRS motor moderate
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain unremarkable; eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Pramipexole modified release titrated to 1.5 mg daily as initial dopamine agonist monotherapy for motor symptoms
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists are associated with higher rates of impulse-control disorders, hallucinations, ankle oedema and sleep attacks in older adults; levodopa is preferred over agonists as first-line in patients over 70. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)

options.text: Levodopa with carbidopa (Sinemet) 100/25 mg three times daily titrated upward to motor response over weeks
options.rationale: Levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor is the most effective symptomatic therapy and is preferred first-line in patients over 70 because of greater motor benefit, fewer neuropsychiatric complications than agonists, and lower fall risk on titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)

options.text: Trihexyphenidyl 2 mg twice daily as initial anticholinergic monotherapy directed primarily at his rest tremor
options.rationale: Anticholinergics in older adults precipitate confusion, urinary retention and cognitive decline; they are not used first-line in patients over 70 with Parkinson's disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)

options.text: Amantadine 100 mg twice daily as oral monotherapy for combined bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor relief
options.rationale: Amantadine has modest motor benefit and is mainly used for dyskinesia later in the disease; its renal clearance and CNS side-effect profile make it unattractive first-line in a 72-year-old with CKD. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)

options.text: Rasagiline 1 mg daily as MAO-B inhibitor monotherapy aiming for modest symptomatic effect in early disease
options.rationale: MAO-B inhibitors have modest symptomatic effect and may be appropriate in early mild disease in younger patients, but in this patient with established motor disability and postural instability, levodopa offers superior symptom control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology 2017)

explanation.summary: Levodopa combined with carbidopa is the most effective symptomatic therapy for Parkinson's disease and is the preferred first-line agent in older patients (over 70) where dopamine agonists carry higher risks of impulse control disorders, hallucinations and falls. Dose is titrated slowly to motor response; the goal in early disease is the lowest effective dose. Long-term motor complications such as dyskinesia and wearing-off are managed with adjuncts including COMT inhibitors and MAO-B inhibitors. Multidisciplinary care, falls prevention and bone health complete the management plan.
key_points: Levodopa first-line in patients aged over 70
Dopamine agonists more often first-line in younger patients with mild disease
Avoid anticholinergics in older adults
Multidisciplinary input - physiotherapy, OT, speech pathology - improves outcomes
explanation.pearls: In a 72-year-old with postural instability and falls, choose Sinemet 100/25 mg three times daily titrated to motor response rather than pramipexole, since the absolute risk of falls and impulse control disorder on agonist therapy outweighs the modest motor-complication advantage.

sources.label: Movement Disorder Society Evidence-Based Medicine Review Update 2018

subtopic_detail: RA early DMARD initiation
stem:
A 46-year-old retail manager presents to your rheumatology outpatient clinic with progressive symmetrical polyarthritis affecting the MCP and PIP joints of both hands and wrists for the past three months, with morning stiffness of 90 minutes and difficulty opening jars. She has no chest, eye or skin symptoms. There is no family history of inflammatory arthritis. She does not smoke.

Her bloods are listed below. Hand x-rays show periarticular osteopenia of MCP joints without erosions. She has no liver disease, no plan to become pregnant, and has had varicella infection in childhood.

data_table.Examination: Synovitis at bilateral MCP 2-5 and PIP 2-3; wrist tenderness; no rheumatoid nodules
data_table.Investigations: CRP 32 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/hr; anti-CCP strongly positive at 180 U/mL; RF positive at 1:160; FBC, UEC, LFTs normal; Hep B and Hep C negative; varicella IgG positive
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 1 g qid

lead_in: Which initial DMARD strategy best matches Australian guidance?

options.text: Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily as solitary DMARD monotherapy for a planned six-month treatment trial
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine is a relatively weak DMARD reserved for milder disease or as a combination partner; in established seropositive RA with high CRP, methotrexate is preferred first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

options.text: Tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily as initial targeted synthetic DMARD therapy ahead of conventional synthetic agents
options.rationale: JAK inhibitors are reserved for failure of methotrexate or other conventional synthetic DMARDs under PBS criteria; they are not Australian first-line therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

options.text: Methotrexate titrating to 15-25 mg weekly with folic acid plus short bridging low-dose oral prednisolone over weeks
options.rationale: Methotrexate is the anchor first-line DMARD for seropositive RA with elevated CRP, titrated to 15-25 mg weekly with folic acid; low-dose corticosteroid bridges disease control while methotrexate takes effect over 6-12 weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

options.text: Indefinite NSAID monotherapy with daily ibuprofen for sustained symptomatic control of inflammatory joint pain
options.rationale: NSAIDs do not modify disease progression in RA and indefinite use risks cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and renal harm; DMARD therapy must be initiated promptly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

options.text: Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 14 days as initial biologic monotherapy without prior conventional DMARDs
options.rationale: Biologic DMARDs require PBS criteria of inadequate response to at least two conventional synthetic DMARDs (including methotrexate at therapeutic dose) for at least three months; not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology 2017)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance and PBS criteria require methotrexate as the anchor first-line DMARD for newly diagnosed seropositive RA. Initial dose is 10 mg weekly titrated to 15-25 mg weekly over 4-8 weeks, with folic acid 5 mg weekly (taken on a different day) to reduce mucosal and hepatic side effects. Bridging low-dose prednisolone (e.g. 10-15 mg daily tapered over 8-12 weeks) controls inflammation while methotrexate reaches therapeutic effect. Biologic and targeted synthetic DMARDs require documented failure of conventional therapy.
key_points: Methotrexate is first-line in seropositive RA
Titrate to 15-25 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg weekly on a separate day
Bridging prednisolone for 8-12 weeks accelerates symptom control
Biologics require failure of two conventional DMARDs per PBS
explanation.pearls: In seropositive RA with CRP over 20 mg/L, start methotrexate at 10 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg on a different day, escalate by 2.5-5 mg every 2-4 weeks to 15-25 mg, and bridge with prednisolone 15 mg daily tapered over 12 weeks.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association methotrexate patient information

subtopic_detail: Acute aortic dissection workup
stem: You are the ED resident assessing a 62-year-old man with sudden severe interscapular tearing pain that started 45 minutes ago while gardening. He is sweaty, anxious, and rates pain 10/10. Past history includes hypertension (often unmonitored) and bicuspid aortic valve. Right arm BP is 178/96 and left arm BP is 142/72. Femoral pulses are present and equal. Cardiac examination reveals a soft early diastolic murmur. The chest is clear. ECG shows sinus rhythm with non-specific lateral T wave changes and no ST elevation. CXR shows a widened mediastinum.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 sinus, BP right 178/96, BP left 142/72, RR 22, SpO2 96%, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Sweaty, distressed, soft early diastolic murmur left sternal edge, no focal neurology, equal femoral pulses
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus, lateral T wave changes; CXR widened mediastinum; hs-troponin 18 ng/L (no rise expected at 45 min); D-dimer pending
data_table.Medications: Irregular perindopril use

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Urgent CT aortogram from the neck through to the femoral bifurcation acquired with arterial-phase contrast
options.rationale: Inter-arm BP differential exceeding 20 mmHg, tearing interscapular pain, widened mediastinum and bicuspid aortic valve make acute aortic dissection the leading diagnosis; CT aortogram is the most sensitive and rapidly available confirmatory test in Australian EDs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)

options.text: Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram by ED clinician as the sole definitive investigation before specialty referral
options.rationale: TTE has limited sensitivity for ascending aortic dissection and cannot adequately visualise the descending aorta; it complements but does not replace cross-sectional imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)

options.text: Coronary angiography to exclude STEMI before any further imaging or treatment decisions are made for this patient
options.rationale: ECG shows no ST elevation and the dominant differential is dissection; angiography could delay diagnosis and cardiac catheterisation in undiagnosed dissection is hazardous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)

options.text: Exercise stress test once analgesia controls his pain to risk-stratify before further investigation choices are made
options.rationale: Stress testing in a patient with suspected dissection is absolutely contraindicated and would not be feasible in this acute presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)

options.text: Outpatient transoesophageal echocardiogram within 24 hours after admission to a chest-pain short-stay observation unit
options.rationale: Suspected acute aortic dissection requires same-hour imaging; deferring to outpatient TOE risks rupture and death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular 2018)

explanation.summary: The combination of tearing interscapular pain, inter-arm BP differential greater than 20 mmHg, a widened mediastinum and a known bicuspid aortic valve makes acute aortic dissection the leading diagnosis. CT aortogram is the most rapidly available high-sensitivity confirmatory test in Australian emergency departments. While imaging is being arranged, target heart rate around 60 using IV beta-blocker (esmolol or metoprolol), then add nitroprusside or GTN to achieve systolic BP 100-120 mmHg, and call the cardiothoracic team for type A dissection.
key_points: Inter-arm BP gap >20 mmHg plus tearing pain is dissection until proven otherwise
CT aortogram is first-line in Australian EDs
Rate control to HR around 60 precedes BP reduction to avoid reflex tachycardia
Type A: emergency surgery; Type B uncomplicated: medical management
explanation.pearls: If the inter-arm systolic gap exceeds 20 mmHg, order CT aortogram and prepare IV esmolol 500 mcg/kg load then 50-200 mcg/kg/min infusion in parallel rather than sending a D-dimer or arranging TTE.

sources.label: ESC Guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of aortic diseases 2014

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis - McDonald criteria
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman who presents with a four-day history of right eye pain on movement and blurring of central vision. She had a self-limited bout of left-sided sensory loss in the leg six months ago lasting two weeks that she did not seek care for. Visual acuity is 6/18 right and 6/6 left with a right RAPD.

Fundus examination shows mild right optic disc swelling. MRI brain shows three T2 hyperintense lesions: one periventricular, one juxtacortical and one infratentorial, with one demonstrating contrast enhancement. MRI of the spinal cord shows a single non-enhancing cervical T2 lesion. CSF analysis is pending.

data_table.Examination: Right RAPD, right central scotoma, otherwise normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: 3 T2 hyperintense lesions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial), one enhancing. MRI cord: cervical T2 lesion non-enhancing. VEP delayed right
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: Which statement best applies the 2017 McDonald criteria here?

options.text: Diagnosis requires a second clinical attack before multiple sclerosis can be confirmed even with current MRI findings
options.rationale: The 2017 McDonald criteria allow MS diagnosis after a single clinical attack if dissemination in space and time are demonstrated by MRI or CSF; a second clinical attack is not mandatory. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

options.text: DIS is met by MRI but dissemination in time requires repeat MRI in three months before MS can be formally diagnosed
options.rationale: Dissemination in time can be met by the simultaneous presence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI, or by CSF-specific oligoclonal bands plus DIS; repeat imaging is not required. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

options.text: DIS and DIT are met on a single MRI but CSF oligoclonal bands are required before MS diagnosis can be formally made
options.rationale: Once DIS and DIT are met by MRI, CSF is not required for the 2017 criteria; CSF supports diagnosis when DIT cannot be demonstrated by MRI alone. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

options.text: Diagnosis cannot be made without first confirming negative aquaporin-4 antibodies plus complete CSF analysis results
options.rationale: NMOSD must be considered and AQP4 testing performed to exclude it, but once excluded and DIS and DIT are met clinically and on MRI, MS can be diagnosed under the 2017 criteria without mandatory CSF. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

options.text: CIS with DIS and DIT satisfied on single MRI fulfils 2017 McDonald criteria allowing diagnosis after exclusion of mimics
options.rationale: DIS is met by lesions in at least 2 of 4 typical locations (this patient has periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord involvement); DIT is met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same scan. Mimics including NMOSD and MOGAD must be excluded; MS can then be diagnosed and DMT discussed. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria - Lancet Neurology 2018)

explanation.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria allow MS diagnosis after a single clinical attack if dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) are demonstrated. DIS requires lesions in at least 2 of 4 typical CNS locations: periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial, or spinal cord. DIT can be met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI, by a new lesion on a later MRI, or by CSF-specific oligoclonal bands together with DIS. Exclusion of mimics (NMOSD, MOGAD, sarcoid, vasculitis) is essential.
key_points: DIS = lesions in 2 of 4 typical CNS locations
DIT = simultaneous enhancing + non-enhancing lesions, OR new lesion on follow-up, OR CSF OCBs + DIS
Always check AQP4 and MOG antibodies to exclude NMOSD and MOGAD before MS label
Early DMT after diagnosis reduces long-term disability
explanation.pearls: If a single MRI in a CIS patient shows lesions in two or more typical locations and at least one enhancing plus one non-enhancing lesion, the 2017 McDonald criteria are satisfied; refer for AQP4/MOG and discuss disease-modifying therapy.

sources.label: MS Australia Clinical Guidelines for Diagnosis 2021

subtopic_detail: Dementia with Lewy bodies - antipsychotic sensitivity
stem: A 78-year-old man with a 14-month history of fluctuating cognition, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations of small animals, mild bradykinesia and REM sleep behaviour disorder is admitted under your geriatrics team with new agitation overnight after a urinary tract infection has been identified. The night staff request a sedating medication. He is not a danger to himself. He is normally on rivastigmine 9.5 mg patch daily and trimethoprim was started six hours ago. He has had no benzodiazepines or antipsychotics previously.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 122/76, RR 18, SpO2 95% on room air, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Disoriented to time and place, mild bradykinesia, no focal neurology, visual hallucinations of cats in the corner
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick leucocytes +++, nitrites positive; FBC, UEC, LFTs within usual range; CXR clear
data_table.Medications: Rivastigmine 9.5 mg/24 h patch; trimethoprim 300 mg started 6 h ago

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate medication choice for sedation tonight?

options.text: Haloperidol 0.5 mg orally as required for agitation overnight with hourly nursing observations of motor status
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics including haloperidol carry up to 50% risk of severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions in DLB, including worsening parkinsonism, autonomic instability and NMS-like syndrome; absolutely avoided. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

options.text: Risperidone 0.5 mg orally as required overnight aiming to reduce hallucinations and agitation during the night shift
options.rationale: Risperidone has D2 affinity comparable to typical antipsychotics in this context and is associated with severe sensitivity in DLB; it should be avoided. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg orally as required overnight as the sedating atypical antipsychotic of choice for nocturnal agitation
options.rationale: Olanzapine has been associated with severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions in DLB and is not recommended; if an antipsychotic is unavoidable, quetiapine at very low dose is preferred. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

options.text: Address reversible delirium triggers with non-pharmacological measures, reserving low-dose quetiapine for refractory severe distress
options.rationale: DLB carries high neuroleptic sensitivity risk; the first response to delirium is to address triggers and use non-pharmacological measures, with low-dose quetiapine reserved for severe distress that cannot be otherwise managed. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg orally as required overnight for sedation as the standard first-line agent in agitated older inpatients
options.rationale: Long-acting benzodiazepines precipitate prolonged sedation, falls and paradoxical worsening of delirium in older adults; if benzodiazepine is unavoidable, short-acting low-dose lorazepam is preferred. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is associated with severe neuroleptic sensitivity (occurring in up to half of patients exposed) which can present as worsening parkinsonism, autonomic instability and NMS-like syndromes. First-line management of delirium superimposed on DLB is to identify and treat reversible causes (infection, dehydration, pain, urinary retention) and use non-pharmacological strategies. If a sedating agent is required for refractory severe distress, low-dose quetiapine (12.5-25 mg) is preferred, but it is not first-line.
key_points: DLB has high neuroleptic sensitivity, especially to typicals and risperidone
Treat reversible delirium triggers first; non-pharmacological measures next
Quetiapine 12.5-25 mg is the least bad choice if pharmacotherapy is unavoidable
Cholinesterase inhibitors can reduce visual hallucinations and behavioural symptoms
explanation.pearls: When DLB patients become agitated with delirium, fix the UTI, hydrate, analgesia and orient first; if pharmacotherapy is unavoidable, use quetiapine 12.5-25 mg orally rather than haloperidol or risperidone, which can precipitate severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guidelines for Dementia 2016

subtopic_detail: VTE duration of anticoagulation
stem: A 56-year-old woman who works as a school administrator is reviewed in your haematology clinic three months after a first unprovoked segmental pulmonary embolism. She presented at the time with breathlessness on exertion and was treated with apixaban with full clinical and radiological recovery. There is no personal or family history of malignancy, no recent surgery, immobilisation or pregnancy, and no oestrogen-containing therapy. A thrombophilia screen at three months shows no high-risk hereditary thrombophilia. Her HAS-BLED score is 1.

data_table.Examination: No leg swelling, no signs of bleeding, normal cardiopulmonary examination
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, coagulation profile normal; thrombophilia screen negative; D-dimer not indicated for treatment decision
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for ongoing anticoagulation?

options.text: Stop apixaban now at the three-month mark with no ongoing oral anticoagulation or antiplatelet substitution prescribed
options.rationale: First unprovoked PE carries a recurrence risk around 30% over five years off anticoagulation; stopping at three months is appropriate for provoked VTE with reversible trigger only. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily for a further nine months and then stop without further haematology review of risk
options.rationale: Stopping at twelve months after an unprovoked event still leaves the patient with substantial annual recurrence risk; current guidance favours indefinite anticoagulation with periodic review unless bleeding risk increases. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)

options.text: Continue extended indefinite anticoagulation with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily with annual bleeding and recurrence review
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance recommend extended anticoagulation after first unprovoked VTE; apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily after the initial treatment period maintains efficacy with reduced bleeding versus full dose. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)

options.text: Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily as ongoing long-term secondary prevention against recurrent venous thromboembolic events
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces recurrence by around 30% versus 80% with anticoagulant therapy after unprovoked VTE; it is not equivalent to extended DOAC therapy. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)

options.text: Switch to warfarin with target INR 2.0-3.0 because of well-established long-term safety data and lower drug acquisition cost
options.rationale: Warfarin and DOACs both have long-term efficacy data; switching to warfarin in a patient stable on apixaban adds INR monitoring burden without clinical benefit. (Source: THANZ guidance on VTE 2019)

explanation.summary: After a first unprovoked VTE, current Australian guidance recommends extended (indefinite) anticoagulation with periodic bleeding-risk review unless bleeding risk becomes prohibitive. Reduced-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) or reduced-dose rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) after the initial 6-month treatment period maintain efficacy versus full dose with lower bleeding risk. Aspirin is inferior to anticoagulation for recurrence prevention. Provoked VTE with a fully reversible trigger is typically anticoagulated for 3 months only.
key_points: First unprovoked VTE: extended anticoagulation with annual review
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily after initial 6 months retains efficacy with less bleeding
Aspirin reduces recurrence less than anticoagulation
Provoked VTE with reversible trigger: 3 months and stop
explanation.pearls: Step apixaban down from 5 mg twice daily to 2.5 mg twice daily at six months in extended therapy for unprovoked VTE; review HAS-BLED score and bleeding history annually to balance ongoing benefit and risk.

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax under mechanical ventilation
stem:
You are the ICU registrar called urgently to bed 4. A 64-year-old man intubated for ARDS secondary to community-acquired pneumonia three days ago suddenly becomes haemodynamically unstable. He is on volume-controlled ventilation with tidal volume 6 mL/kg, PEEP 12 cm H2O, FiO2 0.6. Over the past three minutes, peak airway pressures have risen from 28 to 46 cm H2O, plateau pressures from 22 to 38 cm H2O, BP has fallen from 118/72 to 70/40, HR has risen from 96 to 138 sinus, and SpO2 has dropped from 94% to 80%.

The trachea appears deviated to the left, the right hemithorax is hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, and there is distended neck veins. He is on noradrenaline 0.15 mcg/kg/min already.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 sinus, BP 70/40, SpO2 80%, peak airway pressure 46 cm H2O, plateau 38 cm H2O
data_table.Examination: Tracheal deviation left, hyperresonant right hemithorax, absent right breath sounds, distended neck veins, mottled peripheries
data_table.Investigations: ABG pH 7.18, PaO2 55, PaCO2 64, HCO3 22, lactate 4.6; CXR not yet taken
data_table.Medications: Noradrenaline 0.15 mcg/kg/min, propofol, fentanyl, atracurium infusions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next intervention?

options.text: Immediate finger or needle thoracostomy in the right 4th-5th intercostal space anterior axillary line followed by ICC
options.rationale: Clinical signs match tension pneumothorax superimposed on positive-pressure ventilation; immediate decompression at the safer 4th-5th ICS anterior or mid-axillary site (preferred over 2nd ICS midclavicular in ventilated adults due to chest-wall thickness) restores cardiac output, with definitive ICC to follow. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)

options.text: Briefly disconnect the ventilator and manually bag-mask ventilate to confirm tension pneumothorax before any decompression
options.rationale: Brief disconnection may transiently improve haemodynamics by reducing intrathoracic pressure but delays decompression and is not the definitive next step; the clinical picture mandates immediate thoracostomy. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)

options.text: Obtain an urgent portable supine chest radiograph for tension pneumothorax confirmation before any decompression is performed
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment must not be delayed for imaging; CXR confirmation post-decompression is acceptable. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)

options.text: Increase noradrenaline infusion to 0.5 mcg/kg/min and add vasopressin while continuing current ventilator settings unchanged
options.rationale: Vasopressor escalation cannot overcome obstructive shock from tension pneumothorax; without decompression the patient will arrest. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)

options.text: Increase PEEP to 18 cm H2O and perform a sustained-inflation lung recruitment manoeuvre on the affected hemithorax
options.rationale: Increasing PEEP and recruitment manoeuvres worsen tension pneumothorax by adding gas to the pleural space and dropping venous return further; this risks immediate cardiac arrest. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.5 Special Circumstances)

explanation.summary: Sudden rise in peak and plateau pressures with hypotension, hypoxia, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins and absent unilateral breath sounds in a ventilated patient defines tension pneumothorax. Immediate decompression is the priority and is now recommended at the 4th or 5th intercostal space anterior or mid-axillary line in adults (preferred over the historical 2nd ICS midclavicular site) because of more reliable pleural entry through thinner chest wall. Needle decompression is a temporising measure; definitive intercostal catheter insertion follows. CXR confirmation is post-decompression.
key_points: Tension pneumothorax in ventilated ARDS is the prototype of acute rise in peak/plateau pressure plus shock
Decompress at the 4th-5th ICS anterior or mid-axillary in adults (ATLS update)
Do not delay decompression for CXR confirmation
Definitive ICC follows immediately
explanation.pearls: If peak airway pressure rises more than 10 cm H2O over baseline within minutes alongside hypotension and unilateral absent breath sounds, decompress at the 4th-5th ICS mid-axillary rather than 2nd ICS midclavicular - the lateral approach has higher first-pass success in adults with thick anterior chest walls.

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis Duke criteria
stem:
A 52-year-old man presents to your emergency department with three weeks of fever, anorexia and a 4 kg unintentional weight loss. He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement nine months ago for severe aortic regurgitation. On examination he is febrile, has a soft early diastolic murmur unchanged from baseline, splinter haemorrhages on two fingers and tender nodules on his left finger pad.

Two sets of blood cultures drawn at separate venepuncture sites 12 hours apart have grown Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I). Transthoracic echo shows no clear vegetation but limited views.

data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur unchanged; Janeway lesions, Osler nodes; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Two sets blood cultures positive Streptococcus gallolyticus; CRP 96; WCC 13.2; TTE limited
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg daily; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Transoesophageal echocardiography to evaluate prosthetic valve and assess for vegetations, abscess, or new regurgitation now
options.rationale: TTE has low sensitivity for prosthetic valve endocarditis and abscess; TOE is the test of choice when there is high pretest probability with negative or non-diagnostic TTE in a prosthetic valve patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

options.text: Cardiac CT angiography with delayed-phase imaging as a first-line replacement for echocardiography to detect vegetations and abscess formation
options.rationale: Cardiac CT has a role as an adjunct, particularly for prosthetic valves and pseudoaneurysm assessment, but TOE remains the first-line imaging after non-diagnostic TTE in suspected prosthetic endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

options.text: Cardiac MRI as a first-line imaging modality to evaluate vegetations and associated annular or myocardial extension at presentation
options.rationale: Cardiac MRI is not first-line in suspected endocarditis; its role is limited compared with TOE for vegetation and abscess detection on prosthetic valves. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

options.text: Repeat transthoracic echocardiography in 48 hours with intravenous contrast to improve windows and revisit vegetation question
options.rationale: Repeat TTE adds limited yield over the initial TTE in a prosthetic valve case and delays diagnosis; TOE is significantly more sensitive and is the appropriate next step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

options.text: PET-CT with FDG to localise an occult source of bacteraemia before considering further cardiac imaging in this prosthetic valve patient today
options.rationale: FDG-PET is an adjunct supporting major Duke criteria in prosthetic valve endocarditis after at least three months, not the first imaging step in this acute presentation with persistent bacteraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis 2024)

explanation.summary: Modified Duke criteria require positive blood cultures with typical organisms plus evidence of endocardial involvement. Streptococcus gallolyticus is a typical organism. TTE has limited sensitivity for prosthetic valve endocarditis (around 50%) so TOE is the test of choice when pretest probability is high. Additionally, S. gallolyticus bacteraemia warrants colonoscopy because of its association with colorectal neoplasia. Empirical therapy in prosthetic valve endocarditis is broader than native valve and includes vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin pending sensitivities.
key_points: TTE sensitivity for prosthetic valve endocarditis is around 50%
TOE is first-line imaging when pretest probability is high
S. gallolyticus is a typical Duke organism and warrants colonoscopy
Empirical prosthetic valve cover includes vancomycin, gentamicin and rifampicin
explanation.pearls: When prosthetic valve endocarditis is clinically likely and TTE is non-diagnostic, proceed straight to TOE within 24 to 48 hours and arrange colonoscopy if blood cultures grow S. gallolyticus rather than chasing CT or PET first.

subtopic_detail: Cushing's syndrome workup
stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic with new-onset hypertension (BP 162/96 today), 9 kg weight gain over six months, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness climbing stairs, and oligomenorrhoea. On examination she has central adiposity, supraclavicular fat pads, violaceous abdominal striae greater than 1 cm wide, and thin skin. She drinks two standard drinks weekly and takes no glucocorticoids including inhaled, intra-articular, or topical products. She is otherwise well. You suspect endogenous Cushing's syndrome and need to choose an initial screening investigation.

data_table.Examination: BMI 33; supraclavicular fat pads; wide violaceous striae; proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 8.4 mmol/L (random); K 3.4; HbA1c 7.1%; normal TSH
data_table.Medications: Nil glucocorticoids; nil current antihypertensive

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial screening test?

options.text: Random morning serum cortisol with simultaneous ACTH measurement on a single clinic visit for initial screening at first presentation
options.rationale: Random cortisol has too much diurnal and stress variability to be used as a screening test for Cushing's syndrome and is not recommended at initial workup. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

options.text: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with 8 am cortisol on the following morning after the patient takes 1 mg at bedtime
options.rationale: The 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is one of three recommended first-line screens (alongside 24-hour urinary free cortisol and late-night salivary cortisol) with high sensitivity for endogenous Cushing's. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

options.text: Pituitary MRI with contrast as the initial test to identify a corticotroph adenoma before any biochemical confirmation of hypercortisolism
options.rationale: Pituitary MRI is performed only after biochemical confirmation of ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome; pituitary incidentalomas are common and imaging without biochemistry misleads. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

options.text: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling as the screening investigation to confirm pituitary versus ectopic ACTH source at first review today
options.rationale: Petrosal sinus sampling is reserved for distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH sources after biochemical confirmation and ACTH-dependence, not as a screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

options.text: CT adrenals with contrast as an initial test to identify a primary adrenal tumour before any biochemical confirmation of cortisol excess present
options.rationale: Adrenal imaging is performed after biochemical confirmation; up to 5% of adults have incidentalomas, so imaging without biochemistry leads to overdiagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing's Syndrome Guideline 2008)

explanation.summary: The Endocrine Society recommends one of three first-line screening tests for Cushing's syndrome: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol (two collections), or late-night salivary cortisol (two samples). Two abnormal first-line tests are required before further workup. Imaging is performed only after biochemical confirmation to avoid being misled by incidentalomas. Following confirmation, ACTH level dichotomises ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) causes.
key_points: Three first-line screens: 1 mg DST, 24h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol
Two abnormal screens before further workup
Imaging only after biochemical confirmation
ACTH level dichotomises dependent versus independent disease
explanation.pearls: When a patient presents with new hypertension, central weight gain and wide violaceous striae, screen with overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression (cortisol <50 nmol/L next morning excludes Cushing's) and confirm with a second first-line test before imaging.

subtopic_detail: Septic shock hour-1 vasopressor
stem: A 68-year-old man is brought to your emergency department by ambulance with fever, rigors and confusion. He has urinary frequency for three days and known benign prostatic hyperplasia. After 30 mL/kg of crystalloid over the first hour, his blood pressure remains 84/48 mmHg with MAP 60 mmHg and his lactate has risen from 3.6 to 4.2 mmol/L. Blood cultures and a urine culture have been collected and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics have been administered. There is no current contraindication to central venous access and central venous access can be obtained within 30 minutes.

data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds; mildly confused; tender suprapubic area
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 (was 3.6); WCC 18.2; Cr 142 (baseline 90); urine cloudy, leucocytes 3+
data_table.Medications: Tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next vasoactive therapy?

options.text: Start intravenous dopamine infusion at 5 micrograms per kilogram per minute as first-line vasoactive therapy via reliable peripheral access today
options.rationale: Dopamine has worse outcomes including more arrhythmias than noradrenaline in septic shock and is not recommended as first-line vasopressor. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Administer further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over the next hour as primary therapy before initiating any vasopressor infusion today
options.rationale: Beyond the initial 30 mL/kg, further fluid in vasopressor-resistant septic shock risks pulmonary oedema; vasopressor initiation is preferred to maintain MAP. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Commence intravenous noradrenaline infusion via reliable access targeting mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg and initiate central access
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis recommends commencing noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor after initial fluid resuscitation when MAP remains below 65 mmHg, including via reliable peripheral access while central access is obtained. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Administer intravenous metaraminol boluses to titrate blood pressure rather than initiating any continuous vasopressor infusion at this time today
options.rationale: Bolus metaraminol may temporise during set-up but is not a substitute for noradrenaline infusion in established fluid-refractory septic shock requiring sustained perfusion support. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
