options.text: Withhold vasopressor and re-resuscitate with 1 litre of 4% albumin instead of further crystalloid before reassessment of his perfusion status
options.rationale: Albumin may be used as an adjunct in patients receiving large-volume crystalloid resuscitation, but withholding vasopressor in fluid-refractory septic shock delays haemodynamic stabilisation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: In septic shock with MAP below 65 mmHg despite an initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor. It can be commenced via a reliable peripheral large-bore line for short durations until central venous access is obtained. Vasopressin may be added when escalating noradrenaline doses are required. Beyond the initial bolus, further fluid is guided by dynamic measures rather than empiric repeat boluses to avoid pulmonary oedema.
key_points: Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor in septic shock
Target MAP is 65 mmHg
Vasopressor may be initiated peripherally while central access is sought
Dopamine has worse outcomes than noradrenaline
explanation.pearls: If MAP remains under 65 mmHg after the initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid in septic shock, commence noradrenaline via a reliable large-bore peripheral line while obtaining central access rather than giving further empirical fluid boluses.

subtopic_detail: Hypercalcaemia differentiation
stem: A 62-year-old woman is referred to your general medical clinic after incidental hypercalcaemia on a routine panel. She is asymptomatic but admits to mild constipation. She has osteopenia on a recent bone density scan. She takes no thiazide diuretics, lithium or calcium supplements and does not smoke. Family history includes her sister having a renal stone in her thirties. On examination she is well, with no lymphadenopathy and a normal respiratory and abdominal examination. Repeat fasting bloods on a separate day confirm the abnormality. The result pattern points to a single biochemical category before further imaging.

data_table.Examination: Well; no lymphadenopathy; abdomen soft non-tender; no bony tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Corrected Ca 2.85 (RR 2.10-2.55) mmol/L; PTH 8.6 (RR 1.5-6.5) pmol/L; phosphate 0.74; 25-OH vit D 62; Cr 78; 24h urine Ca/Cr ratio 0.018
data_table.Medications: Cholecalciferol 1000 IU daily; aspirin 100 mg daily

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this biochemical pattern?

options.text: Vitamin D toxicity from prolonged supplementation with appropriately suppressed PTH and hyperphosphataemia from gut calcium absorption excess and bone resorption
options.rationale: Vitamin D toxicity suppresses PTH and is more commonly associated with elevated rather than low-normal phosphate; her PTH is elevated, ruling this out. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)

options.text: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia given inherited calcium-sensing receptor mutation with similar PTH elevation and benign clinical course over years
options.rationale: FHH typically shows a urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01; this patient's ratio of 0.018 excludes FHH on biochemistry. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)

options.text: Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy from PTH-related peptide secretion with suppressed PTH driving phosphate wasting in the renal tubule
options.rationale: Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia typically suppresses PTH; her PTH is elevated, which excludes humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)

options.text: Primary hyperparathyroidism with PTH-driven hypercalcaemia and normocalciuric phosphate-lowering profile consistent with autonomous parathyroid adenoma typically
options.rationale: Elevated calcium with non-suppressed PTH is the diagnostic pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism; the urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio above 0.01 excludes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)

options.text: Sarcoidosis driving 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in granulomas with suppressed PTH and elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in a patient with subclinical disease
options.rationale: Granulomatous hypercalcaemia produces a PTH-suppressed pattern; her elevated PTH and absence of granulomatous features make this implausible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology 2024)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia is divided into PTH-dependent (elevated or non-suppressed PTH) and PTH-independent (suppressed PTH) causes. PTH-dependent causes are primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, separated by the 24-hour urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (less than 0.01 in FHH). PTH-independent causes include malignancy (PTH-rP, lytic lesions, calcitriol-secreting lymphoma), granulomatous disease, vitamin D or A toxicity, milk-alkali syndrome and immobility. Confirmation of primary hyperparathyroidism warrants imaging only when surgery is contemplated.
key_points: Elevated calcium with non-suppressed PTH = PTH-dependent
FHH separated by calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio <0.01
Malignancy and granulomatous causes suppress PTH
Imaging only when surgery is contemplated
explanation.pearls: When hypercalcaemia presents with PTH above mid-normal and calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio above 0.01, diagnose primary hyperparathyroidism without imaging first, then refer for parathyroid scintigraphy or 4D-CT only when surgical management is indicated.

subtopic_detail: Cellulitis vs necrotising fasciitis
stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your emergency department with severe pain in his left lower leg that began yesterday after a minor garden scratch. The pain is dramatically out of proportion to the modest erythema seen on examination. Over six hours in the department the erythema has crept upward and a single haemorrhagic bulla has formed.

He is febrile and tachycardic. His bloods show neutrophil leucocytosis, sodium 130 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78), glucose 14 mmol/L, CRP 320 mg/L and lactate 3.2 mmol/L. Wound swab is pending.

data_table.Examination: Severe pain disproportionate to redness; haemorrhagic bulla; cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22; Na 130; Cr 142 (baseline 78); glucose 14; CRP 320; Hb 132; lactate 3.2; LRINEC 9
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1000 mg BD; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen referral as first-line therapy in suspected necrotising soft tissue infection with planning of operative debridement only afterwards
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is at most an adjunct after surgical debridement and broad antibiotic therapy in selected centres; it does not replace urgent operative source control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g six-hourly for presumed simple cellulitis and reassess clinical progression of the affected limb in 12 hours
options.rationale: Simple cellulitis cover does not address gas-forming organisms or polymicrobial fascial infection, and reassessment delay in suspected necrotising fasciitis costs lives; surgery within 12 hours of presentation reduces mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

options.text: MRI of the lower limb to confirm fascial involvement before any surgical consultation or empirical antibiotic escalation initiated in the department
options.rationale: Imaging delays definitive surgical exploration; necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis and surgery should not be delayed for MRI when the clinical and LRINEC suspicion is high. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin alone for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome cover without immediate surgical consultation or any antibiotic escalation today
options.rationale: IVIG is an adjunct in confirmed streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, not a substitute for source control or appropriate antibiotic combination; delay in surgery is the dominant predictor of mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for operative debridement combined with intravenous meropenem plus clindamycin while resuscitating from sepsis
options.rationale: LRINEC of 9 plus pain disproportionate to erythema, haemorrhagic bullae, rapid progression and sepsis strongly suggests necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical exploration is the only intervention that reduces mortality, with broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection requires urgent operative source control and broad-spectrum antibiotic cover with anti-toxin clindamycin. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, Cr, glucose) above 6 raises and above 8 strongly raises suspicion, but no score replaces clinical assessment. Pain disproportionate to skin findings, rapid progression, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus and systemic toxicity are red flags. Mortality rises sharply with each hour of surgical delay beyond 12 hours of presentation.
key_points: Necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis; do not delay surgery for imaging
LRINEC over 6 raises and over 8 strongly raises suspicion
Empirical cover includes broad-spectrum antibiotic plus clindamycin for toxin suppression
Mortality rises with each hour of operative delay beyond 12 hours
explanation.pearls: When LRINEC is 8 or higher with pain disproportionate to erythema and haemorrhagic bullae, call surgery within minutes and start meropenem plus clindamycin rather than waiting for MRI or persisting with simple cellulitis cover.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections 2024

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion
stem: A 31-year-old man presents to your sexual health clinic with a one-week history of fever, sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy and a faint truncal rash. He reports a high-risk condomless receptive anal intercourse exposure approximately 18 days ago with a partner of unknown serostatus. He took no post-exposure prophylaxis. His fourth-generation HIV combination antigen and antibody test today is negative. He has no other infections identified on EBV serology, throat swab or chest imaging. He asks how confident you are in excluding HIV based on the current result alone today.

data_table.Examination: Cervical lymphadenopathy; mild pharyngeal erythema; truncal maculopapular rash
data_table.Investigations: 4th-gen Ag/Ab HIV: negative; EBV IgM neg; monospot neg; CRP 56
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: HIV-1 RNA viral load by NAAT now to detect acute seroconversion within the eclipse and window phase before antibody seroconversion completes
options.rationale: Fourth-generation Ag/Ab assays can be negative during early viraemia before p24 antigenaemia rises; HIV RNA NAAT detects infection within around 10 days of exposure and is the test of choice when acute seroconversion is suspected and Ag/Ab is negative. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

options.text: Repeat 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab combination test in three months to definitively exclude infection without any further testing required today
options.rationale: A three-month repeat alone misses the acute seroconversion window now and delays diagnosis of likely current acute HIV infection in this high-risk symptomatic presentation. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

options.text: Western blot HIV antibody confirmatory test to override the screening negative and detect early seroconverting antibody bands before clinical resolution
options.rationale: Western blot is a confirmatory antibody test and is also negative in early seroconversion before antibody develops; HIV RNA NAAT is the appropriate sensitive test in this window. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

options.text: Commence empirical antiretroviral therapy now without further testing given the high pretest probability of acute HIV in this clinical presentation today
options.rationale: Empirical antiretroviral therapy without diagnostic confirmation is not standard of care; HIV RNA NAAT provides diagnostic confirmation rapidly to guide treatment initiation. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

options.text: CD4 cell count immediately to identify acute HIV-related lymphopenia as evidence of active infection before any further screening or molecular testing
options.rationale: CD4 count drops transiently in acute HIV but is non-specific and is used to stage established infection rather than diagnose acute infection in the eclipse-window phase. (Source: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy)
source_refs: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion presents 2 to 4 weeks after exposure with a mononucleosis-like illness. Fourth-generation antigen and antibody combination assays narrow but do not eliminate the diagnostic window because p24 antigenaemia can be missed in very early disease. HIV RNA NAAT detects viraemia within around 10 days of exposure and is the recommended test when acute infection is suspected and the fourth-generation result is negative. Early identification matters for prompt initiation of antiretroviral therapy and contact tracing.
key_points: Acute HIV mimics mononucleosis 2 to 4 weeks post-exposure
4th-gen Ag/Ab narrows but does not eliminate the diagnostic window
HIV RNA NAAT detects viraemia from around 10 days post-exposure
Early diagnosis enables immediate ART and contact tracing
explanation.pearls: When a sexually exposed patient presents within four weeks of risk with a mononucleosis-like illness and negative 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab, order HIV RNA NAAT immediately rather than waiting three months to repeat antibody testing.

sources.label: ASHM Australian National HIV Testing Policy

subtopic_detail: DOAC bleeding reversal
stem: A 78-year-old man on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation presents to your emergency department six hours after a witnessed unwitnessed fall at home. CT brain demonstrates a 12 mm right frontal acute subdural haematoma with 4 mm of midline shift. His last apixaban dose was four hours before his fall and his renal function is normal. The neurosurgical registrar advises operative evacuation in the next two hours. His weight is 78 kg, he has no history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and there are no contraindications to specific factor Xa inhibitor reversal.

data_table.Examination: Mild left arm weakness 4/5; PEARL; no other focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122; platelets 188; INR 1.2; Cr 78 (eGFR 78); CT: 12 mm SDH, 4 mm midline shift
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: Which reversal strategy is most appropriate before surgery?

options.text: Administer 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) 50 units per kilogram intravenously as the only available reversal in many Australian hospital sites
options.rationale: PCC is a reasonable option where andexanet alfa is unavailable, but where andexanet alfa is accessible it is the specific direct reversal agent for apixaban with stronger evidence for haemostatic efficacy in intracranial haemorrhage. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

options.text: Administer andexanet alfa via the high-dose intravenous bolus and infusion regimen because last apixaban dose was within eight hours of intracranial haemorrhage
options.rationale: Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors and is recommended for life-threatening or intracranial bleeding when last dose was within hours; the high-dose regimen applies to apixaban over 5 mg or last dose under eight hours ago. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

options.text: Administer fresh frozen plasma 15 mL per kilogram intravenously to dilute circulating apixaban and provide some non-specific factor replacement support
options.rationale: FFP does not reverse direct factor Xa inhibitors and risks volume overload without providing meaningful haemostatic benefit in DOAC-associated bleeding. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

options.text: Administer intravenous vitamin K 10 mg slowly with platelet transfusion to enhance clotting in the face of an ongoing acute intracranial haemorrhage now
options.rationale: Vitamin K does not reverse direct factor Xa inhibitors and platelet transfusion has no role unless the platelet count is critically low; neither addresses the underlying anticoagulant effect. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

options.text: Administer idarucizumab 5 g intravenously as a single dose to reverse direct anticoagulant activity prior to neurosurgical intervention proceeding
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran, not apixaban; using it would have no reversal effect on factor Xa inhibitor activity. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

explanation.summary: Life-threatening bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban is reversed with andexanet alfa where available; the high-dose regimen (800 mg bolus and 8 mg per minute infusion) applies when the apixaban dose was more than 5 mg or taken less than 8 hours before the event. Where andexanet alfa is unavailable, 4-factor PCC at 50 units per kilogram is the accepted alternative. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only. FFP, vitamin K and platelet transfusion are not appropriate substitutes for specific reversal in DOAC-associated bleeding.
key_points: Andexanet alfa specifically reverses factor Xa inhibitor activity
High-dose andexanet for apixaban over 5 mg or last dose under 8 hours ago
Idarucizumab is for dabigatran, not apixaban
4-factor PCC 50 units per kilogram is the alternative when andexanet unavailable
explanation.pearls: For apixaban-associated intracranial haemorrhage with last dose under eight hours ago, give andexanet alfa high-dose (800 mg bolus then 8 mg per minute infusion) rather than reaching for FFP, vitamin K or idarucizumab which provide no factor Xa inhibitor reversal.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion DOAC Reversal Statement 2023

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma alpha block sequencing
stem:
A 41-year-old man is referred to your endocrine inpatient team with episodic severe headache, palpitations and diaphoresis over six months, now with sustained hypertension. He has been resistant to standard agents. He is awake, alert and currently haemodynamically stable. Plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated and CT abdomen shows a 4.5 cm right adrenal mass with classic imaging features. The surgical registrar suggests starting metoprolol now for the tachycardia.

He has no current angina, no asthma, and good background renal function. He is reviewed today for medical preparation prior to laparoscopic adrenalectomy in three weeks.

data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic; otherwise well; no orthostasis on standing today
data_table.Investigations: Plasma metanephrines markedly elevated; CT 4.5 cm right adrenal mass with washout pattern; eGFR 88
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg daily; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medical preparation strategy now?

options.text: Commence amlodipine dose escalation and add an angiotensin receptor blocker alone without any specific catecholamine-targeted pharmacological preparation prior to surgery
options.rationale: Calcium channel and renin-angiotensin blockers are adjuncts only; they do not provide adequate intraoperative haemodynamic protection without alpha-blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

options.text: Commence metoprolol now to control the tachycardia and add prazosin in two weeks once heart rate is consistently below 80 beats per minute on review
options.rationale: Initiating beta-blockade before adequate alpha-blockade in phaeochromocytoma can precipitate severe hypertensive crisis through unopposed alpha vasoconstriction; this sequence is contraindicated. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

options.text: Commence phenoxybenzamine alpha-blockade titrated to mild orthostatic hypotension; introduce beta-blockade only after adequate alpha-blockade is established
options.rationale: Unopposed alpha-receptor stimulation after beta-blockade alone precipitates hypertensive crisis in phaeochromocytoma; non-selective alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine for 10 to 14 days, titrated to mild orthostasis, must precede any beta-blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

options.text: Proceed directly to laparoscopic adrenalectomy within 48 hours without any specific preoperative pharmacological preparation in a young patient at lower operative risk
options.rationale: Unprepared phaeochromocytoma surgery carries unacceptable risk of intraoperative hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia and death; 10 to 14 days of alpha-blockade is standard preparation. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

options.text: Commence labetalol monotherapy as a combined alpha- and beta-blocker for preoperative preparation given its dual receptor activity simplifying medication titration logistics
options.rationale: Labetalol has a beta-blocking effect that exceeds its alpha-blocking effect and is not recommended as monotherapy preparation for phaeochromocytoma surgery. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline 2014)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma requires careful preoperative medical preparation to prevent intraoperative haemodynamic catastrophe. Non-selective alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) or selective alpha-blockade (doxazosin or prazosin) is started 10 to 14 days preoperatively and titrated to mild orthostatic hypotension. Beta-blockade is added only after adequate alpha-blockade because beta-blockade alone unmasks unopposed alpha-vasoconstriction. Salt and fluid loading expand the contracted intravascular volume in the days before surgery. Calcium channel blockers are useful adjuncts when blood pressure remains elevated.
key_points: Alpha-blockade always precedes beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma
Phenoxybenzamine titrated to mild orthostasis for 10 to 14 days
Beta-blockade alone risks hypertensive crisis through unopposed alpha
Salt and fluid loading expand the contracted intravascular volume
explanation.pearls: When a confirmed phaeochromocytoma patient is scheduled for adrenalectomy in three weeks, start phenoxybenzamine and titrate to mild postural drop over 10 to 14 days before adding any beta-blocker, regardless of how prominent the tachycardia or anxiety symptoms appear at baseline.

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem:
A 64-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with 24 hours of rigors and confusion. He has a history of type 2 diabetes on metformin and a recent dental abscess treated with oral amoxicillin 3 days ago. He is now disoriented to time. The triage nurse documents a quick SOFA score of 3 (altered mentation, RR 28, BP 88/50).

Venous blood gas shows lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures have been drawn through a peripheral cannula. No imaging has been performed yet and no source of infection beyond the dental history is clear on initial examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 88/50, RR 28, SpO2 95% room air, Temp 39.0
data_table.Examination: Confused, dry mucous membranes; mild tenderness over right mandible; no rash; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.1, WCC 18.4, CRP 295, creatinine 168 (baseline 90), glucose 14.1

lead_in: What is the single most important next action within the hour-1 bundle?

options.text: Order a contrast-enhanced CT of the head, chest, abdomen and pelvis to identify the source before antibiotic administration
options.rationale: Imaging should not delay antibiotics in septic shock; the source is suggested by recent dental abscess, and antibiotics plus fluids are the priority within the hour-1 bundle. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign / Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Insert a central venous catheter for noradrenaline before any antibiotic administration to avoid extravasation
options.rationale: Noradrenaline can be commenced peripherally short-term while access is upgraded; delaying antibiotics for central access worsens outcome. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, give a 30 mL per kg crystalloid bolus, and start vasopressors if MAP remains below 65
options.rationale: The hour-1 bundle requires lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL per kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and vasopressors if MAP remains under 65 mmHg. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Repeat blood cultures from a second site before any antibiotic administration to maximise culture yield
options.rationale: Two sets from separate sites is ideal but should not delay antibiotics in septic shock; the goal is administration within the hour. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Administer 100 mg of hydrocortisone immediately as the priority over fluid resuscitation and antibiotic delivery
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added when shock is refractory to adequate fluid and vasopressor therapy, not before fluids and antibiotics. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

explanation.summary: Septic shock has a time-dependent mortality and the international hour-1 bundle is operationalised in Australia through Therapeutic Guidelines. Within the first hour clinicians should obtain lactate, draw blood cultures (without delaying antibiotics), administer broad-spectrum antibiotics targeting likely source, and resuscitate hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol per L with 30 mL per kg of crystalloid. Vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line) are added if MAP remains under 65 mmHg after fluids. Source identification and source control follow as resuscitation proceeds.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors if MAP <65 after fluids
Initial crystalloid 30 mL/kg for hypotension or lactate >4
Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor
Source control is parallel to, not before, resuscitation
explanation.pearls: Lactate above 4 mmol/L or MAP below 65 mmHg defines the threshold for full hour-1 resuscitation including 30 mL/kg crystalloid and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition
stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 24 hours of escalating left lower-leg pain, warmth, and a poorly demarcated erythematous patch above the medial malleolus. He is now systemically unwell with rigors. His pain is markedly out of proportion to the visual changes and he describes a numb central zone. There are no obvious skin breaks, no bullae yet, and no necrosis on inspection.

He has not travelled and has not had recent saltwater exposure. He has not had surgery. He uses metformin and atorvastatin and has no known allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 92/56, RR 26, SpO2 95% room air, Temp 39.2
data_table.Examination: Erythema ill-defined; severe pain on light palpation; central anaesthesia; no crepitus; no bullae yet
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4, Na 132, glucose 18, creatinine 158, CRP 320, Hb 132, lactate 3.4; LRINEC 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily and outpatient review in 24 hours for a moderate cellulitis
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and an LRINEC of 9 indicate possible necrotising soft tissue infection; oral therapy and outpatient review is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 6 hourly with limb elevation and re-image at 24 hours
options.rationale: IV flucloxacillin alone does not cover the polymicrobial mix typical of necrotising fasciitis; delaying surgery to await imaging worsens outcome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Activate immediate surgical review for debridement, give intravenous meropenem plus clindamycin, and resuscitate with fluids
options.rationale: An LRINEC score of 6 or more (here 9) combined with pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and central anaesthesia is highly suggestive of necrotising fasciitis; AU practice mandates urgent surgical exploration with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (meropenem) plus clindamycin for toxin suppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Order an urgent MRI of the lower limb and defer surgical consultation until imaging confirms fascial involvement
options.rationale: MRI may have a role in stable patients but should not delay surgical exploration when clinical features and LRINEC strongly suggest necrotising fasciitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence intravenous vancomycin alone empirically pending culture results from initial blood cultures and skin swab
options.rationale: Single agent vancomycin under-covers anaerobes and gram negatives that contribute to type I necrotising fasciitis; broad cover plus clindamycin is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infections classically present with pain out of proportion to visible changes, systemic toxicity, and rapidly evolving skin findings (bullae, anaesthesia, crepitus). The LRINEC score combines CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose to support recognition; a score of 6 or more is suspicious and 8 or more is high risk, although clinical judgement overrides the score. AU first-line empirical therapy is broad-spectrum cover with meropenem (or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin for toxin suppression and vancomycin if MRSA risk; urgent surgical debridement is the definitive intervention.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + systemic toxicity + LRINEC >=6 = act on suspicion
Empirical: meropenem (or pip-taz) + clindamycin + vancomycin (MRSA risk)
Urgent surgical debridement is the definitive therapy
Imaging must not delay theatre when clinical suspicion is high
explanation.pearls: LRINEC score above 6 with pain out of proportion warrants urgent surgical exploration plus meropenem + clindamycin in Australian sepsis pathways.

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated UTI in non-pregnant women
stem:
A 32-year-old non-pregnant woman attends her general practice clinic with 36 hours of dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever, no flank pain, no nausea and no vaginal discharge. She has no history of antibiotic use in the past 6 months and no recent travel. She is otherwise well, sexually active in a stable relationship, and uses combined oral contraception.

A urine dipstick in the surgery is positive for nitrites and leucocyte esterase. There is no history of recurrent UTIs and she has normal renal function.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 80, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no flank tenderness, no signs of systemic illness
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick positive for nitrites and leucocyte esterase; urine MCS not routinely required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days targeting common urinary tract gram-negative pathogen profiles
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved due to resistance and tendinopathy risk; they are not first-line for uncomplicated UTI in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin clavulanate 500 mg three times daily for 5 days as a broad-spectrum first-line agent for cystitis
options.rationale: Amoxicillin clavulanate is broader than necessary and has higher community resistance than the recommended first-line agents. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days as first-line therapy
options.rationale: AU first-line therapy for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women is trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days; both are narrow-spectrum and have low resistance rates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days based on patient preference and reported convenient twice daily dosing
options.rationale: Cefalexin is a second-line agent due to higher resistance and ecological impact; it is not the AU first-line option. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral fosfomycin 3 g as a single dose plus phenazopyridine 200 mg three times daily for symptomatic relief over 48 hours
options.rationale: Fosfomycin is an alternative for resistant organisms; phenazopyridine is not available on PBS in Australia and is not recommended routinely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated UTI in non-pregnant women is diagnosed clinically supported by urine dipstick; routine urine culture is not required unless symptoms recur or fail to respond. AU first-line treatment is trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days; both have favourable resistance and ecological profiles. Pyelonephritis (fever, flank pain, vomiting) requires broader spectrum cover and longer duration. Recurrent UTI (more than 2 in 6 months) warrants behavioural advice, self-start regimens or post-coital prophylaxis depending on triggers.
key_points: Trimethoprim 300 mg for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 5 days is first-line
Urine MCS not routinely required for uncomplicated cystitis
Pyelonephritis needs broader spectrum cover and longer course
Quinolones and broad-spectrum agents are not first-line in Australia
explanation.pearls: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic first-line for uncomplicated UTI: trimethoprim 300 mg for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 5 days.

subtopic_detail: Influenza antiviral indication
stem:
A 72-year-old man with stable congestive heart failure and type 2 diabetes presents to his general practitioner with 36 hours of fever, cough, myalgia and fatigue. There is high influenza activity in the community. He has no chest pain, no haemoptysis, no significant shortness of breath, and his observations are stable. He is fully vaccinated this season. His chest examination is clear.

Nasopharyngeal swab PCR confirms influenza A. He has not been hospitalised this year and lives independently with his wife. His current medications include perindopril, carvedilol, frusemide, metformin and atorvastatin.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 132/82, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air, Temp 38.4
data_table.Examination: Mildly fatigued; chest clear; no peripheral oedema; no signs of respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab PCR positive for influenza A; chest examination clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management decision?

options.text: Reassure, recommend rest and oral fluids, and review only if symptoms worsen significantly over coming days
options.rationale: Symptomatic management alone misses an opportunity to shorten symptom duration and reduce complication risk in a high-risk older adult with comorbidities. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AU Influenza Treatment Guidance)

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days for likely bacterial co-infection given his comorbidities
options.rationale: Antibiotics are reserved for documented or strongly suspected bacterial pneumonia, not routine influenza without focal signs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe inhaled zanamivir 10 mg twice daily for 5 days as the preferred neuraminidase inhibitor for older adults
options.rationale: Inhaled zanamivir is contraindicated in patients with chronic respiratory disease and is less practical for elderly patients; oral oseltamivir is preferred. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days starting today as treatment within 48 hours of symptom onset
options.rationale: Oral oseltamivir within 48 hours of symptom onset shortens illness and reduces complications in high-risk groups (age over 65, comorbidities); 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is the AU standard dose. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Recommend baloxavir marboxil single oral dose for first-line treatment in older adults with influenza A confirmed on PCR
options.rationale: Baloxavir is not currently first-line in Australia and access is limited; oseltamivir remains the AU standard. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Oral oseltamivir is the AU first-line antiviral for influenza, most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset. Indications include severe or progressive illness, hospital admission, and high-risk groups: age over 65, chronic cardiac, respiratory, renal, hepatic, neurological, or metabolic disease, immunosuppression, pregnancy and postpartum, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults, and morbid obesity. Vaccinated status does not preclude treatment in confirmed infection. Antibiotics are reserved for documented bacterial co-infection (otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia).
key_points: Oseltamivir 75 mg BD for 5 days is the AU first-line antiviral
Start within 48 hours of symptom onset for maximal benefit
High-risk groups include age >65, chronic disease, pregnancy, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults
Vaccination does not preclude treatment
explanation.pearls: Oseltamivir 75 mg BD for 5 days within 48 hours of symptom onset is the AU standard for influenza in older or comorbid adults.

subtopic_detail: Spontaneous pneumothorax management
stem: A 24-year-old tall thin male university student presents to the emergency department with 4 hours of sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea while sitting in a lecture. He has no past medical history, does not smoke, and takes no medications. He is haemodynamically stable, breathing comfortably and able to speak in full sentences. His chest radiograph shows a right apical pneumothorax measuring 3 cm from the chest wall at the level of the hilum. The remainder of the chest is unremarkable. There is no tension physiology and no underlying lung disease evident.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 90, BP 122/78, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Reduced breath sounds right apex, mildly hyperresonant percussion right side, trachea midline
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph right apical pneumothorax 3 cm at hilum; no underlying parenchymal disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a 28 French intercostal catheter immediately for definitive drainage and admit under cardiothoracic surgery for observation
options.rationale: Large-bore intercostal catheters are not first-line for primary spontaneous pneumothorax in stable patients; smaller-bore approaches or aspiration are preferred. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)

options.text: Reassure, discharge with simple analgesia and outpatient respiratory review in 4 weeks without any acute intervention
options.rationale: A 3 cm pneumothorax exceeds the AU threshold for conservative management at home; intervention is required as outpatient. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)

options.text: Perform needle thoracostomy at the second intercostal space midclavicular line emergently before any definitive imaging
options.rationale: Needle thoracostomy is reserved for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise; he is stable. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)

options.text: Commence non-invasive positive pressure ventilation to accelerate re-expansion of the visceral pleural defect noted today
options.rationale: Positive pressure ventilation worsens pneumothorax and is contraindicated; it does not accelerate sealing of the visceral pleural defect. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)

options.text: Perform needle aspiration with a 16G catheter and reassess radiologically; if unsuccessful insert a small-bore intercostal drain
options.rationale: AU and BTS guidance for primary spontaneous pneumothorax with size above 2 cm in a stable patient is initial needle aspiration with a small-bore catheter; if aspiration fails (residual size above 2 cm) a small-bore intercostal drain is inserted. (Source: TSANZ/BTS Pneumothorax Guideline)

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically affects tall thin young men and is graded radiologically by size (apex to cupola or chest wall at hilum), with 2 cm a common threshold. AU and BTS guidance support initial needle aspiration over routine large-bore chest drainage for primary spontaneous pneumothorax above 2 cm in stable patients; small-bore intercostal drains are second-line if aspiration fails. Large-bore drains are not first-line. Tension pneumothorax requires immediate needle decompression followed by intercostal drainage. Recurrence prompts surgical bullectomy plus pleurodesis.
key_points: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax above 2 cm in stable patient: needle aspiration first
Small-bore intercostal drain follows failed aspiration
Tension pneumothorax = immediate needle decompression then drainage
Positive pressure ventilation is contraindicated until pneumothorax drained
explanation.pearls: Stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax >2 cm in size is managed first with needle aspiration; small-bore drain follows if residual size remains >2 cm.

subtopic_detail: Myasthenic crisis acute management
stem: A 52-year-old woman with anti-acetylcholine receptor positive myasthenia gravis presents to the emergency department with worsening dyspnoea and dysphagia. She has had a vomiting illness for 36 hours and has missed her last three doses of pyridostigmine. On examination she has bilateral ptosis, a weak head lift, soft voice, paradoxical abdominal breathing, and weak cough. Her forced vital capacity at the bedside is 14 mL/kg and falling. She is alert and orientated but distressed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, RR 28 shallow, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, BP 138/82, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis; weak head lift; paradoxical abdominal breathing; weak cough; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: Bedside FVC 14 mL/kg; ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO2 52, PaO2 80, HCO3 26; CXR clear; CK normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g and admit to a high-dependency bed for monitoring
options.rationale: High-dose steroid alone risks a transient worsening of weakness and does not address the imminent respiratory failure; airway control must come first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Increase the home pyridostigmine dose and treat the underlying vomiting with intravenous ondansetron
options.rationale: Excess pyridostigmine causes a cholinergic crisis with the same neuromuscular picture; in established myasthenic crisis cholinesterase inhibitors are typically withheld until immunotherapy takes effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Trial bilevel non-invasive ventilation overnight while continuing pyridostigmine at maintenance dose
options.rationale: Non-invasive ventilation may be considered in early bulbar-sparing crisis but is unsafe when bulbar weakness, weak cough and a falling FVC compromise secretion clearance and airway protection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Intubate now with a non-depolarising relaxant avoided, then commence intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
options.rationale: Forced vital capacity at 14 mL/kg with rising PaCO2, bulbar weakness, and weak cough is myasthenic crisis; immediate intubation is required, succinylcholine and non-depolarising relaxants are avoided or carefully dose-adjusted, and definitive treatment is IVIG or plasma exchange. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Give intravenous edrophonium as a diagnostic challenge and titrate further therapy to the response
options.rationale: Edrophonium testing is no longer used in established myasthenia because of cardiac risk and adds no information when the diagnosis is already confirmed; the priority is airway control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory failure due to neuromuscular weakness and is precipitated by missed medication, infection, surgery, or new drugs that block neuromuscular transmission. A forced vital capacity below 15 mL/kg, weak cough, bulbar weakness, and rising PaCO2 are indications for intubation; do not rely on SpO2 because hypoxia is a late sign. Once airway is secured, definitive therapy is intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, with corticosteroids commenced under ventilatory cover because of the steroid dip. Pyridostigmine is usually withheld in crisis to avoid cholinergic crisis confusion and reinstated as bulbar function returns.
key_points: Intubate when FVC is below 15 mL/kg or bulbar weakness compromises the airway
Do not rely on SpO2; rising PaCO2 marks the failure
Definitive treatment is IVIG or plasma exchange
Withhold pyridostigmine during crisis to avoid cholinergic crisis overlap
explanation.pearls: The 20-30-40 rule flags impending failure: vital capacity below 20 mL/kg, inspiratory force less negative than -30, or expiratory force below 40 cmH2O. Falling FVC trumps SpO2 every time.

subtopic_detail: Bronchiectasis infective exacerbation
stem: A 58-year-old woman with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis attributable to childhood whooping cough presents to her general practice with 5 days of increased sputum volume, change to thicker yellow-green sputum, low-grade fever, and worsening exertional breathlessness compared with her usual baseline. Her routine sputum cultures over the past 2 years have grown Haemophilus influenzae only. She has not required hospital admission for 3 years and is otherwise well, taking azithromycin three times weekly as maintenance.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 95% room air, BP 128/76, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Coarse crackles at the right base; mild end-expiratory wheeze; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CXR ordered today; previous sputum cultures show Haemophilus influenzae; no Pseudomonas history

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in her antibiotic management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and switch to oral therapy after 48 hours of clinical improvement
options.rationale: Most non-Pseudomonas exacerbations of bronchiectasis are managed as out-patients with oral antibiotics for 14 days; intravenous therapy is reserved for systemic toxicity, hypoxia, or treatment failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Prescribe oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days and review with sputum culture in 1 week
options.rationale: A 5 day course is insufficient for a bronchiectasis exacerbation; standard duration is 14 days to address the infected bronchial pool. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Continue azithromycin only, reinforce airway clearance technique, and review in 7 days
options.rationale: Maintenance azithromycin is for prevention and does not provide adequate cover for an acute exacerbation; an additional 14 day course of targeted antibiotic is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Commence nebulised tobramycin twice daily as monotherapy and review with sputum culture at 48 hours
options.rationale: Inhaled tobramycin is used for chronic Pseudomonas suppression, not for an acute Haemophilus exacerbation; an oral agent with Haemophilus cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Send a sputum culture today and commence oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 14 days
options.rationale: Australian guidance recommends a 14 day oral course directed at recent sputum isolates for a bronchiectasis exacerbation without sepsis; amoxicillin-clavulanate covers Haemophilus influenzae including beta-lactamase producers and concurrent sputum culture refines therapy if treatment fails. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Acute exacerbations of bronchiectasis are defined by an increase in sputum volume or purulence, worsening breathlessness, fever, or constitutional symptoms. Out-patient management is appropriate in the absence of sepsis, hypoxia, or treatment failure. Targeted oral antibiotics for 14 days are selected on the basis of the most recent sputum culture and known colonising organisms; in non-Pseudomonas patients with prior Haemophilus, amoxicillin-clavulanate provides reliable cover. Maintenance azithromycin reduces exacerbation frequency but does not treat an acute event. A fresh sputum culture is taken before treatment to refine therapy if symptoms do not resolve.
key_points: Bronchiectasis exacerbations are treated for 14 days, not 5 to 7 days
Antibiotic choice is guided by previous sputum culture
Maintenance azithromycin reduces exacerbation rate but does not cover acute infection
IV therapy is reserved for sepsis, hypoxia or treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Always send a sputum culture before starting empirical antibiotics in bronchiectasis to capture a possible new Pseudomonas isolate that changes both the agent and the duration.

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment
stem:
A 26-year-old woman who recently arrived from Papua New Guinea attends a refugee health clinic for routine screening. She is asymptomatic, has no cough, no fevers, and no weight loss. Her chest X-ray is reported as normal with no apical scarring or cavitation. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay returns positive. She is HIV negative on rapid testing and not pregnant.

Her vaccination history includes BCG in infancy. She is not currently taking any medications and her sputum culture cannot be collected as she has no productive cough.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 118/72, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Well; chest clear; no lymphadenopathy; no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: CXR: normal lung fields; QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus: positive; HIV: negative; LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: No treatment is needed because she has had BCG and a positive QuantiFERON likely reflects vaccination
options.rationale: Interferon-gamma release assays such as QuantiFERON are not affected by BCG vaccination; a positive result reflects Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and warrants management. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

options.text: Commence empirical four-drug therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol
options.rationale: RIPE is treatment for active tuberculosis; the patient is asymptomatic with a normal chest X-ray, consistent with latent infection that does not require multi-drug therapy. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

options.text: Prescribe isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months with pyridoxine 25 mg daily and monthly LFT monitoring
options.rationale: Australian guidance treats latent TB with isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months plus pyridoxine to prevent peripheral neuropathy, with monthly LFTs to detect hepatitis; this regimen reduces lifetime progression to active TB by approximately 70 percent. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

options.text: Repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus in 3 months and treat only if the result remains positive
options.rationale: Repeating an already positive interferon-gamma release assay does not add information and delays treatment that prevents progression to active tuberculosis. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

options.text: Refer for bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage to obtain a definitive microbiological diagnosis
options.rationale: Invasive sampling is reserved for patients with clinical, radiological, or microbiological features of active tuberculosis; this patient has none. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection is asymptomatic Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection without radiological or microbiological evidence of active disease. QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus and other interferon-gamma release assays are unaffected by BCG vaccination. Once active disease is excluded by a normal chest X-ray and clinical assessment, Australian guidance recommends isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months with pyridoxine to prevent neuropathy, with monthly liver function tests to detect drug-induced hepatitis. Alternative shorter regimens include 4 months of rifampicin or 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine. Treatment reduces the lifetime risk of progression to active tuberculosis by about 70 percent.
key_points: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus is not affected by BCG vaccination
Latent TB is treated with isoniazid 9 months plus pyridoxine in AU first-line
Active disease must be excluded by CXR and symptoms before treating latent
Monthly LFT monitoring captures isoniazid hepatitis early
explanation.pearls: Add pyridoxine 25 mg with every isoniazid course to prevent peripheral neuropathy, especially in pregnant women, diabetics, and people with HIV.

sources.label: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee Australia: Latent TB

subtopic_detail: Parkinson disease initial pharmacotherapy
stem:
A 68-year-old retired carpenter is referred to neurology with a 12 month history of progressive right hand tremor at rest, micrographia, and slowing of fine finger movements. Examination shows asymmetric resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia of right hand finger tapping, and a slowed gait with reduced right arm swing. There is no postural instability and no autonomic or cognitive impairment.

An MRI brain has excluded a structural cause. He continues part-time consultancy and reports that his tremor is interfering with this work. His UPDRS motor score is 22.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 138/82 lying with no postural drop, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Asymmetric resting tremor right > left; cogwheel rigidity; bradykinesia; reduced right arm swing; no postural instability
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: normal; thyroid function normal; copper studies normal; UPDRS-III 22

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Commence carbidopa-levodopa at a low dose with gradual titration to control symptoms while maintaining function
options.rationale: In a 68 year old whose symptoms are interfering with work, levodopa provides the most reliable symptomatic benefit with the lowest short-term adverse effect burden; concerns about long-term motor complications do not justify delaying treatment that preserves function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Initiate the dopamine agonist pramipexole and titrate as tolerated to minimise long-term motor fluctuations
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists are preferred in younger patients to defer motor complications; in a 68 year old they carry significant risk of impulse control disorders, somnolence, and oedema with limited additional benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start the MAO-B inhibitor rasagiline as monotherapy and defer dopamine therapy until functional impairment increases
options.rationale: MAO-B inhibitor monotherapy provides only modest symptomatic benefit; with established functional impairment and a UPDRS of 22, deferring more effective therapy is not appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence amantadine 100 mg twice daily as initial therapy with neurology review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Amantadine has weak symptomatic effect in early Parkinson disease and is typically reserved for treating later-stage dyskinesia rather than first-line motor symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Defer all medication and refer for structured exercise therapy as the sole intervention for 6 months
options.rationale: Exercise is an important adjunct in Parkinson disease but does not substitute for symptomatic therapy in a patient whose tremor is interfering with paid work. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Initial pharmacotherapy in idiopathic Parkinson disease balances symptomatic benefit against the long-term risk of motor complications. Levodopa is the most effective symptomatic agent, has the lowest short-term adverse effect burden, and is preferred in patients over 65 or those with significant functional impairment. Dopamine agonists are favoured in younger patients to defer motor fluctuations but carry impulse control disorder, somnolence, and oedema risks that limit their use in older patients. MAO-B inhibitors provide modest symptomatic benefit. Amantadine is used for dyskinesia later in disease. Levodopa-sparing strategies are no longer recommended in older patients with functional impairment.
key_points: Levodopa is first-line in older patients with functional impairment
Dopamine agonists carry impulse control disorder risk and are avoided in the elderly
MAO-B inhibitors give only modest symptomatic benefit as monotherapy
Withholding effective therapy compromises function without preventing motor complications
explanation.pearls: In a Parkinson patient over 65 whose symptoms threaten function, start levodopa at the lowest effective dose. Reserve dopamine agonists for younger patients with intact impulse control.

subtopic_detail: Pleural effusion Light criteria
stem: A 62-year-old man with a 20 pack-year smoking history presents with 3 weeks of progressive right-sided breathlessness and a dry cough. He has lost 4 kg unintentionally. Chest X-ray shows a moderate right pleural effusion with no other parenchymal abnormality. A diagnostic thoracentesis is performed under ultrasound guidance. The pleural fluid is straw coloured. Pleural protein is 38 g/L, pleural lactate dehydrogenase is 280 U/L, pleural glucose is 4.2 mmol/L, and pleural pH is 7.42. Serum protein is 68 g/L and serum LDH is 200 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 22, SpO2 94% room air, BP 128/76, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Stony dullness, reduced breath sounds, and reduced vocal resonance over the right base; no clubbing or lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Pleural protein 38 g/L, LDH 280 U/L; serum protein 68 g/L, LDH 200 U/L; pleural glucose 4.2, pH 7.42

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Transudate consistent with cardiac failure; commence furosemide and arrange outpatient echocardiogram
options.rationale: A pleural to serum protein ratio of 0.56 and LDH ratio of 1.40 meet Light criteria for an exudate; transudate is not consistent with these values and cardiac failure is unlikely to cause weight loss. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)

options.text: Transudate consistent with hypoalbuminaemia; commence albumin replacement and review with nutrition
options.rationale: Pleural protein is high at 38 g/L; transudates have protein below 25 g/L and a ratio below 0.5; hypoalbuminaemia is not the mechanism here. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)

options.text: Equivocal sample; repeat thoracentesis in 48 hours and review with results of a paired serum sample
options.rationale: The exudate criteria are unequivocally met by both protein and LDH ratios; repeat tap is not required to confirm exudate status. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)

options.text: Chylothorax most likely; check pleural triglycerides and consider lymphatic imaging before further workup
options.rationale: Chylothorax presents with milky fluid and elevated triglycerides; a straw-coloured fluid with these biochemistry values does not fit chylothorax. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)

options.text: Exudate by Light criteria; arrange contrast CT chest and discuss with respiratory for further investigation
options.rationale: Light criteria classify an effusion as exudate if pleural-to-serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, pleural-to-serum LDH ratio exceeds 0.6, or pleural LDH exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH; the ratios here are 0.56 and 1.40, mandating workup for an exudative cause including malignancy. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Light criteria classify a pleural effusion as exudative if any one of the following is met: pleural-to-serum protein ratio above 0.5, pleural-to-serum LDH ratio above 0.6, or pleural LDH exceeding two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Exudates require investigation for cause, with malignancy, parapneumonic effusion, tuberculosis, and connective tissue disease leading the differential. In a smoker with unintentional weight loss and a unilateral exudate, malignancy is the leading concern and contrast CT chest with pleural review for image-guided pleural biopsy is appropriate. Cytology of a single tap is positive in only 60 percent of malignant effusions, so repeat sampling and biopsy may be required.
key_points: Light criteria identify exudate when any one ratio threshold is breached
Smoker with weight loss and unilateral exudate is malignancy until proven otherwise
Cytology sensitivity is around 60 percent on a single tap
Pleural biopsy is often needed to secure the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: An exudate by Light criteria in a smoker with weight loss escalates to contrast CT and respiratory review; do not rely on a single negative cytology.

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection blood pressure target
stem: A 56-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden severe tearing interscapular and chest pain 90 minutes ago. He is diaphoretic, distressed, and complains of a heavy feeling in both legs. His right arm blood pressure is 198/108 and his left arm is 162/92. ECG is in sinus rhythm with no ischaemic changes. A bedside contrast computed tomography aortogram confirms a type B aortic dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian artery with no end-organ malperfusion. He is otherwise haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP right arm 198/108, left arm 162/92, SpO2 98% room air, RR 22, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic; equal radial pulses; bilateral leg heaviness without weakness; clear chest; no peritonitis
data_table.Investigations: CT aortogram: type B dissection distal to left subclavian; troponin negative; lactate 1.4; UEC normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence intravenous glyceryl trinitrate as monotherapy targeting a systolic blood pressure below 120 mmHg
options.rationale: Nitrate monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and increases aortic shear stress; rate control with a beta blocker must precede or accompany vasodilator therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Administer intravenous nicardipine as monotherapy and titrate to systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers without rate control likewise trigger reflex tachycardia and worsen shear stress; rate control through beta blockade is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Administer thrombolysis with intravenous tenecteplase for presumed inferior myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in aortic dissection is catastrophic; the ECG and imaging exclude infarction and confirm dissection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence intravenous esmolol or labetalol to a heart rate below 60 then add nitroprusside if needed
options.rationale: In acute aortic dissection initial therapy is intravenous beta blockade to a heart rate below 60 to reduce aortic shear stress, with a vasodilator such as sodium nitroprusside added if systolic pressure remains above 120 mmHg; the goal is to reduce both pulse pressure and absolute pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Refer for emergency open surgical repair as definitive management of all uncomplicated type B dissections
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B dissection without malperfusion or rupture is initially managed medically; surgery or thoracic endovascular aortic repair is reserved for complicated disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection management focuses on reducing aortic wall shear stress, which is proportional to the rate of rise of pressure and to heart rate. First-line intravenous beta blockade with esmolol or labetalol is titrated to a heart rate below 60 bpm before adding a vasodilator such as sodium nitroprusside to achieve a systolic pressure of 100 to 120 mmHg. Vasodilator monotherapy is contraindicated because reflex tachycardia accelerates dissection propagation. Type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and requires emergency surgery. Uncomplicated type B dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian is managed medically; complicated type B with malperfusion or rupture requires TEVAR or surgery.
key_points: Reduce heart rate to below 60 before adding a vasodilator
Target systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg in acute dissection
Vasodilator monotherapy increases shear stress and is contraindicated
Uncomplicated type B dissection is initially medical, not surgical
explanation.pearls: Esmolol's short half-life allows rapid titration in dissection; achieve heart rate below 60 before reaching for nitroprusside or nicardipine.

sources.label: Heart Foundation Australia: Acute Aortic Syndromes

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis empirical antibiotics
stem: A 45-year-old previously well woman presents to the emergency department with 36 hours of right flank pain, fever, rigors, dysuria, and three episodes of vomiting. She has no history of urinary tract infection and is not pregnant. Examination reveals right costovertebral angle tenderness and a soft non-peritonitic abdomen. Urinalysis shows leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive, and blood 1+. Bloods show a white cell count of 18.5, lactate of 2.4, and creatinine of 95. A urine culture has been sent. She is unable to tolerate oral fluids.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 96/58, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 39.2, RR 22
data_table.Examination: Right costovertebral angle tenderness; soft non-peritonitic abdomen; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive; WCC 18.5; lactate 2.4; creatinine 95; urine culture sent; beta-hCG negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous amoxicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily after senior review of risks
options.rationale: Australian guidance for pyelonephritis requiring admission is IV gentamicin plus IV amoxicillin or ampicillin, with gentamicin dose adjusted for renal function and serum levels monitored; this covers the common Enterobacteriaceae and enterococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 14 days with outpatient follow-up of urine culture
options.rationale: Oral monotherapy is appropriate for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection only; this patient meets pyelonephritis criteria with systemic features and cannot tolerate oral fluids. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 1.5 g loading dose targeting MRSA cover for community-acquired sepsis
options.rationale: Vancomycin is not part of empirical pyelonephritis cover in the absence of MRSA risk factors; Gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae are the dominant pathogens. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous metronidazole 500 mg 8-hourly with intravenous fluconazole pending culture results
options.rationale: Anaerobic and fungal cover is not required for uncomplicated pyelonephritis; the pathogens are Gram-negative aerobes and enterococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 7 days with intravenous fluid resuscitation for vomiting
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin achieves adequate concentration in the bladder but not in renal parenchyma and is contraindicated in pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pyelonephritis requiring admission is treated with intravenous antibiotics targeting Enterobacteriaceae and enterococci. Australian guidance recommends intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin as first-line empirical therapy, with gentamicin dose adjusted for renal function and levels monitored if therapy continues beyond 48 hours. Switch to oral therapy is guided by clinical improvement, ability to tolerate oral intake, and urine culture sensitivities, with a total duration of 10 to 14 days. Nitrofurantoin and oral trimethoprim do not achieve renal parenchymal concentrations and are reserved for uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection. Imaging is considered for treatment failure, recurrent infection, or suspected obstruction.
key_points: Australian first-line empirical pyelonephritis cover is IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin or ampicillin
Nitrofurantoin is reserved for cystitis as renal parenchymal levels are inadequate
Oral switch is guided by clinical improvement and culture sensitivities
Total course is 10 to 14 days
explanation.pearls: Always send a urine culture before starting empirical pyelonephritis cover; the culture refines the second 7 to 10 days of therapy and detects resistance early.

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis clinically isolated syndrome
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 2 weeks of progressive painful loss of central vision in the right eye and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Six months ago she had transient left-sided weakness and numbness that resolved spontaneously over 3 weeks without medical assessment. MRI brain today shows multiple T2 hyperintense lesions in the periventricular and juxtacortical white matter, one of which enhances with gadolinium, plus a non-enhancing lesion in the cervical spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid shows two oligoclonal bands not present in serum. She is otherwise well and has no family history of demyelinating disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 118/72, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Right relative afferent pupillary defect; reduced colour vision; otherwise normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: multiple T2 lesions, one gadolinium enhancing; MRI spine: non-enhancing cervical lesion; CSF: 2 unique oligoclonal bands

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Defer all immunomodulatory therapy until a second clinical relapse confirms relapsing-remitting disease
options.rationale: Current evidence and McDonald 2017 criteria support diagnosis of multiple sclerosis after a single clinical event when imaging and CSF satisfy dissemination in space and time; deferring disease-modifying therapy loses prevention years. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin as a maintenance disease-modifying therapy with quarterly infusions
options.rationale: Intravenous immunoglobulin is not a first-line disease-modifying therapy in multiple sclerosis and is reserved for selected indications such as pregnancy planning; established DMT classes are preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Prescribe oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 6 months as long-term immunosuppression for relapse prevention
options.rationale: Long-term oral corticosteroids do not modify multiple sclerosis disease course and cause cumulative adverse effects; pulse intravenous methylprednisolone is used for acute relapses only. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Plan whole brain irradiation as definitive management of inflammatory demyelinating disease activity
options.rationale: Whole brain irradiation has no role in multiple sclerosis and would cause profound neurotoxicity; immunomodulatory disease-modifying therapy is the standard of care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Treat acute optic neuritis with pulse methylprednisolone and initiate disease-modifying therapy promptly
options.rationale: McDonald 2017 allows multiple sclerosis diagnosis when dissemination in space (multiple typical regions) and time (gadolinium-enhancing plus non-enhancing lesions, or positive CSF oligoclonal bands) are met; treatment is pulse intravenous methylprednisolone for the acute optic neuritis and prompt initiation of disease-modifying therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: McDonald 2017 criteria allow diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis after a single clinical event when dissemination in space and time are demonstrated by imaging or by positive cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands. Acute optic neuritis is treated with pulse intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days, which speeds recovery but does not change long-term outcome. Disease-modifying therapy is initiated as soon as diagnosis is confirmed because early therapy reduces long-term disability; high-efficacy options including ocrelizumab and natalizumab are increasingly used first-line in patients with active disease. Pregnancy planning, comorbidities, and JC virus serology guide drug selection.
key_points: McDonald 2017 allows diagnosis from a single attack when DIS and DIT are met
Positive CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for DIT under McDonald 2017
Pulse methylprednisolone treats acute relapses; DMT modifies disease course
Early initiation of high-efficacy DMT improves long-term outcomes
explanation.pearls: Oligoclonal bands in CSF that are not present in serum substitute for dissemination in time under McDonald 2017, allowing diagnosis from a single relapse.

subtopic_detail: Adult anaphylaxis immediate IM adrenaline dose
stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department after 15 minutes of progressive lip and tongue swelling, audible wheeze, and lightheadedness during a restaurant meal. He has a known allergy to tree nuts and forgot to bring his autoinjector. On arrival he is anxious, generalised urticaria is visible, his tongue is swollen but he is still phonating, and his peripheries are cool. He weighs 78 kg. He has no other medical conditions and is on no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, RR 28, SpO2 92% room air, BP 86/52, Temp 36.5
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria; tongue swelling without stridor; bilateral wheeze; CRT 4 seconds; alert
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; allergy referral after stabilisation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg of 1:1000 solution into the anterolateral mid-thigh and prompt reassessment cycle
options.rationale: ASCIA recommends 0.5 mg IM adrenaline from a 1:1000 ampoule into the anterolateral mid-thigh for adults with anaphylaxis featuring airway or circulatory involvement, repeated every 5 minutes if response is inadequate. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 1 mg of 1:10000 solution given as a slow push under continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline in anaphylaxis is reserved for refractory cases or arrest under intensive monitoring; first-line in spontaneously breathing adults is intramuscular dosing because of the lower arrhythmia risk. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg with intravenous promethazine 25 mg as initial pharmacological treatment given
options.rationale: Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts and do not treat the airway and cardiovascular components of anaphylaxis; delaying adrenaline to give them increases mortality. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg with high-flow oxygen 15 L per minute and a 1 litre crystalloid bolus through wide cannula
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline targets upper airway oedema as adjunct only; systemic anaphylaxis with hypotension requires intramuscular adrenaline as the immediate primary intervention. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Subcutaneous adrenaline 0.5 mg from a 1:1000 ampoule given into the upper arm with airway adjunct preparation
options.rationale: Subcutaneous adrenaline has slow and unpredictable absorption due to peripheral vasoconstriction; intramuscular delivery into the thigh is the correct route. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

explanation.summary: Adult anaphylaxis is treated with 0.5 mg intramuscular adrenaline from a 1:1000 ampoule injected into the anterolateral mid-thigh.
