The dose is repeated every 5 minutes if response is inadequate, with concurrent supine positioning, high-flow oxygen, intravenous crystalloid for hypotension, and salbutamol or nebulised adrenaline as adjuncts. Intravenous adrenaline is reserved for refractory cases under monitoring.
key_points: Adult IM adrenaline dose is 0.5 mg of 1:1000
Anterolateral thigh, not deltoid or subcutaneous
Repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement
IV adrenaline only for refractory anaphylaxis under monitoring
explanation.pearls: ASCIA adult anaphylaxis: 0.5 mg of 1:1000 adrenaline IM into anterolateral mid-thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if needed; IV reserved for refractory cases.

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis modified Duke criteria
stem: A 56-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replaced 14 months ago presents with three weeks of fever, weight loss, and night sweats. He has had two intervening dental procedures without prophylaxis. His blood cultures from two separate venepuncture sites taken 12 hours apart have grown viridans group streptococci. A transthoracic echocardiogram is poor quality and inconclusive. A transoesophageal echo is awaited. The patient is otherwise haemodynamically stable on the ward.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, Temp 38.4
data_table.Examination: Soft early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge; nil splinter haemorrhages or Janeway lesions noted today
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 102 mg/L, Hb 105 g/L, Cr 92 micromol/L; ECG sinus tachycardia, no new conduction; TTE non-diagnostic

lead_in: How is this patient classified under the modified Duke criteria at present?

options.text: Definite infective endocarditis on the strength of pathological criteria from histology and microbiology already
options.rationale: Pathological Duke criteria require tissue or vegetation specimens with histological or microbiological proof; without surgery these are not available, and definite IE must be reached via clinical criteria. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

options.text: Possible infective endocarditis pending transoesophageal echo result and a documented new regurgitant murmur
options.rationale: Possible IE applies when one major and one minor, or three minor criteria, are met; this patient already has two major criteria once typical organism in two cultures is combined with the new regurgitant murmur evidence. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

options.text: Definite infective endocarditis fulfilled by two clinical major criteria from typical organism and new regurgitation
options.rationale: Two separate cultures of viridans streptococci constitute one major criterion, and a new regurgitant murmur in a prosthetic valve patient constitutes the second major (evidence of endocardial involvement); two major criteria satisfy definite IE. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

options.text: Rejected diagnosis because transthoracic echocardiogram failed to visualise vegetations and patient remains stable
options.rationale: A non-diagnostic TTE does not reject IE; in prosthetic valves TOE is required and patients with persistent bacteraemia and typical organisms remain in possible or definite categories. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

options.text: Definite infective endocarditis based on one major criterion only with multiple supportive minor criteria currently
options.rationale: One major plus three minor would meet definite IE, or two major; the question stem documents one major (organism) and the new murmur (a second major), so the categorisation rests on two major criteria rather than the minor mix. (Source: ESC Endocarditis Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Modified Duke criteria diagnose definite IE when two major, or one major and three minor, or five minor clinical criteria are met. Major criteria include typical organisms in two blood cultures from separate sites and evidence of endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, new partial dehiscence, or new regurgitant murmur). Pathological diagnosis requires tissue from surgery or autopsy. A negative TTE does not reject IE; TOE is required in prosthetic valves and high-risk cases.
key_points: Definite IE: 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor
Typical organism in 2 separate cultures = major
New regurgitant murmur or vegetation = major
Negative TTE never rejects IE in prosthetic valves; TOE mandatory
explanation.pearls: Two separate cultures of viridans strep plus a new regurgitant murmur in a prosthetic valve patient = two Duke major criteria = definite IE without needing echo confirmation.

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia CURB-65 site of care
stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 3 days of productive cough, fevers, and dyspnoea. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He lives alone and is independent at baseline. On examination he is alert with focal right basal crepitations, oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, and a respiratory rate of 32. Chest x-ray confirms right lower lobe consolidation. He has not previously had pneumonia and has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Examination: Right basal crackles; no signs of consolidation outside; alert; mildly confused (AMTS 8/10)
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, CRP 162, urea 9.4 mmol/L, Cr 110 micromol/L, BSL 12.4 mmol/L; CXR: right lower lobe consolidation; lactate 1.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate site of care and empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Discharge with oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days and general practitioner review in 48 hours
options.rationale: CURB-65 here is at least 4 (confusion, urea over 7, RR at least 30, BP under 90/60-borderline, age 65+), placing the patient at high risk and mandating inpatient management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

options.text: Admit to short-stay unit on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate with planned discharge within 24 hours of presentation
options.rationale: Short-stay with oral therapy is suited to low-to-moderate severity disease; this patient's vitals and biochemistry place him in moderate-to-severe CAP requiring intravenous therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

options.text: Admit to general medical ward on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Moderate-severity CAP in an Australian inpatient is treated with IV benzylpenicillin plus an atypical-cover agent such as doxycycline; SMART-COP can refine ICU referral but ward admission is appropriate when oxygen and perfusion are correctable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

options.text: Admit to intensive care unit with intravenous meropenem and intravenous vancomycin to cover all resistant organisms
options.rationale: Empiric meropenem and vancomycin are reserved for severe CAP with risk factors for resistant pathogens or in immunocompromise; this presentation lacks those features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

options.text: Admit to general medical ward on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is reserved for moderate-severe CAP with intolerance or local resistance concerns; the Australian first-line in moderate disease is IV benzylpenicillin plus an oral atypical agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - CAP)

explanation.summary: Australian CAP management uses CURB-65 (or SMART-COP) to direct site of care. Score 0 to 1 typically outpatient with oral amoxicillin; 2 inpatient on oral or IV therapy; 3 or more inpatient with IV therapy and consider ICU. Moderate CAP empiric therapy is IV benzylpenicillin with an oral atypical agent (doxycycline preferred over macrolide in Australia for stewardship). Severe disease or septic shock prompts ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and ICU.
key_points: CURB-65 of 3 or more = inpatient IV therapy
AU first line moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin + doxycycline
SMART-COP refines ICU referral
Doxycycline preferred over azithromycin for atypical cover in AU
explanation.pearls: CURB-65 in this case: confusion + urea over 7 + RR over 30 + age 65+ = 4 - inpatient IV therapy mandated; AU first line is benzylpenicillin + doxycycline.

sources.label: TSANZ Position Statement: Community-acquired pneumonia in adults

subtopic_detail: ANCA-associated vasculitis pattern recognition
stem: A 64-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 6 weeks of progressive nasal crusting, recurrent epistaxis, hearing loss, and intermittent haemoptysis. Over the past week she has noticed dark urine. Her bloods are remarkable for raised inflammatory markers and a rising creatinine. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and proteinuria. She is afebrile, alert, and her chest x-ray shows multiple non-cavitating peripheral nodules. ANCA testing has been requested. She is referred urgently to medical assessment.

data_table.Examination: Crusting nasal septum; saddle-nose deformity early; conductive hearing loss; no focal neurology; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Cr 168 micromol/L (baseline 78); urine PCR 280 mg/mmol, RBCs and casts; CRP 92 mg/L; ANCA pending; CXR with multiple non-cavitating peripheral nodules

lead_in: What is the most likely ANCA pattern in this presentation?

options.text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody (anti-GBM) positivity without ANCA positivity in the typical case
options.rationale: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture) causes pulmonary-renal syndrome but is not associated with sinonasal or otological involvement and typically lacks the granulomatous upper airway disease seen here. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)

options.text: Cytoplasmic ANCA pattern targeting proteinase-3 (PR3-ANCA), classically associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis
options.rationale: Upper respiratory tract granulomatous involvement (sinusitis, saddle nose, hearing loss) with renal and pulmonary disease is classic for granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which most commonly shows cytoplasmic ANCA staining with PR3 specificity. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)

options.text: Perinuclear ANCA pattern targeting myeloperoxidase, classically associated with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
options.rationale: EGPA (Churg-Strauss) typically features asthma, blood eosinophilia, and migratory pulmonary infiltrates with peripheral neuropathy; upper airway destructive disease is not its signature. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)

options.text: Atypical ANCA pattern with no recognised target antigen, classically associated with secondary drug-induced vasculitis
options.rationale: Drug-induced ANCA vasculitis is typically MPO-ANCA, and the granulomatous upper airway picture is not characteristic of these atypical patterns. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)

options.text: Negative ANCA testing with positive cryoglobulins and reduced complement levels, classically suggesting cryoglobulinaemia
options.rationale: Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis typically presents with palpable purpura, peripheral neuropathy, and low complement, often with hepatitis C; the destructive upper airway picture is not characteristic. (Source: KDIGO Glomerular Diseases Guideline 2021)

explanation.summary: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener) classically presents with granulomatous involvement of the upper airway (chronic sinusitis, nasal crusting, saddle nose, hearing loss), lower airway (cavitating or non-cavitating nodules), and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with red cell casts and proteinuria. Cytoplasmic ANCA targeting PR3 is the typical pattern. Microscopic polyangiitis is more often pauci-immune renal disease with MPO-ANCA. EGPA features asthma, eosinophilia, and neuropathy.
key_points: GPA: upper airway destruction + pulmonary nodules + RPGN
GPA typically c-ANCA targeting PR3
MPA typically p-ANCA targeting MPO; pauci-immune renal
EGPA: asthma + eosinophilia + neuropathy; often MPO-ANCA
explanation.pearls: Pattern recognition for GPA: saddle nose + sensorineural or conductive hearing loss + cavitating or non-cavitating lung nodules + RPGN with red cell casts = c-ANCA/PR3.

sources.label: EULAR/ERA-EDTA recommendations for the management of ANCA-associated vasculitis

subtopic_detail: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN early recognition
stem: A 32-year-old man on day 14 of carbamazepine for newly diagnosed epilepsy presents with 24 hours of malaise, fever, and a painful pink macular rash on his torso. By the time he reaches the emergency department, he has developed early painful blistering of the oral mucosa, conjunctival hyperaemia, and Nikolsky-positive areas covering an estimated 12 percent of his body surface area. He is haemodynamically stable but visibly uncomfortable. His other medications include paracetamol PRN and a probiotic. There is no preceding upper respiratory infection.

data_table.Examination: Pink macular rash on trunk and limbs; Nikolsky positive on shoulder; lip and oral mucosal erosions; bilateral conjunctival injection
data_table.Investigations: Hb 138 g/L, WCC 11.2 x10^9/L, CRP 64 mg/L, Cr 84 micromol/L, ALT 92 U/L; urea 5.2; bicarbonate 22

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Cease the carbamazepine and arrange urgent transfer to a tertiary burns unit with multidisciplinary support
options.rationale: SJS/TEN is a dermatological emergency; the culprit drug must be ceased and patients should be transferred to a burns unit for fluid balance, wound care, ophthalmology, urology and pain support, especially with epidermal detachment over 10 percent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)

options.text: Continue carbamazepine because of seizure risk and treat the rash with potent topical corticosteroids and emollients
options.rationale: The culprit drug must be stopped immediately; continuing it risks progression to TEN with much higher mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)

options.text: Start empirical intravenous flucloxacillin for presumed staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome until cultures available
options.rationale: SSSS occurs predominantly in children and lacks mucosal involvement; mucosal involvement with a drug exposure makes SJS/TEN the working diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)

options.text: Admit under dermatology to the general ward and commence high-dose oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for skin involvement
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids have mixed evidence in SJS/TEN and are not first-line; burns-unit-level supportive care, often with cyclosporine or IVIG depending on local protocol, is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)

options.text: Wait 48 hours to see whether erythema multiforme resolves spontaneously before triggering specialty referral pathways
options.rationale: Erythema multiforme is target lesions on extremities without significant epidermal detachment; Nikolsky positivity and 12 percent BSA detachment are SJS-TEN overlap and require urgent escalation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology - SCAR)

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis sit on a spectrum defined by epidermal detachment: SJS under 10 percent BSA, overlap 10 to 30, TEN over 30. Carbamazepine is a major culprit and may have HLA-B*15:02 association in some populations. Immediate steps are to cease the culprit drug, transfer to a burns unit, and provide multidisciplinary supportive care including fluids, eye care, urinary, and pain. Mortality rises sharply with later cessation of the culprit drug.
key_points: SJS under 10 percent BSA; overlap 10 to 30; TEN over 30
Cease culprit drug immediately and transfer to burns unit
Carbamazepine is a high-risk culprit
Systemic steroids are not first line; supportive care primary
explanation.pearls: SJS/TEN: cease culprit drug (often allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, sulfa, NSAID) and transfer to burns unit; SCORTEN within 24 h predicts mortality.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists position on SJS/TEN

subtopic_detail: DVT 2-level Wells score and pathway
stem: A 58-year-old woman presents to her general practice with 4 days of left calf swelling, pain, and tenderness. She returned from a 12-hour flight from Singapore 6 days ago. She has a history of stage II breast cancer 18 months ago treated with lumpectomy and tamoxifen, but no active disease. Her left calf is 4.5 cm larger than her right and she has pitting oedema. There is no evidence of an alternative diagnosis on examination. She is haemodynamically stable and walks unaided. She has no history of bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 124/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Left calf 4.5 cm > right; pitting oedema; tenderness along deep venous system; superficial veins not prominent; no cellulitis
data_table.Investigations: FBC and renal function normal; D-dimer pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange D-dimer first and proceed to ultrasound only if positive without calculating a Wells probability score
options.rationale: D-dimer is unreliable as a standalone test; the recommended pathway uses risk stratification first then D-dimer or ultrasound depending on probability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

options.text: Refer immediately for inferior vena cava filter placement to prevent pulmonary embolism while diagnosis is being confirmed
options.rationale: IVC filters are reserved for confirmed VTE with anticoagulation contraindication or breakthrough VTE on anticoagulation; they are not used presumptively. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

options.text: Discharge with leg elevation and a compression stocking and review in 1 week if symptoms have not resolved fully
options.rationale: A patient with multiple risk factors and clinical signs of DVT must not be discharged without proceeding through the diagnostic pathway; missed DVT carries PE risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

options.text: Calculate Wells score; if DVT likely, arrange same-day proximal compression ultrasound and consider therapeutic anticoagulation pending result
options.rationale: With recent immobility, active cancer history, calf swelling over 3 cm, pitting oedema, and tenderness, Wells score is high; the pathway is direct compression ultrasound rather than D-dimer because high pre-test probability undermines D-dimer specificity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

options.text: Commence empirical oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for presumed cellulitis given calf erythema and warmth
options.rationale: Calf swelling with tenderness in a high-risk patient is DVT until proven otherwise; antibiotics for presumed cellulitis without erythema typical of infection delays appropriate investigation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - VTE)

explanation.summary: The 2-level Wells score for DVT stratifies into likely (2 or more) or unlikely (1 or less). DVT-likely patients proceed to proximal compression ultrasound. DVT-unlikely patients have a D-dimer; positive D-dimer triggers ultrasound. Therapeutic anticoagulation is started pending ultrasound when delay is expected and bleeding risk is acceptable. Confirmed proximal DVT is treated with anticoagulation for at least 3 months, with extended duration if unprovoked or cancer-associated.
key_points: Wells 2+ goes to ultrasound directly
Wells under 2 uses D-dimer first
Cancer or active malignancy scores 1
Empirical anticoagulation if delay to scan and acceptable bleeding risk
explanation.pearls: DVT pathway: calculate 2-level Wells - likely (2+) goes to direct USS, unlikely uses D-dimer; high pre-test probability invalidates D-dimer.

subtopic_detail: Hypertension diagnosis confirmation with ABPM
stem: A 48-year-old woman attends her general practice for a routine review. Three separate in-clinic blood pressure readings over 6 weeks have been 152/94, 148/92, and 156/96 using a calibrated upper-arm device. She is asymptomatic, has no diabetes, and has no end-organ damage on initial screening. Her lipids and ECG are unremarkable. Her absolute cardiovascular risk is calculated as moderate. She is keen to know whether she has hypertension that warrants pharmacotherapy or whether further confirmation is appropriate before treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Clinic BP 152/94 (today), HR 76, BMI 26
data_table.Examination: No end-organ examination findings; cardiovascular and respiratory examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm with no LVH criteria; eGFR 92 mL/min; urinary ACR 1.2 mg/mmol; lipids HDL 1.3, LDL 3.4, TG 1.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start perindopril 4 mg daily today based on consistent in-clinic readings above the threshold for stage 1 hypertension
options.rationale: NHF guidance recommends out-of-office confirmation by ABPM or HBPM before commencing pharmacotherapy in most cases to exclude white-coat effect, unless severely elevated or evidence of end-organ damage. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

options.text: Repeat clinic blood pressure measurement in 12 months without confirmatory home or ambulatory blood pressure assessment
options.rationale: Persistent elevated clinic readings require timely confirmation; deferring assessment 12 months risks ongoing exposure to elevated pressures if true hypertension. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

options.text: Arrange polysomnography for obstructive sleep apnoea screening before any further diagnostic blood pressure measurement
options.rationale: OSA assessment is appropriate when there are specific signs or refractory hypertension; it is not the first step in confirming a hypertension diagnosis. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

options.text: Refer to endocrinology for plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio testing to exclude primary hyperaldosteronism before treatment
options.rationale: Secondary hypertension work-up is indicated in resistant, severe, or early-onset disease or with suggestive features; it is not first-line for moderate sustained hypertension. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

options.text: Arrange 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring or 7-day home BP averages, treating if daytime average above 135/85
options.rationale: NHF Australia recommends ABPM or HBPM to confirm hypertension before pharmacotherapy in most patients; the diagnostic threshold is daytime average over 135/85 (ABPM/HBPM), which corresponds to clinic over 140/90. (Source: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

explanation.summary: Australian hypertension diagnosis requires confirmation of sustained elevation, typically by ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring before commencing treatment, except in severely elevated readings or when end-organ damage is present. Diagnostic thresholds: clinic over 140/90, ABPM daytime average over 135/85, HBPM 7-day average over 135/85. Treatment decisions also account for absolute cardiovascular risk and target lower BP thresholds in higher-risk groups.
key_points: Confirm with ABPM or HBPM before treating
ABPM/HBPM threshold 135/85; clinic 140/90
Absolute CV risk drives treatment decisions
Treat immediately if severely elevated or end-organ damage
explanation.pearls: NHF Australia: confirm hypertension with ABPM (daytime average over 135/85) or 7-day HBPM averages over 135/85 before treating; clinic 140/90 alone is insufficient unless severe or end-organ damage.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation Australia Hypertension Guideline 2016

subtopic_detail: Pleural effusion Light's criteria interpretation
stem: A 67-year-old man presents with 2 weeks of progressive dyspnoea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and recently lost 5 kg unintentionally. Chest x-ray shows a large right pleural effusion and CT chest demonstrates pleural thickening with no obvious mass. Diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. The serum LDH is 220 U/L (upper limit of normal 240) and serum protein 68 g/L. The pleural fluid analysis is shown. He is afebrile.

data_table.Examination: Right basal stony dullness; reduced breath sounds; no consolidation; no peripheral oedema; JVP not raised
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid: protein 38 g/L, LDH 220 U/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L, pH 7.36; cytology pending; AFB and culture sent. Serum LDH 220 U/L (ULN 240), serum protein 68 g/L

lead_in: How is this pleural effusion best classified using Light's criteria?

options.text: Transudate because the pleural fluid LDH is below the upper limit of normal serum LDH despite raised protein
options.rationale: Light's criteria require only ONE positive criterion to label exudate; the pleural protein to serum protein ratio above 0.5 already meets criteria, making this an exudate. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)

options.text: Transudate consistent with cardiac failure because the patient has a smoking history and dyspnoea on exertion
options.rationale: Clinical impression cannot override Light's biochemical criteria; pleural protein to serum protein ratio of 0.56 categorically meets exudate criteria. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)

options.text: Exudate, but only if pleural fluid LDH exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH for laboratory comparison
options.rationale: Pleural LDH above two thirds of ULN serum is just one of three criteria; this case meets the protein ratio criterion regardless of whether the LDH criteria is met. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)

options.text: Transudate based on the pleural fluid to serum LDH ratio being below 0.6 and otherwise unremarkable biochemistry
options.rationale: Light's criteria use ANY one of three positive results to label exudate; the protein ratio criterion is met (0.56 over 0.5), making this an exudate irrespective of the LDH ratio. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)

options.text: Exudate because the pleural fluid to serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, requiring investigation for cause including malignancy
options.rationale: Light's criteria: ANY one of pleural protein/serum protein over 0.5, pleural LDH/serum LDH over 0.6, or pleural LDH over two thirds of ULN serum LDH defines exudate; protein ratio 38/68 = 0.56 meets criteria. (Source: Light's Pleural Effusion Criteria)

explanation.summary: Light's criteria classify a pleural effusion as exudative if any one of the following is positive: pleural protein to serum protein ratio over 0.5, pleural LDH to serum LDH ratio over 0.6, or pleural LDH greater than two thirds of upper limit of normal serum LDH. Exudates require workup for causes including malignancy, infection, pulmonary embolism, and connective tissue disease. Pleural fluid cytology, microbiology, and imaging guide further evaluation; thoracoscopy may be needed when cytology is non-diagnostic.
key_points: ANY one positive criterion = exudate
Protein ratio over 0.5 alone is sufficient
Exudates: malignancy, infection, PE, connective tissue disease
Cytology, microbiology, thoracoscopy as needed for cause
explanation.pearls: Light's criteria: ANY one of pleural/serum protein over 0.5, pleural/serum LDH over 0.6, or pleural LDH greater than two thirds ULN serum LDH defines exudate.

subtopic_detail: Glycaemic target in frail elderly with hypoglycaemia history
stem:
An 84-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (diagnosed 22 years ago), background mild cognitive impairment, stage 3a CKD (eGFR 48), polypharmacy and one fall in the past month attends his GP for diabetic review. He lives alone with home care twice daily. His current HbA1c is 6.5 percent (48 mmol/mol). He has had two episodes of symptomatic hypoglycaemia (BSL under 3.5 mmol/L) in the past 6 weeks, one requiring family call-out.

His treatment is metformin 500 mg BD, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, and basal insulin glargine 14 units nocte. He has no known retinopathy and his most recent foot check was satisfactory.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 132/78, BMI 24, weight 68 kg
data_table.Examination: Frail appearance, normal cardiorespiratory, no peripheral oedema, intact monofilament sensation feet, gait slow with frame indoors
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 6.5 percent (48 mmol/mol); eGFR 48; ACR 8 mg/mmol; LFT normal; B12 240 pmol/L; lipids LDL 1.9
data_table.Medications: Metformin 500 mg BD, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily, insulin glargine 14 units nocte, perindopril 4 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in glycaemic management?

options.text: Continue current regimen but add a continuous glucose monitor for 14 days then reassess with the family at the next routine clinic visit
options.rationale: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia and a fall already document inappropriate over-treatment; treatment de-escalation should not wait for further monitoring data before action. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

options.text: Aim for tighter HbA1c at 6 percent (42 mmol/mol) by intensifying basal insulin and adding prandial insulin to reduce risk of long-term diabetic complications
options.rationale: Tight HbA1c targets in frail elderly increase mortality and disability from hypoglycaemia without microvascular benefit at this life-expectancy and disease duration; deintensification is recommended. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

options.text: Cease metformin first to reduce gastrointestinal side effects then review the rest of his diabetes regimen in 6 weeks at the next routine appointment
options.rationale: Metformin is not the cause of hypoglycaemia and is well tolerated; ceasing it leaves the gliclazide and insulin (the drivers of hypoglycaemia) untouched and worsens overall regimen. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

options.text: Switch gliclazide to a daily SGLT2 inhibitor for cardiorenal benefit and continue insulin and metformin at the same doses with weekly home checks
options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors have cardiorenal benefit but bring increased fall risk through volume depletion and increased risk of urinary infection and DKA in frail elderly; first priority is to remove the agent driving hypoglycaemia. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

options.text: Cease gliclazide and reduce insulin glargine by 2 units, targeting HbA1c 7.5 to 8.5 percent (58 to 69 mmol/mol) appropriate for a frail older adult at risk
options.rationale: Frail elderly with limited life expectancy, hypoglycaemia and falls have a relaxed HbA1c target of 7.5 to 8.5 percent (58 to 69 mmol/mol); ceasing the sulfonylurea (highest hypoglycaemia risk drug) and reducing basal insulin is the recommended deintensification. (Source: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults)
source_refs: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults

explanation.summary: Australian guidelines individualise HbA1c targets in older adults with type 2 diabetes by frailty, life expectancy, hypoglycaemia risk and patient preference. Healthy older adults target around 7 percent (53 mmol/mol); frail elderly with multiple comorbidities target 7.5 to 8.5 percent (58 to 69 mmol/mol); end-of-life targets focus on symptom avoidance. Sulfonylureas and insulin are the highest hypoglycaemia risk drugs in this group; metformin (if eGFR appropriate) is preferred for ongoing therapy. Deintensify treatment after hypoglycaemia or falls.
key_points: Healthy older adults: HbA1c ~7 percent.
Frail elderly: HbA1c 7.5-8.5 percent.
End-of-life: symptom-focused.
Sulfonylurea + insulin = highest hypoglycaemia risk; cease first.
explanation.pearls: Document and act on every symptomatic hypoglycaemic episode in elderly diabetes patients; one severe hypoglycaemic event doubles 5-year mortality risk and is a stronger indicator than any HbA1c value.

sources.label: Diabetes Australia: Glycaemic Targets in Older Adults
RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

subtopic_detail: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes acute treatment
stem: A 62-year-old man with stage 4 CKD (baseline creatinine 280, eGFR 18) on long-term perindopril and spironolactone presents to ED with 2 days of vomiting, diarrhoea, and now muscle weakness and palpitations. He has not been eating but has continued his usual medications. He looks unwell, mildly hypovolaemic and dyspnoeic. On examination he is alert. The bedside ECG taken 5 minutes ago shows broad-based QRS at 152 ms with tall symmetrical peaked T waves in all precordial leads and absent P waves. Urgent VBG shows potassium 7.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 58, BP 102/64, RR 22, SpO2 96% air, T 36.4, weight 78 kg
data_table.Examination: Sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, JVP not seen, chest clear, no focal neurology, generalised proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: VBG K 7.4, Na 134, HCO3 16, lactate 1.9, ionised Ca 1.10. Creatinine 412, eGFR 12; ECG: peaked T, broad QRS 152 ms, absent P
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, frusemide 40 mg, paracetamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first step in management?

options.text: Intravenous 10 percent calcium gluconate 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes by slow push with continuous cardiac monitoring throughout the administration
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemic ECG changes with QRS widening require immediate myocardial membrane stabilisation; IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes acts within minutes and is given before any potassium-shifting therapy. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

options.text: Activate the renal registrar for emergency haemodialysis as the first definitive treatment while no other temporising measure is attempted yet
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is the definitive treatment but takes time to mobilise; immediate temporising treatment (calcium then insulin-dextrose) cannot be deferred while waiting for vascular access and dialysis circuit setup. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

options.text: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g orally as a one-off dose to remove potassium from the gut while awaiting renal replacement therapy review
options.rationale: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is slow (hours) and not first-line for life-threatening hyperkalaemia; it does not stabilise the myocardium and risks bowel necrosis in unwell patients. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

options.text: Intravenous actrapid (soluble) insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose over 15 minutes as the first intervention before any other therapy
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose shifts potassium into cells over 30 to 60 minutes but does not stabilise the myocardium; calcium must be given first when ECG changes are present. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

options.text: Salbutamol 10 mg nebulised over 10 minutes as a single agent treatment while ECG monitoring continues with bedside cardiac team
options.rationale: Nebulised salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly but takes 30 minutes to act and is not enough in a haemodynamically unstable patient with QRS broadening; cardiac stabilisation comes first. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Recommendations)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.5 mmol/L or any value with ECG changes) is a medical emergency. The sequence is: cardiac monitoring, IV calcium (10 percent gluconate 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes or 10 percent chloride 10 mL via central line) to stabilise the myocardium, then potassium-shifting therapy with insulin-dextrose (10 units actrapid plus 50 mL 50 percent dextrose), nebulised salbutamol 10 mg, and consideration of sodium bicarbonate if metabolic acidosis. Definitive removal is haemodialysis or correction of cause (cease ACE inhibitor and spironolactone, treat hypovolaemia). Calcium binds to cardiac sodium channels within minutes but does not lower the potassium.
key_points: Calcium first if ECG changes (stabilises myocardium).
Then insulin-dextrose + salbutamol (shifts K intracellularly).
Definitive: dialysis, cease offending drugs.
Repeat ECG and potassium after each intervention.
explanation.pearls: Effect of calcium gluconate lasts only 30 to 60 minutes; repeat if QRS does not narrow within 5 to 10 minutes, and document the potassium and ECG before and after each treatment step to track response.

subtopic_detail: Sacubitril-valsartan initiation after ACE inhibitor in HFrEF
stem:
A 64-year-old man with chronic HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent on most recent echo) attends cardiology for review. He has been on optimal guideline-directed medical therapy with perindopril 8 mg daily, bisoprolol 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, and frusemide 40 mg daily for 4 months. He remains NYHA class II with mild exertional breathlessness on hills.

There has been no hospitalisation. His BP and renal function are stable. He has no symptomatic hypotension. The cardiologist has agreed with him to switch to sacubitril-valsartan for additional mortality benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 64, BP 122/74, RR 14, SpO2 97% air, weight 84 kg
data_table.Examination: Apex non-displaced, soft S3, no JVP elevation, clear chest, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138, potassium 4.2, urea 8.2, creatinine 102 (eGFR 64), NT-proBNP 1860 pg/mL, K stable, no recent hypotension or syncope, eGFR stable
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg, bisoprolol 10 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, dapagliflozin 10 mg, frusemide 40 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initiation regimen for sacubitril-valsartan?

options.text: Continue perindopril 8 mg and add sacubitril-valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily for the first 4 weeks then taper perindopril off over the following month
options.rationale: Concurrent ACE inhibitor and ARNI use is absolutely contraindicated owing to angioedema risk; a full washout, not overlap, is required. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

options.text: Switch perindopril to candesartan 16 mg first, achieve stable ARB dose for 4 weeks, then change candesartan to sacubitril-valsartan with no washout required
options.rationale: An intermediate ARB switch is unnecessary and delays therapy; direct ACE inhibitor to ARNI switch with 36-hour washout is the standard pathway. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

options.text: Stop perindopril and start sacubitril-valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily the same evening, doubling every 2 to 4 weeks as tolerated to target dose
options.rationale: Co-administration of ACE inhibitor and ARNI within 36 hours causes life-threatening angioedema; a 36-hour washout is mandatory before the first ARNI dose. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

options.text: Cease perindopril and bisoprolol simultaneously, wait 36 hours, then start sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily and reintroduce beta-blocker later
options.rationale: Beta-blockers should be continued without interruption (cessation causes rebound and decompensation); only the ACE inhibitor needs washout before ARNI. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

options.text: Cease perindopril, wait 36 hours, then start sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily and uptitrate to 97/103 mg twice daily over 2 to 4 weeks
options.rationale: Standard switch from ACE inhibitor to ARNI requires a 36-hour washout to avoid angioedema; in patients on a therapeutic ACE inhibitor dose with stable BP and renal function, start at the intermediate sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg BD with doubling every 2 to 4 weeks. (Source: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure)
source_refs: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

explanation.summary: Sacubitril-valsartan (ARNI) reduces cardiovascular death and HF hospitalisation compared with enalapril in HFrEF (PARADIGM-HF) and is recommended in place of ACE inhibitor or ARB in patients who remain symptomatic on GDMT. Initiation requires 36-hour washout from the ACE inhibitor (no washout needed if previous ARB). Start dose depends on baseline therapy and BP: 49/51 mg BD for patients on therapeutic ACE inhibitor or ARB with stable BP; 24/26 mg BD for those on low-dose ACE/ARB, low BP (under 110 systolic), or renal impairment. Target 97/103 mg BD if tolerated, doubling every 2 to 4 weeks.
key_points: 36-hour washout from ACE inhibitor before ARNI.
No washout needed switching from ARB.
Start 49/51 mg BD if therapeutic ACE/ARB and BP stable.
Target 97/103 mg BD, doubling every 2-4 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Angioedema risk persists for Black or African heritage patients on ARNI (slightly higher than other populations); monitor K and creatinine 1 to 2 weeks after each titration step.

sources.label: Heart Foundation Guidelines for the Prevention, Detection and Management of Heart Failure

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic indication in COPD exacerbation using Anthonisen criteria
stem:
A 71-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 38 percent predicted, GOLD group D, two exacerbations in the past year) presents to her GP with 5 days of increased breathlessness, increased cough productive of yellow-green sputum (previously clear), and a sense of greater volume of sputum than usual. There is no fever, chest pain, or haemoptysis. She is using her salbutamol inhaler hourly and her usual budesonide-formoterol twice daily.

She tolerates short walks indoors. She has had no recent travel or sick contacts. She has been triple-therapy inhaler optimised for the past 6 months and her routine sputum culture last admission grew Haemophilus influenzae.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 138/82, RR 22, SpO2 92% air (baseline 94%), T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Pursed-lip breathing, mild accessory muscle use, prolonged expiration, expiratory wheeze bilaterally, no focal consolidation, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CXR no consolidation, FBC normal, CRP 32, electrolytes normal, BSL 6.2
data_table.Medications: Budesonide/formoterol 400/12 BD, salbutamol PRN, tiotropium 18 micrograms daily, atorvastatin 40 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days alone with watchful waiting for the green sputum to resolve and review in 48 hours by phone
options.rationale: Anthonisen 3 of 3 (dyspnoea, volume, purulence) is the threshold at which oral antibiotics reduce treatment failure; withholding antibiotics in this group is associated with worse outcomes. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)

options.text: Add roflumilast 500 micrograms daily to current therapy and continue inhalers without commencing antibiotics or corticosteroids at this time
options.rationale: Roflumilast (a PDE-4 inhibitor) is a chronic add-on for severe COPD with frequent exacerbations and chronic bronchitis, not an acute exacerbation treatment. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)

options.text: Hospital admission for intravenous hydrocortisone, intravenous ceftriaxone, and continuous nebulised salbutamol with NIV standby in the medical assessment unit
options.rationale: She is haemodynamically stable, SpO2 only marginally reduced, and not in respiratory failure; inpatient IV therapy is reserved for severe exacerbation with inability to maintain oxygenation, severe acidosis, altered mental state, or social factors. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)

options.text: Switch budesonide-formoterol to fluticasone-vilanterol-umeclidinium triple therapy as a single inhaler and add oral mucolytic with planned review in one week
options.rationale: Single-inhaler triple therapy is a maintenance step-up for frequent exacerbators and would not address the acute exacerbation; the acute event needs steroid plus antibiotic now. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days plus oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days and outpatient review in 48 hours by GP or nurse
options.rationale: She meets all 3 Anthonisen criteria (increased dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence) and antibiotics are indicated; Australian first-line is amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days plus systemic corticosteroid prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days. (Source: COPD-X Concise Guide)

explanation.summary: Antibiotics in COPD exacerbation are indicated when Anthonisen criteria are met (any 2 of 3, especially purulence, or all 3): increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence. Australian first-line is amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days; doxycycline 100 mg daily for 5 days if penicillin allergy. Patients with severe exacerbations, hospital admission, recent antibiotics, or Pseudomonas-risk need broader cover (amoxicillin-clavulanate or ciprofloxacin if Pseudomonas confirmed). Systemic corticosteroid prednisolone 30 to 50 mg for 5 days shortens recovery and reduces relapse. Short-acting bronchodilator and oxygen titrated to SpO2 88 to 92 percent if hypoxic.
key_points: Anthonisen 2+ (esp. purulence) = antibiotics.
First-line amoxicillin 500 mg TDS x 5 days (AU).
Prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days shortens recovery.
Target SpO2 88-92 percent to avoid CO2 retention.
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic-resistant Pseudomonas should be considered in patients with frequent prior courses, recent hospitalisation, severe FEV1 (under 30 percent), or known prior colonisation; ciprofloxacin 750 mg BD covers it but watch QT and tendinopathy.

subtopic_detail: New Graves disease initial pharmacotherapy
stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with 8 weeks of palpitations, 7 kg weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, anxiety, frequent loose stools, and mild bilateral exophthalmos with lid lag. She has a diffusely enlarged smooth thyroid with a soft bruit. She is not pregnant and uses condoms with her partner. There is no proximal weakness, no atrial fibrillation, and no thyroid storm features. She is otherwise well. Investigations come back with overt biochemical hyperthyroidism and positive TSH-receptor antibodies. She is willing to start treatment today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 116 regular, BP 138/68, RR 16, SpO2 99%, T 36.8, weight 56 kg
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, sweaty palms, lid lag, mild proptosis, smooth goitre with bruit, ECG sinus tachycardia, regular rhythm
data_table.Investigations: TSH <0.01 mU/L, free T4 48 pmol/L, free T3 18 pmol/L, TSH receptor antibodies positive at 12 IU/L, FBC normal, LFT mild ALT rise 56, beta-hCG negative
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive (suspends), no other regular medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Atenolol 50 mg daily as monotherapy without thionamide, with reassessment of TFTs in 6 weeks to plan definitive treatment options
options.rationale: Beta-blocker alone controls only adrenergic symptoms and does not reduce thyroid hormone synthesis; a thionamide is required to address the underlying biochemical hyperthyroidism. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for radioactive iodine therapy as definitive treatment without preceding thionamide trial, given the moderate biochemistry and ophthalmic features
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine can transiently worsen Graves orbitopathy and is generally not first-line in active orbitopathy without preceding euthyroidism on thionamide and corticosteroid cover. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

options.text: Carbimazole 30 mg daily for symptom control and beta-blockade with propranolol 20 mg three times daily until thyroid function normalises
options.rationale: Australian first-line for new Graves disease in a non-pregnant adult is a thionamide (carbimazole 15 to 45 mg daily based on severity) plus a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol 20 to 40 mg TDS) for sympathetic symptom control until TFTs normalise. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

options.text: Refer urgently to endocrine surgery for total thyroidectomy as the safest definitive treatment in young women with thyroid eye disease and reproductive plans
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for failed medical management, large goitre with compression, suspected malignancy, or patient preference; it is not first-line for new Graves in a non-pregnant patient. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

options.text: Propylthiouracil 100 mg three times daily as the preferred first-line thionamide for all new Graves disease cases in non-pregnant patients
options.rationale: Propylthiouracil is reserved for first trimester of pregnancy, thyroid storm, and thionamide intolerance because of higher hepatotoxicity risk than carbimazole; not first-line outside these indications. (Source: AMH and ESA Hyperthyroidism Guidelines)

explanation.summary: New Graves disease in non-pregnant adults is treated with carbimazole 15 to 45 mg daily (titrated to TFTs) plus a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol 20 to 40 mg TDS) for symptom relief. Treat for 12 to 18 months to allow remission; 50 percent relapse and may then require definitive treatment with radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy. Monitor TFTs every 4 to 6 weeks initially, then every 3 months. Counsel about agranulocytosis (sore throat or fever; stop drug and check FBC). PTU is preferred in first trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm; methimazole is teratogenic in T1.
key_points: First-line: carbimazole + non-selective beta-blocker.
Treat 12-18 months; 50 percent relapse.
PTU in T1 pregnancy and thyroid storm.
Counsel agranulocytosis warning - sore throat = FBC.
explanation.pearls: Active orbitopathy is a relative contraindication to radioactive iodine without corticosteroid cover (40 mg prednisolone before and tapering over 6 weeks); thyroidectomy is preferred in severe orbitopathy planning.

subtopic_detail: Subarachnoid haemorrhage CT-LP investigation pathway for thunderclap headache
stem:
A 46-year-old woman presents to ED 9 hours after a sudden severe headache that reached maximal intensity within 30 seconds while lifting weights at the gym. The headache is now 8 of 10, occipital and band-like, with nausea but no vomiting, no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no focal neurology, and GCS 15. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. She had no preceding aura, no fever, no recent trauma, and no migraine history.

Non-contrast CT brain performed 30 minutes after arrival (at 9 hours 30 minutes from headache onset) by an experienced neuroradiologist is reported as normal with no haemorrhage and normal grey-white differentiation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 156/92, RR 16, SpO2 99% air, T 36.6, weight 72 kg, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: No meningism, cranial nerves intact, normal fundi (no papilloedema), no focal weakness or sensory deficit, gait normal, no carotid bruits
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT brain at 9.5 h: no haemorrhage. FBC, electrolytes, coagulation, glucose normal. ECG sinus rhythm
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg daily; nil other

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat non-contrast CT brain in 24 hours to detect any progression and discharge home in the interim if symptoms remain stable and there are no new neurological signs
options.rationale: Serial CT does not exclude SAH if the index scan was already insensitive at this timepoint; LP or CTA is required at this presentation, not delayed reimaging. (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)

options.text: Discharge with reassurance and paracetamol because non-contrast CT within 6 hours has greater than 99 percent sensitivity for subarachnoid haemorrhage in a thunderclap headache presentation
options.rationale: The 99 percent sensitivity threshold applies to CT within 6 hours of headache onset; her scan was at 9.5 hours and sensitivity falls to around 92 to 95 percent so SAH must still be excluded by lumbar puncture (or CT angiography). (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)

options.text: Lumbar puncture at the bedside looking for xanthochromia by spectrophotometry on cerebrospinal fluid collected at least 12 hours after headache onset
options.rationale: Once CT is performed beyond 6 hours from onset and is negative, LP for xanthochromia is required; CSF should be collected at least 12 hours after headache onset to allow bilirubin formation, and analysed by spectrophotometry (not visual inspection alone). (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)

options.text: Trial sumatriptan 6 mg subcutaneously and admit overnight for migraine observation given the gym onset suggesting an exertional migraine attack
options.rationale: Sumatriptan is contraindicated in undifferentiated thunderclap headache because vasoconstriction worsens RCVS or cerebral ischaemia; SAH must be excluded first. (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)

options.text: Commence nimodipine 60 mg six-hourly empirically for presumed reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome and admit to the stroke unit for observation
options.rationale: Nimodipine and the diagnosis of RCVS are considered once SAH has been excluded and after vascular imaging; empirical treatment without exclusion of SAH is inappropriate. (Source: NSW Health Headache in ED)

explanation.summary: In thunderclap headache (sudden severe maximal intensity within 60 seconds), non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset has greater than 99 percent sensitivity for SAH; beyond 6 hours the sensitivity falls and further investigation is needed. Two acceptable pathways: lumbar puncture after 12 hours from onset looking for xanthochromia by spectrophotometry, or CT angiography to identify aneurysm. If LP is positive (xanthochromia) or CTA shows aneurysm, neurosurgical referral for coiling or clipping is required. Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours and BP control are standard once SAH is confirmed.
key_points: CT <6 h of onset: 99+ percent sensitivity for SAH.
CT >6 h: LP at 12 h onset for xanthochromia, or CTA.
Xanthochromia by spectrophotometry, not visual.
Confirmed SAH: nimodipine 60 mg/4h + neurosurgery referral.
explanation.pearls: Traumatic tap is distinguished from SAH by a falling red cell count between bottles 1 and 4 and absence of xanthochromia; collect at least 4 bottles and send the final two for cell count and spectrophotometry.

subtopic_detail: Suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy diagnostic pathway
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 28 weeks gestation presents to ED with sudden right pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness over 4 hours. She has mild swelling of the right calf with tenderness along the saphenous vein. She is haemodynamically stable, with no haemoptysis. She has no personal or family VTE history. Bedside echocardiogram shows no right heart strain. CXR is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 116/72, RR 22, SpO2 96% air, T 36.8, weight 78 kg
data_table.Examination: Mild right calf tenderness, no obvious unilateral swelling difference, gravid uterus, fetal heart 142 reactive, no S1Q3T3
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, D-dimer not done (low utility in pregnancy), troponin negative, ECG sinus tachycardia, CXR clear
data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin, iron supplement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic investigation?

options.text: CT pulmonary angiography as the first-line investigation because it has the highest sensitivity and specificity for pulmonary embolism in all patients
options.rationale: CTPA exposes the maternal breast to significant radiation and is reserved for when leg USS is negative and CXR is normal; in pregnancy, leg USS first avoids unnecessary radiation when DVT signs are present. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Ventilation perfusion (V/Q) scan as the first-line investigation in pregnancy because of reduced fetal radiation compared to CT pulmonary angiography
options.rationale: V/Q scan is the chest imaging of choice in pregnancy with a normal CXR if leg USS is negative; however leg USS first is preferred when DVT signs are present because positive USS treats both. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Quantitative D-dimer interpreted against trimester-adjusted age-stratified pregnancy-specific cutoffs to rule out venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
options.rationale: D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy and even with trimester-adjusted cutoffs it has poor diagnostic utility; international guidelines advise against relying on D-dimer to rule out VTE in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound first to look for proximal deep vein thrombosis before any chest imaging in the pregnant patient
options.rationale: RANZCOG and Thrombosis Australia recommend bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound as the first imaging step in suspected PE in pregnancy when DVT signs are present; positive USS confirms VTE and treats both diagnoses with the same anticoagulation, avoiding radiation. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Empirical therapeutic dose enoxaparin without imaging while booking outpatient ultrasound and arranging follow-up cardiology and obstetric review
options.rationale: Empirical anticoagulation without imaging exposes mother and baby to bleeding risk without diagnostic confirmation; bedside lower-limb USS is rapid and usually available. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Suspected PE in pregnancy is investigated with bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound first when DVT signs are present (positive USS confirms VTE and obviates chest imaging). If USS is negative, next imaging is CXR; if CXR is normal, V/Q scan (lower maternal breast radiation) is preferred over CTPA. CTPA is acceptable if V/Q is unavailable or CXR is abnormal. D-dimer is unreliable in pregnancy because of physiological elevation. Empirical therapeutic LMWH is started if there is high clinical suspicion while imaging is arranged.
key_points: Leg USS first if DVT signs - confirms VTE without radiation.
If USS neg + CXR normal: V/Q scan preferred over CTPA.
D-dimer unreliable - elevated by pregnancy.
Empirical LMWH if high suspicion and delay anticipated.
explanation.pearls: Therapeutic enoxaparin in pregnancy is dosed 1 mg/kg twice daily based on early pregnancy weight; monitor anti-Xa levels in extremes of weight, renal impairment or recurrent VTE on treatment.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis management in known Addison disease
stem: A 38-year-old woman with established autoimmune Addison disease (diagnosed 5 years ago) presents to ED with 36 hours of vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain and weakness after attending a friend's wedding. She last took her morning hydrocortisone 20 mg yesterday but has vomited subsequent doses. She normally takes hydrocortisone 20 mg morning, 10 mg lunch, 5 mg evening, and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She wears a medic-alert bracelet. She looks unwell, drowsy but rousable, and is hypotensive.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 76/44, RR 22, SpO2 97% air, T 37.4, weight 56 kg, capillary glucose 3.1
data_table.Examination: Pale, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, JVP not seen, abdomen soft mildly diffusely tender, no peritonism, increased pigmentation creases and gums
data_table.Investigations: Na 124, K 6.0, urea 14.2, creatinine 132, glucose 3.1, lactate 3.8, troponin negative, beta-hCG negative, FBC normal, blood cultures sent
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20/10/5, fludrocortisone 100 micrograms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue her usual oral hydrocortisone regimen at increased dose 40 mg morning then 20 mg lunch, with ondansetron and intravenous saline rehydration overnight
options.rationale: Oral dosing fails in vomiting and adrenal crisis; the patient needs immediate parenteral hydrocortisone, not oral dose adjustment. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.text: Intravenous fludrocortisone 0.1 mg stat as the primary corticosteroid replacement for adrenal crisis along with one litre of isotonic saline boluses
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available intravenously and provides only mineralocorticoid effect; high-dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity at the dose used in crisis. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.text: Defer corticosteroid administration until a short Synacthen test is performed and cortisol baseline is documented to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Synacthen testing is not performed in acute crisis because treatment cannot be delayed; in established Addison disease, immediate hydrocortisone is given on clinical grounds without further confirmatory testing. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus rapid 1 litre intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus and intravenous 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis requires immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus (then 200 mg over 24 hours), aggressive volume resuscitation with isotonic saline, correction of hypoglycaemia, and treatment of any precipitant; mineralocorticoid effect comes from high-dose hydrocortisone so fludrocortisone is not the priority. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 4 mg dispersible tablet with rapid intravenous saline rehydration while awaiting cortisol and ACTH results before commencing further therapy
options.rationale: Oral medication is inappropriate in a vomiting shocked patient and dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid effect; IV hydrocortisone is required immediately. Investigations should not delay treatment. (Source: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)
source_refs: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a clinical emergency in known or suspected adrenal insufficiency presenting with hypotension, vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock. Management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 200 mg over 24 hours (continuous infusion or 50 mg IV/IM every 6 hours), aggressive fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline (1 to 2 litres in the first hour), correction of hypoglycaemia, identification and treatment of precipitant (infection commonest), and electrolyte monitoring. Once recovering, transition to oral hydrocortisone at 2 to 3 times maintenance dose and taper over days. Fludrocortisone is resumed once on usual oral dose.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg/24 h.
Aggressive isotonic saline + glucose if hypoglycaemic.
Treat precipitant - usually infection.
No delay for cortisol testing if clinical adrenal crisis.
explanation.pearls: Every patient with adrenal insufficiency should have an emergency hydrocortisone 100 mg IM ampoule at home, a medic-alert ID, and a sick-day rule (double oral steroid for moderate illness, IM stat for vomiting); educate before discharge.

sources.label: ESA and AMH Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Adult asthma uncontrolled on ICS-LABA step-up
stem: A 42-year-old woman with adult-onset asthma reports daily symptoms requiring her salbutamol 4 times a day, two night-time awakenings per week, and has used three prednisolone courses in the past year. She is fully adherent with budesonide-formoterol 200/6 mcg twice daily plus reliever and has good inhaler technique demonstrated in clinic today. She does not smoke. Spirometry shows FEV1 of 68 percent predicted with 14 percent reversibility post-bronchodilator.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Scattered end-expiratory wheeze, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: FEV1 68 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.65, eosinophils 0.35, IgE 88
data_table.Medications: Budesonide-formoterol 200/6 BID, salbutamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next medication change?

options.text: Add oral montelukast 10 mg daily to current ICS-LABA as third controller for symptom control
options.rationale: Montelukast adds modest benefit and carries TGA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects; LAMA is preferred third controller. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) inhaler as a third controller to current ICS-LABA
options.rationale: Australian asthma guidance recommends LAMA add-on as the preferred step-up when ICS-LABA at medium dose with good adherence and technique fails to control symptoms, before biologics. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Refer immediately for omalizumab biologic therapy without further inhaled corticosteroid trials given symptoms
options.rationale: Biologics are PBS-funded for severe asthma after optimisation of inhaled therapy including LAMA; she has not yet stepped up to triple therapy. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Commence maintenance oral prednisolone 10 mg daily until symptoms have resolved completely
options.rationale: Maintenance oral steroids carry significant long-term morbidity and are reserved for severe refractory asthma after biologic options exhausted. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

options.text: Double the dose of inhaled corticosteroid component within current ICS-LABA combination
options.rationale: Doubling ICS provides only small additional benefit beyond medium dose and increases systemic effects; LAMA add-on is preferred per current guidance. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia)

explanation.summary: Step-up therapy for adult asthma not controlled on medium-dose ICS-LABA, despite good adherence and technique, is triple therapy with addition of a LAMA (tiotropium 5 mcg daily or once-daily ICS-LABA-LAMA combinations). Biologics are PBS-funded for severe asthma based on phenotype: omalizumab (allergic, IgE-driven), mepolizumab/benralizumab (eosinophilic), dupilumab (eosinophilic or type 2 high). Always reassess adherence, inhaler technique, environmental triggers, smoking, comorbidities (rhinitis, reflux, obesity, OSA, mental health) before escalating.
key_points: Confirm adherence and technique before stepping up.
Step 4-5: ICS-LABA medium dose + LAMA add-on.
Biologics for severe disease, phenotype-driven.
Maintenance oral steroids only after biologics fail.
Treat comorbidities: rhinitis, reflux, OSA, obesity, smoking.
explanation.pearls: Always check for vocal cord dysfunction in adult-onset wheeze responding incompletely to maximal therapy - inspiratory wheeze, sudden onset and offset, and laryngoscopy during attack confirm the diagnosis and reduce unnecessary asthma escalation.

subtopic_detail: Native valve infective endocarditis - empiric therapy
stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of degenerative aortic valve disease presents with 10 days of fevers, malaise, weight loss and a new exertional breathlessness. Examination reveals a soft pansystolic murmur not previously documented, splinter haemorrhages in two fingernails and microscopic haematuria on dipstick. Three sets of blood cultures are drawn from separate sites before any antibiotic is given. He has no penicillin allergy and is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 96, BP 118/64, RR 18, SpO2 96 percent room air
data_table.Examination: New apical pansystolic murmur, two splinter haemorrhages, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2, CRP 142, creatinine 96, urinalysis 2+ blood 1+ protein, ECG sinus tachycardia, transthoracic echo pending
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, atorvastatin, aspirin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric intravenous antibiotic regimen while cultures incubate?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as single-agent empiric therapy for community-acquired endocarditis
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not cover staphylococci or enterococci adequately for native valve endocarditis empiric therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours plus flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours
options.rationale: Triple therapy with benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin and low-dose gentamicin gives appropriate coverage of streptococci, methicillin-susceptible staphylococci and enterococci pending culture and susceptibility results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose alone, withholding any beta-lactam until culture identification is available
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy delays optimal beta-lactam therapy for susceptible organisms and is reserved for severe beta-lactam allergy or suspected methicillin-resistant infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g every 8 hours pending culture results given clinical stability and the prolonged subacute history
options.rationale: Endocarditis requires intravenous therapy regardless of clinical stability; oral therapy cannot achieve adequate bactericidal valve concentrations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours as broad spectrum gram-negative cover for the subacute fever syndrome
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam targets gram-negative and anaerobic pathogens that are not the primary cause of native valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Empiric therapy for native valve endocarditis covers viridans streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus and enterococci because these account for the majority of cases. Combination therapy of benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is the Australian guideline regimen pending culture identification. Three separate sets of blood cultures from different venepuncture sites before antibiotics are essential to meet the Duke microbiological criterion. Modified Duke criteria combine clinical, microbiological and echocardiographic findings to support diagnosis. Streamlining of therapy occurs once organism and susceptibilities are known.
key_points: Three separate blood culture sets before antibiotics.
Cover staph, strep and enterococci empirically.
Benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin in Australia.
Vancomycin replaces beta-lactams only for severe allergy or MRSA suspicion.
Streamline once organism and MIC are known.
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours uses the synergy dose, not the once-daily 5-7 mg/kg dose used for gram-negative sepsis; trough should be below 1 mg/L within 5 days of starting.

sources.label: ESC 2023 Guidelines for the management of endocarditis

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion - diagnostic workup
stem: A 28-year-old man presents with 7 days of fever, sore throat, generalised myalgia, headache and a maculopapular rash on his torso. He returned from Bali 4 weeks ago. He reports condomless receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 3 weeks ago. He is on no medications and has no allergies. Examination shows pharyngitis without exudate, fine truncal rash and a few small palpable cervical lymph nodes. There is no meningism.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, HR 102, BP 116/72, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Pharyngitis, maculopapular truncal rash, soft cervical lymphadenopathy, no meningism, no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.1, lymphocytes 0.9, platelets 118, ALT 78, CRP 32, monospot negative
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm acute HIV infection at this stage?

options.text: Fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody combination immunoassay together with quantitative HIV-1 RNA viral load
options.rationale: Fourth-generation combination assay detects p24 antigen and antibody, and quantitative HIV-1 RNA viral load detects acute infection during the antibody window. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

options.text: HIV-1 antibody Western blot alone, since the combination assay is unreliable in the acute window before antibody seroconversion
options.rationale: Western blot is a confirmatory antibody-only test that is negative or indeterminate during acute infection before antibody is detectable. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

options.text: Single CD4 count and CD4 to CD8 ratio measurement, which establishes the diagnosis when the CD4 count is below 500 cells per microlitre
options.rationale: CD4 count quantifies immune status but does not diagnose HIV; lymphopenia can occur in many acute viral infections. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

options.text: EBV serology with monospot and acute and convalescent IgM and IgG titres to exclude infectious mononucleosis before testing for HIV
options.rationale: Treating EBV as a competing diagnosis delays the time-critical diagnosis of acute HIV when post-exposure transmission risk is at its peak. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

options.text: A repeat HIV combination immunoassay in 12 weeks and presumptive empirical treatment with valaciclovir for suspected primary HSV infection
options.rationale: Delaying repeat testing 12 weeks misses the opportunity to confirm acute HIV and initiate early antiretroviral therapy that reduces viral reservoir. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion presents as a mononucleosis-like illness with fever, pharyngitis, rash, lymphadenopathy, and transient cytopenias 2-4 weeks after exposure. Fourth-generation combination immunoassay detects both p24 antigen and HIV antibodies and shortens the window to about 2 weeks. Quantitative HIV-1 RNA confirms infection before antibodies develop and viral loads in acute infection are typically very high. Early ART improves outcomes and reduces forward transmission. Australian framework requires partner notification, contact tracing and consideration of post-exposure prophylaxis for recent contacts.
key_points: Fever, pharyngitis, rash, lymphadenopathy after exposure - test for acute HIV.
Fourth-generation combination assay plus HIV RNA detect acute infection.
Initiate ART promptly to reduce reservoir and transmission.
Counsel about partner notification and confidentiality.
Offer post-exposure prophylaxis to contacts within 72 hours of exposure.
explanation.pearls: If HIV combination assay is positive but RNA undetectable, suspect an elite controller or false-positive serology; repeat both assays from a fresh sample and refer urgently to a HIV s100 prescriber.

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis - QuantiFERON-Plus interpretation
stem: A 34-year-old woman from Vietnam who immigrated to Australia 6 years ago is being assessed before commencing infliximab for inflammatory bowel disease. She has no respiratory symptoms, no contact with anyone with tuberculosis and a normal chest x-ray. She received BCG vaccination in childhood. She is asymptomatic with normal observations.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 72, BP 118/70, SpO2 99 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no lymphadenopathy, well
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray reported as normal, QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus positive with both TB1 and TB2 antigen tubes above cut-off, sputum unable to be obtained
data_table.Medications: Mesalazine, prednisolone 10 mg daily, planned infliximab

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence infliximab immediately because the positive QuantiFERON likely represents BCG vaccination from childhood, not true latent infection
options.rationale: QuantiFERON Gold Plus antigens do not cross-react with BCG vaccination so a positive result indicates Mycobacterium tuberculosis exposure. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)

options.text: Begin a 9-month course of isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily with monthly liver function tests and proceed with infliximab in parallel without further evaluation
options.rationale: Active TB must be excluded before treating as latent, otherwise monotherapy risks resistance and progression on biologic therapy. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)

options.text: Repeat QuantiFERON in 12 weeks to confirm persistent positivity before deciding whether to delay biologic initiation in a symptom-free patient
options.rationale: Repeating QuantiFERON without exclusion of active disease and treatment delays both immunosuppression and tuberculosis management. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)

options.text: Confirm absence of active tuberculosis with sputum induction and CT chest, then treat latent TB with isoniazid plus pyridoxine for 9 months before commencing infliximab
options.rationale: Active TB must first be excluded with directed imaging and microbiology; once excluded, latent TB treatment is given before TNF-alpha inhibitor therapy. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)

options.text: Refer for directly observed RIPE four-drug therapy as latent TB treatment standard before biologic initiation in this high-risk patient population
options.rationale: RIPE four-drug therapy is for active tuberculosis disease; latent TB is treated with isoniazid monotherapy or short rifamycin regimens. (Source: NTAC Latent TB Infection Guideline)

explanation.summary: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus uses TB-specific antigens that do not cross-react with BCG vaccination, so a positive result in this patient indicates Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Active TB must be excluded by clinical assessment, chest imaging and respiratory samples before latent treatment to avoid generating resistance.
