Standard latent TB treatment options include isoniazid 9 months with pyridoxine, rifampicin 4 months or weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid 12 doses. TNF-alpha inhibitors substantially increase risk of reactivation, so treatment should start before biologic initiation when possible. Monitor for hepatotoxicity with monthly liver function tests.
key_points: QuantiFERON-Plus does not cross-react with BCG.
Exclude active TB before treating latent TB.
Isoniazid 9 months with pyridoxine is standard latent therapy.
Start latent TB treatment before TNF-alpha inhibitor.
Monitor LFTs and adherence monthly.
explanation.pearls: Rifapentine plus isoniazid weekly for 12 doses (3HP regimen) is now preferred in many jurisdictions for adherence; rifapentine is not currently widely available in Australia but is on the NTAC option list.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection - recognition and management
stem: A 54-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with 36 hours of severe progressively worsening left lower leg pain following a minor garden injury. The pain is out of proportion to the modest erythema seen at the wound. There is dusky discolouration over a 10 cm area with one tense fluid-filled bulla. He is febrile with tachycardia and feels unwell. He has had paracetamol with no relief.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Lower limb erythema, dusky 10 cm area, tense haemorrhagic bulla, crepitus to palpation, exquisite pain on light touch
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22, neutrophils 19, Na 128, creatinine 142, glucose 16, CRP 320, lactate 4.6, CK 8400, hb 132
data_table.Medications: Metformin, gliclazide, perindopril

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Plain x-ray of the left lower limb followed by venous duplex ultrasound to exclude deep vein thrombosis prior to antibiotic selection
options.rationale: Imaging delays surgical intervention; necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis with definitive treatment in theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and reassess in 24 hours if symptoms have not improved before considering surgical referral
options.rationale: Antibiotic monotherapy without urgent surgical exploration in suspected necrotising fasciitis significantly increases mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Immediate fluid resuscitation, intravenous meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin, and emergent surgical debridement without delay for imaging
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis demands immediate broad spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin for toxin suppression and urgent surgical debridement; imaging must not delay theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Compute LRINEC score using laboratory values and observe in resuscitation area for 6 hours before deciding on surgical exploration if score is below 6
options.rationale: LRINEC supports but does not replace clinical judgement; a low score does not exclude necrotising fasciitis with classic clinical features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Apply topical mupirocin to the wound, elevate the limb and arrange outpatient surgical review for early necrotising fasciitis with negative blood cultures
options.rationale: Outpatient management is inappropriate; necrotising fasciitis requires inpatient resuscitation, IV antibiotics and theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality exceeding 25 percent and rising rapidly with delay. Pain out of proportion to skin findings, systemic toxicity, crepitus, dusky discolouration and haemorrhagic bullae are red flags. Broad spectrum cover with carbapenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin (for toxin suppression in group A streptococcal disease) is started immediately, with surgical debridement within 6 hours as the strongest determinant of survival. The LRINEC score supports but never excludes the diagnosis when clinical features are present. Repeat debridement and ICU admission are usually required.
key_points: Pain out of proportion plus crepitus or bullae - necrotising fasciitis.
Imaging must not delay surgery in clear clinical cases.
Carbapenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin empirically.
Surgical debridement within 6 hours saves lives.
LRINEC supports but does not exclude the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Add clindamycin specifically for ribosomal toxin suppression in group A streptococcal infection; it works even when beta-lactam efficacy is reduced by high bacterial load in the Eagle effect.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Skin and Soft Tissue Infection
WSACS Guidelines for the Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

subtopic_detail: Septic shock - hour 1 bundle priorities
stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department from his nursing home with 6 hours of fever, confusion and reduced urine output. He is normally independent in basic care and lives in the community. He has a history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes and benign prostatic hypertrophy. On arrival he is drowsy and disoriented in time. The triage nurse has applied oxygen and obtained intravenous access.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 124, BP 84/52, RR 28, SpO2 92 percent on 2 L nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, abdomen soft, suprapubic tenderness, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Bedside lactate 4.2, glucose 14, urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive, ECG sinus tachycardia, qSOFA 3
data_table.Medications: Metformin, perindopril, tamsulosin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step within the first hour of resuscitation?

options.text: Send blood cultures and obtain CT abdomen and pelvis before starting antibiotics to identify the urinary source and exclude obstruction first
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay antibiotic administration; first-dose antibiotic within an hour is the strongest hour 1 priority. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Administer oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg single dose while awaiting intravenous access then transfer to a ward bed for ongoing care
options.rationale: Septic shock requires intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics; oral therapy is inadequate and admission requires high-acuity area not a ward. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Draw blood cultures, give intravenous gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam within 1 hour and start 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid resuscitation guided by clinical response
options.rationale: Cultures before antibiotics if achievable without delay, antibiotic within 1 hour and 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension or lactate above 4 are the hour 1 bundle priorities. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Defer all antibiotic therapy until cultures return positive in 24 to 48 hours to ensure susceptibility-targeted treatment with the narrowest agent
options.rationale: Antibiotic delay in septic shock dramatically increases mortality with about 8 percent rise for each hour of delay. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula at 0.05 microgram/kg/min before any intravenous fluid resuscitation is given to maintain organ perfusion
options.rationale: Vasopressors are added after initial fluid resuscitation if MAP remains below 65 mmHg, not as first-line ahead of fluids. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines 2021)

explanation.summary: Septic shock is defined by hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg plus lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluid resuscitation. The hour 1 bundle covers lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within an hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at least 4, and vasopressors if hypotension persists. Source control (urinary obstruction relief, abscess drainage) is essential and should occur within 6-12 hours. Re-measure lactate and reassess perfusion within 2-4 hours.
key_points: Hour 1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors as needed.
Antibiotics within 1 hour - each hour of delay increases mortality.
30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at least 4.
Noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor when MAP below 65 after fluids.
Source control within 6-12 hours of recognition.
explanation.pearls: Use balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte) over 0.9 percent sodium chloride because chloride-restrictive strategies show reduced AKI in critically ill patients (SMART and PLUS trials).

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis - recognition and stress dose steroids
stem: A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily presents to the emergency department with 24 hours of vomiting from gastroenteritis. She has not been able to keep down her morning hydrocortisone dose. She is drowsy with cool peripheries and looks unwell. She normally carries an emergency steroid card and self-injectable hydrocortisone but did not take it.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 124, BP 86/52, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry mucosa, cool peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds, soft abdomen with mild generalised tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Na 124, K 5.6, glucose 3.1, creatinine 142, lactate 2.4, CRP 18, hb 138, WCC 11
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20/10 mg, fludrocortisone 100 micrograms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 L over 30 minutes, intravenous dextrose for hypoglycaemia, then hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is treated with immediate stat 100 mg IV hydrocortisone, rapid volume resuscitation with normal saline, glucose correction and ongoing parenteral steroid replacement. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg stat with antiemetic ondansetron 4 mg intravenously and admit to ward for observation with hourly blood pressure and oral fluid replacement
options.rationale: Oral steroids are inappropriate in vomiting hypotensive patients; parenteral hydrocortisone is required to reverse adrenal crisis. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg stat without further hydrocortisone so that subsequent ACTH stimulation testing can be performed within the next 24 hours for confirmation
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has minimal mineralocorticoid activity required for volume management and giving it first delays definitive treatment unnecessarily. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula at 0.05 microgram/kg/min to address hypotension prior to any glucocorticoid replacement therapy
options.rationale: Vasopressors will not correct cortisol-deficient hypotension which is volume and steroid responsive; treat with fluid and hydrocortisone first. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous fludrocortisone 200 micrograms stat replacement with intravenous bicarbonate to correct mild metabolic acidosis prior to any other interventions
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available intravenously and is irrelevant in crisis when high-dose hydrocortisone already provides mineralocorticoid effect. (Source: AES Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening hypotensive emergency in patients with primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency, typically triggered by infection, vomiting or surgery. Immediate management is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat, rapid volume replacement with normal saline 1 L in 30 minutes (up to 3 L in first hour), correction of hypoglycaemia with dextrose, then hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours. At 100 mg/day mineralocorticoid activity is sufficient so fludrocortisone is not needed acutely. Patient education on sick day rules and emergency hydrocortisone injection is essential to prevent recurrence.
key_points: Sick day rules: double oral dose for fever or stress.
Crisis = IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus saline plus dextrose.
Maintain hydrocortisone 50 mg q6h while ill.
Fludrocortisone not needed at high hydrocortisone doses.
Every patient needs an emergency steroid card and self-injection kit.
explanation.pearls: If hyperpigmentation in a Caucasian patient or postural hypotension persists after starting hydrocortisone, suspect primary (not secondary) adrenal insufficiency and arrange Synacthen test plus aldosterone and renin once the patient is stable.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis - empiric therapy
stem: A 42-year-old non-pregnant woman presents to the emergency department with a 36-hour history of fever, rigors, right flank pain and frequency and dysuria. She has no significant medical history. She has been unable to keep down sips of water for the last 6 hours. Examination demonstrates right loin tenderness and percussion tenderness. She has no allergies. Her vital signs reveal sepsis without shock.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.0, HR 112, BP 108/70, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Right loin tenderness, costovertebral angle tenderness, abdomen soft, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive, WCC 14, neutrophils 12, CRP 86, creatinine 88, lactate 1.4, urine culture pending
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric therapy?

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose followed by oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days after discharge with primary care follow-up
options.rationale: IV gentamicin single dose followed by directed oral therapy is recommended for non-pregnant pyelonephritis without sepsis features in Australian guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days as outpatient management for community-acquired urinary tract infection with mild upper tract features
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate renal parenchymal concentrations and is inappropriate for pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours as broad-spectrum empiric therapy for hospitalised community-acquired pyelonephritis with sepsis
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam is reserved for severe sepsis, complicated pyelonephritis or healthcare-associated infection rather than uncomplicated cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)

options.text: Intravenous ampicillin 2 g every 6 hours plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily until clinically improved, then oral antibiotics directed by urine culture susceptibility
options.rationale: Ampicillin gentamicin combination is broader than necessary; gentamicin alone or single dose plus oral step-down meets the standard regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 10 days at home as first-line empiric therapy for community-acquired pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant adult
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for second-line after culture due to resistance, toxicity (tendinopathy, dysglycaemia) and antimicrobial stewardship in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Pyelonephritis)

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis is upper tract infection with fever, loin pain and lower tract symptoms. In Australian Therapeutic Guidelines, non-pregnant non-septic adults are treated with intravenous gentamicin (5 mg/kg once) plus oral trimethoprim or amoxicillin-clavulanate as step-down, with total duration 10-14 days. Severe sepsis, immunocompromise, obstruction or pregnancy require parenteral broad-spectrum cover such as piperacillin-tazobactam. Urine culture before antibiotics directs targeted therapy. Image (ultrasound or CT) if no improvement at 48-72 hours to exclude obstruction or abscess.
key_points: Gentamicin single dose plus oral step-down for non-pregnant pyelo.
Avoid nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin in pyelonephritis.
Use ciprofloxacin only after culture and stewardship review.
Image at 48-72 hours if no improvement to exclude obstruction.
Total duration 10-14 days with directed oral step-down.
explanation.pearls: Single-dose gentamicin 5 mg/kg leverages concentration-dependent killing with a long post-antibiotic effect, allowing safer transition to oral therapy without ongoing aminoglycoside levels monitoring.

sources.label: Australian Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard

subtopic_detail: Cushing's syndrome - screening tests
stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with 12 months of progressive weight gain centred on her trunk, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness when climbing stairs, irregular periods and newly diagnosed hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance. She takes no glucocorticoid medication. She has wide purple striae on her abdomen and a rounded plethoric face. Her GP has referred her for assessment of suspected Cushing's syndrome.

data_table.Examination: Moon facies, supraclavicular and dorsocervical fat pads, central obesity, purple abdominal striae more than 1 cm wide, proximal weakness 4 of 5
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 8.2 fasting, HbA1c 7.2 percent, K 3.4, ALT normal, eGFR 96, ECG sinus rhythm with LVH
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, nil glucocorticoids

lead_in: Which set of investigations is the most appropriate initial screening?

options.text: Plasma morning ACTH at 09:00 with a paired serum cortisol level as a single measurement combined with an FBC and serum electrolytes panel screen
options.rationale: Random ACTH and cortisol are not diagnostic; Cushing screening requires demonstration of failure of cortisol suppression or elevated unbound cortisol. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)

options.text: Random 24-hour urinary catecholamines and plasma metanephrines as the initial assessment for secondary causes of hypertension in this 38-year-old woman
options.rationale: Catecholamine testing screens for phaeochromocytoma, not Cushing syndrome which requires cortisol assessment. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)

options.text: MRI pituitary as the first-line investigation to identify a 4-6 mm adenoma, followed by inferior petrosal sinus sampling if no adenoma is seen on imaging today
options.rationale: Imaging is performed only after biochemical confirmation; pituitary incidentalomas are common and imaging first leads to misdiagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)

options.text: Insulin tolerance test using 0.1 unit/kg insulin with measurement of cortisol and growth hormone responses to demonstrate adrenal axis activity in this case
options.rationale: Insulin tolerance assesses adrenal sufficiency or growth hormone deficiency, not Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)

options.text: At least two of the following: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, two 24-hour urinary free cortisol collections, and two late-night salivary cortisol samples
options.rationale: Initial Cushing screening requires two positive tests of the three first-line options: 1 mg DST, 24 h UFC, and late night salivary cortisol. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Diagnosis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome screening uses any two of three first-line tests: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol above 50 nmol/L next morning is abnormal), 24-hour urinary free cortisol (twice to confirm), and late-night salivary cortisol (twice). Two positive tests support the diagnosis. Avoid screening during illness, depression, alcohol use disorder, recent dexamethasone interaction with CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin) which causes false negatives. Once Cushing is confirmed biochemically, plasma ACTH discriminates ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) and imaging follows.
key_points: Two positive tests of 1 mg DST, 24 h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol.
Avoid screening during acute illness, recent OCP, alcohol use.
ACTH after confirmation: dependent (pituitary or ectopic) vs independent (adrenal).
Pituitary MRI only after biochemical confirmation.
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling for ACTH-dependent equivocal cases.
explanation.pearls: Oestrogen-containing OCP raises cortisol-binding globulin and falsely elevates urinary free cortisol; stop OCP for 6 weeks before screening, or use late-night salivary cortisol which is not CBG-affected.

subtopic_detail: Influenza - antiviral indication in high-risk adult
stem: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, ischaemic heart disease and COPD on long-acting bronchodilators presents to the general practice with 28 hours of fever, dry cough, myalgia and headache. He had his annual influenza vaccination this year. Nasal swab influenza PCR is positive for influenza A. He is well enough to be managed in the community and has no respiratory distress or hypoxaemia today. He is otherwise stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 96, BP 134/80, RR 18, SpO2 95 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Mild rhinorrhoea, chest with mild expiratory wheeze unchanged from baseline, no consolidation, normal sensorium
data_table.Investigations: Nasal swab influenza A positive, RSV negative, COVID negative, point of care CRP 24
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium, salmeterol-fluticasone, metformin, atorvastatin, aspirin, perindopril

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days starting today and provide written sick-day advice including return precautions for any deterioration
options.rationale: Oseltamivir within 48 hours of symptom onset reduces complications and is recommended for high-risk adults (chronic disease, immunocompromise, age 65+) in Australian guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)

options.text: Reassure that influenza is self-limiting, recommend paracetamol and increased oral fluids, with no role for antivirals when symptom onset is greater than 24 hours ago
options.rationale: Symptom onset within 48 hours is the window for antiviral benefit; this patient is 28 hours in and meets criteria for treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)

options.text: Empirical oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days for community-acquired bacterial superinfection given his chronic respiratory comorbidity and current viral illness
options.rationale: Antibacterial therapy is reserved for bacterial superinfection (high fever returning, focal consolidation, sputum change) not empirically with isolated influenza. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)

options.text: Increase fluticasone propionate metered dose inhaler dose to 500 micrograms twice daily and prescribe a 5-day course of oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for COPD exacerbation
options.rationale: Inhaled steroid escalation and oral prednisolone treat COPD exacerbation, but the diagnosis here is influenza without exacerbation features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)

options.text: Refer to hospital for intravenous remdesivir as recommended antiviral therapy for confirmed influenza A in adults with multiple chronic disease comorbidities
options.rationale: Remdesivir is an antiviral for COVID-19, not influenza; oseltamivir or zanamivir are first-line for influenza in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Influenza)

explanation.summary: Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days started within 48 hours of symptom onset reduces duration, complications and need for antibacterial therapy in influenza. Australian guidelines treat high-risk adults including: age 65+, pregnant or postpartum, chronic respiratory/cardiac/renal/liver/neurological disease, diabetes, immunocompromise, BMI above 40, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults, residential aged care. Treat hospital inpatients regardless of duration. Renal dose-adjust oseltamivir below 60 mL/min. Continue vaccination programs as the primary prevention; treatment is adjunctive.
key_points: Treat influenza in high-risk adults within 48 hours of onset.
Oseltamivir 75 mg BD for 5 days, dose adjust for renal function.
Treat inpatients regardless of symptom duration.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults are a treatment-priority group.
Vaccination remains the primary prevention.
explanation.pearls: Single dose oral baloxavir is a polymerase inhibitor alternative; consider if compliance with 5-day BD oseltamivir is a concern, but resistance can emerge during therapy so it is reserved cases.

sources.label: Australian Influenza Surveillance and Treatment Guidance

subtopic_detail: Primary aldosteronism - aldosterone renin ratio interpretation
stem: A 46-year-old woman is referred for evaluation of resistant hypertension. She is on perindopril, amlodipine and indapamide and her clinic blood pressure remains 168/96. She has spontaneous hypokalaemia and a maternal aunt who had a unilateral adrenal adenoma in her 50s. Her primary care doctor has stopped indapamide for 6 weeks and is considering further investigation before referral. She has had no recent caffeine or strenuous activity before testing.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/96 confirmed, HR 76, BMI 28
data_table.Examination: Clinically euvolaemic, no abdominal bruit, no cushingoid features
data_table.Investigations: Na 142, K 3.0, bicarbonate 30, creatinine 78, eGFR 78, ECG sinus rhythm with U waves
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, amlodipine

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Twenty-four hour urinary fractionated metanephrines collected over 24 hours with parallel plasma metanephrines to screen for an underlying phaeochromocytoma diagnosis
options.rationale: Phaeochromocytoma screening is appropriate for paroxysmal hypertension; this clinical picture with hypokalaemia strongly suggests aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)

options.text: Renal artery duplex ultrasound to exclude renovascular hypertension secondary to fibromuscular dysplasia as a treatable cause of her resistant blood pressure pattern
options.rationale: Renovascular imaging is reasonable in some patterns but does not explain the spontaneous hypokalaemia, which points to primary aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)

options.text: Empirical commencement of spironolactone 25 mg daily and clinical reassessment of blood pressure at 6 weeks without measuring the aldosterone or renin first
options.rationale: Empirical mineralocorticoid blockade obscures subsequent diagnostic testing and prevents confirmation, subtyping and consideration of surgery. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)

options.text: Morning paired plasma aldosterone and renin to calculate aldosterone to renin ratio after replacing potassium and substituting interfering antihypertensives
options.rationale: Aldosterone to renin ratio (after potassium replacement and substituting verapamil/doxazosin for interfering medications) is the recommended screening for primary aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)

options.text: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test to assess cortisol axis and exclude subclinical Cushing syndrome as cause of resistant hypertension and metabolic disturbance
options.rationale: DST screens Cushing syndrome which does not typically cause spontaneous hypokalaemia and is less likely than primary aldosteronism here. (Source: Endocrine Society Primary Aldosteronism Guideline)

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism affects up to 10 percent of resistant hypertension and is associated with disproportionate end-organ damage. Screen with morning plasma aldosterone (PAC) and renin (PRA or direct renin concentration) to calculate ARR. Correct hypokalaemia first; spironolactone, eplerenone and amiloride should be stopped for 6 weeks; beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics may need substitution with verapamil SR or doxazosin. ARR cut-offs vary by assay; confirmatory testing (saline suppression, fludrocortisone suppression, oral salt loading) follows positive screen. Adrenal venous sampling subtypes unilateral vs bilateral for surgical planning.
key_points: Screen resistant HTN, spontaneous hypokalaemia, adrenal incidentaloma with ARR.
Correct potassium and substitute interfering medications before testing.
Confirm with saline suppression or other confirmatory test.
AVS to subtype unilateral vs bilateral disease.
Unilateral disease - laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
explanation.pearls: ACE inhibitors and ARBs suppress aldosterone less than they suppress renin in primary aldosteronism, so an inappropriately measurable PAC with suppressed PRA on these drugs still raises suspicion - do not be reassured by perindopril use.

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal osteoporosis - pharmacological initiation
stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman attends the general practice for review after a low-trauma wrist fracture following a fall from standing height 6 weeks ago. She had a previous Colles fracture 2 years ago. Her mother had a hip fracture aged 78. She is on no current bone-affecting medications. Her DXA shows lumbar spine T-score minus 2.6 and femoral neck T-score minus 2.4. Her calcium and vitamin D levels are within range and her renal function is normal.

data_table.Examination: Healing wrist fracture, height loss 2 cm over past decade, no kyphosis, no spinal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.34, phosphate 1.1, 25-OH vitamin D 78, ALP 88, eGFR 78, PTH 4.2, TSH 1.6
data_table.Medications: Calcium 600 mg with vitamin D 1000 IU daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue calcium and vitamin D supplementation alone with annual DXA scanning and lifestyle advice for the next 12 months without pharmacological bone therapy
options.rationale: Pharmacological therapy is indicated for prior minimal trauma fracture or T-score below minus 2.5; calcium and vitamin D alone are inadequate. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.text: Commence raloxifene 60 mg orally daily as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator for postmenopausal spinal osteoporosis with prior fragility fracture
options.rationale: Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not hip fractures and is second-line behind bisphosphonates or denosumab. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.text: Initiate transdermal estradiol patch 50 micrograms twice weekly with a progestogen for endometrial protection as primary therapy for postmenopausal bone loss
options.rationale: MHT is not first-line bone therapy after 60 due to cardiovascular and breast risks though it may be considered with symptomatic women. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.text: Refer for teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily as first-line anabolic therapy for high fracture risk postmenopausal osteoporosis with a recent fragility fracture
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for very high risk or PBS criteria such as a prior fracture on bisphosphonate; not first-line therapy. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.text: Commence oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium and vitamin D and arrange dental review before starting given the risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw
options.rationale: Alendronate is first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with minimal trauma fracture; dental review reduces ONJ risk and ongoing calcium and vitamin D supports efficacy. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture in a postmenopausal woman is an osteoporotic event regardless of DXA T-score, and is an indication for pharmacological therapy. Alendronate or risedronate are first-line oral options, with zoledronic acid annual IV for poor oral tolerance or compliance, supported by calcium 1000-1300 mg/day and vitamin D 800-2000 IU/day. Dental review and treatment of any active disease before initiation reduces ONJ risk. PBS criteria for funded therapy include T-score at or below minus 2.5, prior minimal trauma fracture, or steroid use. Reassess at 3-5 years; consider drug holiday if low risk and stable.
key_points: Minimal trauma fracture triggers pharmacological therapy regardless of T-score.
Alendronate weekly oral is first-line.
Zoledronic acid IV yearly if oral intolerance.
Pre-treatment dental review reduces ONJ risk.
Calcium 1000-1300 mg and vitamin D 800-2000 IU daily.
explanation.pearls: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously six-monthly is an alternative for renal impairment (eGFR below 35) but stopping abruptly causes rebound vertebral fractures - always transition to a bisphosphonate when ceasing denosumab.

sources.label: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

subtopic_detail: HSV encephalitis - empirical management
stem: A 56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his partner with 3 days of progressive headache, confusion, fever and one witnessed generalised seizure today. He has no significant medical history and is up to date with his vaccinations. He is drowsy with GCS 13, disoriented, has slow word-finding speech and no focal neurology. There is no rash and no neck stiffness on examination. He has had no recent travel or sick contacts.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, HR 102, BP 138/86, RR 18, SpO2 97 percent room air
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3V4M6), disoriented, no meningism, no focal weakness, no rash, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 10, CRP 32, Na 132, glucose 6.4, creatinine 82, ECG sinus rhythm
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours empirically before any imaging or lumbar puncture is performed for suspected herpes simplex viral encephalitis
options.rationale: Empirical aciclovir within 6 hours significantly reduces mortality and morbidity in HSV encephalitis; never delay for imaging or LP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)

options.text: Perform urgent lumbar puncture for CSF analysis and viral PCR before any therapy is commenced to confirm the diagnosis and identify the responsible pathogen accurately
options.rationale: Empirical aciclovir should not be delayed for LP because diagnostic confirmation takes hours and delay increases morbidity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)

options.text: Order urgent non-contrast CT brain and EEG, then commence ceftriaxone 4 g daily plus dexamethasone for bacterial meningitis cover pending further results from investigations
options.rationale: Bacterial meningitis cover alone misses HSV encephalitis; aciclovir must be added immediately to any empirical regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)

options.text: Administer intravenous levetiracetam 1500 mg loading dose for seizure control and observe with neurological observation until brain imaging and CSF results return for review
options.rationale: Anticonvulsants treat seizure activity but do not address the underlying encephalitis; aciclovir is the time-critical intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)

options.text: Treat with intravenous foscarnet 60 mg/kg every 12 hours as first-line antiviral therapy for adult viral encephalitis given the higher potency over standard aciclovir options
options.rationale: Foscarnet is reserved for aciclovir-resistant HSV in immunocompromised patients; aciclovir is first-line empirical therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Encephalitis)

explanation.summary: HSV-1 encephalitis is the most common sporadic viral encephalitis with mortality above 70 percent untreated, falling to 20-30 percent with prompt aciclovir. Classic features are subacute fever, headache, behavioural change, focal seizures and temporal lobe signs, with MRI brain showing asymmetric temporal lobe T2 hyperintensity. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose; HSV PCR is highly sensitive after 48 hours of symptoms. Empirical aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours IV starts before imaging or LP and continues for 14-21 days. Add bacterial meningitis cover (ceftriaxone plus dexamethasone) if meningism present pending results.
key_points: Empirical aciclovir IV before imaging or LP if encephalitis suspected.
Aciclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for 14-21 days.
MRI temporal lobe T2 hyperintensity is classic.
CSF HSV PCR may be negative in first 48 hours - repeat if clinical suspicion.
Add bacterial cover if any meningism or rash.
explanation.pearls: Maintain renal function with prehydration and dose-adjust aciclovir for renal impairment - crystalline nephropathy is a recognised reversible toxicity, monitor creatinine daily during therapy.

subtopic_detail: Adult bacterial meningitis - empiric therapy with dexamethasone
stem: A 32-year-old previously well woman presents with 18 hours of severe headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia and one episode of vomiting. She is alert. Examination demonstrates positive Brudzinski sign and significant neck stiffness. She has no rash. She has no allergies and is not pregnant. The CT brain has been arranged but is delayed and a lumbar puncture has not yet been done. She is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 108, BP 128/76, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, severe neck stiffness, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, no rash, no focal neurology, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18, neutrophils 16, CRP 240, lactate 1.6, Na 138, glucose 7.2, coags normal, blood cultures sent
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate empirical therapy?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours without adjunctive corticosteroid because steroids have inconclusive benefit in adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis
options.rationale: Adjunctive dexamethasone improves outcomes (reduced hearing loss and mortality) in pneumococcal meningitis and is given empirically in Australian guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)

options.text: Defer all antibiotic therapy until non-contrast CT brain excludes raised intracranial pressure followed by diagnostic lumbar puncture for CSF analysis and culture
options.rationale: Antibiotics must not be delayed for imaging or LP in suspected meningitis; first-dose within 1 hour is the primary goal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily with paracetamol as outpatient management for community-acquired meningitis in a well-appearing patient without focal neurology
options.rationale: Suspected bacterial meningitis requires intravenous antibiotics and inpatient management; oral therapy is inadequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose monotherapy and proceed directly to lumbar puncture for CSF testing without empirical beta-lactam coverage first today
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy does not adequately cover meningococcus or Listeria; combination with a third-generation cephalosporin is needed in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg immediately followed by ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours with benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours pending CSF results
options.rationale: Empirical regimen for adult bacterial meningitis is ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin with dexamethasone given just before or with the first dose of antibiotic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Meningitis)

explanation.summary: Adult bacterial meningitis requires immediate empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour of suspicion. The Australian standard regimen is ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h plus benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV q4h for pneumococcus, meningococcus and Listeria cover, with adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h for 4 days given just before or with first antibiotic dose to improve outcomes especially in pneumococcal disease. Add vancomycin if penicillin-resistant pneumococcus is a concern, ampicillin in immunocompromised or above 50 for Listeria. CT before LP if focal neurology, seizures, GCS below 14, immunocompromise or papilloedema. Notify public health for meningococcal disease.
key_points: First-dose IV antibiotic within 1 hour of suspicion.
Ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin empirically in Australia.
Dexamethasone with or just before first dose - reduces hearing loss and mortality.
CT before LP only if focal signs, seizures, GCS below 14, immunocompromise.
Notify public health and give meningococcal prophylaxis to close contacts.
explanation.pearls: Add ampicillin 2 g q4h to cover Listeria in patients over 50, pregnant women, or immunocompromised - cephalosporins have no activity against Listeria and missing this cover increases mortality.

subtopic_detail: Suspected giant cell arteritis - initiation of treatment
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 74-year-old woman with 3 days of severe right-sided temporal headache, jaw claudication after a few minutes of chewing, and a brief episode of blurred vision in her right eye that resolved after 30 minutes this morning. She has been generally fatigued for 6 weeks. Past history includes hypertension and osteoporosis on alendronate. Examination reveals tenderness over the right temporal artery, which is non-pulsatile and feels thickened. Visual acuity is currently 6/6 bilaterally and fundoscopy is normal.

data_table.Examination: Right temporal artery tender, thickened, pulseless; no proximal limb weakness, no scalp necrosis, neuro exam normal, fundoscopy normal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 116, platelets 444, WCC 9.8, ESR 92, CRP 78, ALP normal, creatinine 74
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily; alendronate 70 mg weekly; calcium 600 mg, vitamin D 1000 IU daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg daily immediately, refer urgently for temporal artery biopsy within 1 week, and arrange ophthalmology review the same day for visual symptom assessment
options.rationale: GCA with amaurosis fugax requires immediate high-dose oral or IV steroid to prevent permanent vision loss; biopsy follows within 1 to 2 weeks. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)

options.text: Arrange temporal artery biopsy first to confirm the diagnosis histologically before commencing any corticosteroid therapy that might confound interpretation of the histological vessel inflammation
options.rationale: Delaying steroids risks irreversible visual loss; treat first, biopsy after - histology remains diagnostic for up to 2 weeks. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)

options.text: Prescribe oral aspirin 100 mg daily, refer for urgent vascular ultrasound of the temporal artery, and review the result before deciding on initiation of corticosteroid therapy at a later date
options.rationale: Aspirin alone does not treat the underlying vasculitis and waiting for imaging delays sight-saving steroid. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)

options.text: Prescribe paracetamol regularly for headache, arrange GP review in 1 week with repeat inflammatory markers, and refer to general medicine if the clinical features have not settled by then
options.rationale: Suspected GCA with amaurosis fugax is a sight-threatening emergency; analgesia alone is inadequate. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 15 mg daily and refer to rheumatology outpatients for assessment within 4 weeks, providing patient information about polymyalgia rheumatica and steroid management plan
options.rationale: 15 mg is a polymyalgia rheumatica dose; GCA needs 40 to 60 mg daily (or 1 g pulsed methylprednisolone with visual loss) to suppress vasculitis. (Source: eTG Giant Cell Arteritis)

explanation.summary: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) presents in patients over 50 with new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, transient or permanent visual loss, and constitutional symptoms. ESR and CRP are typically elevated. Treatment must begin immediately on clinical suspicion to prevent irreversible vision loss: oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily (1 mg/kg) without visual symptoms; IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days when visual loss is present. Temporal artery biopsy is the diagnostic gold standard and remains positive for up to 2 weeks after starting steroid. Tocilizumab is steroid-sparing in relapse or intolerance. Bone protection and PPI are added with high-dose steroid.
key_points: Treat on clinical suspicion - do not wait for biopsy.
Visual loss requires IV pulse methylprednisolone.
ESR and CRP usually elevated; biopsy is gold standard.
Biopsy yield preserved for up to 2 weeks on steroid.
Bone protection and PPI with high-dose steroid.
explanation.pearls: The halo sign on temporal artery ultrasound (hypoechoic ring around the vessel wall) has high specificity for GCA and is a non-invasive alternative for diagnostic confirmation when biopsy is delayed.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice Giant Cell Arteritis

subtopic_detail: Adult cellulitis - empirical antibiotic selection
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 56-year-old man with a 2-day history of a painful, hot, expanding erythematous area over his left shin since gardening barefoot last week. There is no systemic upset, no fever, and no diabetes. He has had no previous cellulitis. He has no penicillin allergy. The erythema is sharply demarcated, warm and tender, with no fluctuance, no necrotic centre, and no skin breakdown beyond a small healed abrasion. He is able to weight-bear and there is no joint involvement. He is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Sharply demarcated erythema 12 cm diameter over left anterior shin, warm and tender, no fluctuance, no lymphangitis, small healed abrasion centrally, inguinal nodes not enlarged
data_table.Investigations: Not routinely required for uncomplicated cellulitis
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Oral cephalexin 500 mg orally four times daily for 5 days, with arm or leg elevation, demarcating the leading edge in pen, and review at 48 hours to ensure clinical improvement
options.rationale: Cephalexin is first-line for non-severe cellulitis in Australia, covering Streptococcus pyogenes and methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Oral amoxicillin clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days as broad spectrum cover including Gram negatives, with anti-inflammatory cover using oral ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily
options.rationale: Co-amoxiclav is broader than required for typical limb cellulitis and not first-line; reserved for animal or human bite or polymicrobial wounds. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days to cover community-associated MRSA, accepting that doxycycline gives suboptimal Streptococcus cover compared to a beta lactam antibiotic
options.rationale: Doxycycline is added when MRSA is suspected, not used as monotherapy because of inadequate streptococcal cover. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g six hourly via outpatient parenteral antibiotic service for 5 days, with daily nurse review and observation for failure of erythema demarcation to improve
options.rationale: IV therapy is reserved for severe cellulitis, sepsis or oral failure; non-severe cellulitis is managed with oral cephalexin or dicloxacillin. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

options.text: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days as targeted streptococcal cover, with topical mupirocin to the abrasion site to address the likely entry portal
options.rationale: Penicillin alone misses Staphylococcus aureus which can also cause non-purulent cellulitis; cephalexin or dicloxacillin is preferred. (Source: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

explanation.summary: Cellulitis is a dermal and subcutaneous infection commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus. Non-purulent cellulitis (no abscess) is treated with oral cephalexin or dicloxacillin for 5 days in non-severe disease. Severe cellulitis with systemic features, rapid spread, immunocompromise, or facial location warrants IV flucloxacillin. MRSA cover (doxycycline or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is added for known MRSA colonisation, recent residential aged care, recent IV drug use or recurrent infections. Demarcate the leading edge to monitor response and elevate the limb. Failure to improve at 48 hours warrants reassessment for abscess, necrotising fasciitis, or unusual pathogen.
key_points: Cephalexin 500 mg QID for 5 days is first-line.
IV flucloxacillin for severe disease or sepsis.
Add MRSA cover for known risk factors.
Demarcate margin and elevate the limb.
Reassess at 48 hours if no improvement.
explanation.pearls: Bilateral lower limb erythema is rarely cellulitis - consider venous stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis or contact dermatitis since cellulitis is almost always unilateral.

sources.label: eTG Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

subtopic_detail: Hyperthyroidism in pregnancy - first trimester management
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29-year-old G2P1 at 9 weeks gestation referred by the GP for thyroid abnormalities found on routine bloods. She has tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance and a 3 kg weight loss despite a good appetite. There is no family history of thyroid disease. She has no eye signs. She is not currently taking any medication.

Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated. The midwife notes a goitre is palpable. The infant's heart rate is 158 on Doppler. There is no neck pain or recent viral illness.

data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, smooth diffuse goitre 2x normal size, no nodules palpable, no exophthalmos, no lid lag, no pretibial myxoedema, hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: TSH less than 0.01, free T4 38, free T3 12.4, TSH receptor antibodies positive, beta-hCG 90000, viability scan 9+2
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence carbimazole 15 mg daily and titrate based on monthly free T4, refer to endocrinology and high-risk obstetrics, and aim for free T4 in the upper third of the non-pregnant reference range
options.rationale: Carbimazole is teratogenic in the first trimester (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia); switch to propylthiouracil until end of first trimester. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Commence propylthiouracil 100 mg three times daily, refer to endocrinology and high-risk obstetrics, switch to carbimazole at start of second trimester, and monitor free T4 monthly
options.rationale: Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester because carbimazole has a teratogenic window then; switch to carbimazole after 12 to 14 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Reassure as transient gestational hyperthyroidism, recheck thyroid function at 16 weeks, and reserve antithyroid drug therapy for persistent biochemical abnormality at the second trimester review
options.rationale: Symptomatic Graves disease with positive TSH receptor antibodies is not transient gestational thyrotoxicosis; treatment is required. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange radioactive iodine ablation now to permanently resolve the hyperthyroid state and prevent fetal exposure to antithyroid drugs through the placenta over the remainder of the pregnancy
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy as it crosses the placenta and ablates the fetal thyroid. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

options.text: Commence propranolol 20 mg three times daily as monotherapy for symptom control, defer definitive antithyroid drug therapy until after delivery to avoid placental transfer to the developing fetus
options.rationale: Beta blockers control symptoms but do not treat the underlying hyperthyroidism, which carries fetal and maternal risk if untreated. (Source: RANZCOG Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Untreated Graves disease in pregnancy increases miscarriage, preterm birth, pre-eclampsia, congenital malformations and thyroid storm. Distinguish from transient gestational thyrotoxicosis, which is beta-hCG mediated, peaks at 10 to 12 weeks, occurs without TRAb and resolves by 20 weeks. First-line therapy in Graves in pregnancy is propylthiouracil 50 to 150 mg TDS in the first trimester (carbimazole linked to embryopathy in weeks 6 to 10), switching to carbimazole 5 to 15 mg daily from the second trimester (PTU has higher hepatotoxicity risk). Aim for free T4 at the upper limit of normal. Monitor TRAb in late pregnancy as high levels predict neonatal hyperthyroidism. Beta-blockers add symptom control.
key_points: PTU first trimester, switch to carbimazole second trimester.
Aim for free T4 at upper limit of normal.
Radioactive iodine absolutely contraindicated.
Distinguish Graves from transient gestational thyrotoxicosis.
Monitor TRAb in third trimester for neonatal risk.
explanation.pearls: TSH receptor antibody titre over 3 times the upper limit of normal in the third trimester predicts neonatal Graves disease and warrants paediatric endocrinology handover before delivery.

sources.label: ATA Guidelines on Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Lewy body dementia - antipsychotic avoidance
stem: You are the geriatric medicine registrar reviewing a 73-year-old man in the rehab ward with a 12-month progressive cognitive decline characterised by fluctuating attention, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations of small animals, and bradykinesia with a shuffling gait. His wife reports he acts out his dreams at night. Cognition fluctuates from near-normal to disoriented over hours. He has been agitated overnight on the ward and the after-hours doctor is considering a sedating antipsychotic to manage the night-time disturbance for the rest of the admission.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 78, BP 124/72 lying, BP 102/64 standing, RR 16, SpO2 98%
data_table.Examination: Bradykinesia, mild cogwheel rigidity bilaterally, MMSE 22/30 with marked fluctuation across the assessment, no focal neurology, no seizure activity
data_table.Investigations: Hb 132, UEC normal, TSH 1.9, B12 320, glucose 5.4, CT brain age-related atrophy, MRI excluded vascular dementia, DaTscan reduced striatal uptake
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 5 mg nocte (recently started)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his nocturnal behavioural disturbance?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg at night for behavioural disturbance, with reassessment in 1 week to assess for sedation, parkinsonism worsening, or any other adverse effects on motor function
options.rationale: Antipsychotics, including atypicals such as olanzapine, cause severe sensitivity reactions in Lewy body dementia and are generally avoided. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

options.text: Stop the donepezil because cholinesterase inhibitors may aggravate behavioural disturbance, and substitute with quetiapine 25 mg at night for sedation and management of visual hallucinations
options.rationale: Donepezil should continue - it improves cognition and reduces hallucinations in DLB; stopping it would worsen the clinical picture. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

options.text: Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg at night for hallucinations and behavioural disturbance, accepting the small risk of extrapyramidal side effects in older patients with cognitive impairment
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics like haloperidol are particularly dangerous in DLB, causing severe parkinsonism, cognitive worsening and increased mortality. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

options.text: Optimise non-pharmacological interventions, exclude delirium triggers (infection, constipation, urinary retention, pain), continue cholinesterase inhibitor, and consider low-dose melatonin for sleep regulation
options.rationale: Non-pharmacological approaches with delirium screen and cholinesterase inhibitor optimisation are first-line; antipsychotics carry up to 50% severe sensitivity reaction rate. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

options.text: Commence levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily to address the parkinsonism, accepting that this may worsen hallucinations but provides motor benefit for the patient's gait disturbance
options.rationale: Levodopa is reserved for disabling motor symptoms and used cautiously because it worsens hallucinations and is not first-line in DLB. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) presents with the core triad of fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. Supportive features include REM sleep behaviour disorder, severe neuroleptic sensitivity, and reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake on DaTscan. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) improve cognition and reduce hallucinations and are first-line. Antipsychotics provoke severe sensitivity reactions (parkinsonism, autonomic instability, cognitive worsening, NMS-like crisis, mortality) in up to half of patients; even quetiapine carries risk. Manage behavioural disturbance with delirium screen, environmental measures, sleep hygiene, melatonin and cholinesterase optimisation first. When antipsychotic is unavoidable, very low-dose quetiapine is the least bad option.
key_points: Core DLB: fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism.
REM sleep behaviour disorder is supportive.
Cholinesterase inhibitor first-line for cognition and hallucinations.
Avoid antipsychotics - severe sensitivity in up to 50%.
Screen for delirium and reversible triggers.
explanation.pearls: Reduced striatal uptake on dopamine transporter (DaT) imaging differentiates DLB from Alzheimer disease with high specificity and supports DLB diagnosis when clinical features are equivocal.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice Dementia with Lewy Bodies

subtopic_detail: Provoked VTE - duration of anticoagulation
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man for outpatient follow-up after a confirmed right lower limb deep vein thrombosis 3 months ago. The DVT followed elective right total knee replacement and was diagnosed at day 5 postoperatively. He is on apixaban 5 mg twice daily after a loading dose at presentation. He is otherwise well, has had no symptoms since the event, has no personal or family history of VTE, and is not on hormones. He is back to his usual activity level and his postoperative recovery is otherwise excellent.

data_table.Examination: Knee well healed, no calf swelling, no tenderness, no chest signs, no new neurology
data_table.Investigations: FBE normal, UEC creatinine 78, LFTs normal, INR baseline 1.0, repeat duplex ultrasound shows residual non-occlusive thrombus, no recurrence
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD; paracetamol PRN for occasional knee pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Stop apixaban and commence aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely for secondary prevention against recurrent venous thromboembolism, with review by haematology before any future major surgery
options.rationale: Aspirin gives only modest VTE recurrence reduction; routine prescription is not standard after provoked DVT once anticoagulation is complete. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely because residual thrombus on ultrasound indicates ongoing prothrombotic state and conveys a high risk of recurrence without long-term anticoagulation
options.rationale: Residual venous thrombus alone does not mandate indefinite anticoagulation in surgically provoked DVT; the provoking factor has resolved. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily and continue indefinitely for extended secondary prevention, with annual review of bleeding risk and renal function to maintain ongoing anticoagulation safety
options.rationale: Extended low-dose secondary prevention is for unprovoked VTE with acceptable bleeding risk, not surgically provoked events with no recurrent risk factor. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

options.text: Switch from apixaban to warfarin with INR target 2 to 3 for ongoing therapy and arrange thrombophilia screening including factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation and lupus anticoagulant
options.rationale: Thrombophilia screening is not indicated for provoked VTE because it does not change duration of anticoagulation in this scenario. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

options.text: Stop apixaban now at the standard 3 months and provide written advice on VTE recurrence symptoms with safety net advice for return if any new chest, leg or breathlessness symptoms develop
options.rationale: Provoked DVT with a major transient risk factor (recent surgery) is treated for 3 months; longer therapy does not reduce recurrence risk meaningfully and increases bleeding. (Source: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE)
source_refs: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

explanation.summary: Duration of anticoagulation for VTE depends on whether the event was provoked, unprovoked or cancer-associated. Provoked VTE with a major transient risk factor (surgery, immobilisation, trauma, pregnancy) is treated for 3 months. Unprovoked VTE is treated for at least 3 to 6 months with consideration of extended therapy if bleeding risk is acceptable; rivaroxaban 10 mg or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily are validated extended secondary prevention options. Cancer-associated VTE is treated with a DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban) or LMWH for at least 6 months and continued while cancer is active. Routine thrombophilia screening does not change management in most cases.
key_points: Provoked VTE: 3 months of anticoagulation.
Unprovoked VTE: at least 3 to 6 months, consider extended.
Cancer-associated VTE: DOAC or LMWH while cancer active.
Routine thrombophilia screening rarely changes management.
Extended low-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban for select unprovoked cases.
explanation.pearls: The HERDOO2 rule identifies low-risk women with unprovoked VTE (under 50, no hyperpigmentation/oedema/redness, D-dimer under 250) who can safely stop anticoagulation at 3 months; men have no validated equivalent.

sources.label: ANZSBT and HSANZ Guidance on Anticoagulation in VTE

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection - diagnostic imaging selection
stem:
You are the ED registrar called to see a 62-year-old man with sudden onset severe ripping interscapular and chest pain that began 1 hour ago at rest. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension. On examination there is a 28 mmHg difference between arms with the right side higher, an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge that was not previously documented, and reduced left radial pulse volume.

ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy and no ST elevation. He is alert and his pain remains severe despite 5 mg of intravenous morphine.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 92, BP right arm 178/96, BP left arm 150/90, RR 22, SpO2 97%
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, early diastolic murmur LSE, reduced left radial volume, no focal neurology, chest clear, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus LVH no ST elevation, troponin 28 (mildly raised), chest x-ray widened mediastinum 9 cm, D-dimer 4.8, creatinine 92, lactate 1.6
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 4 mg daily; amlodipine 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence aspirin 300 mg and ticagrelor 180 mg, give a heparin bolus then infusion, and refer to cardiology for emergent percutaneous intervention for likely NSTEMI complicated by acute aortic regurgitation
options.rationale: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is contraindicated in suspected aortic dissection; the clinical picture points to dissection, not NSTEMI. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram on the ward first to confirm the diagnosis before any CT imaging is performed, with cardiology consult once visualisation of the aortic root has been obtained
options.rationale: TTE has poor sensitivity for type B dissection and may delay definitive CT or TOE; contrast CT aortogram is the standard. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Administer thrombolysis with tenecteplase weight-adjusted bolus immediately based on the chest pain and elevated D-dimer, accepting that primary PCI is not available within the standard 120-minute window
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is catastrophic in aortic dissection causing fatal rupture or extension; ECG does not show STEMI. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Commence sodium nitroprusside infusion to rapidly lower blood pressure to target systolic 120, with intravenous morphine for analgesia and observation for spontaneous resolution of pain
options.rationale: Vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic wall stress; beta-blockade must precede or accompany vasodilator. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Commence intravenous esmolol infusion to target heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 120, give intravenous opioid for analgesia, and arrange immediate contrast CT aortogram with surgical consult
options.rationale: Type A or B aortic dissection is treated with impulse control (heart rate then BP) and urgent CT aortogram with cardiothoracic surgical involvement. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular Aortic Dissection)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection presents with sudden severe ripping chest, back or interscapular pain; pulse deficits, blood pressure differential greater than 20 mmHg between arms, new aortic regurgitation, mediastinal widening and end-organ ischaemia are key supportive features. Initial management is impulse control - lower heart rate to under 60 with IV beta-blockade (esmolol or labetalol) THEN reduce systolic BP to 100 to 120 with vasodilator if still elevated; this minimises shear stress on the dissection flap. CT aortogram is the imaging gold standard; TOE is the bedside alternative. Stanford type A (ascending aorta) requires emergent cardiothoracic surgery; type B (descending only) is managed medically unless complicated.
key_points: Rate first then BP with IV beta-blockade.
CT aortogram is the diagnostic gold standard.
Type A = emergent surgery; Type B = medical unless complicated.
Antiplatelet, anticoagulant, thrombolysis contraindicated.
Pulse deficit and BP differential support diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: The pain-pulse-pressure triad of severe chest pain, BP differential greater than 20 mmHg, and pulse deficit identifies dissection earlier than imaging and should mandate empirical impulse control while CT is arranged.

subtopic_detail: STEMI without immediate PCI access
stem: You are the ED registrar in a regional hospital 220 km from the nearest cardiac catheterisation laboratory. A 58-year-old man arrives with 80 minutes of central crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm. He has hypertension and dyslipidaemia and is a current smoker. He took aspirin 300 mg on the ambulance and is haemodynamically stable. The nearest PCI service has confirmed a minimum 150-minute door-to-balloon time including air transfer.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, T 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, chest clear, normal heart sounds, no murmur, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG: 2 mm ST elevation V2-V4 with reciprocal changes in II, III, aVF; troponin pending; no prior ECG available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Commence intravenous metoprolol 5 mg three times to slow heart rate and defer reperfusion until troponin returns
options.rationale: Beta-blockers in STEMI are timed after reperfusion and not before; waiting for troponin delays time-critical therapy. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI)

options.text: Administer intravenous heparin alone and arrange transfer for primary PCI on arrival 150 minutes after first medical contact
options.rationale: Delaying reperfusion to 150 minutes when fibrinolysis can be given within 30 minutes loses myocardium; fibrinolysis is preferred when PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI)

options.text: Continue oral aspirin 300 mg only and arrange transfer for angiography within 24 hours without acute reperfusion
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy alone does not deliver reperfusion in STEMI; either PCI or fibrinolysis is required. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI)

options.text: Administer oral ticagrelor 180 mg load and observe in the coronary care unit without further reperfusion therapy
options.rationale: Ticagrelor is an adjunct after the reperfusion decision and does not substitute for fibrinolysis or PCI. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI)

options.text: Administer intravenous tenecteplase weight-based bolus plus clopidogrel and enoxaparin then transfer for early angiography within 24 hours
options.rationale: When PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact, fibrinolysis with tenecteplase plus adjunctive clopidogrel and enoxaparin followed by pharmaco-invasive transfer is the recommended Australian pathway. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: STEMI; eTG: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: STEMI reperfusion strategy depends on time from symptom onset and door-to-balloon delay. Primary PCI is preferred when it can be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Otherwise, fibrinolysis with tenecteplase is given within 30 minutes of arrival, combined with aspirin, clopidogrel (preferred over prasugrel and ticagrelor pre-fibrinolysis) and enoxaparin, then transfer for early angiography within 3 to 24 hours. Contraindications to fibrinolysis include recent intracranial bleed, ischaemic stroke within 3 months, severe hypertension and active internal bleeding.
key_points: PCI is preferred if achievable within 120 minutes; otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 minutes.
Adjuncts post-fibrinolysis: aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin.
Pharmaco-invasive transfer for angiography is undertaken within 3 to 24 hours.
explanation.pearls: When predicted door-to-balloon exceeds 120 minutes, give intravenous tenecteplase within 30 minutes of arrival plus clopidogrel 300 mg and enoxaparin, then transfer for early angiography.

subtopic_detail: Severe acute pancreatitis
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 54-year-old man admitted overnight with epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea and vomiting. He drinks 80 g of alcohol most evenings. He has been started on intravenous fluids and morphine. At 24 hours after admission you are asked to reassess him because he has become more tachypnoeic, his urine output has fallen and he feels worse. He has no history of cardiac or renal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, RR 28, SpO2 92% on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs, T 38.2°C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen diffusely tender with guarding, no peritonism, no rebound, no rash, no jaundice, urine output 18 mL/hour over the last 3 hours
data_table.Investigations: Lipase 1820 U/L, calcium 1.92 mmol/L, glucose 11.4 mmol/L, urea 14.6 mmol/L, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L, LDH 480 U/L, AST 220 U/L, PaO2 on arterial gas 58 mmHg on supplemental oxygen

lead_in: Which severity stratification action is most appropriate now?

options.text: Apply Ranson criteria at 48 hours and continue current ward-level management until that time point
options.rationale: Ranson criteria are designed for prognostic scoring not real-time triage and delay critical care decisions; clinical and physiological assessment must guide escalation now. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis)

options.text: Commence intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics prophylactically to prevent infected necrosis
options.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics do not reduce mortality or infected necrosis in acute pancreatitis and are not recommended; antibiotics are reserved for documented infection. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis)

options.text: Continue ward-level care with intravenous fluids and morphine and review at 48 hours with repeat lipase
options.rationale: Repeat lipase has no prognostic value and ward-level care is inadequate for a patient meeting organ failure criteria. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis)

options.text: Arrange urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography to relieve presumed gallstone obstruction
options.rationale: ERCP in acute pancreatitis is reserved for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; this presentation is alcohol-related and ERCP is not indicated. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis)

options.text: Transfer urgently to a high-dependency unit because the patient meets organ failure criteria for severe acute pancreatitis
options.rationale: Persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours defines severe acute pancreatitis; tachypnoea with PaO2 under 60 mmHg, oliguria and tachycardia in this patient represent at least respiratory and cardiovascular dysfunction warranting HDU-level care. (Source: GESA: Acute pancreatitis; ANZICS guidance)

explanation.summary: Severity stratification of acute pancreatitis uses the revised Atlanta classification: mild (no organ failure), moderately severe (transient organ failure or local complications) and severe (persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours). Modified Marshall scoring identifies cardiovascular, respiratory and renal dysfunction. Severe disease has 20 to 50% mortality and demands HDU or ICU level care, early enteral nutrition and CT imaging only after 72 hours unless complications are suspected. Prophylactic antibiotics are not supported.
key_points: Persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours defines severe acute pancreatitis.
Modified Marshall score grades respiratory, cardiovascular and renal dysfunction.
Avoid prophylactic antibiotics; reserve CT for after 72 hours.
explanation.pearls: Severe acute pancreatitis is defined by persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours; PaO2 under 60 mmHg, urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/hour or systolic BP under 90 mmHg trigger HDU transfer.

subtopic_detail: Carotid endarterectomy timing
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man in the stroke clinic 3 days after a transient ischaemic attack of right-sided weakness and aphasia lasting 30 minutes that resolved spontaneously. He has hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and is a former smoker. He is on aspirin 100 mg daily and has been started on atorvastatin 80 mg daily. He has no atrial fibrillation on Holter monitoring. His ABCD2 score is 5.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, T 36.7°C, sinus rhythm
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, no carotid bruits audible, no signs of cardiac failure
data_table.Investigations: Carotid duplex: 80% stenosis left internal carotid artery, MRI brain DWI shows small acute left frontal infarct, no haemorrhage, lipids LDL 1.8 mmol/L on statin, HbA1c 6.0%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Add clopidogrel 75 mg daily as long-term dual antiplatelet therapy without carotid surgical or stenting intervention
options.rationale: Long-term DAPT has not been shown to substitute for revascularisation in symptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis and increases bleeding risk. (Source: NSF Stroke)

options.text: Continue medical management alone with aspirin and atorvastatin and arrange surveillance carotid duplex in 6 months
options.rationale: Surgical revascularisation is superior to medical management alone for symptomatic 70 to 99% stenosis; medical-only management is reserved for asymptomatic or surgically high-risk patients. (Source: NSF Stroke)

options.text: Refer for carotid endarterectomy ideally within 2 weeks of the symptomatic event with ongoing aspirin and statin therapy
options.rationale: Symptomatic carotid stenosis between 70% and 99% benefits most from carotid endarterectomy within 14 days of the index event; benefit declines markedly beyond 4 weeks. (Source: NSF Stroke; eTG: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Refer for carotid endarterectomy electively in 3 to 6 months once the patient has fully recovered from the TIA event
