options.rationale: Delaying surgery beyond 14 days reduces the absolute risk reduction in stroke; the highest recurrence risk falls in the first 2 weeks. (Source: NSF Stroke)

options.text: Refer for carotid artery stenting as first-line intervention in this 68-year-old man with high-grade symptomatic stenosis
options.rationale: Carotid endarterectomy remains the standard for symptomatic stenosis in patients over 70 with suitable anatomy; stenting is reserved for surgically high-risk patients or unfavourable anatomy. (Source: NSF Stroke)

explanation.summary: Symptomatic carotid stenosis between 70% and 99% benefits substantially from carotid endarterectomy, with the largest absolute risk reduction when surgery occurs within 14 days of the index event. Number needed to treat to prevent one stroke at 5 years is approximately 6 when surgery happens within 2 weeks but rises sharply with delay. Best medical therapy with aspirin, statin and blood pressure control continues alongside surgery. Carotid artery stenting is an alternative when endarterectomy is contraindicated.
key_points: Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70 to 99% should be operated within 14 days.
Number needed to treat is approximately 6 within 2 weeks and rises with delay.
Continue antiplatelet, statin and BP control alongside surgery.
explanation.pearls: TIA with ipsilateral 70 to 99% carotid stenosis - book carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks; the absolute risk reduction halves if surgery is delayed beyond 4 weeks.

subtopic_detail: HFrEF GDMT in low-BP patient
stem: You are the cardiology registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. His echocardiogram shows LVEF 28% and a moderately dilated left ventricle. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. He is currently on ramipril 5 mg daily, frusemide 40 mg daily and metformin 1 g twice daily. He has been improving over 3 days of hospital admission and is now euvolaemic.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 98/58 mmHg seated, HR 72 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, T 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema, lungs clear, mild left ventricular heave, no murmur
data_table.Investigations: K 4.6 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (eGFR 46 mL/min/1.73 m^2), HbA1c 7.2%, NT-proBNP 1800 pg/mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next medication adjustment?

options.text: Increase ramipril to 10 mg daily aiming for maximum tolerated ACE inhibitor dose
options.rationale: Up-titration of ramipril risks hypotension in a patient with SBP 98 mmHg; further BP-neutral pillars should be added before pushing the ACE inhibitor. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure)

options.text: Switch ramipril to sacubitril-valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily today
options.rationale: Sacubitril-valsartan introduces additional blood pressure-lowering effect and is uncertain in this borderline normotensive patient until SGLT2 inhibitor is established; transition usually requires SBP above 100 mmHg. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure)

options.text: Add spironolactone 25 mg daily today as the next pillar of guideline-directed therapy
options.rationale: MRA addition is appropriate but with current eGFR 46 and potassium 4.6 mmol/L it requires close electrolyte monitoring; SGLT2 inhibition has a more favourable risk profile here as the immediate addition. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure)

options.text: Add empagliflozin 10 mg daily and continue ramipril 5 mg daily without dose changes
options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors provide mortality benefit in HFrEF independent of diabetes status, are tolerated down to eGFR 20 mL/min and do not lower blood pressure significantly when added to background therapy; this is the next step in low-BP HFrEF optimisation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure; AMH)

options.text: Add ivabradine 5 mg twice daily for heart rate control alongside the current therapy
options.rationale: Ivabradine requires sinus rhythm with heart rate above 75 bpm despite maximal beta-blocker therapy; this patient is not yet on a beta-blocker. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ: Heart failure)

explanation.summary: The four pillars of HFrEF therapy are ACE inhibitors or ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors. Modern practice favours rapid sequential introduction of all four pillars at low dose rather than full up-titration of each before adding the next. SGLT2 inhibitors have minimal blood pressure effect and are favoured in low-BP patients. ARNI introduction usually requires SBP above 100 mmHg and a 36-hour ACE inhibitor washout before the first sacubitril-valsartan dose.
key_points: Sequential low-dose introduction of all four HFrEF pillars beats slow uptitration of each.
SGLT2 inhibitors are BP-neutral and effective down to eGFR 20 mL/min.
ARNI introduction generally needs SBP above 100 mmHg and 36-hour ACE inhibitor washout.
explanation.pearls: In low-BP HFrEF the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin or dapagliflozin can be added without dose changes to other pillars and offers mortality benefit within weeks.

subtopic_detail: HIV with cryptococcal antigen positive
stem: You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 38-year-old man newly diagnosed with HIV through community testing. He has a CD4 count of 78 cells/microL and viral load of 350,000 copies/mL. He has no current symptoms of headache, fever or visual changes. As part of baseline workup his serum cryptococcal antigen has returned positive at a titre of 1:160. He has not commenced antiretroviral therapy yet. He has no medication allergies and is not on any current medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/74 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.7°C, weight 72 kg
data_table.Examination: No meningism, no focal neurology, normal fundoscopy, no skin lesions, no oral candidiasis, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Serum cryptococcal antigen positive 1:160, lumbar puncture pending, MRI brain pending, FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits, hepatitis serology negative, tuberculin IGRA negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer all interventions and repeat serum CrAg in 4 weeks to see if the titre declines spontaneously
options.rationale: Untreated cryptococcal infection in advanced HIV progresses to disseminated disease and meningitis; intervention cannot wait. (Source: ASHM: HIV)

options.text: Commence antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Starting ART without first excluding cryptococcal meningitis risks fatal cryptococcal IRIS within weeks of immune reconstitution. (Source: ASHM: HIV)

options.text: Commence oral fluconazole 800 mg daily for 2 weeks then start ART without lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Oral fluconazole alone is inadequate for cryptococcal meningitis induction therapy if disease is present; LP must be performed to know which regimen is required. (Source: ASHM: HIV)

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture today to exclude cryptococcal meningitis before any treatment decision
options.rationale: Asymptomatic serum CrAg positivity in advanced HIV requires lumbar puncture to identify subclinical meningitis, which would mandate induction antifungal therapy with delayed ART start to mitigate IRIS. (Source: ASHM: HIV; BHIVA guidance)

options.text: Refer for primary prophylaxis with oral itraconazole 200 mg daily without further investigation
options.rationale: Itraconazole is not the recommended cryptococcal prophylaxis or treatment agent and does not replace evaluation for CNS involvement. (Source: ASHM: HIV)

explanation.summary: In advanced HIV with CD4 under 100 cells/microL, serum cryptococcal antigen screening identifies subclinical infection. A positive result requires lumbar puncture to exclude cryptococcal meningitis. If meningitis is present, induction antifungal therapy combines intravenous liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine for 2 weeks, followed by consolidation with fluconazole and maintenance. ART is delayed by 4 to 6 weeks after antifungal initiation to reduce cryptococcal IRIS risk.
key_points: Serum CrAg-positive HIV patients with CD4 under 100 cells/microL need LP regardless of symptoms.
Defer ART by 4 to 6 weeks after antifungal start to reduce cryptococcal IRIS risk.
Liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine is the induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis.
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic serum CrAg-positive with CD4 under 100 cells/microL needs LP first; if meningitis is confirmed delay ART by 4 to 6 weeks after antifungal induction.

subtopic_detail: Status epilepticus second-line
stem: You are the medical registrar in resus seeing a 28-year-old woman with known generalised epilepsy on lamotrigine, brought in with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that started 12 minutes before arrival and has continued. Paramedics gave 10 mg intramuscular midazolam without termination. On arrival she received a further intravenous 4 mg lorazepam without effect. She is not pregnant on point-of-care testing. Her airway is patent on a jaw thrust and she has IV access.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/96 mmHg, HR 138 bpm, RR 24, SpO2 94% on 15 L oxygen via non-rebreather, T 37.8°C, BSL 5.8 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Ongoing generalised tonic-clonic seizure, no focal neurology, no rash, no head injury, no needle marks
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.22 with metabolic acidosis, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, lamotrigine level pending, urine drug screen pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg infused over 5 to 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: After two adequate doses of benzodiazepine in established status epilepticus, intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg is the preferred second-line option with rapid onset, broad efficacy and no drug interactions. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus; eTG: Neurology)

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg infused over 30 minutes with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Phenytoin remains an alternative but ESETT-equivalent trial data show levetiracetam achieves seizure cessation at similar rates with fewer cardiovascular side effects in young adults. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus)

options.text: Intravenous propofol 2 mg/kg bolus and infusion to induce general anaesthesia immediately
options.rationale: Anaesthesia is third-line therapy after a failed second-line antiseizure medication; jumping to anaesthesia denies the chance of terminating with a non-anaesthetic agent. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus)

options.text: Intravenous sodium valproate 40 mg/kg infused over 10 minutes with electrolyte monitoring
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is acceptable but is generally avoided in women of childbearing potential due to teratogenicity; levetiracetam is preferred in this group. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus)

options.text: Intravenous midazolam 0.2 mg/kg as a third benzodiazepine dose to attempt termination
options.rationale: After two adequate benzodiazepine doses the failure rate of a third dose is high and respiratory depression accumulates; the standard next step is second-line antiseizure medication. (Source: NSF Status epilepticus)

explanation.summary: Status epilepticus is defined as a seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery between. First-line therapy is benzodiazepine: lorazepam 4 mg IV or midazolam 10 mg IM as a single repeatable dose. After two adequate doses without termination, second-line antiseizure medication is given. Australian and ESETT trial data support levetiracetam, sodium valproate or phenytoin with similar efficacy; levetiracetam is preferred in pregnancy, lactation and young women of childbearing potential.
key_points: Two benzodiazepine doses are first-line; a third is not recommended.
Second-line: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, sodium valproate 40 mg/kg or phenytoin 20 mg/kg.
Levetiracetam is preferred in women of childbearing potential.
explanation.pearls: After two failed benzodiazepine doses in status epilepticus, intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg over 10 minutes is the preferred second-line in women of childbearing potential.

subtopic_detail: Contrast-associated AKI prevention
stem: You are the medical registrar planning a non-emergency CT coronary angiogram in a 74-year-old man with stable angina to clarify the cause of his recurrent chest pain. He has type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease stage 3b with stable eGFR 32, and well-controlled hypertension. He is on perindopril, frusemide 40 mg daily, atorvastatin and metformin. He is not in acute heart failure and has had no recent illness. The cardiologist has requested your input on peri-procedural medication.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/74 mmHg, HR 68 bpm, T 36.6°C, weight 84 kg
data_table.Examination: JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema, lungs clear, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L, eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m^2, K 4.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.8%, urine ACR 14 mg/mmol

lead_in: Which combination of peri-procedural strategies is most appropriate?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1.4% at 3 mL/kg/hour for 1 hour pre-procedure as the sole preventive intervention
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate has not been shown to be superior to sodium chloride 0.9% and is no longer routinely recommended for contrast-associated AKI prevention. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)

options.text: Withhold metformin permanently and give oral N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily for 24 hours pre- and post-procedure
options.rationale: Permanent metformin cessation is unnecessary and oral N-acetylcysteine has been shown to have no benefit in preventing contrast-associated AKI. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)

options.text: Continue all current medications including perindopril, frusemide and metformin without peri-procedural changes
options.rationale: Diuretics increase intravascular volume depletion and metformin should be withheld when eGFR is under 45 mL/min to avoid lactic acidosis if AKI develops. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)

options.text: Withhold metformin for 48 hours from morning of procedure, give intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% at 1 mL/kg/hour pre and post
options.rationale: Patients with eGFR under 45 mL/min undergoing iodinated contrast warrant volume expansion with isotonic saline, minimum contrast volume and temporary metformin withdrawal to prevent lactic acidosis from procedural AKI. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)

options.text: Administer prophylactic intravenous loop diuretic 80 mg immediately pre-contrast to enhance contrast clearance
options.rationale: Diuretic-induced volume depletion worsens contrast nephropathy risk and is contraindicated as prophylaxis. (Source: KHA-CARI; AMH)

explanation.summary: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury risk rises with reduced eGFR, diabetes, heart failure, hypovolaemia and use of nephrotoxic drugs. The most consistently effective preventive strategy is intravenous isotonic crystalloid hydration before and after contrast administration. Metformin is held for 48 hours when eGFR is under 45 mL/min because of the risk of metformin-associated lactic acidosis if AKI develops. Iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast at the smallest necessary volume reduces risk further. N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate are not routinely recommended.
key_points: Intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% pre- and post-procedure is the primary intervention.
Hold metformin for 48 hours when eGFR is under 45 mL/min.
N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate are no longer recommended.
explanation.pearls: For eGFR 30 to 45 mL/min undergoing iodinated contrast, intravenous saline at 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre- and post-procedure with 48-hour metformin pause is the preventive standard.

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative alpha-blockade
stem: You are the endocrine registrar planning the surgical preparation for a 47-year-old woman with a 5.2 cm right adrenal mass producing markedly elevated 24-hour fractionated metanephrines. She has paroxysmal severe headaches with palpitations and pallor. Her resting blood pressure is 168/108 mmHg with episodes recorded to 220/120 mmHg during paroxysms. Her HbA1c is 6.4% and she is not on any current medications. Cardiology review showed normal left ventricular function. Surgery is planned for 14 days from now.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/108 mmHg average over the last day, HR 96 bpm, RR 16, T 36.6°C, weight 64 kg
data_table.Examination: Patient anxious, mild diaphoresis at rest, no signs of cardiac failure, no abdominal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Plasma metanephrines markedly elevated, 24-hour urinary metanephrines elevated, K 3.6 mmol/L, Mg 0.78 mmol/L, ECG sinus tachycardia, MRI confirms 5.2 cm right adrenal lesion

lead_in: Which preoperative regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated against orthostatic BP, add atenolol 25 mg daily after 7 days, high salt diet
options.rationale: The Endocrine Society Australia-aligned regimen starts alpha-blockade 10 to 14 days before surgery, adds a beta-blocker only after adequate alpha-blockade to avoid unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis, and uses sodium loading to expand intravascular volume before tumour resection. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia; eTG: Endocrinology)

options.text: Atenolol 25 mg daily first to control heart rate then add phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily after 5 days, normal salt diet
options.rationale: Starting beta-blockade before adequate alpha-blockade leaves unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Amlodipine 5 mg daily titrated to control blood pressure as the sole preoperative agent for 14 days before surgery
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are second-line additions when alpha-blockade alone is insufficient; they are not preferred monotherapy because they do not blunt catecholamine surge during tumour manipulation. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Proceed directly to surgery without preoperative blockade because the patient has been asymptomatic between paroxysms
options.rationale: Unprepared phaeochromocytoma surgery carries 25 to 50% perioperative mortality from cardiovascular collapse and is contraindicated. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion alone for 14 days before surgery as the sole preoperative blockade agent
options.rationale: Magnesium is a useful intraoperative adjunct but is not the recommended preoperative blockade regimen. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative preparation aims to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia and post-resection hypotension. Alpha-blockade is started 10 to 14 days before surgery with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin titrated against orthostatic blood pressure. Once adequate alpha-blockade is achieved, a beta-blocker can be added to control reflex tachycardia. Sodium and water loading expands intravascular volume to prevent post-resection hypotension. Intraoperative adjuncts include magnesium sulfate, sodium nitroprusside and short-acting beta-blockers.
key_points: Alpha-blockade precedes beta-blockade by at least 7 days.
Phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin titrated against orthostatic BP.
Sodium loading expands intravascular volume for post-resection BP support.
explanation.pearls: Start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily 10 to 14 days before phaeochromocytoma resection and only add a beta-blocker once alpha-blockade is established; reverse sequence risks fatal unopposed alpha-mediated crisis.

subtopic_detail: DOAC choice in atrial fibrillation with CKD stage 3
stem: You are the GP seeing a 78-year-old woman with newly diagnosed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 4 (age over 75, hypertension, prior TIA, female sex not counted in CHA2DS2-VA). Her HAS-BLED is 2. Her eGFR is 38 mL/min/1.73m2 (CKD G3b) and serum creatinine 145 micromol/L. She has no liver disease, no recent bleeding and weighs 62 kg. She is hesitant about warfarin because she cannot easily attend frequent INR checks.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6°C, HR 88 irregular, RR 14, BP 138/82
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no peripheral oedema, no murmurs, no neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG AF, eGFR 38, Cr 145, Hb 128, LFTs normal, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulant strategy?

options.text: Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily titrated against renal function with trough drug sampling
options.rationale: Dabigatran is 80% renally cleared and is not preferred when eGFR is below 50; doses below 30 mL/min are contraindicated. (Source: NHFA)

options.text: Warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 with weekly point-of-care monitoring at her local clinic
options.rationale: Warfarin remains an option (and the only option in mechanical valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis), but DOACs are preferred when not contraindicated, particularly when reliable INR monitoring is difficult. (Source: NHFA)

options.text: Long-term aspirin 100 mg daily as monotherapy for stroke prophylaxis in atrial fibrillation
options.rationale: Aspirin alone is no longer recommended for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF because it offers little stroke benefit at significant bleeding risk. (Source: NHFA)

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily, dose-reduce if two of age 80, weight 60 kg, Cr 133 micromol/L
options.rationale: Apixaban is preferred in CKD G3b because it has the lowest renal clearance of the available DOACs in AU; dose-reduction criteria (any two of age over 80, weight under 60 kg, creatinine over 133 micromol/L) drive the 2.5 mg twice daily dose. (Source: NHFA AF guideline 2023)

options.text: Defer anticoagulation until Holter confirms at least six hours per day of AF burden
options.rationale: Documented paroxysmal AF on ECG with a CHA2DS2-VA score above 1 already meets criteria for anticoagulation; no time-in-AF threshold is required. (Source: NHFA)

explanation.summary: In non-valvular atrial fibrillation with CKD stage 3, apixaban is the preferred DOAC because of its lower dependence on renal clearance compared with dabigatran or rivaroxaban. Apixaban dose reduction criteria are any two of age 80 or more, weight 60 kg or less, or creatinine 133 micromol/L or more. Aspirin alone is not recommended for stroke prevention. Warfarin remains a reasonable option, particularly in valvular AF, but DOACs are preferred when monitoring is difficult.
key_points: Apixaban first-line in CKD stage 3 non-valvular AF.
Dose reduce if two of age 80, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 or more.
Aspirin alone is not appropriate stroke prevention in AF.
explanation.pearls: Recheck the apixaban dose-reduction criteria at each annual review; weight loss in older patients tips many into the 2.5 mg twice daily dose.

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency BP target
stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 56-year-old man with severe occipital headache, blurred vision and nausea for 6 hours. His BP at triage is 222/128 mmHg. He has a background of long-standing untreated hypertension and is normally well. Fundoscopy shows bilateral flame haemorrhages and a single cotton wool spot. He has new mild confusion and his ECG shows LVH with strain. He has no chest pain, no neurological deficit and no recent stroke. The renal function is mildly impaired with creatinine 145 micromol/L.

data_table.Examination: Mildly drowsy, GCS 14, no lateralising signs, fundoscopy as above
data_table.Investigations: Cr 145 micromol/L, K 3.9, troponin negative, ECG LVH strain pattern, CT head no acute haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate blood pressure target and agent in the next hour?

options.text: Discharge home on oral perindopril 5 mg with GP review in 48 hours of presentation
options.rationale: A hypertensive emergency with acute target organ damage cannot be managed as an outpatient; it requires monitored IV therapy. (Source: NHFA)

options.text: Lower the mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25 percent in the first hour with IV labetalol
options.rationale: In hypertensive emergency with acute target-organ damage (encephalopathy, retinopathy, AKI), the standard is a controlled fall in MAP of 20 to 25% over the first hour using IV titratable agents in a monitored setting; abrupt larger reductions risk watershed ischaemia. (Source: Heart Foundation hypertension guideline 2024)

options.text: Defer pharmacological treatment until ambulatory monitoring confirms sustained elevation
options.rationale: Documented hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage warrants immediate treatment without further ambulatory monitoring. (Source: NHFA)

options.text: Commence oral hydralazine plus oral clonidine simultaneously aiming for fast normotension
options.rationale: Oral combination therapy with hydralazine and clonidine is less controllable than IV titratable agents in a hypertensive emergency and can cause unpredictable BP swings. (Source: NHFA)

options.text: Bring BP to 140/90 mmHg within the first 30 minutes using sublingual nifedipine capsules
options.rationale: Rapid uncontrolled drops, particularly with sublingual nifedipine, are associated with watershed cerebral and renal infarction and are not recommended. (Source: NHFA)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is sustained BP elevation with acute target organ damage (encephalopathy, acute LV failure, dissection, eclampsia, retinopathy, AKI). It is managed with IV titratable agents (labetalol, hydralazine, GTN, clevidipine) in a monitored setting, with a controlled 20 to 25 percent reduction in MAP in the first hour to avoid watershed ischaemia. Hypertensive urgency without acute target organ damage is managed with reintroduction or up-titration of oral therapy in primary care or short-stay observation.
key_points: Reduce MAP 20-25% in the first hour, then more gradually.
Use IV titratable agents in a monitored bed.
Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated due to rapid swings.
explanation.pearls: In aortic dissection or pre-eclampsia the BP target is tighter and faster (systolic under 120 within minutes); for encephalopathy aim only for a 20-25% MAP reduction in the first hour.

subtopic_detail: TIA ABCD2 risk stratification and admission threshold
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 72-year-old man with a 25-minute episode of right-sided weakness and dysarthria that resolved 1 hour ago. He has hypertension, diabetes and is in sinus rhythm. CT brain is normal. He has no atrial fibrillation on telemetry. He is on perindopril, metformin and atorvastatin. Carotid Doppler ultrasound is available the next morning at the same site. He has no contraindication to antiplatelet therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/92, HR 78, RR 16, T 36.5 °C, SpO2 98% room air, BSL 8.2
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination now, no carotid bruit, no facial droop, no dysarthria currently
data_table.Investigations: CT brain unremarkable, ECG sinus rhythm, troponin negative; carotid Doppler tomorrow morning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit for inpatient stroke workup, start aspirin 300 mg today and arrange carotid imaging today
options.rationale: ABCD2 score 6 is high-risk for stroke within 48 hours; admit and complete carotid imaging and antiplatelet loading the same day to reduce early recurrence. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

options.text: Discharge home with aspirin 100 mg daily and a routine outpatient carotid Doppler in two weeks time
options.rationale: ABCD2 6 places this patient in the highest-risk group; outpatient management delays urgent revascularisation if a critical stenosis is present. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

options.text: Commence apixaban 5 mg twice daily today and arrange carotid Doppler tomorrow morning as planned
options.rationale: DOACs are reserved for cardioembolic TIA with atrial fibrillation; he is in sinus rhythm and antiplatelet therapy is appropriate. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI brain with diffusion weighting prior to commencing any antiplatelet therapy today
options.rationale: Antiplatelet should not be delayed to wait for MRI; loading dose of aspirin reduces early recurrence and can be given before further imaging. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

options.text: Refer to outpatient TIA clinic in 7 days without commencing any new medication today at all
options.rationale: Delaying assessment and antiplatelet therapy by a week in a high-risk TIA misses the window for preventing early stroke recurrence. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

explanation.summary: ABCD2 score predicts early stroke risk after TIA using age, blood pressure, clinical features, duration and diabetes. Scores of 4 or more, or any TIA with atrial fibrillation, warrant urgent same-day assessment in Australia. Aspirin 300 mg loading then 100 mg daily plus carotid imaging within 24 hours reduces early stroke. Dual antiplatelet with aspirin and clopidogrel for 21 days further reduces recurrence after minor stroke and high-risk TIA. Statin and BP control complete secondary prevention.
key_points: ABCD2 4 or more is high-risk for early stroke recurrence.
Load with aspirin 300 mg then 100 mg daily.
Image carotids and brain within 24 hours.
Use DAPT for 21 days after high-risk TIA or minor stroke.
explanation.pearls: About 5 percent of high-risk TIA patients have an ischaemic stroke within 48 hours; an effective rapid-access TIA clinic combined with same-day antiplatelet loading reduces this risk by approximately 80 percent.

subtopic_detail: AF cardioversion timing and DOAC anticoagulation
stem: You are the ED registrar managing a 64-year-old man with new symptomatic atrial fibrillation. Onset was 18 hours ago by his account during exertion. He has hypertension, diabetes and a CHA2DS2-VA score of 4. He is haemodynamically stable. He has no history of bleeding and no contraindication to anticoagulation. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function and no thrombus visualised. He prefers rhythm control if safe and you have decided cardioversion is appropriate.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 138 irregular, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no chest pain, no signs of heart failure, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142, U&E normal, INR 1.0, ECG atrial fibrillation 132 bpm, TTE LVEF 60% no thrombus, TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan around DC cardioversion?

options.text: Defer cardioversion until 3 weeks of therapeutic apixaban 5 mg twice daily have been completed
options.rationale: Onset under 48 hours allows early cardioversion after pre-procedural anticoagulation; full 3 week pretreatment is for established or uncertain onset AF. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

options.text: Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily now, cardiovert today and continue anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks
options.rationale: AF onset under 48 hours allows early cardioversion after at least one DOAC dose, with at least 4 weeks of anticoagulation afterwards and long-term anticoagulation given high CHA2DS2-VA. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

options.text: Cardiovert immediately without anticoagulation because no thrombus was seen on the transthoracic echo today
options.rationale: Transthoracic echo cannot exclude left atrial appendage thrombus; TOE is required if cardioversion is needed without prior anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

options.text: Bridge with intravenous unfractionated heparin and cardiovert in 7 days after admission to coronary care
options.rationale: Heparin bridging is unnecessary with effective DOAC therapy; modern Australian practice favours single DOAC dose then cardioversion within 48 hour window. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

options.text: Cardiovert without anticoagulation now and start aspirin 100 mg daily for long-term thromboprophylaxis
options.rationale: Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF; CHA2DS2-VA 4 needs full anticoagulation with a DOAC or warfarin. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

explanation.summary: For atrial fibrillation of definite onset under 48 hours, cardioversion can proceed after at least one therapeutic DOAC dose. For uncertain or longer-duration AF, either three weeks of effective anticoagulation or transoesophageal echo exclusion of thrombus is required first. Anticoagulation continues for at least four weeks after cardioversion regardless of CHA2DS2-VA score. Long-term anticoagulation depends on CHA2DS2-VA score; 2 or more warrants ongoing DOAC therapy in non-valvular AF.
key_points: Cardiovert under 48 h after a single DOAC dose.
Use TOE if onset uncertain or anticoagulation incomplete.
Continue anticoagulation 4 weeks after cardioversion.
CHA2DS2-VA 2 or more triggers long-term DOAC.
explanation.pearls: About 5 percent of patients have post-cardioversion stunning and silent thromboembolism even after successful restoration of sinus rhythm; four weeks of post-cardioversion anticoagulation reduces this to under 1 percent in non-valvular AF.

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 bundle and vasopressor choice in septic shock
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with two days of dysuria, fever and rigors. She is hypotensive with cool peripheries. She has no allergies and no chronic disease. Initial intravenous crystalloid 30 mL/kg has been given over the past hour but her mean arterial pressure remains 58 mmHg. Lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. Urine, blood cultures and a chest X-ray have been completed. Empirical antibiotics for severe urosepsis are being prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 122, BP 86/52, MAP 58, RR 24, SpO2 96% room air, UO 0.3 mL/kg/h
data_table.Examination: Warm flushed centrally, cool peripheries, no focal chest signs, suprapubic tenderness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L, CRP 220, creatinine 138, WCC 18 x10^9/L, urinalysis leucocytes and nitrites positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in haemodynamic management?

options.text: Continue further intravenous crystalloid up to 50 mL/kg before commencing any vasopressor support
options.rationale: Fluid above 30 mL/kg without response is unlikely to correct vasodilatory hypotension and increases pulmonary oedema risk; start vasopressor now. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Commence intravenous noradrenaline infusion via large-bore peripheral line targeting MAP 65 mmHg
options.rationale: Septic shock with MAP under 65 after 30 mL/kg fluid requires vasopressor; noradrenaline is first-line and can be initiated peripherally while central access is being secured. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline 1 mg bolus and commence infusion targeting systolic above 100 mmHg
options.rationale: Adrenaline boluses are reserved for cardiac arrest; adrenaline infusion is second line in septic shock when noradrenaline plus vasopressin are insufficient. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Commence dopamine 5 micrograms/kg/min infusion as the recommended first-line vasopressor in septic shock
options.rationale: Dopamine is no longer recommended first line in septic shock due to arrhythmia risk; noradrenaline is preferred. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Defer vasopressor and add intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg per day for refractory hypotension now
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added when noradrenaline doses exceed 0.25 micrograms/kg/min, not as a substitute for vasopressor; treatment of hypotension comes first. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle requires lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, and vasopressor for ongoing hypotension to keep MAP at least 65 mmHg. Noradrenaline is first-line and can be initiated through a large-bore peripheral cannula while central venous access is arranged. Vasopressin is added when the noradrenaline dose exceeds 0.25 to 0.5 micrograms/kg/min. Hydrocortisone 200 mg per day is added for refractory shock.
key_points: Start vasopressor if MAP under 65 after 30 mL/kg fluid.
Noradrenaline is the first-line agent in septic shock.
Vasopressin is added at noradrenaline 0.25 mcg/kg/min.
Hydrocortisone is reserved for refractory shock.
explanation.pearls: Each hour of antibiotic delay in septic shock increases mortality by approximately 7 percent; in Australian EDs the eMR sepsis pathway aims for antibiotic administration within 60 minutes of triage triggered by qSOFA or screening tool.

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection imaging and initial pharmacotherapy
stem: You are the ED registrar at a tertiary hospital seeing a 64-year-old man with sudden severe tearing interscapular pain. BP is 184/108 in the right arm and 142/82 in the left arm. He has a long history of hypertension and is on perindopril. He is now diaphoretic but alert. Pulses are present in all four limbs. ECG shows sinus rhythm with LVH but no ischaemic changes. He has no contrast allergy and creatinine is 92 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 184/108 right arm, 142/82 left arm, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, alert, palpable pulses all four limbs, no focal neurological deficit, no abdominal pain
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm LVH, CXR widened mediastinum, troponin negative, creatinine 92, D-dimer 3.8 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send for urgent transthoracic echocardiogram as the definitive first-line diagnostic test for aortic dissection
options.rationale: TTE has limited sensitivity for descending dissection; CT angiography is the standard first-line investigation with rapid availability. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Commence intravenous heparin infusion empirically until CT pulmonary angiogram has excluded clot
options.rationale: Heparin is contraindicated until dissection is excluded because it can cause catastrophic haemorrhage from the false lumen; image first. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Start intravenous nitroprusside infusion first without beta blocker to drop SBP under 110 mmHg fast
options.rationale: Vasodilator without prior rate control causes reflex tachycardia, increasing shear stress and dissection propagation; beta blocker is initiated first. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Arrange CT angiography of the aorta and start IV esmolol then sodium nitroprusside to control BP
options.rationale: CT angiogram aorta is the first-line investigation in suspected dissection; rate control with esmolol before vasodilator nitroprusside prevents reflex tachycardia and propagation. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Discharge home with oral perindopril increase to 8 mg daily once routine bloodwork is unremarkable
options.rationale: Differential blood pressure with sudden tearing pain and a widened mediastinum is dissection until proven otherwise; discharge would be catastrophic. (Source: NHFA Aortic Dissection)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection presents with tearing chest or back pain, differential pulses or BP, and mediastinal widening. CT angiography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is the standard imaging. Type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and requires urgent cardiothoracic surgery. Type B is medically managed unless complicated. Initial pharmacotherapy targets HR under 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg using intravenous esmolol or labetalol first, then nitroprusside or glyceryl trinitrate for ongoing blood pressure control. Analgesia with morphine is administered alongside.
key_points: Image with CT angiography of the aorta urgently.
Beta blocker before vasodilator to prevent reflex tachycardia.
Type A dissection needs urgent cardiothoracic surgery.
Avoid anticoagulation until dissection is excluded.
explanation.pearls: Initial Type A dissection mortality is around 1 percent per hour for the first 48 hours; phone the on-call cardiothoracic surgeon before the CT report is finalised if the patient is haemodynamically unstable or pulse deficits are progressive.

subtopic_detail: Dabigatran reversal with idarucizumab in major bleeding
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman with a confirmed traumatic intracerebral haemorrhage of 30 mL on CT after a fall. She takes dabigatran 150 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation. Her last dose was 4 hours ago. She has a GCS of 12 and is being prepared for neurosurgical input. She has no other medications and no chronic kidney disease. The hospital pharmacy stocks idarucizumab, prothrombin complex concentrate and tranexamic acid.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 174/96, HR 78, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.6 °C, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Examination: Right hemiparesis MRC 3/5, slurred speech, no other focal deficit, pupils equal reactive
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L, platelets 220, creatinine 85, INR 1.3, dTT pending, CT brain 30 mL right thalamic haematoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer prothrombin complex concentrate 25 IU/kg now and recheck the INR after 30 minutes
options.rationale: PCC is the agent of choice for warfarin or factor Xa inhibitor reversal; dabigatran requires the specific reversal antibody idarucizumab as first-line. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)

options.text: Administer intravenous idarucizumab 5 g as two 2.5 g boluses given 15 minutes apart now urgently
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is the specific monoclonal antibody fragment reversing dabigatran and is indicated for life-threatening bleeding in patients on dabigatran in Australia. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K 10 mg and fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg to correct her coagulopathy quickly
options.rationale: Vitamin K and FFP are for warfarin reversal; they do not reverse the direct thrombin inhibition by dabigatran in significant time. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)

options.text: Commence intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes as the sole haemostatic agent for ICH now
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid does not reverse dabigatran and is not standard therapy for spontaneous ICH; idarucizumab is required for dabigatran reversal. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis to remove dabigatran prior to commencing any specific reversal therapy
options.rationale: Dialysis removes dabigatran but takes hours; idarucizumab acts within minutes and is the first-line intervention in active major bleeding. (Source: NBA DOAC Reversal)

explanation.summary: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with high affinity and reverses anticoagulant effect within minutes. Indications include life-threatening or uncontrolled major bleeding and emergency surgery in patients on dabigatran. Dose is 5 g intravenously as two 2.5 g boluses. Andexanet alfa is the equivalent for apixaban and rivaroxaban, with PCC 25 to 50 IU/kg as alternative when unavailable. Local pharmacy stock and approval pathways should be confirmed in advance for major centres.
key_points: Idarucizumab 5 g IV in two boluses reverses dabigatran fast.
Andexanet alfa or PCC reverses Xa inhibitors.
Vitamin K and FFP do not reverse DOACs.
Confirm pharmacy stock and pathway in advance.
explanation.pearls: About 10 percent of patients re-anticoagulate within 12 to 24 hours after idarucizumab if intrinsic clearance is delayed by renal impairment; recheck thrombin time at 12 and 24 hours and consider a second dose if bleeding recurs.

subtopic_detail: Giant cell arteritis biopsy and steroid timing
stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 76-year-old woman with two weeks of new daily temporal headache, jaw claudication after a few bites, and a tender thickened right temporal artery. Vision is currently normal. She has had no transient visual loss and no diplopia. She has had no prior steroid use and has no diabetes. She has an enlarged thyroid but is biochemically euthyroid. Her ESR is 92 mm/h and CRP is 110 mg/L. The vascular team can perform temporal artery biopsy within 7 days.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 76, RR 16, T 36.7 °C, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Tender thickened right temporal artery, no pulses; visual acuity 6/9 bilaterally, no relative afferent pupillary defect
data_table.Investigations: ESR 92 mm/h, CRP 110 mg/L, FBC normal, platelets 380, no anaemia, eye fundoscopy normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg today and arrange temporal artery biopsy within the next week
options.rationale: Australian guidance recommends immediate high-dose corticosteroid in suspected GCA to prevent visual loss; biopsy within 2 weeks remains diagnostic despite early steroid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)

options.text: Defer all steroid therapy until temporal artery biopsy histology has confirmed the underlying diagnosis
options.rationale: Delay in starting steroid risks permanent visual loss; biopsy remains positive for around 2 weeks after corticosteroid commencement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)

options.text: Start intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days only for any patient with suspected GCA
options.rationale: Pulsed IV steroid is reserved for visual loss or visual symptoms; oral high-dose prednisolone is appropriate in uncomplicated suspected GCA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence indomethacin 50 mg three times daily and review again with ESR result in two weeks time
options.rationale: NSAIDs do not prevent ischaemic complications of GCA and steroid therapy is mandatory; delay is dangerous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence low-dose prednisolone 15 mg daily and arrange same-day temporal artery duplex ultrasound study
options.rationale: Low-dose steroid is insufficient for GCA; ultrasound is adjunctive and does not replace high-dose corticosteroid plus biopsy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Giant cell arteritis is a medical emergency because of risk of permanent vision loss from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Immediate high-dose corticosteroid 1 mg/kg orally is recommended on clinical suspicion before biopsy. Visual symptoms warrant intravenous methylprednisolone 500 to 1000 mg daily for 3 days. Temporal artery biopsy remains diagnostic for around two weeks after starting steroid. Tocilizumab is steroid-sparing for relapsing or refractory disease. Bone protection, gastric prophylaxis and infection screening accompany prolonged glucocorticoid therapy.
key_points: Start prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally on clinical suspicion.
Use IV methylprednisolone if visual symptoms are present.
Biopsy remains positive for about 2 weeks after starting steroid.
Tocilizumab is the steroid-sparing agent for relapsing disease.
explanation.pearls: Once one eye is affected by anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy in GCA, the contralateral eye becomes involved within 1 to 2 weeks in about 25 to 50 percent of untreated cases; immediate steroid plus ophthalmology review is mandatory.

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma crisis alpha then beta blockade
stem: You are the ED registrar managing a 44-year-old man with episodic severe headaches, palpitations and sweating. His BP today is 218/124 with HR 124. He has had no antihypertensive therapy. Recent imaging from an outside hospital showed a 5 cm adrenal mass on CT. Plasma free metanephrines from a prior workup were markedly elevated. He has had no prior cardiovascular events. He is now in the resuscitation cubicle with arterial line and ICU is aware. Endocrine surgery has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 218/124, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, T 36.8 °C, BSL 9.2
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, alert, no focal neurology, no chest pain currently, mild tremor
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia LVH; plasma normetanephrine markedly elevated; CT 5 cm right adrenal mass; troponin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management?

options.text: Start intravenous metoprolol 5 mg now and add phenoxybenzamine after rate control has been achieved
options.rationale: Beta blockade before alpha blockade in phaeochromocytoma causes unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis; this sequence is contraindicated. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Give intravenous hydralazine 10 mg as a single bolus to lower the blood pressure rapidly first now
options.rationale: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia in catecholamine excess and is not first line; alpha blockade is the priority. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Begin intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus to provide combined alpha and beta blockade in one rapid step
options.rationale: Labetalol has predominant beta blockade and weak alpha blockade and is not adequate alpha blockade for phaeochromocytoma crisis. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Commence intravenous phentolamine 5 mg boluses and titrated infusion, defer beta blocker until alpha block is established
options.rationale: Acute phaeochromocytoma crisis is managed with alpha blockade first using IV phentolamine; beta blockade is added once alpha block is established to prevent unopposed alpha effects. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g as a single bolus then continue infusion in lieu of any alpha blocker
options.rationale: Magnesium can be adjunctive in phaeochromocytoma crisis but does not replace alpha blockade which is the cornerstone of management. (Source: ESE Phaeochromocytoma)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma crisis is managed by establishing alpha adrenergic blockade first to prevent unopposed alpha vasoconstriction. Phentolamine intravenously is the agent of choice during a crisis, with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin orally during preparation for surgery. Beta blockade with propranolol or metoprolol is added only after alpha blockade is established, to control reflex tachycardia. Adequate sodium loading and volume repletion are required because chronic catecholamine excess contracts the intravascular volume. Definitive treatment is surgical resection after 7 to 14 days of pre-operative blockade.
key_points: Always block alpha receptors before beta in phaeochromocytoma.
Phentolamine IV is the acute alpha blocker of choice.
Adequate sodium loading precedes surgery.
Definitive treatment is laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
explanation.pearls: Aim for postural blood pressure below 120/80 sitting and not below 90/45 standing on alpha blockade, with mild nasal congestion as a clinical marker of adequate blockade before surgery is planned by the multidisciplinary team.

subtopic_detail: Rhabdomyolysis fluid resuscitation and hyperkalaemia management
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man brought in after 18 hours immobile on the floor following a methamphetamine binge. He has dark urine, swollen tender thighs and is oliguric. His CK is 86,000 IU/L. He has had no prior renal disease. He is alert but distressed by limb pain. Trauma has been excluded by primary and secondary survey. He has no medications. The intensive care registrar has been contacted regarding admission.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82, HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, T 36.9 °C, UO 0.2 mL/kg/h
data_table.Examination: Tense tender swollen thighs bilaterally, sensation intact, distal pulses intact, no compartment syndrome features yet
data_table.Investigations: CK 86,000 IU/L, K 6.4 mmol/L, creatinine 280, urea 18, pH 7.28, bicarbonate 16, urinalysis blood 3+ no RBC, ECG peaked T waves V2-V4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous insulin 10 units with dextrose 25 g only and reassess potassium after 30 minutes today
options.rationale: Insulin and dextrose lower potassium but ECG changes also require immediate membrane stabilisation with calcium before serum potassium-lowering measures. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)

options.text: Give intravenous frusemide 80 mg bolus to drive forced diuresis as the cornerstone of myoglobin clearance
options.rationale: Loop diuretics do not provide protective renal benefit in rhabdomyolysis; volume resuscitation is the priority and frusemide may worsen the situation if hypovolaemic. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)

options.text: Commence haemodialysis empirically to remove myoglobin and lower the serum creatine kinase fast
options.rationale: Myoglobin is not effectively cleared by dialysis; dialysis is reserved for severe AKI with classical indications. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)

options.text: Begin intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg as the recommended renal-protective osmotic diuretic in rhabdomyolysis
options.rationale: Mannitol does not improve renal outcomes in rhabdomyolysis and can worsen AKI if hypovolaemic; isotonic crystalloid is preferred. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)

options.text: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution and start aggressive isotonic crystalloid fluid
options.rationale: ECG changes with K 6.4 require immediate calcium gluconate for membrane stabilisation, plus aggressive isotonic crystalloid to maintain urine output above 200 mL/h in rhabdomyolysis. (Source: KHA-CARI AKI)

explanation.summary: Rhabdomyolysis can cause AKI through myoglobin precipitation, ischaemia and oxidative injury, especially with hypovolaemia. Australian and KDIGO guidance recommends early aggressive isotonic crystalloid to keep urine output around 200 to 300 mL/h. Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is treated with calcium gluconate first for membrane stabilisation, then insulin dextrose, salbutamol and sodium bicarbonate to shift potassium intracellularly. Renal replacement therapy is indicated for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, uraemic complications or volume overload. Compartment syndrome should be reassessed serially.
key_points: Calcium gluconate stabilises membranes immediately.
Aim for urine output 200 to 300 mL/h with isotonic fluid.
Avoid loop diuretics and mannitol routinely.
Dialysis is reserved for refractory complications.
explanation.pearls: Compartment syndrome can develop with high CK and tense tender muscles even after initial neurovascular exam is normal; serial compartment pressure measurement and early fasciotomy consultation with orthopaedics prevents irreversible muscle and nerve damage.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic therapy for native-valve right-sided endocarditis
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 38-year-old man with 4 weeks of fevers, sweats and a 6 kg weight loss. He has injected heroin daily for 4 years. On examination there is a new pansystolic murmur loudest at the lower left sternal edge. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures taken 12 hours apart have already grown methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic echo shows an 8 mm tricuspid vegetation. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 °C, HR 110, BP 118/72, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: New pansystolic murmur at LLSE louder on inspiration; multiple injection sites on forearms; no peripheral stigmata; clear chest; soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures: MSSA in 2 of 2 sets at 12 h apart; TTE: 8 mm tricuspid vegetation, preserved LV function; FBC and U&E unremarkable; HIV non-reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin alone for 6 weeks dosed to target trough 15-20 mg/L
options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for MRSA or beta-lactam allergy; flucloxacillin has superior outcomes for MSSA infective endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours for at least 4 weeks with daily review
options.rationale: MSSA infective endocarditis on a native valve is treated with intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours for at least 4 weeks; right-sided uncomplicated disease may be eligible for shorter courses with specialist input. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous amoxicillin and gentamicin combination for 6 weeks with daily monitoring
options.rationale: Amoxicillin and gentamicin target enterococcal or streptococcal endocarditis; this regimen under-treats Staphylococcus aureus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g once daily as monotherapy for 6 weeks under outpatient OPAT
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone has weaker MSSA activity than flucloxacillin and is not recommended as preferred therapy in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral cephalexin 1 g four times daily with outpatient cardiology review next week
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are insufficient for native-valve endocarditis; intravenous therapy is required with inpatient initiation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Therapeutic Guidelines recommend intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours for native-valve MSSA infective endocarditis for at least 4 weeks, with longer courses for prosthetic valve or complicated disease. Empirical therapy in suspected IE before cultures should cover Staphylococcus aureus (flucloxacillin) and, in prosthetic valve disease or MRSA-prevalent settings, MRSA (vancomycin). All patients need transoesophageal echocardiography for embolic and abscess assessment, daily clinical review, and surgical evaluation for complications.
key_points: Flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly is preferred for native-valve MSSA.
Vancomycin is reserved for MRSA or beta-lactam allergy.
Add gentamicin only as advised for synergy in selected scenarios.
TOE is required to assess complications.
explanation.pearls: Right-sided endocarditis in injecting drug users with uncomplicated MSSA disease, no metastatic abscess, normal renal function and no embolic complications can sometimes be treated with shortened intravenous courses or step-down oral therapy under infectious diseases supervision; never make this decision without specialist input.

subtopic_detail: Vasopressor initiation in fluid-refractory septic shock
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 72-year-old man transferred from the ward 48 hours after admission for community-acquired pneumonia. He has now had 2 litres of intravenous crystalloid in the last hour with no improvement. Blood cultures were drawn and intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam was administered 30 minutes ago. He is confused and looks unwell. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 °C, HR 124, BP 78/40, RR 28, SpO2 92% on 4 L oxygen, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries with capillary refill 5 seconds; coarse crackles right base; warm core; oliguria for 2 hours
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, WCC 21 x10^9/L, CRP 280 mg/L, creatinine 162 micromol/L (baseline 90), procalcitonin elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next intervention?

options.text: Continue with a further 2 L crystalloid bolus before considering vasopressor support
options.rationale: Persistent hypotension and lactate above 4 after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid (achieved at this weight) means further large boluses risk pulmonary oedema; vasopressors should be started now. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Commence dopamine infusion as a first-line vasopressor through a peripheral line first
options.rationale: Dopamine is associated with more arrhythmia and worse outcomes than noradrenaline and is no longer recommended as a first-line vasopressor in septic shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg before starting any vasopressor infusion now
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is reserved for vasopressor-refractory septic shock; it does not substitute for vasopressor initiation when hypotension persists after fluid resuscitation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion through central or large peripheral access targeting MAP ≥65
options.rationale: Fluid-refractory hypotension with lactate above 4 meets septic shock criteria; noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor in Australian and international guidelines, targeting MAP at least 65. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Defer further antibiotic doses until repeat blood cultures and sensitivities are available
options.rationale: Antibiotic therapy must continue without interruption once initiated; deferring doses increases mortality in septic shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

explanation.summary: Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 elements include measuring lactate, drawing blood cultures, administering broad-spectrum antibiotics, giving 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and starting vasopressors if hypotension persists. Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor with a MAP target of at least 65 mmHg. Vasopressin and hydrocortisone are added in vasopressor-refractory disease. Source control and re-evaluation drive the next phase of care.
key_points: Lactate above 4 and persistent hypotension after 30 mL/kg meet shock criteria.
Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor.
MAP target is at least 65 mmHg.
Add vasopressin and hydrocortisone in refractory shock.
explanation.pearls: In Australian practice, peripheral noradrenaline through a well-placed proximal large bore cannula is safe for at least the first few hours while a central line is being arranged; do not delay vasopressor initiation waiting for a central access in deteriorating septic shock.

subtopic_detail: Empirical therapy for adult bacterial meningitis with Listeria cover
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 65-year-old man with 12 hours of fever, severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. GCS is 13. No focal neurology. No skin rash. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He takes no immunosuppressants. Lumbar puncture has been performed and the CSF analysis is back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.5 °C, HR 116, BP 132/82, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Marked neck stiffness; positive Kernig sign; no focal deficit; no skin rash; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: CSF: WCC 1200/microL (90 percent neutrophils), protein 3.2 g/L, glucose 1.2 mmol/L (paired BSL 6.4 mmol/L), Gram stain pending; FBC and U&E unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly as the sole antibiotic until cultures return
options.rationale: In patients over 50 or immunocompromised, Listeria cover with benzylpenicillin is required alongside ceftriaxone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous amoxicillin and gentamicin only awaiting culture and sensitivity results
options.rationale: Amoxicillin and gentamicin under-treat the typical pneumococcal and meningococcal organisms; cephalosporin cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Ceftriaxone with benzylpenicillin Listeria cover and dexamethasone at standard adult doses
options.rationale: Adult patients over 50 or immunocompromised need ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly for pneumococcus and meningococcus, benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly for Listeria, and dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin alone with a target trough of 15-20 mg/L pending sensitivities
options.rationale: Vancomycin alone does not cover Listeria and is reserved for adjunctive cover of penicillin-resistant pneumococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Defer all antibiotics until Gram stain and culture results are available later today
options.rationale: Delaying therapy in bacterial meningitis worsens mortality and neurological outcome; empirical therapy precedes Gram stain results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Empirical therapy for adult bacterial meningitis in Australia is ceftriaxone for pneumococcal and meningococcal cover, with the addition of benzylpenicillin for Listeria in patients over 50, immunocompromised or pregnant. Adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 hours is given with or before the first antibiotic dose for suspected pneumococcal disease to reduce neurological sequelae. Lumbar puncture, blood cultures and CT brain in selected cases guide ongoing therapy.
key_points: Ceftriaxone covers pneumococcus and meningococcus.
Add benzylpenicillin in patients over 50 or immunocompromised for Listeria.
Dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly reduces sequelae in pneumococcal disease.
Do not delay antibiotics for imaging or Gram stain.
explanation.pearls: Indications to do CT before lumbar puncture include focal neurology, GCS under 10, recent seizure or significant immunosuppression; if any are present, draw blood cultures, give empirical antibiotics and dexamethasone immediately, then arrange CT, and proceed to lumbar puncture once safe.

subtopic_detail: Acute management of severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem: You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to assess a 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 3 on perindopril. Routine bloods done by the GP this morning returned a potassium of 6.7 mmol/L. An ECG taken on arrival shows peaked T waves throughout the precordial leads, reduced P wave amplitude and a QRS duration of 110 ms. He is alert and asymptomatic.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/86, HR 64 regular, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented; chest clear; no focal neurology; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 6.7 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L, creatinine 220 micromol/L (baseline 150), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L; ECG: peaked T waves, low P, QRS 110 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2-5 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T, P attenuation, QRS widening) requires immediate cardiac membrane stabilisation; calcium gluconate works in minutes and is the first step. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 20 mg alone as the sole urgent intervention to lower potassium now
options.rationale: Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly but does not stabilise the myocardium; it follows calcium when ECG changes are present. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

options.text: Oral cation exchange resin alone with planned outpatient repeat in 24-48 hours' time
options.rationale: Cation exchange resins remove potassium slowly and are inadequate when ECG changes are present and the K is 6.7. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous insulin and dextrose alone without prior calcium for myocardial stabilisation
options.rationale: Insulin and dextrose shift potassium effectively but do not stabilise the myocardium; calcium should precede them when ECG changes are evident. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

options.text: Cease perindopril alone with a planned repeat potassium check in 48 hours' time
options.rationale: Stopping the ACE inhibitor addresses the cause but does not treat the immediate cardiac risk from severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is a medical emergency. Management proceeds in three steps: stabilise the myocardium with intravenous calcium gluconate within minutes; shift potassium intracellularly using insulin with dextrose and nebulised salbutamol; and remove potassium from the body using diuresis, cation exchange resin or dialysis. Reversible causes including ACE inhibitor or potassium-sparing diuretic therapy should be addressed and follow-up potassium checks scheduled.
key_points: Calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium within minutes.
Insulin-dextrose and salbutamol shift potassium intracellularly.
Resin or dialysis removes potassium from the body.
Cease ACE inhibitor and review longer-term causes.
explanation.pearls: Calcium gluconate has a shorter duration than the potassium shift you generate, so repeat ECGs after 30-60 minutes; an evolving QRS or sine wave despite shifts means it is time for dialysis, not another insulin bolus.

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion diagnosis with negative antibody screen
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old man who has sex with men with a 10-day history of fever, sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy and a maculopapular rash on the trunk. He reports unprotected receptive anal intercourse with a new partner 3 weeks ago. He has had no recent travel. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Fourth-generation HIV combined antigen and antibody assay is negative. Streptococcal throat swab, EBV serology and CMV serology are all negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 96, BP 122/76, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Maculopapular rash on trunk; cervical, axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy; mild pharyngeal erythema; no oral ulceration; no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: HIV combined Ag/Ab fourth generation: negative; EBV IgM negative; CMV IgM negative; throat swab negative for strep; FBC: lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the HIV combined Ag/Ab test in 12 weeks for a definitive negative result
options.rationale: Repeat antibody testing alone delays the diagnosis during the window period when transmission risk to partners is high. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Order HIV RNA viral load PCR now to detect early infection within the window period
options.rationale: Acute HIV viral load PCR detects infection from around 10 days post-exposure and is the appropriate next test when fourth-generation Ag/Ab is negative but clinical suspicion is high. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Send CD4 count alone to assess immune status before deciding on next investigations
options.rationale: CD4 count assesses prognosis in established infection rather than diagnosing acute seroconversion; it is not useful in the window period. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Commence empirical antiretrovirals immediately without diagnostic confirmation now
options.rationale: Antiretrovirals require a confirmed diagnosis and specialist consultation; empirical commencement is not appropriate primary care practice. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Discharge with reassurance and review in 4 weeks if symptoms have not resolved
options.rationale: Symptoms strongly suggest acute seroconversion; reassurance and delayed review risks ongoing transmission and disease progression. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion presents with non-specific viral symptoms including fever, lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis and maculopapular rash within 2 to 4 weeks of exposure. The fourth-generation combined antigen and antibody test detects infection from about 2 weeks. When the fourth-generation test is negative but clinical suspicion is high during the window period, HIV RNA viral load PCR detects infection from about 10 days. Early diagnosis allows partner notification, prevention of transmission and prompt initiation of treatment.
key_points: Fourth-generation Ag/Ab detects from 2 weeks post-exposure.
HIV RNA PCR detects from 10 days; useful in window period.
Treat partners and notify with patient agreement.
Refer for specialist initiation of antiretrovirals.
explanation.pearls: In the same consultation, take the opportunity to discuss post-exposure prophylaxis for any other recent unprotected encounters and pre-exposure prophylaxis once acute infection is excluded; many MSM at risk are not yet aware of PrEP availability through Medicare in Australia.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection time-critical surgical referral
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes who presents with 12 hours of rapidly progressive, severely painful swelling of the left lower leg following trivial garden trauma. He looks toxic with rigors. The leg has dusky erythema with two haemorrhagic bullae and a small area of crepitus over the medial calf. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He has no documented antibiotic allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 95% room air
data_table.Examination: Dusky erythema with two haemorrhagic bullae; crepitus over medial calf; pain out of proportion; brisk capillary refill becomes sluggish at edges
data_table.Investigations: CRP 380 mg/L, WCC 24 x10^9/L, Hb 110 g/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 180 micromol/L, glucose 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L; LRINEC score 11

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Outpatient oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily with review in primary care in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy and outpatient review are dangerously inadequate; the clinical picture is necrotising soft tissue infection with high mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin 2 g 8-hourly as monotherapy without referral for surgical exploration
options.rationale: Antibiotic monotherapy without surgical debridement does not control source in necrotising fasciitis; mortality climbs steeply for every hour of delay to surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange punch skin biopsy first to confirm the diagnosis prior to any surgical consultation
options.rationale: Skin biopsy delays definitive source control; diagnosis of necrotising fasciitis is clinical and surgical, supported by laboratory clues such as LRINEC. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the affected leg before any surgical exploration takes place
options.rationale: MRI delays surgery and adds no value when clinical and laboratory features already strongly indicate necrotising infection; cross-sectional imaging is selectively used. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent surgical exploration with debridement plus IV piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin and vancomycin
options.rationale: Time-critical surgical debridement plus broad empirical antibiotic cover (piperacillin-tazobactam for Gram-negatives and anaerobes, clindamycin for toxin suppression, vancomycin for MRSA) is the Australian standard for necrotising soft tissue infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency. Pain out of proportion, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus and dusky erythema are key clinical clues. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, Hb, sodium, creatinine, glucose) supports clinical suspicion but should never delay surgery. Empirical antibiotics combine broad Gram-negative and anaerobic cover with toxin suppression by clindamycin and MRSA cover by vancomycin. Survival is inversely related to time from presentation to operating theatre.
key_points: Pain out of proportion and crepitus are key clinical clues.
LRINEC supports but does not replace clinical suspicion.
Surgical debridement is time-critical for survival.
Empirical cover: pip-taz plus clindamycin plus vancomycin.
explanation.pearls: Group A streptococcal necrotising fasciitis often presents with hyperacute onset and disproportionate pain before visible skin changes; if the pain story is dramatic and the leg looks deceptively mild, lean towards calling the surgeons early rather than waiting for the rash to declare itself.

sources.label: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy initiation in older-onset Parkinson disease
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 68-year-old retired teacher with an 18-month history of right-hand resting tremor, bradykinesia, mild rigidity, mild gait shuffle and difficulty with handwriting that is interfering with daily activities. There are no falls, no orthostasis, no early visual hallucinations and no cognitive impairment on MoCA (28/30). He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/76 supine, 124/74 standing; HR 70
data_table.Examination: Right-hand resting tremor 4 Hz; cogwheel rigidity at wrist; mild hypomimia; bradykinesia on finger taps; mild shuffling gait; no postural instability; MoCA 28/30
data_table.Investigations: TFTs, B12 and folate normal; FBC and U&E unremarkable; DAT-SPECT abnormal asymmetric nigrostriatal uptake

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Rasagiline 1 mg daily as monotherapy aiming to defer levodopa for at least 12 months
options.rationale: MAO-B inhibitors give only modest symptomatic benefit and are inadequate when handwriting and daily activities are clearly affected in older patients. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)

options.text: Pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily titrating to symptom control with no levodopa
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists in patients over 65 risk hallucinations, daytime sleepiness, impulse control disorders and oedema and are not preferred first-line at this age. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)

options.text: Amantadine 100 mg twice daily alone for symptom control over the next 6-12 months
options.rationale: Amantadine offers only modest benefit and is not standard first-line monotherapy in early Parkinson disease with functional impairment. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)

options.text: Levodopa with peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor titrated from low dose to symptom control
options.rationale: Levodopa with carbidopa or benserazide is first-line in patients over 65 with functional impairment; it produces the largest symptomatic benefit with lower hallucination risk than dopamine agonists in this age group. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for deep brain stimulation now before any oral pharmacotherapy is initiated
options.rationale: Deep brain stimulation is reserved for selected patients with established motor fluctuations or refractory tremor after years of pharmacotherapy; it is not first-line treatment. (Source: MOSAIC Parkinson Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Parkinson disease pharmacotherapy choice balances symptomatic benefit against motor and non-motor complications. In patients over 65 with clear functional impairment, levodopa with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor is first-line because it produces the largest symptomatic benefit with lower risk of hallucinations and impulse control disorders than dopamine agonists.
