Younger patients with mild disease may start a dopamine agonist or MAO-B inhibitor to defer motor fluctuations and dyskinesia. Multidisciplinary care and falls prevention complement pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Levodopa is preferred first-line in patients over 65.
Dopamine agonists risk hallucinations and impulse problems in older patients.
Younger patients may use agonists or MAO-B inhibitors to delay levodopa.
Multidisciplinary care supports long-term function.
explanation.pearls: Sudden withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy can precipitate a parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome that resembles neuroleptic malignant syndrome; always continue or replace dopaminergic therapy during admissions, even when patients cannot swallow, using rotigotine patch or apomorphine if needed.

subtopic_detail: Outpatient anticoagulation for provoked deep venous thrombosis
stem: You are the emergency department resident reviewing a 56-year-old man with a 5-day history of swelling and aching in the right leg. He returned 10 days ago from a 24-hour international flight. He has no chest pain or breathlessness. He has no personal or family history of clotting or bleeding. He is on no regular medications and has no allergies. His weight is 88 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 86, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Swollen erythematous right calf, tender along medial calf, asymmetric calf measurement 38 vs 35 cm, palpable distal pulses, no chest signs
data_table.Investigations: Whole-leg compression ultrasound: non-compressible right popliteal vein with extension to the femoral vein. FBC, U&E and LFTs unremarkable. eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73 m^2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit for intravenous unfractionated heparin titrated to APTT 60 to 80 seconds and bridge to warfarin maintaining INR 2 to 3 over the following days of admission
options.rationale: Inpatient unfractionated heparin and warfarin bridging is reserved for selected populations such as those with severe renal impairment or antiphospholipid syndrome; first-line outpatient management uses a direct oral anticoagulant. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Commence apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for at least 3 months and arrange general practitioner follow-up to plan total duration of anticoagulation
options.rationale: Outpatient apixaban with the 10 mg twice daily lead-in for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily for at least 3 months, is the Australian first-line treatment for provoked proximal DVT in a patient with normal renal function and no contraindications. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Refer urgently for thrombolysis with intravenous alteplase 100 mg over two hours to clear the venous thrombus and prevent post-thrombotic syndrome at long-term follow-up
options.rationale: Catheter-directed thrombolysis is reserved for limb-threatening phlegmasia cerulea dolens; routine thrombolysis is not used for typical proximal DVT. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Place an inferior vena cava filter and start apixaban 5 mg twice daily without a lead-in phase to prevent pulmonary embolism in his routine outpatient anticoagulation pathway
options.rationale: Inferior vena cava filters are reserved for patients with contraindications to anticoagulation; placing one without justification is not standard care. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Defer anticoagulation and arrange weekly compression ultrasounds for the next month to monitor whether the thrombus extends proximally before any treatment is initiated for him
options.rationale: Surveillance without anticoagulation is appropriate only for selected isolated distal DVT, not for confirmed proximal DVT, which carries a high pulmonary embolism risk. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Proximal deep venous thrombosis in a haemodynamically stable patient with adequate renal function is managed as an outpatient with a direct oral anticoagulant. Apixaban or rivaroxaban with the loading-dose regimen are first-line in Australia; warfarin remains used in antiphospholipid syndrome, mechanical heart valves and severe renal impairment. Total duration is at least 3 months for provoked DVT and indefinite for unprovoked or cancer-associated thrombosis. Compression stockings reduce post-thrombotic syndrome risk.
key_points: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily is the loading and treatment regimen
Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily is an equivalent direct oral anticoagulant
Provoked DVT is treated for at least 3 months; unprovoked DVT typically indefinite
Warfarin is preferred in antiphospholipid syndrome and severe renal impairment
IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindications to anticoagulation
explanation.pearls: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated in mechanical heart valves and antiphospholipid syndrome with triple positivity because of inferior outcomes in trials versus warfarin.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease corticosteroid duration
stem: You are the general medical registrar admitting a 68-year-old man with a 3-day worsening of his usual breathlessness and a productive cough with purulent sputum. He has known COPD on tiotropium and salbutamol with two exacerbations in the last 12 months. He is afebrile and able to speak in short sentences. He has no diabetes and no recent antibiotics. His baseline FEV1 is 52% predicted.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0 °C, HR 102, BP 138/82, RR 26, SpO2 90% room air, rising to 94% on 2 L nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Bilateral wheeze, use of accessory muscles, no consolidation, no peripheral oedema, calves soft
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray: hyperinflation, no consolidation. ABG on 2 L: pH 7.36, pCO2 52 mmHg, pO2 68 mmHg, HCO3 28 mmol/L. CRP 38 mg/L, WCC 12.4 x10^9/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of systemic corticosteroid?

options.text: Administer a single intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg dose only with no oral corticosteroid follow-on therapy planned at discharge from the emergency department
options.rationale: A single hydrocortisone dose alone is insufficient; an oral prednisolone course is required to consolidate the anti-inflammatory effect on the airways. (Source: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Prescribe oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 14 days with weekly clinic review during the taper and a brief intravenous methylprednisolone bridge to commence treatment
options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend a 5-day course of oral prednisolone for COPD exacerbations; longer courses do not improve outcomes and increase adverse effects. (Source: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Order intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg every 6 hours for 72 hours and convert to ongoing oral maintenance prednisolone 10 mg daily on discharge for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease control
options.rationale: Continuous maintenance prednisolone is not recommended for COPD because of the side-effect burden; exacerbations are treated with short courses. (Source: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Continue inhaled corticosteroid as currently prescribed with no oral course because this exacerbation is sufficiently mild and self-limiting and additional steroid will not change outcomes
options.rationale: Exacerbations with hypoxia and accessory muscle use require systemic corticosteroids; inhaled steroid alone does not address the acute airway inflammation. (Source: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days without taper and add empirical amoxicillin or doxycycline based on the purulent sputum profile during this exacerbation
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days without taper is the Australian COPD-X recommendation; antibiotics are indicated when at least two of the Anthonisen criteria (increased dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence) are met. (Source: COPD-X Plan)

explanation.summary: Acute exacerbations of COPD are treated with short-acting bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids and selective antibiotics. The COPD-X Plan recommends oral prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days; tapering is unnecessary and does not improve outcomes. Antibiotics are added when at least two of the Anthonisen criteria are met or when ventilatory support is required. Controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 88 to 92% prevents hypercapnic acidosis in CO2 retainers.
key_points: Oral prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days without taper is the recommended course
Antibiotics if 2 of 3 Anthonisen criteria are met: dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence
Controlled oxygen to SpO2 88 to 92% avoids worsening hypercapnia
Non-invasive ventilation is indicated for pH below 7.35 with pCO2 above 45 mmHg
Smoking cessation and pulmonary rehabilitation reduce future exacerbations
explanation.pearls: Eosinophil count above 0.3 x10^9/L during exacerbation predicts greater response to corticosteroids and is increasingly used to guide steroid use in COPD.

subtopic_detail: Metformin initiation in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes confirmed by two fasting glucose readings and an HbA1c. She has no symptoms of polyuria or weight loss. She has hypertension on perindopril. She does not smoke and drinks one glass of wine on weekends. She has no chronic kidney disease history and no acute cardiovascular events. Her body mass index is 31 kg/m^2.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m^2, no peripheral oedema, foot examination intact, fundi unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 7.8%, fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L, eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2, creatinine 86 micromol/L, LFTs normal, urine albumin:creatinine ratio 2.4 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Start basal insulin 10 units at night and uptitrate by 2 units every 3 days targeting a fasting glucose below 6.0 mmol/L without using any oral hypoglycaemic agent first
options.rationale: Basal insulin is reserved for severe hyperglycaemia, symptomatic disease or failure of oral therapy; first-line for new type 2 diabetes is metformin. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.text: Commence empagliflozin 10 mg daily as initial monotherapy and arrange a follow-up appointment in three months for a repeat HbA1c and dose review with a structured plan
options.rationale: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are typically added to metformin or used first-line with confirmed cardiovascular or renal indications; they are not standard initial monotherapy. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.text: Recommend lifestyle measures only and review the HbA1c in 6 months before starting any glucose-lowering medication, regardless of her starting HbA1c or other clinical risk profile
options.rationale: An HbA1c of 7.8% at diagnosis warrants concurrent metformin initiation alongside lifestyle measures; lifestyle alone takes too long to achieve target. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg daily with food, uptitrate over 4 weeks to 1 g twice daily as tolerated and review HbA1c and renal function at 3 months
options.rationale: Metformin is first-line for new type 2 diabetes in Australia with renal function above eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2; gradual titration reduces gastrointestinal side effects and HbA1c review at 3 months guides escalation. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

options.text: Initiate gliclazide modified-release 30 mg daily with breakfast and aim for an HbA1c below 6.5% over the next six months without using any other glucose-lowering therapy
options.rationale: Sulfonylureas are second-line because they cause weight gain and hypoglycaemia; metformin is preferred first-line for new type 2 diabetes. (Source: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

explanation.summary: Metformin remains the first-line pharmacotherapy for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes in Australia, alongside lifestyle modification. It is weight neutral, has no hypoglycaemia risk and reduces cardiovascular events in observational data. Renal function should be monitored: dose reduction is required when eGFR falls below 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 and metformin is contraindicated below 30. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists are added when cardiovascular, renal or weight indications exist.
key_points: Metformin is first-line at HbA1c above 6.5% with eGFR above 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2
Dose reduce at eGFR 30 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m^2 and avoid below eGFR 30
SGLT2 inhibitors are added with cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease
GLP-1 receptor agonists are added with obesity, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or for weight loss
Sulfonylureas remain useful third-line but cause weight gain and hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: Hold metformin for 48 hours around iodinated contrast administration if the eGFR is below 60 mL/min/1.73 m^2 to reduce lactic acidosis risk from contrast-induced renal impairment.

sources.label: RACGP General Practice Management of Type 2 Diabetes

subtopic_detail: Rate control of new-onset atrial fibrillation without heart failure
stem: You are the general medical resident reviewing a 64-year-old man brought in with palpitations and mild exertional breathlessness over 24 hours. He has hypertension on perindopril. He has no chest pain and no history of heart failure or asthma. He has had no fevers, recent surgery or alcohol binge. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He is comfortable at rest and the symptoms are not currently distressing.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 132 irregularly irregular, BP 138/86, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, JVP not elevated, no peripheral oedema, no murmurs, calves soft
data_table.Investigations: ECG: atrial fibrillation, ventricular rate 130s, no ischaemic changes. TSH 1.8 mIU/L, electrolytes normal, troponin not elevated. Bedside echo: preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. CHA2DS2-VA score 2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial rate-control agent?

options.text: Start oral digoxin 250 micrograms twice daily for 48 hours then a maintenance dose of 125 micrograms daily as first-line rate control monotherapy in this stable presentation
options.rationale: Digoxin is reserved as second-line rate control or for patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; beta-blockers are first-line in stable patients with preserved ejection fraction. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily and arrange anticoagulation with apixaban 5 mg twice daily for stroke prevention given his CHA2DS2-VA score
options.rationale: A beta-blocker is the first-line rate-control agent for atrial fibrillation in a stable patient without heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or asthma; concurrent direct oral anticoagulation is started because his CHA2DS2-VA score is 2. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for direct current cardioversion under sedation today within 48 hours of estimated onset, without prior anticoagulation, to restore sinus rhythm as the primary management strategy
options.rationale: Even within a 48-hour window, anticoagulation is recommended at the time of cardioversion in patients with an elevated CHA2DS2-VA score and ongoing thereafter. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

options.text: Start oral amiodarone 200 mg three times daily for one week and then 200 mg daily ongoing as long-term combined rate and rhythm control in this stable patient with preserved function
options.rationale: Amiodarone is reserved for symptomatic rhythm control in patients failing other rhythm-control agents or with structural heart disease; it is not first-line for stable rate control. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous verapamil 5 mg over 5 minutes and arrange oral diltiazem maintenance therapy alongside apixaban for ongoing rate control in this clinically stable patient
options.rationale: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are second-line and avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; beta-blockers are preferred first-line in Australia. (Source: NHFA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)

explanation.summary: New-onset atrial fibrillation in a stable patient is managed with rate control and stroke risk assessment using CHA2DS2-VA. Beta-blockers are first-line rate-control agents in patients without heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or asthma. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are second-line; digoxin is reserved for heart failure or as add-on. A CHA2DS2-VA score of at least 2 in men or at least 3 in women warrants long-term oral anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant.
key_points: Beta-blockers are first-line rate control in stable atrial fibrillation with preserved ejection fraction
CHA2DS2-VA at least 2 in men or at least 3 in women warrants anticoagulation
Direct oral anticoagulants are preferred over warfarin except in mechanical valves or antiphospholipid syndrome
Cardioversion within 48 hours still requires anticoagulation if stroke risk factors are present
Amiodarone is reserved for rhythm control in structural heart disease or refractory cases
explanation.pearls: The CHA2DS2-VA score replaced CHA2DS2-VASc in Australian practice in 2024, removing sex as a stroke risk variable; both men and women are evaluated on the remaining clinical risk factors.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic workup of suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
stem: You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 41-year-old man who arrived from Vietnam six months ago. He has had a 6-week productive cough with night sweats and 4 kg of weight loss. He has had two episodes of streaks of blood in his sputum. He has no chronic medical conditions and is on no medications. He has had no known sick contacts within his immediate household at present.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 96, BP 122/78, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Thin man, no clubbing, fine crackles in the right upper zone, no lymphadenopathy, normal cardiac examination
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray: right upper lobe cavitating consolidation with fibronodular changes. HIV antibody negative. FBC: Hb 124 g/L, WCC 8.4 x10^9/L, lymphocytes 1.6 x10^9/L. ESR 68 mm/h. CRP 56 mg/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Start empirical anti-tuberculosis therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol immediately and obtain microbiological samples after a 14-day clinical response review at the clinic
options.rationale: Empirical treatment before sampling compromises microbiological diagnosis and drug susceptibility testing; airborne isolation and rapid sampling are required first. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

options.text: Place a tuberculin skin test now and proceed to start empirical anti-tuberculosis therapy only if it shows induration above 10 mm at the 48 to 72 hour reading
options.rationale: Tuberculin skin testing assesses latent infection and may be negative in active disease; it does not establish active tuberculosis diagnosis or guide treatment. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

options.text: Arrange a single QuantiFERON-TB Gold-Plus interferon gamma release assay test, place him in airborne isolation pending the assay result and avoid further sputum sampling testing
options.rationale: Interferon gamma release assays detect latent infection and are not diagnostic of active pulmonary tuberculosis; sputum testing for nucleic acid amplification and culture is required. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

options.text: Place him in single-room airborne isolation and collect 3 sputum specimens for acid-fast smear, Xpert MTB/RIF nucleic acid amplification and mycobacterial culture before commencing therapy
options.rationale: Australian guidance requires airborne isolation, three sputum specimens for smear, Xpert MTB/RIF nucleic acid amplification testing and culture; Xpert results within hours allow rapid initiation of treatment with rifampicin resistance information. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

options.text: Order a chest computed tomography scan and bronchoscopy as the first investigation to obtain bronchoalveolar lavage samples for cytology and routine microbiological cultures upfront
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is reserved for sputum-scarce or sputum-negative cases; sputum sampling is the first-line investigation and avoids unnecessary aerosolisation. (Source: NTAC Tuberculosis Management Guideline)

explanation.summary: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is diagnosed by sputum microbiological testing after appropriate airborne infection control. Three early-morning sputum specimens are submitted for acid-fast smear, Xpert MTB/RIF nucleic acid amplification and mycobacterial culture. Xpert provides a rapid result with rifampicin resistance information within hours and is now standard first-line testing in Australia. Treatment with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol is started once microbiological diagnosis is confirmed, ideally with directly observed therapy.
key_points: Airborne isolation in a single negative-pressure room precedes sampling and treatment
Three sputum specimens are submitted for smear, Xpert MTB/RIF and culture
Xpert MTB/RIF provides rapid diagnosis and rifampicin resistance within hours
Tuberculin skin testing and interferon gamma release assays detect latent infection, not active disease
HIV testing is recommended in all newly diagnosed cases of tuberculosis
explanation.pearls: All new diagnoses of active tuberculosis in Australia are notifiable to the relevant state or territory public health authority within 24 hours of suspicion, even before culture confirmation.

subtopic_detail: Massive pulmonary embolism with haemodynamic compromise
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 64-year-old woman 8 days after right hip arthroplasty. She has sudden severe breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. She is on prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily. She has no major bleeding risk factors and no recent stroke or surgery to neck or central nervous system. She has not been thrombolysed for any other condition recently.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 124, BP 86/54, RR 32, SpO2 88% on 10 L Hudson mask
data_table.Examination: Pale, cold peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, raised jugular venous pulse, clear chest, right calf 4 cm larger than left
data_table.Investigations: CT pulmonary angiogram: bilateral central pulmonary emboli with right ventricular dilation, septal bowing. Troponin elevated. ECG: sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start a continuous enoxaparin infusion at 1 mg/kg twice daily and admit for observation and serial echocardiography to assess for right ventricular recovery over the next 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Therapeutic enoxaparin alone is appropriate for haemodynamically stable patients; massive pulmonary embolism with shock requires reperfusion therapy in addition to anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)

options.text: Insert an inferior vena cava filter via the femoral vein under fluoroscopic guidance as the initial intervention before considering further escalation of anticoagulation or reperfusion
options.rationale: Inferior vena cava filters are considered when anticoagulation is contraindicated; they do not address the existing pulmonary embolism causing shock. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)

options.text: Resuscitate with intravenous fluids and noradrenaline targeting MAP above 65 mmHg, give intravenous unfractionated heparin and administer alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours
options.rationale: Massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism with shock requires systemic thrombolysis with alteplase plus heparin and vasopressor support; this regimen reduces mortality in haemodynamically unstable patients. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)

options.text: Switch to oral apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily and discharge home in 24 hours for outpatient follow-up with general practitioner and physiotherapy
options.rationale: Oral apixaban and outpatient management are appropriate for low-risk pulmonary embolism; massive pulmonary embolism with shock requires inpatient reperfusion therapy. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)

options.text: Arrange immediate transfer for surgical pulmonary embolectomy as the first-line reperfusion strategy without prior thrombolysis or anticoagulation in this haemodynamically compromised patient
options.rationale: Surgical embolectomy is reserved for thrombolysis failure or contraindication and centres with cardiothoracic capability; systemic thrombolysis is first-line if no absolute contraindication. (Source: NHFA Pulmonary Embolism Position)

explanation.summary: Massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism is defined by haemodynamic compromise including persistent hypotension or shock. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours plus unfractionated heparin and resuscitation reduces mortality. Submassive (intermediate-risk) pulmonary embolism with right ventricular strain and raised troponin is managed with anticoagulation and close monitoring, with rescue thrombolysis if deterioration occurs. Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed thrombolysis is reserved for contraindications to systemic thrombolysis or thrombolysis failure.
key_points: Massive PE with hypotension or shock warrants systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg
Intermediate-risk PE is anticoagulation with monitoring; rescue thrombolysis if deterioration occurs
Low-risk PE may be treated as outpatient with direct oral anticoagulants
Right ventricular dilation and septal bowing are echocardiographic markers of high risk
Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy is reserved for thrombolysis failure or contraindication
explanation.pearls: Half-dose alteplase 50 mg has been used in catheter-directed thrombolysis trials for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism with reduced bleeding rates, although mortality benefit remains unproven.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis precipitated by intercurrent illness in a patient on long-term steroids
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 52-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency, presenting with 36 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain and progressive drowsiness. She normally takes hydrocortisone 10 mg morning, 5 mg afternoon and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She has not taken her steroids in the last 24 hours because of vomiting. She has not received intramuscular hydrocortisone at home and is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 °C, HR 124, BP 78/46, RR 24, SpO2 97% room air, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dry mucous membranes, hyperpigmented palmar creases, mild abdominal tenderness, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L, K 5.8 mmol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L, creatinine 124 micromol/L, urea 14 mmol/L. ABG: pH 7.30, HCO3 18 mmol/L. ECG sinus tachycardia. CRP 84 mg/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg once and arrange transfer to the medical ward for ongoing rehydration with crystalloid fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity; hydrocortisone is the agent of choice because it provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effect at high dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Triple her oral hydrocortisone dose to 30 mg morning and 15 mg afternoon, give an oral glucose drink and arrange admission for serial monitoring of electrolytes and observation
options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone is inappropriate when the patient is vomiting and in shock; intravenous administration is required, and triple oral dosing is reserved for milder intercurrent illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Restrict fluids to 1 L per 24 hours, give intravenous hypertonic saline 3% for the hyponatraemia and observe for clinical response before commencing any specific steroid therapy
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline and fluid restriction are inappropriate in adrenal crisis with hypovolaemic shock; aggressive isotonic fluid replacement and intravenous hydrocortisone are required first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Withhold any steroid until a random cortisol level has been processed by the laboratory and the result is available, then dose based on the measured cortisol level result
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis; treatment must not be delayed for laboratory results because mortality rises rapidly with delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, commence intravenous 0.9% saline with dextrose 5% and start an empirical sepsis workup with broad-spectrum antibiotic cover
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis treated with stat intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, aggressive crystalloid resuscitation with dextrose, and treatment of any precipitant such as infection; do not delay for laboratory results. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening complication of adrenal insufficiency precipitated by intercurrent illness, vomiting or missed steroid doses. Diagnosis is clinical and treatment must not be delayed for laboratory confirmation. Immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, aggressive crystalloid resuscitation with dextrose to correct hypoglycaemia, and treatment of the precipitant are time-critical. Patients with known adrenal insufficiency should carry a steroid emergency card and have a hydrocortisone autoinjector or intramuscular hydrocortisone available at home.
key_points: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis; do not delay treatment for cortisol levels
Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg six-hourly or 200 mg over 24 hours infusion
Aggressive crystalloid resuscitation with dextrose 5% corrects volume, sodium and hypoglycaemia
Identify and treat precipitants: infection, surgery, vomiting, missed steroid doses
Hydrocortisone at this dose provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity, so fludrocortisone is paused
explanation.pearls: Sick-day rules for patients on long-term steroids include doubling the oral dose for fever above 38 °C and tripling for fever above 39 °C, with intramuscular hydrocortisone for vomiting or unable to take oral medications.

subtopic_detail: Discriminating SIADH from hypovolaemic hyponatraemia in a hospitalised patient
stem: You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 72-year-old woman on day 4 of admission with community-acquired pneumonia. She is on oral amoxicillin and clarithromycin. She had been improving but is now mildly confused and has had three falls overnight. She has been drinking freely from the water jug. She has no diuretics and no recent vomiting. She has not received intravenous fluids in the past 24 hours. Her chest is clearing on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 84, BP 124/76, RR 16, SpO2 96% room air, no postural drop documented
data_table.Examination: Moist mucous membranes, no peripheral oedema, JVP not elevated, abdomen soft, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L (admission 138), K 4.2 mmol/L, urea 3.4 mmol/L, creatinine 60 micromol/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L, plasma osmolality 256 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 56 mmol/L. TSH 1.6 mIU/L. Cortisol 412 nmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer 100 mL of 3% hypertonic saline as a single bolus, recheck sodium in 1 hour and limit total correction to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours and 18 mmol/L in 48 hours
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or coma; this patient has mild confusion only and free water restriction is the first-line measure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence intravenous 0.9% saline at 100 mL/hour and check the sodium every 4 hours for the first 24 hours and adjust the infusion rate accordingly based on the trajectory
options.rationale: Intravenous isotonic saline in SIADH worsens hyponatraemia because the sodium is excreted while water is retained; free water restriction is the correct approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Continue current management without specific sodium intervention and recheck serum sodium and clinical state in 24 hours because the result is likely a pseudohyponatraemia laboratory artefact
options.rationale: Plasma osmolality of 256 mOsm/kg confirms true hyponatraemia; pseudohyponatraemia from severe hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia is excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Restrict free water to 1 L per 24 hours, cease the clarithromycin which is contributing to free water retention and recheck the sodium in 24 hours after these measures are in place
options.rationale: Urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, urine osmolality above 100, low plasma osmolality, euvolaemia and pneumonia as precipitant confirm SIADH; free water restriction is first-line, and reviewing precipitants is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start oral tolvaptan 15 mg daily and recheck the sodium every 6 hours over the next 24 hours, withholding additional treatment if the sodium rises by more than 10 mmol/L in that period
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist used in chronic or refractory SIADH; it is not first-line and risks overcorrection if used without specialist supervision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: SIADH is a euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia diagnosed by low plasma osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine (above 100 mOsm/kg), urine sodium above 30 mmol/L and normal adrenal and thyroid function. Pneumonia, central nervous system disease and many drugs are common precipitants. First-line treatment is fluid restriction to 800 to 1000 mL per day; tolvaptan is reserved for refractory or chronic cases. Correction must not exceed 10 mmol/L in 24 hours and 18 mmol/L in 48 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SIADH criteria: euvolaemia, plasma osmolality below 275, urine osmolality above 100, urine sodium above 30
Free water restriction to 800 to 1000 mL per day is first-line therapy
Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms: seizures, coma or severe confusion
Correction limit is 10 mmol/L in 24 hours and 18 mmol/L in 48 hours
Tolvaptan is used in chronic or refractory SIADH under specialist supervision
explanation.pearls: Overcorrection of chronic hyponatraemia at more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours risks central pontine myelinolysis with locked-in syndrome; if overcorrection occurs, dextrose 5% and desmopressin re-lower the sodium safely.

subtopic_detail: STEMI presenting within PCI window
stem: You are the emergency registrar in a metropolitan hospital with onsite primary percutaneous coronary intervention service. A 58-year-old non-Aboriginal man presents 50 minutes after the onset of central crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm. He has been given aspirin 300 mg orally by the paramedics. He has no contraindications to dual antiplatelet therapy and no bleeding diathesis. His pain is now 7 out of 10 and he is diaphoretic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 96, BP 138/82, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, chest clear, heart sounds dual without murmur, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 2 mm ST elevation V2 to V5 with reciprocal inferior depression, troponin pending, FBE and U&E normal, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence tenecteplase weight-adjusted intravenous bolus and admit to the coronary care unit with rescue percutaneous coronary intervention if no resolution at 90 minutes
options.rationale: Fibrinolysis is reserved for STEMI presenting where primary PCI is not available within 90 minutes from first medical contact; here PCI is onsite and is preferred. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)

options.text: Administer aspirin 300 mg, an additional oral P2Y12 inhibitor and arrange transfer for elective angiography within 24 hours during normal working hours
options.rationale: Delaying revascularisation in a STEMI by 24 hours loses myocardium; reperfusion must be immediate, preferably by primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)

options.text: Loading dose ticagrelor 180 mg orally, intravenous heparin and immediate activation of the cardiac catheter laboratory for primary PCI within 90 minutes of first contact
options.rationale: Anterior STEMI within 12 hours of onset at a PCI-capable hospital requires immediate primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact with dual antiplatelet loading and anticoagulation. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)

options.text: Order CT coronary angiogram to confirm the diagnosis before deciding on revascularisation strategy, given that troponin has not yet been reported back as elevated
options.rationale: STEMI is an ECG diagnosis and immediate reperfusion is not delayed for troponin or CT confirmation; CT coronary angiography has no role in acute STEMI. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)

options.text: Manage medically with intravenous beta-blocker, statin and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor in the coronary care unit and reassess for invasive strategy in 72 hours
options.rationale: Conservative management without reperfusion in STEMI within the window of opportunity results in avoidable myocardial loss and worse outcomes. (Source: CSANZ STEMI Guidelines)

explanation.summary: ST-elevation myocardial infarction within 12 hours of onset requires immediate reperfusion. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention is the preferred strategy where it can be delivered within 90 minutes of first medical contact, or 120 minutes from first medical contact if patient transfer is required. Fibrinolysis is used when PCI cannot be delivered within these windows, followed by routine angiography 3 to 24 hours later (pharmacoinvasive strategy). Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation are commenced before angiography.
key_points: Primary PCI preferred if door-to-balloon within 90 minutes onsite
Fibrinolysis with tenecteplase if PCI not available within 120 minutes from first contact
Pharmacoinvasive strategy: angiography 3 to 24 hours after successful fibrinolysis
Dual antiplatelet loading and anticoagulation before angiography
Cardiogenic shock or mechanical complications mandate immediate angiography regardless of timing
explanation.pearls: Failed fibrinolysis (under 50% ST resolution at 90 minutes) mandates rescue PCI as soon as possible, distinct from the routine pharmacoinvasive angiography window.

subtopic_detail: Community acquired pneumonia outpatient antibiotic
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 42-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with three days of productive cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She has no significant past medical history and no recent hospital admission. She is not pregnant. She lives independently and her partner can supervise her at home. Her SMART-COP score is 0. She is up to date with COVID-19 and influenza vaccinations.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 96, BP 124/74, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Right lower zone crackles and bronchial breath sounds, no oxygen requirement, normal mental state, no signs of dehydration
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray: right lower lobe consolidation; rapid antigen testing for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 500 mg once daily for three days as monotherapy for atypical and typical coverage in the outpatient setting
options.rationale: Azithromycin monotherapy is inadequate empirical cover for typical Streptococcus pneumoniae because of high macrolide resistance rates in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days because it provides broad-spectrum cover for both Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae
options.rationale: Cefalexin has poor pneumococcal coverage compared with amoxicillin and is not the recommended first-line agent for community-acquired pneumonia in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for seven days as broad-spectrum coverage including atypical pathogens in the community setting given the productive cough
options.rationale: Respiratory fluoroquinolones are reserved for severe pneumonia, beta-lactam allergy or proven resistant organisms; routine outpatient use drives resistance and adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for five days with general practice review at 48 hours and safety netting for worsening breathlessness or systemic features
options.rationale: High-dose oral amoxicillin is the first-line agent for low-severity community-acquired pneumonia (SMART-COP 0 to 2) in Australia, with 5 day duration; doxycycline is the macrolide-equivalent alternative for atypical cover when needed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for seven days because of broader beta-lactamase coverage given right lower lobe consolidation on imaging
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for moderate severity, aspiration risk or specific resistant pathogens; it is not first line for low-severity community-acquired pneumonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP triages community-acquired pneumonia severity and disposition: scores of 0 to 2 are low risk and suitable for outpatient management. High-dose oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days is first line in Australia. Doxycycline is added or substituted if atypical pathogens are suspected (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila). Moxifloxacin is reserved for beta-lactam allergy or severe disease. SMART-COP 3 to 4 prompts hospital admission, often with intravenous ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline or azithromycin; SMART-COP 5 or more prompts ICU consideration.
key_points: SMART-COP 0 to 2: outpatient oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days
Doxycycline added if atypical pathogens suspected (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila)
Moxifloxacin reserved for severe penicillin allergy or severe disease
SMART-COP 3 to 4 triggers admission for intravenous therapy
Review at 48 hours and escalate if no improvement
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP allocates 2 points each for systolic BP under 90, oxygen saturation under 90% (or under 94% if under 50 years), and pH under 7.35, while age threshold lowers SpO2 cut-off and other variables get 1 point each.

subtopic_detail: New atrial fibrillation rate versus rhythm control
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 68-year-old non-Aboriginal man with palpitations and breathlessness for three weeks. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. He has had no chest pain or syncope. His exercise tolerance has fallen from 1 km to 200 m. His CHA2DS2-VA score is 4 and he has no bleeding risk factors. He has no history of heart failure or asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 irregular, BP 138/84, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, no thyroid swelling, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation rate 130, TSH normal, echocardiogram pending, electrolytes normal, troponin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.text: Immediate DC cardioversion in the emergency department under conscious sedation and discharge on aspirin 100 mg daily without anticoagulation
options.rationale: Cardioversion without preceding 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or transoesophageal echocardiogram exclusion of left atrial thrombus risks embolic stroke; aspirin is not adequate for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral amiodarone 200 mg three times daily for one week then 200 mg daily and start aspirin 100 mg with cardiology outpatient review in three months
options.rationale: Amiodarone is reserved for specialist-initiated rhythm control because of significant adverse effects, and aspirin is inadequate stroke prevention with CHA2DS2-VA 4. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

options.text: Start digoxin 125 micrograms daily for rate control and aspirin 100 mg daily for stroke prevention with review in two weeks to assess heart rate and symptoms
options.rationale: Digoxin is second line for rate control because it controls only resting rate poorly during activity, and aspirin is inadequate anticoagulation for CHA2DS2-VA 4. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

options.text: Commence apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily titrated for rate control and arrange cardiology review for rhythm-control consideration
options.rationale: Apixaban is first-line anticoagulation in non-valvular atrial fibrillation with CHA2DS2-VA at least 2, and metoprolol is the standard rate-control agent; rhythm control via specialist review remains an option. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for urgent electrophysiology study and pulmonary vein isolation ablation without commencing anticoagulation in the interim while awaiting the procedure
options.rationale: Catheter ablation is reserved for symptomatic rhythm control after failure of antiarrhythmic therapy and never replaces stroke-prevention anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA AF Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Initial management of new atrial fibrillation prioritises stroke risk assessment and rate control. Stroke risk by CHA2DS2-VA: a score of 2 or more in men or women warrants oral anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban or dabigatran) unless contraindicated, with warfarin reserved for moderate to severe mitral stenosis or mechanical valves. Rate control with a beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is first line; rhythm control with cardioversion, flecainide, sotalol or amiodarone is considered when symptoms persist despite rate control, and catheter ablation is an option in symptomatic recurrent disease.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA score of 2 or more triggers oral anticoagulation
DOACs first line for non-valvular AF; warfarin for mechanical valves and severe mitral stenosis
Aspirin has no role in atrial fibrillation stroke prevention
Metoprolol or atenolol first line for rate control
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
explanation.pearls: Apixaban dose is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily if two of: age 80 years or older, body weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher.

subtopic_detail: Moderate adult asthma exacerbation
stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with a four hour history of worsening breathlessness and wheeze on a background of asthma. She has used 12 puffs of salbutamol at home in the last hour without much relief. She is able to speak in short phrases. She has not required steroids in the last six months. She has no penicillin allergy and is up to date with her influenza vaccine.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 116, BP 124/76, RR 26, SpO2 93% room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral expiratory wheeze, mild accessory muscle use, able to complete short sentences, no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Peak expiratory flow 200 L/min (personal best 420 L/min), chest x-ray clear, no fever

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg, nebulised ipratropium and oral antibiotics empirically for presumed lower respiratory tract infection driving the exacerbation
options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis or near-fatal asthma; routine antibiotics are not indicated without features of bacterial infection. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

options.text: Inhaled fluticasone-formoterol four puffs via spacer and discharge home with an updated written asthma action plan after 30 minutes of observation in the department
options.rationale: Discharge after only 30 minutes with a peak flow of 200 L/min and ongoing distress is unsafe; bronchodilator response must be assessed at one hour and oral corticosteroids initiated. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg, intravenous aminophylline loading infusion and admission to high dependency for continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Intravenous corticosteroid offers no advantage over oral in an alert cooperative patient and aminophylline is reserved for severe disease unresponsive to first-line therapy. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

options.text: Salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer (or 5 mg nebulised) every 20 minutes for one hour, oral prednisolone 50 mg, oxygen titrated to SpO2 of 93 to 95%, and reassess at one hour
options.rationale: Moderate asthma exacerbation is managed with repeated salbutamol via spacer or nebuliser every 20 minutes for an hour, early oral prednisolone 50 mg and oxygen targeted to 93 to 95%; reassessment at one hour decides disposition. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

options.text: Heliox-driven salbutamol nebulisation with immediate intubation if no response, and intravenous magnesium sulfate 10 g infused over 30 minutes as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Heliox and intravenous magnesium are reserved for severe or life-threatening asthma after failure of first-line therapy; high-dose magnesium of 10 g is not the standard adult dose. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia Handbook)

explanation.summary: Moderate adult asthma is graded by ability to speak in phrases, heart rate under 120, oxygen saturation 92 to 94% on air and peak expiratory flow 50 to 75% of personal best or predicted. First-line treatment is salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer (or 5 mg nebulised) every 20 minutes for an hour, with oxygen targeted to 93 to 95% and oral prednisolone 50 mg within the first hour. Ipratropium bromide is added in severe exacerbations. Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes is reserved for severe or life-threatening exacerbations not responding to first-line therapy.
key_points: Salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer (or 5 mg nebulised) every 20 minutes for 1 hour
Oral prednisolone 50 mg early; intravenous hydrocortisone only if unable to swallow
Oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95%, not 100%
Ipratropium added for severe exacerbations
Intravenous magnesium 2 g for severe disease unresponsive to first-line therapy
explanation.pearls: Oxygen target in acute asthma is 93 to 95% saturation because higher saturations risk worsening V/Q mismatch and hypercapnia, mirroring the COPD principle.

subtopic_detail: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem: You are the medical registrar urgently reviewing a 72-year-old non-Aboriginal man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 brought in by his wife with weakness and nausea. He takes ramipril, spironolactone, metformin and trimethoprim for a recent urinary tract infection. He missed his haemodialysis-free clinic review last week. He has had no chest pain. He has no contraindication to insulin therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 48, BP 110/68, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, normal mental state, no peripheral oedema, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: K 7.4 mmol/L, Na 136, urea 23.1, creatinine 358 micromol/L, bicarbonate 18, glucose 6.8; ECG sinus bradycardia 48 with peaked T waves, PR 220 ms, broad QRS 124 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous sodium polystyrene sulfonate (resonium) 30 g and oral sodium bicarbonate 1 g three times daily while awaiting renal review later today
options.rationale: Resonium is intravenously inappropriate (oral or rectal) and acts slowly over hours; it does not address the immediate cardiac membrane risk from a potassium of 7.4 with ECG changes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous frusemide 80 mg, oral salbutamol 8 mg and arrange a fast track to outpatient haemodialysis later today via the renal registrar on call team
options.rationale: Loop diuretic is slow and unlikely to be effective in advanced kidney disease, and oral salbutamol is not used; nebulised salbutamol is one of the membrane and shift agents. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guidelines)

options.text: Insulin actrapid 10 units in 50 mL 50% dextrose intravenously and reassess potassium and ECG at 30 minutes without giving any calcium because the patient is haemodynamically stable
options.rationale: ECG changes with severe hyperkalaemia mandate immediate intravenous calcium for cardiac membrane stabilisation before shift therapy; relying on insulin-dextrose alone delays myocardial protection. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guidelines)

options.text: Activate the medical emergency team and prepare for intubation given the bradycardia and broad QRS, with definitive cardiac pacing and central venous access before any drug therapy is administered
options.rationale: Drug therapy for hyperkalaemia is faster than mechanical pacing and resolves the underlying cause; intubation is not required if the patient is alert and ventilating. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution over 5 minutes for cardiac membrane stabilisation, then insulin-dextrose and nebulised salbutamol, and urgent dialysis referral
options.rationale: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes requires immediate calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilisation, then potassium-shifting therapy with insulin-dextrose and salbutamol, and dialysis for definitive removal in this patient with advanced kidney disease. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T waves, broad QRS, sine wave) is a cardiac emergency. Management proceeds in three stages: cardiac membrane stabilisation with intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% (or calcium chloride 10 mL of 10% if central access), potassium shift into cells with insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% dextrose plus nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg, and potassium elimination via dialysis, frusemide if urine output preserved, or oral resin slowly. Identify and reverse contributors: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, trimethoprim, NSAIDs, missed dialysis.
key_points: Calcium gluconate first for ECG changes; effect within 3 minutes, lasts about 30 minutes
Insulin-dextrose and nebulised salbutamol shift potassium intracellularly over 15 to 30 minutes
Dialysis is definitive for advanced CKD or severe refractory hyperkalaemia
Stop ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, trimethoprim and NSAIDs
Repeat ECG and potassium at 30 minutes after intervention
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim and ACE inhibitor combination in advanced CKD is a common precipitant of severe hyperkalaemia through epithelial sodium channel block plus aldosterone suppression.

subtopic_detail: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure
stem: You are the medical registrar called urgently to assess a 65-year-old non-Aboriginal woman who has had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure on the ward. She was admitted three days ago for an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and given intravenous fluids. She drinks no alcohol and is on no diuretics. She is now post-ictal but rousable. Her serum sodium on admission was 138 mmol/L and is now 116 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 92, BP 132/78, RR 18, SpO2 96% on 1 L oxygen via nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Post-ictal, GCS 12, no focal neurological deficit, soft abdomen, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 116 mmol/L, K 4.0, urea 4.2, creatinine 76 micromol/L, serum osmolality 248, urine osmolality 510, urine sodium 68, TSH normal, cortisol normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 1000 mL infusion over 4 hours and restrict free water intake to under 1 L per 24 hours with daily electrolyte review for 3 days
options.rationale: Isotonic saline alone does not correct seizing severe hyponatraemia and may even worsen sodium in SIADH; hypertonic saline is required for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)

options.text: Oral fluid restriction to 800 mL per day combined with oral sodium chloride 1 g three times daily and reassess sodium in 12 hours with intravenous fluids ceased
options.rationale: Oral measures act too slowly for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure; hypertonic saline is required to raise sodium acutely. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)

options.text: Demeclocycline 300 mg twice daily orally for one week and continue current intravenous fluids and supportive care without active sodium correction in the next 6 hours
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is occasionally used in chronic SIADH for outpatients and has no role in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with seizure. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)

options.text: Oral tolvaptan 15 mg single dose now with serial sodium measurements at 2 hours and admission to high dependency for cardiac and respiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Tolvaptan can cause uncontrolled rapid correction and is contraindicated in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; hypertonic saline is preferred. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous 3% sodium chloride 150 mL bolus over 10 minutes, repeat to a maximum of three boluses, with sodium target rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first hour and capped at 10 mmol/L per 24 hours
options.rationale: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure requires immediate hypertonic saline boluses targeting a 4 to 6 mmol/L rise in the first hour, capped at 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, reduced conscious state, vomiting from cerebral oedema) is a neurological emergency. Management is 3% sodium chloride 150 mL intravenous bolus over 10 minutes, repeated up to three times until symptoms resolve, aiming for a 4 to 6 mmol/L rise in the first hour. Total correction must not exceed 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, or 18 mmol/L in 48 hours, to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome. Subsequent management addresses underlying cause: SIADH from drugs, malignancy, central nervous system or pulmonary disease; volume depletion with isotonic saline; or hypervolaemia with diuresis.
key_points: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia mandates 3% saline 150 mL boluses
Target rise 4 to 6 mmol/L in first hour to resolve symptoms
Cap correction at 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, 18 mmol/L in 48 hours
Recheck sodium every 2 hours during active correction
Identify cause: drugs, SIADH triggers, volume status
explanation.pearls: If correction exceeds 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, give 5% dextrose 6 mL/kg over 1 to 2 hours to relower sodium and prevent osmotic demyelination.

subtopic_detail: Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis interpretation
stem: You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 70-year-old non-Aboriginal man with a 60 pack-year smoking history presenting with three days of worsening breathlessness and increased sputum production. He has known severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and was given controlled oxygen by the paramedics. He is drowsy but rousable to voice. He has been on home oxygen 1 L overnight only. He has no chest pain.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 110, BP 138/82, RR 26, SpO2 92% on 28% Venturi mask
data_table.Examination: Pursed lip breathing, accessory muscle use, asterixis, expiratory wheeze and prolonged expiratory phase, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ABG on 28%: pH 7.28, paCO2 70, paO2 62, HCO3 32, base excess +6; chest x-ray hyperinflated with no infiltrate; CRP 42, WCC 12.4

lead_in: Which interpretation of the arterial blood gas is most accurate?

options.text: Acute respiratory acidosis with normal bicarbonate consistent with a primary new pulmonary embolism rather than a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation today
options.rationale: The bicarbonate is elevated at 32 indicating metabolic compensation present, not acute respiratory acidosis alone; the picture fits acute on chronic respiratory acidosis. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)

options.text: Compensated chronic respiratory acidosis at baseline because the pH is only mildly low and the bicarbonate is elevated, requiring no escalation in current ventilation support
options.rationale: If the picture were fully compensated chronic respiratory acidosis the pH would be near normal; pH 7.28 with paCO2 70 indicates acute decompensation on top of chronic retention. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)

options.text: Primary metabolic alkalosis with secondary hyperventilation as compensation, suggesting overuse of bicarbonate-containing antacids or recent vomiting as the dominant disturbance
options.rationale: Metabolic alkalosis would raise pH, not lower it; the low pH and very high paCO2 indicate respiratory acidosis as the primary disturbance. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)

options.text: Hyperoxic hypercapnia from oxygen toxicity alone, which would correct with cessation of supplemental oxygen and switching to room air without ventilation support
options.rationale: Stopping oxygen risks fatal hypoxia; the pattern reflects acute on chronic ventilatory failure requiring non-invasive ventilation, with oxygen titrated to 88 to 92%. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)

options.text: Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation; non-invasive bilevel ventilation is indicated and oxygen should be titrated to a target saturation of 88 to 92%
options.rationale: Elevated bicarbonate indicates chronic CO2 retention with renal compensation, while the acidaemia and very high paCO2 indicate acute decompensation; non-invasive ventilation is indicated and oxygen targeted to 88 to 92% prevents worsening hypercapnia. (Source: TSANZ COPD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis is characterised by acidaemia, raised paCO2 above the chronic baseline and an elevated bicarbonate reflecting prior renal compensation. In COPD exacerbation with pH under 7.35 and paCO2 over 45 despite controlled oxygen and bronchodilator therapy, non-invasive bilevel ventilation is the standard of care because it reduces intubation, mortality and hospital length of stay. Oxygen is titrated to a target saturation of 88 to 92% to avoid worsening hypercapnia from loss of hypoxic drive and reversal of pulmonary vasoconstriction.
key_points: Elevated HCO3 plus acidaemia signals acute on chronic respiratory acidosis
NIV indicated for pH under 7.35 and paCO2 over 45 despite optimal medical therapy
Oxygen target 88 to 92% in COPD to avoid hypercapnia
Bronchodilators, prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally for 5 days and antibiotic if 2 of 3 Anthonisen criteria
Failure of NIV with worsening pH or conscious state prompts invasive ventilation
explanation.pearls: Bilevel non-invasive ventilation typically starts at IPAP 12 and EPAP 5 with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 88 to 92%, with arterial blood gas reassessed at 1 hour.

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage
stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 56-year-old non-Aboriginal man with new severe headache and blurred vision for 6 hours. He has hypertension treated with poorly compliant amlodipine 10 mg daily. He has had no chest pain and no focal limb weakness. He is alert and oriented. His urinalysis is positive for protein and blood. Fundoscopy reveals flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 88, BP 224/132, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, no focal neurological deficit, no carotid bruit, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, fundoscopy with flame haemorrhages and cotton wool spots
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 88), urea 9.4, urinalysis protein 2+ blood 1+, troponin normal, ECG sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for LV hypertrophy, CT brain no haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial blood pressure management?

options.text: Oral captopril 25 mg sublingually with target blood pressure under 140/90 in the first hour and discharge home once below target on the same antihypertensive regimen
options.rationale: Sublingual captopril produces rapid uncontrolled drops in pressure and the target of under 140/90 in the first hour risks cerebral hypoperfusion; admission with parenteral therapy is required. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg every 15 minutes until pressure is below 140/90, then commence oral perindopril and arrange general practice review the following week
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled drops in blood pressure with risk of stroke and myocardial ischaemia and is no longer recommended in any hypertensive presentation. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous frusemide 80 mg bolus and oral metoprolol 100 mg with target pressure under 140/90 in one hour and admission to the general medical ward for observation
options.rationale: Frusemide and oral therapy do not provide the controlled, titrable reduction needed for hypertensive emergency; intravenous infusion of a short-acting agent in a monitored bed is preferred. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

options.text: Increase his amlodipine to 20 mg daily and add irbesartan 300 mg orally with home blood pressure monitoring; arrange cardiology outpatient review within 4 weeks
options.rationale: End-organ damage (acute kidney injury, retinopathy) makes this a hypertensive emergency requiring inpatient parenteral therapy, not titration of oral medications at home. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated in a monitored bed targeting a mean arterial pressure reduction of 20 to 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 6 hours
options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage is treated with a titrated intravenous infusion (GTN or labetalol) in a monitored bed, with mean arterial pressure reduced by 20 to 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours, to avoid hypoperfusion. (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (typically over 180/120) with evidence of acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, retinopathy, acute kidney injury, pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection or eclampsia). It requires immediate admission to a monitored bed and titrated intravenous antihypertensive therapy. The pressure should be lowered by 20 to 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours; faster reduction risks watershed cerebral, renal or coronary infarction. Specific scenarios alter agent choice: labetalol or esmolol with sodium nitroprusside for aortic dissection, GTN for pulmonary oedema, magnesium for eclampsia.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency requires end-organ damage, not just BP above 180/120
Lower mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25% in the first hour, no faster
Then aim for 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours
Intravenous GTN or labetalol in a monitored bed
Sublingual nifedipine and captopril are contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Aortic dissection requires aggressive beta-blockade with labetalol or esmolol first to reduce shear stress before vasodilator therapy, with target systolic 100 to 120 mmHg and heart rate under 60.

subtopic_detail: Cellulitis versus necrotising fasciitis discrimination
stem: You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 62-year-old non-Aboriginal man with type 2 diabetes who presents with 18 hours of worsening lower leg pain disproportionate to the visible cellulitis. He is febrile and tachycardic. His pain has progressed despite paracetamol. He has had no recent injury, IV drug use or travel. His diabetes is poorly controlled with an HbA1c of 9.5%. He takes metformin and gliclazide.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 °C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/54 mmHg, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Right lower leg with patchy violaceous discolouration, two small skin blisters, exquisite tenderness extending beyond the area of erythema, crepitus on palpation, mild lower leg oedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 280 mg/L, lactate 4.1 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, glucose 16.8 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L, Hb 122 g/L, LRINEC score 9, plain X-ray shows soft tissue gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange MRI of the lower leg before deciding management, withhold antibiotics until diagnosis is confirmed, and reassess in 4 hours for repeat clinical examination by the team
options.rationale: MRI is supportive but should never delay surgical exploration in suspected necrotising fasciitis; antibiotics are started empirically without waiting for imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit to the medical ward, commence intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours, mark the erythema boundary and review in 12 hours for response assessment by the medical team
options.rationale: Ward-based monotherapy for presumed cellulitis misses necrotising fasciitis features; delay to debridement increases mortality from around 25% to over 50% beyond 24 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for theatre debridement, commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics including meropenem and clindamycin, and resuscitate with intravenous crystalloid
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, soft tissue gas and LRINEC 6 or above strongly indicate necrotising fasciitis requiring emergency surgical debridement; broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression are commenced concurrently. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: ANZ Surgical Site Infection Prevention Guidelines

options.text: Discharge home on oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily, advise elevation and arrange community nurse review in 24 hours for clinical reassessment of progression
options.rationale: Severe sepsis with hypotension, lactate 4.1 and LRINEC 9 cannot be managed at home; oral cephalexin is inadequate for either severe cellulitis or necrotising fasciitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as primary treatment for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome and continue current ward observation pending surgical review in the morning
options.rationale: IVIG is adjunctive in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome but does not replace surgical debridement or empirical antibiotics; delay to theatre is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency. Hard signs include pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, soft tissue gas and rapid progression. LRINEC score combines CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; 6 or above is high-risk and 8 or above strongly suggestive. Management is urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for streptococcal toxin suppression. Imaging must never delay theatre.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus and gas are necrotising fasciitis red flags
LRINEC 6 or above is high-risk; 8 or above strongly suggests necrotising fasciitis
Urgent surgical debridement is the definitive treatment
Empirical antibiotics include broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin for toxin suppression
Imaging supports but does not delay surgical exploration
explanation.pearls: The finger test (insertion of a gloved finger through a small skin incision under local anaesthetic) yields easy dissection through subcutaneous tissue without bleeding when necrotising fasciitis is present; a positive bedside finger test is diagnostic and prompts immediate theatre.

sources.label: ANZ Surgical Site Infection Prevention Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Adult bacterial meningitis empirical therapy
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 48-year-old non-Aboriginal woman in ED with 12 hours of high fever, severe headache, photophobia and confusion. She has been previously well, with no recent travel or immunosuppression. She has had two episodes of vomiting. There is no rash. She works as a primary school teacher.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 122, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, BP 110/68 mmHg
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, neck stiffness present, no focal neurology, Kernig and Brudzinski positive, no skin rash, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 22 x10^9/L (neutrophils 19), CRP 240 mg/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, glucose 6.8 mmol/L, INR 1.1, platelets 215 x10^9/L, blood cultures taken; CT brain pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture immediately without CT given the absence of focal neurology and papilloedema, send all CSF tubes for analysis, and commence antibiotics after the procedure
options.rationale: Although CT before LP is reserved for specific risk factors, antibiotics should still precede LP when LP is delayed for any reason; sequence matters because of the urgency of antibiotic timing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Defer antibiotics until lumbar puncture results are available, administer paracetamol 1 g intravenously and dexamethasone 10 mg, and reassess after CSF microscopy
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics must not be delayed beyond 30 minutes for any reason in suspected bacterial meningitis; mortality rises with each hour of delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Administer intravenous vancomycin 1.5 g and meropenem 2 g as first-line empirical therapy, given the severity of presentation and risk of cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus in Australia
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added when penicillin or cephalosporin resistance is suspected (e.g. recent foreign travel, recent antibiotic use); empirical first-line in Australia is ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin without vancomycin in the absence of those risks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg with the first dose of ceftriaxone 2 g and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV, then proceed to lumbar puncture once CT is clear
options.rationale: Empirical ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, meningococcus and Listeria for over-50 or vulnerable; dexamethasone given with or just before the first antibiotic dose reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: ASID Adult Bacterial Meningitis Position Statement

options.text: Administer intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours empirically with ceftriaxone, withhold dexamethasone given the uncertain pathogen, and arrange a lumbar puncture in 6 hours
options.rationale: Aciclovir is added when encephalitis is also suspected; this woman has classic meningitis features. Dexamethasone is given with the first antibiotic dose for suspected bacterial meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Australian empirical therapy for adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis is ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV every 4 hours, started within 30 minutes of consideration. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or just before the first antibiotic dose reduces death and neurological sequelae in pneumococcal disease. CT before LP is reserved for focal neurology, papilloedema, immunocompromise or recent seizure. Listeria cover with benzylpenicillin is included for over-50, pregnant or immunocompromised patients.
key_points: Empirical ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin within 30 minutes of consideration
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or just before first antibiotic dose for pneumococcal benefit
CT before LP for focal neurology, papilloedema, immunocompromise or recent seizure
Listeria cover with benzylpenicillin for over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised
Continue dexamethasone for 4 days only if CSF or blood cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone reduces unfavourable outcomes only in pneumococcal meningitis and should be stopped at 48 hours if CSF or blood cultures grow another organism or are negative; continuing in non-pneumococcal cases offers no benefit and risks hyperglycaemia.

sources.label: ASID Adult Bacterial Meningitis Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal in supratherapeutic INR without bleeding
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 76-year-old non-Aboriginal man with atrial fibrillation on warfarin for stroke prevention. He attends the anticoagulant clinic for a routine INR check after starting trimethoprim 5 days ago for a urinary tract infection. He has no signs of bleeding and feels well. He has no recent falls or head injury. His warfarin target range is 2.0 to 3.0. His other medications are bisoprolol and atorvastatin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 72, RR 14, T 36.7 °C
