data_table.Examination: No bruising, gums not bleeding, no haematuria visually, neurologically intact, no flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: INR 9.4 (target 2.0 to 3.0), Hb 134 g/L, platelets 215 x10^9/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, urinalysis nil blood, faecal occult blood not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold warfarin, administer oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg, repeat INR in 24 hours, and review for the need to continue trimethoprim or substitute alternative antibiotic
options.rationale: INR over 9 without bleeding is managed with warfarin cessation and oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg; this corrects INR within 24 hours without overcorrection that complicates rewarfarinisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Withhold warfarin alone for 48 hours, recheck the INR at that point, and continue trimethoprim until urinary culture results return at follow-up in the clinic
options.rationale: INR over 9 carries a high bleeding risk in the next 48 hours; withholding warfarin alone is insufficient and vitamin K is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Administer intravenous vitamin K 10 mg and Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg now, admit to a monitored bed, and recheck the INR at 1 hour after the infusion has completed
options.rationale: Prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K is reserved for major bleeding or emergency surgery; in asymptomatic INR over 9 this overcorrects and risks rebound prothrombotic state. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Administer fresh frozen plasma 4 units intravenously over 4 hours and recheck the INR immediately afterwards, with rewarfarinisation planned the following day in clinic
options.rationale: FFP is no longer first-line for warfarin reversal in Australia due to volume load and slow correction; vitamin K alone is sufficient for asymptomatic supratherapeutic INR. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance

options.text: Continue current warfarin dose, advise to avoid contact activity, and arrange routine INR review at the next scheduled appointment in 7 days at the clinic
options.rationale: Continuing warfarin with INR over 9 risks major haemorrhage; routine 7-day review delays correction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal in supratherapeutic INR follows Australian Red Cross Lifeblood guidance based on INR and bleeding status. INR over 9 without bleeding: stop warfarin and give oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg. INR 4.5 to 9 without bleeding: stop or reduce warfarin and recheck. Major bleeding or emergency surgery: Prothrombinex-VF (PCC) 25 to 50 units/kg plus IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg. FFP is reserved for when PCC is unavailable. Trimethoprim, sulfamethoxazole, metronidazole and amiodarone potentiate warfarin and frequently cause supratherapeutic INRs.
key_points: INR over 9 without bleeding: stop warfarin and oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg
INR 4.5 to 9 without bleeding: stop or reduce warfarin and recheck
Major bleeding: Prothrombinex-VF plus IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg
FFP only when Prothrombinex-VF is unavailable
Trimethoprim, metronidazole and amiodarone are common warfarin potentiators
explanation.pearls: Oral vitamin K is preferred over intravenous in non-emergency reversal because IV doses over 5 mg often cause warfarin resistance for 1 to 2 weeks, complicating re-anticoagulation in a patient who still needs stroke prevention.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Warfarin Reversal Guidance

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax recognition and decompression
stem: You are the medical registrar called urgently to the ward for a 68-year-old non-Aboriginal man with COPD whose dyspnoea has acutely worsened 2 hours after a CT-guided lung biopsy. He is anxious and clammy with marked respiratory distress. He has been on his usual COPD medications and just received nebulised salbutamol with no improvement. His oxygen saturation has fallen rapidly over the last 15 minutes. His ECG is not yet available.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 138, RR 38, SpO2 84% on 8 L/min via Hudson mask, BP 88/52 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Distressed, sweaty, tracheal deviation to the left, absent breath sounds on the right with hyperresonant percussion, raised jugular venous pressure, no peripheral oedema, no flail segment
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound shows absent lung sliding on the right, ABG pH 7.30 pCO2 56 mmHg pO2 56 mmHg lactate 3.4 mmol/L, ECG pending

lead_in: What is the single best initial intervention?

options.text: Arrange an urgent portable chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis, escalate to ICU, and prepare for chest drain insertion once imaging has been formally reported by radiology
options.rationale: Imaging confirmation delays life-saving decompression in tension pneumothorax; the diagnosis is clinical and immediate needle thoracostomy is required. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

options.text: Perform immediate needle thoracostomy at the right 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line, then proceed to intercostal catheter insertion after decompression confirmed by clinical improvement
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax with hypotension, tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds is a clinical emergency; immediate needle decompression at the 5th ICS anterior axillary line (preferred over 2nd ICS midclavicular in adults) followed by formal intercostal catheter is the Australian standard. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

options.text: Commence non-invasive ventilation with bilevel positive airway pressure at 15/5 cm H2O and increase the inspired oxygen fraction, reassess the response in 15 minutes by the team
options.rationale: Positive pressure ventilation in tension pneumothorax worsens the situation by forcing more air into the pleural space; decompression is required first. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

options.text: Administer intravenous fluid bolus 1 litre, increase oxygen flow to 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask, and arrange immediate echocardiogram to exclude cardiac tamponade as the alternative cause
options.rationale: While fluids and oxygen are supportive, they do not address the mechanical obstruction; echocardiography delays decompression and the clinical signs strongly favour pneumothorax over tamponade. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline 50 micrograms boluses titrated to blood pressure response, intubate immediately and ventilate with high tidal volumes to recruit lung units
options.rationale: Intubation and high tidal volume ventilation accelerate tension physiology; adrenaline does not address the underlying mechanical problem. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

explanation.summary: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis based on respiratory distress, hypotension, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance. ANZCOR recommends immediate needle thoracostomy in the 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line in adults (replacing the older 2nd ICS midclavicular site, which fails in around a third of adults due to chest wall thickness). Definitive treatment is intercostal catheter insertion. Imaging must not delay decompression.
key_points: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis
Adult needle thoracostomy site is 5th ICS anterior axillary line per ANZCOR
Imaging must not delay decompression
Definitive treatment is intercostal catheter
Positive pressure ventilation before decompression worsens tension physiology
explanation.pearls: Up to a third of adult needle decompressions at the 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line fail because of chest wall thickness exceeding 5 cm; the 5th intercostal space anterior axillary line is now the ANZCOR-preferred adult site.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 11: Adult Advanced Life Support

subtopic_detail: Cushing syndrome screening with 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 42-year-old non-Aboriginal woman referred from primary care with a 12-month history of progressive central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness and new-onset hypertension. She has stretch marks on her abdomen and her HbA1c has risen from 5.4% to 6.6% over 12 months. She takes no glucocorticoid medication and has not used over-the-counter creams. There is no recent stress or major illness.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/96 mmHg, HR 84, RR 16, T 36.7 °C, BMI 32 kg/m2 (up from 27)
data_table.Examination: Moon facies, supraclavicular fat pads, abdominal striae 1 cm wide and purple, proximal lower limb weakness Medical Research Council grade 4 of 5, multiple bruises on forearms
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.6%, ALT 28 U/L, TSH 1.5 mIU/L, urine drug screen negative, no exogenous steroid use disclosed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order a single random morning serum cortisol with paired ACTH, and refer to endocrinology if the cortisol is greater than 550 nmol/L on that specimen
options.rationale: Random cortisol has poor sensitivity and specificity for Cushing syndrome screening due to diurnal variation and physiological stress effects; structured testing is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

options.text: Order a high-dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test to differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH-driven Cushing syndrome before confirming hypercortisolism with any other screening test
options.rationale: High-dose dexamethasone testing distinguishes pituitary from ectopic source after hypercortisolism is confirmed; it is not the first-step screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

options.text: Arrange overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test and a 24-hour urinary free cortisol, with a confirmatory second test before endocrinology referral and further imaging
options.rationale: Endocrine Society and Australian guidance recommend any 2 of 1 mg overnight dexamethasone, 24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol as initial screening for Cushing syndrome; abnormal results trigger endocrinology referral for confirmation and source identification. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

options.text: Order an MRI pituitary as the first investigation given the clinical features of central weight gain and striae, with endocrine biochemistry to be added once the imaging result is available
options.rationale: Pituitary MRI is performed after biochemical confirmation of hypercortisolism and ACTH-dependent disease; first-line imaging without biochemistry leads to incidental finding misinterpretation. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

options.text: Commence empirical metyrapone 250 mg three times daily while awaiting investigations, with cardiovascular monitoring and review by endocrinology within 2 weeks for further plan
options.rationale: Steroidogenesis inhibitors are commenced only after diagnosis confirmation and under endocrinology supervision; empirical use without diagnosis is not safe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome screening uses any two of three first-line tests: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or late-night salivary cortisol. Two abnormal results trigger specialist confirmation and source localisation. Pituitary MRI follows biochemical evidence of ACTH-dependent disease. Steroidogenesis inhibitors are reserved for confirmed disease under endocrine supervision. Pseudo-Cushing states (depression, alcohol, severe obesity) must be excluded.
key_points: Use any 2 of: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol
Two abnormal results trigger specialist confirmation and source workup
Pituitary MRI follows biochemical evidence of ACTH-dependent disease
Pseudo-Cushing must be excluded: depression, alcohol, severe obesity, late pregnancy
ACTH measurement differentiates ACTH-dependent (pituitary, ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) disease
explanation.pearls: Pregnancy, severe obesity, chronic alcohol use and depression cause pseudo-Cushing with elevated cortisol and incomplete suppression on the 1 mg dexamethasone test; the late-night salivary cortisol is the most specific screening test in obesity because it reflects loss of diurnal variation.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome

subtopic_detail: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy
stem: You are the oncology medicine registrar called to see a 67-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with metastatic breast cancer admitted with 4 days of progressive confusion, polyuria and constipation. Her primary cancer was diagnosed 2 years ago with bone metastases. She has been on letrozole and palbociclib. There is no recent infection or thiazide use. She has had no falls and no head injury.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64 mmHg lying, 86/52 mmHg standing, HR 102, RR 18, T 36.8 °C, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Confused and dehydrated, dry mucous membranes, no focal neurology, no signs of fluid overload, normal cardiovascular examination
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.4 mmol/L (normal 2.10 to 2.55), phosphate 0.8 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78), urea 15 mmol/L, albumin 30 g/L, ECG short QT interval, PTH less than 0.5 pmol/L (suppressed), 25-hydroxy vitamin D 60 nmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence calcitonin 4 units/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours as primary treatment, withhold intravenous fluid in view of the hypotension and dehydration documented
options.rationale: Calcitonin is adjunctive for rapid initial decrease but tachyphylaxis develops in 48 to 72 hours; volume resuscitation is the foundation of treatment, not contraindicated by orthostatic hypotension. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Administer cinacalcet 30 mg orally twice daily as initial therapy and arrange repeat corrected calcium in 24 hours, with further management based on the response to the initial dose given
options.rationale: Cinacalcet is reserved for parathyroid carcinoma and primary hyperparathyroidism, not hypercalcaemia of malignancy where PTH is suppressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Administer 0.9% sodium chloride 4 to 6 litres over 24 hours with cautious monitoring for fluid overload, give intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg over 15 minutes once euvolaemic and renal function stabilises
options.rationale: Australian first-line management is aggressive crystalloid rehydration restoring renal calcium excretion, followed by intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg once euvolaemic; zoledronic acid takes 2 to 4 days to peak effect but provides sustained reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg with concurrent crystalloid replacement to promote calciuresis, withhold bisphosphonates pending an MRI spine to characterise the bone metastases
options.rationale: Routine loop diuretic use without volume overload is no longer recommended for hypercalcaemia management and risks worsening dehydration; bisphosphonate is the standard once euvolaemic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Administer denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously without preceding intravenous fluid resuscitation, with the rationale that denosumab is the preferred agent regardless of renal function
options.rationale: Denosumab is preferred over zoledronic acid in renal impairment (eGFR under 35 mL/min/1.73m2) but volume resuscitation remains the first step in symptomatic hypercalcaemia. (Source: eviQ Hypercalcaemia of Malignancy Protocol)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy presents with polyuria, dehydration, confusion, constipation and short QT interval. Management is staged: aggressive isotonic crystalloid 3 to 6 litres in the first 24 hours to restore renal calcium excretion, then intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg once euvolaemic. Denosumab is preferred when eGFR is under 35 mL/min/1.73m2. Calcitonin is an adjunct for rapid 12 to 48 hour reduction. Loop diuretics are used only for fluid overload, not as primary calciuresis.
key_points: Restore intravascular volume with isotonic crystalloid 3 to 6 litres in 24 hours first
Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV once euvolaemic is the standard antiresorptive
Denosumab preferred when eGFR under 35 mL/min/1.73m2
Calcitonin is adjunctive for the first 48 hours with tachyphylaxis
Loop diuretics are not first-line; reserved for fluid overload during rehydration
explanation.pearls: Zoledronic acid maximal calcium-lowering effect occurs at day 4 to 7, so calcitonin or denosumab is required as bridging therapy in patients with corrected calcium over 3.5 mmol/L or symptomatic neurological involvement requiring faster reduction.

subtopic_detail: Severe community-acquired influenza pneumonia
stem: You are the medical registrar called to ED for a 58-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m2) presenting with 3 days of fever, myalgia, dyspnoea and productive cough during a documented community influenza A outbreak. She works at the local primary school where multiple staff have tested positive for influenza. Her usual medications are metformin and atorvastatin. She has not received this year's influenza vaccine. She lives independently and is otherwise functionally intact.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 124, RR 30, SpO2 90% on 6 L/min via face mask, BP 96/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Toxic appearance, bilateral basal crackles, no rash, no peripheral oedema, GCS 14, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 14 x10^9/L, CRP 220 mg/L, procalcitonin 1.8 micrograms/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, chest X-ray bilateral patchy consolidation, nasopharyngeal PCR pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial plan?

options.text: Commence oseltamivir 30 mg twice daily with renal dose adjustment, ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, send nasopharyngeal PCR, and admit to a monitored bed
options.rationale: Although these antibiotics cover typical and atypical organisms, the oseltamivir dose 30 mg BD is too low for an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73m2; standard dose is 75 mg twice daily until eGFR falls below 30. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily alone, withhold oseltamivir pending nasopharyngeal PCR confirmation, and admit to ED short stay for monitoring over the next 12 hours
options.rationale: Awaiting PCR delays antiviral therapy; oseltamivir is most effective started within 48 hours and should be given empirically to high-risk patients during an outbreak. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence oseltamivir 75 mg IV every 12 hours, intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 4 hours, escalate oxygen and admit to ICU on the basis of CURB-65 score 3 and the lactate
options.rationale: Intravenous oseltamivir is not available in Australian inpatient formularies; oral oseltamivir at appropriate dose is used. Benzylpenicillin alone misses atypicals which are important in severe community-acquired pneumonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily, ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, escalate to ICU for severe community-acquired pneumonia and continue oxygen support
options.rationale: Severe CAP plus suspected influenza during an outbreak warrants combined empirical antibiotic and antiviral therapy; oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily is standard for eGFR 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73m2, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin covers typical and atypical bacterial co-infection, and ICU is indicated for SMART-COP at least 3. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence dexamethasone 6 mg daily as empirical therapy for inflammatory pneumonitis, withhold antiviral therapy in the setting of bacterial co-infection, and admit to a monitored ward bed
options.rationale: Routine corticosteroid use in influenza pneumonia is associated with worse outcomes outside specific indications; antiviral therapy is required for influenza and should not be withheld. (Source: ASID Influenza Antiviral Use Statement)

explanation.summary: Severe influenza pneumonia in vulnerable adults requires combined antibiotic and antiviral therapy. Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily is standard for eGFR over 30 mL/min/1.73m2; the dose is reduced to 30 mg daily for eGFR 10 to 30. Empirical antibiotic cover with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (or doxycycline) addresses bacterial co-infection. Corticosteroids are reserved for specific indications and not routine. Annual influenza vaccination is the foundation of prevention and is funded for at-risk groups in Australia.
key_points: Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily is standard for eGFR over 30 mL/min/1.73m2
Reduce oseltamivir to 30 mg daily for eGFR 10 to 30
Severe CAP with influenza needs both antibiotic and antiviral cover
Corticosteroids are not routine in influenza pneumonia
Annual influenza vaccination is funded for at-risk groups under the National Immunisation Program
explanation.pearls: Bacterial co-infection in severe influenza is dominated by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus; staphylococcal cover with vancomycin is added when there is cavitation, severe sepsis, or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus risk factors.

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 sepsis bundle initial management
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man brought in by ambulance with 12 hours of fever, dysuria, flank pain and rigors. He has a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and an indwelling catheter inserted 3 weeks ago for retention. He has been unable to keep down oral fluids overnight. His Glasgow Coma Scale is 14. He looks unwell with cool peripheries and mottled knees.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 94% room air, BP 92/56 mmHg, capillary refill 4 seconds, urine output 10 mL last hour
data_table.Examination: Reduced peripheral perfusion, mottled lower legs, soft tender suprapubic region, right costovertebral angle tenderness, indwelling urinary catheter in situ with cloudy urine
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.6 mmol/L, FBC WCC 18.4 x10^9/L neutrophils 16.0, CRP 268 mg/L, creatinine 152 micromol/L (baseline 90), urinalysis pyuria nitrites positive, blood cultures and urine culture pending, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Start oral trimethoprim 300 mg as a single stat dose plus 7-day course at home with general practitioner follow-up tomorrow morning, arrange community nursing for catheter change and oral fluid rehydration overnight
options.rationale: Septic shock with hypotension and lactate over 2 requires immediate IV antibiotics, IV crystalloid resuscitation and source control in hospital, not oral antibiotics at home. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Management)

options.text: Send blood cultures only after the patient has received the first dose of intravenous antibiotics to maximise yield and avoid delaying antimicrobial therapy in the initial hour of sepsis bundle delivery in the department
options.rationale: Blood cultures should be obtained before antibiotics where this does not delay therapy beyond 45 minutes; pre-antibiotic cultures retain higher yield. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Wait for blood culture and urine culture results before commencing any antimicrobial therapy because empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure may delay identification of the responsible organism and select for further resistance
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics must be given within 1 hour of recognition of septic shock; waiting for culture results increases mortality. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Send blood and urine cultures, administer 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid intravenously within 3 hours, give intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin or piperacillin-tazobactam empirically within 1 hour, monitor lactate clearance and start vasopressors if hypotension persists
options.rationale: The hour-1 sepsis bundle includes lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours and vasopressor initiation if MAP remains under 65 after fluid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Start non-invasive ventilation with continuous positive airway pressure, give intravenous noradrenaline 0.1 micrograms/kg/min and intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g, and admit for source control work up tomorrow on the morning ward round
options.rationale: Vasopressors are added after a 30 mL/kg crystalloid trial in fluid-responsive sepsis; source control work-up should not be deferred to the next day in pyelonephritis with sepsis. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Management)

explanation.summary: The hour-1 sepsis bundle requires lactate measurement, blood culture before antibiotics, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid within 3 hours for hypotension or lactate over 4, and vasopressor titration to a MAP target of 65 mmHg if hypotension persists. Source control is identified and addressed urgently. Australian empirical cover for urosepsis is typically amoxicillin plus gentamicin or piperacillin-tazobactam. Vasopressors are not commenced before adequate fluid resuscitation.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors as indicated
30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours in hypotension or lactate over 4
Vasopressors target MAP 65 mmHg if hypotension persists
Source control identified and addressed within 6-12 hours
Urosepsis empirical: amoxicillin plus gentamicin or piperacillin-tazobactam
explanation.pearls: In catheter-associated urosepsis remove or change the catheter as part of source control; antibiotics alone without source control are associated with higher mortality and persistent bacteraemia.

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary embolism Wells score and age-adjusted D-dimer
stem: You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 72-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with 24 hours of dyspnoea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She had a right total knee replacement 2 weeks ago and has been mostly bedbound at home. There is no haemoptysis, no calf swelling and no syncope. She has a past history of well-controlled hypertension on perindopril. She is afebrile and clinically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 94% room air, BP 138/82 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mild tachypnoea, normal heart sounds, clear chest, calves symmetrical and non-tender, no signs of right heart strain
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia rate 102 no S1Q3T3 or right strain, chest radiograph clear, FBC and UEC within reference ranges, troponin not elevated, D-dimer 720 ng/mL (laboratory cut-off 500 ng/mL)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with oral apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for 3 months because empirical treatment is more time-efficient than imaging given high pre-test probability and likely VTE in this clinical context
options.rationale: Wells PE score should be calculated first and confirmatory imaging obtained for moderate or high probability before commencing anticoagulation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Reassure that pulmonary embolism is unlikely because the chest radiograph is clear and the ECG shows no evidence of right heart strain or S1Q3T3 pattern and reassess at general practitioner clinic in 48 hours
options.rationale: Chest radiograph and ECG are insensitive for PE and should not be used to exclude the diagnosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Pulmonary Embolism)

options.text: Repeat the D-dimer in 24 hours and admit for observation overnight with serial troponin and ECG monitoring before deciding on definitive imaging or empirical therapeutic anticoagulation in the morning ward round
options.rationale: Repeating D-dimer adds no diagnostic value; the decision is to image or apply age-adjusted threshold (already exceeded here). (Source: BMJ Best Practice Pulmonary Embolism)

options.text: Calculate the Wells score (recent surgery within 4 weeks 1.5, tachycardia 1.5, PE most likely diagnosis 3 equals 6, high probability) and apply the age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off only if Wells is low or moderate before imaging
options.rationale: The Wells score arithmetic shown is incorrect; recent surgery scores 1.5 only if within 4 weeks AND immobilisation criteria are otherwise weighted; more importantly, high pre-test probability bypasses D-dimer and proceeds directly to imaging. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Pulmonary Embolism)

options.text: Calculate the Wells score, determine the patient is at moderate risk, apply age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off (age x 10 ng/mL = 720), find it exceeded and arrange computed tomography pulmonary angiography for diagnostic confirmation
options.rationale: Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off for over-50s is age x 10 ng/mL; 72 x 10 = 720, which equals the D-dimer here so age-adjusted threshold is met and CTPA is indicated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Pulmonary Embolism)

explanation.summary: Suspected PE workup uses the Wells score to estimate pre-test probability. Low-moderate probability patients have D-dimer testing using age-adjusted cut-offs in those over 50 (age x 10 ng/mL). High probability patients proceed directly to imaging without D-dimer. CTPA is the imaging modality of choice. VQ scan is reserved for renal impairment, pregnancy or contrast allergy. Therapeutic anticoagulation follows confirmation of diagnosis or pending imaging if high probability and no contraindication.
key_points: Wells score stratifies low, moderate, high probability
Age-adjusted D-dimer (over 50): age x 10 ng/mL
High pre-test probability: image directly without D-dimer
CTPA is first-line imaging; VQ scan if contraindication
Confirmed PE: anticoagulate (apixaban or rivaroxaban) 3-6 months
explanation.pearls: Age-adjusted D-dimer reduces unnecessary CTPA scans by approximately 12% in older adults with no decrease in sensitivity; the cut-off applies only in low-moderate Wells probability and only in patients aged over 50.

subtopic_detail: Acute kidney injury KDIGO staging and management
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 76-year-old non-Aboriginal man with a 5-day history of fever, productive cough and reduced oral intake. He has community-acquired pneumonia confirmed on chest radiograph and has been on ramipril 10 mg daily and rosuvastatin 20 mg daily for cardiovascular prevention. His baseline creatinine 4 months ago was 95 micromol/L. He has been unable to drink for the past 24 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 92% on 4 L nasal prongs, BP 102/64 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds, urine output 0.4 mL/kg/hour over 6 hours
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, jugular venous pressure not visible at 30 degrees, focal coarse crackles right base, no peripheral oedema, normal heart sounds
data_table.Investigations: Na 134 K 4.8 urea 14.2 mmol/L creatinine 198 micromol/L eGFR 28, FBC WCC 17 x10^9/L Hb 132 platelets 268, urinalysis no blood no protein, urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg, fractional excretion of sodium 0.6%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Continue ramipril for renoprotection given the patient's cardiovascular risk profile and proteinuria history, and add intravenous furosemide 40 mg to maintain urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/hour during the acute illness
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors should be withheld in acute kidney injury related to volume depletion; furosemide does not convert oliguric to non-oliguric AKI in this setting and may worsen hypovolaemia. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)

options.text: Commence intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours empirically for relative adrenal insufficiency in addition to broad-spectrum antibiotics and continue ramipril at the current dose while monitoring renal function trend
options.rationale: Empirical steroids are not indicated for AKI from pre-renal causes; ramipril should be withheld during acute volume depletion. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)

options.text: Arrange immediate haemodialysis given the rise in creatinine to over 2 times baseline meeting KDIGO stage 2 criteria with oliguria and pulmonary involvement to prevent further deterioration of renal function and clinical status
options.rationale: KDIGO indications for renal replacement (AEIOU: acidosis, electrolyte, ingestion, overload, uraemia) are not met here; stage 2 AKI alone without indications is treated with fluid resuscitation and removal of nephrotoxins. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)

options.text: Arrange an urgent renal tract ultrasound to exclude obstruction, withhold ramipril and rosuvastatin temporarily and commence intravenous N-acetylcysteine to attenuate any contrast or sepsis-related acute tubular necrosis insult
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine is not recommended for AKI prevention or treatment in current guidelines; while ultrasound is appropriate, the key intervention is fluid resuscitation. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)

options.text: Diagnose KDIGO stage 2 acute kidney injury, withhold ramipril and rosuvastatin, give a 500 mL bolus of balanced crystalloid then 1 mL/kg/hour, treat the pneumonia, monitor urine output and reassess fluid status hourly
options.rationale: Pre-renal AKI from sepsis and reduced intake (creatinine 2-3 times baseline = KDIGO stage 2) is managed with withholding nephrotoxins, prompt isotonic crystalloid resuscitation, treating the precipitant and monitoring fluid responsiveness. (Source: KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury)

explanation.summary: KDIGO defines AKI by absolute creatinine rise of 26.5 micromol/L within 48 hours, 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours. Stage 1 is 1.5 to 1.9 times baseline, stage 2 is 2 to 2.9 times, stage 3 is 3 times or RRT requirement. Management starts with identifying the cause (pre-renal, intrinsic, post-renal), withholding nephrotoxins, fluid resuscitation if hypovolaemic, and treating the precipitant. RRT indications are AEIOU.
key_points: KDIGO stage 1: 1.5-1.9x baseline; stage 2: 2-2.9x; stage 3: 3x or RRT
Pre-renal AKI: withhold nephrotoxins, isotonic crystalloid, treat precipitant
Investigate cause: pre-renal, intrinsic, post-renal
Ultrasound if obstruction suspected
RRT indications (AEIOU): acidosis, electrolytes, ingestion, overload, uraemia
explanation.pearls: Fractional excretion of sodium under 1% supports pre-renal aetiology in oliguric AKI not on diuretics; if patient is on diuretics use fractional excretion of urea instead (under 35% suggests pre-renal pattern).

subtopic_detail: SIADH workup and management of euvolaemic hyponatraemia
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old non-Aboriginal man with newly diagnosed small-cell lung cancer admitted for chemotherapy planning. He has had a single fall at home, mild headache and mild nausea over the last week. He has no peripheral oedema, normal jugular venous pressure and mucous membranes appear moist. His weight has not changed. He takes amlodipine for hypertension but no diuretics or antidepressants.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 76, RR 14, SpO2 96% room air, BP 124/78 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Mild dehydration not evident, no peripheral oedema, normal heart sounds, breath sounds reduced right base, no focal neurology, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: Na 118 K 4.2 urea 3.4 mmol/L creatinine 78 micromol/L, serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 56 mmol/L, TSH 1.8 mU/L, 9 am cortisol 480 nmol/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L, no current diuretic or SSRI

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence intravenous 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 20 minutes targeting a sodium rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first hour and continue hourly boluses to restore sodium to within normal range over 12 hours of monitoring
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma, severe vomiting); mild symptoms with chronic onset are managed with fluid restriction. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Diagnose syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, commence fluid restriction to 800 mL/24 hours, treat the underlying malignancy and target sodium correction at no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours
options.rationale: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and elevated urine sodium with no diuretic, normal thyroid and cortisol meets SIADH criteria; fluid restriction is first-line with correction limited to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride at 125 mL/hour for 24 hours alongside intravenous demeclocycline and arrange a cosyntropin stimulation test if sodium has not improved within 48 hours from admission
options.rationale: Isotonic saline in SIADH can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia as the sodium is excreted while the free water is retained; demeclocycline is third-line and rarely used. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Commence oral tolvaptan 15 mg daily as first-line therapy with daily sodium monitoring and rapid up-titration to 60 mg daily over 1 week if sodium has not improved by 8 mmol/L within the first 48 hours of treatment
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is reserved for fluid-restriction failure and requires inpatient initiation with cautious titration due to over-rapid correction risk; it is not first-line. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Commence oral salt tablets 1 g three times daily, encourage free fluid intake to thirst and arrange outpatient endocrinology review in 2 weeks once the underlying malignancy is being treated definitively with combination chemotherapy
options.rationale: Free fluid in SIADH worsens dilution; salt tablets without fluid restriction are inadequate. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Hyponatraemia)

explanation.summary: SIADH is diagnosed when there is euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine (over 100 mOsm/kg), urine sodium over 30 mmol/L, normal thyroid and adrenal function and no diuretic. First-line management is fluid restriction to 800 to 1000 mL per day plus treatment of the underlying cause. Correction is limited to under 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Tolvaptan and hypertonic saline are reserved for refractory or severe symptomatic cases.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic hyponatraemia, low serum osmolality, urine osmolality over 100, urine sodium over 30
Exclude thyroid and adrenal insufficiency and diuretic use
First-line: fluid restriction 800-1000 mL/day plus treat the cause
Correct sodium under 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid ODS
Hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia only
explanation.pearls: Small-cell lung cancer is the commonest paraneoplastic cause of SIADH in adults; sodium correction over 10-12 mmol/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination, presenting 2-6 days later with quadriparesis, dysarthria and locked-in syndrome.

subtopic_detail: Acute pancreatitis severity stratification Modified Glasgow
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old non-Aboriginal man with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back over the past 12 hours after a heavy alcohol bout. He has nausea and four episodes of vomiting since onset. He is haemodynamically stable but in significant pain. He has a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use and is not on any regular medications. He has been admitted twice previously with episodes of acute pancreatitis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 °C, HR 112, RR 24, SpO2 92% room air, BP 118/76 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Tender epigastrium with voluntary guarding, no rebound, no Cullen or Grey-Turner signs, bowel sounds reduced but present, jaundice not present
data_table.Investigations: Lipase 1800 U/L, FBC WCC 16.4 x10^9/L Hb 142 platelets 280, Na 136 K 3.8 urea 11.2 creatinine 96 micromol/L glucose 11.6 mmol/L, calcium 1.92 mmol/L corrected, ALT 88 ALP 110 albumin 30 g/L LDH 480 U/L, ABG pH 7.34 pCO2 32 pO2 58 mmHg HCO3 18, CRP 220 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral hydration with electrolyte solution at 100 mL/hour, prescribe oxycodone immediate release 5 mg every 4 hours as needed and arrange ultrasound abdomen within 24 hours to assess for gallstone aetiology
options.rationale: Modified Glasgow score 4 (PaO2 under 60, urea over 16 not present here so 1 fewer; consider 3 with PaO2 + albumin + calcium + glucose) plus CRP 220 indicates severe acute pancreatitis requiring HDU/ICU care with aggressive IV resuscitation, not oral hydration. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)

options.text: Commence parenteral nutrition immediately to rest the pancreas, give intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics with piperacillin-tazobactam empirically and arrange MRCP within 24 hours of admission for biliary evaluation
options.rationale: Enteral nutrition is preferred over parenteral; prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated unless infected necrosis or cholangitis is suspected. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)

options.text: Diagnose severe acute pancreatitis, admit to high-dependency care, commence aggressive intravenous Hartmann's resuscitation, provide opioid analgesia, monitor urine output and arrange contrast-enhanced CT abdomen at 72-96 hours
options.rationale: Severe acute pancreatitis (Modified Glasgow with PaO2, calcium, albumin, glucose abnormalities and CRP over 150 in this index admission) mandates HDU level care, aggressive fluid resuscitation, analgesia and delayed CT (72-96 hours) to assess for necrosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)

options.text: Arrange urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography within 6 hours of admission for sphincterotomy and ductal clearance because of the high lipase and significant systemic inflammatory response in this patient
options.rationale: ERCP is reserved for acute pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; alcohol-related pancreatitis without biliary obstruction does not benefit. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)

options.text: Arrange immediate laparotomy with surgical drainage of pancreatic necrosis and intra-abdominal sepsis source control given the elevated white cell count, raised CRP and clinical features of systemic inflammatory response
options.rationale: Surgery in necrotising pancreatitis is delayed to at least 4 weeks where possible and is reserved for infected necrosis; immediate laparotomy is harmful early in the disease. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Acute Pancreatitis)

explanation.summary: Severe acute pancreatitis is identified by validated scores (Modified Glasgow 3 or more, APACHE II over 8) at 48 hours, organ failure or CRP over 150. Management is HDU/ICU care, aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation to maintain urine output, multimodal analgesia, early enteral nutrition (within 24-72 hours) and contrast CT at 72-96 hours to assess for necrosis. Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated. ERCP is reserved for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction. Necrosectomy is delayed.
key_points: Severity scores: Modified Glasgow 3+, APACHE II over 8, BISAP over 3, CRP over 150
Severe pancreatitis: HDU/ICU, aggressive crystalloid, analgesia
Enteral nutrition preferred and early
CT at 72-96 hours to assess for necrosis
ERCP only for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction
explanation.pearls: Modified Glasgow uses mnemonic PANCREAS: PaO2 under 60, Age over 55, Neutrophils WCC over 15, Calcium under 2, Renal urea over 16, Enzymes LDH over 600 ALT over 200, Albumin under 32, Sugar glucose over 10; 3 or more positive at 48 hours indicates severe disease.

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis empirical therapy native valve
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 52-year-old non-Aboriginal man with a 2-week history of fevers, night sweats, fatigue and 3 kg weight loss. He has a known bicuspid aortic valve under cardiology surveillance and recently had a routine dental cleaning without antibiotic prophylaxis. On examination he has new splinter haemorrhages, two Janeway lesions on the soles and a new early diastolic murmur. He has no penicillin allergy and no recent intravenous drug use.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 °C, HR 104, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, BP 132/56 mmHg with wide pulse pressure
data_table.Examination: New early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, splinter haemorrhages on three fingernails, two Janeway lesions on the right sole, no Osler nodes, no Roth spots on fundoscopy, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 14.2 x10^9/L Hb 116 platelets 220, CRP 168 mg/L ESR 88 mm/h, UEC creatinine 102 micromol/L, blood cultures (3 sets from separate venipunctures over 1 hour pending), transthoracic echocardiogram shows aortic regurgitation with a 12 mm vegetation on the aortic valve

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen pending cultures?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g once daily monotherapy adjusted to culture results when available, continued for a total of 4 weeks of intravenous therapy with follow-up echocardiography at 2 and 6 weeks from initiation of antimicrobial cover
options.rationale: Empirical native valve endocarditis cover requires combination therapy targeting Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci and enterococci; monotherapy ceftriaxone is inadequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours, intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours and intravenous gentamicin 3 mg/kg once daily until culture and sensitivity results are reported by microbiology
options.rationale: Australian native-valve empirical regimen uses benzylpenicillin (not flucloxacillin) for streptococci, plus flucloxacillin OR vancomycin (not both) for staphylococci, plus gentamicin; this option triples antibiotic cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours, intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours, intravenous gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours and a single 1 g dose of intravenous vancomycin upfront for rapid coverage prior to confirmatory blood cultures
options.rationale: A single dose of vancomycin upfront is not appropriate; vancomycin replaces flucloxacillin if MRSA suspected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours, intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours and intravenous gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for an Australian native valve empirical regimen pending culture identification
options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines empirical native valve endocarditis cover is benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin for streptococci, staphylococci and enterococci until culture-directed therapy is possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous meropenem 1 g every 8 hours as broad-spectrum monotherapy and arrange transoesophageal echocardiography within 24 hours for vegetation characterisation and complication assessment before further antibiotic adjustment
options.rationale: Meropenem is not a standard empirical regimen for endocarditis; combination therapy with the specific cover above is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Native-valve infective endocarditis empirical cover targets streptococci, staphylococci and enterococci. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin until cultures are available. Vancomycin replaces flucloxacillin if MRSA is suspected. The modified Duke criteria classify cases as definite, possible or rejected. Transoesophageal echocardiography is performed when transthoracic is inconclusive or to assess for abscess. Surgical indications include heart failure, abscess, large vegetation, fungal aetiology and persistent bacteraemia despite appropriate therapy.
key_points: Empirical native valve: benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin
Replace flucloxacillin with vancomycin if MRSA
Three separate blood culture sets before antibiotics
TOE for inconclusive TTE or to assess abscess
Surgical indications: heart failure, abscess, large vegetation, fungal, persistent bacteraemia
explanation.pearls: Modified Duke criteria definite endocarditis requires 2 major, 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria; major criteria are typical organism in 2 cultures or persistent bacteraemia plus echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement or new valvular regurgitation.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and hydrocortisone dosing
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 42-year-old non-Aboriginal woman known to have primary adrenal insufficiency on regular hydrocortisone 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg at midday and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She has had 24 hours of fever, vomiting and diarrhoea and was unable to take her morning hydrocortisone dose today. She looks unwell, drowsy and hypotensive. Her family is with her and confirms she is fully adherent normally.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 124, RR 24, SpO2 97% room air, BP 82/48 mmHg, capillary refill 4 seconds, capillary glucose 3.0 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, dry mucous membranes, abdomen soft non-tender, no focal neurology, hyperpigmentation of palmar creases consistent with her known underlying condition
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 K 5.8 urea 9.2 mmol/L creatinine 132 micromol/L glucose 3.0 mmol/L, FBC WCC 12.4 x10^9/L, ECG no hyperkalaemic changes, blood cultures sent, urinalysis no nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg, commence intravenous adrenaline infusion 0.1 microgram/kg/min and arrange immediate intensive care admission for ongoing support of shock with vasopressors and inotropes as needed
options.rationale: Adrenaline is not the primary treatment of adrenal crisis; intravenous hydrocortisone with fluid resuscitation is first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Increase her oral hydrocortisone to 30 mg three times daily for the duration of illness, arrange community follow-up tomorrow and provide oral fluid replacement with electrolyte solution overnight
options.rationale: Vomiting prevents oral absorption; she is in established adrenal crisis with hypotension and hypoglycaemia requiring intravenous therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately as a bolus, commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour, give intravenous dextrose for hypoglycaemia and continue intravenous hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours
options.rationale: Established adrenal crisis is treated with immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, intravenous fluid resuscitation with normal saline, glucose correction and ongoing hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours pending stabilisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg as an alternative to hydrocortisone so that a short Synacthen test can be performed within the next 24 hours of admission to confirm the diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: Diagnosis is already established; hydrocortisone is preferred over dexamethasone for its mineralocorticoid activity. Synacthen testing is unnecessary in a known case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Administer intravenous fludrocortisone 200 micrograms as a single dose to correct mineralocorticoid deficiency contributing to hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia and continue her regular oral hydrocortisone schedule
options.rationale: Intravenous fludrocortisone is not available; high-dose intravenous hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity in adrenal crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate intravenous hydrocortisone, intravenous fluid resuscitation, glucose correction and treatment of the precipitant. Standard initial dosing is 100 mg intravenous hydrocortisone followed by 50 mg every 6 hours or a continuous infusion. Hydrocortisone has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity at these doses, so additional fludrocortisone is not needed acutely. Patients with known adrenal insufficiency should be educated to triple oral hydrocortisone during minor illness and use intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg if vomiting.
key_points: Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 50 mg q6h
IV 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation 1 L in first hour
Correct hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose
No need for fludrocortisone acutely at IV hydrocortisone doses
Triple oral dose for minor illness; IM hydrocortisone 100 mg if vomiting
explanation.pearls: Issue every patient with adrenal insufficiency an emergency injection kit (intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg) for vomiting illness or accident; their MedicAlert bracelet and steroid emergency card alert paramedics and ED clinicians to give parenteral steroid before transfer.

subtopic_detail: VTE provoked vs unprovoked anticoagulation duration
stem: You are the general practitioner reviewing a 56-year-old non-Aboriginal man 3 months after a confirmed proximal lower limb deep vein thrombosis. He has been on apixaban since diagnosis. He has no past or family history of thromboembolism, no known thrombophilia and no current malignancy on age-appropriate screening. The DVT occurred 2 weeks after a 12 hour transcontinental flight. He has not had any bleeding complications on apixaban and is keen to discuss duration of treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, BP 124/78 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Resolved calf swelling, no new oedema, no respiratory or cardiac signs of recurrent disease, no signs of malignancy
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC and LFT within reference ranges, d-dimer 380 ng/mL after 4 weeks off anticoagulation simulation not yet performed, age-appropriate cancer screening up to date, thrombophilia screen not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Stop apixaban now at 3 months because this was a provoked deep vein thrombosis with a transient risk factor (long-haul flight), discuss recurrence risk and provide VTE prevention advice for future air travel and immobilisation
options.rationale: DVT provoked by a transient major risk factor (recent long-haul flight) without other risk factors typically requires only 3 months of anticoagulation; longer treatment does not improve outcomes once the provoking factor has resolved. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely because all proximal deep vein thromboses regardless of provoking factor benefit from indefinite anticoagulation based on observational evidence of recurrence reduction without bleeding risk increase
options.rationale: Indefinite anticoagulation is for unprovoked or recurrent VTE; provoked DVT with resolved transient factor does not require indefinite anticoagulation. (Source: BMJ Best Practice DVT)

options.text: Continue apixaban at the reduced dose of 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely as extended-duration secondary prevention because all transcontinental flight-related deep vein thromboses recur at higher rates than other transient provoked thromboses
options.rationale: Reduced-dose extended therapy applies to unprovoked VTE after 6 months of initial full-dose treatment; flight-associated DVT is provoked. (Source: BMJ Best Practice DVT)

options.text: Stop apixaban at 6 months and arrange thrombophilia screening before discontinuation to identify any inherited thrombophilia that would justify ongoing anticoagulation regardless of the transient nature of the provoking risk factor present
options.rationale: Routine thrombophilia screening rarely changes management and is not recommended after a single provoked VTE; identification of low-risk thrombophilias does not extend anticoagulation. (Source: HSANZ Thrombophilia Guidelines)

options.text: Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely as extended secondary prevention because aspirin has shown a meaningful reduction in recurrent VTE risk with a lower bleeding profile than ongoing direct oral anticoagulant therapy in this group
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces recurrent VTE risk less effectively than DOAC or warfarin and is reserved for those who decline ongoing anticoagulation; it is not the standard step after a provoked DVT. (Source: BMJ Best Practice DVT)

explanation.summary: Duration of anticoagulation in VTE depends on whether the event was provoked by a transient major risk factor (3 months typically), provoked by a persistent risk factor (continue while factor present), or unprovoked (consider extended therapy after 6 months). Aspirin reduces recurrence less than anticoagulants and is reserved for those declining anticoagulation. Routine thrombophilia screening after a single VTE rarely changes management. Reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban is an option for extended therapy after unprovoked VTE.
key_points: Provoked by transient factor: 3 months anticoagulation
Provoked by persistent factor: continue while factor present
Unprovoked: consider extended after 6 months
Reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban for extended therapy in unprovoked
Thrombophilia screening rarely alters management after single VTE
explanation.pearls: HERDOO2 and DASH scores can identify a subset of women with unprovoked VTE who can stop anticoagulation safely at 6 to 12 months; men with unprovoked VTE have a higher recurrence rate and benefit from extended therapy.

subtopic_detail: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension recognition and lumbar puncture opening pressure
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the assessment unit reviewing a 26-year-old woman with 6 weeks of progressively worsening daily headache, retro-orbital pressure, pulsatile tinnitus and transient visual obscurations on standing. She has gained 8 kg over 6 months and her BMI is now 32. She is on no regular medication. She has no history of head trauma, neoplasia or immunosuppression.

Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema with peripapillary haemorrhages. MRI brain with venography is normal with no mass, hydrocephalus or sinus thrombosis. Cranial nerve examination shows a bilateral abducens nerve weakness with normal visual acuity.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 78, T 36.7 °C, BMI 32
data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema with peripapillary haemorrhages, bilateral CN VI weakness, otherwise normal cranial nerves and limb examination
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain with venography normal; bloods FBC, UEC, LFTs, B12, TSH normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position with measurement of opening pressure and CSF studies including cell count, glucose and protein to confirm idiopathic intracranial hypertension before initiating treatment
options.rationale: After secondary causes are excluded by neuroimaging (including venography), LP with opening pressure over 250 mmCSF (over 280 in BMI over 30) and normal CSF composition confirms IIH (modified Dandy criteria). (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

options.text: Initiate acetazolamide 250 mg twice daily empirically and arrange follow-up in 2 weeks for review of papilloedema and visual fields without further diagnostic investigation given the typical clinical pattern of IIH
options.rationale: Treatment should follow diagnostic confirmation by LP (Dandy criteria); empirical treatment before confirmation risks missing alternative causes such as hidden venous sinus pathology. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

options.text: Arrange CT venogram or MR venogram to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as the primary cause of raised intracranial pressure given the clinical features and presence of papilloedema and CN VI palsy
options.rationale: She has already had MRI brain WITH venography - this has been done. The next step is LP with opening pressure. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

options.text: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for consideration of optic nerve sheath fenestration and ventriculoperitoneal shunting given the bilateral papilloedema and risk of permanent visual loss without immediate decompression
options.rationale: Surgical interventions are reserved for fulminant IIH or progressive visual loss despite medical therapy; diagnostic workup including LP is required first. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

options.text: Send a lumbar CSF for autoimmune encephalitis and paraneoplastic antibody panels and arrange whole-body PET-CT to look for occult malignancy given the subacute course and weight gain over the last 6 months
options.rationale: Routine paraneoplastic and autoimmune workup is not part of initial IIH evaluation; the clinical and imaging features are typical for IIH and do not suggest paraneoplastic. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

explanation.summary: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects obese women of reproductive age. Modified Dandy criteria: symptoms/signs of raised ICP (headache, papilloedema, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, CN VI palsy), no localising features beyond CN VI, normal CSF composition, opening pressure over 250 mmCSF (over 280 if BMI over 30), no other identifiable cause on neuroimaging including venography. Treatment: weight loss (5 to 10%) is the most effective long-term measure. Acetazolamide first-line pharmacotherapy, topiramate second-line. Surgical options for fulminant or progressive visual loss: optic nerve sheath fenestration, lumboperitoneal or ventriculoperitoneal shunt, or venous sinus stenting where stenosis is documented.
key_points: IIH demographic: obese women of reproductive age
Modified Dandy: symptoms ICP + papilloedema + normal CSF + OP over 250 (280 if BMI over 30)
Imaging must include venography to exclude CVST
First-line: weight loss + acetazolamide; second-line topiramate
Visual loss: ONSF, shunt, or sinus stenting (if stenosis)
explanation.pearls: Visual loss in IIH occurs through papilloedema-induced optic atrophy, not directly from raised ICP; ophthalmology co-management with formal visual fields every 1-3 months in untreated/severe cases drives treatment escalation before permanent loss.

sources.label: RANZCO: Papilloedema and raised intracranial pressure
BMJ Best Practice: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

subtopic_detail: AECOPD ventilatory failure and BiPAP threshold
stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 72-year-old former smoker (75 pack-years) with severe COPD (FEV1 35 percent predicted, GOLD D) presenting with 3 days of increased dyspnoea, purulent sputum and reduced exercise tolerance. He uses tiotropium and salbutamol. On arrival he is using accessory muscles and is drowsy but rousable. He has had nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium plus 40 mg oral prednisolone in the department. Current oxygen is 4 L/min via nasal prongs.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 112, BP 142/82, RR 32, SpO2 92% on 4 L/min nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Pursed-lip breathing, audible polyphonic wheeze and prolonged expiration bilaterally, drowsy but rousable, no asterixis yet, no focal chest signs of consolidation
data_table.Investigations: ABG (on 4 L/min): pH 7.26, pCO2 78 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 30 mmol/L, base excess +4; FBC WCC 12.4, CRP 84, U+E normal, chest X-ray hyperinflation no infiltrate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation without trial of non-invasive ventilation because NIV is contraindicated when the patient has a depressed level of consciousness and a pCO2 over 70 mmHg
options.rationale: NIV is first-line for AECOPD with hypercapnic acidosis even with mild drowsiness due to hypercapnia (it often improves with NIV); intubation is reserved for failure of NIV or absolute contraindication. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)

options.text: Increase the oxygen to 8 L/min via non-rebreather mask to achieve saturations above 95 percent and continue back-to-back nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium without commencing non-invasive ventilation at this stage
options.rationale: High-flow O2 in COPD type 2 failure worsens hypercapnia and acidosis; controlled O2 (target 88-92%) is the rule, and BiPAP is required for the respiratory acidosis. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)

options.text: Reduce oxygen to titrate SpO2 88 to 92 percent via Venturi mask and commence bilevel non-invasive ventilation (IPAP 14 cmH2O EPAP 5 cmH2O) for hypercapnic respiratory failure, with reassessment of ABG in 1 hour
options.rationale: Type 2 respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis (pH under 7.35, pCO2 over 45) despite controlled oxygen and bronchodilator therapy is the trigger for BiPAP in AECOPD per Therapeutic Guidelines Respiratory and TSANZ. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes and intravenous aminophylline 5 mg/kg loading followed by an infusion of 0.5 mg/kg/hr without commencing NIV at this stage and reassess clinical response in 1 hour
options.rationale: Aminophylline is no longer routinely recommended in AECOPD and magnesium has limited evidence; neither replaces NIV for type 2 respiratory failure with acidosis. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)

options.text: Commence oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and continued nebulised bronchodilators on the ward, deferring any ventilatory support because the chest X-ray shows no consolidation to indicate severe infective exacerbation
options.rationale: Antibiotics and bronchodilators are needed but do not address the type 2 respiratory failure with acidosis, which requires NIV. (Source: TSANZ: Non-invasive ventilation in COPD)

explanation.summary: Acute exacerbation of COPD with respiratory acidosis (pH under 7.35, pCO2 over 45 mmHg) despite controlled oxygen and maximal medical therapy is the indication for non-invasive ventilation (bilevel positive airway pressure). Target oxygen saturation 88 to 92 percent using a Venturi mask. Bronchodilators (salbutamol plus ipratropium nebulised), systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 30 to 40 mg daily for 5 days), and antibiotics for infective exacerbations (amoxicillin or doxycycline first-line per Australian guidelines) are concurrent. Reassess ABG at 1 hour - failure of NIV (worsening acidosis, persistent pH under 7.25 at 2 hours, hypoxia, agitation) triggers escalation to intubation.
key_points: AECOPD with pH under 7.35 and pCO2 over 45 = NIV
Controlled O2 88-92% via Venturi mask
Salbutamol + ipratropium nebulised, plus oral prednisolone 5 days
Antibiotics if infective features (amoxicillin or doxycycline)
Reassess ABG at 1 hour, escalate if no improvement at 2 hours
explanation.pearls: Oxygen-induced hypercapnia in chronic CO2 retention is multifactorial: reversal of hypoxic vasoconstriction worsening V/Q mismatch is the main mechanism (not solely loss of hypoxic drive).

subtopic_detail: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema first-line management
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the resuscitation bay reviewing a 68-year-old man with known HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent), previous anterior MI 4 years ago, and hypertension. He has had 6 hours of progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and pink frothy sputum. He is sitting upright, distressed and unable to complete a sentence. His usual medications are perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, frusemide 40 mg twice daily and atorvastatin 40 mg.

He has not been adherent for the last 3 days. He has no chest pain. The 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia and known left bundle branch block without acute ischaemic changes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 184/112, HR 124 sinus, RR 36, SpO2 87% air rising to 92% on 15 L NRB, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Tripod posture, accessory muscle use, fine bibasal crackles to mid-zones, raised JVP, pitting peripheral oedema to knees, peripheral perfusion warm
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly with bilateral perihilar opacities and Kerley B lines; troponin pending; BNP 1842 ng/L; UEC creatinine 110 (baseline 102), K 4.0; ABG pH 7.32 pCO2 48 pO2 60 on NRB

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline 50 mcg as a slow push, intubate immediately and commence noradrenaline infusion at 0.05 mcg/kg/min as first-line therapy for cardiogenic shock pending arrival of the cardiology consult team
options.rationale: He is hypertensive and warm-perfused so not in cardiogenic shock; vasopressors and adrenaline are contraindicated in this hypertensive APO subtype. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

options.text: Commence high-dose intravenous beta blocker with metoprolol 5 mg slow push every 5 minutes and continue current oral diuretic at home dose, deferring nitrate or non-invasive ventilation until heart rate has been controlled below 100
options.rationale: Acute IV beta blocker worsens cardiogenic shock and pulmonary oedema; chronic beta blocker may be continued but not up-titrated in acute decompensation. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

options.text: Administer intravenous morphine 5 mg, an intravenous bolus of 500 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride to support cardiac output, and continue home oral diuretic dose pending observation over the next 4 hours of inpatient management
options.rationale: IV fluids worsen pulmonary oedema; morphine increases mortality in APO per current evidence and is no longer routinely recommended. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

options.text: Sit upright, commence non-invasive bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation, give sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 600 mcg and start an intravenous nitrate infusion titrated to BP, and administer intravenous frusemide 80 mg as initial diuretic dose
options.rationale: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with hypertension and SpO2 under 90 on air is managed with NIV, IV nitrate for preload and afterload reduction and IV loop diuretic per CSANZ heart failure guideline and Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

options.text: Cease all chronic heart failure medications including perindopril and bisoprolol now to avoid contributing to acute decompensation, and start oral metolazone 5 mg in combination with continuing oral frusemide as first-line acute therapy
options.rationale: Chronic ACE inhibitor and beta blocker are continued unless hypotensive or in shock; oral diuretic alone in acute APO is inadequate and IV route is required. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018

explanation.summary: Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema is classified by perfusion and congestion. Hypertensive wet-and-warm (this patient) is treated with sitting upright, NIV (CPAP or BiPAP), IV nitrate infusion titrated to BP (starting 5 to 10 mcg/min), and IV loop diuretic (frusemide 1 to 2 times the home oral daily dose IV). Underlying triggers (ischaemia, AF, infection, non-adherence, NSAIDs, salt load) are sought and managed. Chronic disease-modifying therapy (ACE inhibitor or ARB or sacubitril-valsartan, beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) is continued unless contraindicated by hypotension or shock. Cardiogenic shock (wet-and-cold) needs inotrope or mechanical support.
key_points: Wet-and-warm hypertensive APO: NIV + IV nitrate + IV frusemide
Wet-and-cold cardiogenic shock: inotropes (dobutamine), possible mechanical support
Avoid IV fluids unless RV-dominant or normotensive dry-and-cold
Continue chronic GDMT unless hypotensive
Find and treat the trigger
explanation.pearls: IV nitrate is contraindicated if SBP under 100 mmHg, severe aortic stenosis with low gradient, or recent PDE5 inhibitor use - these are the three traps to avoid before reaching for the GTN infusion.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ: Heart failure guideline 2018
Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Acute heart failure

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes - first-line cardioprotection
stem: You are the medical registrar in a busy emergency department called by the resuscitation nurse with a critical potassium result on a 69-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (baseline eGFR 22) who presented 2 hours ago with worsening lethargy and reduced urine output for 3 days. He takes perindopril 8 mg, spironolactone 25 mg and frusemide 80 mg daily. He started a high-dose oral potassium chloride supplement from a friend last week. He has no chest pain. Routine bloods are back.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 48 bradycardic, RR 16, SpO2 98% air, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, normal cardiovascular exam apart from bradycardia, no peripheral oedema, mild abdominal discomfort, no flank tenderness
data_table.Investigations: K 7.4 mmol/L, Na 136, urea 28, creatinine 280 micromol/L (baseline 220), bicarbonate 18, calcium 2.18, glucose 6.0; ECG: peaked T waves, broad QRS to 140 ms, P waves attenuated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Insert a vascular dialysis catheter and arrange urgent haemodialysis as the sole initial intervention because pharmacological measures are unreliable in chronic kidney disease and only dialysis removes the potassium load definitively
options.rationale: Dialysis is appropriate for refractory or severe hyperkalaemia but is preceded by IV calcium and insulin-dextrose for immediate cardioprotection while access is being arranged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Administer 30 g of oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate (resonium) as first-line therapy because it removes potassium definitively over the next 2 hours and obviates the need for intravenous calcium or insulin-dextrose shift therapy
options.rationale: Resonium has slow onset (hours) and no role in immediate cardioprotection; with ECG changes and K above 6.5, IV calcium and insulin-dextrose are first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Commence intravenous frusemide 80 mg bolus and 1000 mL of 5% dextrose over 2 hours as initial therapy because forced diuresis with isotonic dextrose acts as both potassium shift and excretion in this oliguric kidney patient
options.rationale: Frusemide may help if there is preserved diuresis but is not first-line cardioprotection; with ECG changes IV calcium is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Administer 50 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate as a slow intravenous push as first-line therapy because acidosis-correction shifts potassium intracellularly more rapidly than any other available pharmacological measure
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is an adjunct in significant acidosis and is slower than insulin-dextrose for shifting; not first-line monotherapy in this scenario. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Administer 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate intravenously over 2 to 5 minutes for cardiac membrane stabilisation, then 10 units of intravenous short-acting insulin in 50 mL of 50% dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly, with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: ECG changes with K above 6.5 mmol/L require immediate calcium gluconate for cardiac stabilisation, followed by insulin-dextrose shift therapy and ongoing nebulised salbutamol and definitive potassium removal per Therapeutic Guidelines and KHA-CARI. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T, prolonged PR, wide QRS, sine wave) is a life-threatening emergency. Management priorities are membrane stabilisation, intracellular shift, removal and prevention. First-line: 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate (or 5 mL of 10% calcium chloride via central line) over 2 to 5 minutes - effect within minutes, lasts 30 to 60 minutes, repeat as needed. Shift: 10 units short-acting insulin in 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV over 10 minutes plus nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg.
