Removal: loop diuretic if making urine, oral or rectal cation exchange resin (resonium or patiromer), urgent haemodialysis for refractory or severe disease. Stop ACE inhibitor, MRA, K supplements, NSAIDs. Manage cause (AKI, rhabdomyolysis, adrenal insufficiency).
key_points: ECG changes + K over 6.5 = immediate IV calcium
Calcium stabilises membrane in minutes
Insulin-dextrose 10 U with 50 mL 50% dextrose for shift
Salbutamol nebs adjunct shift
Definitive removal: resonium, diuretic, dialysis
explanation.pearls: Calcium chloride 5 mL of 10% has 3 times the elemental calcium of calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% but requires central venous access due to vesicant risk - gluconate is the safer peripheral option.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection recognition and management
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.9 percent) admitted overnight with a left leg cellulitis from a minor garden injury 3 days ago. Despite intravenous flucloxacillin he has clinically worsened over 8 hours with pain disproportionate to the visible erythema, dusky discolouration extending beyond the marked margin, and new dark haemorrhagic blisters along the medial calf. He is more tachycardic, looks toxic and confused. He has had two intravenous fluid boluses without improvement.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 132, BP 92/58, RR 28, SpO2 95% on 2 L/min, GCS 14, lactate 4.6
data_table.Examination: Confused but rousable, left medial calf swollen tense skin with dusky purpuric discolouration spreading beyond marked margin, two new haemorrhagic bullae, marked tenderness disproportionate to appearance, decreased sensation centrally over the lesion, crepitus on palpation
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 19.8), Hb 122, platelets 165, Na 132, glucose 16.2 mmol/L, creatinine 162, CRP 380 mg/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, INR 1.4, LRINEC score calculated as 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue intravenous flucloxacillin at the current dose, add intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily and arrange routine elective surgical review on the next routine list in 24 to 48 hours pending repeat blood cultures and clinical reassessment
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis demands urgent (not elective) surgical debridement and broader antibiotic cover; flucloxacillin alone misses Gram-negatives, anaerobes and streptococcal toxin suppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Initiate sepsis bundle with intravenous fluid resuscitation, blood cultures, broad-spectrum intravenous meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin and arrange immediate surgical consultation for urgent operative debridement in theatre
options.rationale: LRINEC at or above 8 with clinical features (pain disproportionate, dusky discolouration, bullae, crepitus, toxicity) is necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise; broad-spectrum cover (carbapenem + clindamycin for toxin suppression + vanco for MRSA) and urgent surgical debridement save life. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the limb to confirm necrotising fasciitis before any change in antibiotic therapy or surgical decision making because imaging is required to distinguish soft tissue infection from cellulitis
options.rationale: Imaging may help but never delays surgical debridement in suspected nec fasc; the diagnosis is clinical and surgical findings are confirmatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Apply a topical silver sulfadiazine dressing to the bullae, mark the erythema margins with a black pen and continue intravenous flucloxacillin while observing for response over the next 12 hours of inpatient management
options.rationale: Topical management is inappropriate for necrotising fasciitis; this strategy will result in rapid progression and death without surgical debridement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as monotherapy for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome and observe for 12 hours before considering antibiotic broadening or surgical referral if no clinical improvement has occurred
options.rationale: IVIG may be adjunctive in severe group A streptococcal toxic shock but is not monotherapy and does not replace surgery and broad-spectrum antibiotics. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection (NSTI) is a surgical emergency with mortality 20 to 40 percent. Recognise by pain disproportionate to appearance, rapid progression, dusky or violaceous discolouration, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia of overlying skin and systemic toxicity. LRINEC score at or above 6 raises suspicion (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose), at or above 8 is high probability. Diabetes, immunosuppression and IV drug use are risk factors. Management is urgent surgical debridement (the cornerstone), broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-positives (including MRSA), Gram-negatives and anaerobes (meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin per Australian guidelines), aggressive ICU-level resuscitation, and consideration of IVIG for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.
key_points: Pain disproportionate to appearance + bullae + crepitus + toxicity = NSTI
LRINEC score helps risk-stratify but never delays surgery
Urgent surgical debridement is the cornerstone
Empirical: meropenem + clindamycin (toxin suppression) + vancomycin
ICU support, IVIG for documented strep TSS
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is added not for its antibacterial spectrum but to suppress streptococcal exotoxin production (Eagle effect) - it is included in regimens regardless of the primary antibiotic choice.

sources.label: Surgical Infection Society guideline: Skin and soft tissue infection

subtopic_detail: Septic shock hour-1 bundle and vasopressor selection
stem: You are the medical registrar in the resuscitation area reviewing a 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes admitted with dysuria, frank haematuria and right loin pain progressing over 36 hours. On arrival she is confused, peripherally cool with prolonged capillary refill, and breathing rapidly. She has received 30 mL/kg of intravenous Hartmann's over 90 minutes without improvement. Blood cultures and a urine culture were obtained on arrival. She has been given intravenous ceftriaxone and gentamicin.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 78/40, MAP 53, HR 132 sinus, RR 32, T 39.2, SpO2 96% on 4 L/min, GCS 14, lactate 5.4
data_table.Examination: Confused, cool peripheries, mottled knees, right renal angle tender, no abdominal peritonism, no rash
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19.8 (neutrophils 17.0), CRP 240, creatinine 192 (baseline 88), Na 130, K 4.6, glucose 16.4, ABG pH 7.28 pCO2 30 pO2 90 HCO3 16 BE -8, lactate 5.4 mmol/L, urine dipstick 3+ blood 3+ leucocytes 2+ nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer a further 30 mL/kg of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 minutes and reassess MAP before considering vasopressors, because all sepsis patients need at least 60 mL/kg of resuscitation fluid in the first hour to maximise preload
options.rationale: After 30 mL/kg of fluid with persistent shock, vasopressors are started; further crystalloid risks fluid overload and pulmonary oedema. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Commence an intravenous noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula at 0.05 mcg/kg/min targeting a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg, arrange immediate intensive care review, repeat serum lactate at 2 hours and image the renal tract for obstruction
options.rationale: Septic shock with persistent hypotension after 30 mL/kg fluid is the indication for early vasopressor (noradrenaline first-line) with MAP target of at least 65 mmHg, ICU referral and source control investigation (urinary tract imaging) per the Surviving Sepsis bundle and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Commence intravenous adrenaline 1 mcg/kg/min as first-line vasoactive therapy for septic shock because adrenaline provides both inotropic and vasopressor support and is recommended ahead of noradrenaline in current Australian intensive care guidelines
options.rationale: Noradrenaline is first-line per Surviving Sepsis and ANZICS; adrenaline is added if MAP is inadequate on noradrenaline plus vasopressin. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as initial monotherapy for refractory septic shock before commencing any vasopressor therapy because corticosteroids alone often reverse hypotension by restoring vascular tone
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone (200 mg/day) is added only when MAP is inadequate despite escalating vasopressors; it is not first-line nor monotherapy for septic shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Switch antibiotic therapy to piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g intravenously and meropenem 1 g intravenously as combination Gram-negative cover and observe response over 4 hours before any vasopressor or further fluid resuscitation is started
options.rationale: Antibiotic choice should be optimised but vasopressors cannot be delayed; double Gram-negative cover is not routinely required in community-acquired urinary sepsis. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Sepsis hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures, give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at or above 4 mmol/L, and start vasopressors if hypotensive during or after fluid to maintain MAP at or above 65 mmHg. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor (peripheral acceptable up to 0.2 mcg/kg/min as a bridge to central). Vasopressin 0.03 U/min is added if noradrenaline above 0.25 mcg/kg/min. Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day is added when MAP is inadequate despite noradrenaline plus vasopressin. Source control (drain, debride, decompress) is sought urgently. Reassess lactate at 2 hours and clinical response.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluid, vasopressors
30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4
Noradrenaline first-line; vasopressin add-on, adrenaline rescue
Hydrocortisone for refractory shock on dual vasopressor
Source control is critical
explanation.pearls: Peripheral noradrenaline infusion is safe up to 0.2 mcg/kg/min via a proximal antecubital vein for short periods (under 6 hours) - this avoids delaying haemodynamic support while central access is being secured.

subtopic_detail: Acute type A aortic dissection diagnosis and BP control
stem: You are the medical registrar in resuscitation reviewing a 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension (home BP often 170/100) and a 30 pack-year smoking history who presents with sudden onset severe tearing chest pain radiating through to the interscapular area, starting 40 minutes ago. He looks pale and diaphoretic. On examination there is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge new since last documented review, a 25 mmHg differential between his right and left arms, and weak right radial pulse. ECG shows sinus tachycardia and old left ventricular hypertrophy. Bedside chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum.

data_table.Vital signs: BP right arm 172/108, left arm 144/86, HR 108, RR 20, SpO2 97% air, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, soft early diastolic murmur left sternal edge, weak right radial pulse, normal left radial pulse, no focal neurology, abdomen soft, no leg pulse asymmetry
data_table.Investigations: Troponin marginally raised at 78 ng/L (URL 14), creatinine 102, INR 1.0, lactate 1.8; ECG sinus tachycardia LVH no acute ST changes; CXR widened mediastinum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Refer to the catheter lab for urgent invasive coronary angiography under the suspicion of left main acute coronary syndrome because dissection rarely causes a 25 mmHg interarm differential and the murmur is more likely chronic
options.rationale: Angiography risks instrument-induced dissection extension; CTA aorta is the imaging of choice when dissection is suspected. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

options.text: Administer 300 mg of aspirin orally and 600 mg of clopidogrel as a dual antiplatelet load and arrange urgent coronary angiography because the marginally elevated troponin and chest pain are most consistent with acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: DAPT in aortic dissection causes catastrophic bleeding on aortic repair; the dissection picture (tearing pain, pulse differential, widened mediastinum, AR murmur) trumps the marginal troponin. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

options.text: Commence an intravenous nitroglycerin infusion at 50 mcg/min as initial monotherapy aiming for blood pressure under 120 mmHg without a beta blocker because vasodilator-first management reduces wall shear stress most rapidly in dissection
options.rationale: Vasodilator without prior beta blockade causes reflex tachycardia which increases wall shear stress and propagates dissection; beta blocker is given first. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

options.text: Administer therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily and arrange CT pulmonary angiography urgently for suspected acute pulmonary embolism with right ventricular strain that explains the murmur and asymmetric pulses
options.rationale: PE does not cause pulse differential or AR murmur and anticoagulation is catastrophic in undiagnosed dissection; CTA aorta not CTPA is the correct first imaging. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

options.text: Commence intravenous esmolol or labetalol infusion targeting heart rate 60 to 80 and systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg, manage pain with intravenous opioid, and arrange urgent CT angiogram of the aorta with cardiothoracic surgical consultation in parallel
options.rationale: Suspected type A aortic dissection mandates immediate beta blockade (rate then BP) to reduce shear stress, opioid analgesia, urgent CT angiography of the aorta and cardiothoracic surgical involvement per Heart Foundation and Therapeutic Guidelines. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection presents with sudden severe tearing chest or back pain, pulse differential, new aortic regurgitation murmur, neurological signs (carotid involvement), syncope or limb ischaemia. Type A involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency (mortality 1 to 2 percent per hour without surgery). Type B (descending only) is managed medically unless complicated. Initial management is rate-and-pressure control with intravenous beta blocker (esmolol or labetalol) targeting HR 60 to 80 and SBP 100 to 120, then vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside or GTN) added if BP target not met. Opioid analgesia, large-bore IV access, group and crossmatch and urgent CT angiogram of the whole aorta with cardiothoracic surgical consultation are the immediate steps.
key_points: Sudden tearing chest/back pain + pulse differential + AR murmur
CT angiogram of aorta (CTA) is the imaging of choice
Beta blocker FIRST to reduce shear stress, then vasodilator if needed
Target HR 60-80, SBP 100-120
Type A: surgical emergency. Type B: usually medical
explanation.pearls: A normal D-dimer has high negative predictive value (above 95 percent) for aortic dissection in low-pretest probability patients - a useful rule-out tool when CT angiogram is delayed, but never used to rule out in high-risk presentations.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation: Acute aortic syndromes

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis with intercurrent illness - immediate management
stem: You are the medical registrar at the resuscitation bay reviewing a 38-year-old woman with known primary autoimmune adrenal insufficiency since age 19 on hydrocortisone 10/5/5 mg and fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily. She has had 36 hours of vomiting from gastroenteritis. She told her mother she could not keep her medications down but did not double-dose with sick-day rules. On arrival she is profoundly hypotensive, drowsy, peripherally cool and has been given 1 L of intravenous Hartmann's en route by paramedics. Her partner is reading her steroid emergency card. The endocrine consultant is being paged.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 72/40, HR 130 sinus, RR 24, T 36.4, SpO2 97% air, GCS 13, BSL 3.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, mucous membranes dry, capillary refill 4 sec, generalised hyperpigmentation including palmar creases, no focal neurology, no abdominal peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Na 124 mmol/L, K 6.2, urea 14.8, creatinine 142, glucose 3.4, calcium corrected 2.42, cortisol on arrival drawn at 0830 hours is 84 nmol/L (subnormal); VBG pH 7.30 HCO3 16, lactate 3.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer 100 mg of intravenous hydrocortisone immediately, commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L bolus and 10% dextrose to correct the hypoglycaemia, and start continuous hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours pending source identification of the precipitating illness
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis: rapid IV hydrocortisone 100 mg + IV saline + dextrose for hypoglycaemia, continue hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours (50 mg q6h or infusion), source-control of precipitant, per Australasian Endocrine Society and Therapeutic Guidelines. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

options.text: Administer intravenous fludrocortisone 200 mcg as the priority steroid for the mineralocorticoid deficiency and the hyperkalaemia, and defer hydrocortisone until urgent ACTH stimulation testing has confirmed the adrenal pathway is unresponsive
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available IV and is not first-line in crisis; high-dose IV hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and at-dose mineralocorticoid effect. ACTH testing has no place during a crisis. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg as the first-line glucocorticoid because dexamethasone does not interfere with subsequent cortisol assays and avoids cross-reactivity in the urgent diagnostic ACTH stimulation testing pathway
options.rationale: Dexamethasone can be used if diagnosis is uncertain and stimulation testing is planned, but in established Addison's hydrocortisone is preferred for its combined gluco- and mineralocorticoid actions and immediate efficacy. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

options.text: Insert a central venous access catheter and commence intravenous noradrenaline 0.05 mcg/kg/min titrated to mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg as the first-line haemodynamic support with intravenous hydrocortisone added only after stable blood pressure is achieved
options.rationale: Vasopressor without urgent hydrocortisone replacement will fail because vascular tone is corticosteroid-dependent; immediate IV hydrocortisone with fluid resuscitation is first-line. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

options.text: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% for the hyperkalaemia and intravenous insulin-dextrose for potassium shift while she continues her usual oral hydrocortisone dose once vomiting has settled with intravenous ondansetron antiemetic
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia of adrenal crisis resolves with IV hydrocortisone and saline; oral hydrocortisone will not be absorbed in shock with vomiting and is not an acceptable substitute. (Source: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis)
source_refs: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis presents with hypotension unresponsive to fluids, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and a known or suspected adrenal insufficiency precipitated by intercurrent illness, surgery, missed steroid doses or trauma. It is a clinical diagnosis - treat immediately and confirm later. Management is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg as a bolus, then 200 mg over 24 hours (50 mg every 6 hours or continuous infusion), aggressive isotonic crystalloid resuscitation, dextrose for hypoglycaemia and treatment of the precipitant. Fludrocortisone is unnecessary at hydrocortisone doses above 50 mg/day because the gluco at high dose provides mineralocorticoid activity. Sick-day rules (double oral dose for febrile illness, IM hydrocortisone for vomiting), patient-held steroid emergency card and emergency IM hydrocortisone kit are core education points.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg STAT then 200 mg over 24 hours
IV 0.9% saline aggressive resuscitation
IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Treat precipitant
Sick-day rules + IM emergency kit + steroid emergency card are lifesaving for prevention
explanation.pearls: A morning cortisol drawn during crisis that is over 550 nmol/L effectively excludes adrenal insufficiency; a value under 100 nmol/L while critically unwell is diagnostic for crisis and treatment cannot wait for short Synacthen testing.

sources.label: ESA: Management of adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation duration after unprovoked pulmonary embolism
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man at his 3-month follow-up after an unprovoked submassive pulmonary embolism initially treated with rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days followed by 20 mg daily ongoing. He has had no recurrent venous thromboembolism, no significant bleeding episodes, normal renal function, no active malignancy, no antiphospholipid antibodies, and a normal first-degree family history.

His current symptoms have resolved and he has returned to full-time work. His PESA-style bleeding risk assessment is low. He understands the recurrence risk discussion and asks about whether to stop his anticoagulation now that 3 months have passed without any complications during the initial treatment course.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular and respiratory examination unremarkable, no calf swelling or tenderness, oxygen saturations 98% in air at rest
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 88, Hb 142, platelets 220 x10^9/L; thrombophilia screen negative; CT chest at 3 months shows partial clot resolution

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Switch from rivaroxaban to warfarin with a target international normalised ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 for indefinite anticoagulation and arrange weekly INR monitoring until the patient is stable on the new anticoagulant regimen
options.rationale: DOACs are first-line and at least as effective as warfarin for VTE secondary prevention without monitoring; switching to warfarin in a stable patient introduces inconvenience and bleeding risk without benefit. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

options.text: Continue rivaroxaban at the reduced extended dose of 10 mg once daily indefinitely with annual review of bleeding risk, renal function and the ongoing balance of recurrence risk against bleeding risk to inform continuation
options.rationale: Unprovoked PE has a high recurrence risk (around 10% in year 1, 30 to 40% at 5 years off therapy); current Australian guidance favours indefinite anticoagulation in low-bleed-risk patients, with reduced-dose rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) or apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) for extended therapy. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

options.text: Cease all anticoagulation at 3 months and provide a written plan to recommence rivaroxaban if there are any new symptoms suggesting recurrence, with annual D-dimer testing as a surveillance strategy for asymptomatic recurrence
options.rationale: Ceasing anticoagulation at 3 months after an unprovoked PE leaves the patient with an unacceptably high recurrence rate; routine surveillance D-dimer does not replace ongoing pharmacological prophylaxis in this context. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

options.text: Stop rivaroxaban now and prescribe aspirin 100 mg daily as secondary prevention for the next 12 months, with a planned VTE recurrence review at 12 months to determine whether further intervention is required at that time
options.rationale: Aspirin provides only modest VTE recurrence reduction and is markedly inferior to extended-dose DOAC; it is not a satisfactory substitute when extended anticoagulation is otherwise appropriate. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

options.text: Continue rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily indefinitely without dose reduction and arrange follow-up CT pulmonary angiography in 12 months to assess for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and adjust treatment accordingly
options.rationale: Extended-dose reduction (rivaroxaban 10 mg or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily) is non-inferior for recurrence and lowers bleeding risk; routine surveillance CTPA at 12 months is not standard in an asymptomatic patient with normal saturations and exercise tolerance. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

explanation.summary: After 3 months of treatment-dose anticoagulation for an unprovoked PE, decision-making centres on the recurrence-versus-bleeding balance. Unprovoked PE carries around 10% recurrence in year 1 and 30 to 40% at 5 years off therapy. For low-bleed-risk patients, indefinite anticoagulation is preferred; the AMPLIFY-EXT and EINSTEIN-CHOICE trials support reduced-dose extended therapy (rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily) as non-inferior for recurrence with a halved bleeding rate. Aspirin is markedly inferior. Annual reassessment of bleeding risk and renal function guides ongoing therapy.
key_points: Unprovoked PE recurrence: ~10% year 1, ~30 to 40% at 5 years off anticoagulation
Extended therapy: rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, non-inferior to full-dose with lower bleeding
Provoked PE with reversible risk factor: 3 months total anticoagulation usually sufficient
Annual review: bleeding risk, renal function, ongoing recurrence-risk vs bleeding balance
explanation.pearls: After an unprovoked PE in a low-bleed-risk patient, the default plan is indefinite anticoagulation at extended-reduced dose - aspirin is a fallback only when the patient declines DOAC, not an equivalent option.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: VTE guidance

subtopic_detail: Early rheumatoid arthritis DMARD initiation with methotrexate
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar in clinic reviewing a 46-year-old woman with 10 weeks of progressive symmetrical polyarthritis of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints and wrists, with 90 minutes of early morning stiffness. She has no prior medical history, takes no regular medications, and is up to date with cervical screening. Her bloods show a markedly elevated rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibody, raised inflammatory markers, normal renal and liver function, and a normal full blood count.

Plain hand films are without bony erosion at this point. She is keen to start treatment, lives within 30 minutes of the clinic, has reliable transport, has no plans for pregnancy in the next 12 months and is willing to use reliable contraception during treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76, HR 76, T 37.0 degrees C, BMI 25
data_table.Examination: Bilateral symmetrical MCP and PIP synovitis, both wrists synovitic, no nodules, no extra-articular features, no skin rash
data_table.Investigations: RF 320 IU/mL (RR under 15), anti-CCP 198 U/mL (RR under 20), ESR 64, CRP 38; normal Hb, WCC, platelets, eGFR, LFTs; HBV/HCV/HIV serology negative, latent TB screen negative, varicella immune

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug regimen?

options.text: Commence long-term prednisolone 15 mg daily as monotherapy with calcium and vitamin D and a bisphosphonate for bone protection, with plans for slow gradual taper over the next 12 to 24 months as her symptoms improve over time
options.rationale: Long-term steroid monotherapy in RA causes significant morbidity (diabetes, osteoporosis, infections) without preventing joint damage; steroid is used only as a short bridge while DMARD takes effect. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

options.text: Defer DMARD therapy and commence celecoxib 200 mg twice daily with regular paracetamol 1 g four times daily, plan a 6-month review with a repeat clinical assessment before any decision about disease-modifying therapy is made
options.rationale: Early DMARD initiation within a window of opportunity (under 3 months from symptom onset) improves long-term outcomes; NSAID monotherapy fails to prevent joint damage in seropositive disease. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

options.text: Commence subcutaneous adalimumab 40 mg fortnightly as first-line biologic monotherapy given her highly seropositive disease and the elevated inflammatory markers to maximise rapid suppression of the inflammatory disease burden
options.rationale: Biologic DMARDs are reserved for inadequate response to conventional DMARD therapy after at least 6 months (typically methotrexate plus another csDMARD) under PBS criteria; not first-line. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

options.text: Commence triple oral therapy with hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily, sulfasalazine 1 g twice daily and leflunomide 20 mg daily from the outset to maximise control of disease activity in this newly diagnosed early polyarthritis case
options.rationale: Triple therapy from outset is not first-line in Australia; methotrexate monotherapy with bridging steroid and rapid uptitration with intensified treatment if remission is not achieved at 3 months is preferred. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

options.text: Commence oral methotrexate starting at 10 mg weekly with uptitration to 20 to 25 mg weekly over 8 weeks, prescribe folic acid 5 mg weekly on a non-methotrexate day, and bridge with a short prednisolone taper for symptom control
options.rationale: Methotrexate is first-line DMARD for early seropositive rheumatoid arthritis; rapid uptitration with weekly folate and short-term oral steroid bridging is standard practice with frequent disease activity reassessment. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

explanation.summary: Early seropositive rheumatoid arthritis should be treated with a conventional synthetic DMARD within a window of opportunity, ideally within 3 months of symptom onset, to prevent erosive joint damage. Methotrexate (oral or subcutaneous) is first-line, started at 10 to 15 mg weekly and uptitrated to 20 to 25 mg weekly over 4 to 8 weeks, with weekly folic acid 5 mg on a non-methotrexate day. Short prednisolone bridging (15 to 20 mg with taper over 8 to 12 weeks) controls symptoms while methotrexate takes effect. Pre-treatment workup includes HBV, HCV, HIV and latent TB serology. Biologics are reserved for inadequate response under PBS criteria.
key_points: Methotrexate first-line; start 10 to 15 mg weekly, uptitrate to 20 to 25 mg over 4 to 8 weeks
Weekly folic acid 5 mg on a non-methotrexate day reduces mucositis, hepatotoxicity and gastrointestinal side effects
Short prednisolone bridge while methotrexate takes effect (8 to 12 weeks then taper off)
Pre-treatment screen: HBV, HCV, HIV, latent TB, varicella immunity, baseline LFTs and FBC
explanation.pearls: If oral methotrexate is not achieving remission at maximum tolerated dose, switch to subcutaneous methotrexate before adding biologics - subcutaneous has higher bioavailability and rescues a meaningful proportion of inadequate oral responders.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: RA management guidelines

subtopic_detail: T2DM HbA1c 8.5% second-line therapy with SGLT2 inhibitor
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 62-year-old man with a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin 1 g twice daily for the past 18 months. He has stable albuminuric chronic kidney disease (eGFR 56, urine ACR 38 mg/mmol), well-controlled hypertension on perindopril, established cardiovascular disease with a previous percutaneous coronary intervention 3 years ago, and is on aspirin and high-intensity atorvastatin.

His current HbA1c is 8.5% (target under 7.0%), BMI 29, blood pressure 132/82, no symptomatic hyperglycaemia. He has been adherent with metformin and has implemented dietary changes through dietitian referral for the past 6 months. He has no recent genital or urinary tract infections and no history of diabetic ketoacidosis.

data_table.Examination: No peripheral oedema, palpable foot pulses, no diabetic foot ulceration, normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.5% (RR under 7.0% target), eGFR 56 (RR over 90), urine ACR 38 mg/mmol, LDL 1.8, BP 132/82, no acute clinical infections

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next addition to his diabetes therapy?

options.text: Commence basal insulin glargine 10 units at night and titrate by 2 units every 3 days according to fasting blood glucose with a target fasting glucose between 5 and 7 mmol/L and ongoing review of the dose with his GP
options.rationale: Insulin is generally considered after failure of oral combination therapy or when symptomatic hyperglycaemia or glucotoxicity is present; at an HbA1c of 8.5% on metformin alone the cardiorenal benefits of SGLT2 inhibition take precedence. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

options.text: Add gliclazide modified release 60 mg daily as second-line therapy and arrange diabetes nurse follow-up for self-monitoring of blood glucose and education about hypoglycaemia symptoms with this newly added sulfonylurea agent
options.rationale: Sulfonylureas are not first-choice second-line in a patient with established cardiovascular disease and albuminuric CKD because they provide no cardiorenal benefit and carry hypoglycaemia and weight gain risks. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

options.text: Add sitagliptin 100 mg daily as a DPP-4 inhibitor for its neutral cardiovascular safety profile and lack of weight gain, with monitoring for any pancreatitis-type symptoms and renal function in the months following the addition
options.rationale: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral and well tolerated but provide no cardiovascular or renal protective benefit, making them inferior to SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with established CVD or albuminuric CKD. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

options.text: Increase metformin to 1 g three times daily as the only intensification step at this point and review his HbA1c in 3 months before considering the addition of any second-line agent to his current diabetes regimen
options.rationale: Increasing metformin above 2 g daily yields little additional glucose-lowering and more gastrointestinal effects; he needs a second agent now and his clinical profile favours an SGLT2 inhibitor with cardiorenal benefits. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

options.text: Add empagliflozin 10 mg once daily as an SGLT2 inhibitor for cardiorenal protection in this man with established cardiovascular disease and albuminuric CKD, and arrange short-interval review of his BP, eGFR and ketones
options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors are first-line second-agent in T2DM with established cardiovascular disease or albuminuric chronic kidney disease in Australian guidance because of demonstrated cardiovascular and renal benefits independent of glycaemic effects. (Source: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM)
source_refs: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

explanation.summary: In T2DM with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure or albuminuric chronic kidney disease, the second-line agent in Australia is an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin or ertugliflozin) independent of glycaemic control because of demonstrated cardiorenal benefit. GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, dulaglutide) are also appropriate, especially with obesity or atherosclerotic disease without heart failure. Sulfonylureas and DPP-4 inhibitors lack cardiorenal benefit. SGLT2 inhibitors are contraindicated with frequent genital infections, eGFR below threshold (varies by agent), and require sick-day rules and ketone monitoring counselling.
key_points: T2DM with CVD, HF or albuminuric CKD: SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA as second-line, independent of glycaemic control
SGLT2 inhibitor pre-treatment: counsel on sick-day rules, genital infection risk, euglycaemic DKA, foot care
GLP-1 RA: prefer if obese or atherosclerotic disease without HF; injectable except oral semaglutide
Sulfonylureas: lower cost but hypoglycaemia and weight gain; no cardiorenal benefit
explanation.pearls: For T2DM with CVD or albuminuric CKD, the second drug after metformin is not the cheapest agent that lowers HbA1c - it is the SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist that will prevent his next cardiac event and slow his CKD progression.

sources.label: RACGP: General practice management of T2DM

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis infection household contact management
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 34-year-old asymptomatic Vietnamese-born woman who has lived in Australia for 6 months. She is a contact of her brother, who has just been diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis, and they have been sharing a 2-bedroom flat together. She is well, with no cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Her HIV serology is negative; she is not pregnant and is using effective contraception.

Her chest x-ray is clear with no upper-lobe scarring or cavitation. A QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay returns positive with normal mitogen and negative nil tubes. Her routine bloods including LFTs and FBC are normal. She drinks no alcohol and takes no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74, HR 76, T 36.8 degrees C, BMI 22, SpO2 99% in air
data_table.Examination: No respiratory or systemic symptoms, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: CXR clear; QFT-Plus positive (mitogen and nil normal); HIV negative; LFTs and FBC within normal limits; sputum not produced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Provide reassurance and arrange surveillance with annual chest x-rays for 5 years given her low individual risk of progression to active disease and the side effect burden of isoniazid in an asymptomatic young woman
options.rationale: Recent household contact of smear-positive TB confers around a 10% lifetime risk of progression (highest in the first 2 years), which clearly outweighs the side-effect burden of isoniazid in a young woman without liver disease. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

options.text: Repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay in 8 weeks and only commence treatment if the second test remains positive, given the possibility of an early false positive in a recently arrived migrant from a high-prevalence country
options.rationale: QFT-Plus has excellent specificity (around 99%) and a positive result in a household contact of smear-positive disease is acted upon directly; repeat testing delays appropriate prevention of disease progression. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

options.text: Commence full quadruple anti-tuberculous therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months given the high transmission risk and her recent contact
options.rationale: Quadruple RIPE therapy is for active TB; she has no symptoms, normal CXR and no microbiological evidence of active disease, so latent TB treatment is the correct intervention. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

options.text: Refer her to a respiratory clinic for induced sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage for tuberculosis culture and nucleic acid amplification testing before commencing latent TB therapy, with no treatment until those microbiology results are available
options.rationale: Invasive sampling is not indicated in an asymptomatic contact with a clear chest x-ray; latent TB treatment can begin once symptoms, x-ray and clinical examination exclude active disease. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

options.text: Commence daily oral isoniazid 5 mg/kg up to 300 mg with pyridoxine 25 mg for 6 to 9 months under the state TB service, with monthly clinical and biochemical review and confirmation of active disease exclusion before therapy commences
options.rationale: She has latent TB infection (QFT-Plus positive, asymptomatic, normal CXR) as a household contact of smear-positive pulmonary TB; Australian guidance recommends isoniazid plus pyridoxine for 6 to 9 months under specialist TB service supervision after active TB exclusion. (Source: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance)
source_refs: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

explanation.summary: Latent TB infection in a recent household contact of smear-positive disease has approximately 10% lifetime risk of progression to active disease, with greatest risk in the first 2 years. Australian regimens for LTBI include isoniazid for 6 to 9 months with pyridoxine, or shorter rifamycin-containing regimens (rifampicin 4 months, or weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 12 doses where available). Active TB must be excluded clinically and radiologically before LTBI treatment begins. HIV testing and baseline LFTs are required; treatment is managed by state TB services with monthly clinical and biochemical review.
key_points: LTBI diagnosis: QFT-Plus or T-spot positive, asymptomatic, normal CXR, no microbiological evidence of active TB
Treatment options: isoniazid 6 to 9 months, rifampicin 4 months, isoniazid-rifapentine weekly for 12 doses
Pre-treatment: HIV serology, LFTs, FBC; pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy
Risk of progression: ~10% lifetime, highest in first 2 years and in HIV co-infection
explanation.pearls: Always pair isoniazid with pyridoxine 25 mg daily in adults - peripheral neuropathy is the dose-limiting side effect, and the relative cost of pyridoxine is so low that omitting it is never the right call.

sources.label: NTAC: Latent TB infection treatment guidance

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion testing with 4th generation immunoassay
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man with 6 days of fever, sore throat, generalised maculopapular rash, painful mouth ulcers, marked fatigue and tender cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. He reports condomless receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 18 days ago. He has not been on HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. He has had no other recent illnesses, no travel and no medications.

Routine testing shows lymphopenia, transient transaminitis, and a 4th-generation HIV-1/2 antigen-antibody combination immunoassay returns positive today with a low signal-to-cutoff ratio; the supplemental Western blot is indeterminate. Syphilis serology, hepatitis B and C serology and gonorrhoea NAAT are negative. His past sexual health screening was negative 6 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76, HR 96, T 38.4 degrees C, SpO2 99% in air
data_table.Examination: Maculopapular rash on trunk, tender cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy, painful aphthous oral ulcers, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: 4th gen HIV Ag/Ab assay positive (low S/CO), Western blot indeterminate; lymphopenia 0.8 x10^9/L; AST 78, ALT 92; syphilis/HBV/HCV/GC negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Commence post-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate plus emtricitabine plus dolutegravir empirically for 4 weeks given the recent exposure 18 days ago and reassess his testing situation at the end of the prophylaxis course
options.rationale: Post-exposure prophylaxis must start within 72 hours of exposure; at 18 days post-exposure with reactive screening this is no longer PEP but established acute infection requiring HIV RNA confirmation and ART initiation. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

options.text: Send an HIV-1 RNA viral load assay urgently as the confirmatory test for acute HIV seroconversion, refer to a sexual health or infectious diseases physician for prompt antiretroviral therapy initiation, and arrange partner notification
options.rationale: In suspected acute seroconversion with a reactive 4th-generation Ag/Ab assay and indeterminate Western blot (typical of early seroconversion before band development), HIV RNA viral load is the appropriate confirmatory test; ART is started promptly. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

options.text: Order a CD4 count alone today as the confirmatory test for acute HIV infection and only commence antiretroviral therapy once the CD4 count is below 500 cells per microlitre and confirmation of seroconversion has occurred
options.rationale: CD4 count does not confirm HIV diagnosis; modern ART is started regardless of CD4 count to maximise immunological recovery, suppress viral reservoir and reduce onward transmission. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

options.text: Arrange supportive care alone with paracetamol and oral fluids and rebook for HIV serology in 12 weeks, since most acute seroconversion presentations are self-limiting and the diagnostic uncertainty makes ART premature at this stage of testing
options.rationale: Delaying diagnosis and ART forfeits the substantial benefit of early treatment in acute infection (reduced reservoir, lower set-point, reduced transmission); HIV RNA viral load resolves diagnostic uncertainty today. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

options.text: Repeat the 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab combination immunoassay in 4 weeks before any decision about commencing antiretroviral therapy, since the present indeterminate Western blot does not confirm an HIV-positive result at the present time
options.rationale: Delaying confirmation in suspected acute seroconversion forfeits the substantial individual and public health benefit of early ART; HIV RNA viral load provides definitive same-day confirmation in this scenario. (Source: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion presents with a mononucleosis-like syndrome (fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, maculopapular rash, oral ulcers) typically 2 to 4 weeks after exposure. The 4th-generation Ag/Ab combination assay detects p24 antigen and is reactive earlier than antibody-only assays; however, the Western blot may be indeterminate in early infection before antibody bands have fully developed. HIV-1 RNA viral load is the appropriate confirmatory test (very high viral loads, often above 10^6 copies/mL in acute infection). ART is started promptly regardless of CD4 count: this reduces reservoir size, lowers set-point viral load and prevents transmission, and is referred to a sexual health or infectious diseases physician.
key_points: Acute HIV: 4th-gen Ag/Ab positive plus Western blot often indeterminate before bands develop
Confirmatory test: HIV-1 RNA viral load (typically very high in acute infection)
ART started promptly regardless of CD4 count; reduces reservoir, set-point, transmission
PEP window 72 hours post-exposure only; partner notification and contact tracing essential
explanation.pearls: An indeterminate Western blot after a reactive 4th-generation HIV assay in someone with a mononucleosis-like illness is acute seroconversion until proven otherwise - request HIV RNA the same day and start the referral to sexual health, do not wait 4 weeks to repeat serology.

sources.label: ASHM: HIV testing and management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Abdominal aortic aneurysm 5.5 cm asymptomatic surgical threshold
stem:
You are the vascular surgery registrar reviewing a 72-year-old asymptomatic ex-smoker man (50 pack-year history quit 4 years ago) in clinic after a routine ultrasound surveillance scan demonstrated a 5.6 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, up from 4.8 cm 12 months ago. He has well-controlled hypertension on perindopril, an LDL of 2.0 on atorvastatin, no diabetes, no significant ischaemic heart disease on stress imaging 2 years ago, and an exercise tolerance limited only by mild osteoarthritis.

He has no family history of aortic disease, no Marfan or vascular Ehlers-Danlos features, and the aneurysm morphology is suitable for endovascular repair with a long infrarenal neck of 25 mm and no significant tortuosity.

data_table.Examination: No abdominal tenderness, pulsatile non-tender central abdominal mass, palpable femoral and pedal pulses bilaterally, no distal embolic signs
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal ultrasound: infrarenal AAA 5.6 cm (was 4.8 cm 12 months ago); CT angiogram: 5.6 cm with 25 mm infrarenal neck suitable for EVAR; eGFR 62; LDL 2.0; HbA1c 5.8%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer surgery and arrange repeat surveillance ultrasound in 3 months given the absence of symptoms and the satisfactory exercise tolerance, with intervention only if the aneurysm exceeds 6 cm at the next surveillance scan in 3 months
options.rationale: The Australian and international threshold for elective repair in men is 5.5 cm, not 6 cm; rapid expansion of 0.8 cm over 12 months is an independent indication for intervention. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

options.text: Continue 6-monthly ultrasound surveillance and intensify his medical therapy with the addition of a beta blocker and an angiotensin receptor blocker to slow further aneurysm expansion below the threshold for surgery in the medium term
options.rationale: At 5.6 cm with rapid expansion the annual rupture risk substantially exceeds operative mortality; deferral with intensified medical therapy is not appropriate. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

options.text: Refer for open surgical repair via midline laparotomy as the most durable repair option given his young age and good fitness, with planned admission for around 7 to 10 days of inpatient recovery and pre-operative renal optimisation
options.rationale: EVAR is preferred in patients with suitable anatomy due to lower perioperative mortality; open repair is reserved for unsuitable anatomy, younger patients with long life expectancy, or failed EVAR. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

options.text: Refer for elective endovascular aneurysm repair within the next 1 to 2 months, confirm cardiac fitness for intervention, continue strict blood pressure and lipid control and arrange smoking cessation follow-up given his history of past tobacco use
options.rationale: Surgical repair is indicated at 5.5 cm or greater in men, rapid expansion above 1 cm per year, or symptoms; he meets size, growth and morphology criteria, and EVAR is appropriate where anatomy permits and cardiac fitness allows. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

options.text: Refer for emergency endovascular aneurysm repair within the next 24 hours as the aneurysm exceeds the 5.5 cm threshold and any further delay would substantially increase his risk of imminent and catastrophic aortic rupture
options.rationale: Asymptomatic AAA above 5.5 cm without leakage is electively repaired within weeks, not as an emergency; emergency repair is for symptomatic, leaking or ruptured aneurysms. (Source: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance)
source_refs: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

explanation.summary: Indications for elective AAA repair are: diameter at or above 5.5 cm in men (5.0 cm in women), rapid expansion above 1 cm per year (or above 0.5 cm in 6 months), and symptomatic disease at any size. EVAR is preferred over open repair where anatomy permits (suitable proximal neck length, angulation, iliac access), lower perioperative mortality but higher reintervention rate over time; open repair is more durable in younger fit patients. Medical management focuses on smoking cessation, BP control (avoid statin and antihypertensive omission), and lipid lowering to reduce expansion rate.
key_points: Elective repair threshold: 5.5 cm in men, 5.0 cm in women, or rapid expansion above 1 cm per year
EVAR vs open: EVAR lower 30-day mortality, higher long-term reintervention; open more durable
Suitability for EVAR depends on proximal neck length above 15 to 20 mm, angle, iliac access
Medical therapy: smoking cessation, BP control, statin, no role for routine beta-blocker for expansion
explanation.pearls: Rapid expansion above 1 cm in a year independently triggers repair even below 5.5 cm - growth rate is as important as absolute size, so always document interval growth on serial imaging rather than just the current diameter.

sources.label: Society for Vascular Surgery and Australia and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery joint guidance

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative alpha-then-beta blockade sequencing
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 48-year-old woman with biochemically and radiologically confirmed unilateral 4 cm right adrenal phaeochromocytoma. She presented 3 weeks ago with paroxysmal hypertension to 220/120, headache, palpitations and pallor. Investigations now show plasma free metanephrines 12 times the upper limit of normal, 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines 8 times normal, and a 4 cm right adrenal lesion on MRI with high T2 signal and avid uptake on 68Ga-DOTATATE PET.

She is scheduled for laparoscopic right adrenalectomy in 2 weeks. She has not yet been commenced on any antihypertensive therapy. There is no family history of MEN, neurofibromatosis or von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, and genetic testing has been requested.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/108 lying, drop on standing 18 mmHg systolic; HR 96
data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination, no carotid bruits, no abdominal mass palpable, no neurofibromas or cafe au lait macules
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines x12 ULN, 24h urinary fractionated metanephrines x8 ULN, MRI: 4 cm right adrenal lesion high T2, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET avid; eGFR 92, K 4.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management before surgery?

options.text: Commence phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated upward over 10 to 14 days targeting nasal stuffiness and mild postural hypotension, encourage high salt and fluid intake, then add a beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade is achieved
options.rationale: Pre-operative non-selective alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine for 10 to 14 days, with salt and fluid loading, followed by addition of a beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade is the recognised sequence; starting a beta blocker before alpha blockade risks unopposed alpha effects and hypertensive crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

options.text: Commence metoprolol 25 mg twice daily as initial therapy to control her resting tachycardia and to lower her blood pressure before surgery, then add an alpha blocker once her heart rate has been brought below 80 beats per minute
options.rationale: Starting a beta blocker before alpha blockade in phaeochromocytoma can precipitate hypertensive crisis through unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction; the established sequence is alpha first, then beta. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

options.text: Commence labetalol 100 mg twice daily titrated up over 7 days as a combined alpha and beta blocker as a single-agent strategy and proceed to surgery once she is normotensive on the highest tolerated dose of labetalol
options.rationale: Labetalol has relatively weak alpha-blocking activity and its mixed profile can precipitate unopposed beta effects; phenoxybenzamine (or doxazosin in some centres) followed by a separate beta blocker is preferred. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

options.text: Proceed immediately to laparoscopic right adrenalectomy without further pharmacological preparation given the moderate size of the lesion and the relatively short interval until the scheduled surgical procedure in two weeks time
options.rationale: Operating on an unblockaded phaeochromocytoma carries very high perioperative mortality from intraoperative hypertensive crisis and post-resection hypotension; 10 to 14 days of alpha blockade is mandatory. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

options.text: Commence amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure control and proceed to surgery within 7 days, since calcium channel blockade alone is sufficient pre-operative preparation for laparoscopic adrenalectomy in a haemodynamically stable patient at this time
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockade does not adequately blunt the catecholamine surge of surgical manipulation; alpha blockade for 10 to 14 days with salt and fluid loading is the standard pre-operative preparation. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

explanation.summary: Pre-operative preparation for phaeochromocytoma resection requires 10 to 14 days of alpha-adrenergic blockade (phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated, or doxazosin 2 mg daily titrated) with salt and fluid loading to restore intravascular volume. A beta blocker is added only after adequate alpha blockade to control reflex tachycardia, never before. Adequacy markers: sitting BP under 130/80, standing systolic above 90, nasal congestion, mild postural drop. Post-resection hypotension is managed with fluids and vasopressors. Genetic testing is offered to all (at least 30% have a hereditary cause) and contralateral adrenal preservation is considered in hereditary syndromes.
key_points: Alpha blockade 10 to 14 days pre-op: phenoxybenzamine (irreversible) or doxazosin (selective alpha-1)
Beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade; never first because of unopposed alpha vasoconstriction risk
Salt and fluid loading during alpha blockade to refill the contracted intravascular volume
Genetic testing for all (at least 30% hereditary): SDHB/C/D, RET, VHL, NF1, MAX, TMEM127
explanation.pearls: The single most preventable peri-operative phaeochromocytoma death is starting a beta blocker before alpha blockade - if a surgical team books a phaeochromocytoma case for next week and the patient is on no antihypertensives, your first prescription is phenoxybenzamine, never metoprolol or labetalol.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis empiric antibiotic choice when vomiting
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with 24 hours of right loin pain, fever to 39 degrees, rigors, dysuria and three episodes of vomiting today. She is not pregnant (negative urinary beta-hCG), has no diabetes mellitus, no known renal tract abnormalities and is not immunosuppressed. She has had two prior episodes of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection three years apart, both successfully treated with oral trimethoprim. Today she has been unable to keep down oral fluids or paracetamol since this morning and last passed urine four hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 108, BP 108/68, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, soft abdomen, no peritonism, normal pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick LE++ nit+ blood+; urine MCS sent; bHCG negative; CRP 142, WCC 14.8, Cr 88, eGFR >90; blood cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic plan?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days with paracetamol as required and discharge with advice to drink at least two litres of clear fluid daily and review in general practice in three days
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate when the patient cannot tolerate oral intake due to vomiting and has systemic features, and trimethoprim is no longer a recommended empiric choice for pyelonephritis given resistance rates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

options.text: Admit for IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily plus IV ampicillin 2 g six-hourly with antiemetic and IV fluid resuscitation, narrowing therapy when urine and blood culture sensitivities are available within 48-72 hours
options.rationale: Australian first-line empiric therapy for acute pyelonephritis requiring admission is IV gentamicin plus IV ampicillin, providing cover for E. coli and enterococci with synergy and renal concentration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days commenced in the emergency department with discharge to home if she can tolerate two doses, and outpatient follow-up by her general practitioner within 24 hours
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are not first-line empiric pyelonephritis therapy in Australia due to resistance and adverse effect concerns, and oral therapy is unsuitable when the patient is vomiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

options.text: Admit for IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g eight-hourly with vasopressor on standby and HDU admission given the severity of presentation and to ensure broad coverage of all likely uropathogens including resistant organisms
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam is reserved for severe sepsis, healthcare-associated infection or known resistant pathogens; first-line for community pyelonephritis is gentamicin plus ampicillin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg six-hourly for 5 days with discharge after a single dose of IM ceftriaxone in the emergency department and outpatient antibiotic service follow-up in 24 to 48 hours for assessment
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate tissue or serum concentrations to treat upper urinary tract infection and is contraindicated for pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Pyelonephritis)

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis with systemic features or inability to tolerate oral therapy requires IV antibiotics and admission. Australian first-line empiric therapy is gentamicin (covering most gram-negative uropathogens with renal concentration and synergy) plus ampicillin (for enterococcal cover). De-escalation is guided by culture sensitivity within 48-72 hours. Nitrofurantoin and oral fosfomycin do not penetrate the upper tract and are not used for pyelonephritis.
key_points: Severe pyelonephritis: IV gentamicin + IV ampicillin first-line in Australia
Nitrofurantoin: lower-tract UTI only, not pyelonephritis
Ciprofloxacin: not empiric first-line due to resistance and adverse effect profile
explanation.pearls: If gentamicin contraindicated (significant renal impairment, ototoxicity risk), substitute IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily; consider ESBL coverage if recent healthcare exposure or known carriage.

sources.label: eTG Complete: Urinary tract infections in adults

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition with LRINEC and urgent surgical referral
stem: You are the surgical registrar called to a 65-year-old man admitted 24 hours ago with presumed cellulitis of the left calf treated with IV cefazolin. He is now describing pain markedly out of proportion to examination, has dusky discolouration extending proximally past the original margin marked overnight, and you palpate crepitus at the calf. His T2DM is poorly controlled with HbA1c 9.1 percent and his current observations show septic physiology. The leg has tense bullae that were not present on admission. He had a minor laceration cleaning his garden five days before admission.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 95% room air, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Tense haemorrhagic bullae over anterolateral left calf, crepitus, dusky skin extending beyond marked margin, exquisite tenderness on light palpation, absent dorsalis pedis pulse on Doppler
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19.4, CRP 295, Hb 138, Na 131, glucose 14.3, Cr 145, lactate 4.1, LRINEC score 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent operating theatre for surgical exploration and debridement of fascia, with concurrent IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus IV vancomycin plus IV clindamycin for toxin suppression, and aggressive fluid resuscitation in resus
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency requiring immediate fascial exploration with broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for protein synthesis inhibition and toxin suppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.text: Urgent CT of the lower limb with intravenous contrast to confirm fascial gas and the extent of involvement before booking the operating theatre, with continuation of intravenous cefazolin while awaiting imaging and surgical review
options.rationale: Imaging should never delay surgical intervention in clinically suspected necrotising fasciitis; LRINEC at or above 6 and crepitus already warrant theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.text: Continue IV cefazolin and add IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily, mark the new margin in pen with hourly re-assessment, and reconsider operative debridement only if the patient deteriorates further over the next 6 to 12 hours
options.rationale: Cefazolin plus gentamicin does not cover anaerobes or provide toxin suppression and watchful waiting in necrotising fasciitis carries a mortality penalty for every hour of delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.text: Transfer the patient to a hyperbaric oxygen unit at the tertiary centre for adjunctive therapy as the first intervention given the high LRINEC score, with antibiotics continued during the transfer and surgical exploration planned on arrival
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is at best an adjunct after source control and is not a substitute for or higher priority than urgent fascial debridement at the presenting site. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.text: MRI of the leg with contrast to delineate the extent of fascial involvement and guide surgical planning, with antibiotics escalated to meropenem 1 g eight-hourly while awaiting access to MRI within four to six hours in business hours
options.rationale: MRI sensitivity is high but its delay is unacceptable; clinical and bedside features here already establish the need for theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis supported by pain out of proportion, rapid spread, dusky skin, bullae, crepitus and systemic toxicity. LRINEC at or above 6 indicates intermediate risk and at or above 8 high risk, but no score excludes the diagnosis. Management is immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics including a protein-synthesis inhibitor (clindamycin or linezolid) for toxin suppression, plus urgent surgical fascial exploration and debridement. Imaging should not delay theatre.
key_points: Necrotising fasciitis: surgical emergency; do not wait for imaging
Antibiotics: pip-tazo + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
LRINEC >=6 intermediate, >=8 high risk; clinical features still trump score
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin (or linezolid) is added specifically to inhibit toxin production from group A streptococci and Clostridium species; continue until clinical improvement and de-escalation guided by intra-operative cultures.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infection
Stevens et al IDSA SSTI Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic choice for native valve infective endocarditis in IVDU
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 42-year-old man with a 5-day history of fever, malaise and night sweats. He has been injecting drugs intravenously for 6 years and currently injects daily, most recently in the right antecubital fossa. Examination reveals a new diastolic murmur loudest at the left sternal edge, splinter haemorrhages on three nail beds, a 3-mm tender lesion on the pulp of the left index finger, and no peripheral oedema. Three sets of peripheral blood cultures have been drawn from separate sites within the past hour and transthoracic echocardiography is being arranged today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.5, HR 108, BP 122/68, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: New diastolic murmur LSE, splinter haemorrhages, Osler node on left index finger pulp, no pulmonary oedema, injection sites visible at antecubital fossa
data_table.Investigations: Hb 105, WCC 16, CRP 280, Cr 110, lactate 1.6, blood cultures x 3 drawn, ECG sinus rhythm with first-degree AV block, urine dipstick microhaematuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen while awaiting culture results?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as monotherapy with reassessment when blood cultures are available at 48 to 72 hours, given the broad spectrum of coverage including most likely organisms for native valve endocarditis in this patient population
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not adequately cover MRSA or enterococci, both relevant in IVDU-associated native valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly plus IV gentamicin 1 mg/kg 8-hourly empirically without MRSA cover, with planned addition of vancomycin only if cultures grow MRSA in the next 48 to 72 hours after drawing samples today
options.rationale: In intravenous drug users, MRSA prevalence is high enough that initial empirical cover should include vancomycin while awaiting cultures rather than waiting 48-72 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin (loaded then dosed by TDM) plus IV flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly plus IV gentamicin 1 mg/kg 8-hourly synergistically, awaiting culture and sensitivity results with daily renal function and aminoglycoside trough monitoring
options.rationale: IVDU native valve endocarditis empirical cover includes vancomycin (MRSA), flucloxacillin (MSSA) and gentamicin (synergy, gram-negative cover), with de-escalation after culture sensitivities. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4-hourly as monotherapy until streptococcal endocarditis confirmed on culture, given that viridans streptococci remain the most common organism overall in native valve infective endocarditis across populations
options.rationale: In an IVDU, Staphylococcus aureus is by far the most likely organism and benzylpenicillin alone is inadequate empirical cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective endocarditis)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice daily with discharge on outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy after a single dose of IV ceftriaxone in the emergency department and outpatient antibiotic service review the next day
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate for suspected native valve endocarditis at initial presentation and OPAT before stabilisation is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Native valve infective endocarditis in an intravenous drug user is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA. Empirical therapy should cover MRSA (vancomycin), MSSA (flucloxacillin) and gram-negatives with synergy (gentamicin). De-escalation follows blood culture sensitivities. Three sets of cultures from separate sites are drawn before antibiotics where possible, and echocardiography (transthoracic then transoesophageal if equivocal) confirms vegetations.
key_points: IVDU native valve: vancomycin + flucloxacillin + gentamicin empirical
Three blood culture sets from separate sites before antibiotics
Echocardiography: TTE first, then TOE if equivocal or prosthetic valve
explanation.pearls: PR interval prolongation on ECG can signal aortic root abscess; consider TOE and surgical consult; first-degree AV block here is a red flag.

subtopic_detail: Plasma ACTH measurement after positive screening for Cushing syndrome
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with 12 months of progressive central weight gain (18 kg), purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from a chair), new hypertension at 158/95, and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 7.4 percent. Her initial 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test showed a morning cortisol of 195 nmol/L (suppressed less than 50), and a 24-hour urinary free cortisol is elevated at twice the upper limit of normal on two separate collections. There is no exogenous glucocorticoid exposure (no inhaled, topical or injected steroid).

data_table.Examination: Central adiposity, dorsocervical fat pad, supraclavicular fullness, purple abdominal striae over 1 cm wide, multiple bruises, proximal myopathy
data_table.Investigations: Morning cortisol after 1 mg dexamethasone 195 nmol/L (suppressed if <50), 24 h urinary free cortisol 2x ULN on two collections, late-night salivary cortisol elevated, HbA1c 7.4%, K 3.4, BP 158/95

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test with 8 mg dexamethasone overnight and morning cortisol measurement to distinguish Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH source, with concurrent CRH stimulation if available at the tertiary endocrinology service
options.rationale: High-dose dexamethasone testing is used after ACTH-dependence is established to localise the source, not as the next step after screening positive Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome

options.text: Plasma ACTH measurement on an early-morning sample with appropriate handling on ice, repeated on a separate day to confirm, to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome and guide subsequent localisation imaging
options.rationale: After biochemical confirmation of Cushing syndrome, the next step is plasma ACTH to differentiate ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) disease, which directs subsequent imaging.
