(Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome

options.text: Dedicated pituitary MRI with gadolinium contrast as the next diagnostic step to identify a microadenoma causing Cushing disease, given the higher prevalence of pituitary corticotroph adenomas compared with other causes of endogenous Cushing syndrome
options.rationale: Pituitary MRI is appropriate only after ACTH demonstrates ACTH-dependent disease, since around 20 percent of healthy adults have non-functioning pituitary incidentalomas. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome

options.text: Adrenal CT with adrenal protocol (non-contrast and delayed washout phases) to identify an adrenal adenoma causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome before plasma ACTH is measured, given the presence of biochemical confirmation
options.rationale: Imaging the adrenals before knowing if disease is ACTH-dependent risks pursuing an incidental adrenal nodule when a pituitary or ectopic source is actually responsible. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome

options.text: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation under interventional radiology guidance to localise the corticotroph source as a definitive next step in the diagnostic algorithm for Cushing syndrome with both screening tests positive
options.rationale: IPSS is a tertiary investigation used only when pituitary MRI is negative or equivocal in ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, far downstream of the next-step ACTH measurement. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome

explanation.summary: Once Cushing syndrome is biochemically confirmed with two abnormal screening tests (1 mg DST, 24-hour UFC, late-night salivary cortisol), the next investigation is plasma ACTH to determine ACTH-dependence. Suppressed ACTH indicates ACTH-independent (adrenal) disease and prompts adrenal imaging. Elevated or non-suppressed ACTH indicates ACTH-dependent disease (pituitary Cushing disease or ectopic ACTH), prompting pituitary MRI and then high-dose dex/CRH/IPSS to discriminate.
key_points: Step 1: confirm Cushing biochemically with two screening tests
Step 2: ACTH to determine ACTH-dependence
Step 3: localisation imaging directed by ACTH result
explanation.pearls: Cyclical Cushing syndrome can give intermittently normal screening tests; repeat testing during symptomatic periods is essential if clinical suspicion remains.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushing Syndrome

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency with target end-organ damage and gradual BP reduction
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in the emergency department with a severe occipital headache for 2 hours, blurred vision and one episode of vomiting. His BP is 220/130 in both arms with a regular pulse. Fundoscopy demonstrates bilateral flame-shaped haemorrhages and papilloedema. Creatinine has risen from baseline 90 to 180 with new microscopic haematuria and 2+ proteinuria.

He has no chest pain, focal neurological deficit, or pulmonary oedema, and the GCS is 15. ECG shows sinus rhythm with LVH by voltage criteria. He has not taken his usual amlodipine or perindopril for one week.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 220/130 both arms, HR 88, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, GCS 15, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Bilateral flame haemorrhages and papilloedema, no focal neurology, no carotid bruit, no chest signs, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Cr 180 (baseline 90), urine microscopic haematuria with 2+ proteinuria, ECG sinus rhythm with LVH voltage criteria, CXR no pulmonary oedema, troponin within normal range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit to HDU and commence intravenous labetalol infusion titrated to reduce mean arterial pressure by about 25 percent in the first hour, then to BP around 160/100 over the next 6 hours, while investigating for end-organ damage
options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency requires gradual MAP reduction of around 25 percent in the first hour with a parenteral agent (typically labetalol or GTN) to avoid cerebral or renal hypoperfusion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Hypertensive emergencies)

options.text: Commence IV sodium nitroprusside infusion targeting normalisation of BP to 120/80 within the first hour to minimise the risk of further hypertensive end-organ injury, with arterial line monitoring and cyanide level checking after 24 hours
options.rationale: Rapid normalisation risks cerebral and renal hypoperfusion; the standard target is a gradual ~25% MAP reduction in the first hour, not normalisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Hypertensive emergencies)

options.text: Restart oral amlodipine 10 mg and perindopril 8 mg in the emergency department, allow an oral observation period of 4 to 6 hours and discharge home with general practitioner review in 24 hours for ongoing medication compliance
options.rationale: End-organ damage (papilloedema, AKI) defines hypertensive emergency rather than urgency, requiring IV therapy and admission, not outpatient oral restart. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Hypertensive emergencies)

options.text: Administer sublingual nifedipine 10 mg now and again in 30 minutes if BP remains elevated above 180/110 with bedside continuous monitoring, then transition to oral amlodipine therapy for ongoing maintenance once stable
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled BP drops with rebound and has been associated with stroke and MI; it is contraindicated in hypertensive emergency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Hypertensive emergencies)

options.text: Administer GTN spray 0.4 mg sublingually as needed for symptom control, with repeat as required, alongside oral metoprolol 25 mg as monotherapy in the emergency department before bed-based ward admission for further blood pressure observation
options.rationale: Symptomatic GTN spray is insufficient for true hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage; IV infusion with titration is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Hypertensive emergencies)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is defined by acute or worsening end-organ damage (retinopathy with haemorrhages or papilloedema, AKI, encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection, eclampsia) rather than absolute BP value. Management is admission to HDU/ICU with IV antihypertensive (commonly labetalol, GTN, or nicardipine) titrated to reduce MAP by about 25 percent in the first hour, then to about 160/100 over 6 hours, then normalisation over 24-48 hours. Rapid normalisation causes cerebral hypoperfusion.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency = end-organ damage, regardless of absolute BP
Reduce MAP by 25% in first hour, not faster
Sublingual nifedipine and rapid normalisation are unsafe
explanation.pearls: Exceptions to the 25% rule: aortic dissection (SBP <120 in 20 min), ischaemic stroke (only treat above 220/120 unless thrombolysis), and pre-eclampsia (treat above 160/110 promptly).

subtopic_detail: Levodopa first-line for symptomatic functional impact in older-onset Parkinson disease
stem:
You are the general physician reviewing a 68-year-old retired accountant referred by his GP with 12 months of progressive bradykinesia, an asymmetric right-hand rest tremor, micrographia, and stiffness most evident on his right side. Examination shows cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist, reduced right-arm swing, no postural instability, normal vertical eye movements, and no cerebellar signs. An empirical low-dose levodopa challenge produced a 50 percent reduction in his UPDRS motor score.

He is functionally impaired (struggling with shoelaces and handwriting his usual diary entries), has no cognitive impairment on MoCA 27/30, and has no orthostatic, urinary or REM-sleep behavioural symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 lying, 128/76 standing, HR 68, MoCA 27/30
data_table.Examination: Asymmetric right rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity right wrist, micrographia, reduced right arm swing, no postural instability, normal vertical eye movements, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: Levodopa challenge produced 50% UPDRS motor improvement, MRI brain unremarkable for age, B12 and TSH normal, no medication-induced cause identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Rasagiline 1 mg daily as monotherapy MAO-B inhibitor providing modest symptomatic benefit and good tolerability for early Parkinson disease with minimal functional impact, deferring levodopa until functional decline progresses further
options.rationale: MAO-B inhibitor monotherapy is for very mild disease with minimal functional impact; this patient has clear functional impairment warranting more effective symptom control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily titrated weekly as dopamine agonist monotherapy in order to delay levodopa exposure and reduce the long-term risk of dyskinesia, with monitoring for impulse control disorder and somnolence
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists carry significant impulse control disorder, somnolence, oedema and hallucination risk especially in older men, and are less effective than levodopa for motor symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Amantadine 100 mg twice daily as monotherapy for symptomatic improvement of bradykinesia and tremor in early Parkinson disease, with later addition of levodopa if symptoms progress beyond what can be controlled by amantadine alone
options.rationale: Amantadine has only modest motor benefit and is more often used as add-on for dyskinesia later in disease; it is not an appropriate sole first-line agent for functionally impairing PD. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Defer all pharmacotherapy and refer to a physiotherapist and occupational therapist with movement disorders interest for tailored exercise program, with neurology review in 6 months to reassess and consider levodopa at that time only if needed
options.rationale: Exercise is an important adjunct but does not control functionally impairing motor symptoms; effective drug therapy should be commenced now given functional impact. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Levodopa-carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily titrated to symptoms as first-line therapy, given functional impact, older age, and good response to levodopa challenge, with monitoring for nausea, orthostasis, and later motor fluctuations
options.rationale: Levodopa is the most effective Parkinson disease therapy and is first-line for older patients (over 65-70) with functional impact, where motor fluctuation and dyskinesia risks are lower than in younger patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology: Parkinson disease)

explanation.summary: Initial drug therapy in Parkinson disease depends on patient age, symptom severity, and functional impact. Levodopa remains the most effective agent and is first-line in older patients (typically over 65-70) with functional impairment, because they are less likely to develop motor fluctuations and dyskinesia and more vulnerable to dopamine agonist adverse effects. Dopamine agonists are preferred initial therapy only in younger patients with mild symptoms. MAO-B inhibitors and amantadine are options for very mild disease.
key_points: Levodopa: most effective; first-line in older patients with functional impact
Dopamine agonists: impulse control disorder, somnolence, hallucinations - caution in elderly
Exercise (especially boxing/tai-chi/Lee Silverman big-and-loud) is adjunctive
explanation.pearls: PIGD-predominant atypical features (early postural instability and falls, gaze palsy) suggest PSP/MSA rather than idiopathic PD; absence of vertical gaze palsy here is reassuring.

sources.label: NICE NG71: Parkinson's disease in adults

subtopic_detail: Immediate needle decompression for tension pneumothorax in trauma
stem: You are the emergency department registrar at a level 1 trauma centre receiving a 32-year-old man brought in by ambulance after a high-speed motor vehicle collision 25 minutes ago. He sustained blunt right chest trauma against the steering wheel. He is in severe respiratory distress, agitated and diaphoretic. Trachea is deviated to the left, breath sounds are absent on the right with hyper-resonance to percussion, JVP is markedly elevated, and he is profoundly hypotensive despite a 500 mL crystalloid bolus en route. No chest X-ray has yet been performed and the resuscitation team is in attendance.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.4, HR 132, BP 78/42, RR 38, SpO2 86% on 15 L non-rebreather mask, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Tracheal deviation to left, absent right breath sounds, hyper-resonance to percussion right hemithorax, JVP raised, distended neck veins, no pelvic instability, no obvious external haemorrhage
data_table.Investigations: No CXR or CT yet performed, bedside ultrasound shows absent right lung sliding with lung point at mid-axillary line, FAST otherwise negative, no obvious pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Urgent CT chest with intravenous contrast to confirm the diagnosis of tension pneumothorax and characterise other associated thoracic injuries such as haemothorax, lung contusion, or great vessel injury before any procedural intervention
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and imaging delays in this presentation are life-threatening; immediate decompression is required. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition: Chest Trauma)

options.text: Continue high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask and observe for response over the next 5 to 10 minutes, with reassessment of breath sounds and saturations before any invasive procedure is considered to avoid iatrogenic harm
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is unsafe in tension pneumothorax; cardiovascular collapse and arrest can occur within minutes. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition: Chest Trauma)

options.text: Perform rapid sequence intubation with positive pressure ventilation now using ketamine and rocuronium, before chest decompression, in order to secure the airway given the GCS 14 and ongoing respiratory failure with progressive desaturation
options.rationale: Positive pressure ventilation worsens tension pneumothorax; decompress the chest first before intubation if possible. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition: Chest Trauma)

options.text: Immediate needle decompression with a large-bore cannula at the 4th-5th intercostal space anterior axillary line on the right (or 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line if 5th IC anatomy precludes), followed by definitive intercostal catheter insertion
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical emergency requiring immediate needle decompression then intercostal catheter; ATLS now favours the 4th-5th IC anterior axillary line for greater chest-wall penetration in adults. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition: Chest Trauma)

options.text: Emergency pericardiocentesis via subxiphoid approach with bedside ultrasound guidance as the haemodynamic compromise with raised JVP is most likely due to cardiac tamponade from blunt cardiac injury rather than tension pneumothorax
options.rationale: Examination findings (tracheal deviation, hyper-resonance, absent right breath sounds, ultrasound absent lung sliding) confirm tension pneumothorax rather than tamponade. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition: Chest Trauma)

explanation.summary: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis based on respiratory distress, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance, with progressive haemodynamic compromise from impaired venous return. Immediate needle decompression with a large-bore cannula is the life-saving intervention. ATLS 10th edition favours the 4th-5th intercostal space anterior axillary line in adults because chest wall thickness in obese patients often exceeds standard 14-gauge cannula length at the 2nd IC mid-clavicular line. Definitive intercostal catheter follows.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis; do not delay for imaging
Needle decompression: 4th-5th IC anterior axillary line (or 2nd IC mid-clavicular)
Definitive: intercostal catheter (size 28-32 Fr) in safe triangle
explanation.pearls: Positive pressure ventilation worsens tension physiology; decompress before intubation where possible. Bedside ultrasound (absent lung sliding, lung point) has higher sensitivity than CXR for pneumothorax in trauma.

sources.label: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Trauma resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Mixed cardiogenic and septic shock with line-related bacteraemia post-STEMI
stem:
You are the ICU registrar reviewing a 72-year-old woman day 3 post-large anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI to the LAD. She is now hypotensive on noradrenaline 0.4 mcg/kg/min, with a new fever (38.9) since this morning. WCC is 19, lactate 4.8 (up from 2.1 on day 2). Bedside echo shows severe LV systolic dysfunction (EF 25 percent), no tamponade, no new regional wall motion abnormality.

CVP 18, ScvO2 55 percent, cardiac index by PiCCO 1.6 L/min/m squared, urine output 10 mL/hr over the last 2 hours. Blood cultures from the femoral central line (in situ 4 days) are growing a gram-negative bacillus identified provisionally as E. coli.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 124 sinus tachycardia, BP 78/45 on noradrenaline 0.4 mcg/kg/min, RR 26, SpO2 95% on FiO2 0.5
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries, mottled knees, raised JVP, bibasal crackles, S3 gallop, femoral central line in situ day 4 with mild erythema at site
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.8, ScvO2 55%, CVP 18, CI 1.6 L/min/m sq, EF 25% on echo, no tamponade, blood cultures growing GNB from femoral line and peripheral; urine output 10 mL/hr

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next haemodynamic intervention?

options.text: Increase noradrenaline to 1.0 mcg/kg/min and give a 1 litre Hartmann bolus over 30 minutes to support BP and intravascular volume, with continued current antibiotic regimen and review of inotrope after the fluid bolus
options.rationale: High-dose noradrenaline with low CI 1.6 will worsen afterload and tissue perfusion; a 1 L bolus with CVP 18 and pulmonary congestion risks worsening pulmonary oedema. (Source: ANZICS Septic Shock Guidance; ESC Cardiogenic Shock Position Paper)

options.text: Switch noradrenaline to vasopressin 0.04 units/min as monotherapy and add hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours, without addressing inotropy or source control, while continuing the current empirical antibiotic regimen unchanged
options.rationale: Vasopressin and steroid are appropriate adjuncts in septic shock but do not address the cardiogenic component (low CI, low ScvO2) or the infected line; source control and inotropy are missing. (Source: ANZICS Septic Shock Guidance)

options.text: Diurese aggressively with frusemide 80 mg IV bolus and ongoing infusion targeting negative balance of 1 to 2 litres in 24 hours given the high CVP 18 and bibasal crackles representing pulmonary oedema and fluid overload
options.rationale: Diuresis in distributive plus cardiogenic shock with poor cardiac output worsens organ perfusion; inotropic support and source control take priority. (Source: ESC Cardiogenic Shock Position Paper)

options.text: Add an inotrope (dobutamine 2.5-5 mcg/kg/min targeting CI >2.2), broaden antibiotics to piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin pending sensitivities, remove and replace the infected femoral line, and refer to cardiothoracics for IABP or Impella consideration
options.rationale: Mixed cardiogenic plus septic shock requires inotropic support for the low cardiac output, broader empirical antibiotic cover, source control by removing the infected line, and mechanical circulatory support consideration in refractory cardiogenic shock. (Source: ANZICS Septic Shock Guidance; ESC Cardiogenic Shock Position Paper)

options.text: Defer all changes pending insertion of a pulmonary artery catheter to fully characterise the haemodynamic profile before commencing or modifying any therapy, given the diagnostic uncertainty between predominantly cardiogenic and septic components
options.rationale: PiCCO and ScvO2 already characterise the mixed shock; delaying therapy for PA catheter is not the right priority in this time-critical scenario. (Source: ESC Cardiogenic Shock Position Paper)

explanation.summary: Mixed cardiogenic and septic shock after large anterior STEMI with line-related bacteraemia requires simultaneous management of both components: inotropic support (dobutamine, or milrinone if pulmonary hypertension) for the cardiogenic component evidenced by low CI and low ScvO2; broader empirical antibiotics pending sensitivities for the septic component; source control by removal and replacement of the infected central line; and consideration of mechanical circulatory support (IABP, Impella, or VA-ECMO) for refractory cardiogenic shock. Vasopressors alone or fluid alone worsen outcomes in this profile.
key_points: Mixed shock: support BP (vasopressor) + flow (inotrope) + source control
Source control as urgent as antibiotics (remove infected line)
Mechanical circulatory support considered for refractory cardiogenic shock
explanation.pearls: ScvO2 <60% with low CI in a hypotensive patient indicates inadequate cardiac output and tissue oxygen delivery; lactate clearance is the bedside marker of effective resuscitation.

subtopic_detail: Native valve endocarditis empirical therapy with benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin and gentamicin
stem:
You are the general medical registrar admitting a 45-year-old previously well man with 3 weeks of fevers, night sweats and progressive exertional dyspnoea. He has lost 4 kg, has new finger clubbing, and a recently noted soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. He has no intravenous drug use, no prosthetic valves, no recent dental procedure and no central venous access.

His chest X-ray is unremarkable. Echocardiography has been requested urgently and three sets of blood cultures have been collected at least 30 minutes apart in the emergency department prior to any antibiotic exposure. He is haemodynamically stable but has signs suggestive of mild congestive cardiac failure on examination today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2, HR 104, BP 124/68, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, BMI 24
data_table.Examination: Soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge grade 2/6, splinter haemorrhages bilateral fingernails, bilateral basal fine inspiratory crackles, hepatomegaly, no peripheral oedema, normal neurological examination, no Janeway lesions or Osler nodes
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.6 neutrophilic, CRP 138, Hb 102 normocytic, urinalysis dipstick +2 protein and microscopic haematuria, ECG sinus tachycardia, chest X-ray clear; three sets of blood cultures sent; echocardiography requested urgently

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 2 weeks pending echocardiography results and blood culture sensitivities, with planned admission for definitive intravenous therapy only if echocardiography confirms vegetations on the valves
options.rationale: Endocarditis requires prolonged IV therapy; oral antibiotics are inappropriate as empirical therapy for suspected native valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose then dose-adjusted monotherapy targeting a trough level of 15 to 20 mg/L, providing broad gram-positive cover including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and viridans group streptococci pending culture results
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy is reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy or MRSA risk factors; combination therapy is standard for native valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g four-hourly plus flucloxacillin 2 g four-hourly plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg eight-hourly, with continued cultures, urgent echocardiogram and infectious diseases consultation, narrowing on culture and sensitivity data
options.rationale: Australian first-line empirical therapy for community-acquired native valve endocarditis is benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin to cover viridans streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus and enterococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy until culture results are available, given the broad gram-positive and gram-negative cover and convenient dosing schedule, with reassessment based on the formal echocardiogram and the eventual organism identified
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy is inadequate empirical cover for native valve endocarditis; it misses enterococci and may underdose for Staphylococcus aureus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis)

options.text: Hold all antibiotics pending the echocardiogram and blood culture results in 48 hours, since premature empirical therapy may reduce the diagnostic yield of cultures and complicate identification of the responsible organism in subacute endocarditis presentations
options.rationale: Once three sets of blood cultures are taken at least 30 minutes apart, empirical therapy should be commenced rather than withholding antibiotics in clinically suspected endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Empirical therapy for community-acquired native valve endocarditis in Australia is benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin: benzylpenicillin for viridans group streptococci, flucloxacillin for Staphylococcus aureus, and low-dose gentamicin for enterococcal synergy. Three sets of blood cultures at least 30 minutes apart should be collected before antibiotics. Urgent transthoracic echocardiography (proceeding to transoesophageal if non-diagnostic) confirms diagnosis. Vancomycin replaces benzylpenicillin and flucloxacillin in non-severe beta-lactam allergy or known MRSA carriage. Treatment duration is typically 4 to 6 weeks depending on organism and clinical course.
key_points: BenPen + flucloxacillin + gentamicin is empirical Australian standard for native valve
Three blood cultures at least 30 min apart before antibiotics
Vancomycin substitutes in severe beta-lactam allergy or MRSA risk
explanation.pearls: Surgical indications in infective endocarditis include heart failure from valve dysfunction, persistent bacteraemia despite 5 to 7 days of appropriate antibiotics, large mobile vegetations greater than 10 mm with embolic events, and abscess or fistula formation.

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion diagnosis HIV RNA when fourth-generation antigen antibody is negative
stem:
You are the sexual health clinic registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man with a 5-day history of fevers, sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy, a non-pruritic maculopapular truncal rash and oral ulcers. He had condomless receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 3 weeks ago. He has no previous diagnosis of HIV. Same-day point-of-care fourth-generation antigen-antibody HIV test is negative today. He has had no other recent illnesses and has had no other medications.

He is otherwise systemically well, haemodynamically stable, and not on any antiretroviral therapy currently. He has had no exposure to post-exposure prophylaxis in the past month and is keen to confirm or exclude HIV diagnosis today.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.0, HR 92, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Pharyngeal erythema with bilateral tonsillar exudate, generalised non-tender lymphadenopathy, fine non-blanching truncal maculopapular rash, oral aphthous ulcers, soft non-tender abdomen, no neurology deficit
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody negative; FBC mild leucopenia 3.4 with mild thrombocytopenia 132; LFTs mildly elevated ALT 78; EBV serology and CMV pending; chlamydia, gonorrhoea NAAT and syphilis serology sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm or exclude acute HIV seroconversion?

options.text: Reassure that the negative fourth-generation antigen-antibody test 3 weeks post-exposure effectively excludes HIV given that the p24 antigen detection window opens within 2 weeks, and discharge with safer-sex counselling and routine STI follow-up in 3 months
options.rationale: Fourth-generation tests may still be negative in early seroconversion if HIV RNA is still developing; HIV RNA (viral load) is needed to confirm. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Send Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus serology and a heterophile antibody test to confirm acute infectious mononucleosis as a more probable diagnosis given the lymphadenopathy and pharyngitis, with planned outpatient follow-up in 7 days
options.rationale: EBV/CMV should be considered but does not exclude acute HIV; HIV RNA is essential when seroconversion is clinically suspected. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Treat empirically for secondary syphilis with intramuscular benzathine penicillin 1.8 g stat given the rash and the high-risk exposure, with planned outpatient infectious diseases follow-up to confirm with syphilis serology and consider HIV testing in 3 months
options.rationale: Secondary syphilis can present similarly but does not exclude HIV; HIV RNA testing is essential when acute HIV is suspected. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Commence empirical post-exposure prophylaxis with tenofovir/emtricitabine and dolutegravir for 28 days given the high-risk exposure profile and the clinically suspected seroconversion, with planned repeat HIV testing at week 4 to confirm or exclude
options.rationale: PEP must be commenced within 72 hours of exposure; at 3 weeks post-exposure it is too late and the priority is to confirm or exclude established infection. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Send quantitative HIV RNA viral load testing along with fourth-generation antigen-antibody confirmation, refer urgently to specialist HIV outpatients for confirmation and ART initiation if positive, and counsel on partner notification and testing
options.rationale: When acute seroconversion is suspected and fourth-generation antigen-antibody is negative, HIV RNA viral load is the test of choice as RNA can be detected approximately 10 days post-exposure, before antibody seroconversion. (Source: ASHM: Australian HIV Testing Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion typically presents 2 to 4 weeks post-exposure with a flu-like illness, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, rash, mucocutaneous ulcers, and may show transient cytopenias and mild transaminitis. Fourth-generation antigen-antibody tests detect both p24 antigen and antibody, narrowing the window period to approximately 2 to 3 weeks, but may still be negative in very early seroconversion. HIV RNA (viral load) is detectable from approximately 10 days post-exposure and is the test of choice when acute seroconversion is suspected with a negative serology. Early diagnosis allows immediate ART initiation and partner notification.
key_points: Acute HIV: fevers, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, rash, mucocutaneous ulcers 2-4 weeks post-exposure
HIV RNA detectable approximately 10 days post-exposure
Fourth-generation antigen-antibody window approximately 2-3 weeks
explanation.pearls: PEP must be commenced within 72 hours of exposure; PrEP is for ongoing risk reduction in HIV-negative individuals at high risk and is available on PBS in Australia for eligible patients.

subtopic_detail: Septic shock hour-1 bundle blood cultures antibiotics fluids lactate
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man brought by ambulance with rigors, confusion and hypotension. He has a 2-day history of urinary frequency, dysuria and flank pain. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia. He is alert but disoriented, has dry mucous membranes and warm peripheries. There are no signs of obvious surgical abdomen, no obvious focal infection elsewhere, and no recent hospitalisation, urological instrumentation or known antibiotic-resistant organism colonisation. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn and a peripheral large-bore intravenous line has been placed. His weight is 80 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, HR 122, BP 85/45, RR 26, SpO2 95% room air, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds, mildly tender right flank, soft abdomen, no peritonism, dry mucous membranes, no neurological focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 5.2 mmol/L, WCC 19.4, CRP 256, creatinine 168 (baseline 88), urine dipstick LE+++ nit+ blood+, blood cultures sent, urine MCS sent, chest X-ray no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management within the first hour?

options.text: Commence intravenous noradrenaline infusion through a central venous catheter at 5 micrograms per minute targeting a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg before commencing fluid resuscitation, with admission to the intensive care unit for ongoing management
options.rationale: Initial septic shock management starts with crystalloid resuscitation 30 mL/kg; vasopressors are added if hypotension persists, not before fluid loading. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Australian Adaptation)

options.text: Arrange urgent contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to identify the source of infection and any complicating obstructive uropathy or perinephric abscess prior to commencing antibiotic therapy or significant fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay antibiotics or fluids in septic shock; hour-1 bundle takes priority and imaging follows once stabilised. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Australian Adaptation)

options.text: Prescribe oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for suspected uncomplicated urinary tract infection and discharge home with safety-net advice if blood pressure improves on a single litre normal saline bolus, with general practice review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics and discharge are unsafe in septic shock with lactate 5.2 and hypotension; admission with IV therapy is required. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Australian Adaptation)

options.text: Hold antibiotics and fluids pending urine and blood culture sensitivities to avoid premature empirical antibiotic exposure that may compromise the bacteriological yield from cultures and broaden the patient's antibiotic resistance profile longer term
options.rationale: Delay of antibiotics in septic shock increases mortality by approximately 7% per hour; antibiotics must be commenced empirically within the first hour. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Australian Adaptation)

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour (gentamicin 5 mg/kg plus ampicillin 2 g for suspected urosepsis), administer 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid bolus over 1 to 3 hours, repeat lactate within 2 hours, source control planning and ICU referral
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, take blood cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4 mmol/L, and apply vasopressors if persistent. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Australian Adaptation)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle (endorsed in Australian sepsis pathways) comprises five elements: measure lactate (and remeasure if over 2 mmol/L), obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, begin 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4 mmol/L within 3 hours, and apply vasopressors if hypotension persists during or after fluid resuscitation to target MAP of at least 65 mmHg. Empirical antibiotic choice is guided by suspected source: gentamicin plus ampicillin for community urosepsis. Source control is sought once stabilised.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressors as needed
Antibiotic delay increases mortality approximately 7% per hour in septic shock
MAP target at least 65 mmHg with noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor
explanation.pearls: Balanced crystalloids (Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte) are preferred over normal saline in sepsis to reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis and acute kidney injury, per the SMART and SALT-ED trials.

subtopic_detail: B12 deficiency with neurological involvement parenteral hydroxocobalamin
stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 70-year-old woman with 4 months of progressive lower-limb paraesthesias, an unsteady gait, mild memory disturbance, and exertional dyspnoea. She has no history of bowel surgery, has had a long-standing diagnosis of atrophic gastritis, has never been a vegetarian, and is otherwise self-caring at home. She has not been on metformin or proton pump inhibitor therapy chronically.

On examination she has reduced vibration and proprioception in both lower limbs with brisk knee reflexes and absent ankle reflexes, and a positive Romberg test. She has no jaundice, no glossitis on examination today, and no pancytopenia.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 88, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, no glossitis, neurology with reduced vibration and proprioception lower limbs bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes, brisk knee reflexes, positive Romberg, no focal cortical deficit
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 normocytic transitioning to macrocytic with MCV 108, WCC 4.2, platelets 220, B12 95 (low), serum folate 9 (normal), iron studies normal, TSH normal, anti-intrinsic factor antibody positive, MMA elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence intramuscular hydroxocobalamin 1 mg every second day for 2 weeks then 1 mg every 3 months long-term, monitor neurological recovery and full blood examination at 6 weeks, and screen for autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes given the intrinsic factor antibodies
options.rationale: B12 deficiency with neurological involvement is treated with parenteral hydroxocobalamin loading every second day for 1-2 weeks then 3-monthly maintenance; oral B12 is inadequate when intrinsic factor antibodies are present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency

options.text: Commence oral cyanocobalamin 1 mg daily for 4 months as monotherapy regardless of underlying intrinsic factor antibody positivity, with planned full blood examination and neurological reassessment at week 6 to confirm a satisfactory clinical response
options.rationale: Oral B12 1 mg daily can work in dietary deficiency but is unreliable when intrinsic factor antibodies are present; parenteral therapy is preferred in pernicious anaemia, particularly with neurological involvement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency

options.text: Commence oral folic acid 5 mg daily as initial therapy with planned repeat B12 in 6 weeks to assess response, with parenteral B12 added only if anaemia does not improve adequately on folate monotherapy at the planned 6-week review
options.rationale: Folic acid alone can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration in B12 deficiency and is contraindicated as monotherapy; B12 must be replaced first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency

options.text: Refer urgently to haematology for bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy to characterise the macrocytic anaemia and rule out myelodysplastic syndrome before commencing any B12 replacement therapy, with follow-up neurology assessment within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Bone marrow biopsy is not needed when serum B12 is low with positive intrinsic factor antibodies; diagnosis is established and treatment should commence promptly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency

options.text: Arrange transfusion of two units of packed red cells now to correct the anaemia and improve oxygen delivery, with parenteral B12 commenced after the transfusion is complete and the haemoglobin has stabilised above the threshold of 100 g/L
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for severe symptomatic anaemia or cardiorespiratory compromise; macrocytic anaemia at Hb 96 with B12 deficiency responds to B12 replacement and does not need urgent transfusion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological involvement requires prompt parenteral replacement to limit the risk of irreversible subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Hydroxocobalamin 1 mg intramuscularly every second day for 1 to 2 weeks loads body stores, followed by 1 mg every 3 months for maintenance in pernicious anaemia. Folate must not be given alone in B12 deficiency as it can precipitate neurological deterioration. Pernicious anaemia is associated with autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes, gastric carcinoid tumours, and gastric adenocarcinoma, so surveillance gastroscopy and screening for other autoimmunity (thyroid, adrenal, type 1 diabetes) is offered.
key_points: Parenteral hydroxocobalamin is preferred for neurological involvement or pernicious anaemia
Folate alone is contraindicated as monotherapy in B12 deficiency
Surveillance for autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes and gastric malignancy
explanation.pearls: Methylmalonic acid is the most specific marker for tissue B12 deficiency; homocysteine rises in both B12 and folate deficiency but methylmalonic acid is elevated in B12 deficiency only.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Vitamin B12 Deficiency
BCSH Guideline: Cobalamin and Folate Deficiency

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis intravenous hydrocortisone in known Addison's during gastroenteritis
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency who presents with 36 hours of vomiting, watery diarrhoea, weakness and inability to keep her usual hydrocortisone 20 mg morning, 10 mg afternoon and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily down. Her partner brought her in via ambulance after she became drowsy and complained of generalised weakness.

She is alert but mildly confused on arrival. She has not received any stress-dose steroid before arrival despite her chronic disease management plan instructing her to double her oral dose during illness and seek urgent review if vomiting prevented oral intake.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.0, HR 122, BP 78/50, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, hyperpigmented palmar creases and knuckles, mildly tender abdomen without peritonism, no focal neurology, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Na 122, K 6.0, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, urea 14, creatinine 142 (baseline 78), Hb 138, WCC 14.2, lactate 2.6; ECG sinus tachycardia 122; cortisol pre-treatment not yet available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer oral hydrocortisone 40 mg as a stat dose with antiemetic and oral rehydration solution, with planned review in 2 hours and admission for inpatient observation if there is no improvement in observations and biochemistry at the recheck
options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone is unreliable in vomiting and hypotensive shock; IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus IV fluids is the standard immediate management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg six-hourly, give intravenous normal saline 1 litre stat then ongoing crystalloid resuscitation, treat hypoglycaemia with intravenous 10% dextrose, and admit to high-dependency unit
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is managed with IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg 6-hourly, IV saline for volume resuscitation, IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia, and admission for monitoring; fludrocortisone is not needed acutely as 100 mg IV hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg stat as preferred glucocorticoid as it does not interfere with subsequent cortisol assays for the diagnostic short Synacthen test, give intravenous saline, and admit to the medical ward for ongoing observation
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks the mineralocorticoid effect needed in adrenal crisis and is not first-line; hydrocortisone is preferred in known Addison's during acute illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Hold all glucocorticoid until baseline serum cortisol and ACTH results return to confirm the diagnosis of adrenal crisis, give intravenous fluid resuscitation in the interim, with cortisol assays sent before any steroid administration to avoid biochemical interference
options.rationale: Glucocorticoid must not be delayed for confirmatory testing in suspected adrenal crisis; in known Addison's the diagnosis is established and immediate IV hydrocortisone is life-saving. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Administer intramuscular fludrocortisone 200 micrograms stat with intravenous saline to address her hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia, with planned introduction of oral hydrocortisone once she has tolerated oral intake for 4 hours without further vomiting
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has slow onset and is not for acute adrenal crisis; IV hydrocortisone is the urgent intervention with rapid glucocorticoid and adequate mineralocorticoid effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Adrenal Insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat followed by 50 mg every 6 hours (or continuous infusion of 200 mg per 24 hours), aggressive intravenous saline resuscitation, intravenous dextrose for hypoglycaemia, and admission for ongoing monitoring. In known Addison's disease, treatment should never be delayed for confirmatory testing. Hydrocortisone at high dose provides sufficient mineralocorticoid effect so fludrocortisone is not added acutely; once stable, fludrocortisone is resumed alongside hydrocortisone wean. Sick-day rules and an emergency hydrocortisone kit at home reduce recurrence.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg every 6 hours (or 200 mg/24 h infusion)
IV saline plus IV dextrose if hypoglycaemic
Do not delay treatment for confirmatory testing in known Addison's
explanation.pearls: All patients with primary adrenal insufficiency should carry an emergency hydrocortisone 100 mg vial with needle and syringe, wear a medical alert identifier, and have a written sick-day plan including doubling oral dose for febrile illness.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal Insufficiency Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection intravenous labetalol target heart rate and blood pressure
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 60-year-old hypertensive man with sudden onset severe tearing chest and interscapular pain 1 hour ago. He has poorly controlled hypertension on irbesartan 300 mg daily and amlodipine 10 mg daily. He has had no syncope, no neurology deficit, no abdominal pain, and his ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy but no ischaemic features.

CT aortogram has demonstrated a Stanford type B dissection commencing distal to the left subclavian artery, descending to the level of the renal arteries with patent visceral vessels and no malperfusion. He has been transferred to the resuscitation cubicle with cardiothoracic surgery and intensive care on standby.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 102, BP 186/108 right arm, 124/78 left arm, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Distressed with pain, diaphoretic, no focal neurology, no abdominal tenderness, peripheral pulses present and symmetrical in lower limbs, no clinical features of cardiac tamponade
data_table.Investigations: Trop normal, FBC, UEC, coags normal, ECG sinus tachycardia 102, CXR mediastinum slightly widened, CT aortogram: Stanford type B dissection commencing distal to left subclavian and extending to renal artery level, no end-organ malperfusion, true lumen patent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate medical management?

options.text: Commence oral irbesartan 600 mg as an additional dose plus oral nifedipine modified-release 60 mg orally for blood pressure reduction, with admission to the coronary care unit for cardiac monitoring and serial troponin assessment over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Oral agents have slow onset and unpredictable effect in dissection; IV beta-blocker (labetalol or esmolol) is first-line for acute heart rate and blood pressure control. (Source: CSANZ: Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Administer intravenous adenosine 6 mg rapid push to slow the heart rate to a target less than 60 beats per minute and reduce shear stress on the dissection flap, with continuous cardiac monitoring and repeat doses titrated to clinical response
options.rationale: Adenosine is for paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, not for chronic rate control; labetalol or esmolol infusion is the appropriate agent. (Source: CSANZ: Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Commence intravenous labetalol infusion targeting a heart rate below 60 beats per minute first, then add sodium nitroprusside infusion if systolic blood pressure remains above 120 mmHg, target SBP 100-120 mmHg, opioid for pain, ICU admission
options.rationale: Anti-impulse therapy with IV beta-blocker (target HR less than 60) precedes vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) to avoid reflex tachycardia and shear stress; SBP target 100-120; uncomplicated type B is medically managed initially. (Source: CSANZ: Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Proceed urgently to operating theatre for open surgical repair of the descending aorta given the severity of dissection and high in-hospital mortality of medically managed type B dissection presentations, with cardiopulmonary bypass team standby for the procedure
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically; surgical or endovascular intervention is reserved for malperfusion, rupture, or refractory symptoms. (Source: CSANZ: Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Commence intravenous heparin infusion at 18 units per kilogram per hour to prevent thrombosis within the false lumen and stabilise the dissection flap, with continuous cardiac and APTT monitoring during heparinisation in the intensive care unit
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection due to risk of haemorrhage and aortic rupture; rate and BP control are the priorities. (Source: CSANZ: Aortic Dissection)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection is medically managed with anti-impulse therapy to reduce aortic wall shear stress. IV beta-blocker (labetalol or esmolol infusion) is given first to target heart rate below 60 beats per minute, then a vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside or glyceryl trinitrate) is added to target systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg. Beta-blocker must precede vasodilator to avoid reflex tachycardia. Pain is controlled with opioid. ICU admission for monitoring and cardiothoracic input. Complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or expansion) requires thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) or open surgery.
key_points: Beta-blocker first (HR target less than 60), then vasodilator (SBP 100-120)
Uncomplicated type B: medical management; type A: emergency surgical repair
Anticoagulation contraindicated; opioid for pain
explanation.pearls: Pulse and blood pressure should be measured in both arms in suspected dissection; a difference greater than 20 mmHg in systolic pressure is a classic but non-sensitive sign and absence does not exclude dissection.

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma alpha-blockade prior to beta-blockade before adrenalectomy
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 50-year-old man newly diagnosed with phaeochromocytoma after presenting with paroxysmal headaches, sweating and palpitations, with episodic systolic blood pressures up to 220 mmHg recorded by his general practitioner. Twenty-four-hour fractionated urinary metanephrines and plasma free metanephrines have confirmed the diagnosis. A 5 cm right adrenal mass has been imaged on contrast computed tomography of the abdomen, with no metastatic disease on the staging scans.

He has been referred for elective adrenalectomy and the surgical team has asked for preoperative medical optimisation. He is otherwise well, on no current medications, and has no other comorbidities.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/96 resting (220 systolic during paroxysms), HR 96, BMI 25
data_table.Examination: Mildly tremulous, no thyroid enlargement, normal cardiovascular examination at rest, no abdominal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines and normetanephrines markedly raised, 24-hour urinary metanephrines raised, CT abdomen 5 cm right adrenal mass with classic phaeochromocytoma features and no metastases, MIBG and PET pending; ECG sinus rhythm, normal echocardiogram, normal renal function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preoperative medical preparation?

options.text: Commence atenolol 50 mg daily for 7 days as initial preoperative beta-blockade before introducing alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine, to achieve dual receptor control before the planned surgical excision and avoid intraoperative haemodynamic instability
options.rationale: Beta-blockade before alpha-blockade in phaeochromocytoma causes unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis; alpha-blockade must be commenced first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Proceed directly to adrenalectomy without preoperative medical preparation given the convenience of intraoperative haemodynamic management by experienced anaesthetics and surgical teams, with intravenous phentolamine and sodium nitroprusside available at induction
options.rationale: Preoperative alpha-blockade for 10-14 days reduces mortality from haemodynamic instability during surgery; foregoing preparation is standard of care violation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Commence amlodipine 5 mg daily titrated to blood pressure control as the primary preoperative agent and salt and fluid replacement to optimise intravascular volume, with planned surgery in 2 weeks once normotension is achieved on this regimen
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are second-line adjuncts in phaeochromocytoma; alpha-blockade is mainstay of preoperative preparation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Commence phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily, titrate every 2 to 3 days targeting symptom control and supine BP less than 130/80 with orthostatic systolic above 90, encourage high-salt diet and oral fluids, add a beta-blocker only after established alpha-blockade for residual tachycardia
options.rationale: Phenoxybenzamine for 10-14 days with up-titration, salt and fluid loading, and addition of beta-blocker only after alpha-blockade is established, is standard preoperative preparation for phaeochromocytoma. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Commence metyrosine 250 mg four times daily for catecholamine synthesis inhibition for 7 days preoperatively, with planned introduction of carvedilol after the initial week of metyrosine to provide concurrent alpha and beta receptor antagonism prior to surgery
options.rationale: Metyrosine is reserved for metastatic phaeochromocytoma or refractory cases; not first-line preoperative therapy for surgical candidates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Phaeochromocytoma)

explanation.summary: Preoperative preparation for phaeochromocytoma comprises alpha-adrenergic blockade for 10 to 14 days, traditionally with phenoxybenzamine (non-selective, irreversible) starting at 10 mg twice daily and titrated up to symptom control and target blood pressure less than 130/80 supine with mild orthostatic hypotension. High-salt diet and oral fluid loading reverse the chronically constricted intravascular volume. Beta-blocker is added only after established alpha-blockade to control reflex tachycardia; reversing this order causes unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. Doxazosin (selective alpha-1) is an alternative to phenoxybenzamine.
key_points: Alpha-blockade for 10-14 days before beta-blocker addition
Phenoxybenzamine titrated to BP under 130/80 supine plus orthostasis
High-salt diet and fluid loading reverse chronic vasoconstriction
explanation.pearls: Adequacy of preoperative alpha-blockade is judged by Roizen criteria: BP less than 160/90 for 24 hours, no orthostatic hypotension below 80/45, ECG free of ST-T changes for 1 week, and no more than 5 ectopics per minute.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Phaeochromocytoma

subtopic_detail: Clinically isolated syndrome optic neuritis MRI brain and spine for MS workup
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with 5 days of progressive unilateral painful vision loss in the right eye, worsened by eye movement, with reduced colour vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect on examination. She has had no previous neurological symptoms, no recent infection, no headache outside of the painful eye movements, and is otherwise systemically well.

Fundoscopy shows a mildly swollen optic disc. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension and giant cell arteritis have been excluded clinically. There are no features of inflammatory eye disease, and she has not been exposed to ethambutol, methanol or other optic neurotoxins recently.

data_table.Examination: Right visual acuity 6/36, left 6/6; reduced colour vision right eye; relative afferent pupillary defect right; mild disc swelling right; full extraocular movements with pain on right eye motion; no other cranial nerve deficit; normal upper and lower limb power, tone and reflexes; no sensory deficit
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, ESR, CRP and B12 normal, syphilis serology negative, ANA negative; ECG normal; visual evoked potentials pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation and management plan?

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days empirically for likely optic neuritis with planned outpatient oral prednisolone taper over 3 weeks, with magnetic resonance imaging deferred to outpatient review in 2 weeks once acute treatment is complete
options.rationale: MRI brain and spine should be performed prior to or concurrent with treatment to assess dissemination of demyelinating lesions for MS diagnosis; oral taper after IV steroid is not standard. (Source: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines)
source_refs: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines

options.text: Arrange urgent ocular ultrasound and orbital CT to characterise optic disc oedema and any associated mass lesion compressing the optic nerve, with planned ophthalmology review the next day for visual evoked potentials and consideration of intervention
options.rationale: Ocular ultrasound and CT are not the right imaging for optic neuritis or MS workup; MRI brain and spine with gadolinium is the test of choice. (Source: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines)
source_refs: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines

options.text: Reassure the patient that idiopathic optic neuritis usually resolves spontaneously over 2 to 4 weeks without intervention, advise outpatient ophthalmology review in 1 week and request visual evoked potentials testing without further imaging or systemic therapy
options.rationale: Optic neuritis is the most common first presentation of multiple sclerosis and MRI is required to assess dissemination; treatment with IV steroids may shorten recovery. (Source: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines)
source_refs: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines

options.text: Arrange urgent contrast magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spinal cord to assess for additional demyelinating lesions, refer to neurology and ophthalmology, consider intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days to hasten visual recovery
options.rationale: Optic neuritis suspected as a clinically isolated syndrome requires MRI brain and spine with gadolinium for McDonald criteria assessment, neurology referral, and consideration of IV methylprednisolone (Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial) to hasten recovery. (Source: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines)
source_refs: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines

options.text: Commence empirical ocrelizumab 600 mg intravenously now as disease-modifying therapy for presumed relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, with planned outpatient ophthalmology follow-up in 1 week to monitor visual recovery and treatment tolerability
options.rationale: Disease-modifying therapy is commenced after diagnosis of MS confirmed by clinical and radiological criteria, not for an undiagnosed first event without imaging confirmation. (Source: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines)
source_refs: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: Acute optic neuritis is the most common first manifestation of multiple sclerosis. Diagnostic workup requires contrast magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spinal cord to look for additional demyelinating lesions satisfying McDonald criteria for dissemination in space and time. Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days hastens visual recovery without changing long-term visual outcome (Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial); oral prednisolone alone is associated with worse outcomes and is not recommended. Disease-modifying therapy is initiated after confirmation of MS diagnosis, with selection guided by disease severity and patient factors.
key_points: MRI brain and spine with gadolinium is the imaging modality of choice
IV methylprednisolone hastens visual recovery in optic neuritis (ONTT)
Oral prednisolone monotherapy is harmful and not recommended
explanation.pearls: Aquaporin-4 and MOG antibody testing is added when bilateral, severe, or recurrent optic neuritis is present to identify neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder or MOG antibody-associated disease, which require different long-term immunotherapy.

sources.label: MSA: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis and Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: COPD exacerbation - NIV criteria
stem: A 72-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 38% predicted) is brought in with 3 days of worsening dyspnoea, increased purulent sputum and confusion that started this morning. She has been on tiotropium and combined inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta agonist. She has been treated for two exacerbations in the past year. Controlled oxygen at 28% has been started with target SpO2 88 to 92%.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.4 degrees Celsius, HR 112, RR 30, SpO2 89% on 28% FiO2 venturi, BP 142/86 mmHg, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6)
data_table.Examination: Use of accessory muscles, prolonged expiratory phase, scattered wheeze, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ABG on 28% O2: pH 7.27, PaCO2 78 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 30 mmol/L; chest X-ray hyperinflation, no consolidation or pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous aminophylline as adjunct bronchodilation therapy now
options.rationale: Aminophylline has marginal additional benefit in acute COPD exacerbation, a narrow therapeutic index and significant cardiac toxicity, and is no longer routinely recommended. (Source: TSANZ COPD-X)

options.text: Intubate immediately and transfer to the intensive care unit for ventilation
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for failure of NIV, GCS less than 8, severe haemodynamic instability or contraindication to NIV; mild confusion alone is not such a contraindication when NIV is trialled. (Source: TSANZ COPD-X)

options.text: Increase oxygen flow to 8 L per minute via a Hudson mask to correct hypoxia
options.rationale: High-flow uncontrolled oxygen in hypercapnic COPD worsens CO2 retention and acidosis; targeted SpO2 88 to 92% via controlled delivery is the safer approach. (Source: TSANZ COPD-X)

options.text: Commence non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) with controlled oxygen titration
options.rationale: Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (pH 7.25 to 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) in COPD exacerbation that persists despite controlled oxygen and bronchodilators is a clear indication for NIV. (Source: TSANZ COPD-X)

options.text: Switch to a heliox 70:30 oxygen mixture via a non-rebreather face mask
options.rationale: Heliox is not routinely used in acute COPD exacerbation; it does not address hypercapnic acidosis and is not a substitute for NIV. (Source: TSANZ COPD-X)

explanation.summary: NIV is first-line ventilatory support for acute hypercapnic exacerbations of COPD with pH 7.25 to 7.35 and PaCO2 above 45 mmHg that persist despite controlled oxygen, bronchodilators and steroids. NIV reduces intubation and mortality, with contraindications including GCS less than 8, vomiting, facial trauma and haemodynamic instability. Failure within 1 to 2 hours triggers intubation. Standard medical therapy includes nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally for 5 days, and antibiotics if sputum is purulent.
key_points: NIV is indicated for pH 7.25 to 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mmHg despite controlled oxygen
Controlled oxygen targets SpO2 88 to 92% in COPD
Escalate to intubation if NIV fails or contraindicated
explanation.pearls: COPD-X recommends prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally for 5 days in acute exacerbations; longer courses confer no additional benefit and increase steroid side effects.

subtopic_detail: HFrEF - SGLT2 inhibitor addition
stem: A 64-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 28%) attends his cardiologist for routine review. He is in sinus rhythm, NYHA class II. He is on perindopril 10 mg daily, bisoprolol 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily and frusemide 40 mg daily. eGFR is 62 mL/min/1.73 m2. He has no diabetes. He has been stable for 6 months and is asking what else can be done.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 64, RR 14
data_table.Examination: JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema, chest clear, no third heart sound today
data_table.Investigations: Hb 138, K 4.4, Na 140, urea 7.2, creatinine 110, NT-proBNP 1100 ng/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next addition to his guideline-directed therapy?

options.text: Increase frusemide to 80 mg orally twice daily as the next escalation
options.rationale: He is euvolaemic with no oedema and no orthopnoea; escalating diuretic worsens electrolytes and renal function without prognostic benefit. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ HF Guidelines 2022)

options.text: Add digoxin 125 micrograms orally once daily to his existing regimen
options.rationale: Digoxin reduces HF hospitalisations in symptomatic patients on optimal GDMT but does not reduce mortality and is reserved for ongoing symptoms despite all four pillars. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ HF Guidelines 2022)

options.text: Add ivabradine 5 mg orally twice daily to his existing regimen now
options.rationale: Ivabradine is added in sinus rhythm patients with resting HR above 70 despite maximal beta blocker; this patient has HR 64 so does not meet the heart-rate criterion. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ HF Guidelines 2022)

options.text: Add amlodipine 5 mg orally once daily to his existing regimen now
options.rationale: Amlodipine is acceptable for blood pressure or angina in HFrEF but does not improve HF outcomes; it is not the next pillar of HFrEF GDMT. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ HF Guidelines 2022)

options.text: Add dapagliflozin 10 mg orally once daily to the existing regimen
options.rationale: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin) reduce HF hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFrEF regardless of diabetes status and are now the fourth pillar of GDMT after RAAS inhibitor, beta blocker and MRA. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ HF Guidelines 2022)

explanation.summary: HFrEF GDMT is built on four pillars: an ACE inhibitor or ARB (or sacubitril/valsartan), a beta blocker, an MRA, and an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin). DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced established benefit independent of diabetes status. Sacubitril/valsartan substitutes the ACE inhibitor in suitable patients (typically with NT-proBNP elevated or recent HF hospitalisation). Ivabradine adds when sinus HR remains above 70 on maximal beta blocker. Diuretics control congestion but do not improve prognosis.
key_points: Four pillars: RAAS inhibitor (or sacubitril/valsartan), beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor
SGLT2 inhibitor benefit is independent of diabetes status in HFrEF
Diuretics relieve symptoms but do not change mortality
explanation.pearls: DAPA-HF showed dapagliflozin reduced the composite of CV death and HF hospitalisation by around 26% in non-diabetic HFrEF, with NNT of about 21 over 18 months.

subtopic_detail: AF stroke prevention
stem: A 76-year-old woman is found to have asymptomatic atrial fibrillation on a routine ECG. She has a history of hypertension on amlodipine and type 2 diabetes on metformin. She has no prior stroke or TIA. eGFR is 64 mL/min/1.73 m2. She has no bleeding history.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/82 mmHg, HR 78, irregular, RR 16
data_table.Examination: No murmurs, no heart failure, no carotid bruit, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation rate 78, FBC normal, K 4.3, creatinine 86, HbA1c 7.1%

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate stroke-prevention therapy?

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily as oral anticoagulation
options.rationale: Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 4 (age, hypertension, diabetes), well above the threshold of 2 for oral anticoagulation; DOACs are first-line in non-valvular AF and apixaban is suitable with eGFR 64. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines 2023)

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally once daily as oral antithrombotic
options.rationale: Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF in current Australian guidelines; it is inferior to anticoagulation and offers little or no benefit at her risk. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines 2023)

options.text: Clopidogrel 75 mg orally once daily as oral antithrombotic
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy alone is inferior to anticoagulation for AF stroke prevention; clopidogrel is not first-line and adds bleeding risk without matching DOAC efficacy. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines 2023)

options.text: Warfarin orally with INR target 2.0 to 3.0 as anticoagulation
options.rationale: Warfarin is now reserved for AF with mechanical valves, moderate-severe mitral stenosis, or DOAC contraindication; DOACs are preferred for non-valvular AF in eligible patients. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines 2023)

options.text: No antithrombotic therapy with annual cardiovascular review
options.rationale: Withholding anticoagulation in non-valvular AF with CHA2DS2-VA of 4 carries an unacceptably high annual stroke risk (around 4 to 5%) and is not appropriate. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines 2023)

explanation.summary: The 2023 NHFA/CSANZ AF guideline uses CHA2DS2-VA (sex removed) to assess stroke risk in non-valvular AF; a score of 2 or more is the threshold for oral anticoagulation. DOACs are first-line, with warfarin reserved for mechanical valves, moderate-severe mitral stenosis or DOAC contraindication. DOAC dose reduction follows specific drug criteria (age, weight, renal function, interactions). Antiplatelet therapy is not recommended for AF stroke prevention.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA replaces CHA2DS2-VASc in current Australian guidance
DOACs first-line; warfarin reserved for valvular AF and DOAC contraindications
Antiplatelets are not effective AF stroke prevention
explanation.pearls: Apixaban dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily requires any two of: age 80 or more, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more; this patient meets only one (age) so receives the full 5 mg twice daily dose.

subtopic_detail: Acute migraine - second-line
stem: A 28-year-old woman with episodic migraine without aura presents to her general practitioner. She has 2 attacks per month, each lasting up to 24 hours. Oral ibuprofen 400 mg taken at headache onset has not provided adequate relief in the past 3 attacks. She has no cardiovascular disease, no hemiplegic migraine and is not pregnant. She wants an acute-attack medication she can self-administer.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination between attacks, fundi normal, BP 116/72 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, TFTs normal; no imaging performed as no red flags

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate acute therapy?

options.text: Oral propranolol 40 mg twice daily continuously
options.rationale: Propranolol is a preventive option, not an acute treatment; it is added when attack frequency is 4 or more per month or attacks are disabling despite acute therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Sumatriptan 50 mg orally at headache onset
options.rationale: Triptans are first-line acute migraine treatment when simple analgesia fails or is contraindicated; oral sumatriptan 50 to 100 mg is a standard starting point in Australian practice with no cardiovascular contraindications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Oxycodone 5 mg orally at headache onset
options.rationale: Opioids are not recommended for migraine because of medication-overuse headache risk and dependence; they are not migraine-specific therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Ergotamine 2 mg sublingual tablet at headache onset
options.rationale: Ergotamine has largely been replaced by triptans in Australia because of efficacy, safety and cardiovascular risk profile differences. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg at night every night
options.rationale: Amitriptyline is a preventive option for migraine, not an acute treatment, and would not address an individual attack. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Australian acute migraine management starts with simple analgesia (paracetamol or NSAID) plus antiemetic at the earliest sign of an attack. If this fails or is contraindicated, a triptan is added as second-line acute therapy, taken early when pain is mild. Combination of triptan plus NSAID gives better relief than either alone for some patients. Preventive therapy (propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate or CGRP monoclonal antibodies) is added when attack frequency reaches 4 or more per month or attacks are disabling despite acute treatment. Opioids and ergot derivatives are avoided.
key_points: Triptans are first-line when simple analgesia fails or is contraindicated
Take triptan early when pain is mild for best response
Preventive therapy threshold is around 4 attacks per month or disability
explanation.pearls: Triptans are contraindicated in coronary artery disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine, basilar migraine and pregnancy; they should not be combined with ergot derivatives within 24 hours.

subtopic_detail: Chronic hyponatraemia - correction rate
stem: A 78-year-old man with chronic alcoholism is admitted from a nursing home with confusion and unsteady gait. He has been on a thiazide for years. He has had no seizures. He last ate normally 4 days ago and has been on tea and biscuits. He has no focal neurology. The medical registrar asks about the safe rate of sodium correction.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 88, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mildly confused, no peripheral oedema, mucous membranes dry, no focal neurology, no asterixis
data_table.Investigations: Na 112 mmol/L, K 3.2, urea 4.4, creatinine 92, glucose 5.0, urine osmolality 420 mOsm/kg, urine Na 50 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate sodium-correction strategy in the first 24 hours?

options.text: Aim to correct serum sodium by 20 to 25 mmol/L over the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Rapid correction in chronic hyponatraemia precipitates osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine and extrapontine myelinolysis); the patient is at especially high risk because of age, alcohol and malnutrition. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Give 3% saline 100 mL intravenously over 10 minutes then recheck sodium
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia such as seizures, coma or severe encephalopathy, none of which are present; mild confusion in chronic hyponatraemia is not an indication for bolus therapy. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Aim to correct serum sodium by no more than 8 mmol/L per 24 hours
options.rationale: Chronic hyponatraemia (greater than 48 hours' duration) correction should be limited to 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination, especially in elderly malnourished alcoholic patients. (Source: KHA-CARI / Australian Hyponatraemia Guidance)

options.text: Restrict total fluid intake to 500 mL per 24 hours without other measures
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is a tool but is unlikely to achieve 8 to 10 mmol/L correction safely in the first 24 hours when the patient is symptomatic; the thiazide must also be ceased. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Infuse intravenous 3% saline at 1 mL/kg/hour continuously for 24 hours
options.rationale: Continuous high-rate hypertonic infusion risks over-rapid correction; if hypertonic saline is needed it is bolused in small aliquots with frequent re-measurement, not continuous infusion. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia)
