explanation.summary: Chronic hyponatraemia (greater than 48 hours' duration) correction must be slow to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome. Australian guidance limits correction to 8 mmol/L in the first 24 hours in high-risk patients (alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, age above 65) and 10 mmol/L per 24 hours otherwise. Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures, severe confusion or coma is treated with 3% saline 100 to 150 mL boluses with frequent re-measurement. Over-correction is treated with cessation of saline and reintroduction of free water (oral or 5% glucose), or DDAVP rescue.
key_points: Chronic hyponatraemia: limit correction to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours in high-risk patients
3% saline bolus is reserved for severe symptoms (seizures, coma)
Over-correction: stop saline, start free water, consider DDAVP
explanation.pearls: DDAVP can be used to deliberately slow or reverse over-rapid sodium correction; it is given 1 to 2 micrograms IV/SC every 6 to 8 hours alongside free water replacement when correction has exceeded 8 mmol/L in 24 hours.

subtopic_detail: Intermediate-risk PE - RV strain
stem: A 58-year-old man presents with 2 days of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. He returned from a long-haul flight 5 days ago. His Wells score is 6. CT pulmonary angiography confirms bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli with right ventricular enlargement. He is normotensive on arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 112, RR 24, SpO2 92% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mild dyspnoea, JVP raised 4 cm, lungs clear, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 65 ng/L (cut-off 14), NT-proBNP 920 ng/L, CTPA RV/LV diameter ratio 1.2, ECG sinus tachycardia and S1Q3T3

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge on apixaban with general practitioner review in 7 days from now
options.rationale: Outpatient management is appropriate for low-risk PE (sPESI 0 or Hestia criteria met), not for intermediate-high-risk PE with RV strain and positive biomarkers. (Source: THANZ Position Statement: PE)

options.text: Systemic thrombolysis using intravenous alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is reserved for haemodynamically unstable (massive) PE or intermediate-high-risk PE that decompensates; routine thrombolysis in normotensive intermediate-high-risk PE does not improve mortality and increases major bleeding. (Source: THANZ Position Statement: PE)

options.text: Inferior vena cava filter inserted by interventional radiology in 24 hours
options.rationale: IVC filters are reserved for patients with absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or with recurrent PE despite anticoagulation; the patient can be anticoagulated. (Source: THANZ Position Statement: PE)

options.text: Therapeutic anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin and admission
options.rationale: Intermediate-high-risk PE (normotensive with RV dysfunction plus positive biomarkers) is managed with therapeutic anticoagulation and inpatient monitoring for haemodynamic deterioration, with systemic thrombolysis reserved for decompensation. (Source: TSANZ/Thrombosis & Haemostasis Society Australia)

options.text: Surgical pulmonary embolectomy via median sternotomy on emergency theatre
options.rationale: Surgical embolectomy is reserved for haemodynamically unstable PE with thrombolysis contraindication or failure, or for large central thrombus; it is not first-line in stable intermediate-high-risk PE. (Source: THANZ Position Statement: PE)

explanation.summary: PE risk stratification drives management: high-risk (haemodynamic instability) gets thrombolysis or embolectomy. Intermediate-high-risk (normotensive with RV dysfunction plus positive biomarkers) gets therapeutic anticoagulation with close monitoring for decompensation, when rescue thrombolysis can be deployed. Intermediate-low-risk gets standard anticoagulation, and low-risk patients (sPESI 0, no RV dysfunction, no biomarker elevation) are eligible for outpatient management. Anticoagulation is typically a DOAC for at least 3 months in provoked PE.
key_points: Intermediate-high-risk = RV dysfunction + positive biomarker, normotensive
Anticoagulation with monitoring; thrombolysis if decompensates
Outpatient management requires sPESI 0 (or equivalent) plus social suitability
explanation.pearls: In the PEITHO trial, routine systemic thrombolysis in intermediate-high-risk PE prevented haemodynamic decompensation but did not reduce mortality and increased major bleeding and stroke, which is why current guidance reserves it for decompensation.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal incidentaloma workup
stem: A 56-year-old woman has an incidental 2.8 cm right adrenal mass identified on a CT abdomen done for nephrolithiasis. The CT density is 5 Hounsfield units on the unenhanced phase. She has hypertension on amlodipine and irbesartan, no episodic symptoms, no Cushingoid features, and no family history of endocrine disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/88 mmHg, HR 72, BMI 28 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: No striae, no facial plethora, no proximal myopathy, no palpable mass
data_table.Investigations: CT: right adrenal mass 2.8 cm, 5 HU non-contrast (lipid-rich); FBC, UEC, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with plasma metanephrines
options.rationale: All adrenal incidentalomas are screened for autonomous cortisol secretion (1 mg overnight DST) and phaeochromocytoma (plasma or 24 h urine fractionated metanephrines); aldosterone-renin ratio is added in hypertensive or hypokalaemic patients. (Source: ESE/ENSAT Incidentaloma 2023)

options.text: 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA combined with serum chromogranin A measurement
options.rationale: 5-HIAA and chromogranin A screen for carcinoid and neuroendocrine tumours; they are not part of adrenal incidentaloma workup. (Source: ESE Adrenal Incidentaloma 2023)

options.text: Image-guided fine-needle aspiration of the right adrenal mass this week
options.rationale: FNA is contraindicated until phaeochromocytoma is excluded (catecholamine crisis risk) and rarely changes management for indeterminate adrenal lesions; it is not part of routine workup. (Source: ESE Adrenal Incidentaloma 2023)

options.text: Repeat non-contrast CT abdomen in 6 months without biochemical testing
options.rationale: Imaging surveillance alone misses functioning tumours; biochemical screening for cortisol and metanephrines is mandatory at first identification regardless of imaging features. (Source: ESE Adrenal Incidentaloma 2023)

options.text: Right adrenalectomy without further investigation given size and density
options.rationale: Surgery is considered for masses larger than 4 cm, indeterminate imaging features (above 20 HU) or proven autonomous secretion; this 2.8 cm lipid-rich (5 HU) mass requires biochemical workup, not immediate surgery. (Source: ESE Adrenal Incidentaloma 2023)

explanation.summary: Adrenal incidentaloma evaluation tests two questions: is it functioning, and is it malignant? Functional workup includes 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol greater than 50 nmol/L suggests autonomous secretion), plasma or 24 h urine fractionated metanephrines, and aldosterone-renin ratio if hypertensive or hypokalaemic. Imaging features favouring benign include size below 4 cm, unenhanced CT density below 10 HU (lipid-rich adenoma) and homogeneous appearance. Surgery is considered for masses larger than 4 cm, indeterminate or suspicious imaging, or functional tumours. Non-functional, low-density lesions below 4 cm need re-evaluation as guided by ESE 2023.
key_points: Screen all incidentalomas for cortisol and metanephrines; add ARR if hypertensive/hypokalaemic
Lipid-rich (less than 10 HU) lesions below 4 cm are usually benign adenomas
Surgical referral for size above 4 cm, indeterminate imaging, or proven function
explanation.pearls: In an adrenal mass, an unenhanced CT density of 10 HU or less indicates a lipid-rich adenoma with greater than 98% specificity for benign disease, which is the imaging feature that allows safe biochemical-screening-only workup.

subtopic_detail: Adult sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to ED with 24 hours of fever, dysuria and right flank pain. He is alert but tachycardic. Initial obs show HR 124, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 39.2 degrees Celsius. A bedside lactate is 3.4 mmol/L. He has no allergies. Renal ultrasound is being arranged. You are the receiving registrar in the resuscitation bay deciding the hour-1 plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.2 degrees Celsius, HR 124, RR 28, BP 88/52 mmHg, SpO2 96% in room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds, right renal angle tenderness, no peritonism, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.4 mmol/L, WCC 18 x10^9/L, CRP 220 mg/L, creatinine 156 micromol/L (baseline 90), urinalysis 3+ leukocytes 2+ nitrites, two blood cultures sent

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate hour-1 sepsis bundle?

options.text: Cautious 500 mL crystalloid bolus, intravenous ceftriaxone and start noradrenaline if MAP remains under 65 mmHg
options.rationale: 30 mL/kg crystalloid is the bundle standard in septic shock before vasopressor consideration; restricting to 500 mL initially is inadequate resuscitation in this group. (Source: ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily and 10 mL/kg of crystalloid prior to admission to a medical ward
options.rationale: Septic shock with hypotension and elevated lactate mandates IV antibiotics within an hour and 30 mL/kg fluid resuscitation, not oral monotherapy; ciprofloxacin alone has resistance concerns in urinary sepsis. (Source: ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Crystalloid 30 mL/kg over the first hour, intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam after cultures and serial lactate
options.rationale: Australian sepsis pathways follow the hour-1 bundle of fluid 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 2 mmol/L, blood cultures before broad-spectrum antibiotics targeted at source, and reassessment with serial lactate. Piperacillin-tazobactam covers urinary sepsis with possible Pseudomonas. (Source: ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Activated protein C infusion, intravenous gentamicin alone and hydrocortisone 200 mg as adjunctive therapy
options.rationale: Activated protein C has been withdrawn from sepsis management; gentamicin alone does not cover for resistant Gram-negatives, and routine hydrocortisone is reserved for refractory shock. (Source: ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Delay antibiotics until renal ultrasound has excluded obstructive uropathy and surgical drainage is planned
options.rationale: Antibiotic delay is associated with increased mortality in sepsis; ultrasound is performed in parallel and drainage arranged urgently without delaying empirical antibiotics. (Source: ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard)

explanation.summary: Septic shock with hypotension and raised lactate is managed under the hour-1 bundle. The bundle comprises blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics targeted at the suspected source, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 2 mmol/L, and reassessment with repeat lactate. Source control imaging is arranged in parallel rather than as a reason to delay therapy. Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor when fluid resuscitation alone fails to maintain mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle - cultures, antibiotics, fluid 30 mL/kg, repeat lactate
Piperacillin-tazobactam covers urinary sepsis with possible Pseudomonas risk
Source control imaging occurs in parallel and never delays empirical antibiotics
explanation.pearls: Patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors should have a target MAP of 65 mmHg; noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor and is started after adequate fluid resuscitation.

subtopic_detail: CAP severity scoring
stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to ED with 3 days of cough, fever and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She lives independently and is non-smoker. She has hypertension only. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. She is well perfused and orientated.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 96, RR 24, BP 124/76 mmHg, SpO2 92% on room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Coarse crackles right base, no wheeze, no peripheral oedema, orientated to time and place
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14 x10^9/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, CRP 188 mg/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, multifocal albumin 36 g/L, ABG pH 7.42 PaO2 68 mmHg on room air, blood cultures sent

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate disposition and antibiotic plan?

options.text: Admit for IV moxifloxacin monotherapy as appropriate cover for atypical and typical bacteria in CAP
options.rationale: Quinolone monotherapy is reserved for penicillin allergy or specific situations; first-line for moderate CAP is benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Community-acquired pneumonia)

options.text: Discharge on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Hypoxia with SpO2 92 percent on room air pushes severity to moderate and warrants admission rather than outpatient management. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Community-acquired pneumonia)

options.text: Admit to ICU for intravenous ceftriaxone, azithromycin and noradrenaline support as severe CAP
options.rationale: She does not meet ICU CAP criteria - no shock, no respiratory failure requiring intubation or NIV, no multilobar progression at presentation. ICU admission is over-treatment. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Community-acquired pneumonia)

options.text: Admit for IV benzylpenicillin and oral doxycycline using the moderate-severity community-acquired pneumonia regimen
options.rationale: SMART-COP of 3 (RR 24 - 1 point, SpO2 92 percent - 2 points; albumin 36 g/L is not low enough; urea 6.8 mmol/L is borderline; otherwise 0) indicates moderate severity requiring admission; Australian first-line for moderate CAP is IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Community-acquired pneumonia)

options.text: Admit for IV vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam covering hospital-acquired and aspiration pathogens
options.rationale: This is community-acquired pneumonia in a community-dwelling woman without aspiration risk; antipseudomonal and MRSA cover is not warranted. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Community-acquired pneumonia)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP stratifies community-acquired pneumonia severity. A score of 3 indicates moderate severity requiring admission. Australian first-line therapy for moderate CAP is intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly plus oral doxycycline 100 mg BD. Severe disease (score 5 or higher, ICU need) escalates to IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin. Oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline is appropriate for mild outpatient CAP.
key_points: SMART-COP 0-2 outpatient; 3-4 ward; 5 or higher consider ICU
Moderate CAP - IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline first-line in Australia
Hypoxia (SpO2 under 93 percent on room air) is a major driver of admission decisions
explanation.pearls: Re-evaluate at 48 to 72 hours; non-responders need workup for organising pneumonia, empyema, resistant organism (Legionella, MRSA) and aspiration; CT chest is informative.

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated cystitis women
stem: A 28-year-old non-pregnant woman presents to her GP with 24 hours of dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. She has had two similar episodes in the past year both resolved with antibiotics. She has no fever, no flank pain and no vaginal discharge. She is not sexually active in the past 4 weeks. She has no penicillin allergy and no recent antibiotic use. Urinalysis is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites; midstream urine has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 76, RR 14, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no renal angle tenderness, no peritonism, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis - leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood trace, glucose negative; urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 1 g single dose as empirical therapy covering atypical urinary pathogens
options.rationale: Macrolides do not treat the bacteriuria of cystitis (E. coli is the predominant pathogen); azithromycin is not appropriate cystitis therapy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute cystitis)

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days as effective broad-spectrum first-line cystitis therapy
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for failure or resistance to first-line agents due to collateral resistance and adverse effects; they are not first-line for uncomplicated cystitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute cystitis)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice daily for 5 days as broad cover for uncomplicated cystitis
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate has high E. coli resistance and is not first-line; it is reserved for complicated infection or specific resistance patterns. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute cystitis)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days as a broader cephalosporin cystitis option
options.rationale: Cefalexin is acceptable second-line but trimethoprim is preferred first-line in non-pregnant women without contraindication. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute cystitis)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg orally each night for 3 days as empirical therapy for uncomplicated cystitis
options.rationale: Australian Therapeutic Guidelines list trimethoprim 300 mg orally at night for 3 days as first-line for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women without recent trimethoprim use or culture-confirmed resistance. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Acute cystitis)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women in Australia is treated with trimethoprim 300 mg orally at night for 3 days, or nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6-hourly for 5 days, with cefalexin as a second-line option. Fluoroquinolones are reserved due to resistance and adverse effects. Pregnancy, immunosuppression, flank pain or systemic symptoms shift the decision to complicated UTI pathways.
key_points: Trimethoprim 300 mg nocte for 3 days is first-line for uncomplicated cystitis
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days is an equivalent first-line option
Fluoroquinolones are reserved for resistance or failure of first-line therapy
explanation.pearls: Recurrent cystitis (3 or more episodes per year) warrants behavioural advice and, in selected cases, post-coital or continuous low-dose prophylaxis; non-antibiotic options include topical oestrogen in postmenopausal women.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis recognition
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.2%) presents to ED with 36 hours of right leg pain following a minor abrasion. The pain is out of proportion to the visible skin changes. There is firm induration extending beyond the visible erythema and a small area of grey discolouration with a foul-smelling exudate. Blood pressure has fallen from 134/80 in triage to 92/58 mmHg after analgesia. He is alert. Bedside blood tests have returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.6 degrees Celsius, HR 122, RR 26, BP 92/58 mmHg, SpO2 97% in room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Right calf erythema with central grey patch, woody induration extending proximally, severe tenderness on palpation, palpable peripheral pulses, no crepitus on examination
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L, Hb 124 g/L, Na 130 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, CRP 220 mg/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Activate emergency surgical referral for theatre and commence intravenous meropenem with clindamycin
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, woody induration, skin discolouration, sodium below 135 mmol/L and CRP above 150 mg/L give a LRINEC score consistent with necrotising fasciitis; emergent surgical debridement is the cornerstone of treatment alongside broad-spectrum antibiotics including a toxin suppressor (clindamycin or lincomycin). (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections

options.text: Admit for IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6-hourly and review with the surgical team in the morning round
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis requires same-hour surgical debridement; delay until morning rounds increases mortality. Flucloxacillin alone does not cover Gram-negative or anaerobic streptococcal toxin production. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections

options.text: Arrange contrast-enhanced CT of the right leg before contacting surgery to confirm fascial involvement
options.rationale: Imaging may support diagnosis but should not delay surgical exploration when clinical features and biochemistry strongly suggest necrotising fasciitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections

options.text: Admit to general medical unit for IV vancomycin and serial wound photographs to assess progression
options.rationale: Medical management alone is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis; mortality without prompt surgical debridement is around 70 to 80 percent. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections

options.text: Commence intravenous fluid bolus only, then admit to the diabetic foot service for podiatry review
options.rationale: Septic shock with limb signs requires immediate surgical and antimicrobial therapy; admission to podiatry-led pathways without acute surgery loses critical hours. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency. Pain disproportionate to examination, woody induration beyond erythema, skin discolouration or anaesthesia, plus systemic toxicity should prompt urgent surgical debridement. Broad-spectrum antibiotics include carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus a protein synthesis inhibitor (clindamycin or lincomycin) to suppress streptococcal toxin production. Mortality rises sharply with each hour of delay to debridement.
key_points: Pain out of proportion plus woody induration plus systemic toxicity = surgical emergency
LRINEC supports the diagnosis but absence does not exclude necrotising fasciitis
Add a toxin suppressor (clindamycin or lincomycin) to broad antibiotic cover
explanation.pearls: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is adjunctive in some Australian centres for clostridial myonecrosis but does not replace emergent surgical debridement and broad antimicrobial therapy.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: Necrotising soft tissue infections
ANZ Burns and Plastic Surgery Network: Necrotising fasciitis

subtopic_detail: Adult bacterial meningitis empirical
stem: A 38-year-old previously well man presents to ED with 12 hours of fever, severe headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. He is drowsy but obeying commands. There is no rash. He has no penicillin allergy and no recent overseas travel. CT brain is unremarkable. You are preparing to perform a lumbar puncture but blood cultures are not yet drawn. The bedside team is asking about the order of interventions.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.1 degrees Celsius, HR 108, RR 22, BP 122/76 mmHg, SpO2 98% in room air, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Neck stiffness, photophobia, no rash, no focal neurology, pupils equal and reactive, no papilloedema, alert but drowsy
data_table.Investigations: CT brain no mass lesion no haemorrhage no hydrocephalus, WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 240 mg/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 6.8 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate sequence of interventions?

options.text: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV first then blood cultures then dexamethasone then LP if no focal neurology develops
options.rationale: Blood cultures should be drawn before antibiotics where possible (within minutes) and dexamethasone is given with or just before antibiotics for maximum benefit. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Bacterial meningitis)

options.text: Lumbar puncture first then dexamethasone then ceftriaxone after CSF is in the lab and Gram stain returned
options.rationale: Antibiotic delay while awaiting CSF Gram stain increases mortality; antibiotics and dexamethasone should not wait for LP results. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Bacterial meningitis)

options.text: Blood cultures then dexamethasone 10 mg IV then ceftriaxone 2 g IV then lumbar puncture as feasible
options.rationale: Australian guidance for adult bacterial meningitis is blood cultures first, dexamethasone 10 mg IV just before or with the first antibiotic dose, ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly empirically, and LP performed as soon as safely possible after antibiotics are given. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Bacterial meningitis)

options.text: Vancomycin and meropenem with dexamethasone after MRI brain has excluded an epidural collection
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added only if pneumococcal resistance is suspected; meropenem is for penicillin allergy or atypical history; MRI is not the gating step before antibiotics. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Bacterial meningitis)

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IM in the resuscitation area without further CT or LP because of suspected meningococcal disease
options.rationale: IM penicillin is used pre-hospital when transit will delay IV access; in ED with IV access, IV ceftriaxone is preferred and CT is already done. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Bacterial meningitis)

explanation.summary: Adult bacterial meningitis suspected on clinical grounds is treated with empirical ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly, with dexamethasone 10 mg IV given just before or with the first antibiotic dose to reduce neurological sequelae especially in pneumococcal disease. Blood cultures are drawn before antibiotics where feasible; lumbar puncture follows when safe. Add benzylpenicillin or ampicillin to cover Listeria in those over 50 years, pregnant or immunocompromised.
key_points: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV given just before/with first antibiotic dose reduces neuro sequelae
Empirical ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly; add ampicillin for Listeria risk
Antibiotic delay while awaiting LP or imaging increases mortality
explanation.pearls: Indications for CT before LP include focal neurology, GCS under 12, immunocompromise, papilloedema or seizure within 7 days; in their absence, LP can proceed without CT but antibiotics still come first if LP is delayed.

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion testing
stem: A 27-year-old man presents to a sexual health clinic with 10 days of fever, sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy and a non-pruritic maculopapular rash on his trunk. He had unprotected receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 3 weeks ago. He has no past HIV testing history. He is otherwise well. He asks for the most accurate test for acute HIV at this stage of illness. Examination is consistent with mononucleosis-like illness.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 96, RR 16, BP 118/74 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, faint maculopapular rash on trunk, pharyngeal erythema without exudate, no oral candida, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.8 x10^9/L with lymphocyte 1.0 x10^9/L, ALT 78 U/L, monospot pending, EBV/CMV serology pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate diagnostic test?

options.text: HIV RNA PCR quantitative assay to identify acute infection ahead of antibody seroconversion
options.rationale: During acute HIV seroconversion, viral RNA appears around 10 days post-exposure, before HIV antibody seroconversion (typically 3 to 6 weeks); HIV RNA is the test of choice when acute HIV is suspected. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Fourth-generation HIV antibody-antigen combination test alone with retest at 6 weeks if negative
options.rationale: Fourth-generation tests detect p24 antigen and antibodies and have shorter window than antibody-only tests, but HIV RNA is still more sensitive in the very early acute window. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Western blot HIV antibody confirmation as the gold standard for diagnosis of acute infection presentation
options.rationale: Western blot relies on antibody seroconversion (3 to 6 weeks) and is often negative during acute infection; it is no longer first-line confirmation in Australian practice. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: CD4 lymphocyte subset count alone as the most sensitive test for acute HIV at this stage of illness
options.rationale: CD4 count is used for staging after diagnosis and prognostic monitoring; it is not a diagnostic test for acute HIV. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Rapid point-of-care HIV antibody finger-prick test as the most appropriate initial test in this setting
options.rationale: Point-of-care antibody tests have longer window periods than laboratory fourth-generation or RNA testing and may miss acute infection. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion typically presents 2 to 4 weeks after exposure with a mononucleosis-like illness. HIV RNA PCR is detectable from around 10 days, before fourth-generation antibody-antigen tests, and well before antibody-only or Western blot. Australian sexual health practice combines both fourth-generation serology and HIV RNA when acute HIV is suspected to maximise early detection. Post-test discussion, contact tracing and prompt antiretroviral initiation follow confirmed diagnosis.
key_points: HIV RNA PCR is positive earliest in acute infection (around 10 days post-exposure)
Fourth-generation antibody-antigen tests detect p24 and antibodies, window 2 to 3 weeks
Western blot relies on antibody and is often negative in acute infection
explanation.pearls: Detecting acute HIV is high-yield - viral load is highest in primary infection, so identifying and starting antiretroviral therapy markedly reduces onward transmission and may preserve immune function.

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment
stem: A 34-year-old man recently arrived from Vietnam attends a refugee health clinic for screening. He is asymptomatic. He had BCG vaccination in childhood. His QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus is positive. CXR is normal. Sputum cannot be produced. He is not pregnant, not on immunosuppression and not living with HIV. ALT is normal. He has no household contacts of active TB and no other tuberculosis risk factors apart from being from a high-prevalence country.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.6 degrees Celsius, HR 72, RR 14, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air, BMI 22 kg/m^2
data_table.Examination: Well, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, no scars apart from BCG, abdomen unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: QuantiFERON positive (interferon-gamma response above threshold); CXR no infiltrate, no cavitation, no hilar lymphadenopathy; ALT 28 U/L; HIV negative; hepatitis B and C negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure him that QuantiFERON positivity reflects prior BCG and arrange a repeat test in 2 years
options.rationale: QuantiFERON is not affected by BCG vaccination (the antigens are M. tuberculosis-specific ESAT-6 and CFP-10) - a positive result indicates latent infection in this context. (Source: Australian TB Standards)

options.text: Commence rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol four-drug therapy for 2 months then continue 4 months
options.rationale: RIPE is for active TB, not latent infection; the absence of symptoms, normal CXR and negative sputum exclude active disease. (Source: Australian TB Standards)

options.text: Commence isoniazid 300 mg daily with pyridoxine 25 mg for 6 to 9 months and monitor LFTs at baseline and at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Latent TB in a low-risk adult is treated with isoniazid 300 mg orally daily for 6 to 9 months plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily to prevent peripheral neuropathy; LFTs are checked at baseline and at 4 weeks, then if symptomatic. (Source: Australian TB Standards)

options.text: Refer for sputum induction and bronchoscopy to obtain microbiological samples before any treatment is considered
options.rationale: Sputum induction and bronchoscopy are reserved for suspected active pulmonary TB; he has normal CXR and is asymptomatic so they are not indicated. (Source: Australian TB Standards)

options.text: Commence rifampicin 600 mg daily monotherapy for 4 months as a shorter latent TB regimen for low-risk adults
options.rationale: Rifampicin 4 months is an acceptable shorter alternative for some patients, but isoniazid for 6 to 9 months remains the preferred Australian first-line and the patient has no contraindication to isoniazid. (Source: Australian TB Standards)

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection in an asymptomatic adult with positive QuantiFERON and normal CXR is treated with isoniazid 300 mg daily for 6 to 9 months plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily. LFTs are monitored at baseline and 4 weeks, then symptom-driven. Patient education about hepatotoxicity (anorexia, jaundice, dark urine) and the importance of completion is essential. BCG does not cause false-positive QuantiFERON results.
key_points: Isoniazid 300 mg daily for 6 to 9 months plus pyridoxine is AU first-line for LTBI
QuantiFERON uses M. tuberculosis-specific antigens and is not affected by BCG
Hepatotoxicity monitoring with baseline and 4-week LFTs, then symptom-driven
explanation.pearls: Three-month weekly rifapentine and isoniazid (3HP) directly observed is an effective shorter alternative now available in some Australian centres for selected patients with good follow-up.

subtopic_detail: STEMI reperfusion within PCI window
stem: A 58-year-old man presents to a regional emergency department with 40 minutes of crushing central chest pain radiating to the left jaw. He is a current smoker and has hypertension. He has had no previous cardiac events. The nearest 24-hour cardiac catheterisation laboratory is reached by helicopter within 90 minutes, with an expected total door-to-balloon time of 110 minutes from now. There are no contraindications to fibrinolysis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 140/85, HR 95 sinus, RR 20, SpO2 96% on 2 L oxygen via nasal prongs, temp 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, in pain; chest clear; heart sounds normal with no murmur; peripheries cool
data_table.Investigations: ECG: ST elevation 3 mm V1 to V4 with reciprocal inferior depression; troponin pending; potassium 4.0; creatinine 80

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Weight-based intravenous tenecteplase bolus immediately at the current site of presentation
options.rationale: Fibrinolysis is the alternative when primary PCI is not achievable within 120 minutes; with a door-to-balloon under 120 minutes PCI is preferred. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: STEMI clinical care standard)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: STEMI clinical care standard

options.text: Transfer immediately for primary PCI given expected door-to-balloon under 120 minutes
options.rationale: Australian Heart Foundation guidance recommends primary PCI when first medical contact to device time is under 120 minutes; the expected 110 minutes door-to-balloon makes transfer the preferred reperfusion strategy. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: STEMI clinical care standard)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: STEMI clinical care standard

options.text: Loading dose aspirin and ticagrelor with conservative management given short pain duration
options.rationale: Conservative management does not provide reperfusion in STEMI; antiplatelets are adjuncts but the patient still needs primary PCI or fibrinolysis. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Acute coronary syndromes)

options.text: IV unfractionated heparin alone while organising cath lab transfer the following morning
options.rationale: Delaying reperfusion to the next day in an active STEMI is not acceptable; reperfusion must be expedited within minutes to hours. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: STEMI clinical care standard)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: STEMI clinical care standard

options.text: Hospital admission for serial troponins and ECG monitoring before any reperfusion decision
options.rationale: ST elevation on ECG with typical pain establishes STEMI and mandates immediate reperfusion; waiting for troponin would delay therapy and increase infarct size. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: STEMI clinical care standard)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: STEMI clinical care standard

explanation.summary: Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy in STEMI when first medical contact to device time can be achieved within 120 minutes; otherwise fibrinolysis is given followed by transfer for angiography. Aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor are adjuncts but do not replace reperfusion. Waiting for troponins delays time-critical therapy.
key_points: Primary PCI is preferred when door-to-balloon is within 120 minutes
Fibrinolysis is used when timely PCI is not achievable
ECG ST elevation with typical pain establishes STEMI and mandates reperfusion
explanation.pearls: Pre-treatment includes aspirin 300 mg loading, a P2Y12 inhibitor such as ticagrelor 180 mg, and parenteral anticoagulation; transfer should not be delayed for these.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia: STEMI clinical care standard

subtopic_detail: AECOPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure
stem: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD on triple inhaler therapy presents to the emergency department with 3 days of increasing breathlessness and productive purulent sputum. He uses 1 L of home oxygen overnight. He has been a 60 pack-year smoker who recently quit. He is currently sitting upright and able to speak in short sentences.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 32, SpO2 84% in room air, HR 110, BP 145/85, temp 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tripoding, accessory muscle use, audible expiratory wheeze; chest hyperinflated with bilateral wheeze; mild ankle oedema; GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: ABG in room air: pH 7.28, pCO2 78 mmHg, pO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 28; chest x-ray: hyperinflation, no consolidation

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intubate and mechanically ventilate immediately given the degree of respiratory acidosis on ABG
options.rationale: Invasive ventilation is reserved for NIV failure, severely impaired conscious state or other contraindications to NIV; this patient meets criteria for NIV first. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines for COPD)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines for COPD

options.text: High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask targeting SpO2 above 95 with bronchodilators and steroids
options.rationale: Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen risks worsening hypercapnia in COPD; controlled oxygen via Venturi titrated to SpO2 88-92% is recommended. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines for COPD)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines for COPD

options.text: Controlled oxygen 88-92%, BiPAP NIV, nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics
options.rationale: Hypercapnic AECOPD with pH below 7.35 is treated with controlled oxygen titrated to SpO2 88-92%, BiPAP non-invasive ventilation, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone 30-50 mg and antibiotic if purulent sputum or consolidation. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines for COPD)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines for COPD

options.text: Nebulised magnesium sulfate 2 g and IV aminophylline infusion as bronchodilator escalation therapy
options.rationale: Magnesium and aminophylline are not first-line in AECOPD and add toxicity; standard nebulised bronchodilators with NIV and oxygen control are first-line. (Source: eTG Respiratory: Acute exacerbation of COPD)
source_refs: eTG Respiratory: Acute exacerbation of COPD

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 200 mg with empiric antibiotics pending sputum culture and sensitivity results
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone is as effective as IV hydrocortisone in AECOPD and is preferred; corticosteroids alone do not address hypercapnic failure. (Source: eTG Respiratory: Acute exacerbation of COPD)
source_refs: eTG Respiratory: Acute exacerbation of COPD

explanation.summary: Hypercapnic AECOPD with pH below 7.35 is managed with controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 88-92%, BiPAP non-invasive ventilation, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone 30-50 mg for 5 days, and antibiotics if sputum is purulent. Invasive ventilation is reserved for NIV failure or severe impaired conscious state.
key_points: Target SpO2 88-92% in COPD to avoid worsening hypercapnia
BiPAP reduces intubation in pH below 7.35 hypercapnic AECOPD
Oral prednisolone 30-50 mg for 5 days is as effective as IV steroid
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic choice in AECOPD is doxycycline or amoxicillin in Australia; targeted therapy for Pseudomonas is reserved for severe disease, recent hospitalisation or known colonisation.

sources.label: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines for COPD
eTG Respiratory: Acute exacerbation of COPD

subtopic_detail: Add SGLT2i in T2DM with established ASCVD
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 5 years attends his GP for review. His HbA1c is 8.2 percent, up from 7.5 percent 3 months ago, on metformin extended release 2 g daily. He had a percutaneous coronary intervention to the LAD 2 years ago and is on aspirin, atorvastatin, perindopril and metoprolol. He has no symptoms of hypoglycaemia and his renal function is preserved. His BMI is 31.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal; lower limbs no oedema, foot pulses present, monofilament intact bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 8.2%, eGFR 65, ACR 4, fasting glucose 9.2, LDL 1.8, K 4.1, sodium 138; ECG sinus rhythm

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate add-on glucose-lowering therapy?

options.text: Add gliclazide modified release 60 mg daily for additional glycaemic control today
options.rationale: Sulfonylureas do not provide cardiovascular benefit and risk hypoglycaemia; an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist is preferred in established ASCVD. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: T2DM management algorithm)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: T2DM management algorithm

options.text: Add basal insulin glargine 10 units at night titrated to fasting glucose 4-7 mmol/L
options.rationale: Basal insulin is escalation for refractory hyperglycaemia or symptomatic hyperglycaemia; in established ASCVD an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist is preferred first. (Source: RACGP Handbook: Management of T2 diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP Handbook: Management of T2 diabetes

options.text: Switch metformin to a DPP-4 inhibitor sitagliptin 100 mg daily for ease of administration
options.rationale: DPP-4 inhibitors are glucose-lowering only and lack cardiovascular and renal protective effects; metformin should be retained as background therapy. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: T2DM management algorithm)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: T2DM management algorithm

options.text: Add SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin 10 mg daily for cardiovascular and renal benefit
options.rationale: Australian Diabetes Society guidance recommends adding an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist in T2DM with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease regardless of HbA1c, due to reductions in MACE, heart failure and renal events. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: T2DM management algorithm)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: T2DM management algorithm

options.text: Add thiazolidinedione pioglitazone 30 mg daily for its weight-neutral glycaemic profile
options.rationale: Pioglitazone increases heart failure risk and weight gain and is not preferred in established ischaemic heart disease in current Australian guidance. (Source: RACGP Handbook: Management of T2 diabetes)
source_refs: RACGP Handbook: Management of T2 diabetes

explanation.summary: In T2DM with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist is added regardless of HbA1c due to proven cardiovascular and renal benefits. Sulfonylureas and DPP-4 inhibitors do not provide cardiovascular protection. Basal insulin is reserved for refractory hyperglycaemia.
key_points: Add SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA to metformin in T2DM with established ASCVD
Sulfonylureas and DPP-4 inhibitors lack cardiovascular benefit
Pioglitazone is avoided in known heart failure or high HF risk
explanation.pearls: Counsel patients commencing SGLT2 inhibitors about sick-day rules (withhold during acute illness or dehydration), genital mycotic infection risk and the rare risk of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: T2DM management algorithm
RACGP Handbook: Management of T2 diabetes

subtopic_detail: Levothyroxine initiation elderly with IHD
stem: A 68-year-old woman attends her GP with 4 months of fatigue, cold intolerance, a 4 kg weight gain and constipation. She has a history of stable ischaemic heart disease (PCI 6 years ago) on aspirin, metoprolol and atorvastatin. She is otherwise well and not on any antithyroid medication. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 60 sinus, BMI 28
data_table.Examination: Diffuse goitre; dry skin; bradycardia regular; reflexes slow to relax; no peripheral oedema; ECG sinus rhythm with no ischaemic change
data_table.Investigations: TSH 25 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 8 pmol/L (10-22), TPO antibodies positive at 350; HbA1c 5.5, LFTs normal, troponin negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initiation of thyroid hormone replacement?

options.text: Levothyroxine 1.6 mcg/kg daily (approximately 100 mcg) as a full replacement dose now
options.rationale: Full weight-based replacement in older adults with IHD risks precipitating angina or arrhythmia; low-dose initiation with up-titration is recommended. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hypothyroidism initiation guide)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hypothyroidism initiation guide

options.text: Combined levothyroxine 50 mcg with liothyronine 10 mcg daily for symptom control
options.rationale: Combination therapy is not recommended initially and has no proven advantage over levothyroxine monotherapy in Australian guidance. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hypothyroidism initiation guide)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hypothyroidism initiation guide

options.text: Defer treatment and recheck TSH and free T4 in 6 weeks before commencing therapy
options.rationale: Symptomatic overt primary hypothyroidism with TSH 25 and low free T4 warrants prompt initiation, not deferral. (Source: AMH: Levothyroxine)

options.text: Carbimazole 5 mg daily given the autoimmune thyroid disease features and positive TPO
options.rationale: Carbimazole is an antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism; it is contraindicated in this patient with primary hypothyroidism. (Source: AMH: Levothyroxine)

options.text: Levothyroxine 25 mcg daily for 4 weeks then up-titrate guided by TSH at 6 weekly intervals
options.rationale: Older adults with ischaemic heart disease start levothyroxine at 25 mcg daily and up-titrate every 4 to 6 weeks to avoid precipitating angina or arrhythmia; aim for TSH in the lower half of the normal range. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hypothyroidism initiation guide)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hypothyroidism initiation guide

explanation.summary: Initiation of levothyroxine in older adults with ischaemic heart disease is at a low dose (25 mcg daily) with up-titration every 4 to 6 weeks to avoid precipitating myocardial ischaemia or arrhythmia. Full weight-based replacement is reserved for young, fit adults. TSH is rechecked 6-8 weeks after each dose change.
key_points: Start levothyroxine at 25 mcg/day in older adults with IHD
Up-titrate every 4-6 weeks guided by TSH
Avoid combination T4/T3 as initial therapy in Australian guidance
explanation.pearls: If overt hypothyroidism is severe or there is myxoedema coma, intravenous levothyroxine and hydrocortisone are used and ICU support arranged; this differs from outpatient initiation.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hypothyroidism initiation guide

subtopic_detail: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes first step
stem: A 65-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (baseline eGFR 25) and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on ramipril, spironolactone and bisoprolol presents to the emergency department with 2 days of generalised weakness. She has had no diarrhoea or vomiting. She is alert and orientated. Her medication list has been unchanged for 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 130/80, HR 68 sinus, RR 16, SpO2 98% in room air, temp 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Generalised reduced power 4/5, otherwise unremarkable; no peripheral oedema; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Venous K 7.0 (no haemolysis on sample), Na 138, urea 18, creatinine 240, HCO3 18; ECG: tall peaked T waves, PR 220 ms, QRS 110 ms

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate first step?

options.text: IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 minutes for myocardial membrane stabilisation now
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is a cardiac emergency; intravenous calcium gluconate is the first step to stabilise the cardiac membrane while potassium-shifting and removing therapies are commenced. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of severe hyperkalaemia)

options.text: IV insulin actrapid 10 units in 50 mL of 50% dextrose infused over 15 minutes for shifting
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose shifts potassium intracellularly and is given after calcium gluconate when there are ECG changes; it does not stabilise the cardiac membrane. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg via mask repeated every 20 minutes for intracellular potassium shift
options.rationale: Salbutamol is an adjunct to shift potassium intracellularly; it is not the first action when ECG changes are present, where calcium is given first. (Source: eTG Cardiovascular: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate resonium 30 g and dietary potassium restriction now
options.rationale: Resonium removes potassium slowly over hours; it does not address an acute cardiac emergency with ECG changes. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of severe hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis via temporary vascath insertion as definitive therapy at this point
options.rationale: Dialysis may be needed in refractory cases but immediate calcium gluconate is the first action while organising medical therapy and dialysis if required. (Source: KHA-CARI: Management of severe hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is managed in sequence: IV calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilisation, then insulin-dextrose and salbutamol to shift potassium intracellularly, and finally removal with diuretics, resonium or dialysis. Causative drugs are reviewed. ECG monitoring continues until potassium is below 6.0 mmol/L.
key_points: IV calcium gluconate is the first step in hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
Insulin-dextrose and salbutamol shift potassium intracellularly
Resonium and dialysis remove total body potassium
explanation.pearls: Calcium chloride contains 3 times more calcium than gluconate but is reserved for central access due to severe tissue necrosis if extravasated; calcium gluconate is the safer peripheral option.

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome recognition and management
stem: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder (BMI 16, minimal oral intake for 3 weeks) was admitted 3 days ago for community-acquired pneumonia and commenced on standard hospital meals at 1800 kcal/day from day 1. Today he is more confused, weak and short of breath at rest. He has not received thiamine. He is on IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin for pneumonia.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.0 degrees Celsius, HR 110 sinus, BP 105/60, RR 24, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, confused (AMTS 6/10), peripheral oedema bilateral ankles, fine crackles at right base; weak diffuse weakness in all limbs
data_table.Investigations: PO4 0.3 (0.8-1.5), Mg 0.5 (0.7-1.0), K 3.0, corrected Ca 2.0, Na 134, urea 4, creatinine 60, albumin 22, LFTs ALT 60 AST 90, glucose 5.2

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate priority in management?

options.text: Increase oral feeding to meet the calorie deficit and add a daily oral multivitamin supplement
options.rationale: Continuing or increasing calories without electrolyte and thiamine correction worsens refeeding syndrome and risks cardiac arrhythmia and Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: Refeeding syndrome)

options.text: IV phosphate, magnesium and potassium replacement, IV thiamine 300 mg, and reduce calories to 5-10 kcal/kg/day
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is treated by correcting hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia, giving IV thiamine 300 mg daily for at least 3 days before any carbohydrate, and reducing initial caloric intake to 5-10 kcal/kg/day with slow advancement. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: Refeeding syndrome)

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition at full calorie target to prevent further nutritional deterioration
options.rationale: Aggressive caloric delivery via TPN worsens refeeding shifts and risks cardiac arrhythmia; gradual reintroduction is required. (Source: NICE CG32: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: NICE CG32: Nutrition support in adults

options.text: IV thiamine 100 mg single dose with phosphate-rich oral diet and outpatient dietitian review
options.rationale: A single thiamine dose and dietary measures are insufficient; severe deficiency requires parenteral electrolyte replacement and ongoing parenteral thiamine. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: Refeeding syndrome)

options.text: Cease feeding completely for 48 hours until serum electrolytes normalise then restart full diet
options.rationale: Complete cessation of feeding worsens malnutrition; recommended practice is reduced caloric intake with active electrolyte and thiamine replacement. (Source: NICE CG32: Nutrition support in adults)
source_refs: NICE CG32: Nutrition support in adults

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome occurs when starved patients are fed with carbohydrate, causing insulin surge and intracellular shift of phosphate, magnesium and potassium. Management is electrolyte replacement, IV thiamine 300 mg daily for at least 3 days before any carbohydrate, and slow reintroduction at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolytes for the first week.
key_points: Hypophosphataemia is the cardinal feature of refeeding syndrome
Thiamine 300 mg IV is given before any carbohydrate in at-risk patients
Caloric intake starts at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with slow advancement
explanation.pearls: High-risk features for refeeding are BMI under 16, weight loss above 15% in 3-6 months, minimal nutrition for over 10 days, or low baseline phosphate, magnesium or potassium before feeding.

sources.label: NICE CG32: Nutrition support in adults

subtopic_detail: High-risk TIA DAPT for 21 days
stem: A 70-year-old man presents 2 hours after an episode of right hemiparesis and dysphasia lasting 30 minutes that fully resolved before arrival. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and is a current smoker. He is on perindopril and metformin. He has had no prior cerebrovascular events. There is no history of atrial fibrillation. ECG shows sinus rhythm.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/95, HR 78 sinus, BMI 28, capillary glucose 8.4
data_table.Examination: GCS 15, speech now fluent and clear, no focal weakness or facial droop, gait normal; carotid auscultation no bruit
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: no acute infarct, no haemorrhage; ABCD2 score 5; troponin negative; INR 1.0

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily monotherapy with outpatient clinic review in approximately 4 weeks
options.rationale: Aspirin alone is inadequate for high-risk TIA in the first 3 weeks; dual antiplatelet therapy reduces early recurrent stroke per CHANCE and POINT trials. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Warfarin loading 5 mg daily targeting an INR 2-3 commencing today as anticoagulation now
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is for cardioembolic stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation or other indications; there is no AF demonstrated and warfarin is not indicated for non-cardioembolic TIA. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention

options.text: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, high-intensity statin and urgent stroke clinic review
options.rationale: High-risk TIA (ABCD2 above 4 or minor stroke with NIHSS up to 3) is treated with aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days then aspirin alone, high-intensity statin, BP control and urgent stroke clinic review within 24-48 hours. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: IV thrombolysis with tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg given the high stroke recurrence risk profile
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is reserved for established ischaemic stroke within the eligibility window, not for TIA with resolved symptoms. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Direct oral anticoagulant apixaban 5 mg twice daily empirically pending further investigations
options.rationale: DOACs are not indicated for non-cardioembolic TIA; investigation for AF is appropriate but empirical anticoagulation is not. (Source: National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention

explanation.summary: High-risk TIA (ABCD2 above 4) or minor ischaemic stroke is treated with 21 days of dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) followed by aspirin alone, high-intensity statin, BP and glycaemic control, and urgent stroke clinic review within 24-48 hours. Anticoagulation is reserved for cardioembolic causes.
key_points: ABCD2 above 4 or minor stroke NIHSS up to 3 indicates DAPT for 21 days
Add high-intensity statin and aggressive BP control
Urgent stroke clinic review and AF screening within 24-48 hours
explanation.pearls: Prolonged cardiac monitoring (Holter or implantable loop recorder) is indicated when initial ECG is normal and a cardioembolic source remains a concern after standard workup.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
National Heart Foundation: Secondary stroke prevention

subtopic_detail: TTP recognition and urgent plasma exchange
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 3 days of progressive fatigue, petechial rash on her shins, intermittent confusion and a low-grade fever. She has had no recent infection, no diarrhoea, and is on no medications. She has no personal or family history of bleeding. She is not pregnant. She is alert but mildly drowsy with fluctuating attention.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.0 degrees Celsius, HR 100 sinus, BP 128/76, RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Petechial rash on shins, mild confusion (AMTS 7/10), no focal neurology, no overt bleeding, no splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 75, platelets 12, blood film schistocytes 4+, reticulocytes elevated, LDH 1500, haptoglobin undetectable, total bilirubin 60 (indirect 50), creatinine 130, PT and APTT normal, fibrinogen 3.2, DAT negative; ADAMTS13 activity sample sent

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent platelet transfusion to a count above 50 and IV ceftriaxone empiric sepsis cover today
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is contraindicated in TTP unless life-threatening bleeding, due to risk of worsening microvascular thrombosis; antibiotics do not address the underlying ADAMTS13 deficiency. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura guideline)

options.text: IV immunoglobulin 1 g/kg over 2 days for presumed immune thrombocytopenic purpura disorder
options.rationale: Microangiopathic haemolysis with neurological signs and renal injury and very low platelets fits TTP not ITP; IVIG would delay definitive plasma exchange. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura guideline)

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis given acute kidney injury with electrolyte derangement and uraemia present
options.rationale: AKI in TTP is part of the microangiopathic process and is treated by plasma exchange; haemodialysis is reserved for refractory metabolic indications. (Source: ANZSBT: Therapeutic apheresis indications)

options.text: Urgent therapeutic plasma exchange and IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily while ADAMTS13 pending
options.rationale: Suspected TTP requires urgent initiation of therapeutic plasma exchange (within hours), high-dose corticosteroids, and addition of caplacizumab and rituximab in acquired disease while awaiting ADAMTS13 results; outcome depends on minimising delay. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura guideline)

options.text: Therapeutic anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin for thrombotic microangiopathy syndrome
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is not indicated in TTP and would worsen bleeding with thrombocytopenia; plasma exchange and steroids are first-line. (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura guideline)

explanation.summary: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura presents with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, renal injury and fever; ADAMTS13 activity is very low. Urgent therapeutic plasma exchange and high-dose corticosteroids must be initiated within hours of suspicion. Caplacizumab and rituximab are added in immune TTP. Platelet transfusion is avoided unless life-threatening bleeding.
key_points: TTP pentad: MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurological, renal, fever
Initiate plasma exchange within hours of suspicion, do not wait for ADAMTS13
Platelet transfusion is avoided unless life-threatening bleeding
explanation.pearls: Differentiate TTP from atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (complement-mediated, treated with eculizumab) and from DIC (abnormal coagulation, low fibrinogen, treat the cause).

subtopic_detail: Clostridioides difficile first non-severe episode
stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to ED with 4 days of watery non-bloody diarrhoea 6 times daily after a 7-day course of oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for cellulitis ended 10 days ago. She is haemodynamically stable, mildly dehydrated, and tolerating oral fluids. She has no abdominal distension, no peritonism and no ileus. She takes a proton pump inhibitor for reflux and lives independently with her husband at home.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/76, HR 92, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild lower abdominal tenderness without guarding; bowel sounds present; mucous membranes a little dry
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.4 x10^9/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 70), lactate 1.4 mmol/L, CRP 32 mg/L, stool PCR positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin B gene

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate antimicrobial choice?

options.text: Intravenous metronidazole 500 mg eight hourly for 10 days alongside ongoing oral PPI therapy to suppress gastric acid recurrence
options.rationale: IV metronidazole achieves poor colonic concentrations in CDI; current AU and international guidance favours oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin even for non-severe disease. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)

options.text: Oral loperamide 4 mg followed by 2 mg after each loose stool and no antibiotic therapy initiated until repeat testing in 48 hours
options.rationale: Antimotility agents are contraindicated in CDI because of toxic megacolon risk; treatment should not be delayed in a PCR-positive symptomatic case. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)

options.text: Oral rifaximin 400 mg three times daily for 14 days as the first-line agent for community-acquired Clostridioides difficile infection in adults
options.rationale: Rifaximin is used as a tapered chaser for recurrent CDI in some protocols, not as primary therapy for a first episode. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)

options.text: Faecal microbiota transplant via colonoscopy as the first-line approach for an initial non-severe Clostridioides difficile episode in this patient
options.rationale: FMT is reserved for multiply recurrent CDI after standard antibiotic regimens have failed; it is not first-line for an initial episode. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)

options.text: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days with cessation of the inciting antibiotic and ongoing oral rehydration support
options.rationale: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days is the AU first-line regimen for non-severe CDI; metronidazole is no longer preferred. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: C difficile)

explanation.summary: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days has become first-line for non-severe Clostridioides difficile infection in Australia, displacing metronidazole on the strength of higher cure and reduced recurrence. Fidaxomicin is an alternative, particularly when recurrence risk is high. Severe disease, ileus, megacolon or sepsis prompts admission, oral plus rectal vancomycin and surgical review. Antimotility agents are avoided. FMT is reserved for multiple recurrences.
key_points: Oral vancomycin 125 mg QID for 10 days is first-line in non-severe CDI
Loperamide is contraindicated because of toxic megacolon risk
FMT is reserved for multiply recurrent disease after standard antibiotic failure
explanation.pearls: Stop the inciting antibiotic whenever possible at CDI diagnosis; this alone resolves around a quarter of mild cases before oral vancomycin has finished a 10-day course.

sources.label: ACSQHC: Clostridioides difficile clinical care standard

subtopic_detail: Atrial flutter haemodynamically stable rate control
stem: A 72-year-old man with hypertension and reflux presents to ED with 6 hours of palpitations and mild exertional dyspnoea. He has no chest pain, no syncope, no heart failure symptoms and a known LV ejection fraction of 58 percent on a recent transthoracic echocardiogram. His CHA2DS2-VA score is 3. He is otherwise well, has no chronic kidney disease and weighs 84 kg. There is no obvious precipitant such as alcohol or recent infection.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/86, HR 138 irregularly regular pattern on monitor, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Clear lungs, no peripheral oedema, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: ECG shows sawtooth flutter waves with 2:1 AV conduction, ventricular rate 138; troponin negative; TSH 1.4 mU/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; potassium 4.1 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial rate-control choice?

options.text: Oral metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily commenced now with cardiology follow-up for outpatient anticoagulation decision after CHA2DS2-VA review
options.rationale: Beta blockade is first-line rate control in atrial flutter with preserved LVEF and no heart failure; CHA2DS2-VA above 2 requires anticoagulation review. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)

options.text: Intravenous adenosine 6 mg rapid push then 12 mg as the first-line agent to convert flutter rhythm to sinus rhythm in the emergency department
options.rationale: Adenosine transiently unmasks flutter waves but does not convert flutter; it is diagnostic, not therapeutic, in this rhythm. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 1 hour then 900 mg over 24 hours as the first-line agent for rate control in stable atrial flutter
options.rationale: Amiodarone is reserved for rhythm control in selected patients, often with heart failure; it is not first-line rate control for stable preserved-EF flutter. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)

options.text: Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation despite haemodynamic stability and a duration of arrhythmia under 12 hours without anticoagulation
options.rationale: Elective cardioversion in stable patients with arrhythmia under 48 hours can be considered but is not the routine first step; rate control with anticoagulation review is the AU pathway. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)

options.text: Oral digoxin 250 micrograms daily as monotherapy for rate control in this active 72-year-old with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction and reflux
options.rationale: Digoxin monotherapy provides poor rate control during exertion and is reserved for patients with sedentary lifestyle or as add-on; not first-line in this man. (Source: NHFA atrial fibrillation guideline; CSANZ)

explanation.summary: Stable atrial flutter with preserved LVEF is rate-controlled with a beta blocker (or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker if beta blockade is not tolerated). Digoxin is reserved for sedentary patients or as an add-on. Adenosine has a diagnostic role by transiently unmasking flutter waves but does not convert. Anticoagulation follows CHA2DS2-VA assessment; this man with a score of 3 warrants long-term oral anticoagulation.
key_points: Beta blockers are first-line rate control in flutter with preserved LVEF
Adenosine is diagnostic, not therapeutic, in flutter
CHA2DS2-VA >= 2 prompts oral anticoagulation in Australian guidance
explanation.pearls: A regularly conducted narrow-complex tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise; vagal manoeuvres or adenosine will reveal the sawtooth pattern.

subtopic_detail: Acute gallstone pancreatitis early management
stem: A 54-year-old woman presents to ED with 8 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, with vomiting. She has no fever, no jaundice and no haemodynamic instability. Her lipase is 8 times the upper limit of normal and her ALT is twice normal. An abdominal ultrasound shows gallstones in a non-distended gallbladder, a normal-calibre common bile duct without stones, and no choledocholithiasis. She is haemodynamically stable and tolerates small sips of water in ED.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, Temp 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Epigastric tenderness without peritonism, no guarding; bowel sounds normal; no Cullen or Grey Turner signs
data_table.Investigations: Lipase 1880 U/L, ALT 92 U/L, bilirubin 18 micromol/L, GGT 124 U/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, calcium 2.32 mmol/L, urea 5.2 mmol/L, CRP 24 mg/L; ultrasound as described above

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial in-hospital management plan?

options.text: Urgent endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography within 24 hours regardless of jaundice status or imaging evidence of choledocholithiasis identified
options.rationale: Urgent ERCP is reserved for gallstone pancreatitis with ascending cholangitis or persisting obstruction; without those features there is no early ERCP benefit. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)

options.text: Admit, restrict to nil by mouth for 5 to 7 days, total parenteral nutrition from day 1 and re-image with CT to grade severity at 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Prolonged NBM and TPN are no longer preferred; early enteral feeding within 24 to 48 hours improves outcomes; routine early CT is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or deterioration. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)

options.text: Discharge home with oral analgesia and elective outpatient cholecystectomy in 6 weeks regardless of ongoing pain, hydration status or oral tolerance during the admission today
options.rationale: Acute pancreatitis requires admission for IV fluids and analgesia; discharge from ED with active disease is inappropriate. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g six hourly from admission to prevent peripancreatic infection in this patient with mild gallstone pancreatitis today
options.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics do not improve outcomes in mild pancreatitis and are reserved for proven infection or infected necrosis. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)

options.text: Admit for intravenous Hartmann's resuscitation, parenteral analgesia, early oral or enteral feeding within 24 to 48 hours and same-admission laparoscopic cholecystectomy
options.rationale: AU and GESA guidance recommend goal-directed fluids, early feeding and same-admission cholecystectomy for mild gallstone pancreatitis. (Source: GESA gallstone disease guidance)

explanation.summary: Mild gallstone pancreatitis is managed with goal-directed intravenous crystalloid (Hartmann's preferred), parenteral analgesia, early oral or enteral feeding within 24 to 48 hours, and same-admission laparoscopic cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence. Prophylactic antibiotics do not improve outcomes. Urgent ERCP is reserved for cholangitis or persisting common bile duct obstruction. Severity assessment can be made with bedside scores supplemented by lactate and urea trends.
key_points: Same-admission laparoscopic cholecystectomy is recommended for mild gallstone pancreatitis
Early enteral feeding within 24 to 48 hours improves outcomes versus prolonged NBM
Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated in mild pancreatitis without infection
explanation.pearls: Same-admission cholecystectomy after mild gallstone pancreatitis reduces 30-day readmission for recurrent biliary events by around 75 percent compared with delayed surgery.

subtopic_detail: Mild diabetic foot infection outpatient management
stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 12 years presents to his GP with a 3-day history of a warm, mildly painful 2 cm ulcer over the second metatarsal head with surrounding erythema extending 1 cm from the wound. He has no fever, no streaking lymphangitis and a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse. There is no probe-to-bone and no exposed tendon or capsule. He has no penicillin allergy and his HbA1c is 7.2 percent. He has full ankle range of motion.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82, HR 80, Temp 36.9 degrees Celsius, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: 2 cm shallow plantar ulcer; surrounding cellulitis 1 cm wide; pedal pulses palpable; no probe-to-bone; sensation diminished to 10 g monofilament at first metatarsal head bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: WCC 8.4 x10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L, HbA1c 7.2%, creatinine 88 micromol/L, plain foot X-ray negative for osteomyelitis

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate antimicrobial regimen?

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days, daily dressing changes, off-loading and review at 5 to 7 days with high-risk foot service input as needed
options.rationale: Mild diabetic foot infection in a non-allergic patient is treated with narrow-spectrum oral antistaphylococcal antibiotics; flucloxacillin is AU first-line. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g six hourly for 7 days in hospital with vascular and orthopaedic review on admission to manage anaerobic and Pseudomonas cover today
options.rationale: Mild diabetic foot infection without systemic features does not require IV broad-spectrum therapy or admission. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)

options.text: Topical mupirocin 2 percent ointment three times daily for 7 days without any systemic antibiotic therapy initiated at this presentation in the practice today
options.rationale: Surrounding cellulitis indicates a need for systemic, not topical, antibiotics in diabetic foot infection. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)

options.text: Oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 7 days as the sole antibiotic agent to cover anaerobic skin flora colonising the diabetic ulcer base today
options.rationale: Anaerobic monotherapy misses the dominant Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species in mild infections. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 28 days plus oral clindamycin 450 mg eight hourly for 28 days for a prolonged course of dual-agent therapy
options.rationale: Mild infections require around 7 days of treatment; prolonged dual therapy is reserved for osteomyelitis or moderate-severe infection. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot infection)

explanation.summary: Mild diabetic foot infection (cellulitis under 2 cm wide, no systemic features) is treated with oral narrow-spectrum antistaphylococcal antibiotics. Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days is AU first-line; cefalexin substitutes in non-severe penicillin allergy. Concurrent off-loading, sharp debridement, dressings and glycaemic optimisation are essential. Pseudomonas cover is not required in mild infection. Probe-to-bone or exposed bone prompts MRI and osteomyelitis pathway.
key_points: Flucloxacillin 500 mg QID for 7 days is AU first-line for mild diabetic foot infection
Off-loading and debridement are as important as antibiotics in foot infection
Probe-to-bone or positive bone exposure triggers osteomyelitis workup with MRI
explanation.pearls: Probe-to-bone positivity in a diabetic foot ulcer has a positive predictive value above 80 percent for underlying osteomyelitis and prompts MRI rather than plain film alone.

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection
stem: A 64-year-old man presents to ED with 2 hours of sudden tearing interscapular pain radiating to the lower back. His BP is 178/108 in the right arm and 174/106 in the left arm. There is no neurological deficit, no limb ischaemia and no mesenteric ischaemia features. A CT aortogram shows a dissection flap originating distal to the left subclavian artery extending into the proximal abdominal aorta, with no aortic rupture or visceral malperfusion. He has known hypertension on irregular ramipril.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 178/108, HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius
