data_table.Examination: Equal peripheral pulses, no neurological deficit, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Troponin negative, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L; CT angiogram as described; ECG no ischaemic changes; chest X-ray widened mediastinum

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological priority?

options.text: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 600 micrograms followed by oral amlodipine 10 mg as the priority agent for blood pressure control in this presentation today
options.rationale: Vasodilators alone can reflex-increase shear stress (dP/dt); rate control with a beta blocker must precede or accompany them. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)

options.text: Intravenous fluid loading with 1 litre of 0.9 percent saline followed by oral metoprolol tartrate 50 mg as initial management in this acute aortic syndrome presentation today
options.rationale: Fluid loading is inappropriate in hypertensive dissection and oral beta blockade is too slow for acute shear stress reduction. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)

options.text: Emergent transfer for open thoracotomy and graft repair of the descending aorta as the priority intervention for this uncomplicated type B aortic dissection patient today
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B dissection is initially medical; surgery or TEVAR is reserved for malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)

options.text: Intravenous unfractionated heparin loading at 80 units/kg then a continuous infusion to prevent dissection flap thrombosis and downstream ischaemia in this man today
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection because of haemorrhage and false lumen extension risk. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)

options.text: Intravenous esmolol or labetalol infusion titrated to heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 120 mmHg, plus parenteral analgesia and urgent vascular surgery review
options.rationale: Acute aortic dissection management targets shear stress reduction with IV beta blockade first, BP under 120 systolic, vasodilator added second if needed. (Source: NHFA aortic syndromes statement)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection management centres on reducing aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt). Intravenous beta blockade (esmolol or labetalol) is started first, targeting heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 120 mmHg, with a vasodilator added if BP control is inadequate. Uncomplicated type B dissection is medically managed; complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain) is treated with TEVAR. Type A dissection requires urgent cardiothoracic surgery.
key_points: Target heart rate under 60 and systolic BP under 120 mmHg with IV beta blockade first
Vasodilators are added second after beta blockade to avoid reflex tachycardia and shear stress
Uncomplicated type B dissection is medically managed; complicated type B prompts TEVAR
explanation.pearls: Always start a beta blocker before any vasodilator in aortic dissection because pure vasodilator therapy causes reflex tachycardia and increased dP/dt, worsening shear stress on the dissection flap.

subtopic_detail: Severe acute ulcerative colitis with Truelove-Witts criteria
stem: A 28-year-old man with a 3-year history of ulcerative colitis on oral mesalazine presents with 7 days of worsening bloody diarrhoea now occurring 10 times per day with marked nocturnal symptoms. He has crampy abdominal pain and feels systemically unwell. He has no recent travel, no recent antibiotics, and is up to date with vaccinations. There is no toxic megacolon on plain abdominal X-ray and no peritonism on examination today in the ward bed area.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/70, HR 108, RR 18, Temp 38.1 degrees Celsius, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with diffuse mild tenderness, no guarding, no rebound; bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, platelets 480 x10^9/L, CRP 84 mg/L, albumin 28 g/L; stool C difficile PCR negative, faecal calprotectin elevated; plain abdominal X-ray no megacolon

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg six hourly, VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin, and stool tests including Clostridioides difficile PCR with daily reassessment of response
options.rationale: Truelove-Witts severe UC is treated with IV corticosteroids and VTE prophylaxis; CDI testing rules out the major mimic. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)

options.text: Continue oral mesalazine 4 g daily and add oral budesonide 9 mg daily with outpatient gastroenterology review in 2 weeks once symptoms have plateaued at the current intensity
options.rationale: Oral aminosalicylates and budesonide are inadequate for severe acute UC; IV steroids are required. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)

options.text: Commence empirical oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily and oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for 7 days to cover bacterial overgrowth and travel-related pathogens today
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are not first-line in acute severe UC without infection; they delay definitive immunosuppression. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)

options.text: Commence subcutaneous adalimumab 160 mg loading dose today and 80 mg in 2 weeks as the first-line biologic agent without starting any intravenous corticosteroid therapy beforehand
options.rationale: Biologics are second-line after failure or contraindication to IV corticosteroids in acute severe UC; adalimumab is not first-choice rescue. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)

options.text: Plan urgent total colectomy within 24 hours of admission regardless of corticosteroid response in this patient with acute severe ulcerative colitis presentation now today
options.rationale: Colectomy is for failure of medical rescue, toxic megacolon, perforation or massive haemorrhage; not an immediate first response. (Source: GESA IBD guidance)

explanation.summary: Acute severe ulcerative colitis (Truelove-Witts criteria) is treated by admission, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg six hourly, VTE prophylaxis (despite bleeding), CDI exclusion, and daily clinical reassessment. Day 3 Travis criteria (stool frequency above 8 or CRP above 45 mg/L with 3 to 8 stools) predict steroid failure and trigger rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin and surgical review. Colectomy is reserved for refractory or complicated disease.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg six hourly is first-line in acute severe UC
Day 3 Travis criteria identify steroid non-responders for rescue therapy
VTE prophylaxis is essential despite bloody stools because of pro-thrombotic flare state
explanation.pearls: Day 3 of IV steroids: more than 8 stools per day or CRP above 45 with 3 to 8 stools predicts steroid failure and triggers infliximab or ciclosporin rescue and surgical co-review.

subtopic_detail: Vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological features
stem: A 64-year-old woman presents to her GP with 3 months of progressive fatigue, paraesthesiae of the toes and increasing unsteadiness when walking in the dark. She has type 1 diabetes on insulin and a 20-year history of metformin use was stopped earlier this year. She has no history of pernicious anaemia, no recent bowel surgery and no vegan dietary restriction. She has no recent change in medications and no history of alcohol misuse documented in her file.

data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration sense at the great toes bilaterally; impaired joint position sense; positive Romberg; normal cranial nerves; brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, MCV 108 fL, platelets 220 x10^9/L, WCC 4.6 x10^9/L; serum B12 78 pmol/L (reference > 200 pmol/L); folate 14 nmol/L; TSH 1.4 mU/L; anti-intrinsic factor antibody positive

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin 1000 micrograms every other day for 1 to 2 weeks until neurological progression halts, then maintenance every 3 months for life
options.rationale: Pernicious anaemia with neurological involvement is treated with IM hydroxocobalamin loading then 3-monthly maintenance for life. (Source: AMH: hydroxocobalamin)

options.text: Oral cyanocobalamin 1 mg daily for life without intramuscular loading therapy as the first-line treatment of vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological signs in this Australian outpatient
options.rationale: Oral high-dose B12 is acceptable in dietary deficiency without neurological features; AU practice prefers IM loading for neurological involvement. (Source: AMH: hydroxocobalamin)

options.text: Oral folic acid 5 mg daily for 4 months alone, repeating macrocytic anaemia indices in 4 to 6 weeks, with no B12 supplementation initiated in this presentation in primary care today
options.rationale: Giving folate alone can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. (Source: AMH: folic acid)

options.text: Pack-red-cell transfusion of 2 units in the day ward as the first-line therapy for symptomatic macrocytic anaemia at a haemoglobin of 102 g/L in this older woman today in the GP rooms
options.rationale: Hb 102 with stable cardiorespiratory status does not warrant transfusion; correction of the deficiency restores haematopoiesis. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management)

options.text: Recommence metformin 500 mg twice daily and add iron polymaltose 105 mg once daily to address the macrocytic anaemia she has developed since stopping metformin earlier this year today
options.rationale: Metformin causes B12 deficiency, not macrocytic anaemia from its withdrawal; iron addresses microcytic, not macrocytic anaemia. (Source: AMH: metformin and B12)

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological features (subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns) requires intramuscular hydroxocobalamin loading followed by lifelong maintenance every 3 months in pernicious anaemia. Oral high-dose cyanocobalamin is acceptable in dietary deficiency without neurological involvement. Folate must never precede B12 replacement in macrocytic anaemia because of precipitation risk. Metformin and PPIs are common contributors. Anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies support pernicious anaemia.
key_points: IM hydroxocobalamin loading is preferred in B12 deficiency with neurological features
Never give folate before B12 in macrocytic anaemia because of SCDC precipitation risk
Metformin and PPIs are common contributors to B12 deficiency
explanation.pearls: Hydroxocobalamin 1000 micrograms intramuscular every 2 to 3 days for 2 weeks then 3-monthly for life is the AU regimen for pernicious anaemia with neurological involvement.

subtopic_detail: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy acute management
stem: A 65-year-old woman with newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer presents to ED with 5 days of confusion, polyuria, polydipsia and constipation. She is no longer eating or drinking well. She has no chronic kidney disease, no current bisphosphonate use, no known QT prolongation, no atrial fibrillation, and is not currently on diuretics. Her dental review for jaw clearance was unremarkable last month, and there is no evidence of osteonecrosis of the jaw.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68, HR 102, RR 18, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, GCS 14 (confused), no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.4 mmol/L, phosphate 0.7 mmol/L, albumin 32 g/L, creatinine 124 micromol/L (baseline 78), Mg 0.78 mmol/L; PTH suppressed; PTHrP elevated; ECG QTc 380 ms

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Intravenous frusemide 40 mg eight hourly without prior fluid resuscitation, with hourly monitoring of urine output and serum electrolytes in this woman to forcibly diurese calcium quickly
options.rationale: Loop diuretics are added only after adequate volume repletion in normal renal function; using them first worsens dehydration and hypercalcaemia. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)

options.text: Aggressive intravenous saline rehydration with 3 to 4 litres in the first 24 hours and intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg once renal function permits, plus calcitonin if symptomatic in the meantime
options.rationale: Volume repletion with saline is the first-line move; IV zoledronic acid provides sustained calcium lowering once renal function is restored; calcitonin offers a rapid bridging effect. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis as the first intervention before any intravenous fluid challenge or pharmacological calcium-lowering therapy is administered in this hypercalcaemia of malignancy presentation today
options.rationale: Dialysis is reserved for severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia with renal failure not responsive to fluids and pharmacology; not first-line. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab 120 mg as the immediate first-line therapy for hypercalcaemia of malignancy in this woman with otherwise normal renal function and no prior antiresorptive therapy
options.rationale: Denosumab is used when bisphosphonates fail or are contraindicated by renal failure; it is not first-line monotherapy in initial hypercalcaemia. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)

options.text: Oral cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily commenced from admission as the immediate first-line treatment for hypercalcaemia of malignancy in this woman before any intravenous saline rehydration begins
options.rationale: Cinacalcet is used in parathyroid carcinoma and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, not as first-line for hypercalcaemia of malignancy. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: hypercalcaemia)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy requires aggressive intravenous saline rehydration (3 to 4 litres over 24 hours), correction of magnesium and potassium, and a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid 4 mg IV) once renal function permits. Calcitonin (4 IU/kg 12-hourly) gives faster but short-lived calcium lowering as a bridge in symptomatic patients. Denosumab is used when bisphosphonates fail or in renal failure. Loop diuretics are added only after volume repletion in normal renal function.
key_points: Saline rehydration precedes any pharmacological calcium-lowering therapy
Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV gives sustained calcium lowering within 48 hours
Calcitonin acts within hours but with tachyphylaxis within 48 hours
explanation.pearls: Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV lowers calcium across 48 to 96 hours with effects lasting around 4 weeks; calcitonin 4 IU/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours bridges that delay but loses effect within 48 hours.

subtopic_detail: Hereditary angioedema with laryngeal involvement
stem: A 34-year-old man presents to ED with acute swelling of the lips and tongue and a hoarse voice that started 90 minutes ago. He has had four similar previous episodes of non-pruritic, non-urticarial facial swelling, two with abdominal cramping pain that required admission. His father has the same problem. He is not on any new medications, has had no insect stings, no new foods and no contact with latex. Standard intramuscular adrenaline and intravenous antihistamines have had minimal effect.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82, HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tongue and lip oedema, hoarse voice, no urticaria, no wheeze, no hypotension
data_table.Investigations: Tryptase pending; previous serology: C4 0.04 g/L (low), C1 esterase inhibitor functional activity 22 percent of normal (low) on stored bloods; FBC and UEC normal today

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next therapeutic agent?

options.text: A further dose of intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms with an intravenous adrenaline infusion at low dose as the priority therapy for refractory angioedema in this patient
options.rationale: Adrenaline targets histamine-mediated anaphylaxis; bradykinin-mediated HAE does not respond to adrenaline, antihistamines or corticosteroids. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg, intravenous chlorphenamine 10 mg, and nebulised salbutamol 5 mg as the priority therapy for this severe refractory angioedema episode in the emergency department today
options.rationale: Corticosteroids, antihistamines and beta agonists do not work in bradykinin-mediated HAE; targeted C1-INH replacement or bradykinin pathway inhibition is required. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)

options.text: Intravenous C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate (20 IU/kg) or subcutaneous icatibant 30 mg as targeted bradykinin pathway therapy with airway-ready ENT and anaesthetic backup
options.rationale: HAE laryngeal attacks require C1-INH concentrate or icatibant as first-line; ASCIA recommends airway-ready monitoring. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)

options.text: Oral danazol 200 mg three times daily commenced now as acute therapy for this hereditary angioedema attack, with intravenous antihistamines and observation in the short stay unit afterwards
options.rationale: Danazol is long-term prophylaxis in HAE, not acute attack therapy; onset is far too slow for laryngeal involvement. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)

options.text: Endotracheal intubation under general anaesthesia and observation in the intensive care unit without administering any specific pharmacological angioedema-directed therapy in the meantime
options.rationale: Airway management plans must be in place, but specific HAE therapy is not delayed; C1-INH or icatibant is given concurrently with airway preparation. (Source: ASCIA HAE guidance)

explanation.summary: Hereditary angioedema is bradykinin-mediated and does not respond to adrenaline, antihistamines or corticosteroids. Acute attacks (especially laryngeal) are treated with C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist) or ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor), alongside airway preparedness. Long-term prophylaxis options include attenuated androgens (danazol), tranexamic acid, lanadelumab, and prophylactic C1-INH. C4 is a useful screening test in steady state.
key_points: HAE does not respond to adrenaline, antihistamines or corticosteroids
Acute therapy is C1-INH concentrate or icatibant alongside airway preparedness
Danazol is long-term prophylaxis, not acute attack therapy
explanation.pearls: A persistently low C4 between attacks is the most useful screening test for hereditary angioedema and prompts confirmatory C1 esterase inhibitor antigenic and functional assays.

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma crisis preoperative blockade
stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to ED with episodic palpitations, sweating and severe headaches over 6 months, today with BP 224/128, headache and chest pain. Imaging in the last week showed a 4 cm right adrenal lesion with characteristic features on MRI. 24-hour fractionated urinary metanephrines were elevated at 5 times the upper limit of normal. She has no asthma, no diabetes, no current beta blocker and no contraindications to alpha or beta blockade. She is haemodynamically tachycardic in ED.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 224/128, HR 124, RR 18, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Pale, sweating, no focal neurological deficit, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Investigations: Troponin negative, ECG sinus tachycardia, CT brain normal; 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines 5 x ULN one week ago

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next pharmacological priority?

options.text: Intravenous metoprolol 5 mg increments as the priority agent to immediately bring the resting heart rate to under 80 in this woman with a hypertensive crisis presentation today
options.rationale: Beta blockade before adequate alpha blockade causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and worsens crisis; avoid until alpha-blocked. (Source: AMH: phenoxybenzamine; eTG Endocrinology: phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg as the priority agent to rapidly drop blood pressure into the normotensive range in this woman with hypertensive crisis in the emergency department in front of you
options.rationale: Short-acting sublingual nifedipine causes rapid swings and reflex tachycardia and is not preferred; alpha blockade is the targeted therapy. (Source: AMH: nifedipine)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus then 1 g per hour as the first-line agent to provide vasodilation and antiarrhythmic effect in this woman with severe catecholamine excess and hypertension today
options.rationale: Magnesium is an adjunct in severe phaeochromocytoma crisis but is not first-line monotherapy; alpha blockade is the pillar. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Commence alpha blockade with intravenous phentolamine boluses now and transition to oral phenoxybenzamine over the next 7 to 14 days before adding any beta blocker for sinus tachycardia
options.rationale: Phaeochromocytoma management requires alpha blockade first; beta blockade is added only after alpha blockade is established to avoid unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Refer for urgent laparoscopic adrenalectomy within 24 hours without any pharmacological optimisation in this woman with biochemically confirmed phaeochromocytoma and current hypertensive crisis
options.rationale: Adrenalectomy without 7 to 14 days of alpha blockade and 2 to 3 days of beta blockade is associated with severe intraoperative crisis and mortality. (Source: eTG Endocrinology: phaeochromocytoma)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma crisis is managed with alpha blockade first (intravenous phentolamine in crisis, oral phenoxybenzamine for at least 7 to 14 days preoperatively), followed by beta blockade for tachycardia once alpha blockade is established. Beta blockade alone causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and worsens hypertension. Adequate salt and fluid loading is required during alpha blockade. Surgery is planned after biochemical and haemodynamic optimisation.
key_points: Alpha blockade precedes beta blockade by 7 to 14 days preoperatively in phaeochromocytoma
Beta blockade before alpha blockade causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction
Salt and fluid loading during alpha blockade supports intraoperative haemodynamics
explanation.pearls: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated upward over 7 to 14 days is the standard AU preoperative regimen, with adequate salt and fluid intake to limit postoperative hypotension.

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic therapy for suspected infective endocarditis in an IVDU
stem: A 32-year-old man with active intravenous heroin use presents with 5 days of fevers, rigors and pleuritic chest pain. He is haemodynamically stable but unwell. Three sets of peripheral blood cultures have been drawn from separate sites. Bedside transthoracic echo shows a 9 mm mobile vegetation on the tricuspid valve with mild tricuspid regurgitation. Chest imaging shows multiple peripheral nodular opacities consistent with septic pulmonary emboli.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68, HR 108, RR 22, SpO2 94% on room air, Temp 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Multiple needle track marks both antecubital fossae; soft systolic murmur at lower left sternal edge increasing on inspiration; no peripheral stigmata of left-sided IE
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, CRP 184 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L; troponin negative; ECG sinus tachycardia

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin with intravenous gentamicin empirically while cultures are pending, with daily levels and renal function checks
options.rationale: AU empiric therapy for suspected IE in an IVDU covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus with vancomycin and adds gentamicin for synergy until cultures and susceptibilities return. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as monotherapy, given its broad gram-negative cover and convenient once-daily administration in this presentation
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not reliably cover MRSA, the dominant pathogen in IVDU-associated right-sided IE. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)

options.text: Defer all antibiotics for 48 hours to allow blood cultures to declare a pathogen before any empirical antibiotic exposure
options.rationale: Delaying antibiotics in a febrile patient with vegetations and septic emboli risks progression; empirical cover is started after cultures are drawn. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily with outpatient cardiology follow-up arranged for the following week
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate for the induction phase of IE; intravenous therapy in hospital is required. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g six-hourly as a single agent based on streptococcal cover for community-acquired endocarditis
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin alone misses MRSA and Staphylococcus aureus, the leading IVDU IE pathogens. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: infective endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Empirical therapy for suspected infective endocarditis in an IVDU covers Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA with vancomycin, with gentamicin added for synergy and gram-negative cover until cultures return. Three sets of cultures from separate venepunctures precede antibiotics where time allows. Transthoracic echo identifies right-sided vegetations; transoesophageal echo is indicated if TTE is non-diagnostic or left-sided IE is suspected. Surgical referral applies to large vegetations, heart failure or refractory sepsis.
key_points: IVDU-associated right-sided IE is most commonly Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA
Empiric IV vancomycin plus gentamicin covers MRSA and provides synergy until cultures return
Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites precede antibiotics where the clinical state allows
explanation.pearls: Septic pulmonary emboli with a tricuspid vegetation in an IVDU points to Staphylococcus aureus; start vancomycin with gentamicin once cultures are drawn.

subtopic_detail: Post-exposure prophylaxis after occupational HIV needlestick
stem: A 29-year-old surgical resident sustains a deep hollow-needle injury during arterial line placement in a known HIV-positive patient with an unsuppressed viral load on adherence-poor antiretrovirals. The injury was 40 minutes ago. The resident is healthy, on no medications and not pregnant. She has had a single hepatitis B vaccination course with documented anti-HBs above 100 mIU/mL six months ago. Her last hepatitis C and HIV screens at occupational health 3 months ago were negative.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 84, Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Wound at left index finger pulp, bleeding milked and wound irrigated with saline
data_table.Investigations: Source patient HIV RNA above 100,000 copies/mL on last clinic visit; source HCV antibody negative, HBsAg negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send source patient and worker baseline HIV serology and arrange to start any prophylaxis in the morning once the laboratory has reported results
options.rationale: PEP efficacy declines steeply beyond 24 hours; starting prophylaxis cannot wait for baseline serology when the source is high-risk. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

options.text: Commence tenofovir disoproxil with emtricitabine and dolutegravir as a 28-day three-drug course now and arrange baseline and follow-up testing in parallel
options.rationale: High-risk occupational exposure to a high viral load source mandates three-drug PEP started as soon as possible, ideally within hours, for 28 days. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

options.text: Give a single 50 mg dose of dolutegravir as a pragmatic monotherapy prophylaxis until source results return at the next clinic visit
options.rationale: Single-dose monotherapy is not endorsed PEP; three-drug regimens for 28 days are the standard. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

options.text: Test only the exposed healthcare worker now and defer any prophylaxis until her own baseline serology is available the following day
options.rationale: Worker baseline serology is essential but does not delay PEP initiation in a high-risk exposure. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

options.text: Reassure the worker that her hepatitis B vaccine response covers her, and arrange follow-up serology at 3 months without any antiretroviral therapy
options.rationale: Hepatitis B immunity does not protect against HIV; PEP is required for a needlestick from a viraemic HIV source. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: High-risk occupational HIV exposure (deep hollow-needle injury from a viraemic source) mandates three-drug PEP started as soon as possible, ideally within hours and within 72 hours, for 28 days. The Australian first-line regimen is tenofovir disoproxil plus emtricitabine with dolutegravir or raltegravir. Baseline HIV serology is taken in parallel and repeated at 6 weeks, 3 months and (if indicated) 6 months. Hepatitis B and C status of source and worker are also documented.
key_points: Three-drug PEP within 72 hours, ideally within hours, of high-risk HIV exposure
First-line AU regimen: tenofovir disoproxil with emtricitabine plus dolutegravir for 28 days
Follow-up HIV serology at 6 weeks and 3 months, with earlier symptomatic testing if seroconversion is suspected
explanation.pearls: PEP started within 4 hours and continued for 28 days reduces the risk of HIV seroconversion after needlestick by around 80 percent; tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir is the AU preferred regimen.

sources.label: Australian Society for Infectious Diseases occupational exposure statement

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment in an asymptomatic new migrant
stem: A 28-year-old man newly arrived from a high TB prevalence country attends a refugee health clinic for screening. He has no respiratory or systemic symptoms, no history of treated TB and no known contact with active TB. He is HIV-negative, his BMI is 22 and he has no liver disease. Quantiferon-Gold Plus is positive. Chest radiograph and clinical examination are unremarkable. Sputum induction and AFB testing have not been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 72, Temp 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, chest clear to auscultation
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive; CXR no infiltrate, cavitation or hilar adenopathy; ALT 22 U/L, AST 18 U/L, bilirubin 8 micromol/L; HIV serology negative; HbA1c 5.2%

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence a 6-month rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol regimen empirically as treatment for presumed active pulmonary tuberculosis
options.rationale: RIPE is for active TB; there is no clinical, radiological or microbiological evidence of active disease here. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

options.text: Provide no treatment at this stage and arrange a repeat Quantiferon assay in 12 months as routine follow-up for an asymptomatic positive result
options.rationale: Untreated latent TB has a 5 to 10 percent lifetime reactivation risk; recent migrants from high-prevalence settings benefit from preventive therapy. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

options.text: Offer 9 months of daily isoniazid with pyridoxine, or alternatively 4 months of daily rifampicin, with monthly clinical and liver function review during treatment
options.rationale: Latent TB preventive therapy with isoniazid for 9 months or rifampicin for 4 months reduces reactivation risk by 60 to 90 percent; AU programs accept either, with LFT monitoring. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

options.text: Collect three early-morning sputum samples for AFB smear and culture before deciding on any preventive or active treatment regimen for this man
options.rationale: Sputum AFB is for suspected active TB; without symptoms or CXR changes there is no indication. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

options.text: Repeat the Quantiferon-Gold Plus assay in 4 weeks before any decision is made, on the basis that early conversion windows may produce uncertain results
options.rationale: QFT-Plus does not require routine repeat for confirmation in an asymptomatic positive result with consistent risk factors. (Source: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection)
source_refs: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic QFT-positive new migrants without radiological or microbiological active disease are offered preventive treatment for latent TB infection. AU options are 9 months of isoniazid with pyridoxine or 4 months of rifampicin; the rifampicin regimen has comparable efficacy with fewer hepatotoxicity events. Monthly clinical and LFT review during treatment is standard. Active TB must be excluded before preventive monotherapy.
key_points: Latent TB preventive therapy is offered after excluding active disease with symptoms screen and CXR
9 months isoniazid with pyridoxine or 4 months rifampicin are both accepted AU regimens
Monthly LFTs and symptom review screen for hepatotoxicity during preventive therapy
explanation.pearls: 4 months of daily rifampicin gives equivalent protection to 9 months of isoniazid in latent TB with lower rates of hepatotoxicity and better completion.

sources.label: NTAC Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent TB Infection
Communicable Diseases Network Australia: tuberculosis guideline

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 sepsis bundle in suspected urosepsis
stem: A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought to ED with 24 hours of fevers, rigors and worsening confusion. She has been treated by her GP for a urinary tract infection in the past week. On arrival she is tachypnoeic and hypotensive. Bedside venous blood gas shows pH 7.30 with lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Urinalysis shows leucocyte esterase, nitrites and blood. She has no documented allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 84/52, HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 95% on room air, Temp 38.9 degrees Celsius, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries with prolonged capillary refill, mild left renal angle tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 162 micromol/L (baseline 78), glucose 14.4 mmol/L; cultures and lipase pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Restrict fluids to a single 250 mL crystalloid bolus to avoid pulmonary oedema, then reassess clinically in 60 minutes before any further therapy
options.rationale: 30 mL/kg crystalloid in the first hour is recommended for septic shock; a 250 mL ceiling under-resuscitates. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)

options.text: Withhold all antibiotics until blood and urine cultures have been processed by the laboratory, to optimise the diagnostic yield from microbiology
options.rationale: Antibiotics are given within 1 hour for septic shock; cultures are obtained before antibiotics where possible without delay. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)

options.text: Commence noradrenaline by peripheral line at 0.1 microgram/kg/min before any crystalloid resuscitation, prioritising mean arterial pressure restoration first
options.rationale: Vasopressor support is escalated alongside or after initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid, not before any fluid. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)

options.text: Crystalloid 30 mL/kg over the first hour, intravenous gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam after blood and urine cultures, serial lactates and source imaging within the hour
options.rationale: The AU sepsis pathway delivers a balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg, empiric IV antibiotics within 1 hour after cultures, and lactate trending; gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam covers the likely organism for urosepsis pending sensitivities. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as the immediate first measure for circulatory collapse, plus a single dose of intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is reserved for vasopressor-refractory shock; bicarbonate is not routine in sepsis with pH above 7.15. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; AU sepsis pathway)

explanation.summary: The AU sepsis pathway and Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle for septic shock include lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics, empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg, and vasopressor escalation to target a MAP of at least 65. Source imaging and source control follow. Hydrocortisone is reserved for vasopressor-refractory shock. Empiric agents for urosepsis include gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam.
key_points: Sepsis hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressors to MAP 65
Empiric urosepsis: gentamicin plus piperacillin-tazobactam pending culture sensitivities
Hydrocortisone reserved for vasopressor-refractory shock
explanation.pearls: Lactate above 4 mmol/L with hypotension defines septic shock; 30 mL/kg crystalloid plus broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour reduces mortality.

subtopic_detail: Empiric therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis
stem: A 34-year-old man presents to ED with 12 hours of severe headache, photophobia, neck stiffness and a single rigor. He has no recent travel, no immunosuppression and is on no regular medications. He is alert with no focal neurology. There is no rash. CT brain is reported normal. Lumbar puncture is being prepared by the ED registrar.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 108, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 39.0 degrees Celsius, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Kernig and Brudzinski signs positive, no rash, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: WCC 17.4 x10^9/L, CRP 142 mg/L, lactate 1.9 mmol/L, platelets 198 x10^9/L, INR 1.0; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Proceed straight to lumbar puncture with full opening pressure and CSF cell count, then hold all empirical antibiotics pending the laboratory report
options.rationale: Antibiotics and dexamethasone are not delayed for LP results; doses are given as soon as cultures are drawn. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)

options.text: Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g alone without dexamethasone, on the basis that steroids increase the risk of iatrogenic immunosuppression in young adults
options.rationale: Dexamethasone 10 mg given immediately before or with the first dose reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)

options.text: Start empirical intravenous acyclovir 10 mg/kg alone for presumed herpes simplex encephalitis, with bacterial cover deferred pending CSF PCR results
options.rationale: Bacterial meningitis empirical therapy is given immediately for any suspicion; HSV cover is added when encephalitic features are present. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)

options.text: Defer all therapy until a contrast-enhanced MRI brain has been obtained and reviewed by a neurology registrar to characterise any meningeal enhancement
options.rationale: Imaging beyond non-contrast CT is unnecessary before LP and antibiotics in alert patients with no focal neurology. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g now after a single set of blood cultures, then proceed to lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Empirical dexamethasone 10 mg given before or with the first dose of ceftriaxone reduces neurological sequelae; LP follows immediately. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)

explanation.summary: Suspected bacterial meningitis is treated empirically without delay. In adults under 50 with no immunocompromise the AU regimen is IV ceftriaxone 2 g with IV dexamethasone 10 mg given before or with the first dose. Add benzylpenicillin for Listeria cover when over 50, immunocompromised or pregnant. CT brain is reserved for focal neurology, seizures or impaired conscious level; otherwise LP follows immediately after the first antibiotic dose.
key_points: Empiric IV ceftriaxone 2 g plus IV dexamethasone 10 mg given immediately after blood cultures
Add benzylpenicillin for Listeria cover if over 50, immunocompromised or pregnant
Pre-LP CT is reserved for focal neurology, seizures or impaired conscious level
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV given with or immediately before the first dose of ceftriaxone reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis when started before antibiotics.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: meningococcal disease

subtopic_detail: Oseltamivir initiation in frail nursing home resident with confirmed influenza A
stem: An 84-year-old woman in residential aged care develops fevers, cough and lethargy 36 hours ago, during a documented influenza outbreak in her facility. Point-of-care PCR is positive for influenza A. She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and ischaemic heart disease but no liver or significant renal disease (eGFR 58). She has been vaccinated against influenza this season.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78, HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 91% on room air, Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mildly tachypnoeic, scattered wheeze, no focal consolidation; alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A PCR positive; CXR mild bibasal atelectasis, no consolidation; troponin negative; creatinine 96 micromol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate antiviral plan?

options.text: Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, started today, alongside symptomatic measures and watchful escalation for hypoxia
options.rationale: AU CDNA recommends neuraminidase inhibitor therapy for high-risk individuals such as frail aged-care residents within 48 hours of symptom onset; 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is standard at eGFR above 30. (Source: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units)
source_refs: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units

options.text: Oral oseltamivir 150 mg twice daily for 10 days as an extended high-dose regimen for an outbreak setting in residential aged care
options.rationale: Standard adult dose is 75 mg twice daily for 5 days; routine doubling is not recommended for non-immunocompromised hosts. (Source: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units)
source_refs: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units

options.text: Withhold all antiviral therapy and provide only supportive care, given that symptom onset was more than 24 hours ago in a vaccinated individual
options.rationale: Antivirals retain benefit beyond 48 hours in severe or high-risk influenza; vaccination does not preclude treatment. (Source: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units)
source_refs: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units

options.text: Intravenous peramivir as the first-line antiviral on the basis of mild renal impairment and the convenience of single-dose intravenous therapy
options.rationale: Peramivir is reserved for patients unable to take or tolerate oseltamivir; eGFR 58 does not preclude oral therapy. (Source: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units)
source_refs: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units

options.text: Oral amantadine 100 mg twice daily for 5 days as first-line cover against an A subtype influenza outbreak in this residential setting
options.rationale: Amantadine is no longer recommended due to widespread resistance in circulating influenza A strains. (Source: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units)
source_refs: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units

explanation.summary: Frail older adults in aged care with confirmed influenza receive oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, started as soon as possible after symptom onset. Treatment remains worthwhile beyond 48 hours in severe or high-risk disease. Renal dose adjustment applies at eGFR below 30. Amantadine is obsolete due to resistance. Outbreak control includes droplet precautions, cohort isolation and post-exposure prophylaxis for residents and staff per CDNA guidance.
key_points: Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is first-line for high-risk influenza A
Renal dose adjustment of oseltamivir applies at eGFR below 30
Amantadine is no longer used due to resistance
explanation.pearls: Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days started within 48 hours of symptoms reduces complications and length of illness in high-risk adults including frail aged-care residents.

sources.label: CDNA influenza national guidelines for public health units

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated lower limb cellulitis empirical therapy
stem: A 46-year-old man presents with a 36-hour history of a red, hot, painful lower leg following minor trauma. He is otherwise well, with no diabetes, no immunosuppression and no documented penicillin allergy. There is no fluctuant collection, no necrosis and no crepitus. The leg has well-demarcated erythema below the knee with associated tenderness. He is haemodynamically stable and afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76, HR 80, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Unilateral right calf erythema with central warmth, no fluctuance or abscess, intact distal pulses and sensation
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.4 x10^9/L, CRP 38 mg/L; ultrasound shows no abscess or DVT; HbA1c 5.3%

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly for 7 days as a first-choice agent because of its broader gram-negative cover compared to flucloxacillin
options.rationale: Cefalexin is an acceptable substitute for non-severe penicillin allergy but is not first-line over di/flucloxacillin in non-allergic patients. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)

options.text: Oral di/flucloxacillin 500 mg six-hourly for 5 days as first-line outpatient therapy for non-severe lower limb cellulitis in this patient
options.rationale: Streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus drive uncomplicated cellulitis; di/flucloxacillin covers both and is the AU first-line in non-allergic adults with non-severe disease. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then maintenance per trough level for empirical MRSA cover in a community-acquired skin infection presentation
options.rationale: Empirical MRSA cover is reserved for known colonisation, severe sepsis, recurrent disease or high-risk exposures, none of which apply here. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)

options.text: Topical mupirocin to the affected area three times daily plus oral analgesia, without any systemic antibiotic therapy initiated at this assessment
options.rationale: Topical therapy alone is inadequate for cellulitis; systemic therapy is required. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)

options.text: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily as monotherapy given anaerobic activity and a once-daily option, with no addition of antistreptococcal cover at this time
options.rationale: Doxycycline misses many group A streptococcal isolates and is not first-line monotherapy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis and erysipelas)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cellulitis is typically driven by beta-haemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus. First-line empirical therapy in non-allergic adults is oral di/flucloxacillin 500 mg six-hourly for 5 days; cefalexin substitutes for non-severe penicillin allergy. IV therapy and broader cover are reserved for sepsis, severe local features or rapid spread. MRSA cover is added only for known colonisation, recurrent disease or high-risk exposures. Limb elevation, marking of erythema and 48-hour clinical review identify treatment failure early.
key_points: Di/flucloxacillin is first-line for non-severe cellulitis in non-allergic adults
Cefalexin substitutes for non-severe penicillin allergy
Vancomycin or clindamycin is added only for severe disease or known MRSA risk
explanation.pearls: 5 days of di/flucloxacillin 500 mg six-hourly resolves most uncomplicated lower-limb cellulitis; mark the leading edge and review at 48 hours for failure to improve.

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated lower UTI in a non-pregnant adult woman
stem: A 34-year-old non-pregnant woman presents with 48 hours of urinary frequency, dysuria and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fevers, flank pain, vaginal symptoms or systemic features. She has no significant past medical history, takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies. There is no recent antibiotic exposure. Bedside urinalysis shows leucocyte esterase and nitrites positive.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72, HR 78, Temp 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Suprapubic tenderness only; no flank tenderness, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Bedside urinalysis: leucocytes +++, nitrites positive, blood +; midstream urine sent; not pregnant on serum beta-hCG

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days as empirical first-line therapy in this uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection presentation
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for resistant or complicated infections in Australia; not first-line for uncomplicated lower UTI. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)

options.text: Single 3 g oral dose of fosfomycin as the empirical first-line agent without any further courses required for treatment of this uncomplicated lower UTI
options.rationale: Fosfomycin is a second-line AU option used where first-line agents are unsuitable; not the routine first choice. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 3 days as empirical first-line therapy in this non-pregnant adult woman with uncomplicated lower UTI
options.rationale: Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days is the AU first-line empirical therapy for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant adults; nitrofurantoin for 5 days is an alternative. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily for 7 days as empirical first-line therapy for any culture-positive urinary tract infection in adults regardless of severity
options.rationale: IV therapy is reserved for pyelonephritis, sepsis or oral failure; not first-line for uncomplicated cystitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14 days as a long course of empirical therapy in this uncomplicated lower UTI presentation
options.rationale: Amoxicillin has high E. coli resistance rates in Australia; trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin are preferred and 14 days is excessive. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: urinary tract infections)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cystitis in a non-pregnant adult woman is treated empirically with trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally six-hourly for 5 days. Cefalexin and amoxicillin-clavulanate are alternatives. Fluoroquinolones are reserved for resistant or complicated infections. Pre-treatment midstream urine for culture is not required for sporadic uncomplicated episodes but is sent in recurrent or complicated cases.
key_points: Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days is the AU first-line for uncomplicated cystitis
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg six-hourly for 5 days is an equivalent first-line alternative
Fluoroquinolones are reserved for resistant or complicated UTI
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 3 days resolves most uncomplicated lower UTI in non-pregnant women; switch to nitrofurantoin in late pregnancy or trimethoprim-resistant isolates.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy initiation after low-trauma vertebral fracture
stem: A 72-year-old post-menopausal woman presents with sudden mid-thoracic back pain after a minor stumble. Imaging confirms a wedge compression fracture of T7 without neurological deficit. DXA shows lumbar spine T-score -2.8 and femoral neck T-score -2.4. Renal function and dental status are normal. She is not currently on any antiresorptive or anabolic therapy and has no contraindication to oral bisphosphonates. Calcium and vitamin D intake are documented as low.

data_table.Examination: Localised T7 tenderness, no spinal cord features; vitamin D 38 nmol/L
data_table.Investigations: Calcium corrected 2.32 mmol/L, phosphate 1.0 mmol/L, eGFR 76, magnesium 0.84 mmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, PTH 4.2 pmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate pharmacological plan?

options.text: Oral calcium 1200 mg daily and vitamin D 1000 IU daily alone, deferring any antiresorptive agent until a second fracture occurs in the next year
options.rationale: An incident vertebral fracture with T-score under -2.5 mandates antiresorptive therapy; supplements alone are insufficient. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months without prior bisphosphonate trial and without any transition plan if it is later discontinued
options.rationale: Denosumab is an option but discontinuation without bisphosphonate cover triggers rebound fractures; first-line is usually an oral bisphosphonate. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

options.text: Oestrogen replacement therapy as first-line antifracture therapy in a 72-year-old woman more than 20 years post-menopause with established osteoporosis
options.rationale: Menopausal hormone therapy is not first-line for established osteoporosis in older women given cardiovascular and thromboembolic risks. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

options.text: Oral weekly alendronate 70 mg with daily calcium 1300 mg and vitamin D 1000 IU supplementation, after dental review and adherence counselling for upright dosing
options.rationale: Oral bisphosphonates are AU first-line for post-menopausal osteoporosis with vertebral fracture; calcium and vitamin D repletion plus dental review and upright dosing maximise effectiveness and safety. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

options.text: Daily subcutaneous teriparatide 20 micrograms as initial anabolic therapy without any prior antiresorptive trial in this established post-menopausal osteoporosis
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe disease or bisphosphonate failure under PBS criteria; not first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

explanation.summary: Post-menopausal osteoporosis with incident vertebral fracture meets criteria for antifracture pharmacotherapy. Oral bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate) are AU first-line with weekly dosing on PBS, paired with calcium and vitamin D repletion. Dental review precedes initiation given osteonecrosis risk. Denosumab and teriparatide are subsequent options when bisphosphonates fail or are contraindicated. Hormone therapy is not first-line in older post-menopausal women.
key_points: Vertebral fracture with T-score under -2.5 is an indication for antiresorptive therapy
Oral alendronate or risedronate is AU first-line with calcium and vitamin D repletion
Pre-treatment dental review reduces osteonecrosis risk
explanation.pearls: Alendronate 70 mg weekly reduces vertebral fracture risk by about 45 percent in established osteoporosis; couple with daily calcium 1300 mg and vitamin D 1000 IU when intake is low.

sources.label: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention, diagnosis and management

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation duration after provoked DVT post-orthopaedic surgery
stem: A 38-year-old man develops unilateral left calf swelling 12 days after open reduction internal fixation of an ankle fracture. He has been weight-bearing as tolerated in a moon-boot. Compression duplex ultrasound confirms a non-occlusive popliteal vein deep vein thrombosis. He has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, no malignancy, no thrombophilia screen abnormality and no active bleeding. He is otherwise healthy on no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/74, HR 78, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Left calf 3 cm larger than right, mild tenderness, pulses intact, no respiratory features
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142 g/L, platelets 232 x10^9/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, LFTs normal, INR 1.0; ECG normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Lifelong oral anticoagulation with warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 as definitive therapy for any first proximal deep vein thrombosis episode
options.rationale: Lifelong therapy is reserved for unprovoked or recurrent VTE, malignancy or significant thrombophilia, none of which apply. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)

options.text: Six weeks of oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily without an initial loading dose and then cessation of all anticoagulation with no further review needed
options.rationale: A 6-week course is insufficient for a proximal DVT; standard duration is at least 3 months. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)

options.text: Twelve months of oral apixaban then transition to warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 indefinitely for ongoing secondary prevention of recurrent VTE in this patient
options.rationale: Cross-over to warfarin is not standard; provoked first DVT does not warrant indefinite therapy. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)

options.text: Withhold all anticoagulation in favour of an inferior vena cava filter alone on the basis that this DVT has been provoked by a recent surgical procedure
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is the cornerstone; IVC filters are reserved for active major bleeding or absolute contraindications to anticoagulation. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)

options.text: Oral apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for a total of 3 months, then stop and counsel about recurrence risk and prevention
options.rationale: Provoked proximal DVT in a non-cancer patient is treated for 3 months with a DOAC at standard dosing; the apixaban induction-maintenance schedule is the AU regimen. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand guideline)

explanation.summary: Provoked DVT in a non-cancer patient is treated for 3 months with a direct oral anticoagulant. Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily is the AU regimen; rivaroxaban with a 21-day loading then 20 mg daily is an alternative. Lifelong therapy is reserved for unprovoked or recurrent disease, malignancy or thrombophilia. Counselling on recurrence symptoms and travel prevention closes the encounter.
key_points: Provoked proximal DVT is treated for 3 months with a DOAC at standard dosing
Lifelong therapy is reserved for unprovoked, recurrent, cancer-associated or thrombophilia VTE
IVC filter is reserved for absolute contraindications to anticoagulation
explanation.pearls: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for 3 months is the standard AU regimen for provoked proximal DVT in a non-cancer adult.

subtopic_detail: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state with marked sodium derangement
stem: A 78-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought to ED with 5 days of progressive lethargy and reduced oral intake during a urinary tract infection. He has been incrementally less responsive over 24 hours. He is on metformin and gliclazide; he ran out of insulin three weeks ago. He is dry on examination with a tongue furrow and reduced skin turgor. There is no Kussmaul breathing and no significant ketonuria.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64, HR 112, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air, Temp 37.6 degrees Celsius, GCS 12
data_table.Examination: Markedly dehydrated mucous membranes, no air hunger, lung bases clear
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 52 mmol/L, Na 152 mmol/L, K 4.6 mmol/L, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L, calculated osmolality 358 mOsm/kg, capillary ketones 0.5 mmol/L, pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, urinary nitrites positive

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 15 mL/kg over 1 hour, then insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour after fluid response, with potassium replacement and capped corrected sodium fall
options.rationale: HHS requires cautious volume resuscitation first; insulin starts after fluid response and at lower rates than DKA, with sodium fall capped at 4 to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid pontine myelinolysis or cerebral oedema. (Source: JBDS-IP guideline for HHS adapted for AU practice; ADIPS resources)

options.text: Intravenous 0.45 percent sodium chloride at 1 litre per hour for the first 4 hours with a concurrent insulin bolus of 0.1 units/kg, no potassium addition initially
options.rationale: Rapid hypotonic correction and early insulin bolus risk rapid osmolar shifts, cerebral oedema and hypokalaemia. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS guideline)

options.text: Intravenous insulin bolus 20 units stat followed by 0.1 units/kg/hour insulin infusion and DKA-style high-dose insulin therapy without prior fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: HHS is more dehydrated than acidotic; fluid first, low-dose insulin after fluid response, not DKA-style. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS guideline)

options.text: Hypertonic 3 percent saline 100 mL boluses with reassessment for cerebral oedema and ongoing infusion to correct the hyperosmolar state efficiently
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not used in HHS; it would worsen the hyperosmolar state. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS guideline)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes as initial therapy to correct acidaemia and an empirical insulin infusion at 0.2 units/kg/hour
options.rationale: Acidaemia is mild and not driven by ketoacidosis; bicarbonate is not indicated and high-rate insulin risks rapid osmolar shift. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS guideline)

explanation.summary: HHS presents with marked hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration without significant ketoacidosis. Initial management is cautious volume resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid, gradual correction of osmolality (sodium fall 4 to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours), low-rate insulin (0.05 units/kg/hour) started after fluid response, and potassium replacement when below 5.0 with adequate urine output. Source control of any precipitant (such as UTI) is essential. Cerebral oedema and central pontine myelinolysis are the feared correction-rate complications.
key_points: HHS: fluid first with isotonic crystalloid, then low-rate insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour
Limit corrected sodium fall to 4 to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours
Treat the precipitating infection or omission of insulin
explanation.pearls: Capping the fall in corrected sodium at 8 mmol/L per 24 hours and using insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour after fluid response prevents the cerebral oedema and pontine myelinolysis that follow over-aggressive HHS correction.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society inpatient hyperglycaemia statement

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection in a person with diabetes
stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with rapidly worsening left thigh pain and swelling 36 hours after a minor abrasion. The pain is now out of proportion to visible skin findings. There is dusky discolouration with crepitus on palpation. He is febrile, tachycardic and hypotensive. He has had two episodes of vomiting and is becoming confused. Bedside blood gas shows lactate 5.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/52, HR 132, RR 26, SpO2 96% on room air, Temp 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Left thigh dusky violaceous discolouration, palpable crepitus, exquisite tenderness, anaesthesia in the centre of the lesion
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 318 mg/L, Na 132 mmol/L, glucose 18 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L, lactate 5.8 mmol/L; LRINEC score calculated at 9

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly with discharge home for 24-hour reassessment by the community ambulatory care nurse-led wound clinic and a GP review the following morning
options.rationale: This is necrotising fasciitis with septic shock; oral therapy at home is unsafe. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

options.text: Immediate resuscitation, intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin, blood cultures, urgent surgical consult for theatre-based debridement
options.rationale: Necrotising soft tissue infection requires emergent broad-spectrum antibiotics including a toxin-inhibitor (clindamycin) and MRSA cover, with surgical debridement within hours as the definitive treatment. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as the sole initial modality, with antibiotic therapy and surgical debridement deferred until completion of two sessions
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct after antibiotics and debridement, not a substitute. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

options.text: Topical iodine dressings and limb elevation with intravenous flucloxacillin monotherapy, with surgical review deferred until cultures and imaging confirm a clear diagnosis
options.rationale: Waiting for confirmatory imaging in a clinical necrotising soft tissue infection delays life-saving surgery; monotherapy under-covers the polymicrobial picture. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

options.text: Single dose intravenous vancomycin then discharge home with oral antibiotics, with a community wound nurse review arranged for the following morning
options.rationale: Single-dose therapy and discharge are unsafe in septic shock from necrotising fasciitis; emergency surgery is required. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency. Pain out of proportion, crepitus, dusky skin, bullae and cutaneous anaesthesia raise suspicion; LRINEC above 6 supports it. Management is simultaneous resuscitation, blood cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin or alternatives per eTG), and urgent surgical debridement within hours. Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct after debridement. Delay to theatre is the dominant driver of mortality.
key_points: LRINEC above 6 with clinical features mandates immediate surgical consult
Empiric IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin covers the polymicrobial picture
Surgical debridement is the definitive treatment and is the strongest predictor of survival
explanation.pearls: Debridement within 6 hours of presentation is the single biggest determinant of survival in necrotising soft tissue infection; clindamycin adds toxin suppression to broad-spectrum cover.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: necrotising soft tissue infections

subtopic_detail: Workup of primary aldosteronism in resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia
stem: A 47-year-old woman presents with hypertension refractory to three agents (ACE inhibitor, calcium channel blocker and thiazide) at maximal doses. She has incidentally been found to be hypokalaemic on three separate occasions. She has no family history of hypertension under age 40. She has no episodic features of catecholamine excess. She is not pregnant. A morning aldosterone-to-renin ratio is markedly elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/104 (averaged over 3 readings), HR 76
data_table.Examination: No abdominal bruit, no Cushingoid features, normal funduscopy
data_table.Investigations: K 3.2 mmol/L, Na 142 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L; aldosterone 720 pmol/L, direct renin concentration 5 mIU/L, ARR markedly elevated; 24-hour urinary metanephrines normal; HbA1c 5.4%

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in the workup?

options.text: Cease all antihypertensive agents for 6 weeks with no further investigations performed in the interim period for this patient and arrange a remote phone review
options.rationale: Stopping all antihypertensives without confirmatory testing delays diagnosis and is unsafe at this BP. (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline: case detection, diagnosis, and treatment of primary aldosteronism)

options.text: Proceed directly to laparoscopic adrenalectomy on the basis of the markedly elevated screening aldosterone-to-renin ratio alone without further testing
options.rationale: A screening ARR is not diagnostic; confirmatory suppression and subtyping with adrenal vein sampling are required before surgery. (Source: Endocrine Society guideline: primary aldosteronism)

options.text: Withdraw interfering agents per protocol, repeat the ARR, perform a confirmatory test such as saline suppression or fludrocortisone suppression, then adrenal CT and adrenal vein sampling
options.rationale: The Endocrine Society pathway after a positive screening ARR is medication washout, confirmatory suppression testing, then adrenal imaging and vein sampling to identify a unilateral surgical lesion. (Source: Endocrine Society guideline: primary aldosteronism)

options.text: Empirical lifelong spironolactone 25 mg daily without any confirmatory diagnostic testing for primary aldosteronism in this patient with resistant hypertension
options.rationale: Empirical mineralocorticoid blockade may treat the BP but misses unilateral disease amenable to surgical cure and forfeits the diagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society guideline: primary aldosteronism)

options.text: Send 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and plasma metanephrines as the next step to investigate this hypertension as an endocrine secondary cause
options.rationale: Metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma; here aldosteronism is suggested by the ARR and hypokalaemia. (Source: Endocrine Society guideline: primary aldosteronism)

explanation.summary: A positive aldosterone-to-renin ratio screens for primary aldosteronism but is not diagnostic. Confirmation requires withdrawal of interfering agents (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, betablockers, ACE inhibitors as feasible) and a suppression test (saline, fludrocortisone, oral sodium loading, or captopril). Adrenal CT identifies macroadenomas but is insufficient for lateralisation; adrenal vein sampling localises the source for surgical candidates. Unilateral disease is treated with laparoscopic adrenalectomy; bilateral hyperplasia with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist.
key_points: Confirm primary aldosteronism with a suppression test before any treatment decisions
Adrenal vein sampling is required before adrenalectomy because imaging misses small functioning adenomas
Bilateral hyperplasia is treated medically with spironolactone or eplerenone
explanation.pearls: After a positive ARR, perform a saline suppression test (2 L of 0.9 percent saline over 4 hours): failure of aldosterone to fall below 140 pmol/L confirms autonomous secretion.

subtopic_detail: Pituitary apoplexy with ophthalmoplegia and adrenal insufficiency
stem: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden severe occipital headache, vomiting and binocular diplopia. He has no history of head trauma. Pupillary examination shows a dilated, poorly reactive left pupil and ptosis. He is hypotensive and lethargic. MRI brain shows a 22 mm pituitary macroadenoma with central haemorrhagic transformation. He is on no regular medications. There is no family history of intracranial bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/56, HR 108, Temp 36.4 degrees Celsius, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Left third nerve palsy with dilated pupil and ptosis, bitemporal visual field defect on confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L, K 4.0 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, cortisol (random) 64 nmol/L, TSH 0.4 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L, prolactin 12 microgram/L; MRI confirms haemorrhagic macroadenoma

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine to reduce BP and prevent rebleeding without any concurrent corticosteroid because the diagnosis remains uncertain in this acute setting
options.rationale: Antihypertensives in a hypotensive patient with acute hypopituitarism worsen hypoperfusion; immediate corticosteroid replacement is the priority. (Source: Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance: pituitary apoplexy)
source_refs: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline

options.text: Conservative outpatient management with serial visual field testing in 4 weeks and repeat MRI in 3 months for this acute neuro-ophthalmic presentation in a stable patient
options.rationale: Acute apoplexy with neuro-ophthalmic compromise and adrenal insufficiency is an inpatient emergency, not an outpatient pathway. (Source: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline)
source_refs: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline

options.text: A single dose of intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg only for cerebral oedema, with no subsequent endocrine replacement and no neurosurgical referral arranged
options.rationale: Stress-dose hydrocortisone is required for adrenal insufficiency; dexamethasone alone misses the mineralocorticoid context and curbs further endocrine workup. (Source: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline)
source_refs: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg per 24 hours, fluid resuscitation, urgent neurosurgical and endocrine review for possible transsphenoidal decompression
options.rationale: Acute pituitary apoplexy with hypotension, hyponatraemia and a low random cortisol mandates immediate hydrocortisone replacement; visual field or cranial nerve compromise prompts urgent transsphenoidal decompression. (Source: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline)
source_refs: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline

options.text: Intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg as immediate osmotic therapy alone for the haemorrhagic mass with no corticosteroid replacement or surgical referral arranged at this point
options.rationale: Mannitol does not address adrenal insufficiency or cranial nerve compression; not the first step. (Source: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline)
source_refs: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline

explanation.summary: Pituitary apoplexy is haemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma presenting with thunderclap headache, visual or cranial nerve compromise and acute hypopituitarism. Hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia and a low random cortisol indicate secondary adrenal insufficiency. Immediate management is high-dose IV hydrocortisone, fluid resuscitation and urgent neurosurgical referral for transsphenoidal decompression when there is visual or cranial nerve compromise. Subsequent replacement covers thyroid, gonadal and posterior pituitary axes as required.
key_points: Acute apoplexy is a neurosurgical and endocrine emergency
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours treats secondary adrenal insufficiency
Transsphenoidal decompression is indicated for visual or cranial nerve compromise
explanation.pearls: A low random cortisol below 100 nmol/L with hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia in a patient with a pituitary mass mandates IV hydrocortisone 100 mg before any other intervention.

sources.label: Society for Endocrinology pituitary apoplexy guideline
Endocrine Society guideline: hormonal replacement in hypopituitarism

subtopic_detail: Early disease-modifying therapy in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis
stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with 4 months of symmetrical small joint pain and morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. She has bilateral MCP and PIP synovitis. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are positive. Hand radiographs show early periarticular osteopenia without erosions. She is otherwise well, on no regular medications, not planning pregnancy in the next 18 months and has no liver or lung disease. DAS28 is calculated at 5.4.

data_table.Examination: Synovitis at 8 MCP and 6 PIP joints, two tender swollen wrists, no nodules; ESR 48 mm/hour
data_table.Investigations: RF 86 IU/mL, anti-CCP 320 U/mL, ANA negative, ALT 22 U/L, eGFR 88, hepatitis B and C serology negative, CXR clear, QFT-Plus negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Long-term oral prednisolone 10 mg daily as monotherapy with no addition of any conventional or biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic agent now or in the foreseeable future
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy does not modify joint damage and incurs cumulative toxicity; a conventional synthetic DMARD is mandatory. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association rheumatoid arthritis position statement)

options.text: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily as monotherapy with no escalation plan and no addition of any conventional or biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic agent at any later stage
options.rationale: NSAIDs treat symptoms only; they do not prevent erosive progression in seropositive RA. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association RA statement)

options.text: Defer disease-modifying therapy for 12 months while observing for spontaneous remission and using analgesia as required during the wait-and-watch interval
