options.rationale: Window-of-opportunity data favour DMARD start within 3 months of symptom onset; deferral worsens long-term outcomes. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association RA statement)

options.text: Hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg daily as monotherapy as the sole first-line disease-modifying agent in this seropositive, high-disease-activity rheumatoid arthritis presentation
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy is inadequate for seropositive high-activity RA; it features in combination regimens but not as monotherapy here. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association RA statement)

options.text: Methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid, a tapering bridging course of oral prednisolone, baseline screening completed, plus a treat-to-target plan with biologic step-up if no remission
options.rationale: Methotrexate is the AU anchor DMARD for seropositive RA, started after screening (CXR, hepatitis, eGFR, LFTs), with a short bridging glucocorticoid and a treat-to-target plan stepping to combination or biologic therapy if remission is not achieved. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association RA statement)

explanation.summary: Seropositive RA with high disease activity warrants early DMARD initiation within the window of opportunity. Methotrexate 10 to 15 mg weekly with folic acid is the AU first-line anchor drug, paired with bridging glucocorticoids and a treat-to-target plan. Screening before initiation includes LFTs, eGFR, hepatitis B and C, tuberculosis (QFT-Plus) and pneumococcal vaccination. Step-up to combination conventional synthetic DMARDs or biologic therapy follows failure to reach remission at 3 to 6 months.
key_points: Methotrexate is the AU anchor DMARD for seropositive RA
Early initiation within 3 months of symptom onset preserves joint function
Step-up to combination or biologic therapy when remission is not achieved at 3 to 6 months
explanation.pearls: Methotrexate started at 10 mg weekly with folic acid and titrated to 20 to 25 mg weekly over 6 to 8 weeks reaches remission in around 30 percent of seropositive RA as monotherapy.

subtopic_detail: Suspected giant cell arteritis with new headache and jaw claudication
stem: An 81-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of new bitemporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication when chewing and one episode of transient visual blurring in the right eye 12 hours ago. She has no diabetes, no peptic ulcer disease and no infection. There is no rash and no symptoms of polymyalgia at presentation. Her visual acuity is normal today. There is tenderness over both temporal arteries with reduced pulsatility on the right.

data_table.Examination: Tender thickened right temporal artery, reduced pulse; visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally, fundi normal
data_table.Investigations: ESR 92 mm/hour, CRP 124 mg/L, Hb 108 g/L, platelets 462 x10^9/L, ALT 24 U/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg daily today and arrange urgent temporal artery biopsy within 7 to 14 days, plus aspirin 100 mg daily and bone and gastric protection
options.rationale: Suspected GCA with visual symptoms is started immediately on high-dose corticosteroids; biopsy yield is preserved for 1 to 2 weeks. Aspirin reduces ischaemic events; bone and PPI cover address steroid harms. (Source: BSR guideline on GCA management; eviQ general rheumatology)

options.text: Defer corticosteroid therapy until temporal artery biopsy has been performed and reviewed, even if biopsy is not arranged for several days into the working week
options.rationale: Delaying steroids risks permanent visual loss; biopsy yield is preserved for up to 2 weeks of treatment. (Source: BSR GCA guideline)

options.text: Apply topical ophthalmic prednisolone drops alone to the right eye with no systemic corticosteroid therapy until the biopsy result has been reviewed by the rheumatology team
options.rationale: GCA is systemic; topical therapy does not address arteritis. (Source: BSR GCA guideline)

options.text: Oral naproxen 500 mg twice daily as monotherapy for the headache with reassessment of inflammatory markers and clinical features in 4 weeks at the next planned review
options.rationale: NSAID monotherapy will not control vasculitis and exposes the patient to preventable visual loss. (Source: BSR GCA guideline)

options.text: Initiate subcutaneous tocilizumab as monotherapy without any concurrent oral corticosteroid therapy at the first visit before any biopsy is arranged or organised
options.rationale: Tocilizumab is a steroid-sparing add-on in relapsing or steroid-toxic GCA; not monotherapy at first presentation. (Source: BSR GCA guideline)

explanation.summary: Suspected giant cell arteritis with any visual feature is treated with high-dose corticosteroids before biopsy: oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily for uncomplicated GCA, IV methylprednisolone pulse for vision loss. Temporal artery biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks remains diagnostic; biopsy yield is preserved on early treatment. Aspirin 100 mg daily reduces ischaemic events, while calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonates and a PPI cover steroid harms. Tocilizumab is a steroid-sparing add-on for relapsers.
key_points: Start high-dose corticosteroids immediately on clinical suspicion; do not wait for biopsy
Aspirin 100 mg daily reduces ischaemic events in GCA
Biopsy yield is preserved for 1 to 2 weeks after starting steroids
explanation.pearls: Visual symptoms in suspected GCA prompt IV methylprednisolone 500 to 1000 mg daily for 3 days; otherwise oral prednisolone 60 mg daily, with biopsy within 14 days.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: rheumatology - giant cell arteritis

subtopic_detail: Myasthenic crisis with bulbar and respiratory failure
stem: A 56-year-old woman with seropositive myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine and azathioprine presents with worsening generalised weakness over 5 days following a chest infection. She now has dysphagia, dysphonia and dyspnoea. She has no fevers today. Her forced vital capacity has dropped from a baseline of 3.4 L to 0.9 L. Negative inspiratory force is reduced. She is unable to count to 20 in a single breath.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/76, HR 108, RR 26, SpO2 93% on room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, paradoxical breathing, weak cough, gag reflex reduced
data_table.Investigations: FVC 0.9 L, NIF -22 cmH2O, anti-AChR antibody historically positive, CXR right basal opacity, ABG shows hypercapnia (pCO2 56 mmHg)

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase pyridostigmine fivefold and discharge home with a community nurse review after 24 hours, recommending early follow-up with the treating neurologist
options.rationale: Increasing pyridostigmine in crisis risks cholinergic crisis and does not address respiratory failure; admission is mandatory. (Source: Australian Myasthenic Association clinician resources; eTG Neurology)
source_refs: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

options.text: ICU admission, prepare for non-invasive then invasive ventilation, treat the precipitating chest infection, and initiate intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange
options.rationale: Myasthenic crisis with FVC under 1 L and hypercapnia requires ICU-level airway support, treatment of precipitants, and rapid immunomodulation with IVIG or plasma exchange. (Source: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management)
source_refs: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

options.text: Edrophonium intravenous bolus 10 mg as a diagnostic test before any further therapy is considered, with no ICU referral and no escalation of monitoring in this presentation
options.rationale: Edrophonium is no longer routine in known seropositive disease and does not address respiratory failure. (Source: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management)
source_refs: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

options.text: Oral prednisone titrated outpatient over 6 weeks as the only adjustment, with reassurance and home spirometry monitoring rather than admission for ventilatory support and immunomodulation
options.rationale: Slow steroid titration cannot rescue acute crisis; early steroid up-titration also risks transient worsening. (Source: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management)
source_refs: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

options.text: Single dose intravenous lorazepam 2 mg for anxiety and supportive observation only on the general ward, with no airway escalation arranged or planned at this current encounter
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen ventilatory drive and risk respiratory arrest in neuromuscular failure. (Source: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management)
source_refs: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is bulbar or respiratory failure on a background of myasthenia gravis. Bedside markers include FVC under 1 L (or under 15 mL/kg), single-breath count under 20 and rising pCO2. Management is ICU admission for ventilatory support (NIV trialled cautiously, intubation when paradoxical breathing or rising pCO2 develops), treatment of triggers (infection, drugs such as aminoglycosides), and rapid immunomodulation with IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days or plasma exchange. Steroid up-titration is initiated under cover of immunomodulation given the risk of transient worsening.
key_points: FVC under 1 L or single-breath count under 20 signals impending respiratory failure
IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days or plasma exchange is the rescue therapy of choice
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides and magnesium can precipitate or worsen crisis
explanation.pearls: Single-breath count under 20 or FVC below 15 mL/kg in known myasthenia signals impending respiratory failure; mobilise IVIG or plasma exchange and prepare the airway team.

sources.label: AAN guideline on myasthenia gravis management

subtopic_detail: Clinically isolated syndrome with MRI dissemination meeting McDonald criteria
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 7-day history of painful loss of vision in the right eye and impaired colour perception. Examination confirms right optic neuritis with a relative afferent pupillary defect. She has no prior episodes of neurological symptoms. MRI brain and orbits show right optic nerve enhancement plus three periventricular T2 lesions and one juxtacortical lesion. Both gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions are present. CSF shows two unique oligoclonal bands.

data_table.Examination: Right visual acuity 6/24, RAPD present, normal fundi; remainder of cranial nerves and limbs normal
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: dissemination in space (periventricular plus juxtacortical) and time (enhancing plus non-enhancing) present; CSF oligoclonal bands positive; aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold all disease-modifying therapy and reassess in 12 months with a repeat clinical examination and follow-up MRI, with no further specific action between visits
options.rationale: Active disease meeting McDonald criteria warrants prompt DMT initiation; delay accrues disability. (Source: MS International Federation; MSAANZ DMT consensus)

options.text: Apply five sessions of plasma exchange immediately for this first attack of optic neuritis without any further investigations or commencement of long-term disease-modifying therapy at this point
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is reserved for severe steroid-refractory attacks; it is not first-line acute or maintenance therapy for typical optic neuritis. (Source: MSAANZ DMT consensus)

options.text: Apply the McDonald 2017 criteria, diagnose relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, treat the acute attack with high-dose methylprednisolone, and initiate disease-modifying therapy
options.rationale: Dissemination in space and time on the first MRI satisfies McDonald 2017 criteria and supports diagnosing relapsing-remitting MS, with acute high-dose steroids and prompt DMT to reduce relapse and disability accrual. (Source: McDonald 2017 criteria; MSAANZ DMT consensus)

options.text: Steroid pulse for the attack and immediate cessation of all follow-up plans with no specific disease-modifying therapy initiated and no further specialist review arranged at this time
options.rationale: DMT initiation reduces relapse rate, MRI activity and long-term disability; discharge without DMT misses the window of opportunity. (Source: MSAANZ DMT consensus)

options.text: Wait for a second clinical attack before any treatment is initiated, with no acute corticosteroid for the current optic neuritis and no follow-up MRI planned at this time
options.rationale: Modern McDonald 2017 criteria allow diagnosis after the first attack when imaging shows dissemination in space and time; waiting harms outcomes. (Source: McDonald 2017 criteria)

explanation.summary: Clinically isolated syndrome with MRI findings that satisfy dissemination in space and time meets McDonald 2017 criteria for relapsing-remitting MS. Acute optic neuritis is treated with high-dose methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3 to 5 days; recovery is typically excellent. Early initiation of a disease-modifying therapy (such as fingolimod, ocrelizumab, natalizumab or platform injectable agents per PBS criteria) reduces relapse rate, MRI activity and long-term disability accrual. AQP4 and MOG antibodies are checked to exclude NMOSD and MOGAD.
key_points: McDonald 2017 allows MS diagnosis after a first attack when dissemination in space and time are present on MRI
Treat acute optic neuritis with methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3 to 5 days
Initiate DMT promptly to reduce long-term disability accrual
explanation.pearls: A first demyelinating attack with periventricular and juxtacortical lesions and concurrent gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI satisfies dissemination in space and time under McDonald 2017.

subtopic_detail: Acute chest syndrome in adult sickle cell disease
stem: A 27-year-old man with homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) presents with 24 hours of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. He has been admitted twice in the last year for vaso-occlusive crises. His usual hydroxyurea has been taken regularly. Chest radiograph now shows a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Pulse oximetry shows hypoxia on room air. He has no penicillin allergy. He has had pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccinations.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/74, HR 116, RR 26, SpO2 90% on room air, Temp 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right basal crackles and dullness to percussion; mild jaundice; spleen not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Hb 76 g/L (baseline 92), reticulocytes 11 percent, WCC 14.6 x10^9/L, platelets 388 x10^9/L, LDH 720 U/L, bilirubin 56 micromol/L; CXR confirms right lower lobe infiltrate

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management bundle?

options.text: Exchange transfusion is contraindicated in adults with sickle cell disease, and management is limited to oxygen, analgesia and oral antibiotics on the general ward only
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is a key salvage therapy in severe acute chest syndrome; it is not contraindicated. (Source: BSH guidelines for the management of sickle cell disease; HSANZ paediatric and adult statements)

options.text: NSAIDs as sole analgesia, no antibiotic cover and observation alone with no transfusion or escalation, given hydroxyurea adherence is documented in this patient with sickle cell disease
options.rationale: Acute chest syndrome demands antibiotic cover, oxygen and consideration of transfusion regardless of hydroxyurea status. (Source: BSH sickle cell disease guideline)

options.text: Continuous positive airway pressure as the only intervention without any antibiotic therapy, opioid analgesia, transfusion plan or incentive spirometry while admitted on the medical ward
options.rationale: Non-invasive ventilation is an adjunct; antibiotics, opioid analgesia and transfusion are core therapy. (Source: BSH sickle cell disease guideline)

options.text: Oxygen, intravenous fluids at maintenance, opioid analgesia, intravenous ceftriaxone plus oral azithromycin, incentive spirometry, simple top-up or exchange transfusion, haematology and ICU review
options.rationale: Acute chest syndrome is managed with oxygen, judicious fluids, opioid analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering typical and atypical pathogens, incentive spirometry, and simple top-up transfusion (or exchange transfusion for severe disease), with haematology and ICU involvement. (Source: BSH sickle cell disease guideline)

options.text: Single high-dose acute hydroxyurea bolus as the immediate therapy without any other measures, on the basis that hydroxyurea is the cornerstone of long-term disease modification in this patient
options.rationale: Hydroxyurea is long-term prevention; it does not rescue acute chest syndrome. (Source: BSH sickle cell disease guideline)

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome is a new pulmonary infiltrate with respiratory symptoms in sickle cell disease. Mortality in adults is around 5 to 10 percent. Management is oxygen to maintain saturation above 95 percent, judicious crystalloid (avoiding overload), opioid analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering typical and atypical organisms (eg ceftriaxone plus azithromycin), bronchodilators if reactive airways, incentive spirometry, and simple top-up transfusion or exchange transfusion for severe disease. Haematology and ICU involvement is essential. Triggers (infection, hypoventilation, fat embolism, atelectasis) are sought and addressed.
key_points: Acute chest syndrome: new infiltrate plus respiratory symptoms in sickle cell disease
Broad-spectrum antibiotics cover typical and atypical pathogens
Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe disease (hypoxia, falling Hb, multi-lobar involvement)
explanation.pearls: Adult acute chest syndrome mortality drops with early ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, incentive spirometry every hour while awake, and exchange transfusion when SpO2 falls below 90 percent on supplemental oxygen.

sources.label: HSANZ sickle cell disease position statement

subtopic_detail: Reversal of apixaban-associated intracerebral haemorrhage
stem: A 72-year-old man with non-valvular atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for stroke prevention is brought to ED with sudden dense left hemiparesis 90 minutes after his most recent dose. CT brain shows a 22 mL right basal ganglia haematoma without intraventricular extension or imminent herniation. His baseline INR was 1.0; he is on no antiplatelet therapy. He has no documented liver or significant renal disease. He is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 178/102, HR 88, GCS 13, NIHSS 14
data_table.Examination: Left-sided hemiparesis affecting face, arm and leg; dysarthria; no signs of herniation
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: 22 mL right basal ganglia ICH, no IVH; platelets 218 x10^9/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, INR 1.1, anti-Xa raised (consistent with on-therapy DOAC)

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line reversal strategy?

options.text: Transfusion of 4 units of fresh frozen plasma alone with no additional agent, expecting correction within 60 minutes of the start of transfusion in this DOAC-associated intracranial haemorrhage
options.rationale: FFP does not reverse direct factor Xa inhibitors; specific reversal is required. (Source: THANZ position statement on anticoagulant reversal; AHA/ASA spontaneous ICH guideline)

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg intravenously alone without any other agent, expecting full reversal of apixaban anticoagulant effect within 6 to 12 hours after administration in this patient
options.rationale: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not DOACs; not the agent of choice here. (Source: THANZ anticoagulant reversal statement)

options.text: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous infusion as the sole haemostatic agent with no specific DOAC reversal, no factor concentrate and no further intervention beyond supportive care for this DOAC-associated intracranial haemorrhage
options.rationale: TXA is not a substitute for specific reversal in DOAC ICH; outcome trials show minimal effect on functional outcome. (Source: THANZ anticoagulant reversal statement; TICH-2)

options.text: Defer reversal for 12 hours to allow natural drug clearance, with neurosurgical reassessment only if clinical deterioration occurs and no additional haemostatic intervention is undertaken now in this patient
options.rationale: Active intracerebral bleeding within an apixaban dosing interval requires immediate reversal, not observation. (Source: THANZ anticoagulant reversal statement)

options.text: Andexanet alfa if available, otherwise 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 IU/kg with BP control, neurosurgical referral and reversal of any concurrent antiplatelet therapy
options.rationale: Specific factor Xa reversal with andexanet alfa, or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg when andexanet is unavailable, is the AU pathway for DOAC ICH, alongside BP control under 140 systolic and neurosurgical referral. (Source: THANZ anticoagulant reversal statement; AHA/ASA spontaneous ICH guideline)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulant-associated intracranial haemorrhage requires emergent reversal with the agent specific to the anticoagulant. For factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban), andexanet alfa is the targeted reversal agent where available; otherwise 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 IU/kg is the alternative. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran. Concurrent BP control to 140 systolic, neurosurgical referral for haematoma evacuation candidates, and reversal of antiplatelet therapy with platelet transfusion (selective, in operative cases) complete the package.
key_points: Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban; 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg is the alternative
Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran
BP target under 140 systolic and neurosurgical referral are concurrent priorities
explanation.pearls: In apixaban-associated ICH, andexanet alfa 400 to 800 mg IV bolus followed by infusion (or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg when andexanet unavailable), with BP lowered to under 140 systolic, halves haematoma expansion compared with no specific reversal.

subtopic_detail: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax: ambulatory device versus chest drain
stem: A 22-year-old tall thin male non-smoker presents with sudden onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea over the past 6 hours. He has no past medical history and is on no medications. He is haemodynamically stable. Chest radiograph shows a 3.5 cm rim of air at the level of the hilum with no shift of the trachea or mediastinum. He has no history of underlying lung disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 92, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, T 36.7
data_table.Examination: Reduced air entry and hyperresonance over the right hemithorax, trachea midline, no surgical emphysema
data_table.Investigations: CXR right-sided pneumothorax with 3.5 cm rim of air at hilum; no rib fractures; no underlying lung disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observation only on supplemental high flow oxygen for 24 hours without aspiration or drain
options.rationale: Observation alone for a large primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a symptomatic patient is no longer routine first-line; ambulatory drain or aspiration is preferred. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)

options.text: Insertion of an ambulatory pneumothorax drain with Heimlich valve and discharge planning
options.rationale: Current British Thoracic Society 2023 guidance supports ambulatory management of large primary spontaneous pneumothorax in selected stable patients. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)

options.text: Needle thoracocentesis at the second intercostal space midclavicular line without imaging review
options.rationale: Needle thoracocentesis is reserved for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)

options.text: Insertion of a 28 French chest drain and admission to the high dependency unit for 5 days
options.rationale: Large bore chest drains are reserved for secondary pneumothorax or trauma; primary spontaneous pneumothorax is managed with smaller drains or ambulatory devices. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)

options.text: Referral for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical pleurodesis on the first presentation now
options.rationale: Surgical pleurodesis is for recurrent, bilateral, persistent air leak, or high-risk occupation pneumothorax, not first presentation. (Source: BTS pleural disease guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax management has shifted to a symptom-led approach: stable patients with minimal symptoms may be observed, while symptomatic patients with large pneumothoraces are increasingly managed with ambulatory pneumothorax devices or needle aspiration rather than admission with a chest drain. Tension pneumothorax (haemodynamic compromise, tracheal deviation) is decompressed immediately by needle thoracostomy followed by chest drain. Secondary pneumothorax (underlying lung disease) usually warrants admission and chest drain. Recurrence prevention with VATS and pleurodesis is considered for recurrent disease, persistent air leak over 5 days, bilateral disease, or high-risk occupations (pilots, divers).
key_points: Symptom-led approach replaces strict size cut-offs for primary spontaneous pneumothorax
Ambulatory pneumothorax devices are an option for stable symptomatic primary disease
Surgical pleurodesis is reserved for recurrence, persistent air leak, bilateral disease, or high-risk occupation
explanation.pearls: Needle thoracostomy is reserved for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise; in clinical practice it is replaced by finger thoracostomy in many AU prehospital settings.

subtopic_detail: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with moderate rim
stem: A 23-year-old tall thin male non-smoker presents with 6 hours of right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild breathlessness at rest. He has no preceding trauma. He has had no prior episodes, no underlying lung disease, and no recent travel. He is haemodynamically stable. He has no asthma history and lives 30 minutes from the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98, RR 22, T 36.7, BP 124/76, SpO2 94% room air
data_table.Examination: Reduced breath sounds and hyperresonance on the right; trachea midline; no surgical emphysema
data_table.Investigations: Erect chest x-ray: right pneumothorax with rim of 3 cm at the hilum, no mediastinal shift; computed tomography not performed; no contralateral lung disease

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Insert an 8 to 14 French intercostal catheter into the safe triangle with underwater seal drainage and admit for observation
options.rationale: A primary spontaneous pneumothorax with rim of 2 cm or more or symptomatic at rest warrants intercostal catheter drainage in Australian practice. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

options.text: Aspirate with a 16-gauge cannula at the second intercostal space midclavicular line and discharge if successful
options.rationale: Needle aspiration is an option for small primary pneumothoraces but is less effective than intercostal catheter for rims of 2 cm or more with significant symptoms. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

options.text: Provide oxygen by face mask and observe for 24 hours without any active intervention before considering drainage
options.rationale: Conservative observation alone is for small asymptomatic primary pneumothoraces with rim less than 2 cm and reliable follow-up. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

options.text: Refer for urgent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and pleurodesis on this first presentation today
options.rationale: Definitive surgery is reserved for second ipsilateral pneumothorax, persistent air leak, contralateral history, or occupational indication. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

options.text: Perform emergent needle decompression at the second intercostal space midclavicular line immediately without further imaging
options.rationale: Needle decompression is reserved for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise or tracheal deviation, neither of which is present. (Source: ANZCOR: Adult Advanced Life Support)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance recommends sizing pneumothorax by interpleural distance at the hilum or apex. Rim less than 2 cm and asymptomatic suits conservative observation. Rim of 2 cm or more or symptomatic warrants intercostal catheter, often a small bore 8 to 14 French catheter. Needle aspiration is an alternative but with lower success in larger rims. Tension pneumothorax with tracheal deviation, haemodynamic compromise, or hypoxia requires immediate needle decompression and chest drain placement.
key_points: Rim less than 2 cm and asymptomatic: observe with oxygen
Rim of 2 cm or more or symptomatic: insert intercostal catheter
Tension pneumothorax: immediate needle decompression then drain
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation is the single most important secondary prevention measure after primary spontaneous pneumothorax; the risk of recurrence is halved.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax

subtopic_detail: Lower limb cellulitis empirical antibiotic choice
stem: A 58-year-old presents with 24 hours of right calf erythema, warmth, and tenderness extending from the ankle to the knee with associated low-grade fever. He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin and no known drug allergies. There is no obvious break in the skin and no fluctuance or crepitus. Both legs are otherwise clinically equal in size with no calf tenderness on Homan's manoeuvre.

data_table.Examination: Right calf 2 cm of advancing erythema with warmth and tenderness; no skin necrosis, no crepitus, no lymphangitic streaking; pulses normal; sensation intact
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 12.5 with neutrophilia; CRP 84; eGFR 78; HbA1c 7.6; venous duplex Doppler not yet performed but clinically deep vein thrombosis low likelihood

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial antibiotic plan?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days with same-day general practitioner review of mark and limb elevation
options.rationale: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is broader spectrum and not first-line for uncomplicated cellulitis without diabetic foot ulcer or animal bite. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily for 10 days as first-line treatment for community-acquired soft tissue infection
options.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is reserved for suspected community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus with purulent infection, not non-purulent cellulitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose then 15 mg/kg twice daily as initial empirical therapy until culture results return
options.rationale: Empirical vancomycin is reserved for severe infection, suspected methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, or beta-lactam allergy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)

options.text: Oral clindamycin 450 mg three times daily for 7 days as first-line for non-purulent cellulitis in this presentation
options.rationale: Clindamycin is an alternative in penicillin allergy; it is not first-line in patients tolerant of beta-lactams. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days, with marked limb edge for surveillance and review at 48 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin oral 500 mg four times daily covers Streptococcus and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus for uncomplicated non-purulent cellulitis; recent Australian guidance supports 5 days for clinically improving cases. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: cellulitis)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated non-purulent cellulitis is most commonly caused by Streptococcus species and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Australian first-line therapy is oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days in patients without severity criteria, allergy, or risk factors for community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Marking the erythema edge and reviewing at 48 hours guides response. Intravenous therapy is reserved for severe infection, sepsis criteria, or failure of oral therapy.
key_points: Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days is first-line for uncomplicated cellulitis
Mark the erythema edge and review at 48 hours
Vancomycin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are reserved for specific risk factors
explanation.pearls: Recurrent leg cellulitis often reflects tinea pedis as the portal of entry; treat the fungal foot infection to prevent further episodes.

subtopic_detail: Aldosterone-renin ratio screening in resistant hypertension
stem: A 46-year-old has stage 2 hypertension uncontrolled despite three antihypertensives at full dose: perindopril 8 mg, indapamide 2.5 mg, and amlodipine 10 mg. Home BP averages 158/96. Potassium is 3.2 mmol/L without a diuretic dose change. He has no kidney disease, no obstructive sleep apnoea, and no use of liquorice or nasal decongestants. The endocrinologist plans to investigate for primary hyperaldosteronism.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/96 average home readings; HR 78
data_table.Examination: BMI 31, no Cushingoid features, no abdominal bruit, normal fundi
data_table.Investigations: Na 142, K 3.2, eGFR 82, plasma renin and aldosterone not yet drawn, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 2.5 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate preparation before drawing the aldosterone-renin ratio?

options.text: Continue all current antihypertensive agents unchanged and draw the aldosterone-renin ratio in the morning after 8 hours of overnight recumbency
options.rationale: Some antihypertensives substantially alter the aldosterone-renin ratio and must be adjusted before testing. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)

options.text: Stop all antihypertensive medications for 4 weeks and treat hypertension only with hydralazine plus metoprolol during the washout period before testing
options.rationale: Beta-blockers also suppress renin and increase the aldosterone-renin ratio, generating false positives. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)

options.text: Replace potassium above 4.0 mmol/L, stop any mineralocorticoid antagonist for 4 weeks, and substitute prazosin, hydralazine, moxonidine, or verapamil for sampling
options.rationale: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists must be stopped 4 weeks before sampling; potassium must be replete; non-interfering agents like prazosin, hydralazine, moxonidine, and verapamil can manage hypertension during testing. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)

options.text: Draw aldosterone-renin ratio in the supine position at midnight to maximise diagnostic sensitivity and avoid morning circadian effects
options.rationale: Sampling is done after 2 hours of upright posture in the morning, not in the supine position at midnight. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)

options.text: Restrict dietary sodium to under 80 mmol daily for 2 weeks before sampling to suppress aldosterone secretion and enhance test specificity
options.rationale: Sodium restriction alters the renin-aldosterone axis and is not part of routine screening preparation. (Source: Endocrine Society Guideline: Primary Aldosteronism)

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is a common cause of resistant hypertension, particularly with spontaneous hypokalaemia. Screening uses the aldosterone-renin ratio after potassium repletion and washout of interfering medications. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, eplerenone, and amiloride must be stopped 4 weeks beforehand. Beta-blockers reduce renin and increase the ratio falsely. ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and dihydropyridines may be continued with caution. Sampling is done in the morning after 2 hours upright.
key_points: Replete potassium before sampling
Stop mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists for 4 weeks before testing
Verapamil, prazosin, hydralazine, and moxonidine do not interfere with screening
explanation.pearls: Confirmatory testing with saline loading or fludrocortisone suppression follows a positive screen; do not commit to surgery on a screen alone.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and emergency management
stem: A 38-year-old with primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone 20 mg and fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily presents to the emergency department after 36 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea from gastroenteritis. She has been unable to keep down her morning hydrocortisone. She feels dizzy on standing and has had no urine output today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 22, T 37.1, BP 86/52 lying, SpO2 99%
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds, no focal abdominal signs
data_table.Investigations: Na 128, K 5.6, glucose 3.8, creatinine 132, urea 14, venous blood gas pH 7.31, bicarbonate 18, lactate 2.6

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first action?

options.text: Administer oral hydrocortisone 40 mg now and admit to the short-stay unit for observation and oral rehydration over 6 hours
options.rationale: Persistent vomiting precludes oral absorption; parenteral hydrocortisone is required without delay in adrenal crisis. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg and 1 L of sodium chloride 0.9% over 1 hour, then admit for ongoing hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis requires immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by infusion or repeated doses to total 200 mg over 24 hours, plus aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg and 500 mL of 5% dextrose over 1 hour as first-line treatment for adrenal crisis
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is preferred because it provides mineralocorticoid as well as glucocorticoid coverage; dexamethasone is used only when retaining diagnostic capacity matters. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Administer oral fludrocortisone 0.2 mg and intravenous 5% dextrose at 100 mL/hour to correct hypoglycaemia and electrolyte imbalance
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not needed acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity at 100 mg or more daily. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Defer steroid until plasma cortisol level returns within 2 hours and initiate intravenous antibiotics empirically before any hormonal intervention
options.rationale: Empirical steroids are given immediately in suspected adrenal crisis without waiting for cortisol level results; antibiotics are added if sepsis is suspected. (Source: ESA: Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency requiring immediate intravenous hydrocortisone and aggressive fluid resuscitation. Standard dosing is hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours. Hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid effect at these doses, so fludrocortisone is not required acutely. Glucose monitoring and treatment of hypoglycaemia are essential. Investigation for and treatment of precipitating infection occurs simultaneously.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous followed by 200 mg over 24 hours in adrenal crisis
Fluid resuscitate with sodium chloride 0.9% and treat hypoglycaemia
Identify and treat precipitating illness in parallel
explanation.pearls: All patients with adrenal insufficiency should have hydrocortisone for self-injection at home and stress-dose instructions; an Australian endocrine emergency wristband or card aids identification.

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative blockade sequencing
stem: A 41-year-old has biochemically confirmed phaeochromocytoma with plasma metanephrines 12-fold elevated and a 5 cm right adrenal mass with avid uptake on MIBG. He is referred to the endocrine team for preoperative optimisation. He has paroxysmal palpitations, headaches, and pallor 3 to 4 times weekly. His BP swings between 165/96 during episodes and 138/78 at rest. He has no other comorbidity.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 sinus rhythm, BP 152/92 at rest, no orthostatic drop yet
data_table.Examination: BMI 22, no abdominal mass palpable, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: Plasma metanephrines elevated; MIBG positive at the right adrenal; CT confirms 5 cm right adrenal mass; ECG sinus rhythm, no left ventricular hypertrophy

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate preoperative blockade plan?

options.text: Start metoprolol 25 mg twice daily today and titrate to heart rate under 80 over 2 weeks before initiating alpha blockade
options.rationale: Beta blockade before alpha blockade unopposes alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and can precipitate hypertensive crisis. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Start oral amlodipine 5 mg daily and refer for elective adrenalectomy in 5 to 7 days without preoperative alpha or beta blockade
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockade alone is inadequate preoperative blockade; alpha blockade is mandatory. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Recommend immediate adrenalectomy without preoperative blockade because anaesthetic alpha and beta agents can be titrated intraoperatively
options.rationale: Preoperative blockade for 10 to 14 days reduces intraoperative haemodynamic instability and is mandatory. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily, titrate with high-sodium diet, then add beta-blocker if reflex tachycardia develops, with surgery at 10 to 14 days
options.rationale: Australian and international practice is alpha blockade first, typically phenoxybenzamine, with high-salt diet to expand volume; beta blockade added only if reflex tachycardia, then adrenalectomy at 10 to 14 days. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Start labetalol 100 mg twice daily as a single agent for combined alpha and beta blockade to streamline preoperative preparation
options.rationale: Labetalol has greater beta than alpha activity and can produce paradoxical hypertension in phaeochromocytoma. (Source: ESA: Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

explanation.summary: Preoperative blockade in phaeochromocytoma must be alpha first, beta second, to prevent unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. Phenoxybenzamine is the most common alpha blocker; doxazosin is an alternative when phenoxybenzamine causes troublesome side effects. A high-sodium diet and increased fluid intake expand intravascular volume. Beta blockade is added only after adequate alpha blockade if reflex tachycardia develops. Surgery is generally performed at 10 to 14 days when targets are met.
key_points: Alpha first, beta second for phaeochromocytoma preoperative blockade
Phenoxybenzamine is the standard alpha blocker; doxazosin is an alternative
High-sodium diet and volume expansion are essential adjuncts
explanation.pearls: Labetalol is contraindicated as monotherapy in phaeochromocytoma because the relative beta blockade overshadows the alpha component and can precipitate crisis.

subtopic_detail: Massive pulmonary embolism with haemodynamic compromise
stem: A 62-year-old presents collapsed 90 minutes after returning from a 24-hour flight. She remains haemodynamically unstable on arrival. She has no prior bleeding history, no recent surgery, no head injury, no current anticoagulation, and no known coagulopathy. She is alert and able to consent. The on-call respiratory and cardiology teams have reviewed and agree she has massive pulmonary embolism.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, RR 32, T 36.9, BP 78/48, SpO2 86% on 15 L/min non-rebreather mask
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries, raised jugular venous pressure, prominent right ventricular heave, no audible third heart sound, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Bedside echocardiogram shows severe right ventricular dilatation with septal flattening; troponin elevated; CT pulmonary angiogram shows bilateral central pulmonary emboli; lactate 4.2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours then commence unfractionated heparin once activated partial thromboplastin time normalises
options.rationale: Massive pulmonary embolism with sustained hypotension is a class I indication for systemic thrombolysis, typically alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours, followed by anticoagulation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

options.text: Initiate therapeutic enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily and admit to the medical assessment unit for monitoring with cardiology review tomorrow
options.rationale: Therapeutic anticoagulation alone is inadequate for haemodynamically unstable massive pulmonary embolism; reperfusion is required. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

options.text: Insert an inferior vena cava filter immediately as definitive therapy without anticoagulation or reperfusion treatment
options.rationale: Inferior vena cava filters are reserved for those with contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent emboli despite therapy. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

options.text: Commence non-invasive ventilation with bilevel positive airway pressure and reassess for thrombolysis if not improving after 4 hours of trial
options.rationale: Non-invasive ventilation does not address the haemodynamic obstruction; delay in reperfusion increases mortality. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

options.text: Refer to interventional radiology for outpatient catheter-directed thrombolysis within the next 7 to 10 days after stabilisation on heparin alone
options.rationale: Catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy is considered for those with absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis; delay of 7 days is unacceptable in massive pulmonary embolism. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

explanation.summary: Massive or high-risk pulmonary embolism is defined by sustained hypotension and is a class I indication for systemic thrombolysis. Standard dosing is alteplase 100 mg intravenously over 2 hours followed by unfractionated heparin once activated partial thromboplastin time is approaching normal. Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy is reserved for those with absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis. Intermediate-high risk pulmonary embolism with normotension but right ventricular strain may benefit from selective rescue thrombolysis if deterioration occurs.
key_points: Massive pulmonary embolism with hypotension warrants systemic thrombolysis
Alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours then heparin is standard dosing
Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy is reserved for thrombolysis contraindications
explanation.pearls: Even after thrombolysis many patients have persistent right ventricular strain; follow-up echocardiography at 3 to 6 months screens for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Embolism

subtopic_detail: Suspected osteomyelitis underlying a diabetic foot ulcer
stem: A 64-year-old has had a chronic 2 cm plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head for 8 weeks with surrounding cellulitis and ongoing serous discharge. He has type 2 diabetes for 18 years, HbA1c 8.6, peripheral neuropathy, and palpable pulses. Probe-to-bone with a sterile probe is positive today through the ulcer. There is no acute necrosis.

data_table.Examination: 2 cm plantar ulcer over first metatarsal head with sloughy base; positive probe-to-bone; surrounding 3 cm cellulitis without crepitus; ankle-brachial index 1.0; sensation to 10 g monofilament absent in forefoot
data_table.Investigations: WCC 11.8; CRP 56; ESR 78; HbA1c 8.6; foot x-ray shows cortical erosion of first metatarsal head; MRI not yet performed; previous wound swab grew Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus agalactiae

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue outpatient oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily for a further 4 weeks and review at the diabetic foot clinic in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Outpatient cephalexin is inadequate for suspected osteomyelitis; bone-penetrating broader regimens are required after appropriate sampling. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)

options.text: Order an outpatient bone biopsy in 8 weeks while continuing topical wound dressings and routine podiatry review every 2 weeks
options.rationale: Delay of 8 weeks in suspected osteomyelitis risks progression and amputation; admission and timely sampling are warranted. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)

options.text: Treat empirically with oral metronidazole 400 mg three times daily as monotherapy for 6 weeks and review at the wound clinic monthly
options.rationale: Metronidazole alone does not cover Staphylococcus aureus or aerobic streptococci, which are the dominant pathogens in diabetic foot osteomyelitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)

options.text: Proceed directly to mid-foot amputation today without further investigation or culture-directed antimicrobial therapy as definitive treatment
options.rationale: Surgical resection of infected bone is selective; amputation is reserved for failed medical therapy, extensive necrosis, or limb-threatening sepsis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)

options.text: Admit for orthopaedic and infectious diseases input, bone biopsy with histology and culture, and 6 weeks of culture-directed intravenous then oral antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Positive probe-to-bone with cortical erosion is highly predictive of osteomyelitis; targeted bone biopsy guides 6 weeks of culture-directed antibiotic therapy with surgical input as needed. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: diabetic foot)

explanation.summary: A positive probe-to-bone in a chronic diabetic foot ulcer with raised inflammatory markers and cortical erosion on x-ray is highly predictive of osteomyelitis. Optimal management combines admission for multidisciplinary input including orthopaedic, infectious diseases, vascular, podiatry, and diabetes care. Bone biopsy with histology and culture guides 6 weeks of intravenous followed by oral culture-directed antibiotic therapy. Surgical resection of infected bone is considered when medical therapy fails, when there is extensive necrosis, or when sepsis threatens limb viability.
key_points: Probe-to-bone plus cortical erosion strongly predicts diabetic foot osteomyelitis
Bone biopsy with culture guides 6-week antibiotic therapy
Multidisciplinary care reduces amputation rates
explanation.pearls: Vascular assessment with ankle-brachial index and toe pressures is essential before antibiotic-only management because ischaemia mandates revascularisation.

sources.label: Diabetes Feet Australia: Diabetic Foot Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis on chronic steroid replacement
stem: A 56-year-old woman with Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 10 mg morning and 5 mg afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily is brought to ED by her partner. She has had 24 hours of fevers, cough and progressive lethargy. This morning she vomited her hydrocortisone dose. On arrival she is hypotensive and confused. Her medic-alert bracelet identifies the diagnosis.

data_table.Examination: Confused (GCS 14), warm peripheries, RR 26, no neck stiffness, right basal crackles; capillary refill 3 s
data_table.Investigations: Na 128 mmol/L, K 5.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, urea 9.2, creatinine 124, lactate 3.8, CRP 198 mg/L; CXR right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Double her usual oral hydrocortisone dose and observe in ED with intravenous saline overnight
options.rationale: Oral dosing is inadequate when vomiting and shocked; IV hydrocortisone is required. (Source: ESE 2020)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus crystalloid resuscitation and empirical antibiotics
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis (hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia) on top of sepsis requires immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, IV fluid resuscitation, glucose correction and antibiotics per sepsis pathway. (Source: ESE adrenal crisis 2020; eTG)

options.text: Start IV dexamethasone 4 mg with stim test scheduled before any glucocorticoid replacement therapy
options.rationale: Diagnosis is already established by medic-alert bracelet and clinical picture; do not delay hydrocortisone for biochemical testing in established Addison's. (Source: ESE 2020)

options.text: Administer noradrenaline infusion targeting MAP 65 before any steroid replacement is given
options.rationale: Vasopressors are ineffective without glucocorticoid replacement in established adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone must come first. (Source: ESE 2020)

options.text: Withhold steroid dosing pending confirmation of sepsis source by chest CT before treatment starts
options.rationale: Delay for imaging in shocked adrenal crisis worsens outcome; treat empirically and image after stabilisation. (Source: ESE 2020)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency in patients with primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency, precipitated by infection, surgery, trauma, missed steroid doses, vomiting or stress. Features include hypotension, shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (primary AI only), hypoglycaemia and altered mental state. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat (continuing 200 mg/24 h infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours), IV isotonic saline resuscitation (1 L in first hour), glucose correction, and empirical treatment of the precipitant. Educate patients on sick-day rules: double oral dose for fevers/minor illness, IM hydrocortisone (Solu-Cortef) injection for vomiting.
key_points: Adrenal crisis = hypotension + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia.
Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat.
IV crystalloid 1 L in first hour, then maintenance.
Treat precipitant (sepsis): empirical antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines.
Patient education: double oral dose for minor illness; IM hydrocortisone for vomiting.
explanation.pearls: Patients on regular prednisolone 5 mg or higher for 4 weeks or longer have functional secondary adrenal insufficiency and need stress-dose hydrocortisone for major surgery or sepsis even if their primary disease (eg PMR, asthma) seems quiescent.

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment selection
stem: You are an infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 34-year-old man from a high-prevalence country who arrived in Australia 18 months ago. He is screened before commencing infliximab for severe rheumatoid arthritis. He is asymptomatic, with no cough, fever, or weight loss. His QuantiFERON-Plus assay is positive. Chest X-ray is normal. There are no apical changes or calcified granulomas. He drinks no alcohol, has no past liver disease, and his ALT and AST are normal. He has no household contacts known to have active tuberculosis. He is keen to start his rheumatology treatment as soon as possible.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, Temp 36.7 degrees C, BMI 25 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Cardiorespiratory examination unremarkable, mild synovitis of the MCP joints
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive, CXR normal, ALT 22 U/L, AST 24 U/L, HIV non-reactive, HepBsAg negative, HepC negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for his latent tuberculosis infection?

options.text: Sputum induction for acid-fast bacilli smear and culture before any latent treatment is started
options.rationale: He has no respiratory symptoms and a normal chest X-ray, so sputum sampling is not required. Active TB workup is reserved for symptomatic or radiographically suspicious cases. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Defer treatment and commence infliximab immediately given normal chest imaging and no symptoms
options.rationale: Anti-TNF therapy in the presence of untreated latent TB carries a 4 to 8-fold increase in reactivation, often as extrapulmonary or miliary disease. Treatment of latent TB must precede or run alongside biologic therapy. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Four-drug RIPE therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months then dual therapy for 4 months
options.rationale: RIPE is the regimen for active tuberculosis, not latent infection. Treating latent infection as if it were active causes unnecessary toxicity. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular BCG vaccination as protective immunisation prior to biologic therapy
options.rationale: BCG vaccination does not treat existing latent infection and is contraindicated in immunosuppressed adults due to disseminated BCG risk. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg orally daily with pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 6 months and monthly clinical and LFT review
options.rationale: Isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine for 6 months is a recommended Australian regimen for latent tuberculosis. Treatment should start at least 4 weeks before commencing anti-TNF therapy to reduce the risk of reactivation. Pyridoxine prevents peripheral neuropathy. (Source: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) treatment is offered to those at risk of progression: recent contacts of infectious cases, immunosuppression including anti-TNF therapy, HIV, dialysis, organ transplant, silicosis, and migrants from high-prevalence countries. Acceptable Australian regimens include isoniazid 6 months, isoniazid plus rifampicin 3 months, and rifampicin 4 months. Anti-TNF agents increase reactivation risk 4 to 8-fold; LTBI treatment should begin at least 4 weeks before biologic therapy. Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid peripheral neuropathy.
key_points: Recommended LTBI regimens: 6H, 3HR, or 4R as per NTAC
Anti-TNF therapy increases TB reactivation 4 to 8-fold
LTBI treatment should start at least 4 weeks before biologic therapy
Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy
explanation.pearls: Isoniazid hepatotoxicity rises markedly above age 35 and with alcohol intake - baseline ALT and monthly LFT monitoring during treatment catches early hepatitis and most resolves with prompt drug cessation.

sources.label: NTAC - Position Statement on the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection

subtopic_detail: VTE anticoagulation duration
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 56-year-old man at a 3-month follow-up after an unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis of the right popliteal vein. He has been treated with apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for 3 months and is well. He has had no further symptoms. He has no personal or family history of VTE.

He has no history of cancer, has lost no weight, and a malignancy screen at presentation was unremarkable. There is no thrombophilia identified on a basic screen. His mild hypertension is well controlled. He has no bleeding history.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, BMI 27 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: No leg swelling, no calf tenderness, no signs of post-thrombotic syndrome, no bruising
data_table.Investigations: Hb 142 g/L, platelets 235 x10^9/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, eGFR > 60 mL/min/1.73m2, ALT 24 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Switch to warfarin with target INR 2.0 to 3.0 indefinitely as the most cost-effective long-term option
options.rationale: DOACs are preferred over warfarin for VTE in patients without contraindications because they offer similar efficacy with lower intracranial bleeding rates and avoid INR monitoring. Switching for cost alone is not recommended. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Stop apixaban at 3 months given the patient has completed standard treatment and is asymptomatic
options.rationale: Stopping anticoagulation after 3 months for unprovoked proximal DVT leaves a recurrence risk of around 10% in the first year, with case fatality of recurrent VTE around 5%. Extended therapy is recommended in low-bleeding-risk patients. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily as long-term secondary prevention with no further anticoagulant
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces VTE recurrence by only around 30% compared with around 80% reduction from a DOAC, with similar bleeding rates at the low-dose DOAC extended dose. DOAC is preferred. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely without reducing the dose for extended therapy
options.rationale: Both AMPLIFY-EXT and EINSTEIN-CHOICE showed that reduced-dose DOACs are as effective and safer for extended-phase therapy after the initial 6 months. Full-dose is reserved for higher-risk profiles. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely with annual bleeding-risk review and renal monitoring
options.rationale: After an unprovoked proximal DVT, indefinite anticoagulation is recommended for low bleeding-risk patients because annual recurrence after stopping is around 10% in year one and 5% per year thereafter. Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is the evidence-supported extended-phase dose with similar efficacy and lower bleeding than full-intensity therapy. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: VTE anticoagulation duration depends on whether the event was provoked or unprovoked and on bleeding risk. Provoked VTE (surgery, trauma, immobilisation) is treated for 3 months. Unprovoked proximal DVT or PE warrants extended (indefinite) anticoagulation in low-bleeding-risk patients because recurrence is around 10% in year one without therapy. Reduced-dose DOACs (apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) are as effective and safer than full dose for the extended phase. Annual reassessment of bleeding risk is essential.
key_points: Provoked VTE: 3 months of anticoagulation
Unprovoked proximal VTE: extended therapy if low bleeding risk
Reduced-dose DOAC (apixaban 2.5 mg BID, rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) for extended phase
Annual bleeding-risk reassessment is the cornerstone of extended therapy
explanation.pearls: After the first 6 months of full-dose anticoagulation for unprovoked VTE, reduced-dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) lowers recurrence by approximately 80% compared with placebo with major bleeding rates similar to no anticoagulation.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Septic shock hour-1 bundle
stem:
You are the medical registrar at a metropolitan emergency department. A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 3 days of dysuria, rigors, and now confusion. He has been brought in by his wife. He is alert but confused, peripherally cool, and tachypnoeic. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. He weighs 80 kg. He has no known allergies. He has no known kidney disease.

Intravenous access has been established. A urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leucocytes. A point-of-care lactate has been performed and blood cultures sent. He has received no antibiotics today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 28, Temp 39.4 degrees C, SpO2 95% room air
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13, mottled lower limbs, suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, glucose 12 mmol/L, creatinine 158 micromol/L, WCC 18 x10^9/L, CRP 220 mg/L, urinalysis nitrites and leucocytes positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first-hour intervention?

options.text: Commence intravenous fluid resuscitation at 1 L over 30 minutes then reassess before further bolus
options.rationale: 1 L is well below the recommended 30 mL/kg initial volume for septic shock and inadequate for this 80 kg patient. The Surviving Sepsis bundle calls for 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours, ideally front-loaded in the first hour. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

options.text: Defer antibiotics until urine culture and blood culture results are available to allow targeted therapy
options.rationale: Each hour of delayed antibiotic administration in septic shock increases mortality by 4 to 8%. Cultures are obtained but treatment is not delayed. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

options.text: Administer intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g and commence 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid resuscitation
options.rationale: Septic shock with hypotension and lactate over 2 mmol/L mandates broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour and 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid resuscitation. Piperacillin-tazobactam covers community urinary sepsis with shock per Australian sepsis pathways. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula without fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Noradrenaline is added when fluid resuscitation has failed to restore MAP above 65 mmHg. Starting vasopressors before fluid in this patient bypasses the proven mortality-reducing fluid bolus. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg as first-line therapy for hypotension before fluids
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added only when fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support have failed to maintain MAP above 65 mmHg. It is not a first-hour intervention before fluids and antibiotics. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network)
source_refs: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle for adults with septic shock includes obtaining lactate and blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, and vasopressor support if MAP remains below 65 mmHg after fluid resuscitation. Empirical antibiotic choice follows source: urinary tract sepsis with shock is commonly treated with piperacillin-tazobactam in Australia, narrowed when cultures return. Source control (drainage, surgical intervention) is pursued in parallel for abscess, biliary sepsis, or other surgical foci.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour of septic shock recognition
30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for shock or lactate > 4 mmol/L
Noradrenaline first-line vasopressor target MAP > 65 mmHg
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if vasopressor-dependent shock persists
explanation.pearls: Each hour of delay in appropriate antibiotic administration after recognition of septic shock increases in-hospital mortality by approximately 4 to 8% - early administration is among the highest-yield interventions in sepsis care.

sources.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Australian Sepsis Network
ANZICS Clinical Trials Group - ANZICS Sepsis Resources

subtopic_detail: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 22-year-old previously well thin man with sudden onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild breathlessness 4 hours ago. He has never smoked and has no past medical history. He has no trauma, no fever, and no preceding illness. On examination he has reduced breath sounds on the right with normal trachea midline. Vital signs are stable.

Chest X-ray confirms a moderate right primary pneumothorax with an interpleural distance of 3 cm at the hilum and no mediastinal shift. There is no underlying lung disease on imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Trachea midline, reduced right breath sounds, hyper-resonant percussion right, no surgical emphysema
data_table.Investigations: CXR: right pneumothorax interpleural distance 3 cm at hilum, no shift, no underlying disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Urgent video-assisted thoracoscopic pleurodesis as definitive surgical management for first presentation
options.rationale: VATS pleurodesis is reserved for recurrent pneumothorax, persistent air leak, or first occurrence in high-risk occupations. It is not first-line for a stable primary pneumothorax at first presentation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

options.text: Insertion of a 28F intercostal catheter as the first procedure for any visible primary pneumothorax
options.rationale: Large-bore intercostal catheters cause more pain and longer hospital stays than aspiration or small-bore drains in primary pneumothorax, and are not first-line in a stable patient. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

options.text: Observation only with high-flow oxygen by mask and reassessment with serial chest X-rays at 24 hours
options.rationale: Conservative management is acceptable for small primary pneumothorax (under 2 cm) with minimal symptoms but is not first choice for a 3 cm moderately symptomatic pneumothorax. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

options.text: Needle aspiration of the right pleural space with a 14 to 16 gauge cannula and post-procedure chest X-ray
options.rationale: British Thoracic Society and Australian guidance support needle aspiration as first-line for a symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax with interpleural distance more than 2 cm at the hilum. Aspiration succeeds in around 60% of cases and avoids intercostal catheter insertion. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

options.text: Discharge home with analgesia and outpatient review in 2 weeks with repeat chest X-ray then
options.rationale: A symptomatic moderate primary pneumothorax requires active management before discharge. Home discharge without aspiration or drainage risks progression and tension physiology. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia - Pneumothorax)

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax most commonly affects tall, thin, young men and is managed by size and symptoms. Interpleural distance under 2 cm at the hilum with minimal symptoms is observed. Larger or symptomatic primary pneumothoraces are treated by needle aspiration first, with small-bore intercostal catheter for failure. Tension physiology mandates immediate needle decompression. After a first primary pneumothorax, recurrence rate is approximately 30% within 1 year; VATS pleurodesis or bullectomy is offered after a second event or for persistent air leak.
key_points: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax under 2 cm: observation only
Larger or symptomatic: needle aspiration first-line
Persistent air leak or recurrence: small-bore intercostal catheter then VATS
Recurrence after first event around 30% within 1 year
explanation.pearls: Tall thin young males who smoke have a 7 to 10-fold higher risk of recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax, and smoking cessation is the single most important secondary prevention measure even after surgical pleurodesis.

subtopic_detail: Infective endocarditis empiric therapy
stem: You are the general medical registrar admitting a 58-year-old woman with 3 weeks of low-grade fever, weight loss, and night sweats. She has a known bioprosthetic aortic valve replaced 14 months ago for severe aortic stenosis. Today she has developed a new soft early diastolic murmur on the left sternal edge. There are no embolic phenomena on examination. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn from separate sites and a transthoracic echocardiogram has been ordered. There are no penicillin allergies. The team plans empirical antibiotics while awaiting culture and echocardiographic results.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 124/68 mmHg, Temp 38.4 degrees C, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: New aortic regurgitation murmur, no Janeway lesions, no Osler nodes, no splinter haemorrhages
data_table.Investigations: CRP 88 mg/L, WCC 12 x10^9/L, Hb 108 g/L (normocytic), creatinine 84 micromol/L, ECG sinus rhythm with no new conduction delay

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy as broad-spectrum cover for streptococci and HACEK organisms
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone alone is inadequate for prosthetic valve endocarditis and misses staphylococcal organisms. It is appropriate for native valve streptococcal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin combination for streptococcal native valve endocarditis cover
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin and gentamicin alone cover oral streptococci but miss staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis, which is the dominant pathogen group within 12 months of surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin monotherapy at high dose for community-acquired Staphylococcus aureus cover
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy fails to cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and biofilm-associated organisms typical of early prosthetic valve infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin, and rifampicin combination for early prosthetic valve infective endocarditis cover
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis within 12 months of surgery is treated empirically with vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin to cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci including coagulase-negative species, which dominate this window. Rifampicin penetrates biofilm on prosthetic material. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Defer empirical antibiotics until echocardiographic vegetation is demonstrated to avoid unnecessary therapy
options.rationale: Once endocarditis is clinically suspected with new murmur and persistent fever after sending three culture sets, empirical antibiotics are commenced immediately because delay increases embolic and mortality risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis is classified by valve type and timing. Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (less than 12 months from surgery) is dominated by Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and enterococci, with high methicillin resistance. Empirical therapy is vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin, narrowed when cultures return. Modified Duke criteria require 2 major, 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor for definite IE. Three blood culture sets are drawn from separate sites before antibiotics. Transoesophageal echo has higher sensitivity than transthoracic for prosthetic valve vegetations.
key_points: Early PVE (under 12 months): vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin empirical
Late PVE (over 12 months): treated similarly to native valve disease
Three blood culture sets from separate sites before antibiotics
TOE > TTE sensitivity for prosthetic valve vegetations
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin is added in prosthetic valve endocarditis specifically because of its biofilm penetration; it is not used in native valve disease and has potent CYP3A4 induction with major drug-interaction implications.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand - Endocarditis
ESC Guidelines for the Management of Endocarditis

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage
stem:
You are the medical registrar at a metropolitan emergency department. A 54-year-old man presents with severe headache, blurred vision, and a few hours of dyspnoea. He has poorly controlled essential hypertension on irregular amlodipine. He has no chest pain. He has been working long hours and has not taken his medication for 1 week. Fundoscopy reveals papilloedema and flame haemorrhages.

CXR shows pulmonary oedema. Troponin is mildly elevated and ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with strain. There is no evidence of aortic dissection on the bedside ultrasound. The consultant asks for your initial intravenous antihypertensive plan.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 bpm, BP 232/142 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 91% room air
data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, JVP 4 cm elevated, papilloedema, flame haemorrhages, no focal neurology
