data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 0.08 micrograms/L (peak), creatinine 138 micromol/L, eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m2, urinalysis 2+ blood 2+ protein, CXR pulmonary oedema, ECG sinus tachycardia with LVH

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intravenous antihypertensive strategy?

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to reduce mean arterial pressure by approximately 25% over the first hour
options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema is treated with an intravenous nitrate (GTN) infusion plus loop diuretic, with target reduction in MAP of approximately 25% within the first hour and to 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours to avoid hypoperfusion. GTN reduces both preload and afterload. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

options.text: Oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate release with target normotension within 30 minutes of administration
options.rationale: Oral short-acting nifedipine causes uncontrolled hypotension and rebound stroke or myocardial ischaemia. It is not appropriate for hypertensive emergency. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

options.text: Intravenous esmolol bolus and infusion as monotherapy with target systolic BP under 120 mmHg in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Pure beta-blockade in pulmonary oedema worsens cardiac decompensation and the rapid normalisation target risks cerebral and coronary hypoperfusion. Beta-blockade is reserved for selected scenarios like aortic dissection alongside a vasodilator. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 10 mg bolus repeated every 20 minutes until systolic BP under 140 mmHg
options.rationale: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia (problematic in possible coronary ischaemia) and is unpredictable for titration. It is not first-line in hypertensive emergency outside pregnancy. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

options.text: Oral captopril 25 mg sublingually as rapid renin-angiotensin blockade for malignant hypertension
options.rationale: Sublingual or oral captopril is unpredictable and risks precipitous hypotension and AKI in a patient with rising creatinine. ACE inhibition has no role in acute IV management of hypertensive emergency. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (commonly above 180/120) with acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, retinopathy, pulmonary oedema, acute kidney injury, myocardial ischaemia, aortic dissection). Lowering blood pressure too rapidly causes watershed cerebral and coronary infarction. Targets are approximately 25% reduction in MAP within the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours, except in aortic dissection (systolic under 120 mmHg within 20 minutes) and ischaemic stroke (carefully titrated). IV nitrates, labetalol, and clevidipine are common Australian choices.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency: severe BP plus acute end-organ damage
Target: 25% MAP reduction in first hour, then 160/100 by 2 to 6 hours
Aortic dissection: systolic under 120 mmHg within 20 minutes
Pulmonary oedema: IV nitrate plus loop diuretic; avoid pure beta-blockade
explanation.pearls: Excessive rapid BP lowering in hypertensive emergency causes watershed cerebral infarction because chronic hypertension shifts the cerebral autoregulation curve - aiming for 25% MAP reduction in the first hour respects this rightward shift.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia - Hypertension Guidelines
ESC Guidelines for the Management of Arterial Hypertension

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma crisis management
stem: You are the medical registrar called to the high dependency unit. A 48-year-old woman was admitted yesterday for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During induction of anaesthesia 30 minutes ago she developed extreme hypertension and tachycardia followed by an episode of hypotension. She has now been transferred to the high dependency unit. She had been investigated 6 months ago for episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations but did not attend her endocrine appointment. The surgical team and the anaesthetist suspect an undiagnosed endocrine tumour. Plasma fractionated metanephrines have been sent. She is currently haemodynamically labile.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 bpm (sinus), BP currently 192/118 mmHg fluctuating, RR 22, Temp 37.1 degrees C, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, no focal neurology, no goitre, no abdominal mass palpable, no signs of NF1 stigmata
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, troponin 0.04 micrograms/L, glucose 11 mmol/L, plasma free metanephrines pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive strategy?

options.text: Commence intravenous phentolamine and fluid resuscitation, with a beta-blocker added only after alpha-blockade
options.rationale: Unopposed beta-blockade in suspected phaeochromocytoma crisis precipitates catastrophic alpha-mediated hypertension because circulating catecholamines lose their beta-vasodilatory counter. Phentolamine (non-selective alpha-blocker) is first-line for the acute crisis; sodium nitroprusside is an alternative. Beta-blockade is added only after alpha-blockade is established to control reflex tachycardia. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

options.text: Commence intravenous metoprolol bolus to control the heart rate and reduce myocardial oxygen demand
options.rationale: Unopposed beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma crisis is contraindicated because removal of beta-mediated vasodilation unmasks unopposed alpha-vasoconstriction, causing severe hypertensive crisis and possible cardiogenic shock. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

options.text: Commence intravenous labetalol infusion as combined alpha and beta blockade for catecholamine crisis
options.rationale: Labetalol has a 7:1 beta-to-alpha ratio when given intravenously and is functionally a beta-predominant agent in phaeochromocytoma, risking the same paradoxical hypertension as pure beta-blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

options.text: Commence intravenous amiodarone 300 mg bolus over 20 minutes to suppress sinus tachycardia
options.rationale: The tachycardia is catecholamine-driven and amiodarone is not the appropriate agent. Treatment must address the catecholamine excess via alpha-blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 5 g loading dose with cessation of the surgical procedure
options.rationale: Magnesium is an adjunct but not a primary agent for phaeochromocytoma crisis. Phentolamine or nitroprusside provides specific alpha-mediated vasodilation matched to the pathophysiology. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma crisis arises from massive catecholamine release, often during anaesthesia, surgical manipulation, or interventional procedures in an undiagnosed or inadequately blocked patient. The cardinal management rule is alpha-blockade first, then beta-blockade for tachycardia. Acute IV options include phentolamine (non-selective alpha), sodium nitroprusside, and nicardipine. Volume resuscitation addresses contracted intravascular volume. Once stabilised, oral phenoxybenzamine is used for 10 to 14 days of preoperative blockade before definitive surgical removal. Plasma free metanephrines are the diagnostic test of choice.
key_points: Phaeochromocytoma crisis: alpha-blockade first, beta-blockade only after alpha is established
Acute IV options: phentolamine, nitroprusside, nicardipine
Plasma free metanephrines have the highest sensitivity for diagnosis
Preoperative oral phenoxybenzamine for 10 to 14 days plus volume loading before surgery
explanation.pearls: Unopposed beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma can precipitate fatal hypertensive crisis within minutes because removing beta-mediated vasodilation unleashes catecholamine alpha-vasoconstriction - the order of blockade is non-negotiable.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline - Phaeochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

subtopic_detail: DVT diagnosis Wells score
stem: You are the general medicine RMO assessing a 58-year-old woman presenting with three days of left calf swelling and tenderness. She returned from a 14-hour flight a week ago. She has hypertension on perindopril, no prior VTE, and no active cancer. Examination reveals a swollen tender left calf with 3 cm circumference difference compared to the right and pitting oedema confined to the symptomatic leg.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Left calf swollen with 3 cm circumference difference at 10 cm below tibial tuberosity, tender along deep venous distribution, pitting oedema confined to symptomatic leg, no superficial varicosities
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, paracetamol PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange an MRI venogram of the lower limb to fully characterise venous involvement and exclude alternative diagnoses including muscular and lymphatic pathology
options.rationale: MR venography is reserved for specific cases (pelvic veins, IVC); not first-line for typical leg DVT. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)

options.text: Send a D-dimer level as the first step regardless of pretest probability because a negative result rules out deep vein thrombosis in all patient groups including this one
options.rationale: D-dimer rules out only with low pretest probability; with Wells 3 or more, proceed to imaging directly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)

options.text: Arrange CT venography of the lower limb as the most sensitive imaging test for proximal and distal vein involvement before initiating any further intervention
options.rationale: Compression ultrasound is first-line; CT venography is not standard initial imaging for DVT. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)

options.text: Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with apixaban and arrange ultrasound for confirmation if symptoms have not resolved over the next seven to ten days
options.rationale: Anticoagulation may be commenced empirically if imaging is delayed but diagnosis must still be confirmed promptly; deferring confirmation 7 to 10 days is inappropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)

options.text: Compression duplex ultrasound of the proximal leg veins given her Wells score makes DVT likely and pretest probability favours imaging over D-dimer
options.rationale: Wells score 3 or more (likely DVT) directs straight to compression ultrasound rather than D-dimer; her score totals 3 (calf swelling, pitting oedema unilateral, recent immobilisation). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE)

explanation.summary: DVT workup uses the Wells score to stratify pretest probability. Low probability (under 2) allows D-dimer rule-out. Likely DVT (2 or more) directs straight to compression ultrasound. Therapeutic guidance favours apixaban or rivaroxaban for proximal DVT without cancer or severe renal impairment. Provoked DVT (long-haul flight, surgery, immobilisation) is treated for 3 months; unprovoked DVT requires extended duration consideration.
key_points: Wells score guides whether to use D-dimer or imaging first
Compression duplex ultrasound is first-line imaging
Apixaban or rivaroxaban first-line for non-cancer DVT; 3 months for provoked
explanation.pearls: Cancer-associated thrombosis: LMWH or DOAC (apixaban, edoxaban) both acceptable per ASH 2021; rivaroxaban has higher bleeding risk in GI cancers.

subtopic_detail: Adult anaphylaxis adrenaline timing
stem: You are the ED RMO called to a 38-year-old man who developed widespread urticaria, throat tightness, and wheeze 15 minutes after eating prawns at a work lunch. He has previously had mild oral itching with shellfish. There has been no previous severe reaction. The triage nurse has placed IV access and is preparing equipment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/58, HR 124, RR 26, SpO2 92% room air, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, audible wheeze, mild lip swelling, no stridor, alert
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable for immediate management
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as the first intervention for the systemic inflammatory response before any other pharmacological intervention is undertaken
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have slow onset and are adjunctive; they do not replace adrenaline as the time-critical intervention. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh and position the patient supine while preparing further supportive measures
options.rationale: IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg into anterolateral thigh is first-line for anaphylaxis; delay increases biphasic and fatal reaction risk. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous promethazine 25 mg to manage the urticarial component and reassess the need for adrenaline once the antihistamine has been completed
options.rationale: Antihistamines treat urticaria but not airway or cardiovascular compromise; adrenaline must come first. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer nebulised salbutamol 5 mg as the first treatment for the bronchospasm and reassess oxygen requirements before considering further pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Salbutamol may help bronchospasm but does not address upper airway swelling or hypotension; adrenaline IM is first. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.05 micrograms/kg/min titrated to blood pressure response without prior intramuscular dose of adrenaline at all
options.rationale: IV adrenaline is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after multiple IM doses; IM is first-line due to safer pharmacokinetics. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is defined by acute onset (minutes to hours) with respiratory or cardiovascular compromise plus skin or mucosal involvement, or hypotension after known allergen exposure. IM adrenaline (1:1000) 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg in adults into anterolateral thigh is first-line. Repeat every 5 minutes as needed. Lay patient flat (head up if breathing difficulty), IV fluids for hypotension, salbutamol for persistent wheeze, corticosteroids as adjunct. Observe at least 4 hours.
key_points: IM adrenaline first-line; do not delay for IV access
Lay patient flat; sitting up increases mortality risk in hypotension
Observe 4 hours minimum; biphasic reaction in up to 20%
explanation.pearls: ASCIA action plan emphasises supine positioning; sitting up or standing during anaphylaxis is associated with empty ventricle syndrome and sudden death.

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency BP targets
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 64-year-old man brought to ED with sudden severe headache, vomiting, and confusion. He has known hypertension and stopped his perindopril two months ago. CT brain shows a small right basal ganglia haemorrhage. His GCS is 14, no focal neurology beyond mild left arm weakness, and he is haemodynamically stable. The stroke registrar is on the way.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 218/124 confirmed on repeated manual measurement, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 97%, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), mild left arm weakness 4/5, no neglect, fundi show grade III changes
data_table.Investigations: CT brain: 12 mL right basal ganglia haemorrhage, no IVH, no mass effect; sodium 138, potassium 4.0, creatinine 92
data_table.Medications: Recently stopped perindopril 10 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his blood pressure?

options.text: Commence intravenous nitroprusside infusion with target systolic blood pressure of 100 mmHg within the first thirty minutes to minimise the risk of further bleeding
options.rationale: Nitroprusside risks cyanide accumulation and can raise ICP; aggressive lowering to 100 risks hypoperfusion. Target is 140 systolic. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate release with reassessment every fifteen minutes for further dose titration as needed for ongoing severely elevated blood pressure
options.rationale: Sublingual or oral immediate-release nifedipine causes unpredictable rapid BP drop and is contraindicated in acute stroke. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)

options.text: Resume oral perindopril at 10 mg daily and arrange admission for monitoring without intravenous antihypertensive therapy given the established mild blood pressure background
options.rationale: Oral perindopril has slow onset and cannot control hypertensive emergency; IV agents are needed. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous labetalol with a systolic blood pressure target of 140 mmHg within the first hour as per current intracerebral haemorrhage guidance
options.rationale: Intracerebral haemorrhage with systolic over 180 is treated with IV labetalol targeting systolic 140 within 1 hour per INTERACT2 and AHA guidance; smooth controlled lowering reduces haematoma growth. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)

options.text: Permit permissive hypertension with no antihypertensive therapy in the first six hours to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure and avoid worsening neurological status
options.rationale: Permissive hypertension applies to ischaemic stroke (not for thrombolysis) and not to ICH; ICH benefits from intensive BP lowering. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Living Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute intracerebral haemorrhage with systolic BP over 180 mmHg is managed by smooth controlled BP lowering targeting systolic 140 within 1 hour per INTERACT2. Labetalol is first-line in Australia; alternatives include glyceryl trinitrate or hydralazine. Avoid sublingual nifedipine and nitroprusside. Reverse anticoagulation, neurosurgical consult, and care in stroke unit improve outcomes. Ischaemic stroke uses different targets (permissive unless thrombolysis or over 220/120).
key_points: ICH systolic target 140 within 1 hour per INTERACT2
Ischaemic stroke: permissive hypertension unless over 220/120 or pre-thrombolysis (under 185/110)
Avoid sublingual nifedipine and nitroprusside in acute stroke
explanation.pearls: INTERACT2 showed intensive BP lowering (target 140 systolic) in ICH did not reduce mortality but improved functional outcomes; ATACH-II did not replicate this benefit, but Australian Living Guidelines retain the 140 target.

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion recognition
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man with two weeks of fever, sore throat, fatigue, and a faint maculopapular rash on his trunk and arms. He had unprotected receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner six weeks ago. Initial fourth-generation HIV test was negative two days into symptoms. He is now on day 14 of symptoms and feels worse rather than better.

data_table.Examination: Cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, faint trunk and limb maculopapular rash, pharyngeal injection without exudate
data_table.Investigations: FBC: lymphopenia with platelets 110, ALT 96; EBV and CMV serology pending; rapid Strep negative
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Send HIV RNA viral load by PCR and repeat fourth-generation antigen/antibody combination test with infectious diseases involvement and PEP discussion review
options.rationale: Window period for fourth-generation tests is up to 4 weeks; in symptomatic likely acute HIV, HIV RNA detects earlier and confirms diagnosis with repeat serology. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat fourth-generation HIV serology in three months and provide reassurance that the initial negative result effectively excludes acute HIV infection in this patient
options.rationale: Three-month delay misses time-sensitive acute HIV diagnosis and partner notification opportunities; HIV RNA is indicated now. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral aciclovir empirically for primary Herpes simplex virus seroconversion and arrange swabs of any oral lesions detected on careful examination of the patient
options.rationale: Although HSV is possible, the rash distribution and unprotected sex history with mononucleosis-like illness mandates HIV RNA testing first. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Treat empirically for streptococcal pharyngitis with oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and arrange outpatient review by the immunology service in two to three weeks
options.rationale: Rapid Strep was negative and the pattern fits acute HIV; antibiotics will not address the diagnosis. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange a heterophile antibody (Monospot) test alone to confirm Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis as the most likely diagnosis given the clinical presentation here today
options.rationale: EBV is in the differential but should not be tested in isolation given the high-risk exposure and need to exclude acute HIV. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion (Fiebig stages I to V) presents with mononucleosis-like illness 2 to 4 weeks after exposure: fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, sore throat, myalgia. Fourth-generation antigen/antibody combination tests detect from around 2 weeks; HIV RNA detects from around 10 days. In symptomatic patients with prior negative serology, HIV RNA is the test of choice. Early diagnosis allows ART initiation, reduces transmission risk, and supports partner notification.
key_points: Fourth-generation HIV test window 2 to 4 weeks; HIV RNA from 10 days
Acute seroconversion presents as mononucleosis-like illness 2 to 4 weeks post-exposure
Early ART initiation reduces transmission and preserves CD4
explanation.pearls: Australian U=U (undetectable equals untransmittable) messaging changed HIV care; early ART and treatment-as-prevention are central to ASHM guidance. Discuss PrEP for partners at notification.

subtopic_detail: Latent tuberculosis treatment decision
stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman recently arrived from Vietnam who is being screened by the local refugee health clinic. She is asymptomatic. Her QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus is positive. Chest X-ray is normal. She is HIV negative, hepatitis B and C negative, and has no immunosuppression. She plans to start a medical degree next year and wants to know whether treatment is needed now.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; no lymphadenopathy, normal chest
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive, chest X-ray clear, sputum AFB not sent (asymptomatic), HIV negative, HBV and HCV negative, ALT 22
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her latent TB infection?

options.text: Repeat QFT-Plus in three months to confirm true positive status and exclude transient interferon-gamma release as an alternative explanation for the result obtained
options.rationale: QFT-Plus is reliable; repeat testing is not standard. Treatment should follow a single confirmed positive in appropriate clinical context. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)

options.text: Commence isoniazid monotherapy for nine months (9H) with monthly review and liver function monitoring after baseline aminotransferase establishment in this woman
options.rationale: 9H is acceptable but no longer first-line; shorter rifamycin-containing regimens have better completion and similar efficacy. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)

options.text: Defer treatment until completion of her medical degree and screen with annual QFT-Plus testing until she demonstrates evidence of active infection or symptoms suggesting reactivation
options.rationale: Untreated LTBI has 5 to 10% lifetime risk of reactivation; deferral is not justified in a young healthy person planning healthcare work. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)

options.text: Commence rifampicin and isoniazid (3HR) for three months with monthly liver function tests and counsel about hepatotoxicity and drug interactions
options.rationale: Short-course regimens (3HR daily or 3HP weekly) are equivalent to 6 to 9 months isoniazid with fewer hepatotoxicity events and better completion; first-line in current TB guidance. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange CT chest to exclude subclinical active disease prior to commencing any latent infection treatment regimen given the high prevalence in her country of origin
options.rationale: Asymptomatic with normal chest X-ray in non-immunocompromised does not require CT; this delays treatment. (Source: NTAC LTBI Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Latent TB infection screening with QFT-Plus is offered to people from high-incidence countries, healthcare workers, immunocompromised, and contacts of active TB. Treatment is recommended in those with reactivation risk factors and reasonable expected adherence. First-line regimens are 3HR (3 months rifampicin + isoniazid), 3HP (3 months weekly rifapentine + isoniazid), or 4R (4 months rifampicin); 6H or 9H remain acceptable alternatives. Active TB must be excluded before LTBI therapy.
key_points: Exclude active TB with symptom screen and CXR before treating LTBI
Short rifamycin-containing regimens have better completion than 9H
5 to 10% lifetime reactivation risk in immunocompetent LTBI
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin interacts with combined oral contraceptive pills (reduces efficacy); counsel about alternative contraception during and for 28 days after rifamycin course.

subtopic_detail: Parkinsonism red flags atypical features
stem: You are the geriatrics registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man who was started on levodopa eight months ago for presumed Parkinson disease. He has had limited symptomatic response, frequent backward falls, and now describes difficulty looking down at his food. His wife reports increasing speech difficulties and emotional lability. There is mild axial rigidity but limb tone is relatively preserved on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 supine, 128/76 standing (no postural drop), HR 76
data_table.Examination: Limited downgaze palsy, axial rigidity greater than limb rigidity, postural instability with backward falls on pull test, hypomimia, no resting tremor, no asymmetry
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain shows midbrain atrophy with hummingbird sign; cognitive screen MoCA 22/30 with executive dysfunction
data_table.Medications: Levodopa/carbidopa 100/25 four times daily (limited response)

lead_in: Which feature most strongly suggests an atypical parkinsonian syndrome?

options.text: Slow shuffling gait with reduced arm swing developing gradually over four years without falls, gaze restriction, or autonomic dysfunction during follow-up assessment
options.rationale: Gradual onset shuffling gait without other red flags is typical of idiopathic PD. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)

options.text: Resting tremor with asymmetric onset and a good response to levodopa during the initial six months of treatment after the diagnosis was confirmed by movement disorders
options.rationale: These features support idiopathic Parkinson disease rather than an atypical syndrome. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)

options.text: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with early postural instability, axial rigidity greater than limb rigidity, and poor levodopa response
options.rationale: Progressive supranuclear palsy is identified by vertical (especially downward) supranuclear gaze palsy, early postural instability with backward falls, axial-predominant rigidity, and poor levodopa response. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)

options.text: Mild bradykinesia with bilateral involvement after seven years of levodopa therapy and emergence of dyskinesias with peak-dose involuntary movements over time as therapy progresses
options.rationale: Late dyskinesias and bilateral involvement are typical PD progression rather than atypical features. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)

options.text: Mild hyposmia preceding motor symptoms by several years and REM sleep behaviour disorder with vivid dream enactment occurring during the night with bed partner
options.rationale: Hyposmia and RBD are pre-motor features of idiopathic PD, not red flags for atypical syndromes. (Source: MDS PSP Criteria 2017)

explanation.summary: Atypical parkinsonian syndromes include progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and corticobasal syndrome. Red flags suggesting atypical disease include early postural instability and falls (PSP), vertical gaze palsy (PSP), prominent autonomic failure (MSA), cerebellar signs (MSA-C), pyramidal signs, apraxia and alien limb (CBS), and poor levodopa response. MRI features (hummingbird sign in PSP, hot cross bun in MSA-C) support diagnosis. Survival is shorter than idiopathic PD.
key_points: Early falls + vertical gaze palsy + axial rigidity + poor levodopa = PSP
Autonomic failure + cerebellar signs + parkinsonism = MSA
Asymmetric apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss = CBS
explanation.pearls: Hummingbird sign on midsagittal MRI (midbrain atrophy with preserved pons) is highly specific for PSP; MRI parkinsonism index combines midbrain and pons measurements for improved diagnostic accuracy.

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barre syndrome workup and treatment
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 45-year-old man with five days of ascending lower limb weakness following a self-limited diarrhoeal illness two weeks ago. He now has difficulty climbing stairs and walking. He has noticed mild hand weakness today. He has no bladder or bowel changes. He is otherwise well with no chronic medical conditions.

data_table.Examination: Lower limb power 3/5 proximally, 4/5 distally, areflexia at knees and ankles, upper limb power 5/5 proximally, 4+/5 distally, sensation intact, no fasciculations
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs normal, B12 and TSH normal, MRI spine normal, CSF cell count 2, CSF protein 1.4 g/L, FVC 3.2 L (predicted 4.1 L), Negative inspiratory force minus 60 cmH2O
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 gram daily for five days as the standard initial management of demyelinating neuropathies in adult populations across all settings
options.rationale: Steroids are not effective in GBS (multiple trials) and are not recommended; IVIG or plasma exchange are first-line. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for five days with respiratory monitoring including four-hourly FVC and admission to a monitored bed
options.rationale: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy with cytoalbuminologic dissociation needs IVIG or plasma exchange and respiratory monitoring; FVC under 20 mL/kg or under 60% predicted is an intubation trigger. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange outpatient nerve conduction studies and review in two weeks given preserved walking and absence of any bladder or bowel involvement at this stage
options.rationale: GBS progresses rapidly and respiratory failure can develop within hours; admission is mandatory not optional. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)

options.text: Commence empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed post-infectious sepsis given recent diarrhoeal illness and arrange admission to general medical ward overnight
options.rationale: Post-Campylobacter or Zika GBS does not need antibiotics; the immune-mediated neuropathy is treated by IVIG or PLEX. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange physiotherapy rehabilitation with discharge home as walking remains preserved and respiratory function is currently within reasonable safety margins on assessment
options.rationale: Rapid progression and FVC 78% predicted with ascending weakness requires admission and immunomodulation. (Source: ANZAN GBS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: GBS is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy classically post-Campylobacter or post-viral. CSF shows cytoalbuminologic dissociation (raised protein with normal cell count). Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg total (usually 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) or plasma exchange; both equivalent and steroids do not help. Respiratory monitoring with serial FVC and NIF is critical; FVC under 20 mL/kg or rapidly falling triggers ICU and intubation consideration.
key_points: CSF cytoalbuminologic dissociation: high protein with normal cells
IVIG or plasma exchange equivalent; steroids ineffective
FVC under 20 mL/kg, NIF less negative than minus 30, rapid decline trigger ICU
explanation.pearls: Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score (EGRIS) predicts ventilation risk by combining days since onset, facial or bulbar weakness, and MRC sum score; useful for triage decisions.

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma crisis perioperative management
stem: You are the medical registrar called to a 42-year-old woman admitted yesterday for elective cholecystectomy. She has had episodic palpitations, sweating, and headaches for six months attributed to anxiety. During induction of anaesthesia she developed sudden severe hypertension to 240/140 with arrhythmia. The surgery is now cancelled. She is in ICU. Plasma metanephrines drawn today are markedly elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: BP swings 220/130 to 90/50, HR 130 with ectopics, T 37.8, SpO2 96% on intubation
data_table.Examination: Sedated, diaphoretic, ECG shows multiple VEBs and ischaemic changes
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines 8.4 nmol/L (normal under 0.6), normetanephrines 12.6 nmol/L (normal under 1.0), troponin rising, CT abdomen shows 4.5 cm right adrenal mass
data_table.Medications: ICU sedation; was on no antihypertensives prior to admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological strategy?

options.text: Commence intravenous amiodarone for the ventricular arrhythmias before any other antihypertensive therapy and arrange transfer to cardiology service for further management
options.rationale: Amiodarone does not address catecholamine excess; alpha-blockade is the foundational treatment. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous metoprolol immediately to control the tachycardia and arrhythmia before introducing alpha-blockade after the heart rate has been adequately controlled
options.rationale: Beta-blockade without prior alpha-blockade causes unopposed alpha stimulation and fatal hypertensive crisis; this is a classic catastrophic error. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)

options.text: Proceed to emergency adrenalectomy while she remains anaesthetised to definitively address the source of catecholamines without further preoperative pharmacological preparation
options.rationale: Surgery without alpha-blockade has very high mortality; 10 to 14 days of alpha-blockade with volume repletion is mandatory before resection. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous nitroprusside infusion as monotherapy to control blood pressure with titration to mean arterial pressure target without specific alpha or beta blockade
options.rationale: Nitroprusside controls BP acutely but does not block the underlying catecholamine receptor activation, leaving arrhythmia risk; structured alpha then beta-blockade is standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous phentolamine and titrated phenoxybenzamine, withhold any beta-blockade until alpha-blockade is established, and plan delayed surgical resection
options.rationale: Alpha-blockade must precede beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma to avoid unopposed alpha stimulation and fatal hypertensive crisis; phenoxybenzamine is the standard agent for 10 to 14 days preoperatively. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma crisis requires alpha-blockade before beta-blockade. Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated up over 10 to 14 days is the standard preoperative agent (alternatives doxazosin or prazosin). After alpha-blockade is established, beta-blockade can be added if tachycardia persists (atenolol or metoprolol). Volume expansion with liberal salt intake is essential. Acute crisis management uses phentolamine boluses or infusion. Adrenalectomy follows 10 to 14 days of full blockade.
key_points: Alpha-blockade strictly precedes beta-blockade (10 to 14 days)
Phenoxybenzamine is the standard alpha-blocker; doxazosin or prazosin alternatives
Volume expansion is essential before surgery to prevent post-resection hypotension
explanation.pearls: Genetic counselling and testing for hereditary syndromes (SDHx, VHL, RET, NF1) is recommended in all phaeochromocytoma patients regardless of age; 30 to 40% have an identifiable germline mutation.

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 67-year-old man via ED with two days of dysuria, rigors, and confusion. He has a background of type 2 diabetes on metformin. On arrival he is tachycardic, tachypnoeic, hypotensive, confused and mottled. Urinalysis shows nitrites and leukocytes. He has received 500 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride en route. Initial bloods include a lactate of 4.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Examination: Mottled extremities, dry mucous membranes, mild suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: VBG: lactate 4.8, pH 7.30, HCO3 18, glucose 11.2; FBC: WCC 18.4, Hb 138, plt 122; EUC: Cr 168 (baseline 92); CRP 240; urine: nitrites/leukocytes/blood positive
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g twice daily

lead_in: Which intervention is the highest priority within the next hour?

options.text: Insert central venous catheter for CVP monitoring before commencing fluid resuscitation now
options.rationale: Central access and CVP monitoring should not delay initial fluid bolus and antibiotic; goal-directed CVP targets are no longer mandated by Surviving Sepsis. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to identify the source before any antibiotic is given
options.rationale: Antibiotics should not be delayed for imaging; broad-spectrum antibiotic within 1 hour for septic shock is the priority. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)

options.text: Start IV noradrenaline immediately at 0.05 mcg/kg/min before completion of fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Noradrenaline is added after initial 30 mL/kg crystalloid if MAP <65 persists; starting vasopressor without fluid is not the first step. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)

options.text: IV crystalloid 30 mL/kg with blood cultures then IV antibiotics within the first hour now
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle and ANZICS recommend lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >=4 within the first hour. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Administer IV hydrocortisone 200 mg before commencement of fluid resuscitation now
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is considered if vasopressor-refractory shock after adequate fluid; it is not the first step in the hour-1 bundle. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)

explanation.summary: Australian sepsis pathway (ANZICS, Sepsis Australia) and Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >=4, and start vasopressors if hypotension persists during or after resuscitation to maintain MAP >=65. Source control should be pursued within 6 to 12 hours when feasible. For suspected urosepsis with septic shock, empirical antibiotic typically piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin per local antibiogram. Reassessment at 3 to 6 hours guides further fluid or vasopressor titration. Lactate clearance is a useful marker of response.
key_points: Hour-1: lactate, cultures, broad-spectrum abx, 30 mL/kg crystalloid
Vasopressors if MAP <65 after fluid (target MAP >=65)
Source control within 6-12 hours when feasible
Hydrocortisone for vasopressor-refractory shock only
Lactate clearance is a marker of response
explanation.pearls: Each hour delay in appropriate antibiotic for septic shock increases in-hospital mortality by approximately 7%, which is the basis for the hour-1 bundle.

subtopic_detail: Bacterial meningitis empiric therapy
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 56-year-old previously well man with 12 hours of severe headache, neck stiffness, fever and confusion. He has no rash. He has had no recent travel, no animal exposure and no immunosuppression. The ED has obtained IV access and is preparing to do an LP. He has no focal neurology and no papilloedema on fundoscopy.

data_table.Examination: Neck stiff to passive flexion, Kernig and Brudzinski positive, no rash, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.8, CRP 280, glucose 8.2, lactate 2.1, blood cultures sent; LP pending
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12 hourly with IV benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4 hourly to cover Listeria empirically
options.rationale: Listeria cover (benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin) is added for age >=50 OR immunosuppression OR pregnancy; at 56 with no risk factors this is borderline but the dexamethasone is the critical first dose addition. The cleanest answer per eTG covers pneumococcus + meningococcus, with the Listeria addition for age >=50 specifically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 1.8 g 4 hourly with IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6 hourly given for 4 days
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin alone does not cover ceftriaxone-sensitive but penicillin-resistant pneumococcus; ceftriaxone is the empirical choice in Australian guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV cefotaxime 2 g 6 hourly with vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose IV ceftriaxone alternative
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added if highly penicillin-resistant pneumococcus is suspected (overseas exposure) but is not standard empirical in Australia where resistance rates are low. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV meropenem 2 g 8 hourly with IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6 hourly until cultures available
options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for ceftriaxone allergy or specific resistance patterns; ceftriaxone is first-line empirical in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12 hourly with IV dexamethasone 10 mg 6 hourly given before or with antibiotic
options.rationale: eTG and ANZICS recommend IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12 hourly for empirical bacterial meningitis in adults, with dexamethasone 10 mg 6 hourly before or with first dose to reduce neurological sequelae from pneumococcal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Australian empirical therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults is IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly, with dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly given before or with the first antibiotic dose to reduce neurological sequelae from pneumococcal meningitis. For patients >=50, immunosuppressed, alcohol misuse, or pregnant, add benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly or amoxicillin 2 g 4-hourly for Listeria cover. Vancomycin is added when highly resistant pneumococcus is suspected (e.g. travel to high-resistance regions). Lumbar puncture should follow empirical antibiotic if delay is anticipated >30 minutes or if there are red flags for CT first (GCS <11, new focal neurology, seizures, papilloedema, immunocompromised). Public health notification and contact prophylaxis as required.
key_points: Empirical: ceftriaxone 2 g 12h + dexamethasone 10 mg 6h
Add Listeria cover if age >=50, immunosuppression, alcohol misuse, pregnant
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic dose - mortality and sequelae benefit
CT before LP if GCS <11, focal signs, seizures, papilloedema, immunocompromised
Public health notification + contact prophylaxis for meningococcal disease
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly for 4 days reduces severe hearing loss by about 50% in pneumococcal meningitis if given with or before the first antibiotic dose; the benefit is lost if delayed.

subtopic_detail: Pyelonephritis admission threshold
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman with 36 hours of right loin pain, fever, rigors and dysuria. She has not vomited and is tolerating oral fluids. She is haemodynamically stable. Urinalysis shows nitrites and leukocytes. She has no diabetes, no urological history and is not pregnant. She has had no recent hospitalisation or instrumentation. She lives within 10 minutes of the hospital and has a partner at home.

data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, no peritonism, no costovertebral mass
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2, CRP 96, EUC: Cr 78, lactate 1.8; urinalysis: nitrites/leukocytes/blood
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days with ED safety net and 48 hour GP review
options.rationale: eTG recommends oral ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in haemodynamically stable patients who can tolerate oral fluids; admission is not mandatory when there is no sepsis or complicating feature. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days with GP review in 48 hours and clear safety net
options.rationale: Cefalexin is not recommended first-line for pyelonephritis in Australian eTG because of high E. coli resistance and poor renal tissue concentrations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose then oral switch to amoxicillin-clavulanate after
options.rationale: She does not meet admission criteria (no sepsis, no vomiting, tolerating oral, no complicating factors); admission is unnecessary and IV monotherapy gentamicin then oral switch is not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 8 hourly for 7 days as the broad-spectrum cover
options.rationale: Pip-tazo is unnecessarily broad for community-acquired uncomplicated pyelonephritis without urological history, instrumentation, or sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for 7 days with ED safety net and 48 hour review
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin achieves urinary but not renal tissue concentrations and is unsuitable for pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Australian eTG recommends oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 BD for 14 days for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in haemodynamically stable patients tolerating oral intake. Admission is indicated for sepsis, persistent vomiting, pregnancy, urological abnormality, immunocompromise, age >65 with comorbidities, or social factors limiting safe discharge. Inpatient empirical therapy is gentamicin 4-5 mg/kg IV plus ampicillin or amoxicillin, or alternatively ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, with oral switch when stable. Imaging (CT KUB or renal tract ultrasound) is indicated for recurrence, persistent fever after 48 hours, suspected obstruction or abscess. Recurrent pyelonephritis warrants urology referral.
key_points: eTG outpatient: ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD x 7d OR trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole x 14d
Admit for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, urological abnormality, immunocompromise
Inpatient empirical: gentamicin + amoxicillin, or ceftriaxone
Image if persistent fever >48 hours, recurrence, or suspected obstruction
Avoid cefalexin and nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis
explanation.pearls: Fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli rates have risen to about 15% in Australian community urine isolates, so clinical review at 48 to 72 hours to confirm response is essential.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising fasciitis vs cellulitis
stem: You are the surgical registrar called by ED to review a 52-year-old man with worsening leg redness over 18 hours. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin. He describes pain out of proportion to the visible erythema. He had a fall three days ago with a small abrasion on the calf. On examination there is a 15 cm area of erythema and tense induration with grey discolouration of a 4 cm central patch. He cannot weight-bear. His observations are tachycardic and febrile.

data_table.Examination: Calf erythema with central dusky discolouration, exquisite tenderness extending beyond visible margin, tense induration, no crepitus yet
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.6, Hb 132, CRP 320, Na 132, glucose 14.4, Cr 142 (baseline 88), CK 1840, lactate 3.4; X-ray: no gas in tissues
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6 hourly with limb elevation and review at 24 hours for response
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin alone treats simple cellulitis but is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis where polymicrobial cover and surgical debridement are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, tense induration with dusky discolouration, sepsis physiology and high LRINEC components (CRP 320, WCC 22, Cr 142, Na 132, glucose 14) point to necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical debridement plus piperacillin-tazobactam + vancomycin + clindamycin (for toxin suppression) is the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZICS Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)

options.text: MRI of the leg with contrast urgently to confirm necrotising fasciitis before any surgery
options.rationale: Imaging should not delay surgical exploration when clinical suspicion is high; MRI may help in uncertain cases but is not required before debridement here. (Source: ANZICS NSTI)

options.text: Compute LRINEC score and admit for IV ceftriaxone if score is 6 or higher with review
options.rationale: LRINEC is supportive but not sufficient to drive management; clinical features (pain out of proportion, dusky skin, sepsis) trump LRINEC and indicate immediate surgical referral. (Source: ANZICS NSTI)

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading and admit under medical team for further investigations
options.rationale: Medical admission without surgical involvement is inappropriate; necrotising fasciitis mortality rises sharply with each hour delay to debridement. (Source: ANZICS NSTI)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency where mortality is determined more by time to debridement than by antibiotic choice. Classic features are pain out of proportion to visible inflammation, rapidly advancing erythema, tense induration, dusky or blistered skin, crepitus (late), and systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, Hb, Na, Cr, glucose) supports diagnosis but does not exclude it; clinical features take precedence. Empirical antibiotics combine broad-spectrum (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) plus MRSA cover (vancomycin) plus toxin suppression (clindamycin or linezolid). Surgical exploration with debridement of all necrotic tissue is mandatory and may be repeated daily. Mortality is approximately 25% even with prompt treatment, rising to >50% if delayed beyond 24 hours.
key_points: Pain out of proportion is the key clinical sign
LRINEC score supports but does NOT exclude diagnosis
Triple antibiotic: pip-tazo + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
Surgical debridement is the definitive treatment; do not delay for imaging
Mortality ~25%; rises >50% if delayed >24 hours
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin in necrotising fasciitis suppresses streptococcal exotoxin synthesis, providing mortality benefit independent of bactericidal activity; it is added even when penicillin is in the regimen.

subtopic_detail: Phaeochromocytoma alpha then beta blockade
stem: You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 48-year-old woman with confirmed phaeochromocytoma on 24 hour fractionated metanephrines (urinary metanephrine 12 times upper limit) and a 4 cm right adrenal mass on CT. She has episodic hypertension peaking at 198/118 mmHg with palpitations, sweating and headaches. She is on no antihypertensive. She is scheduled for laparoscopic adrenalectomy in 14 days.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/104 supine, 144/92 standing, HR 88 supine, 110 standing
data_table.Examination: Mild orthostatic symptoms, no tremor, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: 24 hour fractionated metanephrines: metanephrine 12 x ULN; CT abdomen: 4 cm right adrenal mass; ECG: sinus rhythm, no LVH
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological preparation?

options.text: Amlodipine 5 mg daily and salt restriction with surgical referral in seven to fourteen days
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are adjunctive in phaeochromocytoma but do not replace alpha blockade; salt restriction is contraindicated as volume expansion is needed pre-surgery. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Metoprolol 25 mg twice daily for heart rate control then add alpha blocker once stable
options.rationale: Starting beta blocker before alpha blockade in phaeochromocytoma causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and can precipitate severe hypertensive crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated up over 7 to 14 days then add beta blocker if HR high
options.rationale: Australian endocrinology practice and international guidelines: alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine for 7 to 14 days preoperatively to control hypertension and prevent intraoperative crisis; beta blocker is added ONLY after alpha blockade is established, to prevent unopposed alpha vasoconstriction. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline; eTG Endocrinology)

options.text: Combined alpha-beta blocker labetalol 200 mg twice daily as single agent control of BP and HR
options.rationale: Labetalol has predominantly beta over alpha blockade (ratio 7:1 oral) and is not adequate alpha blockade for phaeochromocytoma; phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin is preferred. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

options.text: Spironolactone 25 mg daily to address presumed primary aldosteronism with adrenal mass first
options.rationale: Diagnosis is confirmed phaeochromocytoma by elevated metanephrines; spironolactone is for primary aldosteronism and does not address catecholamine excess. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma preoperative preparation requires alpha-adrenergic blockade for 7 to 14 days to control hypertension and restore intravascular volume. Phenoxybenzamine (non-selective irreversible) or doxazosin (selective alpha-1) are first-line. Beta blockers are added only after alpha blockade is established, to control reflex tachycardia and tachyarrhythmias; starting beta blocker first causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction with risk of fatal hypertensive crisis. High-sodium diet (5 g/day) and oral fluids are recommended to restore volume depleted by catecholamine excess. BP target preoperatively is 130/80 mmHg seated and >90 mmHg systolic standing. Genetic testing (RET, VHL, SDH, NF1, MAX) is indicated for all phaeochromocytomas as 40% are hereditary. Surgical resection is curative in non-metastatic disease.
key_points: Alpha blockade FIRST (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 7-14 days
Beta blocker only AFTER alpha blockade established
High-sodium diet + fluid for volume expansion preoperatively
BP target 130/80 seated, >90 systolic standing
Genetic testing in all phaeochromocytomas (40% hereditary)
explanation.pearls: Phenoxybenzamine is started at 10 mg twice daily and titrated up by 10 to 20 mg every 2 to 3 days until target BP and mild orthostatic symptoms are achieved, indicating adequate blockade.

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis McDonald 2024 criteria
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman with subacute optic neuritis confirmed by ophthalmology three weeks ago, now recovered with steroid. MRI brain today shows 3 periventricular and 2 juxtacortical T2 hyperintense lesions, one of which enhances with gadolinium. MRI spine shows 1 cervical cord lesion without enhancement. CSF (LP performed yesterday) shows oligoclonal bands present (CSF-specific). She has no prior neurological symptoms. There is no fever or recent infection.

data_table.Examination: Visual acuity 6/9 right, 6/6 left (recovered from 6/24); afferent pupillary defect right; remainder normal
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: 5 T2 lesions (3 periventricular, 2 juxtacortical), 1 gadolinium-enhancing; MRI spine: 1 cervical T2 lesion; CSF: oligoclonal bands positive (CSF-specific)
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: Which McDonald 2024 criterion is met to confirm a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?

options.text: Diagnosis cannot be made until a second clinical attack confirms dissemination in time
options.rationale: McDonald 2024 allows diagnosis after a single clinical attack with appropriate paraclinical evidence (DIS on MRI + CSF OCB or simultaneous enhancing/non-enhancing lesions). (Source: McDonald 2024)

options.text: Dissemination in space and time both met clinically without need for paraclinical evidence
options.rationale: She has only one clinical attack (optic neuritis); dissemination in time requires either a second clinical attack or paraclinical evidence. (Source: McDonald 2024)

options.text: Dissemination in time is met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on MRI scan
options.rationale: While the simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing pattern does meet DIT, the more direct criterion fulfilled here under McDonald 2024 is the CSF-specific oligoclonal bands acting as DIT substitute alongside DIS. Both are acceptable but the OCB pathway is the cleanest for clinical decision-making. (Source: McDonald 2024)

options.text: Dissemination in space met clinically; oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time
options.rationale: McDonald 2024 criteria allow a single attack (here optic neuritis) plus DIS demonstrated on MRI plus CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time, confirming MS. (Source: McDonald 2024)

options.text: Diagnosis requires evoked potentials abnormality in addition to current criteria for confirmation
options.rationale: Evoked potentials are no longer required under McDonald 2024 if MRI and CSF criteria are met. (Source: McDonald 2024)

explanation.summary: The McDonald 2024 criteria diagnose MS based on dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT). DIS requires >=1 T2 lesion in >=2 of 4 typical CNS regions (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord). DIT can be met by a second clinical attack OR new T2 or enhancing lesion on follow-up MRI OR simultaneous presence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same scan OR CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (which substitute for DIT). Following confirmation, early initiation of disease-modifying therapy (DMT) is recommended. Australian MBS-funded options include glatiramer acetate, interferon beta, fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide for moderate activity, and natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine for high activity. JC virus serology should be checked before natalizumab.
key_points: McDonald 2024: DIS = T2 lesion in >=2 of 4 CNS regions
DIT = second attack, new MRI lesion, OR simultaneous Gd-enhancing + non-enhancing, OR CSF OCBs
CSF-specific OCBs substitute for DIT after single attack with DIS
Early DMT initiation reduces relapse rate and disability accumulation
JCV serology required before starting natalizumab
explanation.pearls: Ocrelizumab (anti-CD20) is the first DMT approved by TGA for primary progressive MS and is given as IV infusion every 6 months following an initial divided loading dose.

subtopic_detail: Mixed shock recognition
stem:
You are the ICU registrar called to a 72-year-old man on the cardiology ward, day 4 after anterior STEMI treated by primary PCI to LAD, now in shock. He has developed fever and worsening dyspnoea over 6 hours. Bedside echo shows anterior wall hypokinesis (similar to admission), LVEF 35%, no new tamponade, no new VSD, no severe MR. CXR shows new bilateral infiltrates.

Sputum is purulent. Lactate has risen from 1.4 to 3.8 over 6 hours. Cardiac index by non-invasive estimation is 2.0 L/min/m2. Mixed venous saturation by central line is 76%.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 84/52 (was 118/70 yesterday), HR 118, T 38.7, RR 28, SpO2 88% on 6 L/min, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Warm peripheries despite hypotension, no peripheral oedema, no new murmur
data_table.Investigations: CXR: bilateral lower zone infiltrates new; troponin stable from yesterday; CRP 280; WCC 19; lactate 3.8; ScvO2 76%; CI 2.0
data_table.Medications: Aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin, bisoprolol, ramipril, furosemide

lead_in: What is the most likely shock pattern and most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Cardiogenic shock from reinfarction; activate cath lab for repeat PCI within ninety minutes
options.rationale: Stable troponin and stable echo make reinfarction unlikely; fever and infiltrates point to sepsis. (Source: NHFA STEMI Guideline)

options.text: Cardiogenic shock from late stunning post-STEMI; start dobutamine and arrange repeat angiography
options.rationale: Echo shows stable LV function and no mechanical complication; warm peripheries with elevated ScvO2 are not typical of cardiogenic shock. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)

options.text: Hypovolaemic shock from gastrointestinal bleed on dual antiplatelet; transfuse and pause DAPT
options.rationale: No evidence of bleeding; fever, purulent sputum and infiltrates point to infective rather than hypovolaemic cause. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway)

options.text: Obstructive shock from PE post-myocardial infarction; CT pulmonary angiogram and anticoagulate
options.rationale: Bilateral consolidation with purulent sputum and fever fit infective rather than embolic pattern; PE typically shows oligaemic lung fields. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Septic shock from hospital-acquired pneumonia; IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics now
options.rationale: Warm peripheries despite hypotension, fever, new infiltrates, purulent sputum, raised lactate and elevated mixed venous saturation (76% suggests distributive component) point to septic shock from HAP rather than cardiogenic deterioration; treat as septic shock with IV crystalloid and empirical antipseudomonal cover. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Pathway; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Distinguishing shock subtypes at the bedside requires integration of clinical signs, haemodynamic profile and bedside imaging. Cardiogenic shock typically has cold peripheries, low cardiac index, raised PCWP and low mixed venous saturation. Septic shock typically has warm peripheries, normal or high cardiac index after initial fluid, low SVR, and normal or elevated mixed venous saturation. Hypovolaemic shock has cold peripheries, low cardiac index, low PCWP, low ScvO2. Mixed shock is increasingly recognised in critically ill patients with multiple insults. Empirical hospital-acquired pneumonia therapy in Australia is typically piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin if MRSA risk, with anti-pseudomonal cover for HAP onset >=5 days. Reassessment of shock subtype after initial intervention with serial echo, lactate, and central venous oximetry is essential.
key_points: Septic shock: warm, high CI after fluid, low SVR, normal/high ScvO2
Cardiogenic: cold, low CI, raised PCWP, low ScvO2
Hypovolaemic: cold, low CI, low PCWP, low ScvO2
HAP empirical (Australian): pip-tazo +/- vancomycin if MRSA risk
Reassess shock subtype after initial intervention
explanation.pearls: Mixed venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) >70% with hypotension and lactate elevation is classic for distributive shock; ScvO2 <60% favours cardiogenic or hypovolaemic patterns.

subtopic_detail: DOAC choice in AF with renal impairment
stem: You are the cardiology registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman with newly diagnosed permanent atrial fibrillation found on ambulatory monitoring after dizziness. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, prior TIA 2 years ago, and is taking metformin, perindopril, and aspirin. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 5. Her creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault) is 38 mL/min. She has no history of GI bleeding, no liver disease, no drug interactions, and weighs 62 kg. She has reasonable oral intake and good adherence to medications historically.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 88 irregular, T 36.7
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no murmurs, no signs of heart failure, no carotid bruits
data_table.Investigations: ECG: AF rate 88, no ischaemic changes; FBC: Hb 124, plt 240; EUC: Cr 132, eGFR 38, CrCl 38; LFTs normal; HbA1c 7.2%
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD, perindopril 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation choice?

options.text: Continue aspirin 100 mg daily without anticoagulation given her age and the bleeding risk this carries
options.rationale: Aspirin is not effective stroke prevention in AF and is no longer recommended; CHA2DS2-VA 5 with high stroke risk mandates anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Warfarin with INR target 2.0 to 3.0 monitored monthly because DOACs are contraindicated below CrCl 50
options.rationale: DOACs are NOT contraindicated at CrCl 38; apixaban and rivaroxaban have approved dosing down to CrCl 15 to 30 with dose reduction; warfarin is acceptable but not preferred. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily continued with aspirin 100 mg daily for secondary prevention of stroke and TIA
options.rationale: Adding aspirin to oral anticoagulation in AF (without recent ACS or PCI) increases major bleeding without reducing stroke; aspirin should be ceased on starting DOAC. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily with cessation of aspirin in view of bleeding risk on combined antithrombotic therapy
options.rationale: Apixaban 5 mg BD is correct here: dose reduction requires 2 of 3 criteria (age >=80, weight <=60 kg, Cr >=133); she meets 0 to 1 (Cr 132 borderline; age 78 <80; weight 62 >60). Aspirin must be ceased to avoid net bleeding harm; apixaban has best bleeding profile among DOACs especially in CKD and elderly. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline; AMH)

options.text: Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily with cessation of aspirin once anticoagulation is established at steady state
options.rationale: Dabigatran requires dose reduction (110 mg BD) for age >=75 and is renally cleared (80%); contraindicated below CrCl 30 and risky between 30 and 50; apixaban is safer in CKD. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

explanation.summary: NHFA/CSANZ AF guideline: CHA2DS2-VA (Victorian replacement of CHA2DS2-VASc, no sex category) >=2 in men or women is an indication for oral anticoagulation. DOACs are first-line over warfarin for non-valvular AF. Apixaban 5 mg BD (or 2.5 mg BD if 2 of: age >=80, weight <=60 kg, Cr >=133 micromol/L), rivaroxaban 20 mg daily (15 mg if CrCl 15 to 50), dabigatran 150 mg BD (110 mg BD if age >=75 or bleeding risk; contraindicated CrCl <30), edoxaban 60 mg daily (30 mg if CrCl 15 to 50). Warfarin remains preferred for mechanical valves, moderate to severe mitral stenosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, end-stage renal disease. Aspirin should be ceased on starting DOAC unless concurrent recent ACS within 12 months. HAS-BLED guides bleeding risk discussion but is rarely a reason to withhold anticoagulation when stroke risk is high. Annual review of renal function (more often if CKD), weight, age, and bleeding events.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA >=2: anticoagulate (DOAC first-line)
Apixaban dose reduction needs 2 of 3: age >=80, weight <=60, Cr >=133
Dabigatran contraindicated CrCl <30; rivaroxaban/edoxaban reduce at CrCl 15-50
Aspirin offers no stroke benefit in AF and should be ceased on DOAC
Warfarin reserved for mechanical valves, moderate-severe MS, APS
explanation.pearls: Apixaban demonstrated lower major bleeding (especially intracranial haemorrhage) than warfarin in ARISTOTLE, including in patients with CKD and the elderly, making it the preferred DOAC in renal impairment down to CrCl 25 mL/min.

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia outpatient antibiotic
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a previously well 44-year-old man with 4 days of productive cough with green sputum, fevers to 38.6, and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. He has no known comorbidities, takes no regular medications, and has no penicillin allergy. He is tolerating oral fluids and food. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. His SMART-COP score is 1 (multilobar = 0, albumin not done, RR 22 = 0, tachycardia 96 = 0, confusion 0, oxygen 0, pH not done; only SBP 95 which is 1 from threshold; actually SBP 118 so 0). Current vitals are within near-normal range otherwise.

data_table.Examination: Bronchial breath sounds right base with crepitations, dullness to percussion, no signs of effusion, no tracheal deviation, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CXR: right lower lobe consolidation; no bloods needed in primary care setting; SMART-COP estimated score 0; not assessing for severe pneumonia by Australian guideline
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days with safety net and review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Mild CAP (SMART-COP 0 to 2) managed in community: amoxicillin 1 g TDS for 5 days is Australian first-line per eTG; reserve doxycycline for atypical concern or amoxicillin allergy; combination therapy is for moderate to severe CAP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; eTG)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Augmentin + doxycycline is moderate-severity CAP regimen; SMART-COP 0 mild CAP does not need this; broader spectrum is unnecessary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admission for IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6 hourly plus IV doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: IV admission is reserved for moderate to severe CAP (SMART-COP >=3) or social/medical factors preventing oral therapy; not indicated here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days as monotherapy targeting atypical pneumonia pathogens primarily
options.rationale: Macrolide monotherapy is not Australian first-line for CAP due to increasing pneumococcal resistance; reserved for atypical-only presentations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days as monotherapy covering typical and atypical organisms equally
options.rationale: Respiratory fluoroquinolone is reserved for severe penicillin allergy or specific atypical or resistant infections; routine first-line is amoxicillin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP stratifies CAP severity in Australia: Systolic BP <90 (2), Multilobar infiltrate (1), Albumin <35 (1), Respiratory rate >=25 (under 50 = 1, over 50 = 2), Tachycardia >=125 (1), Confusion new (1), Oxygen low (under 50 yo SpO2 <94 or PaO2 <70 = 2; over 50 yo SpO2 <90 or PaO2 <60 = 2), pH <7.35 (2). Score 0 to 2 mild (community oral); 3 to 4 moderate (admit, IV antibiotic); >=5 severe (ICU consideration). Mild CAP empirical: amoxicillin 1 g TDS oral for 5 days. Moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly + oral doxycycline 100 mg BD (or oral azithromycin); switch to oral when stable. Severe CAP: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily + IV azithromycin 500 mg daily +/- oseltamivir in influenza season; ICU consultation. Mycoplasma and Chlamydia coverage with doxycycline or macrolide when atypical features (younger patient, dry cough, extrapulmonary manifestations). Follow-up CXR at 6 weeks to confirm resolution and exclude underlying malignancy especially in smokers over 50.
key_points: SMART-COP: severity stratification (0-2 mild, 3-4 mod, >=5 severe)
Mild oral: amoxicillin 1 g TDS x 5 days
Moderate: IV benzylpenicillin + oral doxycycline
Severe: IV ceftriaxone + IV azithromycin + ICU consult
Repeat CXR at 6 weeks especially in smokers >50
explanation.pearls: Australian eTG shortened first-line amoxicillin duration from 7 to 5 days for mild CAP based on the OAR (Outpatient Antibiotic Reduction) and ANTIC pneumonia trials showing non-inferior outcomes and reduced selection pressure.

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis first-line therapy choice
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 68-year-old postmenopausal woman with a recent low-trauma fracture of the left distal radius from a fall at standing height. She has no other fractures and no back pain. DXA scan today: lumbar spine T-score -2.8, total hip T-score -2.5, femoral neck T-score -2.7. Vitamin D is 78 nmol/L (adequate). Calcium and PTH normal.

eGFR 64 (mildly reduced). No history of dental disease, no planned dental procedures, no oesophageal disease, and no upper GI symptoms. She is otherwise healthy.

data_table.Examination: Healing distal radius fracture in cast, no kyphosis, no other tender vertebrae
data_table.Investigations: DXA: LS T -2.8, hip T -2.5, FN T -2.7; vitamin D 78; calcium 2.32; PTH 4.2; eGFR 64; TSH 1.8; coeliac screen negative; FBC normal; SPEP normal
data_table.Medications: Cholecalciferol 1000 IU daily; calcium dietary

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line osteoporosis therapy?

options.text: Annual IV zoledronic acid 5 mg infusion as first-line therapy without trial of oral therapy initially
options.rationale: IV zoledronic acid is reserved for oral bisphosphonate intolerance, upper GI contraindication, or adherence concerns; oral alendronate is first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for postmenopausal osteoporosis with vertebral fracture prevention
options.rationale: Denosumab is an acceptable alternative but is reserved as second-line for intolerance or contraindication to bisphosphonates per PBS criteria; oral alendronate is preferred first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 mcg daily for 18 months as anabolic therapy for severe postmenopausal osteoporosis
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis (T-score <-3.0 with multiple vertebral fractures) under specialist supervision; not first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Oral raloxifene 60 mg daily as selective oestrogen receptor modulator for postmenopausal osteoporosis treatment
options.rationale: Raloxifene is third-line, reduces vertebral but not hip fractures, and carries VTE risk; not first-line in 68-year-old with hip T-score -2.5. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium and vitamin D continued and 3-yearly DXA monitoring arranged
options.rationale: Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) is Australian first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with prior fragility fracture or T-score <=-2.5; PBS criteria met; no contraindications; eGFR 64 (>35 required for bisphosphonates). (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline; AMH)

explanation.summary: Australian osteoporosis treatment indications: T-score <=-2.5 at any site, or prior minimal trauma vertebral or hip fracture (regardless of T-score), or T-score -1.5 to -2.5 with FRAX 10-year hip fracture risk >=3% or major osteoporotic risk >=20%. First-line oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly) - 50% reduction in vertebral fractures and 40% reduction in hip fractures. Pre-treatment: dental check (BRONJ prevention), correct vitamin D and calcium, exclude secondary causes (multiple myeloma, hyperthyroidism, coeliac, hyperparathyroidism, Cushing). Contraindications: eGFR <35, oesophageal disease (oral), recent or planned invasive dental work (relative). Alternatives: IV zoledronic acid annually (oral intolerance), denosumab 60 mg SC 6-monthly (CKD-compatible but rebound vertebral fracture risk on cessation), teriparatide (severe), romosozumab (very severe), raloxifene (third-line). DXA review at 2 to 3 years. Drug holiday after 5 years oral or 3 years IV in low-risk patients; continue indefinitely if high risk.
key_points: Treat: T <=-2.5, OR prior fragility fracture, OR T -1.5 to -2.5 + high FRAX
First-line: oral alendronate or risedronate (50% vertebral, 40% hip fracture reduction)
Pre-treat: dental check, vitamin D, exclude secondary causes
Contraindications oral: eGFR <35, oesophageal disease
Drug holiday consideration at 5 years oral or 3 years IV
explanation.pearls: Denosumab cessation carries a 10-fold rebound vertebral fracture risk within 12 months if not transitioned to a bisphosphonate, making it a less reversible choice than oral alendronate for patients who may discontinue therapy.

subtopic_detail: Adult acute asthma severity assessment
