The critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency in sepsis is a functional state where cortisol levels may be in the normal range but inadequate for the degree of physiological stress. Delaying treatment for results is inappropriate. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; ADRENAL Trial)

options.text: Transfuse packed red blood cells targeting a haemoglobin of 100 g/L or above
options.rationale: The TRICC trial and subsequent sepsis literature supports a restrictive transfusion threshold of 70 g/L in critically ill patients. This patient's Hb of 96 g/L does not meet the transfusion threshold. Liberal transfusion strategies have not shown benefit in sepsis and carry risks of transfusion reactions and volume overload. (Source: ANZICS; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Vasopressor-refractory septic shock may be due to critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency, where the adrenal response is inadequate for the degree of physiological stress. Stress-dose hydrocortisone (200 mg/day) can restore vascular catecholamine responsiveness and hasten shock reversal. The ADRENAL and APROCCHSS trials provided the evidence base, though mortality benefit remains debated. Treatment should not await cortisol results in life-threatening shock.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day is recommended for vasopressor-refractory septic shock
Do not wait for cortisol results before commencing stress-dose steroids in refractory shock
ADRENAL trial showed faster shock reversal but no overall mortality benefit with hydrocortisone
APROCCHSS trial showed mortality benefit with hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone combined
explanation.pearls: The ADRENAL trial (2018, 3800 patients across 69 Australian and international ICUs) demonstrated hydrocortisone reduced time to vasopressor cessation by approximately 1 day (median 3 vs 4 days) compared with placebo.

subtopic_detail: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension management
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of daily headaches worse on waking and with Valsalva manoeuvres. She reports transient visual obscurations lasting seconds occurring several times daily. Her BMI is 38. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and was commenced on oral tetracycline for acne 3 months ago. An MRI brain is normal with no venous sinus thrombosis on MRV. A lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 32 cmH2O with normal CSF composition.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema (Frisen grade II), visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally, enlarged blind spots on confrontation, full extraocular movements, BMI 38
data_table.Investigations: LP opening pressure 32 cmH2O, CSF protein 0.22 g/L, CSF glucose 3.4 mmol/L (serum 5.2), no cells, MRI brain normal, MRV no venous sinus thrombosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Commence topiramate 25 mg daily for dual headache and weight loss benefit
options.rationale: While topiramate has theoretical benefits of carbonic anhydrase inhibition and weight loss, it is not the recommended first-line agent for IIH. The IIH Treatment Trial (IIHTT) established acetazolamide as the evidence-based first-line therapy. Topiramate may be considered second-line if acetazolamide is not tolerated but lacks the same quality of evidence. (Source: NICE; BMJ Best Practice: IIH)

options.text: Refer for urgent optic nerve sheath fenestration to preserve visual function
options.rationale: Optic nerve sheath fenestration is reserved for rapidly progressive visual loss despite medical therapy, particularly when there is severe papilloedema threatening imminent vision loss. This patient has mild papilloedema (Frisen II) with preserved visual acuity. Medical management should be initiated first. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: IIH; NICE)

options.text: Perform serial lumbar punctures weekly to maintain a normal intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Serial therapeutic lumbar punctures were historically used in IIH management but are no longer recommended as primary therapy. They provide only transient pressure reduction, carry repeated procedural risks, and are inferior to pharmacological management with acetazolamide. They may be used as a temporising measure before surgery in fulminant cases. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: IIH)

options.text: Cease the combined oral contraceptive pill and observe for symptom resolution
options.rationale: While the combined OCP has been associated with IIH, simply ceasing it is insufficient as sole management in a patient with confirmed raised intracranial pressure and papilloedema. The tetracycline should also be ceased as it is a known causative drug. However, active pharmacological treatment with acetazolamide is required alongside medication review and weight management. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: IIH; NICE)

options.text: Cease tetracycline, commence acetazolamide 250 mg BD, and refer for weight management
options.rationale: This is the correct multimodal approach. Tetracycline is a well-known precipitant of IIH and must be ceased. Acetazolamide is the first-line pharmacological treatment per the IIH Treatment Trial, starting at 500 mg daily and titrating up to 4 g daily as tolerated. Weight loss of 5-10% body weight is associated with significant IIH improvement. The combination of removing the drug trigger, reducing CSF production with acetazolamide, and weight management forms the standard initial approach. (Source: NICE; BMJ Best Practice: IIH; IIH Treatment Trial)

explanation.summary: IIH is characterised by raised intracranial pressure without a structural cause, typically affecting young obese women. Drug triggers include tetracyclines, vitamin A derivatives, and the combined OCP. Management involves removing precipitants, acetazolamide as first-line pharmacotherapy, and structured weight loss. Monitoring requires regular visual field assessment and fundoscopy. Surgical options are reserved for refractory cases or acute visual deterioration.
key_points: Tetracyclines are a well-recognised drug cause of IIH and must be ceased
Acetazolamide is first-line pharmacotherapy per the IIH Treatment Trial
Weight loss of 5-10% is associated with significant clinical improvement
Visual field monitoring is essential as papilloedema can cause irreversible optic atrophy
explanation.pearls: The IIH Treatment Trial demonstrated acetazolamide plus weight management improved visual field mean deviation by 1.43 dB more than placebo at 6 months, with the weight loss component contributing independently to improvement.

subtopic_detail: RCVS vs primary CNS vasculitis discrimination
stem:
A 42-year-old woman presents with her fourth thunderclap headache in 10 days. Each episode reaches maximal intensity within 60 seconds, is bilateral, and lasts 1-3 hours. The first episode occurred during sexual intercourse. She takes sertraline 100 mg daily for depression and uses a combined nasal decongestant containing pseudoephedrine. A CT brain and CT angiogram performed after the first episode were normal.

A lumbar puncture showed normal opening pressure and no xanthochromia. She now presents again and a repeat CT angiogram shows multifocal segmental narrowing of the middle and anterior cerebral arteries bilaterally.

data_table.Examination: No focal neurological deficits, no neck stiffness, normal fundoscopy, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: ESR 8 mm/hr, CRP <5 mg/L, CT brain no acute changes, CTA multifocal segmental arterial narrowing, CSF protein 0.28 g/L, no pleocytosis

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome triggered by vasoactive agents
options.rationale: RCVS is characterised by recurrent thunderclap headaches over 1-4 weeks with multifocal segmental vasoconstriction that resolves within 3 months. Key features supporting RCVS over primary CNS vasculitis include: normal inflammatory markers, normal CSF, recurrent thunderclap headaches (rather than insidious headache), no focal neurological deficits, and identifiable vasoactive triggers (sertraline, pseudoephedrine). The initial normal CTA with subsequent abnormal CTA is typical of RCVS, where vasoconstriction develops over days. (Source: BMJ Best Practice; Lancet Neurology RCVS review)

options.text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system with progressive inflammation
options.rationale: Primary CNS vasculitis (PACNS) presents with insidious progressive headache, cognitive decline, and focal neurological deficits over weeks to months. CSF is typically abnormal with elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis. ESR and CRP may be normal but CSF markers are usually deranged. The acute thunderclap headache pattern with normal inflammatory markers and normal CSF strongly favours RCVS over PACNS. (Source: BMJ Best Practice; Lancet Neurology)

options.text: Recurrent subarachnoid haemorrhage from an occult intracranial aneurysm
options.rationale: The normal CT brain and absence of xanthochromia on lumbar puncture effectively exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage. The multifocal segmental narrowing pattern on CTA is characteristic of vasoconstriction rather than vasospasm secondary to aneurysmal SAH, which is typically centred on the circle of Willis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Migraine with aura complicated by persistent vasospastic angiopathy
options.rationale: While migraine can cause reversible vasoconstriction, the thunderclap headache pattern with maximal intensity within seconds is not consistent with migraine. Migrainous headaches typically build over minutes to hours. The recurrent thunderclap pattern with demonstrated multifocal vasoconstriction points specifically to RCVS. (Source: Lancet Neurology; BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with secondary arterial vasospasm
options.rationale: CVST can present with thunderclap headache but typically shows venous sinus occlusion on CTV or MRV. The initial CT angiogram would likely have identified venous pathology. The normal venous imaging and the specific pattern of recurrent arterial segmental narrowing are not consistent with CVST. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: RCVS is an increasingly recognised syndrome characterised by recurrent thunderclap headaches over 1-4 weeks with reversible multifocal segmental cerebral artery vasoconstriction. It is commonly triggered by vasoactive substances including SSRIs, sympathomimetics, triptans, and cannabis. The key discriminator from primary CNS vasculitis is the acute thunderclap presentation, normal inflammatory markers, normal CSF, and absence of focal neurological deficits. Vasoconstriction resolves within 3 months in most cases.
key_points: RCVS presents with recurrent thunderclap headaches over 1-4 weeks
Vasoactive triggers include SSRIs, pseudoephedrine, triptans, cannabis, and postpartum state
Normal ESR/CRP and normal CSF distinguish RCVS from primary CNS vasculitis
Initial angiography may be normal with vasoconstriction developing over subsequent days
explanation.pearls: CTA or MRA may be normal in the first week of RCVS because vasoconstriction typically begins distally and progresses proximally over days; repeating vascular imaging at 1-2 weeks captures the diagnostic window.

subtopic_detail: Frontotemporal dementia vs Alzheimer's discrimination
stem: A 58-year-old accountant is brought by his wife who reports progressive personality change over 18 months. He has become socially disinhibited, making inappropriate sexual comments to colleagues, and was recently dismissed from work. He has developed a rigid daily routine and becomes agitated if meals are served 5 minutes late. He has developed a preference for sweet foods, eating entire packets of biscuits daily. His wife reports he shows no empathy when she is upset. He has no memory complaints and manages household finances without difficulty.

data_table.Examination: MMSE 28/30, ACE-III 82/100 (verbal fluency 4/14, memory 24/26, attention 18/18, visuospatial 15/16, language 21/26), no parkinsonism, no motor neuron signs, primitive reflexes present bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, B12, folate normal, MRI brain shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal lobe atrophy with relative preservation of hippocampi and parietal lobes

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Late-onset bipolar disorder presenting with a prolonged manic episode
options.rationale: While disinhibition and personality change can occur in mania, the progressive nature over 18 months without episodic fluctuation, the presence of compulsive behaviours, loss of empathy, and characteristic frontal atrophy on MRI are inconsistent with bipolar disorder. The ACE-III pattern with impaired verbal fluency but preserved memory further supports a neurodegenerative process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG97)

options.text: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia with frontal predominance
options.rationale: This presentation meets the Rascovsky criteria for behavioural variant FTD: early behavioural disinhibition, early apathy or loss of empathy, early perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality and dietary changes, and a neuropsychological profile with executive deficits but relatively preserved memory and visuospatial function. The MRI showing frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with hippocampal sparing is the characteristic imaging pattern. Onset before age 65 is typical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG97; Lancet Neurology FTD review)

options.text: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease with prominent behavioural symptoms
options.rationale: Early-onset Alzheimer's disease typically presents with progressive episodic memory impairment, visuospatial dysfunction, or language difficulty. Behavioural changes are usually a later feature. The preserved memory on ACE-III (24/26) and preserved visuospatial function with hippocampal sparing on MRI argue strongly against Alzheimer's. (Source: NICE NG97; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Huntington's disease with predominant psychiatric manifestation
options.rationale: Huntington's disease can present with behavioural and psychiatric features before motor onset. However, the MRI would typically show caudate nucleus atrophy rather than frontal-temporal atrophy. Huntington's is also autosomal dominant, and a family history would usually be present. The clinical profile of compulsive eating, social disinhibition, and loss of empathy with frontal atrophy is more consistent with bvFTD. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Dementia with Lewy bodies presenting with predominant behavioural features
options.rationale: DLB is characterised by fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behaviour disorder. This patient has none of these core features. The behavioural profile with loss of empathy, compulsive eating, and social disinhibition with frontal atrophy is not consistent with DLB, which typically shows posterior cortical changes. (Source: NICE NG97; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the most common form of FTD and typically presents before age 65 with progressive personality change, disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behaviours, and hyperorality. Memory and visuospatial function are relatively preserved early in the disease. MRI characteristically shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with hippocampal sparing, distinguishing it from Alzheimer's disease. There is currently no disease-modifying treatment, and management focuses on behavioural strategies and carer support.
key_points: bvFTD presents with personality change, disinhibition, compulsive behaviours, and loss of empathy
Memory and visuospatial function are preserved early, unlike Alzheimer's disease
MRI shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with hippocampal sparing
ACE-III pattern shows impaired verbal fluency with preserved memory domains
explanation.pearls: Verbal fluency (letter and category) is the most sensitive cognitive screening test for bvFTD, often declining years before other cognitive domains; an ACE-III verbal fluency score below 7/14 in the context of preserved memory is a strong discriminator from Alzheimer's disease.

subtopic_detail: Parkinson's disease motor fluctuations
stem: A 67-year-old man with Parkinson's disease diagnosed 8 years ago returns for review. He is taking levodopa-carbidopa 250/25 mg four times daily. He reports that for the past 6 months, his medication wears off predictably 3-3.5 hours after each dose, with return of tremor, stiffness, and difficulty walking. He also experiences involuntary writhing movements of his trunk and limbs at peak dose effect, lasting approximately 1 hour after each dose. His wife reports these dyskinesias are more distressing to her than to him. His cognition is intact.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 64, BP 138/78 lying, 118/70 standing
data_table.Examination: During assessment (2 hours post-dose): moderate choreiform dyskinesia trunk and upper limbs, ON-state mobility good, no freezing, MMSE 28/30
data_table.Investigations: Nil recent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological adjustment?

options.text: Increase each levodopa dose to 375/37.5 mg to overcome the wearing-off periods
options.rationale: Increasing the individual levodopa dose would worsen the already troublesome peak-dose dyskinesias by increasing the peak plasma levodopa level. The therapeutic window narrows as PD progresses, and higher individual doses push further above the dyskinesia threshold. Management of wearing-off with coexisting dyskinesia requires a strategy that smooths the levodopa curve. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG71)

options.text: Switch entirely from levodopa to cabergoline for smoother dopaminergic stimulation
options.rationale: Complete substitution of levodopa with a dopamine agonist at this stage is impractical. Ergot-derived agonists like cabergoline carry valvular fibrosis risk and are avoided. Furthermore, dopamine agonists cannot replicate the efficacy of levodopa in advanced disease. The approach should be to optimise levodopa delivery rather than replace it. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Cease levodopa and commence apomorphine subcutaneous infusion as monotherapy
options.rationale: Apomorphine infusion is reserved for patients with severe motor fluctuations refractory to oral medication optimisation. It is not first-line for managing wearing-off and dyskinesia. Furthermore, ceasing levodopa abruptly risks neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome. Initial pharmacological adjustments to the oral regimen should be attempted first. (Source: NICE NG71; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Reduce individual levodopa doses, increase dosing frequency, and add entacapone
options.rationale: This addresses both problems simultaneously. Reducing individual doses lowers the peak plasma level to reduce peak-dose dyskinesia, while increasing dosing frequency (e.g. 5-6 smaller doses) reduces OFF time. Adding entacapone (a COMT inhibitor) extends the half-life of each levodopa dose by inhibiting peripheral metabolism, further smoothing the plasma level curve. This combination strategy narrows the fluctuation between trough and peak, keeping the patient within the therapeutic window. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG71; AMH)

options.text: Add amantadine 100 mg three times daily specifically for the dyskinesia component
options.rationale: Amantadine can reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesia via NMDA receptor antagonism and is a reasonable adjunct. However, it addresses only the dyskinesia without improving the wearing-off phenomenon. The patient's primary functional problem is the combined pattern of wearing-off plus peak-dose dyskinesia, which requires smoothing the levodopa pharmacokinetic curve. Amantadine may be added later if dyskinesia persists after dose redistribution. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; NICE NG71)

explanation.summary: Motor fluctuations in advanced Parkinson's disease reflect the narrowing therapeutic window between the threshold for motor benefit (below which wearing-off occurs) and the dyskinesia threshold. Management aims to smooth the levodopa plasma concentration curve. Dose redistribution (smaller, more frequent doses) combined with COMT inhibition is the standard approach. Amantadine may be added specifically for residual dyskinesia, and advanced therapies (apomorphine infusion, duodopa, DBS) are reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: Wearing-off with peak-dose dyskinesia indicates a narrow therapeutic window
Reduce individual levodopa doses and increase frequency to smooth the plasma curve
Entacapone extends levodopa half-life by inhibiting peripheral COMT
Amantadine specifically targets dyskinesia but does not address wearing-off
explanation.pearls: Entacapone increases levodopa bioavailability by approximately 35% by inhibiting peripheral catechol-O-methyltransferase, effectively extending the half-life from approximately 1.5 hours to 2.5 hours; the levodopa dose may need to be reduced by 10-30% when entacapone is added to avoid worsening dyskinesia.

subtopic_detail: Submassive PE risk stratification and management
stem: A 54-year-old man presents with acute dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain that began 4 hours ago. He had a left total knee replacement 12 days ago and has been on enoxaparin thromboprophylaxis but missed the past 2 doses. CTPA confirms bilateral segmental and subsegmental pulmonary emboli. His troponin is mildly elevated and an echocardiogram shows right ventricular dilatation with hypokinesis of the RV free wall but preserved apical contractility.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 104/68, RR 24, SpO2 92% on 4 L/min nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Elevated JVP, right parasternal heave, no peripheral oedema, left knee surgical wound healing well
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 124 ng/L (ULN 14), BNP 380 pg/mL, CTPA bilateral segmental PE, RV:LV ratio 1.3, echo McConnell sign positive, lactate 2.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.text: Immediate systemic alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours for massive PE protocol
options.rationale: Systemic thrombolysis is indicated for massive PE with haemodynamic instability (sustained SBP <90 mmHg). This patient has submassive PE with RV dysfunction but is haemodynamically stable (SBP 104). Thrombolysis in this population carries significant bleeding risk, particularly 12 days post-surgery, without proven mortality benefit. The PEITHO trial showed reduced haemodynamic decompensation but increased major bleeding and stroke with thrombolysis in submassive PE. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; PEITHO trial)

options.text: Commence oral rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily and discharge with outpatient review
options.rationale: This patient has submassive PE with RV dysfunction and elevated biomarkers indicating intermediate-high risk. Outpatient management is only appropriate for low-risk PE (sPESI 0, no RV dysfunction, normal biomarkers). This patient requires inpatient monitoring with close observation for haemodynamic deterioration that would trigger escalation to thrombolysis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; ESC PE Guidelines)

options.text: Commence therapeutic dose IV heparin and monitor closely for haemodynamic deterioration
options.rationale: Submassive PE (intermediate-high risk: RV dysfunction plus elevated biomarkers) is managed with therapeutic anticoagulation and close haemodynamic monitoring, with thrombolysis reserved for clinical deterioration. IV unfractionated heparin is preferred over LMWH in this setting because it is titratable and rapidly reversible if thrombolysis or intervention becomes necessary. The recent surgery also favours UFH for its reversibility. Serial assessment for haemodynamic deterioration is essential. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; ESC PE Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis as a lower-bleeding-risk approach
options.rationale: Catheter-directed therapy is an emerging option for submassive PE but is not the standard first-line approach. It requires specialist interventional radiology availability and is typically considered when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or as rescue therapy. Current guidelines still recommend therapeutic anticoagulation with watchful waiting as the primary approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Insert an IVC filter and commence therapeutic anticoagulation concurrently
options.rationale: IVC filters are indicated when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated or when PE recurs despite adequate anticoagulation. This patient can receive anticoagulation. Prophylactic IVC filter insertion in addition to anticoagulation has not shown benefit in reducing PE-related mortality and adds procedural risks and long-term filter complications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; PREPIC2 trial)

explanation.summary: Submassive (intermediate-risk) PE is characterised by RV dysfunction on imaging or echo with elevated cardiac biomarkers but preserved systemic blood pressure. Management is therapeutic anticoagulation with close monitoring. Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for haemodynamic deterioration. The PEITHO trial showed that tenecteplase reduced haemodynamic decompensation in submassive PE but increased major bleeding and stroke, supporting a watchful waiting approach with rescue thrombolysis if needed.
key_points: Submassive PE = RV dysfunction plus elevated biomarkers with stable haemodynamics
IV UFH is preferred for its titrability if escalation to thrombolysis may be needed
McConnell sign (RV free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing) is specific for acute RV strain
Thrombolysis is reserved for haemodynamic deterioration in submassive PE
explanation.pearls: The McConnell sign (RV free wall hypokinesis with preserved apical contractility) has a specificity of approximately 94% for acute PE-related RV strain and distinguishes it from chronic RV dysfunction, where global hypokinesis is more typical.

subtopic_detail: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia management
stem: A 69-year-old woman is being treated in hospital for an acute PE with IV unfractionated heparin. On day 8 of heparin therapy, routine bloods show her platelet count has fallen from 210 x10^9/L on admission to 78 x10^9/L. She has developed new left calf swelling and a compression ultrasound confirms a new left popliteal DVT. She denies bleeding symptoms. Her 4Ts score is calculated at 7 points.

data_table.Examination: Left calf swollen and tender, no skin necrosis at heparin injection sites, no petechiae, no evidence of bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 78 x10^9/L (baseline 210), Hb 124 g/L stable, INR 1.0, APTT 68 seconds (on heparin), fibrinogen 4.2 g/L, 4Ts score 7 (high probability)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease heparin and commence low molecular weight heparin as an alternative
options.rationale: LMWH has significant cross-reactivity with heparin-induced antibodies (approximately 90%) and is absolutely contraindicated in HIT. Switching from UFH to LMWH does not resolve the pathological process and may worsen thrombosis. A non-heparin anticoagulant must be used. (Source: HSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Cease heparin and transfuse platelets to maintain a count above 100 x10^9/L
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in HIT is generally avoided as it may fuel further antibody-mediated platelet activation and thrombosis. The thrombocytopenia in HIT is consumptive due to platelet activation, not due to production failure. Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding or critical procedures. (Source: HSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Cease heparin and commence warfarin 5 mg daily targeting INR 2.0-3.0
options.rationale: Warfarin must not be initiated during acute HIT before platelet recovery. Warfarin causes a transient drop in protein C, creating a prothrombotic state that can precipitate venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis in the setting of HIT. Warfarin may be introduced once platelets have recovered above 150 x10^9/L on a non-heparin anticoagulant. (Source: HSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Continue heparin at the current dose until HIT antibody results are confirmed
options.rationale: With a 4Ts score of 7 (high probability) and new thrombosis, the clinical probability of HIT is very high. Continuing heparin while awaiting confirmatory testing risks further life-threatening thrombotic complications. Heparin must be ceased immediately and a non-heparin anticoagulant started empirically when the clinical suspicion is high. (Source: HSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Cease all heparin and commence IV argatroban infusion with monitoring
options.rationale: Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor that does not cross-react with HIT antibodies. In suspected HIT with high clinical probability (4Ts score >=6) and active thrombosis, all heparin must be ceased immediately and a non-heparin anticoagulant commenced. Argatroban is monitored via APTT and is the preferred agent in Australia for HIT with hepatic dosing adjustment. Danaparoid is an alternative. Confirmatory anti-PF4 antibody testing should be sent but must not delay treatment. (Source: HSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

explanation.summary: HIT is an immune-mediated prothrombotic disorder caused by antibodies against the heparin-PF4 complex. It typically occurs 5-10 days after heparin initiation (or sooner with prior exposure). Despite the thrombocytopenia, the primary risk is thrombosis, not bleeding. Management requires immediate heparin cessation and initiation of a non-heparin anticoagulant. Warfarin must not be started until platelets recover. The 4Ts score guides clinical probability assessment.
key_points: HIT is a prothrombotic condition despite thrombocytopenia
Cease all heparin and commence a non-heparin anticoagulant immediately
LMWH is contraindicated due to >90% cross-reactivity with HIT antibodies
Do not start warfarin until platelets recover above 150 x10^9/L
explanation.pearls: Argatroban is hepatically cleared (preferred in renal impairment) with a half-life of 45 minutes, making it highly titratable; it artificially elevates the INR, so overlap to warfarin requires monitoring with a chromogenic factor X assay rather than INR alone.

subtopic_detail: Type A aortic dissection management decision
stem: A 59-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension and a known bicuspid aortic valve presents to the emergency department with acute severe central chest pain radiating to his back. He is diaphoretic and anxious. A CT angiogram confirms a Stanford Type A aortic dissection with an intimal flap originating 2 cm above the aortic root and extending into the descending aorta. The aortic root measures 5.8 cm. There is a moderate pericardial effusion but no evidence of cardiac tamponade.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 172/96 right arm, 148/84 left arm (>20 mmHg discrepancy), RR 24, SpO2 97%
data_table.Examination: New early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge, reduced left radial pulse compared with right, no focal neurological deficits
data_table.Investigations: CTA: Type A dissection from aortic root to descending aorta, aortic root 5.8 cm, moderate pericardial effusion, troponin 48 ng/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Emergency cardiothoracic surgical repair with aortic root replacement
options.rationale: Stanford Type A aortic dissection is a surgical emergency with approximately 1-2% mortality per hour if untreated. This patient has multiple indications for urgent surgery: Type A dissection, aortic root involvement with dilatation (5.8 cm), new aortic regurgitation (early diastolic murmur), pericardial effusion suggesting haemopericardium risk, and a bicuspid aortic valve. Anti-impulse therapy should be commenced while arranging emergent surgery. (Source: CSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; BMJ Best Practice: Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Conservative medical management with IV esmolol targeting HR below 60 and SBP below 120
options.rationale: Medical management alone is appropriate for uncomplicated Type B dissection but carries unacceptable mortality in Type A dissection (approximately 50% at 2 weeks). The involvement of the ascending aorta poses immediate risk of aortic rupture, tamponade, coronary malperfusion, and acute severe aortic regurgitation. Anti-impulse therapy is essential while awaiting surgery but is not definitive management. (Source: CSANZ; BMJ Best Practice: Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Endovascular stent-graft repair of the descending aortic component only
options.rationale: Endovascular repair (TEVAR) is not appropriate for the ascending aorta due to the proximity of the coronary ostia, aortic valve, and arch vessels. Type A dissections involving the ascending aorta require open surgical repair. TEVAR is used for complicated Type B dissections involving the descending aorta. (Source: CSANZ; BMJ Best Practice: Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Urgent pericardiocentesis followed by reassessment for surgical candidacy
options.rationale: Pericardiocentesis in aortic dissection with haemopericardium is dangerous as it may remove the tamponade effect that is limiting further aortic haemorrhage. Rapid decompression can precipitate fatal exsanguination. Pericardiocentesis is only performed in extremis for imminent cardiac arrest. The pericardial effusion should be managed in the operating theatre during definitive surgical repair. (Source: CSANZ; BMJ Best Practice: Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Transfer to a cardiac catheterisation laboratory for coronary angiography first
options.rationale: Coronary angiography is not required before emergency Type A dissection surgery and delays definitive treatment. The mild troponin elevation may reflect coronary ostial involvement or demand ischaemia. Coronary assessment is performed intraoperatively. The delay associated with catheterisation is unacceptable given the 1-2% per hour mortality rate. (Source: CSANZ; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Type A aortic dissection involving the ascending aorta is a surgical emergency. Without surgery, mortality is approximately 1-2% per hour in the first 48 hours. Medical anti-impulse therapy is commenced immediately but is a bridge to definitive surgical repair. Pericardiocentesis should be avoided unless cardiac arrest is imminent, as removing tamponade may precipitate fatal haemorrhage. Bicuspid aortic valve is a significant risk factor for aortic dissection due to associated aortopathy.
key_points: Type A dissection is a surgical emergency with 1-2% mortality per hour untreated
TEVAR is not suitable for ascending aortic pathology
Pericardiocentesis in dissection-related haemopericardium risks fatal decompression
Bicuspid aortic valve is associated with ascending aortopathy and dissection risk
explanation.pearls: The blood pressure differential >20 mmHg between arms in acute aortic dissection indicates differential subclavian artery involvement by the dissection flap, and the arm with the higher pressure reflects the true aortic pressure for titrating anti-impulse therapy.

subtopic_detail: Denosumab discontinuation rebound fracture risk
stem: A 72-year-old woman has been receiving denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months for 4 years for severe osteoporosis. Her T-scores have improved from -3.4 to -2.1 at the lumbar spine. She now wishes to cease denosumab due to recurrent injection site reactions. She has no history of fragility fractures while on treatment. Her renal function is preserved with an eGFR of 68 mL/min. She takes calcium and vitamin D supplementation.

data_table.Examination: No kyphosis, no tenderness on spinal percussion, BMI 24
data_table.Investigations: DXA T-score lumbar spine -2.1, femoral neck -1.8, eGFR 68 mL/min, corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L, vitamin D 78 nmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to discontinuing denosumab?

options.text: Cease denosumab and arrange repeat DXA in 12 months to reassess bone density
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of denosumab without bisphosphonate consolidation causes rapid rebound bone loss within 12-18 months, with bone mineral density returning to or below pre-treatment levels. This rebound is associated with a significantly increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures. Simply monitoring with DXA is insufficient to prevent this serious complication. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia; AMH)

options.text: Transition to oral alendronate 70 mg weekly starting 6 months after the last denosumab dose
options.rationale: Bisphosphonate consolidation therapy is recommended when discontinuing denosumab to prevent rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures. Oral alendronate should be commenced approximately 6 months after the last denosumab injection (when the next dose would have been due) to maintain anti-resorptive effect during the transition. A minimum of 12 months of bisphosphonate therapy is recommended. This patient's eGFR of 68 permits oral bisphosphonate use. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia; AMH; RACGP)

options.text: Halve the denosumab dose to 30 mg every 6 months as a gradual taper strategy
options.rationale: Dose reduction of denosumab is not an established tapering strategy. Half-dose denosumab does not provide adequate anti-resorptive effect, and there is no evidence that gradual dose reduction prevents the rebound phenomenon. The established approach is sequential bisphosphonate consolidation therapy after the last full dose. (Source: AMH; Osteoporosis Australia)

options.text: Cease denosumab and commence raloxifene 60 mg daily as alternative anti-resorptive
options.rationale: Raloxifene does not have sufficient anti-resorptive potency to prevent the rebound bone loss after denosumab cessation. Bisphosphonates are the only agents with evidence for preventing the post-denosumab rebound phenomenon due to their ability to bind to the bone matrix and provide sustained anti-resorptive effect. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia; AMH)

options.text: Continue denosumab indefinitely as discontinuation is contraindicated at any point
options.rationale: While long-term denosumab use is safe for up to 10 years based on extension studies, discontinuation is not absolutely contraindicated. It requires careful planning with bisphosphonate consolidation therapy. The patient's preference and injection site reactions are valid reasons to transition to an alternative, provided the switch is managed appropriately. (Source: Osteoporosis Australia; RACGP)

explanation.summary: Denosumab cessation triggers rapid rebound bone resorption mediated by a surge in osteoclast activity, with bone density returning to pre-treatment levels within 12-18 months and a significantly increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures. Bisphosphonate consolidation therapy is essential to mitigate this rebound. Oral alendronate commenced at the time of the next scheduled denosumab dose is the standard approach. Monitoring with bone turnover markers at 3-6 months can confirm adequate suppression.
key_points: Denosumab cessation causes rebound bone loss and vertebral fracture risk
Bisphosphonate consolidation is mandatory when stopping denosumab
Alendronate should commence at the time the next denosumab dose would be due
A minimum of 12 months of bisphosphonate therapy after denosumab is recommended
explanation.pearls: The rebound vertebral fracture risk after denosumab cessation peaks at 7-12 months post-last-dose, with an incidence of multiple vertebral fractures of approximately 5-10% in patients who cease without bisphosphonate consolidation, compared with less than 1% in those transitioned appropriately.

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax vs massive haemothorax discrimination
stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance following a high-speed motorcycle collision. He is intubated and ventilated by paramedics due to progressive respiratory distress. He has an obvious right-sided flail chest segment. His ventilation pressures have been rising and his oxygen saturations are falling despite increasing FiO2. The right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion with absent breath sounds. His trachea is deviated to the left. His neck veins are distended.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 78/50, SpO2 82% on FiO2 1.0 via ventilator, peak airway pressure 42 cmH2O
data_table.Examination: Intubated, tracheal deviation to left, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds right, hyper-resonant right chest, right-sided flail segment, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Nil yet available - point-of-care blood gas being processed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Obtain a portable CXR before any intervention to confirm the suspected diagnosis
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate intervention. Delaying treatment for radiological confirmation in a haemodynamically compromised patient risks cardiac arrest from obstructive shock. Imaging should never delay life-saving decompression when the clinical picture is clear. (Source: ATLS; ANZCOR)

options.text: Perform bilateral finger thoracostomies as part of a standard trauma approach
options.rationale: While bilateral finger thoracostomies are part of some rapid sequence approaches in intubated trauma patients, the clinical signs clearly lateralise to the right hemithorax. The left chest has no clinical indication for decompression. Unnecessary bilateral thoracostomies increase procedural risk and delay definitive management of the identified pathology. (Source: ATLS)

options.text: Administer a rapid 1 litre crystalloid bolus to address the obstructive shock first
options.rationale: While fluid resuscitation may provide transient haemodynamic support, the primary pathology is obstructive shock from tension pneumothorax. The mediastinal shift and impaired venous return will not resolve with fluid alone. Decompression of the tension pneumothorax must be performed immediately to restore venous return and cardiac output. (Source: ATLS; ANZCOR)

options.text: Perform immediate right-sided finger thoracostomy followed by intercostal drain insertion
options.rationale: This patient has classic signs of right-sided tension pneumothorax: hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, distended neck veins (impaired venous return), hypotension, and rising ventilation pressures. In an intubated patient, finger thoracostomy (open decompression) in the 4th-5th intercostal space mid-axillary line is preferred over needle decompression due to higher success rate. An intercostal drain should be placed immediately after decompression. (Source: ATLS; ANZCOR)

options.text: Perform right-sided needle decompression at the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line
options.rationale: Needle decompression at the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line is the traditional pre-hospital technique for tension pneumothorax. However, in the ED with an already intubated patient, finger thoracostomy is preferred because needle decompression has a failure rate of up to 40% due to insufficient needle length or catheter kinking, particularly in patients with increased chest wall thickness. (Source: ATLS; ANZCOR)

explanation.summary: Tension pneumothorax in a ventilated trauma patient requires immediate decompression. The distinguishing clinical features from massive haemothorax are hyper-resonance (vs dullness) and distended neck veins (vs flat veins from hypovolaemia). In the ED with an intubated patient, finger thoracostomy is preferred over needle decompression due to higher success rates. The definitive treatment is intercostal drain insertion immediately after decompression.
key_points: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate decompression
Hyper-resonance plus distended neck veins distinguishes tension pneumothorax from massive haemothorax
Finger thoracostomy is preferred over needle decompression in the ED setting
Needle decompression has up to 40% failure rate due to chest wall thickness
explanation.pearls: In trauma, massive haemothorax presents with ipsilateral dullness to percussion and flat neck veins (hypovolaemia), while tension pneumothorax presents with hyper-resonance and distended neck veins (obstructive shock); both cause absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation, making percussion and JVP the key discriminators.

subtopic_detail: Malignant pleural effusion management
stem: A 64-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is reviewed for management of a recurrent right-sided pleural effusion. She has required three therapeutic thoracenteses in the past 6 weeks, each draining approximately 1.5 litres with symptomatic relief lasting only 7-10 days. Pleural fluid cytology has confirmed malignant cells. She has an estimated life expectancy of 4-6 months and her performance status is ECOG 2. She is able to manage activities of daily living with assistance. She wishes to minimise hospital visits.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 94% on room air
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion right base to mid-zone, reduced breath sounds, no contralateral effusion, mild cachexia
data_table.Investigations: CXR: large right pleural effusion, repeat thoracentesis yields 1.6 L straw-coloured exudative fluid, cytology positive for adenocarcinoma, CT shows no trapped lung

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for her recurrent effusion?

options.text: Continue therapeutic thoracentesis as needed every 7-10 days in the clinic
options.rationale: Repeat thoracentesis every 7-10 days is burdensome for a patient who wishes to minimise hospital visits. It does not address the underlying recurrence and exposes the patient to repeated procedural risks including pain, infection, and pneumothorax. A definitive management strategy is preferred for rapidly recurring effusions. (Source: TSANZ; BMJ Best Practice: Malignant Pleural Effusion)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Malignant Pleural Effusion

options.text: Insert a small-bore intercostal drain with talc slurry pleurodesis via the drain
options.rationale: Talc slurry pleurodesis via a chest drain can be effective but requires hospitalisation for several days until the drain output is minimal. For a patient prioritising reduced hospital visits, an indwelling pleural catheter allows outpatient drainage and may achieve spontaneous pleurodesis. The TIME2 trial showed equivalent symptom control between IPC and talc pleurodesis. (Source: TSANZ; TIME2 trial)

options.text: Insert an indwelling pleural catheter for outpatient intermittent drainage
options.rationale: An indwelling pleural catheter (IPC) is the preferred option for this patient. It allows outpatient drainage by the patient or a carer, minimising hospital visits. The TIME2 trial demonstrated equivalent breathlessness control between IPC and talc pleurodesis. IPCs also achieve spontaneous pleurodesis in approximately 45-50% of cases. For patients with limited life expectancy who prioritise staying out of hospital, IPC is the recommended approach per TSANZ guidelines. (Source: TSANZ; BMJ Best Practice: Malignant Pleural Effusion)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Malignant Pleural Effusion

options.text: Refer for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with mechanical pleurodesis
options.rationale: VATS pleurodesis has the highest success rate for achieving pleurodesis but requires general anaesthesia and several days of hospitalisation. For a patient with ECOG 2, limited life expectancy, and a preference to minimise hospital visits, this is disproportionately invasive. It is more appropriate for patients with better performance status and longer expected survival. (Source: TSANZ; BMJ Best Practice: Malignant Pleural Effusion)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Malignant Pleural Effusion

options.text: Commence systemic chemotherapy optimisation to reduce pleural fluid production
options.rationale: While systemic therapy may reduce effusion recurrence in chemosensitive tumours, it does not provide immediate symptomatic relief and its effect on pleural fluid is unpredictable. The recurrent effusion requires a mechanical drainage solution regardless of systemic therapy optimisation. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Malignant Pleural Effusion)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Malignant Pleural Effusion

explanation.summary: Recurrent malignant pleural effusion management depends on patient performance status, life expectancy, lung re-expansion capacity, and patient preference. Indwelling pleural catheters offer equivalent symptom control to talc pleurodesis with the advantage of outpatient management. The TIME2 trial is the landmark study comparing these approaches. Talc pleurodesis is preferred when the patient has good performance status and the lung fully re-expands. Trapped lung is a contraindication to pleurodesis as the visceral and parietal pleura cannot appose.
key_points: IPC is preferred for patients prioritising reduced hospital visits and limited life expectancy
TIME2 trial showed equivalent breathlessness control between IPC and talc pleurodesis
IPCs achieve spontaneous pleurodesis in approximately 45-50% of patients
Trapped lung (failure of lung re-expansion) is a contraindication to pleurodesis
explanation.pearls: The AMPLE-2 trial demonstrated that daily IPC drainage (vs symptom-guided drainage) increased spontaneous pleurodesis rates from 24% to 47% at 12 weeks, suggesting an aggressive early drainage strategy when aiming for catheter removal.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Malignant Pleural Effusion

subtopic_detail: Hypertensive emergency organ-specific targets
stem: A 56-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden severe chest pain and dyspnoea. He has not taken his usual antihypertensives for the past 2 weeks. His ECG shows LVH with strain pattern and sinus tachycardia but no ST-elevation. A CXR shows bilateral pulmonary oedema with upper lobe diversion. His troponin is mildly elevated. An echocardiogram shows severely impaired LV systolic function (LVEF 25%) with no regional wall motion abnormalities. A CT aortogram excludes aortic dissection.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 228/132, RR 32, SpO2 88% on 15 L/min non-rebreather mask
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, bilateral coarse crackles to mid-zones, elevated JVP, S3 gallop, no peripheral oedema, equal arm pressures
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, LVH with strain, troponin 68 ng/L, BNP 1840 pg/mL, creatinine 142 micromol/L, CXR bilateral pulmonary oedema, echo LVEF 25%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological approach to blood pressure reduction?

options.text: IV labetalol 20 mg boluses targeting a 25% BP reduction over 6-8 hours
options.rationale: IV labetalol is a reasonable agent for many hypertensive emergencies but is relatively contraindicated in acute decompensated heart failure due to its beta-blocking effect, which may further depress cardiac output in a patient with LVEF 25%. Vasodilator therapy is preferred in hypertensive emergency complicated by acute pulmonary oedema. (Source: NHFA; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Oral amlodipine 10 mg and oral perindopril 5 mg as urgent oral stepdown therapy
options.rationale: Oral antihypertensives have slow and unpredictable onset in the acute setting. This patient has a hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema requiring rapid, titratable blood pressure reduction. IV therapy is mandatory. Oral agents may be introduced once the acute crisis is stabilised. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; NHFA)

options.text: IV sodium nitroprusside infusion starting at 0.3 mcg/kg/min with arterial line monitoring
options.rationale: Sodium nitroprusside is effective but carries risks of cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity, reflex tachycardia, and coronary steal phenomenon. In the setting of acute heart failure with possible myocardial ischaemia (elevated troponin), GTN infusion is preferred as it reduces preload and afterload with a favourable coronary blood flow profile. Nitroprusside is reserved for refractory cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; NHFA)

options.text: IV hydralazine 5 mg boluses every 20 minutes targeting SBP below 160 mmHg
options.rationale: Hydralazine causes direct arteriolar vasodilation with reflex tachycardia and increased cardiac output, which may worsen myocardial oxygen demand. It is poorly titratable due to unpredictable dose response and prolonged duration. In acute heart failure, agents that reduce preload are preferred to pure afterload reducers. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: IV GTN infusion starting at 10-20 mcg/min titrated to symptom relief and BP target
options.rationale: IV glyceryl trinitrate is the preferred agent for hypertensive emergency complicated by acute pulmonary oedema. It reduces both preload (venodilatation) and afterload at higher doses, providing rapid symptom relief. It has a favourable coronary vasodilatory profile relevant to this patient's elevated troponin. The target is a 25% MAP reduction in the first hour. Concurrent IV furosemide and non-invasive ventilation address the pulmonary oedema. (Source: NHFA; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency management is organ-specific. In acute pulmonary oedema, IV GTN is preferred because it reduces preload and afterload while providing coronary vasodilatation. Beta-blockers are avoided in acute decompensated heart failure due to negative inotropic effects. The blood pressure target is a 25% MAP reduction in the first hour, not normalisation, to avoid organ hypoperfusion. Concurrent management with diuretics, oxygen, and consideration of non-invasive ventilation is essential.
key_points: IV GTN is first-line for hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema
Beta-blockers are relatively contraindicated in acute decompensated heart failure
Target 25% MAP reduction in the first hour to avoid organ hypoperfusion
IV furosemide and non-invasive ventilation are concurrent therapies
explanation.pearls: GTN at low doses (10-40 mcg/min) primarily causes venodilatation reducing preload, while at higher doses (>100 mcg/min) it additionally causes arteriolar dilatation reducing afterload; this dose-dependent pharmacology allows titration from pure preload reduction to combined preload-afterload reduction.

subtopic_detail: Initial IV antihypertensive selection and BP target
stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a severe headache and blurred vision for 4 hours. He has a background of poorly controlled hypertension and stopped taking his amlodipine 3 weeks ago. On examination he has bilateral papilloedema and bilateral retinal haemorrhages consistent with hypertensive retinopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 bpm, BP 232/138 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: GCS 15, papilloedema bilaterally, flame haemorrhages, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Cr 148 micromol/L (baseline 90), K 4.2 mmol/L, urinalysis protein 2+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: IV glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to reduce MAP by 25% in the first hour
options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage (retinopathy, AKI) requires controlled IV BP reduction. The target is to reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour to avoid watershed ischaemia, then gradually toward 160/100 mmHg over the next 2 to 6 hours. IV GTN or sodium nitroprusside are appropriate first-line agents. (Source: eTG: Cardiovascular; NHFA/CSANZ)

options.text: Oral amlodipine 10 mg and observe for 6 hours before reassessing blood pressure
options.rationale: Oral agents are too slow and unpredictable in hypertensive emergency with acute end-organ damage. IV therapy is required for controlled, titratable reduction. Oral agents are appropriate for hypertensive urgency without end-organ damage. (Source: eTG: Cardiovascular)

options.text: IV labetalol bolus titrated to normalise blood pressure to below 140/90 within 1 hour
options.rationale: While IV labetalol is an appropriate agent, targeting normal BP within 1 hour risks cerebral hypoperfusion and watershed infarction. The initial target is a 25% MAP reduction, not normalisation. Autoregulation is shifted rightward in chronic hypertension. (Source: eTG: Cardiovascular; NHFA/CSANZ)

options.text: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 600 mcg repeated every 5 minutes until BP is controlled
options.rationale: Sublingual GTN causes unpredictable and precipitous drops in blood pressure that cannot be titrated. IV infusion allows minute-to-minute control, which is essential to avoid overshoot and ischaemic complications. (Source: eTG: Cardiovascular)

options.text: IV hydralazine 10 mg bolus and arrange urgent CT brain before further BP management
options.rationale: IV hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and unpredictable BP drops, making it a less ideal first-line choice. While neuroimaging is reasonable to exclude stroke, it should not delay initiation of controlled IV antihypertensive therapy. (Source: eTG: Cardiovascular; NHFA/CSANZ)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is defined by severely elevated blood pressure with evidence of acute end-organ damage, including retinopathy, encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, aortic dissection, or acute pulmonary oedema. Management requires admission to a monitored bed with intravenous antihypertensive therapy titrated to reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour. Further gradual reduction toward 160/100 mmHg occurs over the following 2 to 6 hours. The choice of IV agent depends on the specific end-organ involvement and contraindications.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency requires IV antihypertensive therapy, not oral agents
Target MAP reduction of no more than 25% in the first hour to avoid watershed ischaemia
Autoregulation is shifted rightward in chronic hypertension so rapid normalisation is dangerous
IV GTN, sodium nitroprusside, and labetalol are all acceptable first-line agents
explanation.pearls: In chronic hypertension the cerebral autoregulatory curve shifts rightward, meaning a MAP that is normal for a healthy person may be below the ischaemic threshold in a chronically hypertensive patient - this is why the 25% MAP reduction ceiling exists.

subtopic_detail: BP target variation by end-organ involvement - aortic dissection vs stroke
stem: A 66-year-old man presents with acute-onset tearing interscapular pain radiating to his abdomen. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension. CT aortogram confirms a Stanford type B aortic dissection extending from the left subclavian artery to the infrarenal aorta without malperfusion syndrome. There is no evidence of contained rupture or visceral ischaemia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104 bpm, BP 218/126 mmHg (right arm), BP 196/112 mmHg (left arm), RR 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air
data_table.Investigations: Cr 102 micromol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, Hb 138 g/L, troponin I 12 ng/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate blood pressure target within the first hour?

options.text: Reduce MAP by no more than 25% and reassess at 6 hours in a monitored setting
options.rationale: The 25% MAP reduction target applies to most hypertensive emergencies but is insufficient for aortic dissection, where more aggressive SBP lowering is required to reduce aortic wall shear stress and limit propagation. (Source: eTG: Cardiovascular; ESC Aortic Disease Guidelines 2024)

options.text: Target SBP 100 to 120 mmHg and HR below 60 bpm using IV esmolol or labetalol
options.rationale: Acute aortic dissection requires aggressive SBP reduction to 100 to 120 mmHg and HR below 60 bpm to minimise aortic wall shear stress. IV beta-blockers (esmolol or labetalol) are first-line. Beta-blockade should precede vasodilators to avoid reflex tachycardia. Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically. (Source: eTG: Cardiovascular; ESC Aortic Disease Guidelines 2024)

options.text: Target SBP below 180 mmHg using IV sodium nitroprusside as the sole first-line agent
options.rationale: Sodium nitroprusside as monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia, which increases aortic wall shear stress and may worsen dissection propagation. If used, it must follow adequate beta-blockade. The SBP target of below 180 mmHg is also too liberal for dissection. (Source: ESC Aortic Disease Guidelines 2024)

options.text: Target SBP 140 to 160 mmHg using IV hydralazine and arrange urgent surgical repair
options.rationale: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and is contraindicated in aortic dissection. Uncomplicated Stanford type B dissection without malperfusion, rupture, or refractory pain is managed medically, not surgically. Surgical or endovascular repair is reserved for complicated type B. (Source: ESC Aortic Disease Guidelines 2024; eTG: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Target SBP 100 to 120 mmHg using IV esmolol and arrange emergent endovascular repair
options.rationale: While the BP target is correct, emergent endovascular repair is not indicated for uncomplicated type B dissection. The absence of malperfusion, rupture, or refractory symptoms means medical management alone is appropriate. Endovascular repair may be considered electively. (Source: ESC Aortic Disease Guidelines 2024)

explanation.summary: Aortic dissection has a unique BP target compared with other hypertensive emergencies. The goal is SBP 100 to 120 mmHg and HR below 60 bpm, achieved primarily with IV beta-blockers to reduce both blood pressure and the rate of pressure rise (dP/dt). Stanford type B dissections are classified as uncomplicated or complicated. Complicated features include malperfusion syndrome, contained rupture, refractory pain, or rapid expansion, which mandate urgent endovascular or surgical intervention. Uncomplicated type B is managed with medical therapy and surveillance imaging.
key_points: Aortic dissection target is SBP 100 to 120 mmHg and HR below 60 bpm
IV beta-blockers are first-line to reduce both BP and dP/dt
Vasodilators must follow beta-blockade to prevent reflex tachycardia
Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically
Complicated type B requires endovascular or surgical intervention
explanation.pearls: IV esmolol is preferred over labetalol in aortic dissection when rapid titration is needed because its half-life is only 9 minutes, allowing minute-to-minute control if hypotension or bradycardia develops.

subtopic_detail: PRES in eclampsia-mimicking presentation with atypical features
stem: A 34-year-old woman who is 3 days postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery presents with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. She had no pre-eclampsia during pregnancy and her antenatal blood pressures were all normal. She is currently breastfeeding and takes no regular medications. On arrival she is postictal with a GCS of 11. A repeat seizure occurs in the emergency department.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108 bpm, BP 198/124 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 95% on 6 L face mask, T 37.4 C
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 198 x10^9/L, ALT 32 U/L, Cr 68 micromol/L, urate 0.32 mmol/L, urine protein:creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol, MRI brain shows bilateral symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the parieto-occipital white matter without restricted diffusion

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Eclampsia - administer IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose and commence IV labetalol infusion
options.rationale: Eclampsia typically occurs in the setting of pre-eclampsia features (hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopaenia, elevated transaminases). This patient has normal platelets, normal ALT, normal urate, and minimal proteinuria. While magnesium sulfate would not be harmful, the MRI findings of parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema without restricted diffusion are characteristic of PRES, not eclampsia per se. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: PRES; RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis - commence IV heparin and arrange CT venography
options.rationale: CVST can present postpartum with seizures and headache, but MRI typically shows venous infarction with restricted diffusion and parenchymal haemorrhage, not bilateral symmetrical parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema. The MRI pattern here is characteristic of PRES. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: PRES; Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome - commence IV labetalol and IV levetiracetam
options.rationale: The combination of acute severe hypertension, seizures, and bilateral parieto-occipital T2/FLAIR hyperintensity without restricted diffusion on MRI is the hallmark of PRES. The absence of pre-eclampsia features (normal platelets, normal ALT, minimal proteinuria) argues against eclampsia. PRES can occur postpartum even without preceding pre-eclampsia. Management centres on aggressive BP control and seizure treatment. PRES is typically reversible with prompt BP management. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: PRES; RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Postpartum pre-eclampsia with seizures - administer IV magnesium sulfate and IV hydralazine
options.rationale: Post-partum pre-eclampsia can develop de novo after delivery, but the diagnostic criteria require hypertension plus at least one of proteinuria, thrombocytopaenia, renal impairment, elevated transaminases, or neurological features. Here the only feature is hypertension with seizures, and the MRI pattern specifically supports PRES. Hydralazine is also less favoured than labetalol due to unpredictable hypotension. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)

options.text: Subarachnoid haemorrhage - arrange urgent CT angiography and neurosurgical consultation
options.rationale: SAH typically shows subarachnoid blood on CT or xanthochromia on LP. MRI in SAH does not show bilateral symmetrical parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema. The presentation with severe hypertension and this specific MRI pattern points to PRES rather than a vascular event. (Source: Stroke Foundation; BMJ Best Practice: PRES)

explanation.summary: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome is a clinico-radiological diagnosis characterised by acute hypertension, seizures, headache, and visual disturbance with bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema on MRI. It can occur postpartum even without a history of pre-eclampsia, and is thought to result from a failure of cerebral autoregulation leading to vasogenic oedema. The key MRI discriminator is T2/FLAIR hyperintensity WITHOUT restricted diffusion, distinguishing it from ischaemic stroke. Management is prompt blood pressure control and seizure treatment. Despite the name, PRES is not always reversible if treatment is delayed.
key_points: PRES shows bilateral parieto-occipital T2/FLAIR hyperintensity without restricted diffusion
Can occur postpartum without preceding pre-eclampsia
Eclampsia and PRES have overlapping features but differing biochemical profiles
Prompt BP control is the cornerstone of PRES management
Despite its name PRES can cause permanent injury if untreated
explanation.pearls: The absence of restricted diffusion on DWI-MRI distinguishes the vasogenic oedema of PRES from the cytotoxic oedema of ischaemic stroke - this single imaging discriminator often clinches the diagnosis when clinical features overlap with eclampsia or CVST.

subtopic_detail: Influenza antiviral timing and indications for oseltamivir
stem: A 32-year-old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant presents to the emergency department in July with 2 days of high fever, myalgia, dry cough, and rhinorrhoea. She has no significant medical history and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. A point-of-care influenza rapid antigen test is positive for influenza A.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, T 39.1 C
data_table.Examination: Clear chest on auscultation bilaterally, no signs of respiratory distress, uterine size consistent with dates, normal fetal movements reported

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure that influenza is self-limiting and prescribe paracetamol for symptomatic relief only
options.rationale: Pregnant women are at significantly higher risk of severe influenza complications including pneumonia, hospitalisation, and preterm birth. Antiviral therapy is recommended for all pregnant women with confirmed or suspected influenza regardless of symptom duration. Withholding treatment exposes both mother and fetus to avoidable risk. (Source: RANZCOG; eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe zanamivir inhaled 10 mg twice daily as the preferred antiviral in pregnancy
options.rationale: Zanamivir is an alternative when oseltamivir is not tolerated, but oseltamivir remains the first-line antiviral in pregnancy because it has a larger evidence base for safety and efficacy in pregnant women. Inhaled zanamivir may also be poorly tolerated in women with respiratory symptoms. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic; RANZCOG)

options.text: Delay antiviral therapy until respiratory swab PCR confirms the diagnosis
options.rationale: Treatment should not be delayed awaiting confirmatory PCR when a rapid antigen test is positive in the appropriate clinical context. PCR has higher sensitivity but the clinical decision to treat should not await it, particularly in a high-risk patient. Empiric treatment based on clinical suspicion alone is also acceptable in pregnancy. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days without delay regardless of duration
options.rationale: Oseltamivir is the first-line antiviral for influenza in pregnancy and should be commenced as soon as possible. Although benefit is greatest within 48 hours of symptom onset, treatment is recommended regardless of duration in high-risk groups including pregnant women. Oseltamivir is safe in all trimesters. The standard treatment dose is 75 mg twice daily for 5 days. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic; RANZCOG)

options.text: Admit for IV antibiotics and oseltamivir given the high risk of secondary bacterial pneumonia
options.rationale: This patient has normal oxygen saturation, clear lungs, and no signs of respiratory distress or sepsis. There is no indication for IV antibiotics or admission at this stage. Outpatient oral oseltamivir with safety-net advice and planned review is appropriate. Admission would be warranted if she developed hypoxia or respiratory distress. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pregnant women are an established high-risk group for influenza complications due to altered immune function, increased oxygen consumption, and reduced functional residual capacity. Australian guidelines recommend oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days for all pregnant women with confirmed or suspected influenza, regardless of symptom duration. Treatment should commence as soon as possible and should not be delayed for confirmatory testing. Vaccination remains the most important preventive strategy and is funded under the National Immunisation Program for all pregnant women.
key_points: Pregnant women are high-risk for severe influenza and should receive antiviral treatment
Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is first-line regardless of trimester
Treatment should not be delayed for confirmatory PCR when clinical suspicion is high
Influenza vaccination is recommended for all pregnant women at any gestation
Admission is indicated only if there are signs of severe disease or complications
explanation.pearls: Oseltamivir provides the greatest benefit when started within 48 hours of symptom onset, but Australian guidelines recommend treatment at any duration in high-risk groups including pregnant women, immunosuppressed patients, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and those aged 65 years and over.
